From men of corrupt principles, atheistical profane men, who make it their business to debauch young men's judgments, and instil into their minds prejudices against religion and arguments for vice: "It will <hi type="italic">deliver thee from the way of the evil man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.12">v. 12</reference>), and a blessed deliverance it will be, as from the very jaws of death, <hi type="italic">from the way</hi> in which he walks, and in which he would persuade thee to walk." The enemy is spoken of as one (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.12">v. 12</reference>), an <hi type="italic">evil man,</hi> but afterwards as many (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.13">v. 13</reference>); there is a club, a gang of them, that are in confederacy against religion, and join hand in hand for the support of the devil's kingdom and the interests of it. [1.] They have a spirit of contradiction to that which is good: They <hi type="italic">speak froward things;</hi> they say all they can against religion, both to show their own enmity to it and to dissuade others from it. They are advocates for Satan; they plead for Baal, and <hi type="italic">pervert the right ways of the Lord.</hi> How peevishly will profane wits argue for sin, and with what frowardness will they carp at the word of God! Wisdom will keep us either from conversing with such men or at least from being ensnared by them. [2.] They are themselves apostates from that which is good, and such are commonly the most malicious and dangerous enemies religion has, witness Julian (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">They leave the paths of uprightness,</hi> which they were trained up in and had set out in, shake off the influences of their education, and break off the thread of their hopeful beginnings, <hi type="italic">to walk in the ways of darkness,</hi> in those wicked ways which hate the light, in which men are led blindfold by ignorance and error, and which lead men into utter darkness. The ways of sin are ways of darkness, uncomfortable and unsafe; what fools are those that leave the plain, pleasant, lightsome paths of uprightness, to walk in those ways! <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Ps. lxxxii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.11">1 John ii. 11</reference>. [3.] They take a pleasure in sin, both in committing it themselves and in seeing others commit it (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.14">v. 14</reference>): They <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> in an opportunity <hi type="italic">to do evil,</hi> and in the accomplishment and success of any wicked project. It is sport to fools to do mischief; nor is any sight more grateful to them than to see <hi type="italic">the frowardness of the wicked,</hi> to see those that are hopeful drawn into the ways of sin, and then to see them hardened and confirmed in those ways. They are pleased if they can discern that the devil's kingdom gets ground (see <reference osisRef="Rom.1.32">Rom. i. 32</reference>), such a height of impiety have they arrived at. [4.] They are resolute in sin (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">v. 15</reference>): Their <hi type="italic">ways are crooked,</hi> a great many windings and turnings to escape the pursuit of their convictions and break the force of them; some sly excuse, some subtle evasion or other, their deceitful hearts furnish them with, for the strengthening of their hands in their wickedness; and in the crooked mazes of that labyrinth they secure themselves from the arrests of God's word and their own consciences; for they are <hi type="italic">froward in their paths,</hi> that is, they are resolved to go on in them, whatever is said against it. Every wise man will shun the company of such as these. <div eID="gen13366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13367" type="x-p"/> (2.) From women of corrupt practices. The former lead to spiritual wickednesses, the lusts of the unsanctified mind; these lead to <hi type="italic">fleshly lusts,</hi> which defile the body, that living temple, but withal <hi type="italic">war against the soul.</hi> The adulteress is here called <hi type="italic">the strange woman,</hi> because no man that has any wisdom or goodness in him will have any acquaintance with her; she is to be shunned by every Israelite as if she were a heathen, and a stranger to that sacred commonwealth. A strange woman indeed! utterly estranged from all principles of reason, virtue, and honour. It is a great mercy to be delivered from the allurements of the adulteress, considering, [1.] How false she is. Who will have any dealings with those that are made up of treachery? She is a strange woman; for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> She is false to him whom she entices. She speaks fair, tells him how much she admires him above any man, and what a kindness she has for him; but she <hi type="italic">flatters with her words;</hi> she has no true affection for him, nor any desire of his welfare, any more than Delilah had of Samson's. All she designs is to pick his pocket and gratify a base lust of her own. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> She is false to her husband, and violates the sacred obligation she lies under to him. He was <hi type="italic">the guide of her youth;</hi> by marrying him she chose him to be so, and submitted herself to his guidance, with a promise to attend him only, and forsake all others. But she has <hi type="italic">forsaken</hi> him, and therefore it cannot be thought that she should be faithful to any one else; and whoever entertains her is partaker with her in her falsehood. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> She is false to God himself: She <hi type="italic">forgets the covenant of her God,</hi> the marriage-covenant (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">v. 17</reference>), to which God is not only a witness, but a party, for, he having instituted the ordinance, both sides vow to him to be true to each other. It is not her husband only that she sins against, but her God, who <hi type="italic">will judge whoremongers and adulterers</hi> because they despise the oath and break the covenant, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.18">Ezek. xvii. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.2.14">Mal. ii. 14</reference>. [2.] How fatal it will prove to those that fall in league with her, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.18-Prov.2.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. Let the sufferings of others be our warnings. Take heed of the sin of whoredom; for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> The ruin of those who are guilty of it is certain and unavoidable, if they do not repent. It is a sin that has a direct tendency to the killing of the soul, the extinguishing of all good affections and dispositions in it, and the exposing of it to the wrath and curse of God and the sword of his justice. Those that live in forbidden pleasures are dead while they live. Let discretion preserve every man, not only from the evil woman, but from the evil house, for the <hi type="italic">house inclines to death;</hi> it is in the road that leads directly to eternal death; <hi type="italic">and her paths unto Rephaim,</hi> to the <hi type="italic">giants</hi> (so some read it), the sinners of the old world, who, living in luxury and excess of riot, were cut down out of time, and their foundation was overthrown with a flood. Our Lord Jesus deters us from sinful pleasures with the consideration of everlasting torments which follow them. <hi type="italic">Where the worm dies not, nor is the fire quenched.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28-Matt.5.29">Matt. v. 28, 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Their repentance and recovery are extremely hazardous: <hi type="italic">None,</hi> or next to none, <hi type="italic">that go unto her, return again.</hi> It is very rare that any who are caught in this snare of the devil recover themselves, so much is the heart hardened, and the mind blinded, by the deceitfulness of this sin. Having once lost their <hi type="italic">hold of the paths of life,</hi> they know not how to take hold of them again, but are perfectly besotted and bewitched with those base lusts. Many learned interpreters think that this caution against the <hi type="italic">strange woman,</hi> besides the literal sense, is to be understood figuratively, as a caution, 1. Against idolatry, which is spiritual whoredom. Wisdom will keep thee from all familiarity with the worshippers of images, and all inclination to join with them, which had for many ages been of such pernicious consequence to Israel and proved so to Solomon himself. 2. Against the debauching of the intellectual powers and faculties of the soul by the lusts and appetites of the body. Wisdom will keep thee from being captivated by the carnal mind, and from subjecting the spirit to the dominion of the flesh, that notorious adulteress which <hi type="italic">forsakes its guide,</hi> violates the <hi type="italic">covenant of our God,</hi> which <hi type="italic">inclines to death,</hi> and which, when it has got an undisturbed dominion, makes the case of the soul desperate. <div eID="gen13367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13368" type="x-p"/> II. This wisdom will be of use to guide and direct us in that which is good (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">That thou mayest walk in the way of good men.</hi> We must avoid the way of the <hi type="italic">evil man,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">strange woman,</hi> in order that we may walk in good ways; we must <hi type="italic">cease to do evil,</hi> in order that we may <hi type="italic">learn to do well.</hi> Note, 1. There is a way which is peculiarly the way of good men, the way in which good men, as such, and as far as they have really been such, have always walked. 2. It will be our wisdom to walk in that way, to ask for the good old way and walk therein, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer. vi. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.12">Heb. vi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">xii. 1</reference>. And we must not only walk in that way awhile, but we must keep it, keep in it, and never turn aside out of it: <hi type="italic">The paths of the righteous</hi> are the paths of life, which all that are wise, having taken hold of, will keep their hold of. "That thou mayest imitate those excellent persons, the patriarchs and prophets (so bishop Patrick paraphrases it), and be preserved in <hi type="italic">the paths of those righteous</hi> men who followed after them." We must not only choose our way in general by the good examples of the saints, but must also take directions from them in the choice of our particular paths; observe the track, and go forth by the footsteps of the flock. Two reasons are here given why we should thus choose:—(1.) Because men's integrity will be their establishment, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.21">v. 21</reference>. It will be the establishment, [1.] Of their persons: <hi type="italic">The upright shall dwell in the land,</hi> peaceably and quietly, as long as they live; and their uprightness will contribute to it, as it settles their minds, guides their counsels, gains them the good-will of their neighbours, and entitles them to God's special favour. [2.] Of their families: <hi type="italic">The perfect,</hi> in their posterity, <hi type="italic">shall remain in it.</hi> They shall dwell and remain for ever in the heavenly Canaan, of which the earthly one was but a type. (2.) Because men's iniquity will be their destruction, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.22">v. 22</reference>. See what becomes of <hi type="italic">the wicked,</hi> who choose the way of <hi type="italic">the evil man;</hi> they <hi type="italic">shall be cut off,</hi> not only from heaven hereafter and all hopes of that, but <hi type="italic">from the earth</hi> now, on which they set their affections, and in which they lay up their treasure. They think to take root in it, but they and their families <hi type="italic">shall be rooted out of it,</hi> in judgment to them, but in mercy to the earth. There is a day coming which <hi type="italic">shall leave them neither root nor branch,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">Mal. iv. 1</reference>. Let that wisdom then <hi type="italic">enter into our hearts,</hi> and be <hi type="italic">pleasant to our souls,</hi> which will keep us out of a way that will end thus.  <chapter eID="Prov.2"/> <div eID="gen13368" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen13371" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13370" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Communion Conferred by Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen13372" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My son, forget not my law; but let thine heart keep my commandments: <hi type="super">2</hi> For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to thee. <hi type="super">3</hi> Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart: <hi type="super">4</hi> So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man. <hi type="super">5</hi> Trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. <hi type="super">6</hi> In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. <div eID="gen13372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13373" type="x-p"/> We are here taught to live a life of communion with God; and without controversy great is this mystery of godliness, and of great consequence to us, and, as is here shown, will be of unspeakable advantage. <div eID="gen13373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13374" type="x-p"/> I. We must have a continual regard to God's precepts, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.1-Prov.3.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen13374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13375" type="x-p"/> 1. We must, (1.) Fix God's law, and his commandments, as our rule, by which we will in every thing be ruled and to which we will yield obedience. (2.) We must acquaint ourselves with them; for we cannot be said to forget that which we never knew. (3.) We must remember them so that they may be ready to us whenever we have occasion to use them. (4.) Our wills and affections must be subject to them and must in every thing conform to them. Not only our heads, but our hearts, must <hi type="italic">keep God's commandments;</hi> in them, as in the ark of the testimony, both the tables of the law must be deposited. <div eID="gen13375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13376" type="x-p"/> 2. To encourage us to submit ourselves to all the restraints and injunctions of the divine law, we are assured (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.2">v. 2</reference>) that it is the certain way to long life and prosperity. (1.) It is the way to be long-lived. God's commandments <hi type="italic">shall add to us length of days;</hi> to a good useful life on earth, they shall add an eternal life in heaven, <hi type="italic">length of days for ever and ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.21.4">Ps. xxi. 4</reference>. God shall be our life and the length of our days, and that will be indeed long life, with an addition. But, because length of days may possibly become a burden and a trouble, it is promised, (2.) That it shall prove the way to be easy too, so that even the days of old age shall not be evil days, but days in which thou shalt have pleasure: <hi type="italic">Peace shall they</hi> be continually <hi type="italic">adding to thee.</hi> As grace increases, peace shall increase; and <hi type="italic">of the increase of Christ's government and peace,</hi> in the heart as well as in the world, <hi type="italic">there shall be no end. Great</hi> and growing <hi type="italic">peace have those that love the law.</hi> <div eID="gen13376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13377" type="x-p"/> II. We must have a continual regard to God's promises, which go along with his precepts, and are to be received, and retained, with them (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let not mercy and truth forsake thee,</hi> God's mercy in promising, and his truth in performing. Do not forfeit these, but live up to them, and preserve thy interest in them; do not forget these, but live upon them, and take the comfort of them. <hi type="italic">Bind them about thy neck,</hi> as the most graceful ornament." It is the greatest honour we are capable of in this world to have an interest in the mercy and truth of God. "<hi type="italic">Write to them upon the table of thy heart,</hi> as dear to thee, thy portion, and most delightful entertainment; take a pleasure in applying them and thinking them over." Or it may be meant of the mercy and truth which are our duty, piety and sincerity, charity towards men, fidelity towards God. Let these be fixed and commanding principles in thee. To encourage us to do this we are assured (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.4">v. 4</reference>) that this is the way to recommend ourselves both to our Creator and fellow-creatures: <hi type="italic">So shalt thou find favour and good understanding.</hi> 1. A good man seeks the favour of God in the first place, is ambitious of the honour of being accepted of the Lord, and he shall find that favour, and with it a good understanding; God will make the best of him, and put a favourable construction upon what he says and does. He shall be owned as one of Wisdom's children, and shall have praise with God, as one having that <hi type="italic">good understanding</hi> which is ascribed to all those <hi type="italic">that do his commandments.</hi> 2. He wishes to have favour with men also (as Christ had, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.52">Luke ii. 52</reference>), to be <hi type="italic">accepted of the multitude of his brethren</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.10.3">Esth. x. 3</reference>), and that he shall have; they shall understand him aright, and in his dealings with them he shall appear to be prudent, shall act intelligently and with discretion. <hi type="italic">He shall have good success</hi> (so some translate it), the common effect of good understanding. <div eID="gen13377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13378" type="x-p"/> III. We must have a continual regard to God's providence, must own and depend upon it in all our affairs, both by faith and prayer. 1. By faith. We must repose an entire confidence in the wisdom, power, and goodness of God, assuring ourselves of the extent of his providence to all the creatures and all their actions. We must therefore <hi type="italic">trust in the Lord with all our hearts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.5">v. 5</reference>); we must believe that he is able to do what he will, wise to do what is best, and good, according to his promise, to do what is best for us, if we love him, and serve him. We must, with an entire submission and satisfaction, depend upon him to perform all things for us, and not <hi type="italic">lean to our own understanding,</hi> as if we could, by any forecast of our own, without God, help ourselves, and bring our affairs to a good issue. Those who know themselves cannot but find their own understanding to be a broken reed, which, if they lean to, will certainly fail them. In all our conduct we must be diffident of our own judgment, and confident of God's wisdom, power, and goodness, and therefore must follow Providence and not force it. That often proves best which was least our own doing. 2. By prayer (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">In all thy ways acknowledge God.</hi> We must not only in our judgment believe that there is an over-ruling hand of God ordering and disposing of us and all our affairs, but we must solemnly own it, and address ourselves to him accordingly. We must ask his leave, and not design any thing but what we are sure is lawful. We must ask his advice and beg direction from him, not only when the case is difficult (when we know not what to do, no thanks to us that we have our eyes up to him), but in every case, be it ever so plain, We must ask success of him, as those who know <hi type="italic">the race is not to the swift.</hi> We must refer ourselves to him as one from whom our judgment proceeds, and patiently, and with a holy indifferency, wait his award. <hi type="italic">In all our ways</hi> that prove direct, and fair, and pleasant, in which we gain our point to our satisfaction, we must acknowledge God with thankfulness. <hi type="italic">In all our ways</hi> that prove cross and uncomfortable, and that are hedged up with thorns, we must acknowledge God with submission. Our eye must be ever towards God; to him we must, in every thing, make our requests known, as Jephthah <hi type="italic">uttered all his words before the Lord in Mizpeh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.11.11">Judg. xi. 11</reference>. For our encouragement to do this, it is promised, "<hi type="italic">He shall direct thy paths,</hi> so that thy way shall be safe and good and the issue happy at last." Note, Those that put themselves under a divine guidance shall always have the benefit of it. God will give them that wisdom which is profitable to direct, so that they shall not turn aside into the by-paths of sin, and then will himself so wisely order the event that it shall be to their mind, or (which is equivalent) for their good. Those that faithfully follow the pillar of cloud and fire shall find that though it may lead them about it leads them the right way and will bring them to Canaan at last.

<div eID="gen13378" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Consecration to God.</title> <div sID="gen13379" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and depart from evil. <hi type="super">8</hi> It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones. <hi type="super">9</hi> Honour the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase: <hi type="super">10</hi> So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine. <hi type="super">11</hi> My son, despise not the chastening of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; neither be weary of his correction: <hi type="super">12</hi> For whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son <hi type="italic">in whom</hi> he delighteth. <div eID="gen13379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13380" type="x-p"/> We have here before us three exhortations, each of them enforced with a good reason:— <div eID="gen13380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13381" type="x-p"/> I. We must live in a humble and dutiful subjection to God and his government (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Fear the Lord,</hi> as your sovereign Lord and Master; be ruled in every thing by your religion and subject to the divine will." This must be, 1. A humble subjection: <hi type="italic">Be not wise in thy own eyes.</hi> Note, There is not a greater enemy to the power of religion, and the fear of God in the heart, than conceitedness of our own wisdom. Those that have an opinion of their own sufficiency think it below them, and a disparagement to them, to take their measures from, much more to hamper themselves with, religion's rules. 2. A dutiful subjection: <hi type="italic">Fear the Lord, and depart from evil;</hi> take heed of doing any thing to offend him and to forfeit his care. To <hi type="italic">fear the Lord,</hi> so as to <hi type="italic">depart from evil,</hi> is true <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> and <hi type="italic">understanding</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job xxviii. 28</reference>); those that have it are truly wise, but self-denyingly so, and not <hi type="italic">wise in their own eyes.</hi> For our encouragement thus to live in the fear of God it is here promised (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">v. 8</reference>) that it shall be as serviceable even to the outward man as our necessary food. It will be nourishing: <hi type="italic">It shall be health to thy navel.</hi> It will be strengthening: It shall be <hi type="italic">marrow to thy bones.</hi> The prudence, temperance, and sobriety, the calmness and composure of mind, and the good government of the appetites and passions, which religion teaches, tend very much not only to the health of the soul, but to a good habit of body, which is very desirable, and without which our other enjoyments in this world are insipid. Envy is <hi type="italic">the rottenness of the bones;</hi> the sorrow of the world dries them; but hope and joy in God are marrow to them. <div eID="gen13381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13382" type="x-p"/> II. We must make a good use of our estates, and that is the way to increase them, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.9-Prov.3.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen13382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13383" type="x-p"/> 1. A precept which makes it our duty to serve God with our estates: <hi type="italic">Honour the Lord with thy substance.</hi> It is the end of our creation and redemption to honour God, to be to him for a name and a praise; we are no other way capable of serving him than in his honour. His honour we must show forth and the honour we have for him. We must honour him, not only <hi type="italic">with our bodies and spirits which are his,</hi> but with our estates too, for they also are his: we and all our appurtenances must be devoted to his glory. Worldly wealth is but poor substance, yet, such as it is, we must honour God with it, and then, if ever, it becomes substantial. We must honour God, (1.) <hi type="italic">With our increase.</hi> Where riches increase we are tempted to honour ourselves (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.17">Deut. viii. 17</reference>) and to set our hearts upon the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.10">Ps. lxii. 10</reference>); but the more God gives us the more we should study to honour him. It is meant of the increase of the earth, for we live upon annual products, to keep us in constant dependence on God. (2.) <hi type="italic">With all our increase.</hi> As God has prospered us in every thing, we must honour him. Our law will allow a prescription for a <hi type="italic">modus decimandi—a mode of tithing,</hi> but none <hi type="italic">de non decimando—for exemption from paying tithes.</hi> (3.) <hi type="italic">With the first-fruits of all,</hi> as Abel, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.4">Gen. iv. 4</reference>. This was the law (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.19">Exod. xxiii. 19</reference>), and the prophets, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.10">Mal. iii. 10</reference>. God, who is the first and best, must have the first and best of every thing; his right is prior to all other, and therefore he must be served first. Note, It is our duty to make our worldly estates serviceable to our religion, to use them and the interest we have by them for the promoting of religion, to do good to the poor with what we have and abound in all works of piety and charity, <hi type="italic">devising liberal things.</hi> <div eID="gen13383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13384" type="x-p"/> 2. A promise, which makes it our interest to serve God with our estates. It is the way to make a little much, and much more; it is the surest and safest method of thriving: <hi type="italic">So shall thy barns be filled with plenty.</hi> He does not say thy bags, but thy barns, not thy wardrobe replenished, but thy presses: "God shall bless thee with an increase of that which is for use, not for show or ornament—for spending and laying out, not for hoarding and laying up." Those that do good with what they have shall have more to do more good with. Note, If we make our worldly estates serviceable to our religion we shall find our religion very serviceable to the prosperity of our worldly affairs. <hi type="italic">Godliness has the promise of the life that now is</hi> and most of the comfort of it. We mistake if we think that giving will undo us and make us poor. No, giving for God's honour will make us rich, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.19">Hag. ii. 19</reference>. What we gave we have. <div eID="gen13384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13385" type="x-p"/> III. We must conduct ourselves aright under our afflictions, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.11-Prov.3.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. This the apostle quotes (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.5">Heb. xii. 5</reference>), and calls it <hi type="italic">an exhortation which speaks unto us as unto children,</hi> with the authority and affection of a father. We are here in a world of troubles. Now observe, <div eID="gen13385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13386" type="x-p"/> 1. What must be our care when we are in affliction. We must neither despise it nor be weary of it. His exhortation, before, was to those that are rich and in prosperity, here to those that are poor and in adversity. (1.) We must not despise an affliction, be it ever so light and short, as if it were not worth taking notice of, or as if it were not sent on an errand and therefore required no answer. We must not be stocks, and stones, and stoics, under our afflictions, insensible of them, hardening ourselves under them, and concluding we can easily get through them without God. (2.) We must not be weary of an affliction, be it ever so heavy and long, not <hi type="italic">faint</hi> under it, so the apostle renders it, not be dispirited, dispossessed of our own souls, or driven to despair, or to use any indirect means for our relief and the redress of our grievances. We must not think that the affliction either presses harder or continues longer than is meet, not conclude that deliverance will never come because it does not come so soon as we expect it. <div eID="gen13386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13387" type="x-p"/> 2. What will be our comfort when we are in affliction. (1.) That it is a divine correction; it is <hi type="italic">the chastening of the Lord,</hi> which, as it is a reason why we should submit to it (for it is folly to contend with a God of incontestable sovereignty and irresistible power), so it is a reason why we should be satisfied in it; for we may be sure that a God of unspotted purity does us no wrong and that a God of infinite goodness means us no hurt. It is from God, and therefore must not be despised; for a slight put upon the messenger is an affront to him that sends him. It is from God, and therefore we must not be weary of it, for he knows our frame, both what we need and what we can bear. (2.) That it is a fatherly correction; it comes not from his vindictive justice as a Judge, but his wise affection as a Father. The father corrects <hi type="italic">the son whom he</hi> loves, nay, and because he loves him and desires he may be wise and good. He delights in that in his son which is amiable and agreeable, and therefore corrects him for the prevention and cure of that which would be a deformity to him, and an alloy to his delight in him. Thus God hath said, <hi type="italic">As many as I love I rebuke and chasten,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.19">Rev. iii. 19</reference>. This is a great comfort to God's children, under their afflictions, [1.] That they not only consist with, but flow from, covenant-love. [2.] That they are so far from doing them any real hurt that, by the grace of God working with them, they do a great deal of good, and are happy means of their satisfaction.

<div eID="gen13387" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Excellency of Wisdom; Happiness of Those Who Find Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen13388" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Happy <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man <hi type="italic">that</hi> findeth wisdom, and the man <hi type="italic">that</hi> getteth understanding. <hi type="super">14</hi> For the merchandise of it <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold. <hi type="super">15</hi> She <hi type="italic">is</hi> more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her. <hi type="super">16</hi> Length of days <hi type="italic">is</hi> in her right hand; <hi type="italic">and</hi> in her left hand riches and honour. <hi type="super">17</hi> Her ways <hi type="italic">are</hi> ways of pleasantness, and all her paths <hi type="italic">are</hi> peace. <hi type="super">18</hi> She <hi type="italic">is</hi> a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and happy <hi type="italic">is every one</hi> that retaineth her. <hi type="super">19</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding hath he established the heavens. <hi type="super">20</hi> By his knowledge the depths are broken up, and the clouds drop down the dew. <div eID="gen13388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13389" type="x-p"/> Solomon had pressed us earnestly to seek diligently for wisdom (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.1">ch. ii. 1</reference>, &c.), and had assured us that we should succeed in our sincere and constant pursuits. But the question is, What shall we get by it when we have found it? Prospect of advantage is the spring and spur of industry; he therefore shows us how much it will be to our profit, laying this down for an unquestionable truth, <hi type="italic">Happy is the man that findeth wisdom,</hi> that true wisdom which consists in the knowledge and love of God, and an entire conformity to all the intentions of his truths, providences, and laws. Now observe, <div eID="gen13389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13390" type="x-p"/> I. What it is to find wisdom so as to be made happy by it. <div eID="gen13390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13391" type="x-p"/> 1. We must get it. He is the happy man who, having found it, makes it his own, gets both an interest in it and the possession of it, who <hi type="italic">draws out understanding</hi> (so the word it), that is, (1.) Who derives it from God. Having it not in himself, he draws it with the bucket of prayer from the fountain of all wisdom, <hi type="italic">who gives liberally.</hi> (2.) Who takes pains for it, as he does who draws ore out of the mine. It if do not come easily, we must put the more strength to draw it. (3.) Who improves in it, who, having some understanding, draws it out by growing in knowledge and making five talents ten. (4.) Who does good with it, who draws out from the stock he has, as wine from the vessel, and communicates to others, for their instruction, <hi type="italic">things new and old.</hi> That is well got, and to good purpose, that is thus used to good purpose. <div eID="gen13391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13392" type="x-p"/> 2. We must trade for it. We read here of the merchandise of wisdom, which intimates, (1.) That we must make it our business, and not a by-business, as the merchant bestows the main of his thoughts and time upon his merchandise. (2.) That we must venture all in it, as a stock in trade, and be willing to part with all for it. This is that pearl of great price which, when we have found it, we must willingly sell all for the purchase of, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.45-Matt.13.46">Matt. xiii. 45, 46</reference>. <hi type="italic">Buy the truth,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.23">Prov. xxiii. 23</reference>); he does not say at what rate, because we must buy it at any rate rather than miss it. <div eID="gen13392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13393" type="x-p"/> 3. We must lay hold on it as we lay hold on a good bargain when it is offered to us, which we do the more carefully if there be danger of having it taken out of our hands. We must apprehend with all our might, and put forth our utmost vigour in the pursuit of it, lay hold on all occasions to improve in it, and catch at the least of its dictates. <div eID="gen13393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13394" type="x-p"/> 4. We must retain it. It is not enough to lay hold on wisdom, but we must keep our hold, hold it fast, with a resolution never to let it go, but to persevere in the ways of wisdom to the end. We must <hi type="italic">sustain it</hi> (so some read it), must embrace it with all our might, as we do that which we would sustain. We must do all we can to support the declining interests of religion in the places where we live. <div eID="gen13394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13395" type="x-p"/> II. What the happiness of those is who do find it. <div eID="gen13395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13396" type="x-p"/> 1. It is a transcendent happiness, more than can be found in the wealth of this world, if we had ever so much of it, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.14-Prov.3.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. It is not only a surer, but a more gainful merchandise to trade for wisdom, for Christ, and grace, and spiritual blessings, than for silver, and gold, and rubies. Suppose a man to have got these in abundance, nay, to have all the things he can desire of this world (and who is it that ever had?), yet, (1.) All this would not purchase heavenly wisdom; no, it would <hi type="italic">utterly be contemned;</hi> it <hi type="italic">cannot be gotten for gold,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.15">Job xxviii. 15</reference>, &c. (2.) All this would not countervail the want of heavenly wisdom nor be the ransom of a soul lost by its own folly. (3.) All this would not make a man half so happy, no, not in this world, as those are who have true wisdom, though they have none of all these things. (4.) Heavenly wisdom will procure that for us, and secure that to us, which silver, and gold, and rubies, will not be the purchase of. <div eID="gen13396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13397" type="x-p"/> 2. It is a true happiness; for it is inclusive of, and equivalent to, all those things which are supposed to make men happy, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.16-Prov.3.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Wisdom is here represented as a bright and bountiful queen, reaching forth gifts to her faithful and loving subjects, and offering them to all that will submit to her government. (1.) Is length of days a blessing? Yes, the most valuable; life includes all good, and therefore she offers that <hi type="italic">in her right hand.</hi> Religion puts us into the best methods of prolonging life, entitles us to the promises of it, and, though our days on earth should be no more than our neighbour's, yet it will secure to us everlasting life in a better world. (2.) Are riches and honour accounted blessings? They are so, and them she reaches out with <hi type="italic">her left hand.</hi> For, as she is ready to embrace those that submit to her with both arms, so she is ready to give out to them with both hands. They shall have the wealth of this world as far as Infinite Wisdom sees good for them; while the true riches, by which men are rich towards God, are secured to them. Nor is there any honour, by birth or preferment, comparable to that which attends religion; it makes the <hi type="italic">righteous more excellent than his neighbour,</hi> recommends men to God, commands respect and veneration with all the sober part of mankind, and will in the other world make those that are now buried in obscurity to <hi type="italic">shine forth as the sun.</hi> (3.) Is pleasure courted as much as any thing? It is so, and it is certain that true piety has in it the greatest true pleasure. <hi type="italic">Her ways are ways of pleasantness;</hi> the ways in which she has directed us to walk are such as we shall find abundance of delight and satisfaction in. All the enjoyments and entertainments of sense are not comparable to the pleasure which gracious souls have in communion with God and doing good. That which is the only right way to bring us to our journey's end we must walk in, fair or foul, pleasant or unpleasant; but the way of religion, as it is the right way, so it is a pleasant way; it is smooth and clean, and strewed with roses: <hi type="italic">All her paths are peace.</hi> There is not only peace in the end, but peace in the way; not only in the way of religion in general, but in the particular paths of that way, in all her paths, all the several acts, instances, and duties of it. One does not embitter what the other sweetens, as it is with the allays of this world; but they are all peace, not only sweet, but safe. The saints enter into peace on this side heaven, and enjoy a present sabbatism. <div eID="gen13397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13398" type="x-p"/> 3. It is the happiness of paradise (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">She is a tree of life.</hi> True grace is that to the soul which the tree of life would have been, from which our first parents were shut out for eating of the forbidden tree. It is a seed of immortality, a <hi type="italic">well of living waters, springing up to life eternal.</hi> It is an earnest of the New Jerusalem, in the midst of which is <hi type="italic">the tree of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.2">Rev. xxii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.7">ii. 7</reference>. Those that feed and feast on this heavenly wisdom shall not only be cured by it of every fatal malady, but shall find an antidote against age and death; they shall <hi type="italic">eat and live for ever.</hi> <div eID="gen13398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13399" type="x-p"/> 4. It is a participation of the happiness of God himself, for wisdom is his everlasting glory and blessedness, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.19-Prov.3.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. This should make us in love with the wisdom and understanding which God gives, that <hi type="italic">the Lord by wisdom founded the earth,</hi> so that it cannot be removed, nor can ever fail of answering all the ends of its creation, to which it is admirably and unexceptionably fitted. <hi type="italic">By understanding he has</hi> likewise <hi type="italic">established the heavens</hi> and directed all the motions of them in the best manner. The heavenly bodies are vast, yet there is no flaw in them—numerous, yet no disorder in them—the motion rapid, yet no wear or tear; the depths of the sea are broken up, and thence come the waters beneath the firmament, and <hi type="italic">the clouds drop down the dews,</hi> the waters from above the firmament, and all this by the divine wisdom and knowledge; therefore <hi type="italic">happy is the man that finds wisdom,</hi> for he will thereby be <hi type="italic">thoroughly furnished for every good word and work.</hi> Christ is that Wisdom, by whom the worlds were made and still consist; happy therefore are those to whom he is <hi type="italic">made of God wisdom,</hi> for he has wherewithal to make good all the foregoing promises of long life, riches, and honour; for all the wealth of heaven, earth, and seas, is his.

<div eID="gen13399" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Excellency of Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen13400" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> My son, let not them depart from thine eyes: keep sound wisdom and discretion: <hi type="super">22</hi> So shall they be life unto thy soul, and grace to thy neck. <hi type="super">23</hi> Then shalt thou walk in thy way safely, and thy foot shall not stumble. <hi type="super">24</hi> When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet. <hi type="super">25</hi> Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it cometh. <hi type="super">26</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken. <div eID="gen13400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13401" type="x-p"/> Solomon, having pronounced those happy who not only lay hold on wisdom, but retain her, here exhorts us therefore to retain her, assuring us that we ourselves shall have the comfort of doing so. <div eID="gen13401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13402" type="x-p"/> I. The exhortation is, to have religion's rules always in view and always at heart, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.21">v. 21</reference>. 1. To have them always in view: "<hi type="italic">My son, let them not depart from thy eyes;</hi> let not thy eyes ever depart from them to wander after vanity. Have them always in mind, and do not forget them; be ever and anon thinking of them, and conversing with them, and never imagine that thou hast looked upon them long enough and that it is time now to lay them by; but, as long as thou livest, keep up and cultivate thy acquaintance with them." He who learns to write must always have his eye upon his copy, and not let that be out of his sight; and to the words of wisdom must those, in like manner, have a constant respect, who will walk circumspectly. 2. To have them always at heart; for it is in that treasury, the hidden man of the heart, that we must <hi type="italic">keep sound wisdom and discretion,</hi> keep to the principles of it and keep in the ways of it. It is wealth that is worth keeping. <div eID="gen13402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13403" type="x-p"/> II. The argument to enforce this exhortation is taken from the unspeakable advantage which wisdom, thus kept, will be of to us. 1. In respect of strength and satisfaction: "It will be <hi type="italic">life to thy soul</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.22">v. 22</reference>); it will quicken thee to thy duty when thou beginnest to be slothful and remiss; it will revive thee under thy troubles when thou beginnest to droop and despond. It will be thy spiritual life, an earnest of life eternal." Life to the soul is life indeed. 2. In respect of honour and reputation: It shall be <hi type="italic">grace to thy neck,</hi> as a chain of gold, or a jewel. <hi type="italic">Grace to thy jaws</hi> (so the word is), grateful to thy <hi type="italic">taste and relish</hi> (so some); it shall infuse <hi type="italic">grace into all thou sayest</hi> (so others), shall furnish thee with acceptable words, which shall gain thee credit. 3. In respect of safety and security. This he insists upon in <reference osisRef="Prov.3.23-Prov.3.26">four verses</reference>, the scope of which is to show that <hi type="italic">the effect of righteousness</hi> (which is the same with <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> here) is <hi type="italic">quietness and assurance for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Isa. xxxii. 17</reference>. Good people are taken under God's special protection, and therein they may have an entire satisfaction. They are safe and may be easy, (1.) In their motions by day, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.23">v. 23</reference>. If our religion be our companion, it will be our convoy: "<hi type="italic">Then shalt thou walk in thy way safely.</hi> The natural life, and all that belongs to it, shall be under the protection of God's providence; the spiritual life, and all its interests, are under the protection of his grace; so that thou shalt be kept from falling into sin or trouble." Wisdom will direct us into, and keep us in, the safe way, as far as may be, from temptation, and will enable us to walk in it with holy security. The way of duty is the way of safety. "We are in danger of falling, but wisdom will keep thee, that <hi type="italic">thy foot shall not stumble</hi> at those things which are an offence and overthrow to many, but which thou shalt know how to get over." (2.) In their rest by night, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.24">v. 24</reference>. In our retirements we lie exposed and are most subject to frights. "But keep up communion with God, and keep a good conscience, and then <hi type="italic">when thou liest down thou shalt not be afraid</hi> of fire, or thieves, or specters, or any of the terrors of darkness, knowing that when we, and all our friends, are asleep, yet <hi type="italic">he that keeps Israel</hi> and every true-born Israelite <hi type="italic">neither slumbers nor sleeps,</hi> and to him thou hast committed thyself and taken shelter under the shadow of his wings. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt lie down,</hi> and not need to sit up to keep guard; having lain down, thou shalt sleep, and not have thy eyes held waking by care and fear; and <hi type="italic">thy sleep shall be sweet</hi> and refreshing to thee, being not disturbed by any alarms from without or from within," <reference osisRef="Ps.4.8">Ps. iv. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.7">cxvi. 7</reference>. The way to have a good night is to keep a good conscience; and the sleep, as of the labouring man, so of the wise and godly man, is sweet. (3.) In their greatest straits and dangers. Integrity and uprightness will preserve us, so that we need <hi type="italic">not be afraid of sudden fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.3.25">v. 25</reference>. The harms that surprise us, unthought of, giving us no time to arm ourselves by consideration, are most likely to put us into confusion. But let not the wise and good man forget himself, and then he will not give way to any fear that has torment, be the alarm ever so sudden. Let him not fear the <hi type="italic">desolation of the wicked, when it comes,</hi> that is, [1.] The desolation which the wicked ones make of religion and the religious; though it comes, and seems to be just at the door, yet be not afraid of it; for, though God may make use of the wicked as instruments of his people's correction, yet he will never suffer them to be the authors of their desolation. Or rather, [2.] The desolation which wicked men will be brought into in a moment. It will come, and timorous saints may be apprehensive that they shall be involved in it; but let this be their comfort, that though judgments lay waste generally, at least promiscuously, yet God knows who are his and how to separate between the precious and the vile. Therefore be not afraid of that which appears most formidable, for (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.26">v. 26</reference>) "<hi type="italic">the Lord shall be</hi> not only thy protector to keep thee safe, but <hi type="italic">thy confidence</hi> to keep thee secure, so that thy foot <hi type="italic">shall not be taken</hi> by thy enemies nor ensnared by thy own fears." God has engaged to keep the feet of his saints.

<div eID="gen13403" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Justice and Kindness Recommended; Caution against Envy.</title> <div sID="gen13404" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">28</hi> Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee. <hi type="super">29</hi> Devise not evil against thy neighbour, seeing he dwelleth securely by thee. <hi type="super">30</hi> Strive not with a man without cause, if he have done thee no harm. <hi type="super">31</hi> Envy thou not the oppressor, and choose none of his ways. <hi type="super">32</hi> For the froward <hi type="italic">is</hi> abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but his secret <hi type="italic">is</hi> with the righteous. <hi type="super">33</hi> The curse of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the house of the wicked: but he blesseth the habitation of the just. <hi type="super">34</hi> Surely he scorneth the scorners: but he giveth grace unto the lowly. <hi type="super">35</hi> The wise shall inherit glory: but shame shall be the promotion of fools. <div eID="gen13404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13405" type="x-p"/> True wisdom consists in the due discharge of our duty towards man, as well as towards God, in honesty as well as piety, and therefore we have here divers excellent precepts of wisdom which relate to our neighbour. <div eID="gen13405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13406" type="x-p"/> I. We must render to all their due, both in justice and charity, and not delay to do it (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.27-Prov.3.28">v. 27, 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Withhold not good from those to whom it is due</hi> (either for want of love to them or through too much love to thy money) <hi type="italic">when it is in the power of thy hand to do it,</hi> for, if it be not, it cannot be expected; but it was thy great fault if thou didst, by thy extravagances, disable thyself to do justly and show mercy, and it ought to be the greatest of thy griefs if God had disabled thee, not so much that thou art straitened in thy own comforts and conveniences as that thou hast not wherewithal to give to those to whom it is due." <hi type="italic">Withhold</hi> it not; this implies that it is called for and expected, but that the hand is drawn in and the <hi type="italic">bowels of compassion are shut up.</hi> We must not hinder others from doing it, not be ourselves backward to it. "If thou hast it by thee to-day, hast it in the power of thy hand, say not to thy neighbour, <hi type="italic">Go thy way for this time,</hi> and come at a more convenient season, and I will then see what will be done; <hi type="italic">to-morrow I will give;</hi> whereas thou art not sure that thou shalt live till to-morrow, or that to-morrow thou shalt <hi type="italic">have it by thee.</hi> Be not thus loth to part with thy money upon a good account. Make not excuses to shift off a duty that must be done, nor delight to keep thy neighbour in pain and in suspense, nor to show the authority which the giver has over the beggar; but readily and cheerfully, and from a principle of conscience towards God, give good to <hi type="italic">those to whom it is due,</hi>" to the <hi type="italic">lords and owners of it</hi> (so the word is), to those who upon any account are entitled to it. This requires us, 1. To pay our just debts without fraud, covin, or delay. 2. To give wages to those who have earned them. 3. To provide for our relations, and those that have dependence on us, for to them it is due. 4. To render dues both to church and state, magistrates and ministers. 5. To be ready to all acts of friendship and humanity, and in every thing to be neighbourly; for these are things that are due by the law of doing as we would be done by. 6. To be charitable to the poor and necessitous. If others want the necessary supports of life, and we have wherewithal to supply them, we must look upon it as due to them and not withhold it. Alms are called <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> because they are a debt to the poor, and a debt which we must not defer to pay, <hi type="italic">Bis dat, qui cito dat</hi>—<hi type="italic">He gives twice who gives speedily.</hi> <div eID="gen13406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13407" type="x-p"/> II. We must never design any hurt or harm to any body (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.29">v. 29</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Devise not evil against thy neighbour;</hi> do not contrive how to do him an ill-turn undiscovered, to prejudice him in his body, goods, or good name, and the rather because <hi type="italic">he dwells securely by thee,</hi> and, having given thee no provocation, entertains no jealousy or suspicion of thee, and therefore is off his guard." It is against the laws both of honour and friendship to do a man an ill-turn and give him no warning. <hi type="italic">Cursed be he that smites his neighbour secretly.</hi> It is a most base ungrateful thing, if our neighbours have a good opinion of us, that we will do them no harm, and we thence take advantage to cheat and injure them. <div eID="gen13407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13408" type="x-p"/> III. We must not be quarrelsome and litigious (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.30">v. 30</reference>): "Do not <hi type="italic">strive with a man without cause;</hi> contend not for that which thou hast no title to; resent not that as a provocation which peradventure was but an oversight. Never trouble thy neighbour with frivolous complaints and accusations, or vexatious law-suits, when either there is no harm done thee or none worth speaking of, or thou mightest right thyself in a friendly way." Law must be the last refuge; for it is not only our duty, but our interest, <hi type="italic">as much as in us lies, to live peaceably with all men.</hi> When accounts are balanced, it will be found there is little got by striving. <div eID="gen13408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13409" type="x-p"/> IV. We must not envy the prosperity of evil-doers, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.31">v. 31</reference>. This caution is the same with that which is so much insisted on, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1 Ps.37.7-Ps.37.9">Ps. xxxvii.</reference> "<hi type="italic">Envy not the oppressor;</hi> though he be rich and great, though he live in ease and pleasure, and make all about him to stand in awe of him, yet do not think him a happy man, nor wish thyself in his condition. <hi type="italic">Choose none of his ways;</hi> do not imitate him, nor take the courses he takes to enrich himself. Never think of doing as he does, though thou wert sure to get by it all that he has, for it would be dearly bought." Now, to show what little reason saints have to envy sinners, Solomon here, in the <reference osisRef="Prov.3.32-Prov.3.35">last four verses</reference> of the chapter, compares the condition of sinners and saints together (as his father David had done, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.22">Ps. xxxvii.</reference>), sets the one over against the other, that we may see how happy the saints are, though they be oppressed, and how miserable the wicked are, though they be oppressors. Men are to be judged of as they stand with God, and as he judges of them, not as they stand in the world's books. Those are in the right who are of God's mind; and, if we be of his mind, we shall see, whatever pretence one sinner may have to envy another, that saints are so happy themselves that they have no reason at all to envy any sinner, though his condition be ever so prosperous. For, 1. Sinners are hated of God, but saints are beloved, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">v. 32</reference>. The froward sinners, who are continually going from-ward him, whose lives are a perverse contradiction to his will, are <hi type="italic">abomination to the Lord.</hi> He that hates nothing that he has made yet abhors those who have thus marred themselves; they are not only abominable in his sight, but an abomination. The righteous therefore have no reason to envy them, for they have his secret with them; they are his favourites; he has that communion with them which is a secret to the world and in which they have a joy that a stranger does not intermeddle with; he communicates to them the secret tokens of his love; his covenant is with them; they know his mind, and the meanings and intentions of his providence, better than others can. <hi type="italic">Shall I hide from Abraham the thing that I do?</hi> 2. Sinners are under the curse of God, they and their houses; saints are under his blessing, they and their habitation, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.33">v. 33</reference>. The wicked has a house, a strong and stately dwelling perhaps, but <hi type="italic">the curse of the Lord</hi> is upon it, it is <hi type="italic">in it,</hi> and, though the affairs of the family may prosper, yet the very blessings are curses, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.2">Mal. ii. 2</reference>. There is <hi type="italic">leanness in the soul,</hi> when the body is fed to the full, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.15">Ps. cvi. 15</reference>. The curse may work silently and slowly; but it is as a fretting leprosy; it will consume the <hi type="italic">timber thereof and the stones thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.5.4">Zech. v. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.11">Hab. ii. 11</reference>. The just have a habitation, a poor cottage (the word is used for sheep-cotes), a very mean dwelling; but God blesses it; he is continually blessing it, from the beginning of the year to the end of it. The curse or blessing of God is upon the house according as the inhabitants are wicked or godly; and it is certain that a blessed family, though poor, has no reason to envy a cursed family, though rich. 3. God puts contempt upon sinners, but shows respect to saints, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.34">v. 34</reference>. (1.) Those who exalt themselves shall certainly be abased: <hi type="italic">Surely he scorns the scorners.</hi> Those who scorn to submit to the discipline of religion, scorn to take God's yoke upon them, scorn to be beholden to his grace, who scoff at godliness and godly people, and take a pleasure in bantering and exposing them, God will scorn them, and lay them open to scorn before all the world. He despises their impotent malice, <hi type="italic">sits in heaven and laughs at them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Ps. ii. 4</reference>. He retaliates upon them (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.26">Ps. xviii. 26</reference>); he <hi type="italic">resists the proud.</hi> (2.) Those who humble themselves shall be exalted, for <hi type="italic">he gives grace to the lowly;</hi> he works that in them which puts honour upon them and for which they are <hi type="italic">accepted of God and approved of men.</hi> Those who patiently bear contempt from scornful men shall have respect from God and all good men, and then they have no reason to envy the scorners or to choose their ways. 4. The end of sinners will be everlasting shame, the end of saints endless honour, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.35">v. 35</reference>. (1.) Saints are wise men, and act wisely for themselves; for though their religion now wraps them up in obscurity, and lays them open to reproach, yet they are sure to inherit glory at last, the far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. They shall have it, and have it by inheritance, the sweetest and surest tenure. God gives them grace (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.34">v. 34</reference>), and therefore they shall inherit glory, for grace is glory, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. It is glory begun, the earnest of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Ps. lxxxiv. 11</reference>. (2.) Sinners are fools, for they are not only preparing disgrace for themselves, but at the same time flattering themselves with a prospect of honour, as if they only took the way to be great. Their end will manifest their folly: <hi type="italic">Shame shall be their promotion.</hi> And it will be so much the more their punishment as it will come instead of their promotion; it will be all the promotion they must ever expect, that God will be glorified in their everlasting confusion.  <chapter eID="Prov.3"/> <div eID="gen13409" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen13412" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13411" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Parental Instructions.</title> <div sID="gen13413" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know understanding. <hi type="super">2</hi> For I give you good doctrine, forsake ye not my law. <hi type="super">3</hi> For I was my father's son, tender and only <hi type="italic">beloved</hi> in the sight of my mother. <hi type="super">4</hi> He taught me also, and said unto me, Let thine heart retain my words: keep my commandments, and live. <hi type="super">5</hi> Get wisdom, get understanding: forget <hi type="italic">it</hi> not; neither decline from the words of my mouth. <hi type="super">6</hi> Forsake her not, and she shall preserve thee: love her, and she shall keep thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> Wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> the principal thing; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding. <hi type="super">8</hi> Exalt her, and she shall promote thee: she shall bring thee to honour, when thou dost embrace her. <hi type="super">9</hi> She shall give to thine head an ornament of grace: a crown of glory shall she deliver to thee. <hi type="super">10</hi> Hear, O my son, and receive my sayings; and the years of thy life shall be many. <hi type="super">11</hi> I have taught thee in the way of wisdom; I have led thee in right paths. <hi type="super">12</hi> When thou goest, thy steps shall not be straitened; and when thou runnest, thou shalt not stumble. 13 Take fast hold of instruction; let <hi type="italic">her</hi> not go: keep her; for she <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy life. <div eID="gen13413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13414" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen13414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13415" type="x-p"/> I. The invitation which Solomon gives to his children to come and receive instruction from him (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.1-Prov.4.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hear, you children, the instruction of a father.</hi> That is, 1. "Let my own children, in the first place, receive and give good heed to those instructions which I set down for the use of others also." Note, Magistrates and ministers, who are entrusted with the direction of larger societies, are concerned to take a more than ordinary care for the good instruction of their own families; from this duty their public work will by no means excuse them. This charity must begin at home, though it must not end there; for he that has not his children in subjection with all gravity, and does not take pains in their good education, how shall he do his duty as he ought <hi type="italic">to the church of God?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.4-1Tim.3.5">1 Tim. iii. 4, 5</reference>. The children of those that are eminent for wisdom and public usefulness ought to improve in knowledge and grace in proportion to the advantages they derive from their relation to such parents. Yet it may be observed, to save both the credit and the comfort of those parents whose children do not answer the hopes that arose from their education, that Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, was far from being either one of the wisest or one of the best. We have reason to think that thousands have got more good by Solomon's proverbs than his own son did, to whom they seem to have been dedicated. 2. Let all young people, in the days of their childhood and youth, take pains to get knowledge and grace, for that is their learning age, and then their minds are formed and seasoned. He does not say, <hi type="italic">My</hi> children, but <hi type="italic">You</hi> children. We read but of one son that Solomon had of his own; but (would you think it?) he is willing to set up for a schoolmaster, and to teach other people's children! for at that age there is most hope of success; the branch is easily bent when it is young and tender. 3. Let all that would receive instruction come with the disposition of children, though they be grown persons. Let all prejudices be laid aside, and the mind be as white paper. let them be dutiful, tractable, and self-diffident, and take the word as the word of a father, which comes both with authority and with affection. We must see it coming from God as <hi type="italic">our Father in heaven,</hi> to whom we pray, from whom we expect blessings, the Father of our spirits, to whom we ought to be in subjection, that we may live. We must look upon our teachers as our fathers, who love us and seek our welfare; and therefore though the instruction carry in it reproof and correction, for so the word signifies, yet we must bid it welcome. Now, (1.) To recommend it to us, we are told, not only that it is the <hi type="italic">instruction of a father,</hi> but that it is <hi type="italic">understanding,</hi> and therefore should be welcome to intelligent creatures. Religion has reason on its side, and we are taught it by fair reasoning. It is a law indeed (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.2">v. 2</reference>), but that law is founded upon doctrine, upon unquestionable principles of truth, upon <hi type="italic">good doctrine,</hi> which is not only faithful, but worthy of all acceptation. If we admit the doctrine, we cannot but submit to the law. (2.) To rivet it in us, we are directed to receive it as a gift, to attend to it with all diligence, to attend so as to know it, for otherwise we cannot do it, and not to forsake it by disowning the doctrine or disobeying the law. <div eID="gen13415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13416" type="x-p"/> II. The instructions he gives them. Observe, <div eID="gen13416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13417" type="x-p"/> 1. How he came by these instructions; he had them from his parents, and teaches his children the same that they taught him, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.3-Prov.4.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. Observe, (1.) His parents loved him, and therefore taught him: <hi type="italic">I was my father's son.</hi> David had many sons, but Solomon was his son <hi type="italic">indeed,</hi> as Isaac is called (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.19">Gen. xvii. 19</reference>) and for the same reason, because on him the covenant was entailed. He was his father's darling, above any of his children. God had a special kindness for Solomon (the prophet called him <hi type="italic">Jedidiah,</hi> because the Lord loved him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.25">2 Sam. xii. 25</reference>), and for that reason David had a special kindness for him, for he was a man after God's own heart. If parents may ever love one child better than another, it must not be till it plainly appears that God does so. He was <hi type="italic">tender, and only beloved, in the sight of his mother.</hi> Surely there was a manifest reason for making such a distinction when both the parents made it. Now we see how they showed their love; they catechised him, kept him to his book, and held him to a strict discipline. Though he was a prince, and heir-apparent to the crown, yet they did not let him live at large; nay, therefore they tutored him thus. And perhaps David was the more strict with Solomon in his education because he had seen the ill effects of an undue indulgence in Adonijah, whom he had not <hi type="italic">crossed in any thing</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.6">1 Kings i. 6</reference>), as also in Absalom. (2.) What his parents taught him he teaches others. Observe, [1.] When Solomon was grown up he not only remembered, but took a pleasure in repeating, the good lessons his parents taught him when he was a child. He did not forget them, so deep were the impressions they made upon him. He was not ashamed of them, such a high value had he for them, nor did he look upon them as the childish things, the mean things, which, when he became a man, a king, he should put away, as a disparagement to him; much less did he repeat them: as some wicked children have done, to ridicule them, and make his companions merry with them, priding himself that he had got clear from grave lessons and restraints. [2.] Though Solomon was a wise man himself, and divinely inspired, yet, when he was to teach wisdom, he did not think it below him to quote his father and to make use of his words. Those that would learn well, and teach well, in religion, must not affect new-found notions and new-coined phrases, so as to look with contempt upon the knowledge and language of their predecessors; if we must keep to the good old way, why should we scorn the good old words? <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer. vi. 16</reference>. [3.] Solomon, having been well educated by his parents, thought himself thereby obliged to give his children a good education, the same that his parents had given him; and this is one way in which we must requite our parents for the pains they took with us, even by showing piety at home, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">1 Tim. v. 4</reference>. They taught us, not only that we might learn ourselves, but that we might teach our children, the good knowledge of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.6">Ps. lxxviii. 6</reference>. And we are false to a trust if we do not; for the sacred deposit of religious doctrine and law was lodged in our hands with a charge to transmit it pure and entire to those that shall <hi type="italic">come after us,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.2">2 Tim. ii. 2</reference>. [4.] Solomon enforces his exhortations with the authority of his father David, a man famous in his generation upon all accounts. Be it taken notice of, to the honour of religion, that the wisest and best men in every age have been most zealous, not only for the practice of it themselves, but for the propagating of it to others; and we should therefore <hi type="italic">continue in the things which we have learned, knowing of whom we have learned them,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.14">2 Tim. iii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen13417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13418" type="x-p"/> 2. What these instructions were, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.4-Prov.4.13">v. 4-13</reference>. <div eID="gen13418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13419" type="x-p"/> (1.) By way of precept and exhortation. David, in teaching his son, though he was a child of great capacity and quick apprehension, yet to show that he was in good earnest, and to affect his child the more with what he said, expressed himself with great warmth and importunity, and inculcated the same thing again and again. So children must be taught. <reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">Deut. vi. 7</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt whet them diligently upon thy children.</hi> David, though he was a man of public business, and had tutors for his son, took all this pains with him himself. <div eID="gen13419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13420" type="x-p"/> [1.] He recommends to him his Bible and his catechism, as the means, his father's <hi type="italic">words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.4">v. 4</reference>), the <hi type="italic">words of his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.5">v. 5</reference>), his <hi type="italic">sayings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.10">v. 10</reference>), all the good lessons he had taught him; and perhaps he means particularly the book of Psalms, many of which were <hi type="italic">Maschils—psalms of instruction,</hi> and two of them are expressly said to be <hi type="italic">for Solomon.</hi> These, and all his other words, Solomon must have an eye to. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He must <hi type="italic">hear and receive them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.10">v. 10</reference>), diligently attend to them, and imbibe them, <hi type="italic">as the earth drinks in the rain that comes often upon it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.7">Heb. vi. 7</reference>. God thus bespeaks our attention to his word: <hi type="italic">Hear, O my son! and receive my sayings. Secondly,</hi> He must <hi type="italic">hold fast the form of sound words</hi> which his father gave him (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let thy heart retain my words;</hi> and except the word be hid in the heart, lodged in the will and affections, it will not be retained. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He must govern himself by them: <hi type="italic">Keep my commandments,</hi> obey them, and that is the way to increase in the knowledge of them, <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He must stick to them and abide by them: "<hi type="italic">Decline not from the words of my mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.5">v. 5</reference>), as fearing they will be too great a check upon thee, but <hi type="italic">take fast hold of instruction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.13">v. 13</reference>), as being resolved to keep thy hold and never let it go." Those that have a good education, though they strive to shake it off, will find it hang about them a great while, and, if it do not, their case is very sad. <div eID="gen13420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13421" type="x-p"/> [2.] He recommends to him wisdom and understanding as the end to be aimed at in the use of these means; that <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> which is the <hi type="italic">principal wisdom,</hi> get that. <hi type="italic">Quod caput est sapientia eam acquire sapientiam—Be sure to mind that branch of wisdom which is the top branch of it,</hi> and that is the <hi type="italic">fear of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">ch. i. 7</reference>. Junius and Tremellius. A principle of religion in the heart is the one thing needful; therefore, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Get this <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> get this <hi type="italic">understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.5">v. 5</reference>. And again, "<hi type="italic">Get wisdom,</hi> and <hi type="italic">with all thy getting, get understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.7">v. 7</reference>. Pray for it, take pains for it, give diligence in the use of all appointed means to attain it. <hi type="italic">Wait at wisdom's gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.34">Prov. viii. 34</reference>. Get dominion over thy corruptions, which are thy follies: get possession of wise principles and the habits of wisdom. Get wisdom by experience, get it <hi type="italic">above all thy getting;</hi> be more in care and take more pains to get this than to get the wealth of this world; whatever thou forgettest, get this, reckon it a great achievement, and pursue it accordingly." True wisdom is God's gift, and yet we are here commanded to get it, because God gives it to those that labour for it; yet, after all, we must not say, <hi type="italic">Our might and the power of our hand have gotten us this wealth. Secondly, Forget her not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">forsake her not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">let her not go</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">but keep her.</hi> Those that have got this wisdom must take heed of losing it again by returning to folly: it is indeed a good part, that shall not be <hi type="italic">taken from us;</hi> but then we must take heed lest we throw it from us, as those do that forget it first, and let it slip out of their minds, and then forsake it and turn out of its good ways. That good thing which is committed to us we must keep, and not let it drop, through carelessness, nor suffer it to be forced from us, nor suffer ourselves to be wheedled out of it; never let go such a jewel. <hi type="italic">Thirdly, Love her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.6">v. 6</reference>), and <hi type="italic">embrace her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.8">v. 8</reference>), as worldly men love their wealth and set their hearts upon it. Religion should be very dear to us, dearer than any thing in this world; and, if we cannot reach to be great masters of wisdom, yet let us be true lovers of it; and what grace we have let us embrace it with a sincere affection, as those that admire its beauty. <hi type="italic">Fourthly, "Exalt her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.8">v. 8</reference>. Always keep up high thoughts of religion, and do all thou canst to bring it into reputation, and maintain the credit of it among men. Concur with God in his purpose, which is to magnify the law and make it honourable, and do what thou canst to serve that purpose." Let <hi type="italic">Wisdom's</hi> children not only justify her, but magnify her, and prefer her before that which is dearest to them in this world. In honouring those that fear the Lord, though they are low in the world, and in regarding a <hi type="italic">poor wise man,</hi> we exalt wisdom. <div eID="gen13421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13422" type="x-p"/> (2.) By way of motive and inducement thus to labour for wisdom, and submit to the guidance of it, consider, [1.] It is the main matter, and that which ought to be the chief and continual care of every man in this life (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wisdom is the principal thing;</hi> other things which we are solicitous to get and keep are nothing to it. It is the <hi type="italic">whole of man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.13">Eccl. xii. 13</reference>. It is that which recommends us to God, which beautifies the soul, which enables us to answer the end of our creation, to live to some good purpose in the world, and to get to heaven at last; and therefore it is the principal thing.
