[2.] It has reason and equity on its side (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have taught thee in the way of wisdom,</hi> and so it will be found to be at last. <hi type="italic">I have led thee,</hi> not in the crooked ways of carnal policy, which does wrong under colour of wisdom, but <hi type="italic">in right paths,</hi> agreeable to the eternal rules and reasons of good and evil." The rectitude of the divine nature appears in the rectitude of all the divine laws. Observe, David not only taught his son by good instructions, but led him both by a good example and by applying general instructions to particular cases; so that nothing was wanting on his part to make him wise. [3.] It would be much for his own advantage: "If thou be wise and good, thou shalt be so for thyself." <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "It will be thy life, thy comfort, thy happiness; it is what thou canst not live without:" <hi type="italic">Keep my commandments and live,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.4">v. 4</reference>. That of our Saviour agrees with this, <hi type="italic">If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.19.17">Matt. xix. 17</reference>. It is upon pain of death, eternal death, and in prospect of life, eternal life, that we are required to be religious. "Receive wisdom's sayings, <hi type="italic">and the years of thy life shall be many</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.10">v. 10</reference>), as many in this world as Infinite Wisdom sees fit, and in the other world thou shalt live that life the years of which shall never be numbered. <hi type="italic">Keep her</hi> therefore, whatever it cost thee, <hi type="italic">for she is thy life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.13">v. 13</reference>. All thy satisfaction will be found in this;" and a soul without true wisdom and grace is really a dead soul. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "It will be thy guard and guide, thy convoy and conductor, through all the dangers and difficulties of thy journey through this wilderness. Love wisdom, and cleave to her, and she shall <hi type="italic">preserve thee, she shall keep thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.6">v. 6</reference>) from sin, the worst of evils, the worst of enemies; she shall keep thee from hurting thyself, and then none else can hurt thee." As we say, "Keep thy shop, and thy shop will keep thee;" so, "Keep thy wisdom, and thy wisdom will keep thee." It will keep us from straits and stumbling-blocks in the management of ourselves and our affairs, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.12">v. 12</reference>. 1. That our steps be not straitened when we go, that we bring not ourselves into such straits as David was in, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.14">2 Sam. xxiv. 14</reference>. Those that make God's word their rule shall walk at liberty, and be at ease in themselves. 2. That our feet do not stumble when we run. If wise and good men be put upon sudden resolves, the certain rule of God's word which they go by will keep them even then from stumbling upon any thing that may be pernicious. Integrity and uprightness will preserve us. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> "It will be thy honour and reputation (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Exalt</hi> wisdom (do thou but show thy good-will to her advancement) and though she needs not thy service she will abundantly recompense it, <hi type="italic">she shall promote thee, she shall bring thee to honour.</hi>" Solomon was to be a king, but his wisdom and virtue would be more his honour than his crown or purple; it was that for which all his neighbours had him so much in veneration; and no doubt, in his reign and David's, wise and good men stood fairest for preferment. However, religion will, first or last, bring all those <hi type="italic">to honour</hi> that cordially <hi type="italic">embrace her;</hi> they shall be accepted of God, respected by all wise men, owned in the great day, and shall inherit everlasting glory. This he insists on (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">She shall give to thy head an ornament of grace</hi> in this world, shall recommend thee both to God and man, and in the other world <hi type="italic">a crown of glory shall she deliver to thee,</hi> a crown that shall never totter, a crown of glory that shall never wither." That is the true honour which attends religion. <hi type="italic">Nobilitas sola est atique unica virtus—Virtue is the only nobility!</hi> David having thus recommended wisdom to his son, no marvel that when God bade him ask what he would he prayed, Lord, <hi type="italic">give me a wise and an understanding heart.</hi> We should make it appear by our prayers how well we are taught.

<div eID="gen13422" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions against Bad Company.</title> <div sID="gen13423" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil <hi type="italic">men.</hi> <hi type="super">15</hi> Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away. <hi type="super">16</hi> For they sleep not, except they have done mischief; and their sleep is taken away, unless they cause <hi type="italic">some</hi> to fall. <hi type="super">17</hi> For they eat the bread of wickedness, and drink the wine of violence. <hi type="super">18</hi> But the path of the just <hi type="italic">is</hi> as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day. <hi type="super">19</hi> The way of the wicked <hi type="italic">is</hi> as darkness: they know not at what they stumble. <div eID="gen13423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13424" type="x-p"/> Some make David's instructions to Solomon, which began <reference osisRef="Prov.4.4">v. 4</reference>, to continue to the end of the chapter; nay, some continue them to the end of the ninth chapter; but it is more probable that Solomon begins here again, if not sooner. In these verses, having exhorted us to walk in the paths of wisdom, he cautions us against the path of the wicked. 1. We must take heed of the ways of sin and avoid them, every thing that looks like sin and leads to it. 2. In order to this we must keep out of the ways of sinners, and have no fellowship with them. For fear of falling into wicked courses, we must shun wicked company. Here is, <div eID="gen13424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13425" type="x-p"/> I. The caution itself, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.14-Prov.4.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. 1. We must take heed of falling in with sin and sinners: <hi type="italic">Enter not into the paths of the wicked.</hi> Our teacher, having like a faithful guide shown us the <hi type="italic">right paths</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.11">v. 11</reference>), here warns us of the by-paths into which we are in danger of being drawn aside. Those that have been well educated, and trained up in the way they should go, let them never turn aside into the way they should not go; let them not so much as enter into it, no, not to make trial of it, lest it prove a dangerous experiment and difficult to retreat with safety. "Venture not into the company of those that are infected with the plague, no, not though thou think thyself guarded with an antidote." 2. If at any time we are inveigled into an evil way, we must hasten out of it. "If, ere thou wast aware, thou didst enter in at the gate, because it was wide, <hi type="italic">go not</hi> on <hi type="italic">in the way of evil men.</hi> As soon as thou art made sensible of thy mistake, retire immediately, take not a step more, stay not a minute longer, in the way that certainly leads to destruction." 3. We must dread and detest the ways of sin and sinners, and decline them with the utmost care imaginable. "<hi type="italic">The way of evil men</hi> may seem a pleasant way and sociable, and the nearest way to the compassing of some secular end we may have in view; but it is an evil way, and will end ill, and therefore if thou love thy God and thy soul <hi type="italic">avoid it, pass not by it,</hi> that thou mayest not be tempted to enter into it; and, if thou find thyself near it, <hi type="italic">turn from it and pass away,</hi> and get as far off it as thou canst." The manner of expression intimates the imminent danger we are in, the need we have of this caution, and the great importance of it, and that our watchmen are, or should be, in good earnest, in giving us warning. It intimates likewise at what a distance we should keep from sin and sinners; he does not say, Keep at a due distance, but at a great distance, the further the better; never think you can get far enough from it. <hi type="italic">Escape for thy life: look not behind thee.</hi> <div eID="gen13425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13426" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons to enforce this caution. <div eID="gen13426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13427" type="x-p"/> 1. "Consider the character of the men whose way thou art warned to shun." They are mischievous men (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.16-Prov.4.17">v. 16, 17</reference>); they not only care not what hurt they do to those that stand in their way, but it is their business to do mischief, and their delight, purely for mischief-sake. They are continually designing and endeavouring to <hi type="italic">cause some to fall,</hi> to ruin them body and soul. Wickedness and malice are in their nature, and violence is in all their actions. They are spiteful in the highest degree; for, (1.) Mischief is rest and sleep to them. As much satisfaction as a covetous man has when he has got money, an ambitious man when he has got preferment, and a good man when he has done good, so much have they when they have said or done that which is injurious and ill-natured; and they are extremely uneasy if they cannot get their envy and revenge gratified, as Haman, to whom every thing was unpleasant as long as Mordecai was unhanged. It intimates likewise how restless and unwearied they are in their mischievous pursuits; they will rather be deprived of sleep than of the pleasure of being vexatious. (2.) Mischief is meat and drink to them; they feed and feast upon it. <hi type="italic">They eat the bread of the wickedness (they eat up my people as they eat bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.14.4">Ps. xiv. 4</reference>) <hi type="italic">and drink the wine of violence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">drink iniquity like water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.16">Job xv. 16</reference>. All they eat and drink is got by rapine and oppression. Do wicked men think the time lost in which they are not doing hurt? Let good men make it as much their business and delight to do good. <hi type="italic">Amici, diem perdidi—Friends, I have lost a day.</hi> And let all that are wise, and wish well to themselves, avoid the society of the wicked; for, [1.] It is very scandalous; for there is no disposition of mind that is a greater reproach to human nature, a greater enemy to human society, a bolder defiance to God and conscience, that has more of the devil's image in it, or is more serviceable to his interests, than a delight to do mischief and to vex, and hurt, and ruin every body. [2.] It is very dangerous. "Shun those that delight to do mischief as thou tenderest thy own safety; for, whatever friendship they may pretend, one time or other they will do thee mischief; thou wilt ruin thyself if thou dost concur with them (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>) and they will ruin thee if thou dost not." <div eID="gen13427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13428" type="x-p"/> 2. "Consider the character of the way itself which thou art warned to shun, compared with the right way which thou art invited to walk in." <div eID="gen13428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13429" type="x-p"/> (1.) The way of righteousness is light (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The path of the just,</hi> which they have chosen, and in which they walk, <hi type="italic">is as light;</hi> the <hi type="italic">light shines on their ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.22.28">Job xxii. 28</reference>) and makes them both safe and pleasant. Christ is <hi type="italic">their way</hi> and he is <hi type="italic">the light.</hi> They are guided by the word of God and that is <hi type="italic">a light to their feet;</hi> they themselves are <hi type="italic">light in the Lord</hi> and they <hi type="italic">walk in the light as he is in the light.</hi> [1.] It is a <hi type="italic">shining light.</hi> Their way shines to themselves in the joy and comfort of it; it shines before others in the lustre and honour of it; <hi type="italic">it shines before men, who see their good works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">Matt. v. 16</reference>. They go on in their way with a holy security and serenity of mind, as those that <hi type="italic">walk in the light.</hi> It is as the morning-light, which <hi type="italic">shines out of obscurity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.8">Isa. lviii. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">10</reference>) and puts an end to the <hi type="italic">works of darkness.</hi> [2.] It is a growing light; it <hi type="italic">shines more and more,</hi> not like the light of a meteor, which soon disappears, or that of a candle, which burns dim and burns down, but like that of the rising sun, which goes forward shining, mounts upward shining. Grace, the guide of this way, is growing; <hi type="italic">he that has clean hands shall be stronger and stronger.</hi> That joy which is the pleasure of this way, that honour which is the brightness of it, and all that happiness which is indeed its light, shall be still increasing. [3.] It will arrive, in the end, at <hi type="italic">the perfect day.</hi> The light of the dayspring will at length be noon-day light, and it is this that the enlightened soul is pressing towards. The saints will not be perfect till they come to heaven, but there they shall themselves <hi type="italic">shine as the sun when he goes forth in his strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">Matt. xiii. 43</reference>. Their graces and joys shall be all consummate. Therefore it is our wisdom to keep close to <hi type="italic">the path of the just.</hi> <div eID="gen13429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13430" type="x-p"/> (2.) The <hi type="italic">way of</hi> sin <hi type="italic">is as darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">v. 19</reference>. The works he had cautioned us not to have fellowship with are <hi type="italic">works of darkness.</hi> What true pleasure and satisfaction can those have who know no pleasure and satisfaction but what they have in doing mischief? What sure guide have those that cast God's word behind them? <hi type="italic">The way of the wicked is dark,</hi> and therefore dangerous; for they stumble and yet <hi type="italic">know not at what they stumble.</hi> They fall into sin, but are not aware which way the temptation came by which they were overthrown, and therefore know not how to avoid it the next time. They fall into trouble, but never enquire wherefore God contends with them; they <hi type="italic">consider not that they do evil,</hi> nor what will be in the end of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Ps. lxxxii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.5-Job.18.6">Job xviii. 5, 6</reference>. This is the way we are directed to shun.

<div eID="gen13430" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Parental Instructions.</title> <div sID="gen13431" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> My son, attend to my words; incline thine ear unto my sayings. <hi type="super">21</hi> Let them not depart from thine eyes; keep them in the midst of thine heart. <hi type="super">22</hi> For they <hi type="italic">are</hi> life unto those that find them, and health to all their flesh. <hi type="super">23</hi> Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it <hi type="italic">are</hi> the issues of life. <hi type="super">24</hi> Put away from thee a froward mouth, and perverse lips put far from thee. <hi type="super">25</hi> Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee. <hi type="super">26</hi> Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established. <hi type="super">27</hi> Turn not to the right hand nor to the left: remove thy foot from evil. <div eID="gen13431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13432" type="x-p"/> Solomon, having warned us not to do evil, here teaches us how to do well. It is not enough for us to shun the occasions of sin, but we must study the methods of duty. <div eID="gen13432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13433" type="x-p"/> I. We must have a continual regard to the word of God and endeavour that it may be always ready to us. <div eID="gen13433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13434" type="x-p"/> 1. The sayings of wisdom must be our principles by which we must govern ourselves, our monitors to warn us of duty and danger; and therefore, (1.) We must receive them readily: "<hi type="italic">Incline thy ear to them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.20">v. 20</reference>); humbly bow to them; diligently listen to them." The attentive hearing of the word of God is a good sign of a work of grace begun in the heart and a good means of carrying it on. It is to be hoped that those are resolved to do their duty who are inclined to know it. (2.) We must retain them carefully (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.21">v. 21</reference>); we must lay them before us as our rule: "<hi type="italic">Let them not depart from thy eyes;</hi> view them, review them, and in every thing aim to conform to them." We must lodge them within us, as a commanding principle, the influences of which are diffused throughout the whole man: "<hi type="italic">Keep them in the midst of thy heart,</hi> as things dear to thee, and which thou art afraid of losing." Let the word of God be written in the heart, and that which is written there will remain. <div eID="gen13434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13435" type="x-p"/> 2. The reason why we must thus make much of the words of wisdom is because they will be both food and physic to us, like <hi type="italic">the tree of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.2">Rev. xxii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.12">Ezek. xlvii. 12</reference>. Those that seek and find them, find and keep them, shall find in them, (1.) Food: <hi type="italic">For they are life unto those that find them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.22">v. 22</reference>. As the spiritual life was begun by the word as the instrument of it, so by the same word it is still nourished and maintained. We could not live without it; we may by faith live upon it. (2.) Physic. They are <hi type="italic">health to all their flesh,</hi> to the whole man, both body and soul; they help to keep both in good plight. They are <hi type="italic">health to all flesh,</hi> so the LXX. There is enough to cure all the diseases of this distempered world. They are <hi type="italic">a medicine to all their flesh</hi> (so the word is), to all their corruptions, for they are called flesh, to all their grievances, which are as thorns in the flesh. There is in the word of God a proper remedy for all our spiritual maladies. <div eID="gen13435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13436" type="x-p"/> II. We must keep a watchful eye and a strict hand upon all the motions of our inward man, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.23">v. 23</reference>. Here is, 1. A great duty required by the laws of wisdom, and in order to our getting and preserving wisdom: <hi type="italic">Keep thy heart with all diligence.</hi> God, who gave us these souls, gave us a strict charge with them: Man, woman, <hi type="italic">keep thy heart; take heed to thy spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.9">Deut. iv. 9</reference>. We must maintain a holy jealousy of ourselves, and set a strict guard, accordingly, upon all the avenues of the soul; keep our hearts from doing hurt and getting hurt, from being defiled by sin and disturbed by trouble; keep them as our jewel, as our vineyard; keep a conscience void of offence; keep out bad thoughts; keep up good thoughts; keep the affections upon right objects and in due bounds. <hi type="italic">Keep them with all keepings</hi> (so the word is); there are many ways of keeping things—by care, by strength, by calling in help, and we must use them all in keeping our hearts; and all little enough, so deceitful are they, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.9">Jer. xvii. 9</reference>. Or <hi type="italic">above all keepings;</hi> we must keep our hearts with more care and diligence than we keep any thing else. We must keep our eyes (<reference osisRef="Job.31.1">Job xxxi. 1</reference>), keep our tongues (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.13">Ps. xxxiv. 13</reference>), keep our feet (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1">Eccl. v. 1</reference>), but, above all, keep our hearts. 2. A good reason given for this care, because <hi type="italic">out of it are the issues of life.</hi> Out of a heart well kept will flow living issues, good products, to the glory of God and the edification of others. Or, in general, all the actions of the life flow from the heart, and therefore keeping that is making the tree good and healing the springs. Our lives will be regular or irregular, comfortable or uncomfortable, according as our hearts are kept or neglected. <div eID="gen13436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13437" type="x-p"/> III. We must set a <hi type="italic">watch before the door of our lips,</hi> that we offend not with out tongue (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Put away from thee a froward mouth and perverse lips.</hi> Our hearts being naturally corrupt, out of them a great deal of corrupt communication is apt to come, and therefore we must conceive a great dread and detestation of all manner of evil words, cursing, swearing, lying, slandering, brawling, filthiness, and foolish talking, all which come from a <hi type="italic">froward mouth and perverse lips,</hi> that will not be governed either by reason or religion, but contradict both, and which are as unsightly and ill-favoured before God as a crooked distorted mouth drawn awry is before men. All manner of tongue sins, we must, by constant watchfulness and stedfast resolution, <hi type="italic">put from us,</hi> put <hi type="italic">far from us,</hi> abstaining from all words that have an appearance of evil and fearing to learn any such words. <div eID="gen13437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13438" type="x-p"/> IV. We must make a covenant with our eyes: "Let them <hi type="italic">look right on and straight before thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.24">v. 24</reference>. Let the eye be fixed and not wandering; let it not rove after every thing that presents itself, for then it will be diverted form good and ensnared in evil. Turn it from beholding vanity; let thy eye be single and not divided; let thy intentions be sincere and uniform, and look not asquint at any by-end." We must keep our eye upon our Master, and be careful to approve ourselves to him; keep our eye upon our rule, and conform to that; keep our eye upon our mark, the <hi type="italic">prize of the high calling,</hi> and direct all towards that. <hi type="italic">Oculum in metam</hi>—<hi type="italic">The eye upon the goal.</hi> <div eID="gen13438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13439" type="x-p"/> V. We must act considerately in all we do (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ponder the path of thy feet, weigh it</hi> (so the word is); "put the word of God in one scale, and what thou hast done, or art about to do, in the other, and see how they agree; be nice and critical in examining whether thy way be good before the Lord and whether it will end well." We must consider our past ways and examine what we have done, and our present ways, what we are doing, whither we are going, and <hi type="italic">see that we walk circumspectly.</hi> It concerns us to consider what are the duties and what the difficulties, what are the advantages and what the dangers, of our way, that we may act accordingly. "Do nothing rashly." <div eID="gen13439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13440" type="x-p"/> VI. We must act with steadiness, caution, and consistency: "<hi type="italic">Let all thy ways be established</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.26">v. 26</reference>) and be not unstable in them, as the double-minded man is; halt not between two, but go on in an even uniform course of obedience; <hi type="italic">turn not to the right hand not to the left,</hi> for there are errors on both hands, and Satan gains his point if he prevails to draw us aside either way. Be very careful to <hi type="italic">remove thy foot from evil;</hi> take heed of extremes, for in them there is evil, and <hi type="italic">let thy eyes look right on,</hi> that thou mayest keep the golden mean." Those that would approve themselves wise must always be watchful.  <chapter eID="Prov.4"/> <div eID="gen13440" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen13443" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13442" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Parental Instructions; Cautions against Sensuality.</title> <div sID="gen13444" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My son, attend unto my wisdom, <hi type="italic">and</hi> bow thine ear to my understanding: <hi type="super">2</hi> That thou mayest regard discretion, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> thy lips may keep knowledge. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the lips of a strange woman drop <hi type="italic">as</hi> an honeycomb, and her mouth <hi type="italic">is</hi> smoother than oil: <hi type="super">4</hi> But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword. <hi type="super">5</hi> Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold on hell. <hi type="super">6</hi> Lest thou shouldest ponder the path of life, her ways are moveable, <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou canst not know <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> Hear me now therefore, O ye children, and depart not from the words of my mouth. <hi type="super">8</hi> Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house: <hi type="super">9</hi> Lest thou give thine honour unto others, and thy years unto the cruel: <hi type="super">10</hi> Lest strangers be filled with thy wealth; and thy labours <hi type="italic">be</hi> in the house of a stranger; <hi type="super">11</hi> And thou mourn at the last, when thy flesh and thy body are consumed, <hi type="super">12</hi> And say, How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof; <hi type="super">13</hi> And have not obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor inclined mine ear to them that instructed me! <hi type="super">14</hi> I was almost in all evil in the midst of the congregation and assembly. <div eID="gen13444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13445" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen13445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13446" type="x-p"/> I. A solemn preface, to introduce the caution which follows, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.1-Prov.5.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Solomon here addresses himself to his son, that is, to all young men, as unto his children, whom he has an affection for and some influence upon. In God's name, he demands attention; for he writes by divine inspiration, and is a prophet, though he begins not with, <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord. "Attend, and bow thy ear;</hi> not only hear what is said, and read what is written, but apply thy mind to it and consider it diligently." To gain attention he urges, 1. The excellency of his discourse: "It is <hi type="italic">my wisdom, my understanding;</hi> if I undertake to teach thee wisdom I cannot prescribe any thing to be more properly called so; moral philosophy is my philosophy, and that which is to be learned in my school." 2. The usefulness of it: "Attend to what I say," (1.) "That thou mayest act wisely—<hi type="italic">that thou mayest regard discretion.</hi>" Solomon's lectures are not designed to fill our heads with notions, with matters of nice speculation, or doubtful disputation, but to guide us in the government of ourselves, that we may act prudently, so as becomes us and so as will be for our true interest. (2.) "That thou mayest speak wisely—<hi type="italic">that thy lips may keep knowledge,</hi> and thou mayest have it ready at thy tongue's end" (as we say), "for the benefit of those with whom thou dost converse." The priest's lips are said to <hi type="italic">keep knowledge</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.2.7">Mal. ii. 7</reference>); but those that are ready and mighty in the scriptures may not only in their devotions, but in their discourses, be spiritual priests. <div eID="gen13446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13447" type="x-p"/> II. The caution itself, and that is to abstain from fleshly lusts, from adultery, fornication, and all uncleanness. Some apply this figuratively, and by the adulterous woman here understand idolatry, or false doctrine, which tends to debauch men's minds and manners, or the sensual appetite, to which it may as fitly as any thing be applied; but the primary scope of it is plainly to warn us against seventh-commandment sins, which youth is so prone to, the temptations to which are so violent, the examples of which are so many, and which, where admitted, are so destructive to all the seeds of virtue in the soul that it is not strange that Solomon's cautions against it are so very pressing and so often repeated. Solomon here, as a faithful watchman, gives fair warning to all, as they regard their lives and comforts, to dread this sin, for it will certainly be their ruin. Two things we are here warned to take heed of:— <div eID="gen13447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13448" type="x-p"/> 1. That we do not listen to the charms of this sin. It is true <hi type="italic">the lips of a strange woman drop as a honey-comb</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.3">v. 3</reference>); the pleasures of fleshly lust are very tempting (like the wine that <hi type="italic">gives its colour in the cup</hi> and <hi type="italic">moves itself aright</hi>); its mouth, the kisses of its mouth, the words of its mouth, are <hi type="italic">smoother than oil,</hi> that the poisonous pill may go down glibly and there may be no suspicion of harm in it. But consider, (1.) How fatal the consequences will be. What fruit will the sinner have of his honey and oil when the end will be, [1.] The terrors of conscience: It <hi type="italic">is bitter as wormwood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.4">v. 4</reference>. What was luscious in the mouth rises in the stomach and turns sour there; it cuts, in the reflection, like <hi type="italic">a two-edged sword;</hi> take it which way you will, it wounds. Solomon could speak by experience, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Eccl. vii. 26</reference>. [2.] The torments of hell. If some that have been guilty of this sin have repented and been saved, yet the direct tendency of the sin is to destruction of body and soul; the <hi type="italic">feet</hi> of it <hi type="italic">go down to death,</hi> nay, they <hi type="italic">take hold on hell,</hi> to pull it to the sinner, as if the damnations slumbered too long, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.4">v. 4</reference>. Those that are entangled in this sin should be reminded that there is but a step between them and hell, and that they are ready to drop into it. (2.) Consider how false the charms are. The adulteress flatters and speaks fair, her words are honey and oil, but she will deceive those that hearken to her: <hi type="italic">Her ways are movable, that thou canst not know them;</hi> she often changes her disguise, and puts on a great variety of false colours, because, if she be rightly known, she is certainly hated. Proteus-like, she puts on many shapes, that she may keep in with those whom she has a design upon. And what does she aim at with all this art and management? Nothing but to keep them from <hi type="italic">pondering the path of life,</hi> for she knows that, if they once come to do that, she shall certainly lose them. Those are <hi type="italic">ignorant of Satan's devices</hi> who do not understand that the great thing he drives at in all his temptations is, [1.] To keep them from choosing the path of life, to prevent them from being religious and from going to heaven, that, being himself shut out from happiness, he may keep them out from it. [2.] In order hereunto, to keep them from pondering the path of life, from considering how reasonable it is that they should walk in that path, and how much it will be for their advantage. Be it observed, to the honour of religion, that it certainly gains its point with all those that will but allow themselves the liberty of a serious thought and will weigh things impartially in an even balance, and that the devil has no way of securing men in his interests but by diverting them with continual amusements of one kind or another from the calm and sober consideration of the <hi type="italic">things that belong to their peace.</hi> And uncleanness is a sin that does as much as any thing blind the understanding, sear the conscience, and keep people from pondering the path of life. Whoredom <hi type="italic">takes away the heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.4.11">Hos. iv. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen13448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13449" type="x-p"/> 2. That we do not approach the borders of this sin, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.7-Prov.5.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen13449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13450" type="x-p"/> (1.) This caution is introduced with a solemn preface: "<hi type="italic">Hear me now therefore, O you children!</hi> whoever you are that read or hear these lines, take notice of what I say, and mix faith with it, treasure it up, and <hi type="italic">depart not from the words of my mouth,</hi> as those will do that hearken to the words of the strange woman. Do not only receive what I say, for the present merely, but cleave to it, and let it be ready to thee, and of force with thee, when thou art most violently assaulted by the temptation." <div eID="gen13450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13451" type="x-p"/> (2.) The caution itself is very pressing: "<hi type="italic">Remove thy way far from her;</hi> if thy way should happen to lie near her, and thou shouldst have a fair pretence of being led by business within the reach of her charms, yet change thy way, and alter the course of it, rather than expose thyself to danger; <hi type="italic">come not nigh the door of her house;</hi> go on the other side of the street, nay, go through some other street, though it be about." This intimates, [1.] That we ought to have a very great dread and detestation of the sin. We must fear it as we would a place infected with the plague; we must loathe it as the odour of carrion, that we will not come near. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> we are likely to preserve our purity when we conceive a rooted antipathy to all fleshly lusts. [2.] That we ought industriously to avoid every thing that may be an occasion of this sin or a step towards it. Those that would be kept from harm must keep out of harm's way. Such tinder there is in the corrupt nature that it is madness, upon any pretence whatsoever, to come near the sparks. If we thrust ourselves into temptation, we mocked God when we prayed, <hi type="italic">Lead us not into temptation.</hi> [3.] That we ought to be jealous over ourselves with a godly jealousy, and not to be so confident of the strength of our own resolutions as to venture upon the brink of sin, with a promise to ourselves that <hi type="italic">hitherto we will come and no further.</hi> [4.] That whatever has become a snare to us and an occasion of sin, though it be as a <hi type="italic">right eye</hi> and a <hi type="italic">right hand,</hi> we must <hi type="italic">pluck it out, cut it off, and cast it from us,</hi> must part with that which is dearest to us rather than hazard our own souls; this is our Saviour's command, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28-Matt.5.30">Matt. v. 28-30</reference>. <div eID="gen13451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13452" type="x-p"/> (3.) The arguments which Solomon here uses to enforce this caution are taken from the same topic with those before, the many mischiefs which attend this sin. [1.] It blasts the reputation. "Thou wilt <hi type="italic">give thy honour unto others</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.9">v. 9</reference>); thou wilt lose it thyself; thou wilt put into the hand of each of thy neighbours a stone to throw at thee, for they will all, with good reason, cry shame on thee, will despise thee, and trample on thee, as a foolish men." Whoredom is a sin that makes men contemptible and base, and no man of sense or virtue will care to keep company with one that keeps company with harlots. [2.] It wastes the time, gives <hi type="italic">the years,</hi> the years of youth, the flower of men's time, <hi type="italic">unto the cruel,</hi> "that base lust of thine, which with the utmost cruelty <hi type="italic">wars against the soul,</hi> that base harlot which pretends an affection for thee, but really hunts for the precious life." Those years that should be given to the honour of a gracious God are spent in the service of a cruel sin. [3.] It ruins the estate (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Strangers</hi> will be <hi type="italic">filled with thy wealth,</hi> which thou art but entrusted with as a steward for thy family; and the fruit of <hi type="italic">thy labours,</hi> which should be provision for thy own house, will be in <hi type="italic">the house of a stranger,</hi> that neither has right to it nor will ever thank thee for it." [4.] It is destructive to the health, and shortens men's days: <hi type="italic">Thy flesh and thy body</hi> will be <hi type="italic">consumed</hi> by it, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.11">v. 11</reference>. The lusts of uncleanness not only <hi type="italic">war against the soul,</hi> which the sinner neglects and is in no care about, but they war against the body too, which he is so indulgent of and is in such care to please and pamper, such deceitful, such foolish, such hurtful lusts are they. Those that give themselves to work uncleanness with greediness waste their strength, throw themselves into weakness, and often have their bodies filled with loathsome distempers, by which the number of their months is cut off in the midst and they fall unpitied sacrifices to a cruel lust. [5.] It will fill the mind with horror, if ever conscience be awakened. "Though thou art merry now, <hi type="italic">sporting thyself in thy own deceivings,</hi> yet thou wilt certainly <hi type="italic">mourn at the last,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.11">v. 11</reference>. Thou art all this while making work for repentance, and laying up matter for vexation and torment in the reflection, when the sin is set before thee in its own colours." Sooner or later it will bring sorrow, either when the soul is humbled and brought to repentance or when the <hi type="italic">flesh and body are consumed,</hi> either by sickness, when conscience flies in the sinner's face, or by the grave; when the body is rotting there, the soul is racking in the torments of hell, where the worm dies not, and "<hi type="italic">Son, remember,</hi>" is the constant peal. Solomon here brings in the convinced sinner reproaching himself, and aggravating his own folly. He will then most bitterly lament it. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That because he hated to be reformed he therefore hated to be informed, and could not endure either to be taught his duty (<hi type="italic">How have I hated</hi> not only the discipline of being instructed, but the <hi type="italic">instruction</hi> itself, though all true and good!) or to be told of his faults—<hi type="italic">My heart despised reproof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.12">v. 12</reference>. He cannot but own that those who had the charge of him, parents, ministers, had done their part; they had been his teachers; they had instructed him, had given him good counsel and fair warning (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.13">v. 13</reference>); but to his own shame and confusion does he speak it, and therein justifies God in all the miseries that were brought upon him, he had not <hi type="italic">obeyed their voice,</hi> for indeed he <hi type="italic">never inclined his ear to those that instructed him,</hi> never minded what they said nor admitted the impressions of it. Note, Those who have had a good education and do not live up to it will have a great deal to answer for another day; and those who will not now remember what they were taught, to conform themselves to it, will be made to remember it as an aggravation of their sin, and consequently of their ruin. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That by the frequent acts of sin the habits of it were so rooted and confirmed that his heart was fully set in him to commit it (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was almost in all evil in the midst of the congregation and assembly.</hi> When he came into the synagogue, or into the courts of the temple, to worship God with other Israelites, his unclean heart was full of wanton thoughts and desires and his eyes of adultery. Reverence of the place and company, and of the work that was doing, could not restrain him, but he was almost as wicked and vile there as any where. No sin will appear more frightful to an awakened conscience than the profanation of holy things; nor will any aggravation of sin render it more exceedingly sinful than the place we are honoured with in the congregation and assembly, and the advantages we enjoy thereby. Zimri and Cozbi avowed their villany <hi type="italic">in the sight of Moses and all the congregation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.25.6">Num. xxv. 6</reference>), and heart-adultery is as open to God, and must needs be most offensive to him, when we draw nigh to him in religious exercises. <hi type="italic">I was in all evil</hi> in defiance of the magistrates and judges, and their assemblies; so some understand it. Others refer it to the evil of punishment, not to the evil of sin: "I was made an example, a spectacle to the world. I was under almost all God's sore judgments <hi type="italic">in the midst of the congregation of Israel,</hi> set up for a mark. <hi type="italic">I stood up and cried in the congregation,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.30.28">Job xxx. 28</reference>. Let that be avoided which will be thus rued at last.

<div eID="gen13452" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Conjugal Fidelity Enjoined.</title> <div sID="gen13453" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well. <hi type="super">16</hi> Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad, <hi type="italic">and</hi> rivers of waters in the streets. 17 Let them be only thine own, and not strangers' with thee. 18 Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth. <hi type="super">19</hi> <hi type="italic">Let her be as</hi> the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love. <hi type="super">20</hi> And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger? <hi type="super">21</hi> For the ways of man <hi type="italic">are</hi> before the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he pondereth all his goings. <hi type="super">22</hi> His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins. <hi type="super">23</hi> He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall go astray. <div eID="gen13453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13454" type="x-p"/> Solomon, having shown the great evil that there is in adultery and fornication, and all such lewd and filthy courses, here prescribes remedies against them. <div eID="gen13454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13455" type="x-p"/> I. Enjoy with satisfaction the comforts of lawful marriage, which was ordained for the prevention of uncleanness, and therefore ought to be made use of in time, lest it should not prove effectual for the cure of that which it might have prevented. Let none complain that God has dealt unkindly with them in forbidding them those pleasures which they have a natural desire of, for he has graciously provided for the regular gratification of them. "Thou mayest not indeed eat of every tree of the garden, but choose thee out one, which thou pleasest, and of that thou mayest freely eat; nature will be content with that, but lust with nothing." God, in thus confining men to one, has been so far from putting any hardship upon them that he has really consulted their true interest; for, as Mr. Herbert observes, "<hi type="italic">If God had laid all common, certainly man would have been the encloser.</hi>"—Church-porch. Solomon here enlarges much upon this, not only prescribing it as an antidote, but urging it as an argument against fornication, that the allowed pleasures of marriage (however wicked wits may ridicule them, who are factors for the unclean spirit) far transcend all the false forbidden pleasures of whoredom. <div eID="gen13455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13456" type="x-p"/> 1. Let young men marry, marry and not burn. Have <hi type="italic">a cistern,</hi> a <hi type="italic">well of thy own</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.15">v. 15</reference>), even the wife <hi type="italic">of thy youth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Wholly abstain, or wed.</hi>—Herbert. "The world is wide, and there are varieties of accomplishments, among which thou mayest please thyself." <div eID="gen13456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13457" type="x-p"/> 2. Let him that is married take delight in his wife, and let him be very fond of her, not only because she is the wife that he himself has chosen and he ought to be pleased with his own choice, but because she is the wife that God in his providence appointed for him and he ought much more to be pleased with the divine appointment, pleased with her because she is his own. <hi type="italic">Let thy fountain be blessed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.18">v. 18</reference>); think thyself very happy in her, look upon her as a blessed wife, let her have thy blessing, pray daily for her, and then <hi type="italic">rejoice with her.</hi> Those comforts we are likely to have joy of that are sanctified to us by prayer and the blessing of God. It is not only allowed us, but commanded us, to be pleasant with our relations; and it particularly becomes yoke-fellows to rejoice together and in each other. Mutual delight is the bond of mutual fidelity. It is not only taken for granted that the <hi type="italic">bridegroom rejoices over his bride</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Isa. lxii. 5</reference>), but given for law. <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.9">Eccl. ix. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of thy life.</hi> Those take not their comforts where God has appointed who are jovial and merry with their companions abroad, but sour and morose with their families at home. <div eID="gen13457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13458" type="x-p"/> 3. Let him be fond of his wife and love her dearly (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let her be as the loving hind and the pleasant roe,</hi> such as great men sometimes kept tame in their houses and played with. Desire no better diversion from severe study and business than the innocent and pleasant conversation of thy own wife; let her lie in thy bosom, as the poor man's ewe-lamb did in his (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.3">2 Sam. xii. 3</reference>), and do thou repose thy head in hers, and let that <hi type="italic">satisfy thee at all times;</hi> and seek not for pleasure in any other. "<hi type="italic">Err thou always in her love.</hi> If thou wilt suffer thy love to run into an excess, and wilt be dotingly fond of any body, let it be only of thy own wife, where there is least danger of exceeding." This is <hi type="italic">drinking waters,</hi> to quench the thirst of thy appetite, <hi type="italic">out of thy own cistern,</hi> and <hi type="italic">running waters,</hi> which are clear, and sweet, and wholesome, <hi type="italic">out of thy own well,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.15">v. 15. 1 Cor. vii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2-1Cor.7.3">3</reference>. <div eID="gen13458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13459" type="x-p"/> 4. Let him take delight in his children and look upon them with pleasure (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.16-Prov.5.17">v. 16, 17</reference>): "Look upon them as streams from thy own pure fountains" (the Jews are said to <hi type="italic">come forth out of the waters of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Isa. xlviii. 1</reference>), "so that they are parts of thyself, as the streams are of the fountain. Keep to thy own wife, and thou shalt have," (1.) "A numerous offspring, like <hi type="italic">rivers of water,</hi> which run in abundance, and they shall be dispersed abroad, matched into other families, whereas those that <hi type="italic">commit whoredom</hi> shall <hi type="italic">not increase,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Hos.4.10">Hos. iv. 10</reference>. (2.) "A peculiar offspring, which shall be <hi type="italic">only thy own,</hi> whereas the children of whoredom, that are fathered upon thee, are, probably, not so, but, for aught thou knowest, are the offspring of strangers, and yet thou must keep them." (3.) "A creditable offspring, which are an honour to thee, and which thou mayest send abroad, and appear with, in the streets, whereas a spurious brood is thy disgrace, and that which thou art ashamed to own." In this matter, virtue has all the pleasure and honour in it; justly therefore it is called <hi type="italic">wisdom.</hi> <div eID="gen13459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13460" type="x-p"/> 5. Let him then scorn the offer of forbidden pleasures when he is <hi type="italic">always ravished with the love</hi> of a faithful virtuous wife; let him consider what an absurdity it will be for him to be <hi type="italic">ravished with a strange woman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.20">v. 20</reference>), to be in love with a filthy harlot, and <hi type="italic">embrace the bosom of a stranger,</hi> which, if he had any sense of honour or virtue, he would loathe the thoughts of. "Why wilt thou be so sottish, such an enemy to thyself, as to prefer puddle-water, and that poisoned too and stolen, before pure living waters out of thy own well?" Note, If the dictates of reason may be heard, the laws of virtue will be obeyed. <div eID="gen13460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13461" type="x-p"/> II. "See the eye of God always upon thee and let his fear rule in thy heart," <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21">v. 21</reference>. Those that live in this sin promise themselves secresy (<hi type="italic">the eye of the adulterer waits for the twilight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.24.15">Job xxiv. 15</reference>); but to what purpose, when it cannot be hidden from God? For, 1. He sees it. <hi type="italic">The ways of man,</hi> all his motions, all his actions, are <hi type="italic">before the eyes of the Lord,</hi> all the workings of the heart and all the outgoings of the life, that which is done ever so secretly and disguised ever so artfully. God sees it in a true light, and knows it with all its causes, circumstances, and consequences. He does not cast an eye upon men's ways now and then, but they are always actually in his view and under his inspection; and darest thou sin against God in his sight, and do that wickedness under his eye which thou durst not do in the presence of a man like thyself? 2. He will call the sinner to an account for it; for he not only sees, but <hi type="italic">ponders all his goings,</hi> judges concerning them, as one that will shortly judge the sinner for them. Every action is <hi type="italic">weighed,</hi> and shall be <hi type="italic">brought into judgment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.14">Eccl. xii. 14</reference>), which is a good reason why we should <hi type="italic">ponder the path of our feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.26">ch. iv. 26</reference>), and so <hi type="italic">judge ourselves</hi> that we <hi type="italic">may not be judged.</hi> <div eID="gen13461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13462" type="x-p"/> III. "Foresee the certain ruin of those that go on still in their trespasses." Those that live in this sin promise themselves impunity, but they deceive themselves; their sin will find them out, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.22-Prov.5.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. The apostle gives the sense of these verses in a few words. <reference osisRef="Heb.13.4">Heb. xiii. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.</hi> 1. It is a sin which men with great difficulty shake off the power of. When the sinner is old and weak his lusts are strong and active, in <hi type="italic">calling to remembrance the days of his youth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.19">Ezek. xxiii. 19</reference>. Thus <hi type="italic">his own iniquities</hi> having <hi type="italic">seized the wicked himself</hi> by his own consent, and he having voluntarily surrendered himself a captive to them, he is <hi type="italic">held in the cords of his own sins,</hi> and such full possession they have gained of him that he cannot extricate himself, but in the <hi type="italic">greatness of his folly</hi> (and what greater folly could there be than to yield himself a servant to such cruel task-masters?) he shall <hi type="italic">go astray,</hi> and wander endlessly. Uncleanness is a sin from which, when once men have plunged themselves into it, they very hardly and very rarely recover themselves. 2. It is a sin which, if it be not forsaken, men cannot possibly escape the punishment of; it will unavoidably be their ruin. As their own iniquities do arrest them in the reproaches of conscience and present rebukes (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.19">Jer. vii. 19</reference>), so their own iniquities shall arrest them and bind them over to the judgments of God. There needs no prison, no chains; they shall be <hi type="italic">holden in the cords of their own sins,</hi> as the fallen angels, being incurably wicked, are thereby <hi type="italic">reserved in chains of darkness.</hi> The sinner, who, having been <hi type="italic">often reproved, hardens his neck,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">die at length without instruction.</hi> Having had general warnings sufficient given him already, he shall have no particular warnings, but he shall die without seeing his danger beforehand, shall die because he would not receive instruction, but <hi type="italic">in the greatness of his folly</hi> would <hi type="italic">go astray;</hi> and so shall his doom be, he shall never find the way home again. Those that are so foolish as to choose the way of sin are justly left of God to themselves to go in it till they come to that destruction which it leads to, which is a good reason why we should guard with watchfulness and resolution against the allurements of the sensual appetite.  <chapter eID="Prov.5"/> <div eID="gen13462" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen13465" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13464" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Cautions against Suretiship.</title> <div sID="gen13466" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, <hi type="italic">if</hi> thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou art snared with the words of thy mouth, thou art taken with the words of thy mouth. <hi type="super">3</hi> Do this now, my son, and deliver thyself, when thou art come into the hand of thy friend; go, humble thyself, and make sure thy friend. <hi type="super">4</hi> Give not sleep to thine eyes, nor slumber to thine eyelids. <hi type="super">5</hi> Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand <hi type="italic">of the hunter,</hi> and as a bird from the hand of the fowler. <div eID="gen13466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13467" type="x-p"/> It is the excellency of the word of God that it teaches us not only divine wisdom for another world, but human prudence for this world, that we may order our affairs with discretion; and this is one good rule, To avoid suretiship, because by it poverty and ruin are often brought into families, which take away that comfort in relations which he had recommended in the foregoing chapter. 1. We must look upon suretiship as a snare and decline it accordingly, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. "It is dangerous enough for a man to be bound for his friend, though it be one whose circumstances he is well acquainted with, and well assured of his sufficiency, but much more to <hi type="italic">strike the hands with a stranger,</hi> to become surety for one whom thou dost not know to be either able or honest." Or the stranger here with whom the hand is stricken is the creditor, "the usurer to whom thou art become bound, and yet as to thee he is a stranger, that is, thou owest him nothing, nor hast had any dealings with him. If thou hast rashly entered into such engagements, either wheedled into them or in hopes to have the same kindness done for thee another time, know that <hi type="italic">thou art snared with the words of thy mouth;</hi> it was easily done, with a word's speaking; it was but setting thy hand to a paper, a bond is soon sealed and delivered, and a recognizance entered into. But it will not be so easily got clear of; thou art <hi type="italic">in a snare</hi> more than thou art aware of." See how little reason we have to make light of tongue-sins; if by a word of our mouth we may become indebted to men, and lie open to their actions, by the words of our mouth we may become obnoxious to God's justice, and even so may be snared. It is false that words are but wind: they are often snares. 2. If we have been drawn into this snare, it will be our wisdom by all means, with all speed, to get out of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.3-Ps.6.5">v. 3-5</reference>. It sleeps for the present; we hear nothing of it. The debt is not demanded; the principal says, "Never fear, we will take care of it." But still the bond is in force, interest is running on, the creditor may come upon thee when he will and perhaps may be hasty and severe, the principal may prove either knavish or insolvent, and then thou must rob thy wife and children, and ruin thy family, to pay that which thou didst neither nor drink for. And therefore <hi type="italic">deliver thyself;</hi> rest not till either the creditor give up the bond or the principal give thee counter-security; when <hi type="italic">thou art come into the hand of thy friend,</hi> and he has advantage against thee, it is no time to threaten or give ill language (that will provoke and make ill worse), but <hi type="italic">humble thyself,</hi> beg and pray to be discharged, go down on thy knees to him, and give him all the fair words thou canst; engage thy friends to speak for thee; leave no stone unturned till thou hast agreed with thy adversary and compromised the matter, so that thy bond may not come against thee or thine. This is a care which may well break thy sleep, and let it do so till thou hast got through. "<hi type="italic">Give not sleep to thy eyes</hi> till thou hast <hi type="italic">delivered thyself.</hi> Strive and struggle to the utmost, and hasten with all speed, <hi type="italic">as a roe</hi> or a <hi type="italic">bird</hi> delivers herself out of this snare of <hi type="italic">the fowler</hi> or hunter. Delays are dangerous, and feeble efforts will not serve." See what care God, in his word, has taken to make men good husbands of their estates, and to teach them prudence in the management of them. <hi type="italic">Godliness</hi> has precepts, as well as promises, relating to <hi type="italic">the life that now is.</hi> <div eID="gen13467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13468" type="x-p"/> But how are we to understand this? We are not to think it is unlawful in any case to become surety, or bail, for another; it may be a piece of justice or charity; he that has friends may see cause in this instance to show himself friendly, and it may be no piece of imprudence. Paul became bound for Onesimus, <reference osisRef="Phlm.1.19">Philem. 19</reference>. We may help a young man into business that we know to be honest and diligent, and gain him credit by passing our word for him, and so do him a great kindness without any detriment to ourselves. But, 1. It is every man's wisdom to keep out of debt as much as may be, for it is an incumbrance upon him, entangles him in the world, puts him in danger of doing wrong or suffering wrong. The <hi type="italic">borrower is servant to the lender,</hi> and makes himself very much a slave to this world. Christians therefore, who are <hi type="italic">bought with a price,</hi> should not thus, without need, make themselves <hi type="italic">the servants of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.23">1 Cor. vii. 23</reference>. 2. It is great folly to entangle ourselves with necessitous people, and to become bound for their debts, that are ever and anon taking up money, and lading, as we say, out of one hole into another, for it is ten to one but, some time or other, it will come upon us. A man ought never to be bound as surety for more than he is both able and willing to pay, and can afford to pay without wronging his family, in case the principal fail, for he ought to look upon it as his own debt. <reference osisRef="Sir.8.13">Ecclesiasticus viii. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">Be not surety above thy power, for, if thou be surety, thou must take care to pay it.</hi> 3. It is a necessary piece of after-wit, if we have foolishly entangled ourselves, to get out of the snare as fast as we can, to lose no time, spare no pains, and stick at no submission to make ourselves safe and easy, and get our affairs into a good posture. It is better to humble ourselves for an accommodation than to ruin ourselves by our stiffness and haughtiness. <hi type="italic">Make sure thy friend</hi> by getting clear from thy engagements from him; for rash suretiship is as much the bane of friendship as that which is prudent is sometimes the bond of it. Let us take heed lest we any way make ourselves guilty of other men's sins against God (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">1 Tim. v. 22</reference>), for that is worse, and much more dangerous, than being bound for other men's debts; and, if we must be in all this care to get our debts to men forgiven, much more to get our peace made with God. "<hi type="italic">Humble thyself</hi> to him; <hi type="italic">make sure</hi> of Christ <hi type="italic">thy friend,</hi> to intercede for thee; pray earnestly that thy sins may be pardoned, and thou mayest be delivered from going down to the pit, and it shall not be in vain. <hi type="italic">Give not sleep to thy eyes nor slumber to thy eye lids,</hi> till this be done."

<div eID="gen13468" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Slothfulness Reproved.</title> <div sID="gen13469" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: <hi type="super">7</hi> Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, <hi type="super">8</hi> Provideth her meat in the summer, <hi type="italic">and</hi> gathereth her food in the harvest. <hi type="super">9</hi> How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? 10 <hi type="italic">Yet</hi> a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: <hi type="super">11</hi> So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man. <div eID="gen13469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13470" type="x-p"/> Solomon, in these verses, addresses himself to the sluggard who loves his ease, lives in idleness, minds no business, sticks to nothing, brings nothing to pass, and in a particular manner is careless in the business of religion. Slothfulness is as sure a way to poverty, though not so short a way, as rash suretiship. He speaks here to the sluggard, <div eID="gen13470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13471" type="x-p"/> I. By way of instruction, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.6-Ps.6.8">v. 6-8</reference>. He sends him to school, for sluggards must be schooled. He is to take him to school himself, for, if the scholar will take no pains, the master must take the more; the sluggard is not willing to come to school to him (dreaming scholars will never love wakeful teachers) and therefore he has found him out another school, as low as he can desire. Observe, <div eID="gen13471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13472" type="x-p"/> 1. The master he is sent to school to: <hi type="italic">Go to the ant, to the bee,</hi> so the LXX. Man is taught more than the beasts of the earth, and made wiser that the fowls of heaven, and yet is so degenerated that he may learn wisdom from the meanest insects and be shamed by them. When we observe the wonderful sagacities of the inferior creatures we must not only give glory to the God of nature, who has made them thus strangely, but receive instruction to ourselves; by spiritualizing common things, we may make the things of God both easy and ready to us, and converse with them daily. <div eID="gen13472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13473" type="x-p"/> 2. The application of mind that is required in order to learn of this master: <hi type="italic">Consider her ways.</hi> The sluggard is so because he does not consider; nor shall we ever learn to any purpose, either by the word or the works of God, unless we set ourselves to consider. Particularly, if we would imitate others in that which is good, we must consider their ways, diligently observe what they do, that we may do likewise, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.17">Phil. iii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen13473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13474" type="x-p"/> 3. The lesson that is to be learned. In general, learn wisdom, <hi type="italic">consider, and be wise;</hi> that is the thing we are to aim at in all our learning, not only to be knowing, but to be wise. In particular, learn to <hi type="italic">provide meat in summer;</hi> that is, (1.) We must prepare for hereafter, and not mind the present time only, not eat up all, and lay up nothing, but in gathering time treasure up for a spending time. Thus provident we must be in our worldly affairs, not with an anxious care, but with a prudent foresight; lay in for winter, for straits and wants that may happen, and for old age; much more in the affairs of our souls. We must provide meat and food, that which is substantial and will stand us in stead, and which we shall most need. In the enjoyment of the means of grace provide for the want of them, in life for death, in time for eternity; in the state of probation and preparation we must provide for the state of retribution. (2.) We must take pains, and labour in our business, yea, though we labour under inconveniences. Even <hi type="italic">in summer,</hi> when the weather is hot, the ant is busy in <hi type="italic">gathering food</hi> and laying it up, and does not indulge her ease, nor take her pleasure, as the grasshopper, that sings and sports in the summer and then perishes in the winter. The ants help one another; if one have a grain of corn too big for her to carry home, her neighbours will come in to her assistance. (3.) We must improve opportunities, we must gather when it is to be had, as the ant does in summer and harvest, in the proper time. It is our wisdom to improve the season while that favours us, because that may be done then which cannot be done at all, or not so well done, at another time. <hi type="italic">Walk while you have the light.</hi> <div eID="gen13474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13475" type="x-p"/> 4. The advantages which we have of learning this lesson above what the ant has, which will aggravate our slothfulness and neglect if we idle away our time. She has <hi type="italic">no guides, overseers,</hi> and <hi type="italic">rulers,</hi> but does it of herself, following the instinct of nature; the more shame for us who do not in like manner follow the dictates of our own reason and conscience, though besides them we have parents, masters, ministers, magistrates, to put us in mind of our duty, to check us for the neglect of it, to quicken us to it, to direct us in it, and to call us to an account about it. The greater helps we have for working out our salvation the more inexcusable shall we be if we neglect it. <div eID="gen13475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13476" type="x-p"/> II. By way of reproof, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.9-Ps.6.11">v. 9-11</reference>. In these verses, <div eID="gen13476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13477" type="x-p"/> 1. He expostulates with the sluggard, rebuking him and reasoning with him, calling him to his work, as a master does his servant that has over-slept himself: "<hi type="italic">How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?</hi> How long wouldst thou sleep if one would let thee alone? <hi type="italic">When wilt thou</hi> think it time to <hi type="italic">arise?</hi>" Sluggards should be roused with a <hi type="italic">How long?</hi> This is applicable, (1.) To those that are slothful in the way of work and duty, in the duties of their particular calling as men or their general calling as Christians. "<hi type="italic">How long wilt thou</hi> waste thy time, and <hi type="italic">when wilt thou</hi> be a better husband of it? <hi type="italic">How long wilt thou</hi> love thy ease, and <hi type="italic">when wilt thou</hi> learn to deny thyself, and to take pains? <hi type="italic">How long wilt thou</hi> bury thy talents, and <hi type="italic">when wilt thou</hi> begin to trade with them? <hi type="italic">How long wilt thou</hi> delay, and put off, and trifle away thy opportunities, as one regardless of hereafter; and <hi type="italic">when wilt thou</hi> stir up thyself to do what thou hast to do, which, if it be not done, will leave thee for ever undone?" (2.) To those that are secure in the way of sin and danger: "Hast thou not slept enough? Is it not far in the day? Does not thy Master call? Are not the Philistines upon thee? When then wilt thou arise?" <div eID="gen13477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13478" type="x-p"/> 2. He exposes the frivolous excuses he makes for himself, and shows how ridiculous he makes himself. When he is roused he stretched himself, and begs, as for alms, for more <hi type="italic">sleep,</hi> more <hi type="italic">slumber;</hi> he is well in his warm bed, and cannot endure to think of rising, especially of rising to work. But, observe, he promises himself and his master that he will desire but <hi type="italic">a little</hi> more <hi type="italic">sleep, a little</hi> more <hi type="italic">slumber,</hi> and then he will get up and go to his business. But herein he deceives himself; the more a slothful temper is indulged the more it prevails; let him sleep awhile, and slumber awhile, and still he is in the same tune; still he asks for <hi type="italic">a little</hi> more <hi type="italic">sleep, yet a little</hi> more; he never thinks he has enough, and yet, when he is called, pretends he will come presently. Thus men's great work is left undone by being put off yet a little longer, <hi type="italic">de die in diem—from day to day;</hi> and they are cheated of all their time by being cheated of the present moments. A little more sleep proves an everlasting sleep. <hi type="italic">Sleep on now, and take your rest.</hi> <div eID="gen13478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13479" type="x-p"/> 3. He gives him fair warning of the fatal consequences of his slothfulness, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.11">v. 11</reference>. (1.) <hi type="italic">Poverty and want</hi> will certainly come upon those that are slothful in their business. If men neglect their affairs, they not only will not go forward, but they will go backward. He that leaves his concerns at sixes and sevens will soon see them go to wreck and ruin, and bring his noble to nine-pence. Spiritual poverty comes upon those that are slothful in the service of God; those will want oil, when they should use it, that provide it not in their vessels. (2.) "It will come silently and insensibly, will grow upon thee, and come step by step, <hi type="italic">as one that travels,</hi> but will without fail come at last." <hi type="italic">It will leave thee as naked as if thou wert stripped by a highwayman;</hi> so bishop Patrick. (3.) "It will come irresistibly, <hi type="italic">like an armed man,</hi> whom thou canst not oppose nor make thy part good against."

<div eID="gen13479" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Seven Abominations.</title> <div sID="gen13480" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth. <hi type="super">13</hi> He winketh with his eyes, he speaketh with his feet, he teacheth with his fingers; <hi type="super">14</hi> Frowardness <hi type="italic">is</hi> in his heart, he deviseth mischief continually; he soweth discord. <hi type="super">15</hi> Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy. <hi type="super">16</hi> These six <hi type="italic">things</hi> doth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hate: yea, seven <hi type="italic">are</hi> an abomination unto him: <hi type="super">17</hi> A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood, <hi type="super">18</hi> An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief, <hi type="super">19</hi> A false witness <hi type="italic">that</hi> speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren. <div eID="gen13480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13481" type="x-p"/> Solomon here gives us, <div eID="gen13481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13482" type="x-p"/> I. The characters of one that is mischievous to man and dangerous to be dealt with. If the slothful are to be condemned, that do nothing, much more those that do ill, and contrive to do all the ill they can. It is a <hi type="italic">naughty person</hi> that is here spoken of, Heb. <hi type="italic">A man of Belial;</hi> I think it should have been so translated, because it is a term often used in scripture, and this is the explication of it. Observe, <div eID="gen13482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13483" type="x-p"/> 1. How a man of Belial is here described. He is <hi type="italic">a wicked man,</hi> that makes a trade of doing evil, especially with his tongue, for he <hi type="italic">walks</hi> and works his designs <hi type="italic">with a froward mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.12">v. 12</reference>), by lying and perverseness, and a direct opposition to God and man. He says and does every thing, (1.) Very artfully and with design. He has the subtlety of the serpent, and carries on his projects with a great deal of craft and management (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">with his eyes, with his feet, with his fingers.</hi> He expresses his malice <hi type="italic">when he dares not speak out</hi> (so some), or, rather, thus he carries on his plot; those about him, whom he makes use of as the tools of his wickedness, understand the ill meaning of a wink of his eye, a stamp of his feet, the least motion of his fingers. He gives orders for evil-doing, and yet would not be thought to do so, but has ways of concealing what he does, so that he may not be suspected. He is a close man, and upon the reserve; those only shall be let into the secret that would do any thing he would have them to do. He is a cunning man, and upon the trick; he has a language by himself, which an honest man is not acquainted with, nor desires to be. (2.) Very spitefully and with ill design. It is not so much ambition or covetousness that <hi type="italic">is in his heart,</hi> as downright <hi type="italic">frowardness,</hi> malice, and ill nature. He aims not so much to enrich and advance himself as to do an ill turn to those about him. He is <hi type="italic">continually devising</hi> one <hi type="italic">mischief</hi> or other, purely for mischief-sake—a man of Belial indeed, of the devil, resembling him not only in subtlety, but in malice. <div eID="gen13483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13484" type="x-p"/> 2. What his doom is (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">His calamity shall come</hi> and <hi type="italic">he shall be broken;</hi> he that devised mischief shall fall into mischief. His ruin shall come, (1.) Without warning. It shall come suddenly: <hi type="italic">Suddenly shall he be broken,</hi> to punish him for all the wicked arts he had to surprise people into his snares. (2.) Without relief. He shall be irreparably broken, and never able to piece again: <hi type="italic">He shall be broken without remedy.</hi> What relief can he expect that has disobliged all mankind? <hi type="italic">He shall come to his end and none shall help him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.45">Dan. xi. 45</reference>. <div eID="gen13484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13485" type="x-p"/> II. A catalogue of those things which are in a special manner odious to God, all which are generally to be found in those men of Belial whom he had described in the foregoing verses; and the last of them (which, being the seventh, seems especially to be intended, because he says they are six, yea, seven) is part of his character, that he <hi type="italic">sows discord.</hi> God hates sin; he hates every sin; he can never be reconciled to it; he hates nothing but sin. But there are some sins which he does in a special manner hate; and all those here mentioned are such as are injurious to our neighbour. It is an evidence of the good-will God bears to mankind that those sins are in a special manner provoking to him which are prejudicial to the comfort of human life and society. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> the men of Belial must expect their ruin to <hi type="italic">come suddenly,</hi> and <hi type="italic">without remedy,</hi> because their practices are such as the Lord hates and <hi type="italic">are an abomination to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.6.16">v. 16</reference>. Those things which God hates it is no thanks to us to hate in others, but we must hate them in ourselves. 1. Haughtiness, conceitedness of ourselves, and contempt of others—<hi type="italic">a proud look.</hi> There are seven things that God hates, and pride is the first, because it is at the bottom of much sin and gives rise to it. God sees the pride in the heart and hates it there; but, when it prevails to that degree that the show of men's countenance witnesses against them that they overvalue themselves and undervalue all about them, this is in a special manner hateful to him, for then pride is proud of itself and sets shame at defiance. 2. Falsehood, and fraud, and dissimulation. Next to a <hi type="italic">proud look</hi> nothing is more an abomination to God than <hi type="italic">a lying tongue;</hi> nothing more sacred than truth, nor more necessary to conversation than speaking truth. God and all good men hate and abhor lying. 3. Cruelty and blood-thirstiness. The devil was, from the beginning, a liar and a murderer (<reference osisRef="John.8.44">John viii. 44</reference>), and therefore, as <hi type="italic">a lying tongue,</hi> so <hi type="italic">hands that shed innocent blood</hi> are hateful to God, because they have in them the devil's image and do him service. 4.
