Subtlety in the contrivance of sin, wisdom to do evil, <hi type="italic">a heart that</hi> designs and a head that <hi type="italic">devises wicked imaginations,</hi> that is acquainted with the depths of Satan and knows how to carry on a covetous, envious, revengeful plot, most effectually. The more there is of craft and management in sin the more it is an abomination to God. 5. Vigour and diligence in the prosecution of sin—<hi type="italic">feet that are swift in running to mischief,</hi> as if they were afraid of losing time or were impatient of delay in a thing they are so greedy of. The policy and vigilance, the eagerness and industry, of sinners, in their sinful pursuits, may shame us who go about that which is good so awkwardly and so coldly. 6. False-witness bearing, which is one of the greatest mischiefs that the wicked imagination can devise, and against which there is least fence. There cannot be a greater affront to God (to whom in an oath appeal is made) nor a greater injury to our neighbour (all whose interests in this world, even the dearest, lie open to an attack of this kind) than knowingly to give in a false testimony. There are seven things which God hates, and lying involves two of them; he hates it, and doubly hates it. 7. Making mischief between relations and neighbours, and using all wicked means possible, not only to alienate their affections one from another, but to irritate their passions one against another. The God of love and peace hates <hi type="italic">him that sows discord among brethren,</hi> for he delights in concord. Those that by tale-bearing and slandering, by carrying ill-natured stories, aggravating every thing that is said and done, and suggesting jealousies and evil surmises, blow the coals of contention, are but preparing for themselves a fire of the same nature.

<div eID="gen13485" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Parental Cautions; Cautions against Impurity.</title> <div sID="gen13486" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> My son, keep thy father's commandment, and forsake not the law of thy mother: <hi type="super">21</hi> Bind them continually upon thine heart, <hi type="italic">and</hi> tie them about thy neck. <hi type="super">22</hi> When thou goest, it shall lead thee; when thou sleepest, it shall keep thee; and <hi type="italic">when</hi> thou awakest, it shall talk with thee. 23 For the commandment <hi type="italic">is</hi> a lamp; and the law <hi type="italic">is</hi> light; and reproofs of instruction <hi type="italic">are</hi> the way of life: <hi type="super">24</hi> To keep thee from the evil woman, from the flattery of the tongue of a strange woman. <hi type="super">25</hi> Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids. 26 For by means of a whorish woman <hi type="italic">a man is brought</hi> to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life. <hi type="super">27</hi> Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned? <hi type="super">28</hi> Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned? <hi type="super">29</hi> So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife; whosoever toucheth her shall not be innocent. 30 <hi type="italic">Men</hi> do not despise a thief, if he steal to satisfy his soul when he is hungry; <hi type="super">31</hi> But <hi type="italic">if</hi> he be found, he shall restore sevenfold; he shall give all the substance of his house. 32 <hi type="italic">But</hi> whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding: he <hi type="italic">that</hi> doeth it destroyeth his own soul. 33 A wound and dishonour shall he get; and his reproach shall not be wiped away. <hi type="super">34</hi> For jealousy <hi type="italic">is</hi> the rage of a man: therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance. 35 He will not regard any ransom; neither will he rest content, though thou givest many gifts. <div eID="gen13486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13487" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general exhortation faithfully to adhere to the word of God and to take it for our guide in all our actions. <div eID="gen13487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13488" type="x-p"/> 1. We must look upon the word of God both as a light (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.23">v. 23</reference>) and as a law, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.20">v. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.23">23</reference>. (1.) By its arguments it is a light, which our understandings must subscribe to; it <hi type="italic">is a lamp</hi> to our eyes for discovery, and so to our feet for direction. The word of God reveals to us truths of eternal certainty, and is built upon the highest reason. Scripture-light is the sure light. (2.) By its authority it is a law, which our wills must submit to. As never such a light shone out of the schools of the philosophers, so never such a law issued from the throne of any prince, so well framed, and so binding. It is such a law as is a lamp and a light, for it carries with it the evidence of its own goodness. <div eID="gen13488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13489" type="x-p"/> 2. We must receive it as <hi type="italic">our father's commandment</hi> and <hi type="italic">the law of our mother,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.6.20">v. 20</reference>. It is God's commandment and his law. But, (1.) Our parents directed us to it, put it into our hands, trained us up in the knowledge and observance of it, its original and obligation being most sacred. We believe indeed, not for their saying, for we have tried it ourselves and find it to be of God; but we were beholden to them for recommending it to us, and see all the reason in the world to <hi type="italic">continue in the things we have learned, knowing of whom we have learned them.</hi> (2.) The cautions, counsels, and commands which our parents gave us agree with the word of God, and therefore we must hold them fast. Children, when they are grown up, must remember <hi type="italic">the law of</hi> a good <hi type="italic">mother,</hi> as well as the <hi type="italic">commandment</hi> of a good <hi type="italic">father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Sir.3.2">Ecclesiasticus iii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord has given the father honour over the children and has confirmed the authority of the mother over the sons.</hi> <div eID="gen13489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13490" type="x-p"/> 3. We must retain the word of God and the good instructions which our parents gave us out of it. (1.) We must never cast them off, never think it a mighty achievement (as some do) to get clear of the restraints of a good education: "<hi type="italic">Keep thy father's commandment,</hi> keep it still, and never forsake it." (2.) We must never lay them by, no, not for a time (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Bind them continually,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">upon thy hand</hi> (as Moses had directed, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.8">Deut. vi. 8</reference>) but <hi type="italic">upon thy heart.</hi> Phylacteries upon the hand were of no value at all, any further than they occasioned pious thoughts and affections in the heart. There the word must be written, there it must be hid, and laid close to the conscience. <hi type="italic">Tie them about thy neck,</hi> as an ornament, a bracelet, or gold chain,—<hi type="italic">about thy throat</hi> (so the word is); let them be a guard upon that pass; tie them about thy throat, that no forbidden fruit may be suffered to go in nor any evil word suffered to go out through the throat; and thus a great deal of sin would be prevented. Let the word of God be always ready to us, and let us feel the impressions of it, as of that which is bound upon our hearts and about our necks. <div eID="gen13490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13491" type="x-p"/> 4. We must make use of the word of God and of the benefit that is designed us by it. If we bind it continually upon our hearts, (1.) It will be our guide, and we must follow its direction. "<hi type="italic">When thou goest, it shall lead thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.22">v. 22</reference>); it shall lead thee into, and lead thee in, the good and right way, shall lead thee from, and lead thee out of, every sinful dangerous path. It will say unto thee, when thou art ready to turn aside, <hi type="italic">This is the way; walk in it.</hi> It will be that to thee that the pillar of cloud and fire was to Israel in the wilderness. Be led by that, let it be thy rule, and then thou shalt be led by the Spirit; he will be thy monitor and support." (2.) It will be our guard, and we must put ourselves under the protection of it: "<hi type="italic">When thou sleepest,</hi> and liest exposed to the malignant powers of darkness, <hi type="italic">it shall keep thee;</hi> thou shalt be safe, and shalt think thyself so." If we govern ourselves by the precepts of the word all day, and make conscience of the duty God has commanded to us, we may shelter ourselves under the promises of the word at night, and take the comfort of the deliverances God does and will command for us. (3.) It will be our companion, and we must converse with it: "<hi type="italic">When thou awakest</hi> in the night, and knowest not how to pass away thy waking minutes, if thou pleasest, <hi type="italic">it shall talk with thee,</hi> and entertain thee with pleasant meditations in the night-watch; <hi type="italic">when thou awakest</hi> in the morning, and art contriving the work of the day, <hi type="italic">it shall talk with thee</hi> about it, and help thee to contrive for the best," <reference osisRef="Ps.1.2">Ps. i. 2</reference>. The word of God has something to say to us upon all occasions, if we would but enter into discourse with it, would ask it what it has to say, and give it the hearing. And it would contribute to our close and comfortable walking with God all day if we would begin with him in the morning and let his word be the subject of our first thoughts. <hi type="italic">When I awake I am still with thee;</hi> we are so if the word be still with us. (4.) It will be our life; for, as the law <hi type="italic">is a lamp</hi> and <hi type="italic">a light</hi> for the present, so the <hi type="italic">reproofs of instruction are the way of life.</hi> Those reproofs of the word which not only show us our faults, but instruct us how to do better, are the way that leads to life, eternal life. Let not faithful reproofs therefore, which have such a direct tendency to make us happy, ever make us uneasy. <div eID="gen13491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13492" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a particular caution against the sin of uncleanness. <div eID="gen13492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13493" type="x-p"/> 1. When we consider how much this iniquity abounds, how heinous it is in its own nature, of what pernicious consequence it is, and how certainly destructive to all the seeds of the spiritual life in the soul, we shall not wonder that the cautions against it are so often repeated and so largely inculcated. (1.) One great kindness God designed men, in giving them his law, was to preserve them from this sin, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.24">v. 24</reference>. "The reproofs of instruction are therefore <hi type="italic">the way of life</hi> to thee, because they are designed <hi type="italic">to keep thee from the evil woman,</hi> who will be certain death to thee, from being enticed by <hi type="italic">the flattery of the tongue of a strange woman,</hi> who pretends to love thee, but intends to ruin thee." Those that will be wrought upon by flattery make themselves a very easy prey to the tempter; and those who would avoid that snare must take well-instructed reproofs as great kindnesses and be thankful to those that will deal faithfully with them, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.5-Prov.27.6">Prov. xxvii. 5, 6</reference>. (2.) The greatest kindness we can do ourselves is to keep at a distance from this sin, and to look upon it with the utmost dread and detestation (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lust not after her beauty,</hi> no, not <hi type="italic">in thy heart,</hi> for, if thou dost, thou hast <hi type="italic">there</hi> already <hi type="italic">committed adultery with her.</hi> Talk not of the charms in her face, neither be thou smitten with her amorous glances; they are all snares and nets; <hi type="italic">let her</hi> not <hi type="italic">take thee with her eye-lids.</hi> Her looks are arrows and fiery darts; they wound, they kill, in another sense than what lovers mean; they call it a pleasing captivity, but it is a destroying one, it is worse than Egyptian slavery." <div eID="gen13493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13494" type="x-p"/> 2. Divers arguments Solomon here urges to enforce this caution against the sin of whoredom. <div eID="gen13494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13495" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is a sin that impoverishes men, wastes their estates, and reduces them to beggary (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">By means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread;</hi> many a man has been so, who has purchased the ruin of his body and soul at the expense of his wealth. The prodigal son spent his living on harlots, so that he brought himself to be fellow-commoner with the swine. And that poverty must needs lie heavily which men bring themselves into by their own folly, <reference osisRef="Job.31.12">Job xxxi. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen13495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13496" type="x-p"/> (2.) It threatens death; it kills men: <hi type="italic">The adulteress will hunt for the precious life,</hi> perhaps designedly, as Delilah for Samson's, at least, eventually, the sin strikes at the life. Adultery was punished by the law of Moses as a capital crime. <hi type="italic">The adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death.</hi> Every one knew this. Those therefore who, for the gratifying of a base lust, would lay themselves open to the law, could be reckoned no better than self-murderers. <div eID="gen13496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13497" type="x-p"/> (3.) It brings guilt upon the conscience and debauches that. He that <hi type="italic">touches his neighbour's wife,</hi> with an immodest touch, cannot <hi type="italic">be innocent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.6.29">v. 29</reference>. [1.] He is in imminent danger of adultery, as he that <hi type="italic">takes fire in his bosom,</hi> or <hi type="italic">goes upon hot coals,</hi> is in danger of being <hi type="italic">burnt.</hi> The way of this sin is down-hill, and those that venture upon the temptations to it hardly escape the sin itself. The fly fools away her life by playing the wanton with the flames. It is a deep pit, which it is madness to venture upon the brink of. He that keeps company with those of ill fame, that goes in with them, and touches them, cannot long preserve his innocency; he thrusts himself into temptation and so throws himself out of God's protection. [2.] He that commits adultery is in the high road to destruction. The bold presumptuous sinner says, "I may venture upon the sin and yet escape the punishment; I shall have peace though I go on." He might as well say, I will <hi type="italic">take fire into my bosom and not burn my clothes,</hi> or I will <hi type="italic">go upon hot coals and not burn my feet. He that goes into his neighbour's wife,</hi> however he holds himself, God will not hold him guiltless. The fire of lust kindles the fire of hell. <div eID="gen13497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13498" type="x-p"/> (4.) It ruins the reputation and entails perpetual infamy upon that. It is a much more scandalous sin than stealing is, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.30-Ps.6.33">v. 30-33</reference>. Perhaps it is not so in the account of men, at least not in our day. A thief is sent to the stocks, to the gaol, to Bridewell, to the gallows, while the vile adulterer goes unpunished, nay, with many, unblemished; he dares boast of his villanies, and they are made but a jest of. But, in the account of God and his law, adultery was much the more enormous crime; and, if God is the fountain of honour, his word must be the standard of it. [1.] As for the sin of stealing, if a man were brought to it by extreme necessity, if he stole meat for the <hi type="italic">satisfying of his soul when he was hungry,</hi> though that will not excuse him from guilt, yet it is such an extenuation of his crime that <hi type="italic">men do not despise</hi> him, do not expose him to ignominy, but pity him. Hunger will break through stone-walls, and blame will be laid upon those that brought him to poverty, or that did not relieve him. Nay, though he have not that to say in his excuse, <hi type="italic">if he be found</hi> stealing, and the evidence be ever so plain upon him, yet he shall only make restitution <hi type="italic">seven-fold.</hi> The law of Moses appointed that he who stole a sheep should restore four-fold, and an ox five-fold (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.1">Exod. xxii. 1</reference>); accordingly David adjudged, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.6">2 Sam. xii. 6</reference>. But we may suppose in those cases concerning which the law had not made provision the judges afterwards settled the penalties in proportion to the crimes, according to the equity of the law. Now, if he that stole an ox out of a man's field must restore five-fold, it was reasonable that he that stole a man's goods out of his house should <hi type="italic">restore seven-fold;</hi> for there was no law to put him to death, as with us, for burglary and robbery on the highway, and of this worst kind of theft Solomon here speaks; the greatest punishment was that a man might be forced to <hi type="italic">give all the substance of his house</hi> to satisfy the law and his blood was not attainted. But, [2.] Committing adultery is a more heinous crime; Job calls it so, and <hi type="italic">an iniquity to be punished by the judge,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.11">Job xxxi. 11</reference>. When Nathan would convict David of the evil of his adultery he did it by a parable concerning the most aggravated theft, which, in David's judgment, deserved to be punished with death (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.5">2 Sam. xii. 5</reference>), and then showed him that his sin was <hi type="italic">more exceedingly sinful</hi> than that. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is a greater reproach to a man's reason, for he cannot excuse it, as a thief may, by saying that it was to satisfy his hunger, but must own that it was to gratify a brutish lust which would break the hedge of God's law, not for want, but for wantonness. Therefore <hi type="italic">whoso commits adultery with a woman lacks understanding,</hi> and deserves to be stigmatized as an arrant fool. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is more severely punished by the law of God. A thief suffered only a pecuniary mulct, but the adulterer suffered death. The thief <hi type="italic">steals to satisfy his soul,</hi> but the adulterer <hi type="italic">destroys his own soul,</hi> and falls an unpitied sacrifice to the justice both of God and man. "Sinner, thou hast destroyed thyself." This may be applied to the spiritual and eternal death which is the consequence of sin; <hi type="italic">he that does it</hi> wounds his conscience, corrupts his rational power, extinguishes all the sparks of the spiritual life, and exposes himself to the wrath of God for ever, and thus <hi type="italic">destroys his own soul. Thirdly,</hi> The infamy of it is indelible, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.33">v. 33</reference>. It will be <hi type="italic">a wound</hi> to his good name, a <hi type="italic">dishonour</hi> to his family, and, though the guilt of it may be done away by repentance, the <hi type="italic">reproach</hi> of it never will, but will stick to his memory when he is gone. David's sin in the matter of Uriah was not only a perpetual blemish upon his own character, but gave occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme his name too. <div eID="gen13498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13499" type="x-p"/> (5.) It exposes the adulterer to the rage of the jealous husband, whose honour he puts such an affront upon, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.34-Ps.6.35">v. 34, 35</reference>. He that touches his neighbour's wife, and is familiar with her, gives him occasion for jealousy, much more he that debauches her, which, if kept ever so secret, might then be <hi type="italic">discovered by the waters of jealousy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.5.12">Num. v. 12</reference>. "When discovered, thou hadst better meet a bear robbed of her whelps than the injured husband, who, in the case of adultery, will be as severe an avenger of his own honour as, in the case of manslaughter, of his brother's blood. If thou art not afraid of the wrath of God, yet be afraid of the <hi type="italic">rage of a man.</hi> Such jealousy is; it is <hi type="italic">strong as death</hi> and <hi type="italic">cruel as the grave.</hi> In the <hi type="italic">day of vengeance,</hi> when the adulterer comes to be tried for his life, the prosecutor will not spare any pains or cost in the prosecution, will not relent towards thee, as he would perhaps towards one that had robbed him. He will not accept of any commutation, any composition; <hi type="italic">he will not regard any ransom.</hi> Though thou offer to bribe him, and <hi type="italic">give him many gifts</hi> to pacify him, he <hi type="italic">will not rest content</hi> with any thing less than the execution of the law. Thou must be <hi type="italic">stoned to death.</hi> If <hi type="italic">a man would give all the substance of his house,</hi> it would atone for a theft (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.31">v. 31</reference>), but not for adultery; in that case it would utterly be contemned. <hi type="italic">Stand in awe therefore, and sin not;</hi> expose not thyself to all this misery for a moment's sordid pleasure, which will be bitterness in the end."  <chapter eID="Prov.6"/> <div eID="gen13499" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen13502" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13501" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Word of God Recommended.</title> <div sID="gen13503" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My son, keep my words, and lay up my commandments with thee. <hi type="super">2</hi> Keep my commandments, and live; and my law as the apple of thine eye. <hi type="super">3</hi> Bind them upon thy fingers, write them upon the table of thine heart. <hi type="super">4</hi> Say unto wisdom, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my sister; and call understanding <hi type="italic">thy</hi> kinswoman: <hi type="super">5</hi> That they may keep thee from the strange woman, from the stranger <hi type="italic">which</hi> flattereth with her words. <div eID="gen13503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13504" type="x-p"/> These verses are an introduction to his warning against fleshly lusts, much the same with that, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.20">ch. vi. 20</reference>, &c., and ending (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.5">v. 5</reference>) as that did (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.24">v. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">To keep thee from the strange woman;</hi> that is it he aims at; only there he had said, <hi type="italic">Keep thy father's commandment,</hi> here (which comes all to one), <hi type="italic">Keep my commandments,</hi> for he speaks to us as unto sons. He speaks in God's name; for it is God's <hi type="italic">commandments</hi> that we are to <hi type="italic">keep,</hi> his <hi type="italic">words,</hi> his <hi type="italic">law.</hi> The word of God must be to us, 1. As that which we are most careful of. We must keep it as our treasure; we must <hi type="italic">lay up God's</hi> commandments with us, lay them up safely, that we may not be robbed of them by the wicked one, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.1">v. 1</reference>. We must keep it as our life: <hi type="italic">Keep my commandments and live</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.2">v. 2</reference>), not only, "Keep them, and you shall live;" but, "Keep them as you would your life, as those that cannot live without them." It would be death to a good man to be deprived of the word of God, for by it he lives, and not <hi type="italic">by bread alone.</hi> 2. As that which we are most tender of: Keep <hi type="italic">my law as the apple of thy eye.</hi> A little thing offends the eye, and therefore nature has so well guarded it. We pray, with David, that God would keep us as the apple of his eye (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Ps. xvii. 8</reference>), that our lives and comforts may be precious in his sight; and they shall be so (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.8">Zech. ii. 8</reference>) if we be in like manner tender of his law and afraid of the least violation of it. Those who reproach strict and circumspect walking, as needless preciseness, consider not that the law is to be kept as the apple of the eye, for indeed it is the <hi type="italic">apple of our eye;</hi> the law is light; the law in the heart is the eye of the soul. 3. As that which we are proud of and would be ever mindful of (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Bind them upon thy fingers;</hi> let them be precious to thee; look upon them as an ornament, as a diamond-ring, as the <hi type="italic">signet on thy right hand;</hi> wear them continually as thy wedding-ring, the badge of thy espousals to God. Look upon the word of God as putting an honour upon thee, as an ensign of thy dignity. <hi type="italic">Bind them on thy fingers,</hi> that they may be constant memorandums to thee of thy duty, that thou mayest have them always in view, as that which is <hi type="italic">graven upon the palms of thy hands.</hi>" 4. As that which we are fond of and are ever thinking of: <hi type="italic">Write them upon the table of thy heart,</hi> as the names of the friends we dearly love, we say, are written in our hearts. <hi type="italic">let the word of God dwell richly in us,</hi> and be written there where it will be always at hand to be read. Where sin was written (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.1">Jer. xvii. 1</reference>) let the word of God be written. It is the matter of a promise (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">Heb. viii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will write my law in their hearts</hi>), which makes the precept practicable and easy. 5. As that which we are intimately acquainted and conversant with (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister,</hi> whom I dearly love and take delight in; <hi type="italic">and call understanding thy kinswoman,</hi> to whom thou art nearly allied, and for whom thou hast a pure affection; call her thy friend, whom thou courtest." We must make the word of God familiar to us, consult it, and consult its honour, and take a pleasure in conversing with it. 6. As that which we make use of for our defence and armour, to keep us <hi type="italic">from the strange woman,</hi> from sin, that flattering but destroying thing, that adulteress; particularly from the sin of uncleanness, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.5">v. 5</reference>. Let the word of God confirm our dread of that sin and our resolutions against it; let it discover to us its fallacies and suggest to us answers to all its flatteries.

<div eID="gen13504" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Foolish Young Man; Enticements of the Adulteress.</title> <div sID="gen13505" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> For at the window of my house I looked through my casement, <hi type="super">7</hi> And beheld among the simple ones, I discerned among the youths, a young man void of understanding, <hi type="super">8</hi> Passing through the street near her corner; and he went the way to her house, <hi type="super">9</hi> In the twilight, in the evening, in the black and dark night: <hi type="super">10</hi> And, behold, there met him a woman <hi type="italic">with</hi> the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart. 11 (She <hi type="italic">is</hi> loud and stubborn; her feet abide not in her house: 12 Now <hi type="italic">is she</hi> without, now in the streets, and lieth in wait at every corner.) <hi type="super">13</hi> So she caught him, and kissed him, <hi type="italic">and</hi> with an impudent face said unto him, <hi type="super">14</hi> <hi type="italic">I have</hi> peace offerings with me; this day have I paid my vows. 15 Therefore came I forth to meet thee, diligently to seek thy face, and I have found thee. <hi type="super">16</hi> I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved <hi type="italic">works,</hi> with fine linen of Egypt. <hi type="super">17</hi> I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. <hi type="super">18</hi> Come, let us take our fill of love until the morning: let us solace ourselves with loves. <hi type="super">19</hi> For the goodman <hi type="italic">is</hi> not at home, he is gone a long journey: <hi type="super">20</hi> He hath taken a bag of money with him, <hi type="italic">and</hi> will come home at the day appointed. <hi type="super">21</hi> With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him. 22 He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks; <hi type="super">23</hi> Till a dart strike through his liver; as a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it <hi type="italic">is</hi> for his life. <div eID="gen13505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13506" type="x-p"/> Solomon here, to enforce the caution he had given against the sin of whoredom, tells a story of a young man that was ruined to all intents and purposes by the enticements of an adulterous woman. Such a story as this would serve the lewd profane poets of our age to make a play of, and the harlot with them would be a heroine; nothing would be so entertaining to the audience, nor give them so much diversion, as her arts of beguiling the young gentleman and drawing in the country squire; her conquests would be celebrated as the triumphs of wit and love, and the comedy would conclude very pleasantly; and every young man that saw it acted would covet to be so picked up. Thus <hi type="italic">fools make a mock at sin.</hi> But Solomon here relates it, and all wise and good men read it, as a very melancholy story. The impudence of the adulterous woman is very justly looked upon, by all that have any sparks of virtue in them, with the highest indignation, and the easiness of the young man with the tenderest compassion; and the story concludes with sad reflections, enough to make all that read and hear it afraid of the snares of fleshly lusts and careful to keep at the utmost distance from them. It is supposed to be a parable, or imagined case, but I doubt it was too true, and, which is worse, that notwithstanding the warning it gives of the fatal consequences of such wicked courses it is still too often true, and the agents for hell are still playing the same game and with similar success. <div eID="gen13506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13507" type="x-p"/> Solomon was a magistrate, and, as such, inspected the manners of his subjects, looked often through his casement, that he might see with his own eyes, and made remarks upon those who little thought his eye was upon them, that he might know the better how to make the sword he bore a terror to evil-doers. But here he writes as a minister, a prophet, who is by office a watchman, to give warning of the approach of the enemies, and especially where they lie in ambush, that we may not be ignorant of Satan's devices, but may know where to double our guard. This Solomon does here, where we may observe the account he gives, <div eID="gen13507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13508" type="x-p"/> I. Of the person tempted, and how he laid himself open to the temptation, and therefore must thank himself if it end in his destruction. 1. He was a <hi type="italic">young man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.7.7">v. 7</reference>. Fleshly lusts are called <hi type="italic">youthful lusts</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22">2 Tim. ii. 22</reference>), not to extenuate them as tricks of youth, and therefore excusable, but rather to aggravate them, as robbing God of the first and best of our time, and, by debauching the mind when it is tender, laying a foundation for a bad life ever after, and to intimate that young people ought in a special manner to fortify their resolutions against this sin. 2. He was a young man <hi type="italic">void of understanding,</hi> that went abroad into the world, not principled as he ought to have been with wisdom and the fear of God, and so ventured to sea without ballast, without pilot, cord, or compass; he knew not how to depart from evil, which is the best understanding, <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job xxviii. 28</reference>. Those become an easy prey to Satan who, when they have arrived to the stature of men, have scarcely the understanding of children. 3. He kept bad company. He was a <hi type="italic">young man among the youths,</hi> a silly young man <hi type="italic">among the simple</hi> ones. If, being conscious of his own weakness, he had associated with those that were older and wiser than himself, there would have been hopes of him. Christ, at twelve years old, conversed with the doctors, to set young people an example of this. But, if those that are simple choose such for their companions as are like themselves, simple they will still be, and hardened in their simplicity. 4. He was sauntering, and had nothing to do, but <hi type="italic">passed through the street</hi> as one that knew not how to dispose of himself. One of the sins of filthy Sodom was <hi type="italic">abundance of idleness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.49">Ezek. xvi. 49</reference>. He went in a starched stately manner, so (it is said) the word signifies. He appeared to be a nice formal fop, the top of whose accomplishments was to dress well and walk with a good air; fit game for that bird of prey to fly at. 5. He was a night-walker, that hated and scorned the business that is to be done by day-light, from which the evening calls men in to their repose; and, having fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, he begins to move <hi type="italic">in the twilight in the evening,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.7.9">v. 9</reference>. And he chooses <hi type="italic">the black and dark night</hi> as fittest for his purpose, not the moonlight nights, when he might be discovered. 6. He steered his course towards the house of one that he thought would entertain him, and that he might be merry with; he went <hi type="italic">near her corner,</hi> the <hi type="italic">way to her house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.8">v. 8</reference>), contrary to Solomon's advice (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.8">ch. v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Come not night the door of her house.</hi> Perhaps he did not know it was the way to an infamous house, but, however, it was a way that he had no business in; and when we have nothing to do the devil will quickly find us something to do. We must take heed, not only of idle days, but of idle evenings, lest they prove inlets to temptation. <div eID="gen13508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13509" type="x-p"/> II. Of the person tempting, not a common prostitute, for she was a married wife (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.19">v. 19</reference>), and, for aught that appears, lived in reputation among her neighbours, not suspected of any such wickedness, and yet, in the <hi type="italic">twilight of the evening,</hi> when her husband was abroad, abominably impudent. She is here described, 1. By her dress. She had the <hi type="italic">attire of a harlot</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.10">v. 10</reference>), gaudy and flaunting, to set her off as a beauty; perhaps she was painted as Jezebel, and went with her neck and breasts bare, loose, and <hi type="italic">en deshabille.</hi> The purity of the heart will show itself in the modesty of the dress, which <hi type="italic">becomes women professing godliness.</hi> 2. By her craft and management. She is <hi type="italic">subtle of heart,</hi> mistress of all the arts of wheedling, and knowing how by all her caresses to serve her own base purposes. 3. By her temper and carriage. <hi type="italic">She is loud and stubborn,</hi> talkative and self-willed, noisy and troublesome, wilful and headstrong, all tongue, and will have her saying, right or wrong, impatient of check and control, and cannot bear to be counselled, much less reproved, by husband or parents, ministers or friends. She is a <hi type="italic">daughter of Belial,</hi> that will endure no yoke. 4. By her place, not her own house; she hates the confinement and employment of that; her <hi type="italic">feet abide not there</hi> any longer than needs must. She is all for gadding abroad, changing place and company. <hi type="italic">Now is she without</hi> in the country, under pretence of taking the air, now <hi type="italic">in the streets</hi> of the city, under pretence of seeing how the market goes. She is here, and there, and every where but where she should be. She <hi type="italic">lies in wait at every corner,</hi> to pick up such as she can make a prey of. Virtue is a penance to those to whom home is a prison. <div eID="gen13509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13510" type="x-p"/> III. Of the temptation itself and the management of it. She met the young spark. Perhaps she knew him; however she knew by his fashions that he was such a one as she wished for; so she <hi type="italic">caught him about</hi> the neck and <hi type="italic">kissed</hi> him, contrary to all the rules of modesty (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.13">v. 13</reference>), and waited not for his compliments or courtship, but <hi type="italic">with an impudent face</hi> invited him not only to <hi type="italic">her house,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">her bed.</hi> <div eID="gen13510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13511" type="x-p"/> 1. She courted him to sup with her (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.14-Prov.7.15">v. 14, 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have peace-offerings with me.</hi> Hereby she gives him to understand, (1.) Her prosperity, that she was compassed about with so many blessings that she had occasion to offer peace-offerings, in token of joy and thankfulness; she was before-hand in the world, so that he needed not fear having his pocket picked. (2.) Her profession of piety. She had been to-day at the temple, and was as well respected there as any that worshipped in the courts of the Lord. She had paid her vows, and, as she thought, made all even with God Almighty, and therefore might venture upon a new score of sins. Note, The external performances of religion, if they do not harden men against sin, harden them in it, and embolden carnal hearts to venture upon it, in hopes that when they come to count and discount with God he will be found as much in debt to them for their peace-offerings and their vows as they to him for their sins. But it is sad that a show of piety should become the shelter of iniquity (which really doubles the shame of it, and makes it more exceedingly sinful) and that men should baffle their consciences with those very things that should startle them. The Pharisees made long prayers, that they might the more plausibly carry on their covetous and mischievous provisions. The greatest part of the flesh of the peace-offerings was by the law returned back to the offerers, to feast upon with their friends, which (if they were peace-offerings of thanksgiving) was to be all eaten <hi type="italic">the same day</hi> and <hi type="italic">none of it left until the morning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.7.15">Lev. vii. 15</reference>. This law of charity and generosity is abused to be a colour for gluttony and excess: "Come," says she, "come home with me, for I have good cheer enough, and only want good company to help me off with it." It was a pity that the peace-offerings should thus become, in a bad sense, sin-offerings, and that what was designed for the honour of God should become the food and fuel of a base lust. But this is not all. (4.) To strengthen the temptation, [1.] She pretends to have a very great affection for him above any man: "<hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because I have a good supper upon the table, <hi type="italic">I came forth to meet thee,</hi> for no friend in the world shall be so welcome to it as thou shalt, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.15">v. 15</reference>. Thou art he whom I came on purpose to seek, to <hi type="italic">seek diligently,</hi> came myself, and would not send a servant." Surely he cannot deny her his company when she put such a value upon it, and would take all this pains to obtain the favour of it. Sinners take pains to do mischief, and are as the roaring lion himself; they <hi type="italic">go about seeking to devour,</hi> and yet pretend they are seeking to oblige. [2.] She would have it thought that Providence itself countenanced her choice of him for her companion; for how quickly had she found him whom she sought! <div eID="gen13511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13512" type="x-p"/> 2. She courted him to lie with her. They will sit down to eat and drink, and then rise up to play, to play the wanton, and there is a bed ready for them, where he shall find that which will be in all respects agreeable to him. To please his eye, it is <hi type="italic">decked with coverings of tapestry</hi> and <hi type="italic">carved works,</hi> exquisitely fine; he never saw the like. To please his touch, the sheets are not of home-spun cloth; they are far-fetched and dear bought; they are of <hi type="italic">fine linen of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.7.16">v. 16</reference>. To gratify his smell, it is <hi type="italic">perfumed</hi> with the sweetest scents, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.17">v. 17</reference>. Come, therefore, and <hi type="italic">let us take our fill of love,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.7.18">v. 18</reference>. Of <hi type="italic">love,</hi> does she say? Of <hi type="italic">lust</hi> she means, brutish lust; but it is a pity that the name of love should be thus abused. True love is from heaven; this is from hell. How can those pretend to solace themselves and love one another who are really ruining themselves and one another? <div eID="gen13512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13513" type="x-p"/> 3. She anticipated the objection which he might make of the danger of it. Is she not another man's wife, and what if her husband should catch them in adultery, in the very act? he will make them pay dearly for their sport, and where will the solace of their love be then? "Never fear," says she, "the <hi type="italic">good man is not at home</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.19">v. 19</reference>); she does not call him her <hi type="italic">husband,</hi> for she <hi type="italic">forsakes the guide of her youth</hi> and <hi type="italic">forgets the covenant of her God;</hi> but "the <hi type="italic">good man</hi> of the house, whom I am weary of." Thus Potiphar's wife, when she spoke of her husband, would not call him so, but <hi type="italic">he,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.39.14">Gen. xxxix. 14</reference>. It is therefore with good reason taken notice of, to Sarah's praise, that she spoke respectfully of her husband, calling him <hi type="italic">lord.</hi> She pleases herself with this that he is not at home, and therefore she is melancholy if she have not some company, and therefore whatever company she has she may be free with them, for she is from under his eye, and he shall never know. But will he not return quickly? No: "he has <hi type="italic">gone a long journey,</hi> and cannot return on a sudden; he <hi type="italic">appointed the day</hi> of his return, and he never comes home sooner than he says he will. <hi type="italic">He has taken a bag of money with him,</hi> either," (1.) "To trade with, to buy goods with and he will not return till he has laid it all out. It is a pity that an honest industrious man should be thus abused, and advantage taken of his absence, when it is upon business, for the good of his family." Or, (2.) "To spend and revel with." Whether justly or not, she insinuates that he was a bad husband; so she would represent him, because she was resolved to be a bad wife, and must have that for an excuse; it is often groundlessly suggested, but is never a sufficient excuse. "He follows his pleasures, and wastes his estate abroad" (says she), "and why should not I do the same at home?" <div eID="gen13513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13514" type="x-p"/> IV. Of the success of the temptation. Promising the young man every thing that was pleasant, and impunity in the enjoyment, she gained her point, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.21">v. 21</reference>. It should seem, the youth, though very simple, had no ill design, else a word, a beck, a wink, would have served, and there would have been no need of all this harangue; but though he did not intend any such thing, nay, had something in his conscience that opposed it, yet <hi type="italic">with her much fair speech she caused him to yield.</hi> His corruptions at length triumphed over his convictions, and his resolutions were not strong enough to hold out against such artful attacks as these, but <hi type="italic">with the flattery of her lips she forced him;</hi> he could not stop his ear against such a charmer, but surrendered himself her captive. Wisdom's maidens, who plead her cause, and have reason on their side, and true and divine pleasures to invite men to, have a deaf ear turned to them, and with all their rhetoric cannot compel men to come in, but such is the dominion of sin in the hearts of men that its allurements soon prevail by falsehood and flattery. With what pity does Solomon here look upon this foolish young man, when he sees him follow the adulterous woman! (1.) He gives him up for gone; alas! he is undone. he goes to the slaughter (for houses of uncleanness are slaughter-houses to precious souls); a dart will presently <hi type="italic">strike through his liver;</hi> going without his breast-plate, he will receive his death's wound, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.23">v. 23</reference>. It is his life, his precious life, that is thus irrecoverably thrown away, he is perfectly lost to all good; his conscience is debauched; a door is opened to all other vices, and this will certainly end in his endless damnation. (2.) That which makes his case the more piteous is that he is not himself aware of his misery and danger; he goes blindfold, nay, he goes laughing to his ruin. The ox thinks he is led to the pasture when he is led to the slaughter; <hi type="italic">the fool</hi> (that is, the drunkard, for, of all sinners, drunkards are the greatest fools) is led <hi type="italic">to the correction of the stocks,</hi> and is not sensible of the shame of it, but goes to it as if he were going to a play. The <hi type="italic">bird</hi> that <hi type="italic">hastes to the snare</hi> looks only at the bait, and promises herself a good bit from that, and considers not that <hi type="italic">it is for her life.</hi> Thus this unthinking unwary young man dreams of nothing but the pleasures he shall have in the embraces of the harlot, while really he is running headlong upon his ruin. Though Solomon does not here tell us that he put the law in execution against this base harlot, yet we have no reason to think but that he did, he was himself so affected with the mischief she did and had such an indignation at it.

<div eID="gen13514" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Seduction of a Youth.</title> <div sID="gen13515" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Hearken unto me now therefore, O ye children, and attend to the words of my mouth. <hi type="super">25</hi> Let not thine heart decline to her ways, go not astray in her paths. <hi type="super">26</hi> For she hath cast down many wounded: yea, many strong <hi type="italic">men</hi> have been slain by her. <hi type="super">27</hi> Her house <hi type="italic">is</hi> the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death. <div eID="gen13515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13516" type="x-p"/> We have here the application of the foregoing story: "<hi type="italic">Hearken to me therefore,</hi> and not to such seducers (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.24">v. 24</reference>); give ear to a father, and not to an enemy." 1. "Take good counsel when it is given you. <hi type="italic">Let not thy heart decline to her ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.25">v. 25</reference>); never leave the paths of virtue, though strait and narrow, solitary and up-hill, for the way of the adulteress, though green, and broad, and crowded with company. Do not only keep thy feet from those ways, but let not so much as thy heart incline to them; never harbour a disposition this way, nor think otherwise than with abhorrence of such wicked practices as these. Let reason, and conscience, and the fear of God ruling in the heart, check the inclinations of the sensual appetite. If thou goest in her paths, in any of the paths that lead to this sin, thou goest astray, thou art out of the right way, the safe way; therefore take heed, <hi type="italic">go not astray,</hi> lest thou wander endlessly." 2. "Take fair warning when it is given you." (1.) "Look back, and see what mischief this sin has done. The adulteress has been the ruin not of here and there one, but she has <hi type="italic">cast down many wounded.</hi>" Thousands have been undone, now and for ever, by this sin; and those not only the weak and simple youths, such as he was of whom he had now spoken, but <hi type="italic">many strong men have been slain by her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.7.26">v. 26</reference>. Herein, perhaps, he has an eye especially to Samson, who was slain by this sin, and perhaps to David too, who by this sin entailed a sword upon his house, though so far the Lord took it away that he himself should not die. These were men not only of great bodily strength, but of eminent wisdom and courage, and yet their fleshly lusts prevailed over them. <hi type="italic">Howl, fir-trees, if the cedars be shaken. Let him that thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.</hi> (2.) "Look forward with an eye of faith, and see what will be in the end of it," <reference osisRef="Prov.7.27">v. 27</reference>. Her house, though richly decked and furnished, and called a <hi type="italic">house of pleasure,</hi> is the <hi type="italic">way to hell;</hi> and her chambers are the stair-case that goes down to the <hi type="italic">chambers of death</hi> and everlasting darkness. The cup of fornication must shortly be exchanged for the cup of trembling; and the flames of lust, if not quenched by repentance and mortification, will burn to the lowest hell. Therefore <hi type="italic">stand in awe and sin not.</hi>  <chapter eID="Prov.7"/> <div eID="gen13516" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen13519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13518" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Invitation of Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen13520" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Doth not wisdom cry? and understanding put forth her voice? <hi type="super">2</hi> She standeth in the top of high places, by the way in the places of the paths. <hi type="super">3</hi> She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors. 4 Unto you, O men, I call; and my voice <hi type="italic">is</hi> to the sons of man. <hi type="super">5</hi> O ye simple, understand wisdom: and, ye fools, be ye of an understanding heart. <hi type="super">6</hi> Hear; for I will speak of excellent things; and the opening of my lips <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> right things. <hi type="super">7</hi> For my mouth shall speak truth; and wickedness <hi type="italic">is</hi> an abomination to my lips. <hi type="super">8</hi> All the words of my mouth <hi type="italic">are</hi> in righteousness; <hi type="italic">there is</hi> nothing froward or perverse in them. <hi type="super">9</hi> They <hi type="italic">are</hi> all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge. <hi type="super">10</hi> Receive my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold. <hi type="super">11</hi> For wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it. <div eID="gen13520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13521" type="x-p"/> The will of God revealed to us for our salvation is here largely represented to us as easy to be known and understood, that none may have an excuse for their ignorance or error, and as worthy to be embraced, that none may have an excuse for their carelessness and unbelief. <div eID="gen13521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13522" type="x-p"/> I. The things revealed are easy to be known, for they <hi type="italic">belong to us and to our children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">Deut. xxix. 29</reference>), and we need not soar up to heaven, or dive into the depths, to get the knowledge of them (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.11">Deut. xxx. 11</reference>), for they are published and proclaimed in some measure by the works of the creation (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.1">Prov. xix. 1</reference>), more fully by the consciences of men and the eternal reasons and rules of good and evil, but most clearly by Moses and the prophets; let them hear them. The precepts of wisdom may easily be known; for, 1. They are proclaimed aloud (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Does not Wisdom cry?</hi> Yes, she cries aloud, and does not spare (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">Isa. lviii. 1</reference>); she <hi type="italic">puts forth her voice,</hi> as one in earnest and desirous to be heard. <hi type="italic">Jesus stood and cried,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.37">John vii. 37</reference>. The curses and blessings were read with a loud voice by the Levites, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.14">Deut. xxvii. 14</reference>. And men's own hearts sometimes speak aloud to them; there are clamours of conscience, as well as whispers. 2. They are proclaimed from on high (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">She stands in the top of high places;</hi> it was from the top of Mount Sinai that the law was given, and Christ expounded it in a sermon upon the mount. Nay, if we slight divine revelation, we <hi type="italic">turn away from him that speaks from heaven,</hi> a high place indeed, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.25">Heb. xii. 25</reference>. The adulterous woman spoke in secret, the oracles of the heathen muttered, but Wisdom speaks openly; truth seeks no corners, but gladly appeals to the light. 3. They are proclaimed <hi type="italic">in the places of concourse,</hi> where multitudes are gathered together, the more the better. Jesus spoke <hi type="italic">in the synagogues and in the temple, whither the Jews always resorted,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.20">John xviii. 20</reference>. Every man that passes by on the road, of what rank or condition soever, may know what is good, and what the Lord requires of him, if it be not his own fault. There is no speech nor language where Wisdom's voice is not heard; her discoveries and directions are given to all promiscuously. <hi type="italic">He that has ears to hear, let him hear.</hi> 4. They are proclaimed where they are most needed. They are intended for the guide of our way, and therefore are published <hi type="italic">in the places of the paths,</hi> where many ways meet, that travellers may be shown, if they will but ask, which is the right way, just then when they are at a loss; thou shalt then <hi type="italic">hear the word behind thee, saying, This is the way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.21">Isa. xxx. 21</reference>. The foolish man <hi type="italic">known not how to go to the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.15">Eccl. x. 15</reference>), and therefore Wisdom stands ready to direct him, stands <hi type="italic">at the gates, at the entry of the city,</hi> ready to tell him where the seer's house is, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.18">1 Sam. ix. 18</reference>. Nay, she follows men to their own houses, and cries to them <hi type="italic">at the coming in at the doors,</hi> saying, <hi type="italic">Peace be to this house; and, if the son of peace be there,</hi> it shall certainly abide upon it. God's ministers are appointed to testify to people both publicly and from house to house. Their own consciences follow them with admonitions wherever they go, which they cannot be out of the hearing of while they carry their own heads and hearts about with them, which are a law unto themselves. 5. They are directed to the children of men. We attend to that discourse in which we hear ourselves named, though otherwise we should have neglected it; therefore Wisdom speaks to us: "<hi type="italic">Unto you, O men! I call</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.4">v. 4</reference>), not to angels (they need not these instructions), not to devils (they are past them), not to the brute-creatures (they are not capable of them), but <hi type="italic">to you, O men!</hi> who are taught more than the beasts of the earth and made wiser than the fowls of heaven. To you is this law given, to you is the word of this invitation, this exhortation sent. <hi type="italic">My voice is to the sons of men,</hi> who are concerned to receive instruction, and to whom, one would think, it should be very welcome. It is not, to you, O Jews! only, that Wisdom cries, nor to you, O gentlemen! not to you, O scholars! but <hi type="italic">to you, O men! O sons of men!</hi> even the meanest." 6. They are designed to make them wise (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.5">v. 5</reference>); they are calculated not only for men that are capable of wisdom, but for sinful men, fallen men, foolish men, that need it, and are undone without it: "<hi type="italic">O you simple ones! understand wisdom.</hi> Though you are ever so simple, Wisdom will take you for her scholars, and not only so, but, if you will be ruled by her, will undertake to give you <hi type="italic">an understanding heart.</hi>" When sinners leave their sins, and become truly religious, then the <hi type="italic">simple understand wisdom.</hi> <div eID="gen13522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13523" type="x-p"/> II. The things revealed are worthy to be known, well worthy of all acceptation. We are concerned to hear; for, 1. They are of inestimable value. They are <hi type="italic">excellent things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">princely things,</hi> so the word is. Though they are level to the capacity of the meanest, yet there is that in them which will be entertainment for the greatest. They are divine and heavenly things, so excellent that, in comparison with them, all other learning is but children's play. Things which relate to an eternal God, an immortal soul, and an everlasting state, must needs be <hi type="italic">excellent things.</hi> 2. They are of incontestable equity, and carry along with them the evidence of their own goodness. They are <hi type="italic">right things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">all in righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.8">v. 8</reference>), and <hi type="italic">nothing froward or perverse in them.</hi> All the dictates and directions of revealed religion are consonant to, and perfective of, the light and law of nature, and there is nothing in them that puts any hardship upon us, that lays us under any undue restraints, unbecoming the dignity and liberty of the human nature, nothing that we have reason to complain of. <hi type="italic">All God's precepts concerning all things are right.</hi> 3. They are of unquestionable truth. Wisdom's doctrines, upon which her laws are founded, are such as we may venture our immortal souls upon: <hi type="italic">My mouth shall speak truth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.7">v. 7</reference>), the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, for it is a testimony to the world. Every word of God is true; there are not so much as pious frauds in it, nor are we imposed upon in that which is told us for our good. Christ is a faithful witness, is the truth itself; <hi type="italic">wickedness</hi> (that is, lying) <hi type="italic">is an abomination to his lips.</hi> Note, Lying is wickedness, and we should not only refrain from it, but it should be an abomination to us, and as far from what we say as from what God says to us. His word to us is <hi type="italic">yea, and amen;</hi> never then let ours be <hi type="italic">yea and nay.</hi> 4. They are wonderfully acceptable and agreeable to those who take them aright, who understand themselves aright, who have not their judgments blinded and biassed by the world and the flesh, are not under the power of prejudice, are taught of God, and whose understanding he has opened, who impartially <hi type="italic">seek knowledge,</hi> take pains for it, and have found it in the enquiries they have hitherto made. To them, (1.) They are all <hi type="italic">plain,</hi> and not hard to be understood. If the book is sealed, it is to those who are willingly ignorant. <hi type="italic">If our gospel is hidden, it is hidden to those who are lost;</hi> but to those who <hi type="italic">depart from evil,</hi> which <hi type="italic">is understanding,</hi> who have that <hi type="italic">good understanding</hi> which those have who <hi type="italic">do the commandments,</hi> to them <hi type="italic">they are all plain</hi> and there is nothing difficult in them. The way of religion is a highway, and <hi type="italic">the way-faring men, though fools, shall not err therein,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>. Those therefore do a great wrong to the common people who deny them the use of the scripture under pretence that they cannot understand it, whereas it is plain for plain people. (2.) They are all <hi type="italic">right,</hi> and not hard to be submitted to. Those who discern things that differ, who know good and evil, readily subscribe to the rectitude of all Wisdom's dictates, and therefore, with out murmuring or disputing, govern themselves by them. <div eID="gen13523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13524" type="x-p"/> III. From all this he infers that the right knowledge of those things, such as transforms us into the image of them, is to be preferred before all the wealth of this world (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.10-Prov.8.11">v. 10, 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Receive my instruction, and not silver.</hi> Instruction must not only be heard, but received. We must bid it welcome, receive the impressions of it, and submit to the command of it; and this <hi type="italic">rather than choice gold,</hi> that is, 1. We must prefer religion before riches, and look upon it that, if we have the knowledge and fear of God in our hearts, we are really more happy and better provided for every condition of life than if we had ever so much silver and gold. <hi type="italic">Wisdom is</hi> in itself, and therefore must be in our account, <hi type="italic">better than rubies.</hi> It will bring us in a better price, be to us a better portion; show it forth, and it will be a better ornament than jewels and precious stones of the greatest value. Whatever we can sit down and wish for of the wealth of this world would, if we had it, be unworthy to be compared with the advantages that attend serious godliness. 2. We must be dead to the wealth of this world, that we may the more closely and earnestly apply ourselves to the business of religion. We must receive instruction as the main matter, and then be indifferent whether we receive silver or no; nay, we must not receive it as our portion and reward, as the rich man in his life-time <hi type="italic">received his good things.</hi>

<div eID="gen13524" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Advantages of Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen13525" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions. <hi type="super">13</hi> The fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate. 14 Counsel <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine, and sound wisdom: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> understanding; I have strength. <hi type="super">15</hi> By me kings reign, and princes decree justice. <hi type="super">16</hi> By me princes rule, and nobles, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all the judges of the earth. <hi type="super">17</hi> I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me. <hi type="super">18</hi> Riches and honour <hi type="italic">are</hi> with me; <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> durable riches and righteousness. <hi type="super">19</hi> My fruit <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver. <hi type="super">20</hi> I lead in the way of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of judgment: <hi type="super">21</hi> That I may cause those that love me to inherit substance; and I will fill their treasures. <div eID="gen13525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13526" type="x-p"/> Wisdom here is Christ, <hi type="italic">in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge;</hi> it is Christ in the word and Christ in the heart, not only Christ revealed to us, but Christ revealed in us. It is the word of God, the whole compass of divine revelation; it is God the Word, in whom all divine revelation centres; it is the soul formed by the word; it is Christ formed in the soul; it is religion in the purity and power of it. Glorious things are here spoken of this excellent person, this excellent thing. <div eID="gen13526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13527" type="x-p"/> I. Divine wisdom gives men good heads (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I Wisdom dwell with prudence,</hi> not with carnal policy (the wisdom that is from above is contrary to that, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.12">2 Cor. i. 12</reference>), but with true discretion, which serves for the right ordering of the conversation, that wisdom of the prudent which is to <hi type="italic">understand his way</hi> and is in all cases <hi type="italic">profitable to direct,</hi> the wisdom of the serpent, not only to guard from harm, but to guide in doing good. <hi type="italic">Wisdom dwells with prudence;</hi> for prudence is the product of religion and an ornament to religion; and there are more <hi type="italic">witty inventions</hi> found out with the help of the scripture, both for the right understanding of God's providences and for the effectual countermining of Satan's devices and the doing of good in our generation, than were ever discovered by the learning of the philosophers or the politics of statesmen. We may apply it to Christ himself; he <hi type="italic">dwells with prudence,</hi> for his whole undertaking is the <hi type="italic">wisdom of God in a mystery,</hi> and in it God <hi type="italic">abounds towards us in all wisdom and prudence.</hi> Christ <hi type="italic">found out the knowledge of</hi> that great <hi type="italic">invention,</hi> and a costly one it was to him, man's salvation, by his satisfaction, an admirable expedient. We had found out many inventions for our ruin; he found out one for our recovery. The covenant of grace is so well ordered in all things that we must conclude that he who ordered it <hi type="italic">dwelt with prudence.</hi> <div eID="gen13527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13528" type="x-p"/> II. It gives men good hearts, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.13">v. 13</reference>. True religion, consisting in <hi type="italic">the fear of the Lord,</hi> which is the wisdom before recommended, teaches men, 1. To hate all sin, as displeasing to God and destructive to the soul: <hi type="italic">The fear of the Lord is to hate evil, the evil way,</hi> to hate sin as sin, and therefore to <hi type="italic">hate every false way.</hi> Wherever there is an awe of God there is a dread of sin, as an evil, as only evil. 2. Particularly to hate pride and passion, those two common and dangerous sins. Conceitedness of ourselves, <hi type="italic">pride and arrogancy,</hi> are sins which Christ hates, and so do all those who have the Spirit of Christ; every one hates them in others, but we must hate them in ourselves. <hi type="italic">The froward mouth,</hi> peevishness towards others, God hates, because it is such an enemy to the peace of mankind, and therefore we should hate it. Be it spoken to the honour of religion that, however it is unjustly accused, it is so far from making men conceited and sour that there is nothing more directly contrary to it than pride and passion, nor which it teaches us more to detest. <div eID="gen13528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13529" type="x-p"/> III. It has a great influence upon public affairs and the well-governing of all societies, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.14">v. 14</reference>. Christ, as God, has strength and wisdom; wisdom and might are his; as Redeemer, he is <hi type="italic">the wisdom of God and the power of God.</hi> To all that are his he is made of God both <hi type="italic">strength</hi> and <hi type="italic">wisdom;</hi> in him they are laid up for us, that we may both know and do our duty. He is the wonderful counsellor and gives that grace which alone is <hi type="italic">sound wisdom.</hi> He <hi type="italic">is understanding</hi> itself, and <hi type="italic">has strength</hi> for all those that strengthen themselves in him. True religion gives men the best counsel in all difficult cases, and helps to make their way plain. Wherever it is, it is <hi type="italic">understanding,</hi> it has <hi type="italic">strength;</hi> it will be all that to us that we need, both for services and sufferings. Where the word of God dwells richly it makes a man <hi type="italic">perfect</hi> and <hi type="italic">furnishes him thoroughly for every good word and work.</hi> Kings, princes, and judges, have of all men most need of wisdom and strength, of counsel and courage, for the faithful discharge of the trusts reposed in them, and that they may be blessings to the people over whom they are set. And therefore Wisdom says, <hi type="italic">By me kings reign</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.15-Prov.8.16">v. 15, 16</reference>), that is, 1. Civil government is a divine institution, and those that are entrusted with the administration of it have their commission from Christ; it is a branch of his kingly office that <hi type="italic">by him kings reign;</hi> from him to whom all judgment is committed their power is derived. They reign by him, and therefore ought to reign for him. 2. Whatever qualifications for government any kings or princes have they are indebted to the grace of Christ for them; he gives them the spirit of government, and they have nothing, no skill, no principles of justice, but what he endues them with. <hi type="italic">A divine sentence is in the lips of the king;</hi> and kings are to their subjects what he makes them. 3. Religion is very much the strength and support of the civil government; it teaches subjects their duty, and so <hi type="italic">by it kings reign</hi> over them the more easily; it teaches kings their duty, and so <hi type="italic">by it kings reign</hi> as they ought; they <hi type="italic">decree justice,</hi> while they <hi type="italic">rule in the fear of God.</hi> Those rule well whom religion rules. <div eID="gen13529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13530" type="x-p"/> IV. It will make all those happy, truly happy, that receive and embrace it. <div eID="gen13530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13531" type="x-p"/> 1. They shall be happy in the love of Christ; for he it is that says, <hi type="italic">I love those that love me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.17">v. 17</reference>. Those that <hi type="italic">love the Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity</hi> shall be beloved of him with a peculiar distinguishing love: he will <hi type="italic">love them and manifest himself to them.</hi> <div eID="gen13531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13532" type="x-p"/> 2. They shall be happy in the success of their enquiries after him: "<hi type="italic">Those that seek me early,</hi> seek an acquaintance with me and an interest in me, seek me <hi type="italic">early,</hi> that is, seek me earnestly, seek me first before any thing else, that begin betimes in the days of their youth to seek me, they shall find what they seek." Christ shall be theirs, and they shall be his. He never said, <hi type="italic">Seek in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen13532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13533" type="x-p"/> 3. They shall be happy in the wealth of the world, or in that which is infinitely better. (1.) They shall have as much riches and honour as Infinite Wisdom sees good for them (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.18">v. 18</reference>); they are <hi type="italic">with Christ,</hi> that is, he has them to give, and whether he will see fit to give them to us must be referred to him. Religion sometimes helps to make people rich and great in this world, gains them a reputation, and so increases their estates; and the riches which Wisdom gives to her favourites have these two advantages:— [1.] That they are <hi type="italic">riches and righteousness,</hi> riches honestly got, not by fraud and oppression, but in regular ways, and riches charitably used, for alms are called <hi type="italic">righteousness.</hi> Those that have their wealth from God's blessing on their industry, and that have a heart to do good with it, have <hi type="italic">riches and righteousness.</hi> [2.] That therefore they are <hi type="italic">durable riches.</hi> Wealth gotten by vanity will soon be diminished, but that which is well got will wear well and will be left to the children's children, and that which is well spent in works of piety and charity is put out to the best interest and so will be durable; for the friends made by <hi type="italic">the mammon of unrighteousness when we fail will receive us into everlasting habitations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.9">Luke xvi. 9</reference>. It will be found after many days, for the days of eternity. (2.) They shall have that which is infinitely better, if they have not riches and honour in this world (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My fruit is better than gold,</hi> and will turn to a better account, will be of more value in less compass, <hi type="italic">and my revenue better than</hi> the <hi type="italic">choicest silver,</hi> will serve a better trade." We may assure ourselves that not only Wisdom's products at last, but her income in the mean time, not only her fruit, but her revenue, is more valuable than the best either of the possessions or of the reversions of this world. <div eID="gen13533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13534" type="x-p"/> 4. They shall be happy in the grace of God now; that shall be their guide in the good way, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.20">v. 20</reference>. This is that fruit of wisdom which is <hi type="italic">better than gold, than fine gold,</hi> it <hi type="italic">leads us in the way of righteousness,</hi> shows us that way and goes before us in it, the way that God would have us walk in and which will certainly bring us to our desired end. It leads <hi type="italic">in the midst of the paths of judgment,</hi> and saves us from deviating on either hand. <hi type="italic">In medio virtus—Virtue lies in the midst.</hi> Christ by his Spirit guides believers into all truth, and so <hi type="italic">leads them in the way of righteousness,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">walk after the Spirit.</hi> <div eID="gen13534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13535" type="x-p"/> 5. They shall be happy in the glory of God hereafter, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">v. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> Wisdom <hi type="italic">leads in the paths of righteousness,</hi> not only that she may keep her friends in the way of duty and obedience, but that she may <hi type="italic">cause them to inherit substance</hi> and may <hi type="italic">fill their treasures,</hi> which cannot be done with the things of this world, nor with any thing less than God and heaven. The happiness of those that love God, and devote themselves to his service, is substantial and satisfactory. (1.) It is substantial; it is substance itself. It is a happiness which will subsist of itself, and stand alone, without the accidental supports of outward conveniences. Spiritual and eternal things are the only real and substantial things. Joy in God is substantial joy, solid and well-grounded. The promises are their bonds, Christ is their surety, and both substantial. They <hi type="italic">inherit substance;</hi> that is, their inheritance hereafter is substantial; it is a weight of glory; it is substance, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.34">Heb. x. 34</reference>. All their happiness they have as heirs; it is grounded upon their sonship. (2.) It is satisfying; it will not only fill their hands, but <hi type="italic">fill their treasures,</hi> not only maintain them, but make them rich. The things of this world may fill men's bellies (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>), but not their treasures, for they cannot in them secure to themselves <hi type="italic">goods for many years;</hi> perhaps they may be deprived of them <hi type="italic">this night.</hi> But let the treasures of the soul be ever so capacious there is enough in God, and Christ, and heaven, to fill them. In Wisdom's promises believers have goods laid up, not for days and years, but for eternity; her fruit therefore <hi type="italic">is better than gold.</hi>
