<div eID="gen13535" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Wisdom Eternal and Divine.</title> <div sID="gen13536" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old. 23 I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was. <hi type="super">24</hi> When <hi type="italic">there were</hi> no depths, I was brought forth; when <hi type="italic">there were</hi> no fountains abounding with water. <hi type="super">25</hi> Before the mountains were settled, before the hills was I brought forth: <hi type="super">26</hi> While as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the highest part of the dust of the world. <hi type="super">27</hi> When he prepared the heavens, I <hi type="italic">was</hi> there: when he set a compass upon the face of the depth: <hi type="super">28</hi> When he established the clouds above: when he strengthened the fountains of the deep: <hi type="super">29</hi> When he gave to the sea his decree, that the waters should not pass his commandment: when he appointed the foundations of the earth: <hi type="super">30</hi> Then I was by him, <hi type="italic">as</hi> one brought up <hi type="italic">with him:</hi> and I was daily <hi type="italic">his</hi> delight, rejoicing always before him; <hi type="super">31</hi> Rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth; and my delights <hi type="italic">were</hi> with the sons of men. <div eID="gen13536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13537" type="x-p"/> That it is an intelligent and divine person that here speaks seems very plain, and that it is not meant of a mere essential property of the divine nature, for Wisdom here has personal properties and actions; and that intelligent divine person can be no other than the Son of God himself, to whom the principal things here spoken of wisdom are attributed in other scriptures, and we must explain scripture by itself. If Solomon himself designed only the praise of wisdom as it is an attribute of God, by which he made the world and governs it, so to recommend to men the study of that wisdom which belongs to them, yet the Spirit of God, who indited what he wrote, carried him, as David often, to such expressions as could agree to no other than the Son of God, and would lead us into the knowledge of great things concerning him. All divine revelation is <hi type="italic">the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him,</hi> and here we are told who and what he is, as God, designed in the eternal counsels to be the Mediator between God and man. The best exposition of these verses we have in the <reference osisRef="John.1.1-John.1.4">first four verses</reference> of St. John's gospel. <hi type="italic">In the beginning was the Word,</hi> &c. Concerning the Son of God observe here, <div eID="gen13537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13538" type="x-p"/> I. His personality and distinct subsistence, one with the Father and of the same essence, and yet a person of himself, whom <hi type="italic">the Lord possessed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.22">v. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">who was set up</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.23">v. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">was brought forth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.24-Prov.8.25">v. 24, 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">was by him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">v. 30</reference>), for he was <hi type="italic">the express image of his person,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb. i. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen13538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13539" type="x-p"/> II. His eternity; he was begotten of the Father, for <hi type="italic">the Lord possessed</hi> him, as his own Son, his beloved Son, laid him in his bosom; he was <hi type="italic">brought forth as the only-begotten of the Father,</hi> and this <hi type="italic">before all worlds,</hi> which is most largely insisted upon here. The Word was eternal, and had a being before the world, before the beginning of time; and therefore it must follow that it was from eternity. <hi type="italic">The Lord possessed him in the beginning of his way,</hi> of his eternal counsels, for those were <hi type="italic">before his works.</hi> This way indeed had no beginning, for God's purposes in himself are eternal like himself, but God speaks to us in our own language. Wisdom explains herself (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was set up from everlasting.</hi> The Son of God was, in the eternal counsels of God, designed and advanced to be the wisdom and power of the Father, light and life, and all in all both in the creation and in the redemption of the world. That he <hi type="italic">was brought forth</hi> as to his being, and <hi type="italic">set up</hi> as to the divine counsels concerning his office, before the world was made, is here set forth in a great variety of expressions, much the same with those by which the eternity of God himself is expressed. <reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">Ps. xc. 2</reference>, <hi type="italic">Before the mountains were brought forth.</hi> 1. <hi type="italic">Before the earth was,</hi> and that was made <hi type="italic">in the beginning,</hi> before man was made; therefore the second Adam had a being before the first, for the first Adam was <hi type="italic">made of the earth,</hi> the second had a being <hi type="italic">before the earth,</hi> and therefore is <hi type="italic">not of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.31">John iii. 31</reference>. 2. Before the sea was (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.24">v. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">when there were no depths</hi> in which the waters were gathered together, <hi type="italic">no fountains</hi> from which those waters might arise, none of that deep on which the Spirit of God moved for the production of the visible creation, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen. i. 2</reference>. 3. Before the mountains were, the everlasting mountains, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.25">v. 25</reference>. Eliphaz, to convince Job of his inability to judge of the divine counsels, asks him (<reference osisRef="Job.15.7">Job xv. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Wast thou made before the hills?</hi> No, thou wast not. But <hi type="italic">before the hills was</hi> the eternal Word <hi type="italic">brought forth.</hi> 4. Before the habitable parts of the world, which men cultivate, and reap the profits of (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.26">v. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">the fields</hi> in the valleys and plains, to which the mountains are as a wall, which are <hi type="italic">the highest part of the dust of the world;</hi> the <hi type="italic">first part of the dust</hi> (so some), the atoms which compose the several parts of the world; <hi type="italic">the chief or principal part of the dust,</hi> so it may be read, and understood of man, who was made of the dust of the ground and is dust, but is the principal part of the dust, dust enlivened, dust refined. The eternal Word had a being before man was made, for <hi type="italic">in him was the life of men.</hi> <div eID="gen13539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13540" type="x-p"/> III. His agency in making the world. He not only had a being before the world, but he was present, not as a spectator, but as the architect, when the world was made. God silenced and humbled Job by asking him, "<hi type="italic">Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? Who hath laid the measures thereof?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.4">Job xxxviii. 4</reference>, &c.). Wast thou that eternal Word and wisdom, who was the prime manager of that great affair? No; thou art of yesterday." But here the Son of God, referring, as it should seem, to the discourse God had with Job, declares himself to have been engaged in that which Job could not pretend to be a witness of and a worker in, the creation of the world. <hi type="italic">By him God made the worlds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.9">Eph. iii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">Heb. i. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col. i. 16</reference>. 1. When, on the first day of the creation, in the very beginning of time, God said, <hi type="italic">Let there be light,</hi> and with a word produced it, this eternal Wisdom was that almighty Word: Then <hi type="italic">I was there, when he prepared the heavens,</hi> the fountain of that light, which, whatever it is here, is there substantial. 2. He was no less active when, on the second day, he stretched out the firmament, the vast expanse, and <hi type="italic">set</hi> that as <hi type="italic">a compass upon the face of the depth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.27">v. 27</reference>), surrounded it on all sides with that canopy, that curtain. Or it may refer to the exact order and method with which God framed all the parts of the universe, as the workman marks out his work with his line and compasses. The work in nothing varied from the plan of it formed in the eternal mind. 3. He was also employed in the third day's work, when the <hi type="italic">waters above the heavens,</hi> were gathered together by <hi type="italic">establishing the clouds above,</hi> and those under the heavens by <hi type="italic">strengthening the fountains of the deep,</hi> which send forth those waters (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.28">v. 28</reference>), and by preserving the bounds of the sea, which is the receptacle of those waters, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.29">v. 29</reference>. This speaks much the honour of this eternal Wisdom, for by this instance God proves himself a God greatly to be feared (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jer. v. 22</reference>) that <hi type="italic">he has placed the sand for the bound of the sea,</hi> that the dry land might continue to appear above water, fit to be a habitation for man; and thus he has <hi type="italic">appointed the foundation of the earth.</hi> How able, how fit, is the Son of God to be the Saviour of the world, who was the Creator of it! <div eID="gen13540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13541" type="x-p"/> IV. The infinite complacency which the Father had in him, and he in the Father (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was by him, as one brought up with him.</hi> As by an eternal generation he was brought forth of the Father, so by an eternal counsel he was brought up with him, which intimates, not only the infinite love of the Father to the Son, who is therefore called <hi type="italic">the Son of his love</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.13">Col. i. 13</reference>), but the mutual consciousness and good understanding that were between them concerning the work of man's redemption, which the Son was to undertake, and about which the <hi type="italic">counsel of peace was between them both,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zech. vi. 13</reference>. He was <hi type="italic">alumnus patris—the Father's pupil,</hi> as I may say, trained up from eternity for that service which in time, in the fulness of time, he was to go through with, and is therein taken under the special tuition and protection of the Father; he is <hi type="italic">my servant whom I uphold,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>. He did what he saw the Father do (<reference osisRef="John.5.19">John v. 19</reference>), pleased his Father, sought his glory, did according to the commandment he received from his Father, and all this <hi type="italic">as one brought up with him.</hi> He was <hi type="italic">daily his Father's delight (my elect, in whom my soul delighteth,</hi> says God, <reference osisRef="Isa.43.1">Isa. xliii. 1</reference>), and he also <hi type="italic">rejoiced always before him.</hi> This may be understood either, 1. Of the infinite delight which the persons of the blessed Trinity have in each other, wherein consists much of the happiness of the divine nature. Or, 2. Of the pleasure which the Father took in the operations of the Son, when he <hi type="italic">made the world;</hi> God saw every thing that the Son made, <hi type="italic">and, behold, it was very good,</hi> it pleased him, and therefore his Son was <hi type="italic">daily,</hi> day by day, during the six days of the creation, upon that account, <hi type="italic">his delight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.39.43">Exod. xxxix. 43</reference>. And the Son also did himself <hi type="italic">rejoice before him</hi> in the beauty and harmony of the whole creation, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.31">Ps. civ. 31</reference>. Or, 3. Of the satisfaction they had in each other, with reference to the great work of man's redemption. The Father delighted in the Son, as Mediator between him and man, was well-pleased with what he proposed (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>), and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> loved him because he undertook to <hi type="italic">lay down his life for the sheep;</hi> he put a confidence in him that he would go through his work, and not fail nor fly off. The Son also <hi type="italic">rejoiced always before him,</hi> delighted to do his will (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.8">Ps. xl. 8</reference>), adhered closely to his undertaking, as one that was well-satisfied in it, and, when it came to the setting to, expressed as much satisfaction in it as ever, saying, <hi type="italic">Lo, I come,</hi> to do <hi type="italic">as in the volume of the book it is written of me.</hi> <div eID="gen13541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13542" type="x-p"/> V. The gracious concern he had for mankind, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.31">v. 31</reference>. Wisdom <hi type="italic">rejoiced,</hi> not so much in the rich products of the earth, or the treasures hid in the bowels of it, as <hi type="italic">in the habitable parts of</hi> it, for her <hi type="italic">delights were with the sons of men;</hi> not only in the creation of man is it spoken with a particular air of pleasure (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Gen. i. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let us make man,</hi> but in the redemption and salvation of man. The Son of God was <hi type="italic">ordained, before the world,</hi> to that great work, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.20">1 Pet. i. 20</reference>. A remnant of the sons of men were given him to be brought, through his grace, to his glory, and these were those in whom his delights were. His church was the habitable part of his earth, made habitable for him, <hi type="italic">that the Lord God might dwell</hi> even <hi type="italic">among those</hi> that had been rebellious; and this he rejoiced in, in the prospect of seeing his seed. Though he foresaw all the difficulties he was to meet with in his work, the services and sufferings he was to go through, yet, because it would issue in the glory of his Father and the salvation of those sons of men that were given him, he looked forward upon it with the greatest satisfaction imaginable, in which we have all the encouragement we can desire to come to him and rely upon him for all the benefits designed us by his glorious undertaking.

<div eID="gen13542" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Wisdom's Exhortation.</title> <div sID="gen13543" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> Now therefore hearken unto me, O ye children: for blessed <hi type="italic">are they that</hi> keep my ways. <hi type="super">33</hi> Hear instruction, and be wise, and refuse it not. <hi type="super">34</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man that heareth me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at the posts of my doors. <hi type="super">35</hi> For whoso findeth me findeth life, and shall obtain favour of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">36</hi> But he that sinneth against me wrongeth his own soul: all they that hate me love death. <div eID="gen13543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13544" type="x-p"/> We have here the application of Wisdom's discourse; the design and tendency of it is to bring us all into an entire subjection to the laws of religion, to make us wise and good, not to fill our heads with speculations, or our tongues with disputes, but to rectify what is amiss in our hearts and lives. In order to this, here is, <div eID="gen13544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13545" type="x-p"/> I. An exhortation to hear and obey the voice of Wisdom, to attend and comply with the good instructions that the word of God gives us, and in them to discern the voice of Christ, as the sheep know the shepherd's voice. <div eID="gen13545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13546" type="x-p"/> 1. We must be diligent <hi type="italic">hearers of the word;</hi> for how can we believe in him of whom we have not heart? "<hi type="italic">Hearken unto me, O you children!</hi>" <reference osisRef="Prov.8.32">v. 32</reference>. "Read the word written, sit under the word preached, bless God for both, and hear him in both speaking to you." Let children age, and what they hearken to then, it is likely, they will be so seasoned by as to be governed by all their days. Let Wisdom's children justify Wisdom by hearkening to her and show themselves to be indeed her children. We must hear Wisdom's words, (1.) Submissively, and with a willing heart (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.33">v. 33</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hear instruction, and refuse it not,</hi> either as that which you need not or as that which you like not; it is offered you as a kindness, and it is at your peril if you refuse it." Those that reject the counsel of God reject it against themselves, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.30">Luke vii. 30</reference>. "Refuse it not now, lest you should not have another offer." (2.) Constantly, and with an attentive ear. We must hear Wisdom so as to <hi type="italic">watch daily at her gates,</hi> as beggars to receive an alms, as clients and patients to receive advice, and to wait as servants, with humility, and patience, and ready observance, <hi type="italic">at the posts of her doors.</hi> See here what a good house Wisdom keeps, for every day is dole-day; what a good school, for every day is lecture-day. While we have God's works before our eyes, and his word in our hand, we may be every day hearing Wisdom, and learning instruction from her. See here what a dutiful and diligent attendance is required of all Christ's disciples; they must <hi type="italic">watch at the gates.</hi> [1.] We must lay hold on all opportunities of getting knowledge and grace, and must get into, and keep in, a constant settled course of communion with God. [2.] We must be very humble in our attendance on divine instructions, and be glad of any place, even the meanest, so we may but be within hearing of them, as David, who would gladly be a door-keeper in the house of God. [3.] We must raise our expectations of these instructions, and hearken to them with care, and patience, and perseverance, must watch and wait, as Christ's hearers, that <hi type="italic">hanged on him</hi> to hear him, as the word in the original is (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.48">Luke xix. 48</reference>) and (<reference osisRef="Prov.21.38">ch. xxi. 38</reference>) <hi type="italic">came early in the morning to hear him.</hi> <div eID="gen13546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13547" type="x-p"/> 2. We must be conscientious <hi type="italic">doers of the work,</hi> for we are <hi type="italic">blessed only in our deed.</hi> It is not enough to hearken unto Wisdom's words, but we must <hi type="italic">keep her ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.32">v. 32</reference>), do every thing that she prescribes, keep within the hedges of her ways, and not transgress them, keep in the tracks of her ways, proceed and persevere in them. "<hi type="italic">Hear instruction and be wise;</hi> let it be a means to make you wise in ordering your conversation." What we know is known in vain if it do not make us wise, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.33">v. 33</reference>. <div eID="gen13547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13548" type="x-p"/> II. An assurance of happiness to all those that do hearken to Wisdom. They are blessed, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.32">v. 32</reference>, and again <reference osisRef="Prov.8.34">v. 34</reference>. Those are blessed that watch and wait at Wisdom's gates; even their attendance there is their happiness; it is the best place they can be in. Those are blessed that wait there, for they shall not be put to wait long; let them continue to knock awhile and it shall be opened to them. They are seeking Wisdom, and they shall find what they seek. But will it make them amends if they do find it? Yes (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whoso finds me finds life,</hi> that is, all happiness, all that good which he needs or can desire. He finds life in that grace which is the principle of spiritual life and the pledge of eternal life. He <hi type="italic">finds life,</hi> for he shall <hi type="italic">obtain favour of the Lord,</hi> and <hi type="italic">in his favour is life.</hi> If the king's favour is towards a wise son, much more the favour of the King of kings. Christ is Wisdom, and he that finds Christ, that obtains an interest in him, he <hi type="italic">finds life;</hi> for Christ is life to all believers. <hi type="italic">He that has the Son of God has life,</hi> eternal life, and he <hi type="italic">shall obtain favour of the Lord,</hi> who is well-pleased with all those that are in Christ; nor can we obtain God's favour, unless we find Christ and be found in him. <div eID="gen13548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13549" type="x-p"/> III. The doom passed upon all those that reject Wisdom and her proposals, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">v. 36</reference>. They are left to ruin themselves, and Wisdom will not hinder them, because they have set at nought all her counsel. 1. Their crime is very great; they <hi type="italic">sin against Wisdom,</hi> rebel against its light and laws, thwart its designs, and by their folly offend it. They <hi type="italic">sin against Christ;</hi> they act in contempt of his authority, and in contradiction to all the purposes of his life and death. This is construed into hating Wisdom, hating Christ; they are his enemies, who will not have him to reign over them. What can appear worse than hating him who is the centre of all beauty and fountain of all goodness, love itself? 2. Their punishment will be very just, for they wilfully bring it upon themselves. (1.) Those that offend Christ do the greatest wrong to themselves; they <hi type="italic">wrong their own souls;</hi> they wound their own consciences, bring a blot and stain upon their souls, which renders them odious in the eyes of God, and unfit for communion with him; they deceive themselves, disturb themselves, destroy themselves. Sin is a wrong to the soul. (2.) Those that are at variance with Christ are in love with their own ruin: <hi type="italic">Those that hate me love death;</hi> they love that which will be their death, and put that from them which would be their life. Sinners die because they will die, which leaves them inexcusable, makes their condemnation the more intolerable, and will for ever justify God when he judges. <hi type="italic">O Israel! thou hast destroyed thyself.</hi>  <chapter eID="Prov.8"/> <div eID="gen13549" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen13552" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13551" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Invitation of Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen13553" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars: <hi type="super">2</hi> She hath killed her beasts; she hath mingled her wine; she hath also furnished her table. <hi type="super">3</hi> She hath sent forth her maidens: she crieth upon the highest places of the city, <hi type="super">4</hi> Whoso <hi type="italic">is</hi> simple, let him turn in hither: <hi type="italic">as for</hi> him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him, <hi type="super">5</hi> Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine <hi type="italic">which</hi> I have mingled. <hi type="super">6</hi> Forsake the foolish, and live; and go in the way of understanding. <hi type="super">7</hi> He that reproveth a scorner getteth to himself shame: and he that rebuketh a wicked <hi type="italic">man getteth</hi> himself a blot. <hi type="super">8</hi> Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee. <hi type="super">9</hi> Give <hi type="italic">instruction</hi> to a wise <hi type="italic">man,</hi> and he will be yet wiser: teach a just <hi type="italic">man,</hi> and he will increase in learning. <hi type="super">10</hi> The fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy <hi type="italic">is</hi> understanding. <hi type="super">11</hi> For by me thy days shall be multiplied, and the years of thy life shall be increased. <hi type="super">12</hi> If thou be wise, thou shalt be wise for thyself: but <hi type="italic">if</hi> thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen13553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13554" type="x-p"/> Wisdom is here introduced as a magnificent and munificent queen, very great and very generous; that Word of God is this Wisdom in which God makes known his goodwill towards men; God the Word is this Wisdom, to whom the Father has committed all judgment. He who, in the chapter before, showed his grandeur and glory as the Creator of the world, here shows his grace and goodness as the Redeemer of it. The word is plural, <hi type="italic">Wisdoms;</hi> for in Christ are hid treasures of wisdom, and in his undertaking appears the manifold wisdom of God in a mystery. Now observe here, <div eID="gen13554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13555" type="x-p"/> I. The rich provision which Wisdom has made for the reception of all those that will be her disciples. This is represented under the similitude of a sumptuous feast, whence it is probable, our Saviour borrowed those parables in which he compared the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven</hi> to a great supper, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.2">Matt. xxii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.16">Luke xiv. 16</reference>. And so it was prophesied of, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa. xxv. 6</reference>. It is such a feast as Ahasuerus made to <hi type="italic">show the riches of his glorious kingdom.</hi> The grace of the gospel is thus set before us in the ordinance of the Lord's supper. To bid her guests welcome, 1. Here is a stately palace provided, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.1">v. 1</reference>. Wisdom, not finding a house capacious enough for all her guests, has built one on purpose, and, both to strengthen it and to beautify it, she has <hi type="italic">hewn out her seven pillars,</hi> which make it to be very firm, and look very great. Heaven is the house which Wisdom has built to entertain all her guests that are called to the marriage-supper of the Lamb; that is her Father's house, where there are many mansions, and whither she has gone to prepare places for us. She has hanged the earth upon nothing, there in it we have no continuing city; but heaven is a city that has foundations, has pillars. The church is Wisdom's house, to which she invites her guests, supported by the power and promise of God, as by <hi type="italic">seven pillars.</hi> Probably, Solomon refers to the temple which he himself had lately built for the service of religion, and to which he would persuade people to resort, both to worship God and to receive the instructions of Wisdom. Some reckon the schools of the prophets to be here intended. 2. Here is a splendid feast got ready (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">She has killed her beasts; she has mingled her wine;</hi> plenty of meat and drink are provided, and all of the best. <hi type="italic">She has killed her sacrifice</hi> (so the word is); it is a sumptuous, but a sacred feast, a feast upon a sacrifice. Christ has offered up himself a sacrifice for us, and it is <hi type="italic">his flesh</hi> that is <hi type="italic">meat indeed</hi> and <hi type="italic">his blood</hi> that is <hi type="italic">drink indeed.</hi> The Lord's supper is a feast of reconciliation and joy upon the sacrifice of atonement. The wine is <hi type="italic">mingled</hi> with something richer than itself, to give it a more than ordinary spirit and flavour. <hi type="italic">She has</hi> completely <hi type="italic">furnished her table</hi> with all the satisfactions that a soul can desire-righteousness and grace, peace and joy, the assurances of God's love, the consolations of the Spirit, and all the pledges and earnests of eternal life. Observe, It is all Wisdom's own doing; <hi type="italic">she</hi> has killed the beasts, <hi type="italic">she</hi> has mingled the wine, which denotes both the love of Christ, who makes the provision (he does not leave it to others, but takes the doing of it into his own hands), and the excellency of the preparation. That must needs be exactly fitted to answer the end which Wisdom herself has the fitting up of. <div eID="gen13555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13556" type="x-p"/> II. The gracious invitation she has given, not to some particular friends, but to all in general, to come and take part of these provisions. 1. She employs her servants to carry the invitation round about in the country: <hi type="italic">She has sent forth her maidens,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.9.3">v. 3</reference>. The ministers of the gospel are commissioned and commanded to give notice of the preparations which God has made, in the everlasting covenant, for all those that are willing to come up to the terms of it; and they, with maiden purity, not corrupting themselves or the word of God, and with an exact observance of their orders, are to call upon all they meet with, even in <hi type="italic">the highways and hedges,</hi> to come and feast with Wisdom, for <hi type="italic">all things are now ready,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.14.23">Luke xiv. 23</reference>. 2. She herself <hi type="italic">cries upon the highest places of the city,</hi> as one earnestly desirous of the welfare of the children of men, and grieved to see them rejecting their own mercies for lying vanities. Our Lord Jesus was himself the publisher of his own gospel; when he had sent forth his disciples he followed them to confirm what they said; nay, it <hi type="italic">began to be spoken by the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.3">Heb. ii. 3</reference>. He stood, and cried, <hi type="italic">Come unto me.</hi> We see who invited; now let us observe, <div eID="gen13556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13557" type="x-p"/> (1.) To whom the invitation is given: <hi type="italic">Whoso is simple</hi> and <hi type="italic">wants understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.9.4">v. 4</reference>. If we were to make an entertainment, of all people we should not care for, much less court, the company of such, but rather of philosophers and learned men, that we might hear their wisdom, and whose table-talk would be improving. "Have I need of madmen?" But Wisdom invites such, because what she has to give is what they most need, and it is their welfare that she consults, and aims at, in the preparation and invitation. He that is simple is invited, that he may be made wise, and he that <hi type="italic">wants a heart</hi> (so the word is) let him come hither, and he shall have one. Her preparations are rather physic than food, designed for the most valuable and desirable cure, that of the mind. Whosoever he be, the invitation is general, and excludes none that do not exclude themselves; though they be ever so foolish, yet, [1.] They shall be welcome. [2.] They may be helped; they shall neither be despised nor despaired of. Our Saviour came, <hi type="italic">not to call the righteous, but sinners,</hi> not the wise in their own eyes, who say they see (<reference osisRef="John.9.41">John ix. 41</reference>), but the simple, those who are sensible of their simplicity and ashamed of it, and him that is willing to <hi type="italic">become a fool, that he may be wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18">1 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen13557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13558" type="x-p"/> (2.) What the invitation is. [1.] We are invited to Wisdom's house: <hi type="italic">Turn in hither.</hi> I say <hi type="italic">we</hi> are, for which of us is there that must not own the character of the invited, that are <hi type="italic">simple and want understanding?</hi> Wisdom's doors stand open to such, and she is desirous to have some conversation with them, one word for their good, nor has she any other design upon them. [2.] We are invited to her table (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Come, eat of my bread,</hi> that is, taste of the true pleasures that are to be found in the knowledge and fear of God. By faith acted on the promises of the gospel, applying them to ourselves and taking the comfort of them, we feed, we feast, upon the provisions Christ has made for poor souls. What we eat and drink we make our own, we are nourished and refreshed by it, and so are our souls by the word of God; it has that in it which is <hi type="italic">meat and drink</hi> to those that have understanding. <div eID="gen13558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13559" type="x-p"/> (3.) What is required of those that may have the benefit of this invitation, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.6">v. 6</reference>. [1.] They must break off from all bad company: "<hi type="italic">Forsake the foolish,</hi> converse not with them, conform not to their ways, have no fellowship with the works of darkness, or with those that deal in such works." The first step towards virtue is to shun vice, and therefore to shun the vicious. <hi type="italic">Depart from me, you evil-doers.</hi> [2.] They must awake and arise from the dead; they must live, not in pleasure (for those that do so are dead while they live), but in the service of God; for those only that do so live indeed, live to some purpose. "Live not a mere animal-life, as brutes, but now, at length, live the life of men. <hi type="italic">Live</hi> and you <hi type="italic">shall live;</hi> live spiritually, and you shall live eternally," <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Eph. v. 14</reference>. [3.] They must choose the paths of Wisdom, and keep to them: "<hi type="italic">Go in the way of understanding;</hi> govern thyself henceforward by the rules of religion and right reason." It is not enough to forsake the foolish, but we must join ourselves with those that walk in wisdom, and walk in the same spirit and steps. <div eID="gen13559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13560" type="x-p"/> III. The instructions which Wisdom gives to the maidens she sends to invite, to the ministers and others, who in their places are endeavouring to serve her interests and designs. She tells them, <div eID="gen13560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13561" type="x-p"/> 1. What their work must be, not only to tell in general what preparation is made for souls, and to give a general offer of it, but they must address themselves to particular persons, must tell them of their faults, <hi type="italic">reprove, rebuke,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.9.7-Prov.9.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. They must instruct them how to amend—<hi type="italic">teach,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.9.9">v. 9</reference>. The word of God is intended, and therefore so is the ministry of that word, <hi type="italic">for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness.</hi> <div eID="gen13561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13562" type="x-p"/> 2. What different sorts of persons they would meet with, and what course they must take with them, and what success they might expect. <div eID="gen13562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13563" type="x-p"/> (1.) They would meet with some <hi type="italic">scorners</hi> and <hi type="italic">wicked men</hi> who would mock the messengers of the Lord, and misuse them, would <hi type="italic">laugh those to scorn</hi> that invite them to the feast of the Lord, as they did, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.10">2 Chron. xxx. 10</reference>, would <hi type="italic">treat them spitefully,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.22.6">Matt. xxii. 6</reference>. And, though they are not forbidden to invite those simple ones to Wisdom's house, yet they are advised not to pursue the invitation by reproving and rebuking them. <hi type="italic">Reprove not a scorner; cast not these pearls before swine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Matt. vii. 6</reference>. Thus Christ said of the Pharisees, <hi type="italic">Let them alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.14">Matt. xv. 14</reference>. "Do not reprove them." [1.] "In justice to them, for those have forfeited the favour of further means who scorn the means they have had. Those that are thus <hi type="italic">filthy, let them be filthy still;</hi> those that are <hi type="italic">joined to idols, let them alone; lo, we turn to the Gentiles.</hi>" [2.] "In prudence to yourselves; because, if you reprove them," <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "You lose your labour, and so <hi type="italic">get to yourselves shame</hi> for the disappointment." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "You exasperate them; do it ever so wisely and tenderly, if you do it faithfully, they will hate you, they will load you with reproaches, and say all the ill they can of you, and so you will get a blot; therefore you had better not meddle with them, for your reproofs will be likely to do more hurt than good." <div eID="gen13563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13564" type="x-p"/> (2.) They would meet with others, who are wise, and good, and just; thanks be to God, all are not scorners. We meet with some who are so wise for themselves, to just to themselves, as to be willing and glad to be taught; and when we meet with such, [1.] If there be occasion, we must reprove them; for wise men are not so perfectly wise but there is that in them which needs a reproof; and we must not connive at any man's faults because we have a veneration for his wisdom, nor must a <hi type="italic">wise man</hi> think that his wisdom exempts him from reproof when he says or does any thing foolishly; but the more wisdom a man has the more desirous he should be to have his weaknesses shown him, because a <hi type="italic">little folly</hi> is a great blemish to <hi type="italic">him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour.</hi> [2.] With our reproofs we must <hi type="italic">give</hi> them <hi type="italic">instruction,</hi> and must <hi type="italic">teach</hi> them, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.9">v. 9</reference>. [3.] We may expect that our doing so will be taken as a kindness, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Ps. cxli. 5</reference>. A wise man will reckon those his friends who deal faithfully with him: "Rebuke such a one, and <hi type="italic">he will love thee</hi> for thy plain dealing, will thank thee, and desire thee to do him the same good turn another time, if there be occasion." It is as great an instance of wisdom to take a reproof well as to give it well, [4.] Being taken well, it will do good, and answer the intention. A <hi type="italic">wise man</hi> will be made wiser by the reproofs and instructions that are given him; he <hi type="italic">will increase in learning,</hi> will grow in knowledge, and so grow in grace. None must think themselves too wise to learn, nor so good that they need not be better and therefore need not be taught. We must still press forward, and follow on to know till we come to the perfect man. <hi type="italic">Give to a wise man</hi> (so it is in the original), give him advice, give him reproof, give him comfort, and <hi type="italic">he will be yet wiser; give him occasion</hi> (so the LXX.), occasion to show his wisdom, and he will show it, and the acts of wisdom will strengthen the habits. <div eID="gen13564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13565" type="x-p"/> IV. The instructions she gives to those that are invited, which her maidens must inculcate upon them. <div eID="gen13565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13566" type="x-p"/> 1. Let them know wherein true wisdom consists, and what will be their entertainment at Wisdom's table, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.10">v. 10</reference>. (1.) The heart must be principled with <hi type="italic">the fear of God;</hi> that <hi type="italic">is the beginning of wisdom.</hi> A reverence of God's majesty, and a dread of his wrath, are that fear of him which is the beginning, the first step towards true religion, whence all other instances of it take rise. This fear may, at first, have torment, but love will, by degrees, cast out the torment of it. (2.) The head must be filled with the knowledge of the things of God. <hi type="italic">The knowledge of holy things</hi> (the word is plural) <hi type="italic">is understanding,</hi> the things pertaining to the service of God (those are called <hi type="italic">holy things</hi>), that pertain to our own sanctification; reproof is called <hi type="italic">that which is holy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Matt. vii. 6</reference>. Or the knowledge which holy men have, which was taught by the holy prophets, of those things which <hi type="italic">holy men spoke as they were moved by the holy Ghost,</hi> this <hi type="italic">is understanding;</hi> it is the best and most useful understanding, will stand us in most stead and turn to the best account. <div eID="gen13566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13567" type="x-p"/> 2. Let them know what will be advantages of this wisdom (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">By me thy days shall be multiplied.</hi> It will contribute to the health of thy body, and so <hi type="italic">the years of thy life</hi> on earth <hi type="italic">shall be increased,</hi> while men's folly and intemperance shorten their days. It will bring thee to heaven, and there thy days shall be multiplied <hi type="italic">in infinitum—to infinity,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">years of thy life shall be increased without end.</hi>" There is no true wisdom but in the say of religion and no true life but in the end of that way. <div eID="gen13567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13568" type="x-p"/> 3. Let them know what will be the consequence of their choosing or refusing this fair offer, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.12">v. 12</reference>. Here is, (1.) The happiness of those that embrace it: "<hi type="italic">If thou be wise, thou shalt be wise for thyself;</hi> thou wilt be the gainer by it, not Wisdom." A man cannot be profitable to God. It is to our own good that we are thus courted. "Thou wilt not leave the gain to others" (as we do our worldly wealth when we die, which is therefore called <hi type="italic">another man's,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.12">Luke xvi. 12</reference>), "but thou shalt carry it with thee into another world." Those that are wise for their souls are wise for themselves, for the soul is the man; nor do any consult their own true interest but those that are truly religious. This recommends us to God, and recovers us from that which is our folly and degeneracy; it employs us in that which is most beneficial in this world, and entitles us to that which is much more so in the world to come. (2.) The shame and ruin of those that slight it: "<hi type="italic">If thou scornest</hi> Wisdom's proffer, <hi type="italic">thou alone shalt bar it.</hi>" [1.] "Thou shalt bear the blame of it." Those that are good must thank God, but those that are wicked may thank themselves; it is not owing to God (he is not the author of sin); Satan can only tempt, he cannot force; and wicked companions are but his instruments; so that all the fault must lie on the sinner himself. [2.] "Thou shalt bear the loss of that which thou scornest; it will be to thy own destruction; thy blood will be upon thy own head, and the consideration of this will aggravate thy condemnation. <hi type="italic">Son, remember,</hi> that thou hadst this fair offer made thee, and thou wouldst not accept it; thou stoodest fair for life, but didst choose death rather."

<div eID="gen13568" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Invitation of Folly.</title> <div sID="gen13569" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> A foolish woman <hi type="italic">is</hi> clamorous: <hi type="italic">she is</hi> simple, and knoweth nothing. <hi type="super">14</hi> For she sitteth at the door of her house, on a seat in the high places of the city, 15 To call passengers who go right on their ways: <hi type="super">16</hi> Whoso <hi type="italic">is</hi> simple, let him turn in hither: and <hi type="italic">as for</hi> him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him, <hi type="super">17</hi> Stolen waters are sweet, and bread <hi type="italic">eaten</hi> in secret is pleasant. 18 But he knoweth not that the dead <hi type="italic">are</hi> there; <hi type="italic">and that</hi> her guests <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the depths of hell. <div eID="gen13569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13570" type="x-p"/> We have heard what Christ has to say, to engage our affections to God and godliness, and one would think the whole world should go after him; but here we are told how industrious the tempter is to seduce unwary souls into the paths of sin, and with the most he gains his point, and Wisdom's courtship is not effectual. Now observe, <div eID="gen13570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13571" type="x-p"/> I. Who is the tempter—<hi type="italic">a foolish woman,</hi> Folly herself, in opposition to Wisdom. Carnal sensual pleasure I take to be especially meant by this <hi type="italic">foolish woman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.13">v. 13</reference>); for that is the great enemy to virtue and inlet to vice; that defiles and debauches the mind, stupefies conscience, and puts out the sparks of conviction, more than any thing else. This tempter is here described to be, 1. Very ignorant: <hi type="italic">She is simple and knows nothing,</hi> that is, she has no sufficient solid reason to offer; where she gets dominion in a soul she works out all the knowledge of holy things; they are lost and forgotten. <hi type="italic">Whoredom, and wine, and new wine, take away the heart;</hi> they besot men, and make fools of them. (2.) Very importunate. The less she has to offer that is rational the more violent and pressing she is, and carries the day often by dint of impudence. She <hi type="italic">is clamorous</hi> and noisy (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.13">v. 13</reference>), continually haunting young people with her enticements. <hi type="italic">She sits at the door of her house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.14">v. 14</reference>), watching for a prey; not as Abraham at his tent-door, seeking an opportunity to do good. <hi type="italic">She sits on a seat (on a throne,</hi> so the word signifies) <hi type="italic">in the high places of the city,</hi> as if she had authority to give law, and we were all <hi type="italic">debtors to the flesh, to live after the flesh,</hi> and as if she had reputation, and were in honour, and thought worthy of <hi type="italic">the high places of the city;</hi> and perhaps she gains upon many more by pretending to be fashionable than by pretending to be agreeable. "Do not all persons of rank and figure in the world" (says she) "give themselves a greater liberty than the strict laws of virtue allow; and why shouldst thou humble thyself so far as to be cramped by them?" Thus the tempter affects to seem both kind and great. <div eID="gen13571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13572" type="x-p"/> II. Who are the tempted—young people who have been well educated; these she will triumph most in being the ruin of. Observe, 1. What their real character is; they are <hi type="italic">passengers that go right on their ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.15">v. 15</reference>), that have been trained up in the paths of religion and virtue and set out very hopefully and well, that seemed determined and designed for good, and are not (as that young man, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.8">ch. vii. 8</reference>) <hi type="italic">going the way to her house.</hi> Such as these she has a design upon, and lays snares for, and uses all her arts, all her charms, to pervert them; if they <hi type="italic">go right on,</hi> and will not look towards her, she will call after them, so urgent are these temptations. (2.) How she represents them. She calls them <hi type="italic">simple</hi> and <hi type="italic">wanting understanding,</hi> and therefore courts them to her school, that they may be cured of the restraints and formalities of their religion. This is the method of the stage (which is too close an exposition of this paragraph), where the sober young man, that has been virtuously educated, is the fool in the play, and the plot is to make him <hi type="italic">seven times more a child of hell</hi> than his profane companions, under colour of polishing and refining him, and setting him up for a wit and a beau. What is justly charged upon sin and impiety (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.4">v. 4</reference>), that it is folly, is here very unjustly retorted upon the ways of virtue; but the day will declare who are the fools. <div eID="gen13572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13573" type="x-p"/> III. What the temptation is (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Stolen waters are sweet.</hi> It is to water and bread, whereas Wisdom invites to the beasts she has killed and the wine she has mingled; however, bread and water are acceptable enough to those that are hungry and thirsty; and this is pretended to be more <hi type="italic">sweet</hi> and <hi type="italic">pleasant</hi> than common, for it is <hi type="italic">stolen water and bread eaten in secret,</hi> with a fear of being discovered. The pleasures of prohibited lusts are boasted of as more relishing than those of prescribed love; and dishonest gain is preferred to that which is justly gotten. Now this argues, not only a bold contempt, but an impudent defiance, 1. Of God's law, in that the waters are the sweeter for being stolen and come at by breaking through the hedge of the divine command. <hi type="italic">Nitimur in vetitum—We are prone to what is forbidden.</hi> This spirit of contradiction we have from our first parents, who thought the forbidden tree of all others <hi type="italic">a tree to be desired.</hi> 2. Of God's curse. The <hi type="italic">bread is eaten in secret,</hi> for fear of discovery and punishment, and the sinner takes a pride in having so far baffled his convictions, and triumphed over them, that, notwithstanding that fear, he dares commit the sin, and can make himself believe that, being eaten in secret, it shall never be discovered or reckoned for. Sweetness and pleasantness constitute the bait; but, by the tempter's own showing, even that is so absurd, and has such allays, that it is a wonder how it can have any influence upon men that pretend to reason. <div eID="gen13573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13574" type="x-p"/> IV. An effectual antidote against the temptation, in a few words, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">v. 18</reference>. He that so far wants understanding as to be drawn aside by these enticements is led on, ignorantly, to his own inevitable ruin: <hi type="italic">He knows not,</hi> will not believe, does not consider, the tempter will not let him know, <hi type="italic">that the dead are there,</hi> that those who live in pleasure are <hi type="italic">dead while they live, dead in trespasses and sins.</hi> Terrors attend these pleasures like the terrors of death itself. The giants are there—<hi type="italic">Rephaim.</hi> It was this that ruined the sinners of the old world, the giants that were <hi type="italic">in the earth in those days. Her guests,</hi> that are treated with those <hi type="italic">stolen waters,</hi> are not only in the highway to hell and at the brink of it, but they are already <hi type="italic">in the depths of hell,</hi> under the power of sin, led captive by Satan at his will, and ever and anon lashed by the terrors of their own consciences, which are a hell upon earth. The depths of Satan are <hi type="italic">the depths of hell;</hi> remorseless sin is remediless ruin, it is the bottomless pit already. Thus does Solomon show the hook; those that believe him will not meddle with the bait.  <chapter eID="Prov.9"/> <div eID="gen13574" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen13577" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13576" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div sID="gen13578" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son <hi type="italic">is</hi> the heaviness of his mother. <div eID="gen13578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13579" type="x-p"/> Solomon, speaking to us as unto children, observes here how much the comfort of parents, natural, political, and ecclesiastical, depends upon the good behaviour of those under their charge, as a reason, 1. Why parents should be careful to give their children a good education, and to train them up in the ways of religion, which, if it obtain the desired effect, they themselves will have the comfort of it, or, if not, they will have for their support under their heaviness that they have done their duty, have done their endeavour. 2. Why children should conduct themselves wisely and well, and live up to their good education, that they may gladden the hearts of their parents, and not sadden them. Observe, (1.) It adds to the comfort of young people that are pious and discreet that thereby they do something towards recompensing their parents for all the care and pains they have taken with them, and occasion pleasure to them in the evil days of old age, when they most need it; and it is the duty of parents to rejoice in their children's wisdom and well-doing, yea, though it arrive at such an eminency as to eclipse them. (2.) It adds to the guilt of those that conduct themselves ill that thereby they grieve those whom they ought to be a joy to, and are a heaviness particularly to their poor mothers who bore them with sorrow, but with greater sorrow see them wicked and vile.

<div eID="gen13579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13580" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death. <hi type="super">3</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish: but he casteth away the substance of the wicked. <div eID="gen13580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13581" type="x-p"/> These two verses speak to the same purport, and the latter may be the reason of the former. 1. That wealth which men get unjustly will do them no good, because God will blast it: <hi type="italic">Treasures of wickedness profit nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.2">v. 2</reference>. The treasures of wicked people, much more the treasure which they have made themselves masters of by any wicked people, by oppression of fraud, though it be ever so much, as a treasure, and laid up ever so safely, though it be hidden treasure, yet it <hi type="italic">profits nothing;</hi> when profit and loss come to be balanced the profit gained by the treasures will by no means countervail the loss sustained by the wickedness, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Matt. xvi. 26</reference>. They do not profit the soul; they will not purchase any true comfort or happiness. They will stand a man in no stead at death, or in the judgment of the great day; and the reason is because God <hi type="italic">casts away the substance of the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.3">v. 3</reference>); he takes that from them which they have unjustly gotten; he rejects the consideration of it, not regarding the rich more than the poor. We often see that scattered by the justice of God which has been gathered together by the injustice of men. How can the treasures of wickedness profit, when, though it be counted substance, God casts it away and it vanishes as a shadow? 2. That which is honestly got will turn to a good account, for God will bless it. <hi type="italic">Righteousness delivers from death,</hi> that is, wealth gained, and kept, and used, in a right manner (righteousness signifies both honesty and charity); it answers the end of wealth, which is to keep us alive and be a defence to us. It will deliver from those judgments which men bring upon themselves by their wickedness. It will profit to such a degree as to deliver, though not from the stroke of death, yet from the sting of it, and consequently from the terror of it. For <hi type="italic">the Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.3">v. 3</reference>), and so their <hi type="italic">righteousness delivers from death,</hi> purely by the favour of God to them, which is their life and livelihood, and which will keep them alive in famine. The soul of the righteous shall be kept alive by the word of God, and faith in his promise, when <hi type="italic">young lions shall lack and suffer hunger.</hi>

<div eID="gen13581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13582" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> He becometh poor that dealeth <hi type="italic">with</hi> a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich. <div eID="gen13582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13583" type="x-p"/> We are here told, 1. Who those are who, though rich, are in a fair way to <hi type="italic">become poor</hi>—those <hi type="italic">who deal with a slack hand,</hi> who are careless and remiss in their business, and never mind which end goes foremost, nor ever set their hands vigorously to their work or stick to it; those <hi type="italic">who deal with a deceitful hand</hi> (so it may be read); those who think to enrich themselves by fraud and tricking will, in the end, impoverish themselves, not only by bringing the curse of God on what they have, but by forfeiting their reputation with men; none will care to deal with those who deal with sleight of hand and are honest only with good looking to. 2. Who those are who, though poor, are in a fair way to become rich—those who are diligent and honest, who are careful about their affairs, and, what their hands find to do, do it with all their might, in a fair and honourable way, those are likely to increase what they have. <hi type="italic">The hand of the acute</hi> (so some), of those who are sharp, but not sharpers; <hi type="italic">the hand of the active</hi> (so others); the stirring hand gets a penny. This is true in the affairs of our souls as well as in our worldly affairs; slothfulness and hypocrisy lead to spiritual poverty, but those who are <hi type="italic">fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,</hi> are likely to be <hi type="italic">rich in faith</hi> and <hi type="italic">rich in good works.</hi>

<div eID="gen13583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13584" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> He that gathereth in summer <hi type="italic">is</hi> a wise son: <hi type="italic">but</hi> he that sleepeth in harvest <hi type="italic">is</hi> a son that causeth shame. <div eID="gen13584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13585" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The just praise of those who improve their opportunities, who take pains to gather and increase what they have, both for soul and body, who provide for hereafter while provision is to be made, who <hi type="italic">gather in summer,</hi> which is gathering time. He who does so <hi type="italic">is a wise son,</hi> and it is his honour; he acts wisely for his parents, whom, if there be occasion, he ought to maintain, and he gives reputation to himself, his family, and his education. 2. The just reproach and blame of those who trifle away these opportunities: <hi type="italic">He who sleeps,</hi> loves his ease, idles away his time, and neglects his work, especially <hi type="italic">who sleeps in harvest,</hi> when he should be laying in for winter, who lets slip the season of furnishing himself with that which he will have occasion for, <hi type="italic">is a son that causes shame;</hi> for he is a foolish son; he prepares shame for himself when winter comes, and reflects shame upon all his friends. He who gets knowledge and wisdom in the days of his youth <hi type="italic">gathers in summer,</hi> and he will have the comfort and credit of his industry; but he who idles away the days of his youth will bear the shame of his indolence when he is old.

<div eID="gen13585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13586" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Blessings <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon the head of the just: but violence covereth the mouth of the wicked. <div eID="gen13586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13587" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. <hi type="italic">The head of the just</hi> crowned with <hi type="italic">blessings,</hi> with the blessings both of God and man. Variety of blessings, abundance of blessings, shall descend from above, and visibly abide on the head of good men, real blessings; they shall not only be spoken well of, but done well to. Blessings shall be on their head as a coronet to adorn and dignify them and as a helmet to protect and secure them. 2. <hi type="italic">The mouth of the wicked covered</hi> with <hi type="italic">violence.</hi> Their mouths shall be stopped with shame for the violence which they have done; they shall not have a word to say in excuse for themselves (<reference osisRef="Job.5.16">Job v. 16</reference>); their breath shall be stopped with the violence that shall be done to them, when their violent dealings shall return on their heads, shall be returned to their teeth.

<div eID="gen13587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13588" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The memory of the just <hi type="italic">is</hi> blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot. <div eID="gen13588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13589" type="x-p"/> Both the just and the wicked, when their days are fulfilled, must die. Between their bodies in the grave thee is no visible difference; between the souls of the one and the other, in the world of spirits, thee is a vast difference, and so there is, or ought to be, between their memories, which survive them. <div eID="gen13589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13590" type="x-p"/> I. Good men are and ought to be well spoken of when they are gone; it is one of the blessings that <hi type="italic">comes upon the head of the just,</hi> even when their head is laid. Blessed men leave behind them blessed memories. 1. It is part of the dignity of the saints, especially those who excel in virtue and are eminently useful, that they are remembered with respect when they are dead. Their good name, their name with good men, for good things, is then in a special manner as <hi type="italic">precious ointment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Eccl. vii. 1</reference>. Those that honour God he will thus honour, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.3">Ps. cxii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">9</reference>. <hi type="italic">The elders</hi> by faith <hi type="italic">obtained a good report</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.2">Heb. xi. 2</reference>), and, being dead, are yet spoken of. 2. It is part of the duty of the survivors: <hi type="italic">Let the memory of the just be blessed,</hi> so the Jews read it, and observe it as a precept, not naming an eminently just man that is dead without adding, <hi type="italic">Let his memory be blessed.</hi> We must delight in making an honourable mention of good men that are gone, bless God for them, and for his gifts and graces that appeared in them, and especially be followers of them in <hi type="italic">that which is good.</hi> <div eID="gen13590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13591" type="x-p"/> II. Bad men are and shall be forgotten, or spoken of with contempt. When their bodies are putrefying in the grave their <hi type="italic">names</hi> also <hi type="italic">shall rot.</hi> Either they shall not be preserved at all, but buried in oblivion (no good can be said of them, and therefore the greatest kindness that can be done them will be to say nothing of them), or they shall be loathsome, and mentioned with detestation, and that rule of honour, <hi type="italic">De mortuis nil nisi bonum</hi>—<hi type="italic">Say nothing to the disadvantage of the dead,</hi> will not protect them. Where the wickedness has been notorious, and cannot but be mentioned, it ought to be mentioned with abhorrence.

<div eID="gen13591" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Marks of Wisdom and of Folly.</title> <div sID="gen13592" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The wise in heart will receive commandments: but a prating fool shall fall. <div eID="gen13592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13593" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The honour and happiness of the obedient. They <hi type="italic">will receive commandments;</hi> they will take it as a privilege, and really an ease to them, to be under government, which saves them the labour of deliberating and choosing for themselves; and they will take it as a favour to be told their duty and admonished concerning it. And this is their wisdom; those are <hi type="italic">wise in heart</hi> who are tractable, and those who thus bend, thus stoop, shall stand and be established, shall prosper, being well advised. 2. The shame and ruin of the disobedient, that will not be governed, nor endure any yoke, that will not be taught, nor take any advice. They are fools, for they act against themselves and their own interest; they are commonly <hi type="italic">prating fools,</hi> fools of lips, full of talk, but full of nonsense, boasting of themselves, prating spitefully against those that admonish them (<reference osisRef="3John.1.10">3 John 10</reference>), and pretending to give counsel and law to others. Of all fools, none more troublesome than the <hi type="italic">prating fools,</hi> nor that more expose themselves; but they <hi type="italic">shall fall</hi> into sin, into hell, because they received not commandments. Those that are full of tongue seldom look well to their feet, and therefore stumble and fall.

<div eID="gen13593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13594" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> He that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known. <div eID="gen13594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13595" type="x-p"/> We are here told, and we may depend upon it, 1. That men's integrity will be their security: <hi type="italic">He that walks uprightly</hi> towards God and man, that is faithful to both, that designs as he ought and means as he says, <hi type="italic">walks surely;</hi> he is safe under a divine protection and easy in a holy security. He goes on his way with a humble boldness, being well armed against the temptations of Satan, the troubles of the world, and the reproaches of men. He knows what ground he stands on, what guide he follows, what guard he is surrounded with, and what glory he is going to, and therefore proceeds with assurance and <hi type="italic">great peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Isa. xxxii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15-Isa.33.16">xxxiii. 15, 16</reference>. Some understand it as part of the character of an upright man, that he <hi type="italic">walks surely,</hi> in opposition to walking at all adventures. He will not dare to do that which he is not fully satisfied in his own conscience concerning the lawfulness of, but will see his way clear in every thing. 2. That men's dishonesty will be their shame: <hi type="italic">He that perverts his way,</hi> that turns aside into crooked paths, that dissembles with God and man, looks one way and rows another, though he may for a time disguise himself, and pass current, <hi type="italic">shall be known</hi> to be what he is. It is a thousand to one but some time or other he betrays himself; at least, God will discover him in the great day. <hi type="italic">He that perverts his ways documento erit</hi>—<hi type="italic">shall be made an example of,</hi> for warning to others; so some.

<div eID="gen13595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13596" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> He that winketh with the eye causeth sorrow: but a prating fool shall fall. <div eID="gen13596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13597" type="x-p"/> Mischief is here said to attend, 1. Politic, designing, self-disguising sinners: <hi type="italic">He that winks with the eye,</hi> as if he took no notice of you, when at the same time he is watching an opportunity to do you an ill turn, that makes signs to his accomplices when to come into assist him in executing his wicked projects, which are all carried on by trick and artifice, <hi type="italic">causes sorrow</hi> both to others and to himself. Ingenuity will be no excuse for iniquity, but the sinner must either repent or do worse, either rue it or be ruined by it. 2. Public, silly, self-exposing sinners: A <hi type="italic">prating fool,</hi> whose sins go before unto judgment, <hi type="italic">shall fall,</hi> as was said before, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.8">v. 8</reference>. But his case is less dangerous of the two, and, though he destroys himself, he does not create so much sorrow to others as <hi type="italic">he that winks with his eyes.</hi> The dog that bites is not always the dog that barks.

<div eID="gen13597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13598" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> The mouth of a righteous <hi type="italic">man is</hi> a well of life: but violence covereth the mouth of the wicked. <div eID="gen13598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13599" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How industrious a good man is, by communicating his goodness, to do good with it: <hi type="italic">His mouth,</hi> the outlet of his mind, <hi type="italic">is a well of life;</hi> it is a constant spring, whence issues good discourse for the edification of others, like streams that water the ground and make it fruitful, and for their consolation, like streams that quench the thirst of the weary traveller. It is like <hi type="italic">a well of life,</hi> that is pure and clean, not only not poisoned, but not muddled, with any corrupt communication. 2. How industrious a bad man is, by concealing his badness, to do hurt with it: <hi type="italic">The mouth of the wicked covers violence,</hi> disguises the designed mischief with professions of friendship, that it may be carried on the more securely and effectually, as Joab kissed and killed, Judas kissed and betrayed; this is his sin, to which the punishment answers (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Violence covers the mouth of the wicked;</hi> what he got by violence shall by violence be taken from him, <reference osisRef="Job.5.4-Job.5.5">Job v. 4, 5</reference>.

<div eID="gen13599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13600" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins. <div eID="gen13600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13601" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The great mischief-maker, and that is malice. Even where there is no manifest occasion of strife, yet <hi type="italic">hatred</hi> seeks occasion and so <hi type="italic">stirs it up</hi> and does the devil's work. Those are the most spiteful ill-natured people that can be who take a pleasure in setting their neighbours together by the ears, by tale-bearing, evil surmises, and misrepresentations, blowing up the sparks of contention, which had lain buried, into a flame, at which, with an unaccountable pleasure, they warm their hands. 2. The great peace-maker, and that is <hi type="italic">love,</hi> which <hi type="italic">covers all sins,</hi> that is, the offences among relations which occasion discord. Love, instead of proclaiming and aggravating the offence, conceals and extenuates it as far as it is capable of being concealed and extenuated. Love will excuse the offence which we give through mistake and unadvisedly; when we are able to say that there was no ill intended, but it was an oversight, and we love our friend notwithstanding, this covers it. It will also overlook the offence that is given us, and so cover it, and make the best of it: by this means strife is prevented, or, if begun, peace is recovered and restored quickly. The apostle quotes this, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.8">1 Pet. iv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Love will cover a multitude of sins.</hi>

<div eID="gen13601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13602" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> In the lips of him that hath understanding wisdom is found: but a rod <hi type="italic">is</hi> for the back of him that is void of understanding. <div eID="gen13602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13603" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Wisdom and grace are the honour of good men: He <hi type="italic">that has understanding,</hi> that good understanding which those have that do the commandments, <hi type="italic">wisdom is found in his lips,</hi> that is, it is discovered to be there, and consequently that he has within a good treasure of it, and it is derived thence for the benefit of others. It is a man's honour to have wisdom, but much more to be instrumental to make others wise. 2. Folly and sin are the shame of bad men: <hi type="italic">A rod is for the back of him that is void of understanding—of him that wants a heart;</hi> he exposes himself to the lashes of his own conscience, to the scourges of the tongue, to the censures of the magistrate, and to the righteous judgments of God. Those that foolishly and wilfully go on in wicked ways are preparing rods for themselves, the marks of which will be their perpetual disgrace.

<div eID="gen13603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13604" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> lay up knowledge: but the mouth of the foolish <hi type="italic">is</hi> near destruction. <div eID="gen13604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13605" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. It is the wisdom of the wise that they treasure up a stock of useful knowledge, which will be their preservation: <hi type="italic">Wisdom is</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">found in their lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.13">v. 13</reference>), because it is laid up in their hearts, out of which store, like the good householder, they bring things new and old. Whatever knowledge may be at any time useful to us we must <hi type="italic">lay it up,</hi> because we know not but some time or other we may have occasion for it. We must continue laying up as long as we live; and be sure to lay it up safely, that it may not be to seek when we want it. 2. It is the folly of fools that they lay up mischief in their hearts, which is ready to them in all they say, and works terror and destruction both to others and to themselves. They <hi type="italic">love devouring words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.4">Ps. lii. 4</reference>), and these come uppermost. Their <hi type="italic">mouth is near destruction,</hi> having the <hi type="italic">sharp arrows of bitter words</hi> always at hand to throw about.

<div eID="gen13605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13606" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The rich man's wealth <hi type="italic">is</hi> his strong city: the destruction of the poor <hi type="italic">is</hi> their poverty. <div eID="gen13606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13607" type="x-p"/> This may be taken two ways:—1. As a reason why we should be diligent in our business, that we may avoid that sinking dispiriting uneasiness which attends poverty, and may enjoy the benefit and comfort which those have that are beforehand in the world. Taking pains is really the way to make ourselves and our families easy. Or, rather, 2. As a representation of the common mistakes both of rich and poor, concerning their outward condition. (1.) Rich people think themselves happy because they are rich; but it is their mistake: <hi type="italic">The rich man's wealth is,</hi> in his own conceit, <hi type="italic">his strong city,</hi> whereas the worst of evils it is too weak and utterly insufficient to protect them from. It will prove that they are not so safe as they imagine; nay, their wealth may perhaps expose them. (2.) Poor people think themselves undone because they are poor; but it is their mistake: <hi type="italic">The destruction of the poor is their poverty;</hi> it sinks their spirits, and ruins all their comforts; whereas a man may live very comfortably, though he has but a little to live on, if he be but content, and keep a good conscience, and live by faith.

<div eID="gen13607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13608" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> The labour of the righteous <hi type="italic">tendeth</hi> to life: the fruit of the wicked to sin. <div eID="gen13608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13609" type="x-p"/> Solomon here confirms what his father had said (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.16">Ps. xxxvii. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">A little that a righteous man has is better than the riches of many wicked.</hi> 1. Perhaps a righteous man has no more than what he works hard for; he eats only <hi type="italic">the labour of his hands,</hi> but that <hi type="italic">labour tends to life;</hi> he aims at nothing but to get an honest livelihood, covets not to be rich and great, but is willing to live and maintain his family. Nor does it tend only to his own life, but he would enable himself to do good to others; he labours <hi type="italic">that he may have to give</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>); all his business turns to some good account or other. Or it may be meant of his labour in religion; he takes most pains in that which has a tendency to eternal life; he <hi type="italic">sows to the Spirit,</hi> that he may <hi type="italic">reap life everlasting.</hi> 2. Perhaps a wicked man's wealth is fruit which he did not labour for, but came easily by, but it tends <hi type="italic">to sin.</hi> He makes it the food and fuel of his lusts, his pride and luxury; he gets hurt with it and not good; he gets hurt by it and is hardened by it in his wicked ways. The things of this world are good or evil, life or death, as they are used, and as those are that have them.

<div eID="gen13609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13610" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> He <hi type="italic">is in</hi> the way of life that keepeth instruction: but he that refuseth reproof erreth. <div eID="gen13610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13611" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. That those are in the right that do not only receive instruction, but retain it, that do not let it slip through carelessness, as most do, nor let it go to those that would rob them of it, that <hi type="italic">keep instruction</hi> safely, keep it pure and entire, keep it for their own use, that they may govern themselves by it, keep it for the benefit of others, that they may instruct them; those that do so are <hi type="italic">in the way of life,</hi> the way that has true comfort in it and eternal life at the end of it. 2. That those are in the wrong that do not only not receive instruction, but wilfully and obstinately refuse it when it is offered them. They will not be taught their duty because it discovers their faults to them; that instruction which carries reproof in it they have a particular aversion to, and certainly they err; it is a sign that they err in judgment, and have false notions of good and evil; it is a cause of their erring in conversation. The traveller that has missed his way, and cannot bear to be told of it and shown the right way, must needs err still, err endlessly; he certainly misses <hi type="italic">the way of life.</hi>
