<div eID="gen13611" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Proper of the Use of the Tongue.</title> <div sID="gen13612" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> He that hideth hatred <hi type="italic">with</hi> lying lips, and he that uttereth a slander, <hi type="italic">is</hi> a fool. <div eID="gen13612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13613" type="x-p"/> Observe here, Malice is folly and wickedness. 1. It is so when it is concealed by flattery and dissimulation: He <hi type="italic">is a fool,</hi> though he may think himself a politician, <hi type="italic">that hides hatred with lying lips,</hi> lest, if it break out, he should be ashamed before men and should lose the opportunity of gratifying his malice. <hi type="italic">Lying lips</hi> are bad enough of themselves, but have a peculiar malignity in them when they are made <hi type="italic">a cloak of maliciousness.</hi> But he <hi type="italic">is a fool</hi> who thinks to hide any thing from God. 2. It is no better when it is vented in spiteful and mischievous language: <hi type="italic">He that utters slander is a fool</hi> too, for God will sooner or later bring forth that righteousness as the light which he endeavours to cloud, and will find an expedient to roll the reproach away.

<div eID="gen13613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13614" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise. <div eID="gen13614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13615" type="x-p"/> We are here admonished concerning the government of the tongue, that necessary duty of a Christian. 1. It is good to say little, because <hi type="italic">in the multitude of words there wanteth not sin,</hi> or <hi type="italic">sin doth not cease.</hi> Usually, those that speak much speak much amiss, and among many words there cannot but be many idle words, which they must shortly give an account of. Those that love to hear themselves talk do not consider what work they are making for repentance; for that will be wanted, and first or last will be had, where <hi type="italic">there wanteth not sin.</hi> 2. It is therefore good to <hi type="italic">keep our mouth as with a bridle: He that refrains his lips,</hi> that often checks himself, suppresses what he has thought, and holds in that which would transpire, is a wise man; it is an evidence of his wisdom, and he therein consults his own peace. Little said is soon amended, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.13">Amos v. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.19">Jam. i. 19</reference>.

<div eID="gen13615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13616" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> The tongue of the just <hi type="italic">is as</hi> choice silver: the heart of the wicked <hi type="italic">is</hi> little worth. <hi type="super">21</hi> The lips of the righteous feed many: but fools die for want of wisdom. <div eID="gen13616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13617" type="x-p"/> We are here taught how to value men, not by their wealth and preferment in the world, but by their virtue. <div eID="gen13617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13618" type="x-p"/> I. Good men are good for something. Though they may be poor and low in the world, and may not have power and riches to do good with, yet, as long as they have a mouth to speak, that will make them valuable and useful, and upon that account we must honour those that fear the Lord, because <hi type="italic">out of the good treasure of their heart they bring forth good things.</hi> 1. This makes them valuable: <hi type="italic">The tongue of the just is as choice silver;</hi> they are sincere, freed from the dross of guile and evil design. God's words are compared to <hi type="italic">silver purified</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Ps. xii. 6</reference>), for they may be relied on; and such are the words of just men. They are of weight and worth, and will enrich those that hear them with wisdom, which is better than <hi type="italic">choice silver.</hi> 2. It makes them useful: <hi type="italic">The lips of the righteous feed many;</hi> for they are full of the word of God, which is the bread of life, and that sound doctrine wherewith souls are nourished up. Pious discourse is spiritual food to the needy, to the hungry. <div eID="gen13618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13619" type="x-p"/> II. Bad men are good for nothing. 1. One can get no good by them: <hi type="italic">The heart of the wicked is little worth,</hi> and therefore that which comes out of the abundance of his heart cannot be worth much. His principles, his notions, his thoughts, his purposes, and all the things that fill him, and affect him, are worldly and carnal, and therefore of no value. <hi type="italic">He that is of the earth speaks of the earth,</hi> and neither understands nor relishes the things of God, <reference osisRef="John.3.31">John iii. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1 Cor. ii. 14</reference>. The wicked man pretends that, though he does not talk of religion as the just do, yet he has it within him, and thanks God that his heart is good; but he that searches the heart here says the contrary: <hi type="italic">It is nothing worth.</hi> 2. One can do no good to them. While many are fed by <hi type="italic">the lips of the righteous, fools die for want of wisdom;</hi> and fools indeed they are to die for want of that which they might so easily come by. <hi type="italic">Fools die for want of a heart</hi> (so the word is); they perish for want of consideration and resolution; they have no heart to do any thing for their own good. While the righteous feed others fools starve themselves.

<div eID="gen13619" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Advantages of the Righteous.</title> <div sID="gen13620" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> The blessing of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it. <div eID="gen13620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13621" type="x-p"/> Worldly wealth is that which most men have their hearts very much upon, but they generally mistake both in the nature of the thing they desire and in the way by which they hope to obtain it; we are therefore told here, 1. What that wealth is which is indeed desirable, not having abundance only, but having it and <hi type="italic">no sorrow with it,</hi> no disquieting care to get and keep it, no vexation of spirit in the enjoyment of it, no tormenting grief for the loss of it, no guilt contracted by the abuse of it—to have it and to have a heart to take the comfort of it, to do good with it and to serve God with joyfulness and gladness of heart in the use of it. 2. Whence this desirable wealth is to be expected, not by making ourselves drudges to the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Ps. cxxvii. 2</reference>), but by <hi type="italic">the blessing of God.</hi> It is this that <hi type="italic">makes rich and adds no sorrow;</hi> what comes from the love of God has the grace of God for its companion, to preserve the soul from those turbulent lusts and passions of which, otherwise, the increase of riches is commonly the incentive. He had said (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">The hand of the diligent makes rich,</hi> as a means; but here he ascribes it to <hi type="italic">the blessing of the Lord;</hi> but that blessing is upon <hi type="italic">the hand of the diligent.</hi> It is thus in spiritual riches. Diligence in getting them is our duty, but God's blessing and grace must have all the glory of that which is acquired, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.17-Deut.8.18">Deut. viii. 17, 18</reference>.

<div eID="gen13621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13622" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> as sport to a fool to do mischief: but a man of understanding hath wisdom. <div eID="gen13622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13623" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Sin exceedingly sinful: <hi type="italic">It is as laughter to a fool to do mischief;</hi> it is as natural to him, and as pleasant, as it is to a man to laugh. <hi type="italic">Wickedness is his Isaac</hi> (that is the word here); it is his delight, his darling, and that in which he pleases himself. He makes a laughing matter of sin. When he is warned not to sin, from the consideration of the law of God and the revelation of his wrath against sin, he makes a jest of the admonition, and laughs at the shaking of the spear; when he has sinned, instead of sorrowing for it, he boasts of it, ridicules reproofs, and laughs away the convictions of his own conscience, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.9">ch. xiv. 9</reference>. 2. Wisdom exceedingly wise, for it carries along with it the evidence of its own excellency; it may be predicated of itself, and this is encomium enough; you need say no more in praise of <hi type="italic">a man of understanding</hi> than this, "He is an <hi type="italic">understanding man;</hi> he <hi type="italic">has wisdom;</hi> he is so wise as not to do mischief, or if he has, through oversight, offended, he is so wise as not to make a jest of it." Or, to pronounce wisdom wise indeed, read it thus: <hi type="italic">As it is a sport to a fool to do mischief, so it is to a man of understanding to have wisdom and to show it.</hi> Besides the future recompence, a good man has as much present pleasure in the restraints and exercises of religion as sinners can pretend to in the liberties and enjoyments of sin, and much more, and much better.

<div eID="gen13623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13624" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> The fear of the wicked, it shall come upon him: but the desire of the righteous shall be granted. <hi type="super">25</hi> As the whirlwind passeth, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> the wicked no <hi type="italic">more:</hi> but the righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> an everlasting foundation. <div eID="gen13624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13625" type="x-p"/> It is here said, and said again, to the righteous, that <hi type="italic">it shall be well with them,</hi> and to the wicked, <hi type="italic">Woe to them;</hi> and these are set the one over against the other, for their mutual illustration. <div eID="gen13625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13626" type="x-p"/> I. It shall be as ill with the wicked as they can fear, and as well with the righteous as they can desire. 1. The wicked, it is true, buoy themselves up sometimes in their wickedness with vain hopes which will deceive them, but at other times they cannot but be haunted with just fears, and those <hi type="italic">fears shall come upon them;</hi> the God they provoke will be every whit as terrible as they, when they are under their greatest damps, apprehend him to be. <hi type="italic">As is thy fear, so is thy wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.11">Ps. xc. 11</reference>. Wicked men fear the punishment of sin, but they have not wisdom to improve their fears by making their escape, and so the thing they feared comes upon them, and their present terrors are earnests of their future torments. 2. The righteous, it is true, sometimes have their fears, but their desire is towards the favour of God and a happiness in him, and that <hi type="italic">desire shall be granted.</hi> According to their faith, not according to their fear, it shall be <hi type="italic">unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Ps. xxxvii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen13626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13627" type="x-p"/> II. The prosperity of the wicked shall quickly end, but the happiness of the righteous shall never end, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">v. 25</reference>. The wicked make a great noise, hurry themselves and others, like a <hi type="italic">whirlwind,</hi> which threatens to bear down all before it; but, like a <hi type="italic">whirlwind,</hi> they are presently gone, and they pass irrecoverably; they are <hi type="italic">no more;</hi> all about them are quiet and glad when the storm is over, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.10 Ps.37.36">Ps. xxxvii. 10, 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.5">Job xx. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">The righteous,</hi> on the contrary, make no show; they lie hid, like a <hi type="italic">foundation,</hi> which is low and out of sight, but they are fixed in their resolution to cleave to God, established in virtue, and they shall be an <hi type="italic">everlasting foundation,</hi> immovably good. He that is holy shall be holy still and immovably happy; his hope is built on a rock, and therefore not shocked by the storm, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.24">Matt. vii. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">The righteous is the pillar of the world</hi> (so some read it); the world stands for their sakes; the holy seed is the substance thereof.

<div eID="gen13627" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Righteous Exclusively Happy.</title> <div sID="gen13628" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> the sluggard to them that send him. <div eID="gen13628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13629" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Those that are of a slothful disposition, that love their ease and cannot apply their minds to any business, are not fit to be employed, no, not so much as to be sent on an errand, for they will neither deliver a message with any care nor make any haste back. Such therefore are very unmeet to be ministers, Christ's messengers; he will not own the sending forth of sluggards into his harvest. 2. Those that are guilty of so great an oversight as to entrust such with any affair, and put confidence in them, will certainly have vexation with them. A slothful servant is to his master as uneasy and troublesome as <hi type="italic">vinegar to the teeth</hi> and <hi type="italic">smoke to the eyes;</hi> he provokes his passion, as vinegar sets the teeth on edge, and occasions him grief to see his business neglected and undone, as smoke sets the eyes a weeping.

<div eID="gen13629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13630" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> The fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened. <hi type="super">28</hi> The hope of the righteous <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> gladness: but the expectation of the wicked shall perish. <div eID="gen13630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13631" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Religion lengthens men's lives and crowns their hopes. <hi type="italic">What man is he that loves life?</hi> Let him <hi type="italic">fear God,</hi> and that will secure him from many things that would prejudice his life, and secure to him life enough in this world and eternal life in the other; <hi type="italic">the fear of the Lord</hi> will add days more than was expected, will add them endlessly, will prolong them to the days of eternity. <hi type="italic">What man is he that would see good days?</hi> Let him be religious, and then his days shall not only be many, but happy, very happy as well as very many, for <hi type="italic">the hope of the righteous shall be gladness;</hi> they shall have what they hope for, to their unspeakable satisfaction. It is something future and unseen that they place their happiness in (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.24-Rom.8.25">Rom. viii. 24, 25</reference>), not what they have in hand, but what they have in hope, and their hope will shortly be swallowed up in fruition, and it will be their everlasting <hi type="italic">gladness. Enter thou into the joy of thy Lord.</hi> 2. Wickedness shortens men's lives, and frustrates their hopes: <hi type="italic">The years of the wicked,</hi> that are spent in the pleasures of sin and the drudgery of the world, <hi type="italic">shall be shortened.</hi> Cut down the trees that cumber the ground. And whatever comfort or happiness a wicked man promises himself, in this world or the other, he will be frustrated; for <hi type="italic">the expectation of the wicked shall perish;</hi> his hope shall be turned into endless despair.

<div eID="gen13631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13632" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> The way of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> strength to the upright: but destruction <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> to the workers of iniquity. <hi type="super">30</hi> The righteous shall never be removed: but the wicked shall not inhabit the earth. <div eID="gen13632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13633" type="x-p"/> These two verses are to the same purport with those next before, intimating the happiness of the godly and the misery of the wicked; it is necessary that this be inculcated upon us, so loth are we to believe and consider it. 1. Strength and stability are entailed upon integrity: <hi type="italic">The way of the Lord</hi> (the providence of God, the way in which he walks towards us) <hi type="italic">is strength to the upright,</hi> confirms him in his uprightness. All God's dealings with him, merciful and afflictive, serve to quicken him to his duty and animate him against his discouragements. Or <hi type="italic">the way of the Lord</hi> (the way of godliness, in which he appoints us to walk) is <hi type="italic">strength to the upright;</hi> the closer we keep to that way, the more our hearts are enlarged to proceed in it, the better fitted we are both for services and sufferings. A good conscience, kept pure from sin, gives a man boldness in a dangerous time, and constant diligence in duty makes a man's work easy in a busy time. The more we do for God the more we may do, <reference osisRef="Job.17.9">Job xvii. 9</reference>. That <hi type="italic">joy of the Lord</hi> which is to be found only in the <hi type="italic">way of the Lord</hi> will be our strength (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Neh. viii. 10</reference>), and therefore <hi type="italic">the righteous shall never be removed.</hi> Those that have an established virtue have an established peace and happiness which nothing can rob them of; they <hi type="italic">have an everlasting foundation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">v. 25</reference>. 2. Ruin and destruction are the certain consequences of wickedness. <hi type="italic">The wicked shall not</hi> only not inherit the earth, though they lay up their treasure in it, but they shall not so much as <hi type="italic">inhabit the earth;</hi> God's judgments will root them out. <hi type="italic">Destruction,</hi> swift and sure destruction, <hi type="italic">shall be to the workers of iniquity,</hi> destruction from the presence of the Lord and the glory of his power. Nay, that way of the Lord which is the strength of the upright is consumption and terror <hi type="italic">to the workers of iniquity;</hi> the same gospel which to the one is a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life</hi> to the other is a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death;</hi> the same providence, like the same sun, softens the one and hardens the other, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">Hos. xiv. 9</reference>.

<div eID="gen13633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13634" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> The mouth of the just bringeth forth wisdom: but the froward tongue shall be cut out. <hi type="super">32</hi> The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable: but the mouth of the wicked <hi type="italic">speaketh</hi> frowardness. <div eID="gen13634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13635" type="x-p"/> Here, as before, men are judged of, and, accordingly, are justified or condemned, by their words, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.37">Matt. xii. 37</reference>. 1. It is both the proof and the praise of a man's wisdom and goodness that he speaks wisely and well. A good man, in his discourse, <hi type="italic">brings forth wisdom</hi> for the benefit of others. God gives him wisdom as a reward of his righteousness (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Eccl. ii. 26</reference>), and he, in gratitude for that gift and justice to the giver, does good with it, and with his wise and pious discourses edifies many. He <hi type="italic">knows what is acceptable,</hi> what discourse will be pleasing to God (for that is it that he studies more than to oblige the company), and what will be agreeable both to the speaker and to the hearers, what will become him and benefit them, and that he will speak. 2. It is the sin, and will be the ruin, of a wicked man, that he speaks wickedly like himself. <hi type="italic">The mouth of the wicked speaks frowardness,</hi> that which is displeasing to God and provoking to those he converses with; and what is the issue of it? Why, <hi type="italic">the froward tongue shall be cut out,</hi> as surely as the <hi type="italic">flattering one,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.12.3">Ps. xii. 3</reference>.  <chapter eID="Prov.10"/> <div eID="gen13635" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen13636" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div sID="gen13637" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> A false balance <hi type="italic">is</hi> abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but a just weight <hi type="italic">is</hi> his delight. <div eID="gen13637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13638" type="x-p"/> As religion towards God is a branch of universal righteousness (he is not an honest man that is not devout), so righteousness towards men is a branch of true religion, for he is not a godly man that is not honest, nor can he expect that his devotion should be accepted; for, 1. Nothing is more offensive to God than deceit in commerce. <hi type="italic">A false balance</hi> is here put for all manner of unjust and fraudulent practices in dealing with any person, which are all an <hi type="italic">abomination to the Lord,</hi> and render those abominable to him that allow themselves in the use of such accursed arts of thriving. It is an affront to justice, which God is the patron of, as well as a wrong to our neighbour, whom God is the protector of. Men make light of such frauds, and think there is no sin in that which there is money to be got by, and, while it passes undiscovered, they cannot blame themselves for it; a blot is no blot till it is hit, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.7-Hos.12.8">Hos. xii. 7, 8</reference>. But they are not the less an abomination to God, who will be the avenger of those that are defrauded by their brethren. 2. Nothing is more pleasing to God than fair and honest dealing, nor more necessary to make us and our devotions acceptable to him: <hi type="italic">A just weight is his delight.</hi> He himself goes by a just weight, and holds the scale of judgment with an even hand, and therefore is pleased with those that are herein followers of him. A balance cheats, under pretence of doing right most exactly, and therefore is the greater abomination to God.

<div eID="gen13638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13639" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="italic">When</hi> pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly <hi type="italic">is</hi> wisdom. <div eID="gen13639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13640" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. How he that exalts himself is here abased, and contempt put upon him. <hi type="italic">When pride comes then comes shame.</hi> Pride is a sin which men have reason to be themselves ashamed of; it is a shame to a man who springs out of the earth, who lives upon alms, depends upon God, and has forfeited all he has, to be proud. It is a sin which others cry out shame on and look upon with disdain; he that is haughty makes himself contemptible; it is a sin for which God often brings men down, as he did Nebuchadnezzar and Herod, whose ignominy immediately attended their vain-glory; for God <hi type="italic">resists the proud,</hi> contradicts them, and counterworks them, in the thing they are proud of, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa. ii. 11</reference>, &c. 2. How he that humbles himself is here exalted, and a high character is given him. As with the proud there is folly, and will be shame, so <hi type="italic">with the lowly there is wisdom,</hi> and will be honour, for a man's wisdom gains him respect and makes his face to shine before men; or, if any be so base as to trample upon the humble, God will give them grace which will be their glory. Considering how safe, and quiet, and easy, those are that are of a humble spirit, what communion they have with God and comfort in themselves, we will say, <hi type="italic">With the lowly is wisdom.</hi>

<div eID="gen13640" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Advantages of the Righteous.</title> <div sID="gen13641" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them. <div eID="gen13641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13642" type="x-p"/> It is not only promised that God will guide the upright, and threatened that he will destroy the transgressors, but, that we may be the more fully assured of both, it is here represented as if the nature of the thing were such on both sides that it would do it itself. 1. The integrity of an honest man will itself be his guide in the way of duty and the way of safety. His principles are fixed, his rule is certain, and therefore his way is plain; his sincerity keeps him steady, and he needs not tack about every time the wind turns, having no other end to drive at than to keep a good conscience. <hi type="italic">Integrity and uprightness</hi> will <hi type="italic">preserve</hi> men, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">Ps. xxv. 21</reference>. 2. The iniquity of a bad man will itself be his ruin. As the plainness of a good man will be his protection, though he is ever so much exposed, so the perverseness of sinners will be their destruction, though they think themselves ever so well fortified. They shall fall into pits of their own digging, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.22">ch. v. 22</reference>.

<div eID="gen13642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13643" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death. <div eID="gen13643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13644" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The <hi type="italic">day of death</hi> will be a <hi type="italic">day of wrath.</hi> It is a messenger of God's wrath; therefore when Moses had meditated on man's mortality he takes occasion thence to admire <hi type="italic">the power of God's anger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.11">Ps. cx. 11</reference>. It is a debt owing, not to nature, but to God's justice. <hi type="italic">After death the judgment,</hi> and that is a <hi type="italic">day of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.17">Rev. vi. 17</reference>. 2. Riches will stand men in no stead that day. They will neither put by the stroke nor ease the pain, much less take out the sting; what profit will this world's birth-rights be of then? In the day of public judgments riches often expose men rather than protect them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Ezek. vii. 19</reference>. 3. It is righteousness only that will <hi type="italic">deliver from</hi> the evil of <hi type="italic">death.</hi> A good conscience will make death easy, and take off the terror of it; it is the privilege of the righteous only not to be hurt of the second death, and so not much hurt by the first.

<div eID="gen13644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13645" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> The righteousness of the perfect shall direct his way: but the wicked shall fall by his own wickedness. <hi type="super">6</hi> The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: but transgressors shall be taken in <hi type="italic">their own</hi> naughtiness. <div eID="gen13645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13646" type="x-p"/> These two verses are, in effect, the same, and both to the same purport with <reference osisRef="Prov.11.3">v. 3</reference>. For the truths are here of such certainty and weight that they cannot be too often inculcated. Let us govern ourselves by these principles. <div eID="gen13646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13647" type="x-p"/> I. That the ways of religion are plain and safe, and in them we may enjoy a holy security. A living principle of honesty and grace will be, 1. Our best direction in the right way, in every doubtful case to say to us, <hi type="italic">This is the way, walk in it.</hi> He that acts without a guide looks right on and sees his way before him. 2. Our best deliverance from every false way: <hi type="italic">The righteousness of the upright</hi> shall be armour of proof to them, to deliver them from the allurements of the devil and the world, and from their menaces. <div eID="gen13647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13648" type="x-p"/> The ways of wickedness are dangerous and destructive: <hi type="italic">The wicked shall fail</hi> into misery and ruin <hi type="italic">by their own wickedness,</hi> and be <hi type="italic">taken in their own naughtiness</hi> as in a snare. <hi type="italic">O Israel! thou hast destroyed thyself.</hi> Their sin will be their punishment; that very thing by which they contrived to shelter themselves will make against them.

<div eID="gen13648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13649" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> When a wicked man dieth, <hi type="italic">his</hi> expectation shall perish: and the hope of unjust <hi type="italic">men</hi> perisheth. <div eID="gen13649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13650" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Even wicked men, while they live, may keep up a confident expectation of a happiness when they die, or at least a happiness in this world. The hypocrite has his hope, in which he wraps himself as the spider in her web. The worldling expects great matters from his wealth; he calls it <hi type="italic">goods laid up for many years,</hi> and hopes to take his ease in it and to be merry; but in death their expectation will be frustrated: the worldling must leave this world which he expected to continue in and the hypocrite will come short of that world which he expected to remove to, <reference osisRef="Job.27.8">Job xxvii. 8</reference>. 2. It will be the great aggravation of the misery of wicked people that their hopes will sink into despair just when they expect them to be crowned with fruition. When a godly man dies his expectations are out-done, and all his fears vanish; but when a wicked man dies his expectations are dashed, dashed to pieces; in that very day his thoughts perish with which he had pleased himself, his hopes vanish.

<div eID="gen13650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13651" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead. <div eID="gen13651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13652" type="x-p"/> As always in death, so sometimes in life, the righteous are remarkably favoured and the wicked crossed. 1. Good people are helped out of the distresses which they thought themselves lost in, and their feet are set in a large room, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Ps. lxvi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">xxxiv. 19</reference>. God has found out a way to deliver his people even when they have despaired and their enemies have triumphed, as if the wilderness had shut them in. 2. The wicked have fallen into the distresses which they thought themselves far from, nay, which they had been instrumental to bring the righteous into, so that they seem to come in their stead, as a ransom for the just. Mordecai is saved from the gallows, Daniel from the lion's den, and Peter from the prison; and their persecutors <hi type="italic">come in their stead.</hi> The Israelites are delivered out of the Red Sea and the Egyptians drowned in it. So precious are the saints in God's eye that he <hi type="italic">gives men for them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.3-Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 3, 4</reference>.

<div eID="gen13652" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Common Truths.</title> <div sID="gen13653" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> An hypocrite with <hi type="italic">his</hi> mouth destroyeth his neighbour: but through knowledge shall the just be delivered. <div eID="gen13653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13654" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Hypocrisy designing ill. It is not only the murderer with his sword, but the <hi type="italic">hypocrite with his mouth,</hi> that <hi type="italic">destroys his neighbour,</hi> decoying him into sin, or into mischief, by the specious pretences of kindness and good-will. <hi type="italic">Death and life are in the power of the tongue,</hi> but no tongue more fatal than the flattering tongue. 2. Honesty defeating the design and escaping the snare: <hi type="italic">Through knowledge</hi> of the devices of Satan <hi type="italic">shall the just be delivered</hi> from the snares which the hypocrite has laid for him; seducers shall not deceive the elect. By the knowledge of God, and the scriptures, and their own hearts, shall the just be delivered from those that lie in wait to deceive, and so to destroy, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.18-Rom.16.19">Rom. xvi. 18, 19</reference>.

<div eID="gen13654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13655" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> When it goeth well with the righteous, the city rejoiceth: and when the wicked perish, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> shouting. <hi type="super">11</hi> By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked. <div eID="gen13655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13656" type="x-p"/> It is here observed, <div eID="gen13656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13657" type="x-p"/> I. That good men are generally well-beloved by their neighbours, but nobody cares for wicked people. 1. It is true there are some few that are enemies to the righteous, that are prejudiced against God and godliness, and are therefore vexed to see good men in power and prosperity; but all indifferent persons, even those that have no great stock of religion themselves, have a good word for a good man; and therefore <hi type="italic">when it goes well with the righteous,</hi> when they are advanced and put into a capacity of doing good according to their desire, it is so much the better for all about them, and <hi type="italic">the city rejoices.</hi> For the honour and encouragement of virtue, and as it is the accomplishment of the promise of God, we should be glad to see virtuous men prosper in the world, and brought into reputation. 2. Wicked people may perhaps have here and there a well-wisher among those who are altogether such as themselves, but among the generality of their neighbours they get ill-will; they may be feared, but they are not loved, and therefore <hi type="italic">when they perish there is shouting;</hi> every body takes a pleasure in seeing them disgraced and disarmed, removed out of places of trust and power, chased out of the world, and wishes no greater loss may come to the town, the rather because they hope <hi type="italic">the righteous may come in their stead,</hi> as they into trouble instead of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.8">v. 8</reference>. Let a sense of honour therefore keep us in the paths of virtue, that we may live desired and die lamented, and not be hissed off the stage, <reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job xxvii. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.52.6">Ps. lii. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen13657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13658" type="x-p"/> II. That there is good reason for this, because those that are good do good, but (<hi type="italic">as saith the proverb of the ancients) wickedness proceeds from the wicked.</hi> 1. <hi type="italic">Good men are public blessings</hi>—<hi type="italic">Vir bonus est commune bonum. By the blessing of the upright,</hi> the blessings with which they are blessed, which enlarge their sphere of usefulness,—by the blessings with which they bless their neighbours, their advice, their example, their prayers, and all the instances of their serviceableness to the public interest,—by the blessings with which God blesses others for their sake,—by these <hi type="italic">the city is exalted</hi> and made more comfortable to the inhabitants, and more considerable among its neighbours. 2. Wicked men are public nuisances, not only the burdens, but the plagues of their generation. The city is <hi type="italic">overthrown by the mouth of the wicked,</hi> whose evil communications corrupt good manners, are enough to debauch a town, to ruin virtue in it, and bring down the judgments of God upon it.

<div eID="gen13658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13659" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> He that is void of wisdom despiseth his neighbour: but a man of understanding holdeth his peace. <hi type="super">13</hi> A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter. <div eID="gen13659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13660" type="x-p"/> I. Silence is here recommended as an instance of true friendship, and a preservative of it, and therefore an evidence, 1. Of wisdom: <hi type="italic">A man of understanding,</hi> that has rule over his own spirit, if he be provoked, <hi type="italic">holds his peace,</hi> that he may neither give vent to his passion nor kindle the passion of others by any opprobrious language or peevish reflections. 2. Of sincerity: <hi type="italic">He that is of a faithful spirit,</hi> that is true, not only to his own promise, but to the interest of his friend, <hi type="italic">conceals every matter</hi> which, if divulged, may turn to the prejudice of his neighbour. <div eID="gen13660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13661" type="x-p"/> II. This prudent friendly concealment is here opposed to two very bad vices of the tongue:—1. Speaking scornfully of a man to his face: <hi type="italic">He that is void of wisdom</hi> discovers his folly by this; he <hi type="italic">despises his neighbour,</hi> calls him <hi type="italic">Raca,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Thou fool,</hi> upon the least provocation, and tramples upon him as not worthy to be set with the dogs of his flock. He undervalues himself who thus undervalues one that is made of the same mould. 2. Speaking spitefully of a man behind his back: <hi type="italic">A tale-bearer,</hi> that carries all the stories he can pick up, true or false, from house to house, to make mischief and sow discord, <hi type="italic">reveals secrets</hi> which he has been entrusted with, and so breaks the laws, and forfeits all the privileges, of friendship and conversation.

<div eID="gen13661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13662" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Where no counsel <hi type="italic">is,</hi> the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors <hi type="italic">there is</hi> safety. <div eID="gen13662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13663" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The bad omen of a kingdom's ruin: <hi type="italic">Where no counsel is,</hi> no consultation at all, but every thing done rashly, or no prudent consultation for the common good, but only caballing for parties and divided interests, <hi type="italic">the people fall,</hi> crumble into factions, fall to pieces, fall together by the ears, and fall an easy prey to their common enemies. Councils of war are necessary to the operations of war; two eyes see more than one; and mutual advice is in order to mutual assistance. 2. The good presage of a kingdom's prosperity: <hi type="italic">In the multitude of counsellors,</hi> that see their need one of another, and act in concert and with concern for the public welfare, <hi type="italic">there is safety;</hi> for what prudent methods one discerns not another may. In our private affairs we shall often find it to our advantage to advise with many; if they agree in their advice, our way will be the more clear; if they differ, we shall hear what is to be said on all sides, and be the better able to determine.

<div eID="gen13663" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Rewards of Righteousness.</title> <div sID="gen13664" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> He that is surety for a stranger shall smart <hi type="italic">for it:</hi> and he that hateth suretiship is sure. <div eID="gen13664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13665" type="x-p"/> Here we are taught, 1. In general, that we may not use our estates as we will (he that gave them to us has reserved to himself a power to direct us how we shall use them, for they are not our own; we are but stewards), and further that God in his law consults our interests and teaches us that charity which begins at home, as well as that which must not end there. There is a good husbandry which is good divinity, and a discretion in ordering our affairs which is part of the character of a good man, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.5">Ps. cxii. 5</reference>. Every man must be just to his family, else he is not true to his stewardship. 2. In particular, that we must not enter rashly into suretiship, (1.) Because there is danger of bringing ourselves into trouble by it, and our families too when we are gone: <hi type="italic">He that is surety for a stranger,</hi> for any one that asks him and promises him to be bound for him another time, for one whose person perhaps he knows, and thinks he knows his circumstances, but is mistaken, he <hi type="italic">shall smart for it. Contritione conteretur—he shall be certainly and sadly crushed and broken by it,</hi> and perhaps become a bankrupt. Our Lord Jesus was surety for us when we were strangers, nay, enemies, and he smarted for it; <hi type="italic">it pleased the Lord to bruise him.</hi> (2.) Because he that resolves against all such suretiship keeps upon sure grounds, which a man may do if he take care not to launch out any further into business than his own credit will carry him, so that he needs not ask others to be bound for him.

<div eID="gen13665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13666" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> A gracious woman retaineth honour: and strong <hi type="italic">men</hi> retain riches. <div eID="gen13666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13667" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. It is allowed that <hi type="italic">strong men retain riches,</hi> that those who bustle in the world, who are men of spirit and interest, and are able to make their part good against all who stand in their way, are likely to keep what they have and to get more, while those who are weak are preyed upon by all about them. 2. It is taken for granted that <hi type="italic">a gracious woman</hi> is as solicitous to preserve her reputation for wisdom and modesty, humility and courtesy, and all those other graces that are the true ornaments of her sex, as strong men are to secure their estates; and those women who are truly gracious will, in like manner, effectually secure their honour by their prudence and good conduct. <hi type="italic">A gracious woman</hi> is as honourable as a valiant man and her honour is as sure.

<div eID="gen13667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13668" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> cruel troubleth his own flesh. <div eID="gen13668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13669" type="x-p"/> It is a common principle, Every one for himself. <hi type="italic">Proximus egomet mihi—None so near to me as myself.</hi> Now, if this be rightly understood, it will be a reason for the cherishing of gracious dispositions in ourselves and the crucifying of corrupt ones. We are friends or enemies to ourselves, even in respect of present comfort, according as we are or are not governed by religious principles. 1. A <hi type="italic">merciful,</hi> tender, good humoured <hi type="italic">man, does good to his own soul,</hi> makes and keeps himself easy. He has the pleasure of doing his duty, and contributing to the comfort of those that are to him as <hi type="italic">his own soul;</hi> for <hi type="italic">we are members one of another.</hi> He that waters others with his temporal good things shall find that God will water him with his spiritual blessings, which will do the best <hi type="italic">good to his own soul.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa. lviii. 7</reference>, &c. <hi type="italic">If thou hide not thy eyes from thy own flesh,</hi> but do good to others, as to thyself, if thou do good with thy own soul and <hi type="italic">draw that out to the hungry,</hi> thou wilt do good to thy own soul; for the Lord shall <hi type="italic">satisfy thy soul</hi> and <hi type="italic">make fat thy bones.</hi> Some make it part of the character of a <hi type="italic">merciful man,</hi> that he will make much of himself; that disposition which inclines him to be charitable to others will oblige him to allow himself also that which is convenient and to <hi type="italic">enjoy the good of all his labour.</hi> We may by the <hi type="italic">soul</hi> understand the <hi type="italic">inward man,</hi> as the apostle calls it, and then it teaches us that the first and great act of mercy is to provide well for our own souls the necessary supports of the spiritual life. 2. A <hi type="italic">cruel,</hi> froward, ill-natured man, <hi type="italic">troubles his own flesh,</hi> and so his sin becomes his punishment; he starves and dies for want of what he has, because he has not a heart to use it either for the good of others of for his own. He is vexatious to his nearest relations, that are, and should be, to him as his own flesh, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.29">Eph. v. 29</reference>. Envy, and malice, and greediness of the world, are the rottenness of the bones and the consumption of the flesh.

<div eID="gen13669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13670" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> The wicked worketh a deceitful work: but to him that soweth righteousness <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a sure reward. <div eID="gen13670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13671" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Sinners put a most fatal cheat upon themselves: <hi type="italic">The wicked works a deceitful work,</hi> builds himself a house upon the sand, which will deceive him when the storm comes, promises himself <hi type="italic">that</hi> by his sin which he will never gain; nay, it is cutting his throat when it smiles upon him. <hi type="italic">Sin deceived me, and by it slew me.</hi> 2. Saints lay up the best securities for themselves: He <hi type="italic">that sows righteousness,</hi> that is good, and makes it his business to do good, with an eye to a future recompence, he shall have <hi type="italic">a sure reward;</hi> it is made as sure to him as eternal truth can make it. If the seedness fail not, the harvest shall not, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.8">Gal. vi. 8</reference>.

<div eID="gen13671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13672" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> As righteousness <hi type="italic">tendeth</hi> to life: so he that pursueth evil <hi type="italic">pursueth it</hi> to his own death. <div eID="gen13672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13673" type="x-p"/> It is here shown that righteousness, not only by the divine judgment, will end in life, and wickedness in death, but that righteousness, in its own nature, has a direct tendency to life and wickedness to death. 1. True holiness is true happiness; it is a preparative for it, a pledge and earnest of it. <hi type="italic">Righteousness</hi> inclines, disposes, and leads, the soul <hi type="italic">to life.</hi> 2. In like manner, those that indulge themselves in sin are fitting themselves for destruction. The more violent a man is in sinful pursuits the more eagerly bent he is upon his own destruction; he awakens it when it seemed to slumber and hastens it when it seemed to linger. <div eID="gen13673" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div sID="gen13674" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> They that are of a froward heart <hi type="italic">are</hi> abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but <hi type="italic">such as are</hi> upright in <hi type="italic">their</hi> way <hi type="italic">are</hi> his delight. <div eID="gen13674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13675" type="x-p"/> It concerns us to know what God hates and what he loves, that we may govern ourselves accordingly, may avoid his displeasure and recommend ourselves to his favour. Now here we are told, 1. That nothing is more offensive to God than hypocrisy and double-dealing, for these are signified by the word which we translate <hi type="italic">frowardness,</hi> pretending justice, but intending wrong, walking in crooked ways, to avoid discovery. Those <hi type="italic">are of a froward heart</hi> who act in contradiction to that which is good, under a profession of that which is good, and such are, more than any sinners, an <hi type="italic">abomination to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Isa. lxv. 5</reference>. 2. That nothing is more pleasing to God than sincerity and plain-dealing: <hi type="italic">Such as are upright in their way,</hi> such as aim and act with integrity, such as have their conversation in the world <hi type="italic">in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom,</hi> these God delights in, these he even boasts of (<hi type="italic">Hast thou considered my servant Job?</hi>) and will have us to admire. <hi type="italic">Behold an Israelite indeed!</hi>

<div eID="gen13675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13676" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> <hi type="italic">Though</hi> hand <hi type="italic">join</hi> in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered. <div eID="gen13676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13677" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. That confederacies in sin shall certainly be broken, and shall not avail to protect the sinners: <hi type="italic">Though hand join in hand,</hi> though there are many that concur by their practice to keep wickedness in countenance, and engage to stand by one another in defending it against all the attacks of virtue and justice,—though they are in league for the support and propagation of it,—though wicked children tread in the steps of their wicked parents, and resolve to keep up the trade, in defiance of religion,—yet all this will not protect them from the justice of God; they shall not be held guiltless; it will not excuse them to say that they did as the most did and as their company did; they <hi type="italic">shall not be unpunished;</hi> witness the flood that was brought upon a whole world of ungodly men. Their number, and strength, and unanimity in sin will stand them in no stead when the day of vengeance comes. 2. That entails of religion shall certainly be blessed: <hi type="italic">The seed of the righteous,</hi> that follow the steps of their righteousness, though they may fall into trouble, shall, in due time, <hi type="italic">be delivered.</hi> Though justice may come slowly to punish the wicked, and mercy may come slowly to save the righteous, yet both will come surely. Sometimes <hi type="italic">the seed of the righteous,</hi> though they are not themselves righteous, are delivered for the sake of their godly ancestors, as Israel often, and the seed of David.

<div eID="gen13677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13678" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, <hi type="italic">so is</hi> a fair woman which is without discretion. <div eID="gen13678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13679" type="x-p"/> By <hi type="italic">discretion</hi> here we must understand <hi type="italic">religion</hi> and <hi type="italic">grace,</hi> a true taste and relish (so the word signifies) of the honours and pleasures that attend an unspotted virtue; so that <hi type="italic">a woman without discretion</hi> is a woman of a loose and dissolute conversation; and then observe, 1. It is taken for granted here that beauty or comeliness of body is <hi type="italic">as a jewel of gold,</hi> a thing very valuable, and, where there is wisdom and grace to guard against the temptations of it, it is a great ornament, (<hi type="italic">Gratior est pulchro veniens de corpore virtus—Virtue appears peculiarly graceful when associated with beauty</hi>); but a foolish wanton woman, of a light carriage, is fitly compared to a swine, though she be ever so handsome, wallowing in the mire of filthy lusts, with which the mind and conscience are defiled, and, though washed, returning to them. 2. It is lamented that beauty should be so abused as it is by those that have not modesty with it. It seems ill-bestowed upon them; it is quite misplaced, <hi type="italic">as a jewel in a swine's snout,</hi> with which he roots in the dunghill. If beauty be not guarded by virtue, the virtue is exposed by the beauty. It may be applied to all other bodily endowments and accomplishments; it is a pity that those should have them who have not discretion to use them well.

<div eID="gen13679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13680" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> The desire of the righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> only good: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the expectation of the wicked <hi type="italic">is</hi> wrath. <div eID="gen13680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13681" type="x-p"/> This tells us what <hi type="italic">the desire</hi> and <hi type="italic">expectation of the righteous</hi> and <hi type="italic">of the wicked</hi> are and how they will prove, what they would have and what they shall have. 1. <hi type="italic">The righteous</hi> would have <hi type="italic">good, only good;</hi> all they desire is that it may go well with all about them; they wish no hurt to any, but happiness to all; as to themselves, their desire is not to gratify any evil lust, but to obtain the favour of a good God and to preserve the peace of a good conscience; and good they shall have, that good which they desire, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Ps. xxxvii. 4</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">The wicked</hi> would have <hi type="italic">wrath;</hi> they desire the woeful day, that God's judgments may gratify their passion and revenge, may remove those that stand in their way, and that they may make an advantage to themselves by fishing in troubled waters; and wrath they shall have, so shall their doom be. They expect and desire mischief to others, but it shall return upon themselves; as they loved cursing, they shall have enough of it.

<div eID="gen13681" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Praise of Liberality.</title> <div sID="gen13682" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> that withholdeth more than is meet, but <hi type="italic">it tendeth</hi> to poverty. <div eID="gen13682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13683" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is possible a man may grow rich by prudently spending what he has, may scatter in works of piety, charity, and generosity, and yet may increase; nay, by that means may increase, as the corn is increased by being sown. By cheerfully using what we have our spirits are exhilarated, and so fitted for the business we have to do, by minding which closely what we have is increased; it gains a reputation which contributes to the increase. But it is especially to be ascribed to God; he blesses the giving hand, and so makes it a getting hand, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.20">2 Cor. ix. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Give, and it shall be given you.</hi> 2. It is possible a man may grow poor by meanly sparing what he has, <hi type="italic">withholding more than is meet,</hi> not paying just debts, not relieving the poor, not providing what is convenient for the family, not allowing necessary expenses for the preservation of the goods; this <hi type="italic">tends to poverty;</hi> it cramps men's ingenuity and industry, weakens their interest, destroys their credit, and forfeits the blessing of God: and, let men be ever so saving of what they have, if God blast it and blow upon it, it comes to nothing. <hi type="italic">A fire not blown</hi> shall <hi type="italic">consume it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">Hag. i. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">9</reference>.

<div eID="gen13683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13684" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself. <div eID="gen13684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13685" type="x-p"/> So backward we are to works of charity, and so ready to think that giving undoes us, that we need to have it very much pressed upon us how much it is for our own advantage to do good to others, as before, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.17">v. 17</reference>. 1. We shall have the comfort of it in our own bosoms: <hi type="italic">The liberal soul,</hi> the soul of blessing, that prays for the afflicted and provides for them, that scatters blessings with gracious lips and generous hands, that soul <hi type="italic">shall be made fat</hi> with true pleasure and enriched with more grace. 2. We shall have the recompence of it both from God and man: <hi type="italic">He that waters</hi> others with the streams of his bounty <hi type="italic">shall be also watered himself;</hi> God will certainly return it in the dews, in the plentiful showers, of his blessing, which he will <hi type="italic">pour out, till there be not room enough to receive it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.10">Mal. iii. 10</reference>. Men that have any sense of gratitude will return it if there be occasion; the <hi type="italic">merciful shall find mercy</hi> and the kind be kindly dealt with. 3. We shall be enabled still to do yet more good: <hi type="italic">He that waters, even he shall be as rain</hi> (so some read it); he shall be recruited as the clouds are which return after the rain, and shall be further useful and acceptable, as the rain to the new-mown grass. <hi type="italic">He that teaches shall learn</hi> (so the Chaldee reads it); he that uses his knowledge in teaching others shall himself be taught of God; to him that has, and uses what he has, more shall be given.

<div eID="gen13685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13686" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> upon the head of him that selleth <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen13686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13687" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What use we are to make of the gifts of God's bounty; we must not hoard them up merely for our own advantage, that we may be enriched by them, but we must bring them forth for the benefit of others, that they may be supported and maintained by them. It is a sin, when corn is dear and scarce, to withhold it, in hopes that it will still grow dearer, so to keep up and advance the market, when it is already so high that the poor suffer by it; and at such a time it is the duty of those that have stocks of corn by them to consider the poor, and to be willing to sell at the market-price, to be content with moderate profit, and not aim to make a gain of God's judgments. It is a noble and extensive piece of charity for those that have stores wherewithal to do it to help to keep the markets low when the price of our commodities grows excessive. 2. What regard we are to have to the voice of the people. We are not to think it an indifferent thing, and not worth heeding, whether we have the ill will and word, or the good will and word, of our neighbours, their prayers or their curses; for here we are taught to dread their curses, and forego our own profit rather than incur them; and to court their blessings, and be at some expense to purchase them. Sometimes, <hi type="italic">vox populi est vox Dei</hi>—<hi type="italic">the voice of the people is the voice of God.</hi>

<div eID="gen13687" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Folly and Misery of Sinners.</title> <div sID="gen13688" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour: but he that seeketh mischief, it shall come unto him. <div eID="gen13688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13689" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Those that are industrious to do good in the world get themselves beloved both with God and man: <hi type="italic">He that rises early to that which is good</hi> (so the word is), that seeks opportunities of serving his friends and relieving the poor, and lays out himself therein, <hi type="italic">procures favour.</hi> All about him love him, and speak well of him, and will be ready to do him a kindness; and, which is better than that, better than life, he has God's lovingkindness. 2. Those that are industrious to do mischief are preparing ruin for themselves: <hi type="italic">It shall come unto them;</hi> some time or other they will be paid in their own coin. And, observe, <hi type="italic">seeking mischief</hi> is here set in opposition to <hi type="italic">seeking good;</hi> for those that are not doing good are doing hurt.

<div eID="gen13689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13690" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch. <div eID="gen13690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13691" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Our riches will fail us when we are in the greatest need: <hi type="italic">He that trusts in them,</hi> as if they would secure him the favour of God and be his protection and portion, <hi type="italic">shall fall,</hi> as a man who lays his weight on a broken reed, which will not only disappoint him, but run into his hand and pierce him. 2. Our righteousness will stand us in stead when our riches fail us: <hi type="italic">The righteous shall</hi> then <hi type="italic">flourish as a branch,</hi> the branch of righteousness, like a tree whose leaf shall not wither, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Ps. i. 3</reference>. Even in death, when riches fail men, the <hi type="italic">bones</hi> of the righteous <hi type="italic">shall flourish as a herb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.14">Isa. lxvi. 14</reference>. When those that take root in the world wither those that are grafted into Christ and partake of his root and fatness shall be fruitful and flourishing.

<div eID="gen13691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13692" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> He that troubleth his own house shall inherit the wind: and the fool <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> servant to the wise of heart. <div eID="gen13692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13693" type="x-p"/> Two extremes in the management of family-affairs are here condemned and the ill consequences of them foretold:—1. Carefulness and carnal policy, on the one hand. There are those that by their extreme earnestness in pursuit of the world, their anxiety about their business and fretfulness about their losses, their strictness with their servants and their niggardliness towards their families, <hi type="italic">trouble their own houses</hi> and give continual vexation to all about them; while others think, by supporting factions and feuds in their families, which are really a trouble to their houses, to serve some turn for themselves, and either to get or to save by it. But they will both be disappointed; they will <hi type="italic">inherit the wind.</hi> All they will get by these arts will not only be empty and worthless as the wind, but noisy and troublesome, vanity and vexation. 2. Carelessness and want of common prudence, on the other. He that is a fool in his business, that either minds it not or goes awkwardly about it, that has no contrivance and consideration, no only loses his reputation and interest, but becomes a <hi type="italic">servant to the wise in heart.</hi> He is impoverished, and forced to work for his living; while those that manage wisely raise themselves, and come to have dominion over him, and others like him. It is rational, and very fit, that <hi type="italic">the fool</hi> should <hi type="italic">be servant to the wise in heart,</hi> and upon that account, among others, we are bound to submit our wills to the will of God, and to be subject to him, because we are fools and he is infinitely wise.

<div eID="gen13693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13694" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> The fruit of the righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> a tree of life; and he that winneth souls <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise. <div eID="gen13694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13695" type="x-p"/> This shows what great blessings good men are, especially those that are eminently wise, to the places where they live, and therefore how much to be valued. 1. The righteous are as <hi type="italic">trees of life;</hi> the fruits of their piety and charity, their instructions, reproofs, examples, and prayers, their interest in heaven, and their influence upon earth, are like the fruits of that tree, precious and useful, contributing to the support and nourishment of the spiritual life in many; they are the ornaments of paradise, God's church on earth, for whose sake it stands. 2. The wise are something more; they are as trees of knowledge, not forbidden, but commanded knowledge. <hi type="italic">He that is wise,</hi> by communicating his wisdom, <hi type="italic">wins souls,</hi> wins upon them to bring them in love with God and holiness, and so wins them over into the interests of God's kingdom among men. The wise are said to <hi type="italic">turn many to righteousness,</hi> and that is the same with winning souls here, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.3">Dan. xii. 3</reference>. Abraham's proselytes are called <hi type="italic">the souls that he had gotten,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.12.5">Gen. xii. 5</reference>. Those that would win souls have need of wisdom to know how to deal with them; and those that do win souls show that they are wise.

<div eID="gen13695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13696" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> Behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth: much more the wicked and the sinner. <div eID="gen13696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13697" type="x-p"/> This, I think, is the only one of Solomon's proverbs that has that note of attention prefixed to it, <hi type="italic">Behold!</hi> which intimates that it contains not only an evident truth, which may be beheld, but an eminent truth, which must be considered. 1. Some understand both parts of a recompence in displeasure: <hi type="italic">The righteous,</hi> if they do amiss, shall be punished for their offences in this world; much more shall wicked people be punished for theirs, which are committed, not through infirmity, but with a high hand. If judgment begin at the house of God, what will become of the ungodly? <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17-1Pet.4.18">1 Pet. iv. 17, 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.31">Luke xxiii. 31</reference>. 2. I rather understand it of a recompence of reward to the righteous and punishment to sinners. Let us behold providential retributions. There are some recompences <hi type="italic">in the earth,</hi> in this world, and in the things of this world, which prove that <hi type="italic">verily there is a God that judges in the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.11">Ps. lviii. 11</reference>); but they are not universal; many sins go unpunished in the earth, and services unrewarded, which indicates that there is a judgment to come, and that there will be more exact and full retributions in the future state. Many times <hi type="italic">the righteous</hi> are <hi type="italic">recompensed</hi> for their righteousness here <hi type="italic">in the earth,</hi> though that is not the principal, much less the only reward either intended for them or intended by them; but whatever the word of God has promised them, or the wisdom of God sees good for them, they shall have <hi type="italic">in the earth. The wicked</hi> also, <hi type="italic">and the sinner,</hi> are sometimes remarkably punished in this life, nations, families, particular persons. And if the righteous, who do not deserve the least reward, yet have part of their recompence here on earth, much more shall the wicked, who deserve the greatest punishment, have part of their punishment on earth, as an earnest of worse to come. Therefore <hi type="italic">stand in awe and sin not.</hi> If those have two heavens that merit none, much more shall those have two hells that merit both.  <chapter eID="Prov.11"/> <div eID="gen13697" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv27"/><title type="x-s3">Advantages of the Righteous.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv27"/> <div sID="gen13699" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof <hi type="italic">is</hi> brutish. <div eID="gen13699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13700" type="x-p"/> We are here taught to try whether we have grace or no by enquiring how we stand affected to the means of grace. 1. Those that have grace and love it will delight in all the instructions that are given them by way of counsel; admonition, or reproof, by the word or providence of God; they will value a good education, and think it not a hardship, but a happiness, to be under a strict and prudent discipline. Those that love a faithful ministry, that value it, and sit under it with pleasure, make it to appear that they <hi type="italic">love knowledge.</hi> 2. Those show themselves not only void of grace, but void of common sense, that take it as an affront to be told of their faults, and an imposition upon their liberty to be put in mind of their duty: <hi type="italic">He that hates reproof is</hi> not only foolish, but <hi type="italic">brutish,</hi> like the horse and the mule that have no understanding, or the ox that kicks against the goad. Those that desire to live in loose families and societies, where they may be under no check, that stifle the convictions of their own consciences, and count those their enemies that tell them the truth, are the <hi type="italic">brutish</hi> here meant.

<div eID="gen13700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13701" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> A good <hi type="italic">man</hi> obtaineth favour of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but a man of wicked devices will he condemn. <div eID="gen13701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13702" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. We are really as we are with God. Those are happy, truly happy, for ever happy, that <hi type="italic">obtain favour of the Lord,</hi> though the world frown upon them, and they find little favour with men; for in God's favour is life, and that is the fountain of all good. On the other hand those are miserable whom <hi type="italic">he condemns,</hi> however men may applaud them, and cry them up; whom he condemns he condemns to the second death. 2. We are with God as we are with men, as we have our conversation in this world. Our Father judges of his children very much by their conduct one to another; and therefore <hi type="italic">a good man,</hi> that is merciful, and charitable, and does good, <hi type="italic">draws out favour from the Lord</hi> by his prayers; but a malicious man, that devises wickedness against his neighbours, <hi type="italic">he will condemn,</hi> as unworthy of a place in his kingdom.

<div eID="gen13702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13703" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> A man shall not be established by wickedness: but the root of the righteous shall not be moved. <div eID="gen13703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13704" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Though men may advance themselves by sinful arts, they cannot by such arts settle and secure themselves; though they may get large estates they cannot get such as will abide: <hi type="italic">A man shall not be established by wickedness;</hi> it may set him in high places, but they are slippery places, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.18">Ps. lxxiii. 18</reference>. That prosperity which is raised by sin is built on the sand, and so it will soon appear. 2. Though good men may have but little of the world, yet that little will last, and what is honestly got will wear well: <hi type="italic">The root of the righteous shall not be moved,</hi> though their branches may be shaken. Those that by faith are rooted in Christ are firmly fixed; in him their comfort and happiness are so rooted as never to be rooted up.

<div eID="gen13704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13705" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> A virtuous woman <hi type="italic">is</hi> a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed <hi type="italic">is</hi> as rottenness in his bones. <div eID="gen13705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13706" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. He that is blessed with a good wife is as happy as if he were upon the throne, for she is no less than <hi type="italic">a crown</hi> to him. <hi type="italic">A virtuous woman,</hi> that is pious and prudent, ingenious and industrious, that is active for the good of her family and looks well to the ways of her household, that makes conscience of her duty in every relation, a woman of spirit, that can bear crosses without disturbance, such a one owns her husband for her head, and therefore she <hi type="italic">is a crown</hi> to him, not only a credit and honour to him, as <hi type="italic">a crown</hi> is an ornament, but supports and keeps up his authority in his family, as <hi type="italic">a crown</hi> is an ensign of power. She is submissive and faithful to him and by her example teaches his children and servants to be so too. 2. He that is plagued with a bad wife is as miserable as if he were upon the dunghill; for she is no better than <hi type="italic">rottenness in his bones,</hi> an incurable disease, besides that <hi type="italic">she makes him ashamed.</hi> She that is silly and slothful, wasteful and wanton, passionate and ill-tongued, ruins both the credit and comfort of her husband. If he go abroad, his head is hung down, for his wife's faults turn to his reproach. If he retire into himself, his heart is sunk; he is continually uneasy; it is an affliction that preys much upon the spirits.

<div eID="gen13706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13707" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> The thoughts of the righteous <hi type="italic">are</hi> right: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the counsels of the wicked <hi type="italic">are</hi> deceit. <div eID="gen13707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13708" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The word of God is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart, and judges them. We mistake if we imagine that thoughts are free. No, they are under the divine cognizance, and therefore under the divine command. 2. We ought to be observers of the thoughts and intents of our own hearts, and to judge of ourselves by them; for they are the first-born of the soul, that have most of its image undisguised. Right thoughts are a righteous man's best evidences, as nothing more certainly proves a man wicked than wicked contrivances and designs. A good man may have in his mind bad suggestions, but he does not indulge them and harbour them till they are ripened into bad projects and resolutions. 3. It is a man's honour to mean honestly, and to have his thoughts right, though a word or action may be misplaced, or mistimed, or at least misinterpreted. But it is a man's shame to lie always at catch, to act with deceit, with trick and design, not only with a long reach, but with an overreach.

<div eID="gen13708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13709" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> The words of the wicked <hi type="italic">are</hi> to lie in wait for blood: but the mouth of the upright shall deliver them. <div eID="gen13709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13710" type="x-p"/> In the foregoing verse the <hi type="italic">thoughts</hi> of the wicked and righteous were compared; here their <hi type="italic">words,</hi> and those are as the abundance of the heart is. 1. Wicked people speak mischief to their neighbours; and wicked indeed those are whose <hi type="italic">words</hi> are to <hi type="italic">lie in wait for blood;</hi> their tongues are swords to those that stand in their way, to good men whom they hate and persecute. See an instance, <reference osisRef="Luke.20.20-Luke.20.21">Luke xx. 20, 21</reference>. 2. Good men speak help to their neighbours: The <hi type="italic">mouth of the upright</hi> is ready to be opened in the cause of those that are oppressed (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.8">ch. xxxi. 8</reference>), to plead for them, to witness for them, and so to <hi type="italic">deliver them,</hi> particularly those whom the wicked <hi type="italic">lie in wait</hi> for. A man may sometimes do a very good work with one good word.

<div eID="gen13710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13711" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The wicked are overthrown, and <hi type="italic">are</hi> not: but the house of the righteous shall stand. <div eID="gen13711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13712" type="x-p"/> We are here taught as before (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.3 Prov.10.25 Prov.10.30">v. 3 and ch. x. 25, 30</reference>), 1. That the <hi type="italic">triumphing of the wicked is short.</hi> They may be exalted for a while, but in a little time they are <hi type="italic">overthrown and are not;</hi> their trouble proves their overthrow, and those who made a great show disappear, and their place knows them no more. <hi type="italic">Turn the wicked, and they are not;</hi> they stand in such a slippery place that the least touch of trouble brings them down, like the apples of Sodom, which look fair, but touch them and they go to dust. 2. That the prosperity of the righteous has a good bottom and will endure. Death will remove them, but their <hi type="italic">house</hi> shall <hi type="italic">stand,</hi> their families shall be kept up, and the generation of the upright shall be blessed.

<div eID="gen13712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13713" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> A man shall be commended according to his wisdom: but he that is of a perverse heart shall be despised. <div eID="gen13713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13714" type="x-p"/> We are here told whence to expect a good name. Reputation is what most have a high regard to and stand much upon. Now it is certain, 1. The best reputation is that which attends virtue and serious piety, and the prudent conduct of life: <hi type="italic">A man shall be commended</hi> by all that are wise and good, in conformity to the judgment of God himself, which we are sure is <hi type="italic">according to truth,</hi> not according to his riches or preferments, his craft and subtlety, but <hi type="italic">according to his wisdom,</hi> the honesty of his designs and the prudent choice of means to compass them. 2. The worst reproach is that which follows wickedness and an opposition to that which is good: <hi type="italic">He that is of a perverse heart,</hi> that turns aside to crooked ways, and goes on frowardly in them, <hi type="italic">shall be despised.</hi> Providence will bring him to poverty and contempt, and all that have a true sense of honour will despise him as unworthy to be dealt with and unfit to be trusted, as a blemish and scandal to mankind.

<div eID="gen13714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13715" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is</hi> despised, and hath a servant, <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than he that honoureth himself, and lacketh bread. <div eID="gen13715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13716" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is the folly of some that they covet to make a great figure abroad, take place, and take state, as persons of quality, and yet want necessaries at home, and, if their debts were paid, would not be worth a morsel of bread, nay, perhaps, pinch their bellies to put it on their backs, that they may appear very gay, because fine feathers make fine birds. 2. The condition and character of those is every way better who content themselves in a lower sphere, where they are despised for the plainness of their dress and the meanness of their post, that they may be able to afford themselves, not only necessaries, but conveniences, in their own houses, not only bread, but a servant to attend them and take some of their work off their hands.
