Those that contrive to live plentifully and comfortably at home are to be preferred before those that affect nothing so much as to appear splendid abroad, though they have not wherewithal to maintain their appearance, whose hearts are unhumbled when their condition is low.

<div eID="gen13716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13717" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> A righteous <hi type="italic">man</hi> regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked <hi type="italic">are</hi> cruel. <div eID="gen13717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13718" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. To how great a degree a good man will be merciful; he has not only a compassion for the human nature under its greatest abasements, but he regards even <hi type="italic">the life of his beast,</hi> not only because it is his servant, but because it is God's creature, and in conformity to Providence, which <hi type="italic">preserves man and beast.</hi> The beasts that are under our care must be provided for, must have convenient food and rest, must in no case be abused or tyrannised over. Balaam was checked for beating his ass. The law took care for oxen. Those therefore are unrighteous men that are not just to the brute-creatures; those that are furious and barbarous to them evidence, and confirm in themselves, a habit of barbarity, and help to make the creation groan, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.22">Rom. viii. 22</reference>. 2. To how great a degree a wicked man will be unmerciful; even his <hi type="italic">tender mercies</hi> are <hi type="italic">cruel;</hi> that natural compassion which is in him, as a man, is lost, and, by the power of corruption, is turned into hard-heartedness; even that which they will have to pass for compassion is really cruel, as Pilate's resolution concerning Christ the innocent, <hi type="italic">I will chastise him and let him go.</hi> Their pretended kindnesses are only a cover for purposed cruelties.

<div eID="gen13718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13719" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread: but he that followeth vain <hi type="italic">persons is</hi> void of understanding. <div eID="gen13719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13720" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is men's wisdom to mind their business and follow an honest calling, for that is the way, by the blessing of God, to get a livelihood: <hi type="italic">He that tills his land,</hi> of which he is either the owner or the occupant, that keeps to his word and is willing to take pains, if he do not raise an estate by it (what need is there of that?), yet he <hi type="italic">shall be satisfied with bread,</hi> shall have food convenient for himself and his family, enough to bear his charges comfortably through the world. Even the sentence of wrath has this mercy in it, Thou shalt <hi type="italic">eat bread,</hi> though it be <hi type="italic">in the sweat of thy face.</hi> Cain was denied this, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.12">Gen. iv. 12</reference>. Be busy, and that is the true way to be easy. Keep thy shop and thy shop will keep thee. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt eat the labour of thy hands.</hi> 2. It is men's folly to neglect their business. Those are <hi type="italic">void of understanding</hi> that do so, for then they fall in with idle companions and follow them in their evil courses, and so come to want bread, at least bread of their own, and make themselves burdensome to others, eating the bread out of other people's mouths.

<div eID="gen13720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13721" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The wicked desireth the net of evil <hi type="italic">men:</hi> but the root of the righteous yieldeth <hi type="italic">fruit.</hi> <div eID="gen13721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13722" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What is the care and aim of a wicked man; he would do mischief: He <hi type="italic">desires the net of evil men.</hi> "Oh that I were but as cunning as such a man, to make a hand of those I deal with, that I had but his art of over-reaching, that I could but take my revenge on one I have spite to as effectually as he can!" He desires the <hi type="italic">strong-hold, or fortress,</hi> of evil men (so some read it), to act securely in doing mischief, that it may not turn upon him. 2. What is the care and aim of a good man: His <hi type="italic">root yields fruit,</hi> and is his strength and stability, and that is it that he desires, to do good and to be fixed and confirmed in doing good. The wicked desires only a net wherewith to fish for himself; the righteous desires to yield fruit for the benefit of others and God's glory, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.6">Rom. xiv. 6</reference>.  <div eID="gen13722" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv28"/><title type="x-s3">Truth and Falsehood.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv28"/> <div sID="gen13723" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> The wicked is snared by the transgression of <hi type="italic">his</hi> lips: but the just shall come out of trouble. <div eID="gen13723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13724" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. The wicked entangling themselves in trouble by their folly, when God in justice leaves them to themselves. They are often <hi type="italic">snared by the transgression of their lips</hi> and their throats are cut with their own tongues. By <hi type="italic">speaking evil of dignities</hi> they expose themselves to public justice; by giving ill language they become obnoxious to private resentments, are sued for defamation, and actions on the case for words are brought against them. Many a man has paid dearly in this world for the transgression of his lips, and has felt the lash on his back for want of a bridle upon his tongue, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. 2. The righteous extricating themselves out of trouble by their own wisdom, when God in mercy comes in for their succour: <hi type="italic">The just shall come out</hi> of such troubles as the wicked throw themselves headlong into. It is intimated that the just may perhaps come into trouble; but, <hi type="italic">though they fall, they shall not be utterly cast down,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">Ps. xxxiv. 19</reference>.

<div eID="gen13724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13725" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of <hi type="italic">his</hi> mouth: and the recompence of a man's hands shall be rendered unto him. <div eID="gen13725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13726" type="x-p"/> We are here assured, for our quickening to every good word and work, 1. That even good words will turn to a good account (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">A man shall be satisfied with good</hi> (that is, he shall gain present comfort, that inward pleasure which is truly satisfying) <hi type="italic">by the fruit of his mouth,</hi> by the good he does with his pious discourse and prudent advice. While we are teaching others we may ourselves learn, and feed on the bread of life we break to others. 2. That good works, much more, will be abundantly rewarded: The <hi type="italic">recompence of a man's hands</hi> for all his work and labour of love, all he has done for the glory of God and the good of his generation, <hi type="italic">shall be rendered unto him,</hi> and he shall reap as he has sown. Or it may be understood of the general rule of justice; God will <hi type="italic">render to every man according to his work,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.6">Rom. ii. 6</reference>.

<div eID="gen13726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13727" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The way of a fool <hi type="italic">is</hi> right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise. <div eID="gen13727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13728" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What it is that keeps a fool from being wise: <hi type="italic">His way is right in his own eyes;</hi> he thinks he is in the right in every thing he does, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> asks no advice, because he does not apprehend he needs it; he is confident he knows the way, and cannot miss it, and therefore never enquires the way. The rule he goes by is to do that which is <hi type="italic">right in his own eyes,</hi> to walk in the way of his heart. <hi type="italic">Quicquid libet, licet—He makes his will his law.</hi> He is a fool that is governed by his eye, and not by his conscience. 2. What it is that keeps a wise man from being a fool; he is willing to be advised, desires to have counsel given him, and <hi type="italic">hearkens to counsel,</hi> being diffident of his own judgment and having a value for the direction of those that are wise and good. He is wise (it is a sign he is so, and he is likely to continue so) whose ear is always open to good advice.

<div eID="gen13728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13729" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> A fool's wrath is presently known: but a prudent <hi type="italic">man</hi> covereth shame. <div eID="gen13729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13730" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Passion is folly: <hi type="italic">A fool is known by his anger</hi> (so some read it); not but that a wise man may be angry when there is just cause for it, but then he has his anger under check and direction, is <hi type="italic">lord of his anger,</hi> whereas a fool's anger lords it over him. He that, when he is provoked, breaks out into indecent expressions, in words or behaviour, whose passion alters his countenance, makes him outrageous, and leads him to forget himself, <hi type="italic">Nabal</hi> certainly is his name and <hi type="italic">folly is with him. A fool's indignation is known in the day;</hi> he proclaims it openly, whatever company he is in. Or it is known in the day he is provoked; he cannot defer showing his resentments. Those that are soon angry, that are quickly put into a flame by the least spark, have not that rule which they ought to have over their own spirits. 2. Meekness is wisdom: <hi type="italic">A prudent man covers shame.</hi> (1.) He covers the passion that is in his own breast; when his <hi type="italic">spirit is stirred,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">heart hot within him,</hi> he keeps his mouth as with a bridle, and suppresses his resentments, by smothering and stifling them. Anger is shame, and, though a wise man be not perfectly free from it, yet he is ashamed of it, rebukes it, and suffers not the evil spirit to speak. (2.) He covers the provocation that is given him, the indignity that is done him, winks at it, covers it as much as may be from himself, that he may not carry his resentments of it too far. It is a kindness to ourselves, and contributes to the repose of our own minds, to extenuate and excuse the injuries and affronts that we receive, instead of aggravating them and making the worst of them, as we are apt to do.

<div eID="gen13730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13731" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">He that</hi> speaketh truth sheweth forth righteousness: but a false witness deceit. <div eID="gen13731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13732" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A faithful witness commended for an honest man. <hi type="italic">He that</hi> makes conscience of <hi type="italic">speaking truth,</hi> and representing every thing fairly, to the best of his knowledge, whether in judgment or in common conversation, whether he be upon his oath or no, he <hi type="italic">shows forth righteousness;</hi> he makes it to appear that he is governed and actuated by the principles and laws of righteousness, and he promotes justice by doing honour to it and serving the administration of it. 2. A false witness condemned for a cheat; he <hi type="italic">shows forth deceit,</hi> not only how little conscience he makes of deceiving those he deals with, but how much pleasure he takes in it, and that he is possessed by a lying spirit, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.3-Jer.9.5">Jer. ix. 3-5</reference>. We are all concerned to possess ourselves with a dread and detestation of the sin of lying (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.163">Ps. cxix. 163</reference>) and with a reigning principle of honesty.

<div eID="gen13732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13733" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise <hi type="italic">is</hi> health. <div eID="gen13733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13734" type="x-p"/> The tongue is death or life, poison or medicine, as it is used. 1. There are words that are cutting and killing, that are <hi type="italic">like the piercings of a sword.</hi> Opprobrious words grieve the spirits of those to whom they are spoken, and cut them to the heart. Slanders, like a sword, wound the reputation of those of whom they are uttered, and perhaps incurably. Whisperings and evil surmises, like a sword, divide and cut asunder the bounds of love and friendship, and separate those that have been dearest to each other. 2. There are words that are curing and healing: <hi type="italic">The tongue of the wise is health,</hi> closing up those wounds which the backbiting tongue had given, making all whole again, restoring peace, and accommodating matters in variance and persuading to reconciliation. Wisdom will find out proper remedies against the mischiefs that are made by detraction and evil-speaking.

<div eID="gen13734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13735" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue <hi type="italic">is</hi> but for a moment. <div eID="gen13735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13736" type="x-p"/> Be it observed, to the honour of truth, that sacred thing, 1. That, if truth be spoken, it will hold good, and, whoever may be disobliged by it and angry at it, yet it will keep its ground. Great is the truth and will prevail. What is true will be always true; we may abide by it, and need not fear being disproved and put to shame. 2. That, if truth be denied, yet in time it will transpire. A <hi type="italic">lying tongue,</hi> that puts false colours upon things, <hi type="italic">is but for a moment.</hi> The lie will be disproved. The liar, when he comes to be examined, will be found in several stories, and not consistent with himself as he is that speaks truth; and, when he is found in a lie, he cannot gain his point, nor will he afterwards be credited. Truth may be eclipsed, but it will come to light. Those therefore that make a lie their refuge will find it a refuge of lies.  <div eID="gen13736" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv29"/><title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv29"/> <div sID="gen13737" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Deceit <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the heart of them that imagine evil: but to the counsellors of peace <hi type="italic">is</hi> joy. <div eID="gen13737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13738" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that devise mischief contrive, for the accomplishing of it, how to impose upon others; but it will prove, in the end, that they deceive themselves. Those that <hi type="italic">imagine evil,</hi> under colour of friendship, have their hearts full of this and the other advantage and satisfaction which they shall gain by it, but it is all a cheat. Let them imagine it ever so artfully, deceivers will be deceived. 2. Those that consult the good of their neighbours, that study the things which make for peace and give peaceable advice, promote healing attempts and contrive healing methods, and, according as their sphere is, further the public welfare, will have not only the credit, but the comfort of it. They will have joy and success, perhaps beyond their expectation. <hi type="italic">Blessed are the peace-makers.</hi>

<div eID="gen13738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13739" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> There shall no evil happen to the just: but the wicked shall be filled with mischief. <div eID="gen13739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13740" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Piety is a sure protection. If men be sincerely righteous, the righteous God has engaged that no evil shall happen to them. He will, by the power of his grace in them, that principle of justice, keep them from the evil of sin; so that, though they be tempted, yet they shall not be overcome by the temptation, and though they may come into trouble, into many troubles, yet to them those troubles shall have no evil in them, whatever they have to others (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.10">Ps. xci. 10</reference>), for they shall be overruled to work for their good. 2. Wickedness is as sure a destruction. Those that live in contempt of God and man, that are set on mischief, with mischief they <hi type="italic">shall be filled.</hi> They shall be more mischievous, shall be <hi type="italic">filled with all unrighteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.29">Rom. i. 29</reference>. Or they shall be made miserable with the mischiefs that shall come upon them. Those that delight in mischief shall have enough of it. Some read the whole verse thus, <hi type="italic">There shall no evil happen to the just, though the wicked be filled with mischief</hi> and spite against them. They shall be safe under the protection of Heaven, though hell itself break loose upon them.

<div eID="gen13740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13741" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Lying lips <hi type="italic">are</hi> abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but they that deal truly <hi type="italic">are</hi> his delight. <div eID="gen13741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13742" type="x-p"/> We are here taught, 1. To hate lying, and to keep at the utmost distance from it, because it is an abomination to the Lord, and renders those abominable in his sight that allow themselves in it, not only because it is a breach of his law, but because it is destructive to human society. 2. To make conscience of truth, not only in our words, but in all our actions, because those that <hi type="italic">deal truly</hi> and sincerely in all their dealings are <hi type="italic">his delight,</hi> and he is well pleased with them. We delight to converse with, and make use of, those that are honest and that we may put a confidence in; such therefore let us be, that we may recommend ourselves to the favour both of God and man.

<div eID="gen13742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13743" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> A prudent man concealeth knowledge: but the heart of fools proclaimeth foolishness. <div eID="gen13743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13744" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. He that is wise does not affect to proclaim his wisdom, and it is his honour that he does not. He communicates his knowledge when it may turn to the edification of others, but he conceals it when the showing of it would only tend to his own commendation. Knowing men, if they be prudent men, will carefully avoid every thing that savours of ostentation, and not take all occasions to show their learning and reading, but only to use it for good purposes, and then let <hi type="italic">their own works praise them. Ars est celare artem—The perfection of art is to conceal it.</hi> 2. He that is foolish cannot avoid proclaiming his folly, and it is his shame that he cannot: <hi type="italic">The heart of fools,</hi> by their foolish words and actions, <hi type="italic">proclaims foolishness;</hi> either they do not desire to hide it, so little sense have they of good and evil, honour and dishonour, or they know not how to hide it, so little discretion have they in the management of themselves, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.3">Eccl. x. 3</reference>.

<div eID="gen13744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13745" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> The hand of the diligent shall bear rule: but the slothful shall be under tribute. <div eID="gen13745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13746" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Industry is the way to preferment. Solomon advanced Jeroboam because he saw that he was an industrious young man, and minded his business, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.28">1 Kings xi. 28</reference>. Men that take pains in study and serviceableness will thereby gain such an interest and reputation as will give them a dominion over all about them, by which means many have risen strangely. He that has been <hi type="italic">faithful in a few things</hi> shall be made <hi type="italic">ruler over many things.</hi> The elders, that <hi type="italic">labour in the word and doctrine,</hi> are <hi type="italic">worthy of double honour;</hi> and those that are diligent when they are young will get that which will enable them to rule, and so to rest, when they are old. 2. Knavery is the way to slavery: <hi type="italic">The slothful</hi> and careless, or rather the <hi type="italic">deceitful</hi> (for so the word signifies), <hi type="italic">shall be under tribute.</hi> Those that, because they will not take pains in an honest calling, live by their shifts and arts of dishonesty, are paltry and beggarly, and will be kept under. Those that are diligent and honest when they are apprentices will come to be masters; but those that are otherwise are the fools who, all their days, must be <hi type="italic">servants to the wise in heart.</hi>

<div eID="gen13746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13747" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad. <div eID="gen13747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13748" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The cause and consequence of melancholy. It is <hi type="italic">heaviness in the heart;</hi> it is a load of care, and fear, and sorrow, upon the spirits, depressing them, and disabling them to exert themselves with any vigour on what is to be done or fortitude in what is to borne; it makes them stoop, prostrates and sinks them. Those that are thus oppressed can neither do the duty nor take the comfort of any relation, condition, or conversation. Those therefore that are inclined to it should watch and pray against it. 2. The cure of it: <hi type="italic">A good word</hi> from God, applied by faith, <hi type="italic">makes it glad;</hi> such a word is that (says one of the rabbin), <hi type="italic">Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee;</hi> the good word of God, particularly the gospel, is designed to make the hearts glad that are weary and heavy-laden, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Matt. xi. 28</reference>. Ministers are to be helpers of this joy.

<div eID="gen13748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13749" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> The righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> more excellent than his neighbour: but the way of the wicked seduceth them. <div eID="gen13749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13750" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. That good men do well for themselves; for they have in themselves an excellent character, and they secure to themselves an excellent portion, and in both they excel other people: <hi type="italic">The righteous is more abundant than his neighbour</hi> (so the margin); he is richer, though not in this world's goods, yet in the graces and comforts of the Spirit, which are the true riches. There is a true excellency in religion; it ennobles men, inspires them with generous principles, makes them substantial; it is an excellency which is, in the sight of God, of great price, who is the true Judge of excellency. His neighbour may make a greater figure in the world, may be more applauded, but the righteous man has the intrinsic worth. 2. That wicked men do ill for themselves; they walk in a way which <hi type="italic">seduces them.</hi> It seems to them to be not only a pleasant way, but the right way; it is so agreeable to flesh and blood that they therefore flatter themselves with an opinion that it cannot be amiss, but they will not gain the point they aim at, nor enjoy the good they hope for. It is all a cheat; and therefore the righteous is wiser and happier than his neighbour, that yet despise him and trample upon him.

<div eID="gen13750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13751" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> The slothful <hi type="italic">man</hi> roasteth not that which he took in hunting: but the substance of a diligent man <hi type="italic">is</hi> precious. <div eID="gen13751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13752" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. That which may make us hate slothfulness and deceit, for the word here, as before, signifies both: <hi type="italic">The slothful</hi> deceitful <hi type="italic">man</hi> has roast meat, but that which he roasts is not what he himself <hi type="italic">took in hunting,</hi> no, it is what others took pains for, and he lives upon the fruit of their labours, like the drones in the hive. Or, if slothful deceitful men have taken any thing by hunting (as sportsmen are seldom men of business), yet they do not roast it when they have taken it; they have no comfort in the enjoyment of it; perhaps God in his providence cuts them short of it. 2. That which may make us in love with industry and honesty, that the <hi type="italic">substance of a diligent man,</hi> though it be not great perhaps, <hi type="italic">is</hi> yet <hi type="italic">precious.</hi> It comes from the blessing of God; he has comfort in it; it does him good, and his family. It is his own daily bread, not bread out of other people's mouths, and therefore he sees God gives it to him in answer to his prayer.

<div eID="gen13752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13753" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> In the way of righteousness <hi type="italic">is</hi> life; and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the pathway <hi type="italic">thereof there is</hi> no death. <div eID="gen13753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13754" type="x-p"/> The way of religion is here recommended to us, 1. As a straight, plain, easy way; it is <hi type="italic">the way of righteousness.</hi> God's commands (the rule we are to walk by) are all holy, just, and good. Religion has right reason and equity on its side; it is a <hi type="italic">path-way,</hi> a way which God has cast up for us (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>); it is a highway, the king's highway, the King of kings' highway, a way which is tracked before us by all the saints, the good old way, full of the footsteps of the flock. 2. As a safe, pleasant, comfortable way. (1.) There is not only life at the end, but there is life in the way; all true comfort and satisfaction. The favour of God, which is better than life; the Spirit, who is life. (2.) There is not only life in it, but so as that in it <hi type="italic">there is no death,</hi> none of that sorrow of the world which works death and is an allay to our present joy and life. There is no end of that life that is in the way of righteousness. Here there is life, but there is death too. <hi type="italic">In the way of righteousness</hi> there <hi type="italic">is life, and no death,</hi> life and immortality.  <chapter eID="Prov.12"/> <div eID="gen13754" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv30"/><title type="x-s3">Moral Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv30"/> <div sID="gen13756" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> A wise son <hi type="italic">heareth</hi> his father's instruction: but a scorner heareth not rebuke. <div eID="gen13756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13757" type="x-p"/> Among the children of the same parents it is no new thing for some to be hopeful and others the contrary; now here we are taught to distinguish. 1. There is great hope of those that have a reverence for their parents, and are willing to be advised and admonished by them. He is <hi type="italic">a wise son,</hi> and is in a far way to be wiser, that <hi type="italic">hears his father's instruction,</hi> desires to hear it, regards it, and complies with it, and does not merely give it the hearing. 2. There is little hope of those that will not so much as <hi type="italic">hear rebuke</hi> with any patience, but scorn to submit to government and scoff at those that deal faithfully with them. How can those mend a fault who will not be told of it, but count those their enemies who do them that kindness?

<div eID="gen13757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13758" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> A man shall eat good by the fruit of <hi type="italic">his</hi> mouth: but the soul of the transgressors <hi type="italic">shall eat</hi> violence. <div eID="gen13758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13759" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. If that which comes from within, out of the heart, be good, and from a good treasure, it will return with advantage. Inward comfort and satisfaction will be daily bread; nay, it will be a continual feast to those who delight in that communication which is <hi type="italic">to the use of edifying.</hi> 2. Violence done will recoil in the face of him that does it: <hi type="italic">The soul of the transgressors</hi> that harbours and plots mischief, and vents it by word and deed, <hi type="italic">shall eat violence;</hi> they shall have their belly full of it. <hi type="italic">Reward her as she has rewarded thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">Rev. xviii. 6</reference>. Every man shall drink as he brews, eat as he speaks; for by our words we must be justified or condemned, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.37">Matt. xii. 37</reference>. As our fruit is, so will our food be, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.21-Rom.6.22">Rom. vi. 21, 22</reference>.

<div eID="gen13759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13760" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life: <hi type="italic">but</hi> he that openeth wide his lips shall have destruction. <div eID="gen13760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13761" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A guard upon the lips is a guard to the soul. He that is cautious, that thinks twice before he speaks once, that, if he have <hi type="italic">thought evil, lays his hand upon his mouth</hi> to suppress it, that keeps a strong bridle on his tongue and a strict hand on that bridle, he <hi type="italic">keeps his soul</hi> from a great deal both of guilt and grief and saves himself the trouble of many bitter reflections on himself and reflections of others upon him. 2. There is many a one ruined by an ungoverned tongue: <hi type="italic">He that opens widely his lips,</hi> to let our <hi type="italic">quod in buccam venerit—whatever comes uppermost,</hi> that loves to bawl, and bluster, and make a noise, and affects such a liberty of speech as bids defiance both to God and man, he <hi type="italic">shall have destruction.</hi> it will be the destruction of his reputation, his interest, his comfort, and his soul for ever, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.6">Jam. iii. 6</reference>.

<div eID="gen13761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13762" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> The soul of the sluggard desireth, and <hi type="italic">hath</hi> nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat. <div eID="gen13762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13763" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The misery and shame of the slothful. See how foolish and absurd they are; they desire the gains which the diligent get, but they hate the pains which the diligent take; they covet every thing that is to be coveted, but will do nothing that is to be done; and therefore it follows, They have nothing; for he that will not labour let him hunger, and let him not <hi type="italic">eat,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.10">2 Thess. iii. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">The desire of the slothful,</hi> which should be his excitement, is his torment, which should make him busy, makes him always uneasy, and is really a greater toil to him than labour would be. 2. The happiness and honour of the diligent: Their <hi type="italic">soul shall be made fat;</hi> they shall have abundance, and shall have the comfortable enjoyment of it, and the more for its being the fruit of their diligence. This is especially true in spiritual affairs. Those that rest in idle wishes know not what the advantages of religion are; whereas those that take pains in the service of God find both the pleasure and profit of it.  <div eID="gen13763" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv31"/><title type="x-s3">The Righteous Exclusively Happy.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv31"/> <div sID="gen13764" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> A righteous <hi type="italic">man</hi> hateth lying: but a wicked <hi type="italic">man</hi> is loathsome, and cometh to shame. <div eID="gen13764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13765" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Where grace reigns sin is loathsome. It is the undoubted character of every <hi type="italic">righteous man</hi> that he <hi type="italic">hates lying</hi> (that is, all sin, for every sin is a lie, and particularly all fraud and falsehood in commerce and conversation), not only that he will not tell a lie, but he abhors lying, from a rooted reigning principle of love to truth and justice, and conformity to God. 2. Where sin reigns the <hi type="italic">man is loathsome.</hi> If his eyes were opened, and his conscience awakened, he would be so to himself, he would <hi type="italic">abhor himself and repent in dust and ashes;</hi> however, he is so to God and all good men; particularly, he makes himself so by lying, than which there is nothing more detestable. And, though he may think to face it out awhile, yet he will <hi type="italic">come to shame</hi> and contempt at last and will blush to show his face, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan. xii. 2</reference>.

<div eID="gen13765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13766" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Righteousness keepeth <hi type="italic">him that is</hi> upright in the way: but wickedness overthroweth the sinner. <div eID="gen13766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13767" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. Saints secured from ruin. Those that are <hi type="italic">upright in their way,</hi> that mean honestly in all their actions, adhere conscientiously to the sacred and eternal rules of equity, and deal sincerely both with God and man, their integrity will keep them from the temptations of Satan, which shall not prevail over them, the reproaches and injuries of evil men, which shall not fasten upon them, to do them any real mischief, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">Ps. xxv. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen13767" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen13768"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13769"/>Hic murus aheneus esto, nil conscire sibi.<l eID="gen13769" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13770"/>Be this thy brazen bulwark of defence,<l eID="gen13770" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13771"/>Still to preserve thy conscious innocence.<l eID="gen13771" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen13768"/> <div sID="gen13772" type="x-p"/> 2. Sinners secured for ruin. Those that are wicked, even their wickedness will be their overthrow at last, and they are held in the cords of it in the mean time. Are they corrected, destroyed? It is their own wickedness that corrects them, that destroys them; they alone shall bear it.

<div eID="gen13772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13773" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> There is that maketh himself rich, yet <hi type="italic">hath</hi> nothing: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> that maketh himself poor, yet <hi type="italic">hath</hi> great riches. <div eID="gen13773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13774" type="x-p"/> This observation is applicable, <div eID="gen13774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13775" type="x-p"/> I. To men's worldly estate. The world is a great cheat, not only the things of the world, but the men of the world. <hi type="italic">All men are liars.</hi> Here is an instance in two sore evils under the sun:—1. Some that are really poor would be thought to be rich and are thought to be so; they trade and spend as if they were rich, make a great bustle and a great show as if they had hidden treasures, when perhaps, if all their debts were paid, they are not worth a groat. This is sin, and will be shame; many a one hereby ruins his family and brings reproach upon his profession of religion. Those that thus live above what they have choose to be subject to their own pride rather than to God's providence, and it will end accordingly. 2. Some that are really rich would be thought to be poor, and are thought to be so, because they sordidly and meanly live below what God has given them, and choose rather to bury it than to use it, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.1-Eccl.6.2">Eccl. vi. 1, 2</reference>. In this there is an ingratitude to God, injustice to the family and neighbourhood, and uncharitableness to the poor. <div eID="gen13775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13776" type="x-p"/> II. To their spiritual state. Grace is the riches of the soul; it is true riches; but men commonly misrepresent themselves, either designedly or through mistake and ignorance of themselves. 1. There are many presuming hypocrites, that are really poor and empty of grace and yet either think themselves rich, and will not be convinced of their poverty, or pretend themselves rich, and will not own their poverty. 2. There are many timorous trembling Christians, that are spiritually rich, and full of grace, and yet think themselves poor, and will not be persuaded that they are rich, or, at least, will not own it; by their doubts and fears, their complaints and griefs, they <hi type="italic">make themselves poor.</hi> The former mistake is destroying at last; this is disquieting in the mean time.

<div eID="gen13776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13777" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The ransom of a man's life <hi type="italic">are</hi> his riches: but the poor heareth not rebuke. <div eID="gen13777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13778" type="x-p"/> We are apt to judge of men's blessedness, at least in this world, by their wealth, and that they are more or less happy accordingly as they have more or less of this world's goods; but Solomon here shows what a gross mistake it is, that we may be reconciled to a poor condition, and may neither covet riches ourselves nor envy those that have abundance. 1. Those that are rich, if by some they are respected for their riches, yet, to balance that, by others they are envied and struck at, and brought in danger of their lives, which therefore they are forced to ransom with their riches. <hi type="italic">Slay us not, for we have treasures in the field,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.41.8">Jer. xli. 8</reference>. Under some tyrants, it has been crime enough to be rich; and how little is a man beholden to his wealth when it only serves to redeem that life which otherwise would not have been exposed! 2. Those that are poor, if by some, that should be their friends, they are despised and overlooked, yet, to balance that, they are also despised and overlooked by others that would be their enemies if they had any thing to lose: <hi type="italic">The poor hear not rebuke,</hi> are not censured, reproached, accused, nor brought into trouble, as the rich are; for nobody thinks it worth while to take notice of them. When the rich Jews were carried captives to Babylon <hi type="italic">the poor of the land were left,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.12">2 Kings xxv. 12</reference>. Welcome nothing, once in seven years. <hi type="italic">Cantabit vacuus coram latrone viator</hi>—<hi type="italic">When a traveller is met by a robber he will rejoice at not having much property about him.</hi>

<div eID="gen13778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13779" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> The light of the righteous rejoiceth: but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out. <div eID="gen13779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13780" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The comfort of good men flourishing and lasting: <hi type="italic">The light of the righteous rejoices,</hi> that is, it increases, and makes them glad. Even their outward prosperity is their joy, and much more those gifts, graces, and comforts, with which their souls are illuminated; these <hi type="italic">shine more and more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">ch. iv. 18</reference>. The Spirit is their light, and he gives them a fulness of joy, and <hi type="italic">rejoices to do them good.</hi> 2. The comfort of bad men withering and dying: <hi type="italic">The lamp of the wicked</hi> burns dimly and faint; it looks melancholy, like a taper in an urn, and it will shortly <hi type="italic">be put out</hi> in utter darkness, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.11">Isa. l. 11</reference>. The light of the righteous is as that of the sun, which may be eclipsed and clouded, but will continue; that of the wicked is as a lamp of their own kindling, which will presently go out and is easily put out.

<div eID="gen13780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13781" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Only by pride cometh contention: but with the well advised <hi type="italic">is</hi> wisdom. <div eID="gen13781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13782" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Foolish pride is the great make-bate. Would you know <hi type="italic">whence come wars and fightings?</hi> They come from this root of bitterness. Whatever hand other lusts may have in contention (passion, envy, covetousness), pride has the great hand; it is its pride that it will itself sow discord and needs no help. Pride makes men impatient of contradiction in either their opinions or their desires, impatient of competition and rivalship, impatient of contempt, or any thing that looks like a slight, and impatient of concession, and receding, from a conceit of certain right and truth on their side; and hence arise quarrels among relations and neighbours, quarrels in states and kingdoms, in churches and Christian societies. Men will be revenged, will not forgive, because they are proud. 2. Those that are humble and peaceable are wise and <hi type="italic">well advised.</hi> Those that will ask and take advice, that will consult their own consciences, their Bibles, their ministers, their friends, and will do nothing rashly, are wise, as in other things, so in this, that they will humble themselves, will stoop and yield, to preserve quietness and prevent quarrels.

<div eID="gen13782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13783" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Wealth <hi type="italic">gotten</hi> by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase. <div eID="gen13783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13784" type="x-p"/> This shows that riches wear as they are won and woven. 1. That which is won ill will never wear well, for a curse attends it which will waste it, and the same corrupt dispositions which incline men to the sinful ways of getting well incline them to the like sinful ways of spending: <hi type="italic">Wealth gotten by vanity</hi> will be bestowed upon vanity, and then it <hi type="italic">will be diminished.</hi> That which is got by such employments as are not lawful, or not becoming Christians, such as only serve to feed pride and luxury, that which is got by gaming or by the stage, may as truly be said to be <hi type="italic">gotten by vanity</hi> as that which is got by fraud and lying, and <hi type="italic">will be diminished. De male quæsitis vix gaudet tertius hæres—Ill-gotten wealth will scarcely be enjoyed by the third generation.</hi> 2. That which is got by industry and honesty will grow more, instead of growing less; it will be a maintenance; it will be an inheritance; it will be an abundance. <hi type="italic">He that labours, working with his hands, shall</hi> so <hi type="italic">increase</hi> as that he shall <hi type="italic">have to give to him that needs</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>); and, when it comes to that, it will increase yet more and more.

<div eID="gen13784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13785" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but <hi type="italic">when</hi> the desire cometh, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> a tree of life. <div eID="gen13785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13786" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Nothing is more grievous than the disappointment of a raised expectation, though not in the thing itself by a denial, yet in the time of it by a delay: <hi type="italic">Hope deferred makes the heart sick</hi> and languishing, fretful and peevish; but hope quite dashed kills the heart, and the more high the expectation was raised the more cutting is the frustration of it. It is therefore our wisdom not to promise ourselves any great matters from the creature, not to feed ourselves with any vain hopes from this world, lest we lay up matter for our own vexation; and what we do hope for let us prepare to be disappointed in, that, if it should prove so, it may prove the easier; and let us not be hasty. 2. Nothing is more grateful than to enjoy that, at last, which we have long wished and waited for: <hi type="italic">When the desire does come</hi> it puts men into a sort of paradise, a garden of pleasure, for <hi type="italic">it is a tree of life.</hi> It will aggravate the eternal misery of the wicked that their hopes will be frustrated; and it will make the happiness of heaven the more welcome to the saints that it is what they have earnestly longed for as the crown of their hopes.

<div eID="gen13786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13787" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Whoso despiseth the word shall be destroyed: but he that feareth the commandment shall be rewarded. <div eID="gen13787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13788" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The character of one that is marked for ruin: He that <hi type="italic">despises the word</hi> of God, and has no regard to it, no veneration for it, nor will be ruled by it, certainly he <hi type="italic">shall be destroyed,</hi> for he slights that which is the only means of curing a destructive disease and makes himself obnoxious to that divine wrath which will certainly be his destruction. Those that prefer the rules of carnal policy before divine precepts, and the allurements of the world and the flesh before God's promises and comforts, despise his word, giving the preference to those things that stand in competition with it; and it is to their own just destruction: they would not take warning. 2. The character of one that is sure to be happy: <hi type="italic">He that fears the commandment,</hi> that stands in awe of God, pays a deference to his authority, has a reverence for his word, is afraid of displeasing God and incurring the penalties annexed to the commandment, shall not only escape destruction, but <hi type="italic">shall be rewarded</hi> for his godly fear. <hi type="italic">In keeping the commandment there is great reward.</hi>

<div eID="gen13788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13789" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The law of the wise <hi type="italic">is</hi> a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death. <div eID="gen13789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13790" type="x-p"/> By <hi type="italic">the law of the wise</hi> and righteous, here, we may understand either the principles and rules by which they govern themselves or (which comes all to one) the instructions which they give to others, which ought to be as a law to all about them; and if they be so, 1. They will be constant springs of comfort and satisfaction, as <hi type="italic">a fountain of life,</hi> sending forth streams of living water; the closer we keep to those rules the more effectually we secure our own peace. 2. They will be constant preservatives from the temptations of Satan. Those that follow the dictates of this law will keep at a distance from the snares of sin, and so escape <hi type="italic">the snares of death</hi> which those run into that forsake <hi type="italic">the law of the wise.</hi>

<div eID="gen13790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13791" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Good understanding giveth favour: but the way of transgressors <hi type="italic">is</hi> hard. <div eID="gen13791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13792" type="x-p"/> If we compare not only the end, but the way, we shall find that religion has the advantage; for, 1. The way of saints is pleasant and agreeable: <hi type="italic">Good understanding</hi> gains <hi type="italic">favour</hi> with God and man; our Saviour grew in that favour when he <hi type="italic">increased in wisdom.</hi> Those that conduct themselves prudently, and order their conversation aright in every thing, that <hi type="italic">serve Christ in righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost,</hi> are <hi type="italic">accepted of God and approved of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17-Rom.14.18">Rom. xiv. 17, 18</reference>. And how comfortably will that man pass through the world who is well understood and is therefore well accepted! 2. The way of sinners is rough and uneasy, and, for <hi type="italic">this</hi> reason, unpleasant to themselves, because unacceptable to others. It is <hi type="italic">hard,</hi> hard upon others, who complain of it, hard to the sinner himself, who can have little enjoyment of himself while he is doing that which is disobliging to all mankind. The service of sin is perfect slavery, and the road to hell is strewed with the thorns and thistles that are the products of the curse. Sinners labour in the very fire.

<div eID="gen13792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13793" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Every prudent <hi type="italic">man</hi> dealeth with knowledge: but a fool layeth open <hi type="italic">his</hi> folly. <div eID="gen13793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13794" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is wisdom to be cautious. <hi type="italic">Every prudent</hi> discreet <hi type="italic">man</hi> does all <hi type="italic">with knowledge</hi> (considering with himself and consulting with others), acts with deliberation and is upon the reserve, is careful not to meddle with that which he has not some knowledge of, not to launch out into business which he has not acquainted himself with, will not <hi type="italic">deal with</hi> those that he has not some <hi type="italic">knowledge</hi> of, whether they may be confided in. He is still dealing in knowledge, that he may increase the stock he has. 2. It is folly to be rash, as the <hi type="italic">fool</hi> is, who is forward to talk of things he knows nothing of and undertake that which he is no way fit for, and so <hi type="italic">lays open his folly</hi> and makes himself ridiculous. He <hi type="italic">began to build and was not able to finish.</hi>

<div eID="gen13794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13795" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> A wicked messenger falleth into mischief: but a faithful ambassador <hi type="italic">is</hi> health. <div eID="gen13795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13796" type="x-p"/> Here we have, 1. The ill consequences of betraying a trust. <hi type="italic">A wicked messenger,</hi> who, being sent to negotiate any business, is false to him that employed him, divulges his counsels, and so defeats his designs, cannot expect to prosper, but will certainly <hi type="italic">fall into</hi> some <hi type="italic">mischief</hi> or other, will be discovered and punished, since nothing is more hateful to God and man than the treachery of those that have a confidence reposed in them. 2. The happy effects of fidelity: An <hi type="italic">ambassador</hi> who <hi type="italic">faithfully</hi> discharges his trust, and serves the interests of those who employ him, <hi type="italic">is health;</hi> he is health to those by whom and for whom he is employed, heals differences that are between them, and preserves a good understanding; he is health to himself, for he secures his own interest. This is applicable to ministers, Christ's messengers and ambassadors; those that are wicked and false to Christ and the souls of men do mischief and <hi type="italic">fall into mischief,</hi> but those that are faithful will find sound words to be healing words to others and themselves.

<div eID="gen13796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13797" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Poverty and shame <hi type="italic">shall be to</hi> him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured. <div eID="gen13797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13798" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. He that is so proud that he scorns to be taught will certainly be abased. He that <hi type="italic">refuses</hi> the good <hi type="italic">instruction</hi> offered him, as if it were a reflection upon his honour and an abridgment of his liberty, <hi type="italic">poverty and shame shall be to him:</hi> he will become a beggar and live and die in disgrace; every one will despise him as foolish, and stubborn, and ungovernable. 2. He that is so humble that he takes it well to be told of his faults shall certainly be exalted: <hi type="italic">He that regards a reproof,</hi> whoever gives it to him, and will mend what is amiss when it is shown him, gains respect as wise and candid; he avoids that which would be a disgrace to him and is in a fair way to make himself considerable.

<div eID="gen13798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13799" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> The desire accomplished is sweet to the soul: but <hi type="italic">it is</hi> abomination to fools to depart from evil. <div eID="gen13799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13800" type="x-p"/> This shows the folly of those that refuse instruction, for they might be happy and will not. 1. They might be happy. There are in man strong desires of happiness; God has provided for the accomplishment of those desires, and that would be <hi type="italic">sweet to the soul,</hi> whereas the pleasures of sense are grateful only to the carnal appetite. <hi type="italic">The desire</hi> of good men towards the favour of God and spiritual blessings brings that which <hi type="italic">is sweet to their souls;</hi> we know those that can say so by experience, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6-Ps.4.7">Ps. iv. 6, 7</reference>. 2. Yet they will not be happy; for <hi type="italic">it is</hi> an <hi type="italic">abomination to</hi> them <hi type="italic">to depart from evil,</hi> which is necessary to their being happy. Never let those expect any thing truly sweet to their souls that will not be persuaded to leave their sins, but that roll them under their tongues as a sweet morsel.

<div eID="gen13800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13801" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> He that walketh with wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed. <div eID="gen13801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13802" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that would be good must keep good company, which is an evidence for them that they would be good (men's character is known by the company they choose) and will be a means of making them good, of showing them the way and of quickening and encouraging them in it. He that would be himself wise must walk with those that are so, must choose such for his intimate acquaintance, and converse with them accordingly; must ask and receive instruction from them, and keep up pious and profitable talk with them. <hi type="italic">Miss not the discourse of the elders, for they also learned of their fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Sir.8.9">Ecclesiasticus viii. 9.</reference> And (<reference osisRef="Sir.6.35">Ecclesiasticus vi. 35</reference>), <hi type="italic">Be willing to hear every godly discourse, and let not the parables of understanding escape thee.</hi> 2. Multitudes are brought to ruin by bad company: <hi type="italic">A companion of fools shall be broken</hi> (so some), <hi type="italic">shall be known</hi> (so the LXX.), known to be a fool; <hi type="italic">noscitur ex socio—he is known by his company.</hi> He <hi type="italic">will be like them</hi> (so some), <hi type="italic">will be made wicked</hi> (so others); it comes all to one, for all those, and those only, that make themselves wicked, will <hi type="italic">be destroyed,</hi> and those that associate with evil-doers are debauched, and so undone, and at last ascribe their death to it.

<div eID="gen13802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13803" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Evil pursueth sinners: but to the righteous good shall be repayed. <div eID="gen13803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13804" type="x-p"/> Here see, 1. How unavoidable the destruction of sinners is; the wrath of God pursues them, and all the terrors of that wrath: <hi type="italic">Evil pursues</hi> them closely wherever they go, as the avenger of blood pursued the manslayer, and they have no city of refuge to flee to; they attempt an escape, but in vain. Whom God pursues he is sure to overtake. They may prosper for a while and grow very secure, but their damnation slumbers not, though they do. 2. How indefeasible the happiness of the saints is; the God that cannot lie has engaged that <hi type="italic">to the righteous good shall be repaid.</hi> They shall be abundantly recompensed for all the good they have done, and all the ill they have suffered, in this world; so that, though many have been losers for their righteousness, they shall not be losers by it. Though the recompence do not come quickly, it will come in the day of payment, in the world of retribution; and it will be an abundant recompence.

<div eID="gen13804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13805" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> A good <hi type="italic">man</hi> leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner <hi type="italic">is</hi> laid up for the just. <div eID="gen13805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13806" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How <hi type="italic">a good man's</hi> estate lasts: He <hi type="italic">leaves an inheritance to his children's children.</hi> It is part of his praise that he is thoughtful for posterity, that he does not lay all out upon himself, but is in care to do well for those that come after him, not by withholding more than is meet, but by a prudent and decent frugality. He trains up his children to this, that they may leave it to their children; and especially he is careful, both by justice and charity, to obtain the blessing of God upon what he has, and to entail that blessing upon his children, without which the greatest industry and frugality will be in vain: <hi type="italic">A good man,</hi> by being good and doing good, by honouring the Lord with his substance and spending it in his service, secures it to his posterity; or, if he should not leave them much of this world's goods, his prayers, his instructions, his good example, will be the best entail, and the promises of the covenant will be an inheritance to his <hi type="italic">children's children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.17">Ps. ciii. 17</reference>. 2. How it increases by the accession of <hi type="italic">the wealth of the sinner</hi> to it, for that <hi type="italic">is laid up for the just.</hi> If it be asked, How should good men grow so rich, who are not so eager upon the world as others are and who commonly suffer for their well-doing? It is here answered, God, in his providence, often brings into their hands that which wicked people had laid up for themselves. <hi type="italic">The innocent shall divide the silver,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.27.16-Job.27.17">Job xxvii. 16, 17</reference>. The Israelites shall spoil the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.36">Exod. xii. 36</reference>) and <hi type="italic">eat the riches of the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">Isa. lxi. 6</reference>.

<div eID="gen13806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13807" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Much food <hi type="italic">is in</hi> the tillage of the poor: but there is <hi type="italic">that is</hi> destroyed for want of judgment. <div eID="gen13807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13808" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How a small estate may be improved by industry, so that a man, by making the best of every thing, may live comfortably upon it: <hi type="italic">Much food is in the tillage of the poor,</hi> the poor farmers, that have but a little, but take pains with that little and husband it well. Many make it an excuse for their idleness that they have but a little to work on, a very little to be doing with; but the less compass the field is of the more let the skill and labour of the owner be employed about it, and it will turn to a very good account. Let him dig, and he needs not beg. 2. How a great estate may be ruined by indiscretion: <hi type="italic">There is that</hi> has a great deal, but it <hi type="italic">is destroyed</hi> and brought to nothing <hi type="italic">for want of judgment,</hi> that is, prudence in the management of it. Men over-build themselves or over-buy themselves, keep greater company, or a better table, or more servants, than they can afford, suffer what they have to go to decay and do not make the most of it; by taking up money themselves, or being bound for others, their estates are sunk, their families reduced, and all <hi type="italic">for want of judgment.</hi>

<div eID="gen13808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13809" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes. <div eID="gen13809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13810" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. To the education of children in that which is good there is necessary a due correction of them for what is amiss; every child of ours is a child of Adam, and therefore has that foolishness bound up in its heart which calls for rebuke, more or less, the rod and reproof which give wisdom. Observe, It is <hi type="italic">his</hi> rod that must be used, the rod of a parent, directed by wisdom and love, and designed for good, not the rod of a servant. 2. It is good to begin betimes with the necessary restraints of children from that which is evil, before vicious habits are confirmed. The branch is easily bent when it is tender. 3. Those really hate their children, though they pretend to be fond of them, that do not keep them under a strict discipline, and by all proper methods, severe ones when gentle ones will not serve, make them sensible of their faults and afraid of offending. They abandon them to their worst enemy, to the most dangerous disease, and therefore hate them. Let this reconcile children to the correction their good parents give them; it is from love, and for their good, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.7-Heb.12.9">Heb. xii. 7-9</reference>.

<div eID="gen13810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13811" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> The righteous eateth to the satisfying of his soul: but the belly of the wicked shall want. <div eID="gen13811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13812" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is the happiness of the righteous that they shall have enough and that they know when they have enough. They desire not to be surfeited, but, being moderate in their desires, they are soon satisfied. Nature is content with a little and grace with less; enough is as good as a feast. Those that feed on the bread of life, that feast on the promises, meet with abundant satisfaction of soul there, eat, and are filled. 2. It is the misery of the wicked that, through the insatiableness of their own desires, they are always needy; not only their souls shall not be satisfied with the world and the flesh, but even their <hi type="italic">belly shall want;</hi> their sensual appetite is always craving. In hell they shall be denied a drop of water.  <chapter eID="Prov.13"/> <div eID="gen13812" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv32"/><title type="x-s3">Wisdom and Folly.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv32"/> <div sID="gen13814" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands. <div eID="gen13814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13815" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A good wife is a great blessing to a family. By a fruitful wife a family is multiplied and replenished with children, and so built up. But by a prudent wife, one that is pious, industrious, and considerate, the affairs of the family are made to prosper, debts are paid, portions raised, provision made, the children well educated and maintained, and the family has comfort within doors and credit without; thus is the house built. She looks upon it as her own to take care of, though she knows it is her husband's to bear rule in, <reference osisRef="Esth.1.22">Esth. i. 22</reference>. 2. Many a family is brought to ruin by ill housewifery, as well as by ill husbandry. A <hi type="italic">foolish</hi> woman, that has no fear of God nor regard to her business, that is wilful, and wasteful, and humoursome, that indulges her ease and appetite, and is all for jaunting and feasting, cards and the play-house, though she come to a plentiful estate, and to a family beforehand, she will impoverish and waste it, and will as certainly be the ruin of her house as if she <hi type="italic">plucked it down with her hands;</hi> and the husband himself, with all his care, can scarcely prevent it.

<div eID="gen13815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13816" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> He that walketh in his uprightness feareth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> perverse in his ways despiseth him. <div eID="gen13816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13817" type="x-p"/> Here are, 1. Grace and sin in their true colours. Grace reigning is a reverence of God, and gives honour to him who is infinitely great and high, and to whom all honour is due, than which what is more becoming or should be more pleasing to the rational creature? Sin reigning is no less than a contempt of God. In <hi type="italic">this,</hi> more than in any thing, sin appears exceedingly sinful, that it despises God, whom angels adore. Those that despise God's precepts, and will not be ruled by them, his promises, and will not accept of them, despise God himself and all his attributes. 2. Grace and sin in their true light. By this we may know a man that has grace, and the fear of God, reigning in him, <hi type="italic">he walks in his uprightness,</hi> he makes conscience of his actions, is faithful both to God and man, and every stop he makes, as well as every step he takes, is by rule; here is one that honours God. But, on the contrary, <hi type="italic">he that is perverse in his ways,</hi> that wilfully follows his own appetites and passions, that is unjust and dishonest and contradicts his profession in his conversation, however he may pretend to devotion, he is a wicked man, and will be reckoned with as a despiser of God himself.

<div eID="gen13817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13818" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> In the mouth of the foolish <hi type="italic">is</hi> a rod of pride: but the lips of the wise shall preserve them. <div eID="gen13818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13819" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. A proud fool exposing himself. Where there is pride in the heart, and no wisdom in the head to suppress it, it commonly shows itself in the words: <hi type="italic">In the mouth there is pride,</hi> proud boasting, proud censuring, proud scorning, proud commanding and giving law; this is the <hi type="italic">rod,</hi> or branch, <hi type="italic">of pride;</hi> the word is used only here and <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa. xi. 1</reference>. It grows from that root of bitterness which is in the heart; it is a rod from that stem. The root must be plucked up, or we cannot conquer this branch, or it is meant of a smiting beating rod, a <hi type="italic">rod of pride</hi> which strikes others. The proud man with his tongue lays about him and deals blows at pleasure, but it will in the end be a rod to himself; the proud man shall come under an ignominious correction by the words of his own mouth, not cut as a soldier, but caned as a servant; and herein he will be beaten with his own rod, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. 2. A humble wise man saving himself and consulting his own good: <hi type="italic">The lips of the wise shall preserve them</hi> from doing that mischief to others which proud men do with their tongues, and from bringing that mischief on themselves which haughty scorners are often involved in.

<div eID="gen13819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13820" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Where no oxen <hi type="italic">are,</hi> the crib <hi type="italic">is</hi> clean: but much increase <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the strength of the ox. <div eID="gen13820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13821" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The neglect of husbandry is the way to poverty: <hi type="italic">Where no oxen are,</hi> to till the ground and tread out the corn, <hi type="italic">the crib</hi> is empty, <hi type="italic">is clean;</hi> there is no straw for the cattle, and consequently no bread for the service of man. Scarcity is represented by <hi type="italic">cleanness of teeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.4.6">Amos iv. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Where no oxen are</hi> there is nothing to be done at the ground, and then nothing to be had out of it; <hi type="italic">the crib</hi> indeed <hi type="italic">is clean</hi> from dung, which pleases the neat and nice, that cannot endure husbandry because there is so much dirty work in it, and therefore will sell their oxen to keep the crib clean; but then not only the labour, but even the dung of the ox is wanted. This shows the folly of those who addict themselves to the pleasures of the country, but do not mind the business of it, who (as we say) keep more horses than kine, more dogs than swine; their families must needs suffer by it. 2. Those who take pains about their ground are likely to reap the profit of it. Those who keep that about them which is for use and service, not for state and show, more husbandmen than footmen, are likely to thrive. <hi type="italic">Much increase is by the strength of the ox;</hi> that is made for our service, and is profitable alive and dead.

<div eID="gen13821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13822" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> A faithful witness will not lie: but a false witness will utter lies. <div eID="gen13822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13823" type="x-p"/> In the administration of justice much depends upon the witnesses, and therefore it is necessary to the common good that witnesses be principled as they ought to be; for, 1. A witness that is conscientious will not dare to give in a testimony that is in the least untrue, nor, for good-will or ill-will, represent a thing otherwise than according to the best of his knowledge, whoever is pleased or displeased, and then judgment runs down like a river. 2. But a witness that will be bribed, and biassed, and browbeaten, <hi type="italic">will utter lies</hi> (and not stick nor startle at it), with as much readiness and assurance as if what he said were all true.

<div eID="gen13823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13824" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> A scorner seeketh wisdom, and <hi type="italic">findeth it</hi> not: but knowledge <hi type="italic">is</hi> easy unto him that understandeth. <div eID="gen13824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13825" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The reason why some people seek wisdom, and do not find it, is because they do not seek it from a right principle and in a right manner. They are scorners, and it is in scorn that they ask instruction, that they may ridicule what is told them and may cavil at it. Many put questions to Christ, tempting him, and that they might have whereof to accuse him, but they were never the wiser. No marvel if those who seek wisdom, as Simon Magus sought the gifts of the Holy Ghost, to serve their pride and covetousness, do not find it, for they seek amiss. Herod desired to see a miracle, but he was a scorner, and therefore it was denied him, <reference osisRef="Luke.23.8">Luke xxiii. 8</reference>. Scorners speed not in prayer. 2. To those who understand aright, who <hi type="italic">depart from evil</hi> (for <hi type="italic">that is understanding</hi>), the <hi type="italic">knowledge</hi> of God and of his will <hi type="italic">is easy.</hi> The parables which harden scorners in their scorning, and make divine things more difficult to them, enlighten those who are willing to learn, and make the same things more plain, and intelligible, and familiar to them, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.11">Matt. xiii. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.15">15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.16">16</reference>. The same word which to the scornful <hi type="italic">is a savour of death unto death</hi> to the humble and serious <hi type="italic">is a savour of life unto life.</hi> He <hi type="italic">that understands,</hi> so as to <hi type="italic">depart from evil</hi> (for <hi type="italic">that is understanding</hi>), to quit his prejudices, to lay aside all corrupt dispositions and affections, will easily apprehend instruction and receive the impressions of it.

<div eID="gen13825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13826" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Go from the presence of a foolish man, when thou perceivest not <hi type="italic">in him</hi> the lips of knowledge. <div eID="gen13826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13827" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How we may discern a fool and discover him, a wicked man, for he is <hi type="italic">a foolish man.</hi> If we <hi type="italic">perceive not in him the lips of knowledge,</hi> if we find there is no relish or savour of piety in his discourse, that his communication is all corrupt and corrupting, and nothing in it <hi type="italic">good and to the use of edifying,</hi> we may conclude the treasure is bad. 2. How we must decline such a one and depart from him: <hi type="italic">Go from his presence,</hi> for <hi type="italic">thou perceivest</hi> there is no good to be gotten by his company, but danger of getting hurt by it. Sometimes the only way we have of reproving wicked discourse and witnessing against it is by leaving the company and going out of the hearing of it.

<div eID="gen13827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13828" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The wisdom of the prudent <hi type="italic">is</hi> to understand his way: but the folly of fools <hi type="italic">is</hi> deceit. <div eID="gen13828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13829" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. The good conduct of a wise and good man; he manages himself well. It is not the wisdom of the learned, which consists only in speculation, that is here recommended, but <hi type="italic">the wisdom of the prudent,</hi> which is practical, and is of use to direct our counsels and actions. Christian prudence consists in a right <hi type="italic">understanding of our way;</hi> for we are travellers, whose concern it is, not to spy wonders, but to get forward towards their journey's end. It <hi type="italic">is to understand our own way,</hi> not to be critics and busybodies in other men's matters, but to look well to ourselves and <hi type="italic">ponder the path of our feet,</hi> to understand the directions of our way, that we may observe them, the dangers of our way, that we may avoid them, the difficulties of our way, that we may break through them, and the advantages of our way, that we may improve them—to understand the rules we are to walk by and the ends we are to walk towards, and walk accordingly. 2. The bad conduct of a bad man; he puts a cheat upon himself. He does not rightly understand his way; he thinks he does, and so misses his way, and goes on in his mistake: <hi type="italic">The folly of fools is deceit;</hi> it cheats them into their own ruin. The folly of him that built on the sand was deceit.

<div eID="gen13829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13830" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Fools make a mock at sin: but among the righteous <hi type="italic">there is</hi> favour. <div eID="gen13830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13831" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How wicked people are hardened in their wickedness: they <hi type="italic">make a mock at sin.</hi> They make a laughing matter of the sins of others, making themselves and their companions merry with that for which they should mourn, and they make a light matter of their own sins, both when they are tempted to sin and when they have committed it; they <hi type="italic">call evil good and good evil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.20">Isa. v. 20</reference>), turn it off with a jest, rush into sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jer. viii. 6</reference>) and say they shall have peace though they go on. They care not what mischief they do by their sins, and laugh at those that tell them of it. They are advocates for sin, and are ingenious at framing excuses for it. <hi type="italic">Fools make a mock at the sin-offering</hi> (so some); those that make light of sin make light of Christ. Those are fools that make light of sin, for they make light of that which God complains of (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.13">Amos ii. 13</reference>), which lay heavily upon Christ, and which they themselves will have other thoughts of shortly. 2. How good people are encouraged in their goodness: <hi type="italic">Among the righteous there is favour;</hi> if they in any thing offend, they presently repent and obtain the favour of God. They have a goodwill one to another; and among them, in their societies, there is mutual charity and compassion in cases of offences, and no mocking.

<div eID="gen13831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13832" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy. <div eID="gen13832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13833" type="x-p"/> This agrees with <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.11">1 Cor. ii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">What man knows the things of a man,</hi> and the changes of his temper, <hi type="italic">save the spirit of a man?</hi> 1. Every man feels most from his own burden, especially that which is a burden upon the spirits, for that is commonly concealed and the sufferer keeps it to himself. We must not censure the griefs of others, for we know not what they feel; their stroke perhaps is heavier than their groaning. 2. Many enjoy a secret pleasure, especially in divine consolations, which others are not aware of, much less are sharers in; and, as the sorrows of a penitent, so the joys of a believer are such as a <hi type="italic">stranger does not intermeddle with</hi> and therefore is no competent judge of.

<div eID="gen13833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13834" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> The house of the wicked shall be overthrown: but the tabernacle of the upright shall flourish. <div eID="gen13834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13835" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Sin is the ruin of great families: <hi type="italic">The house of the wicked,</hi> though built ever so strong and high, <hi type="italic">shall be overthrown,</hi> shall be brought to poverty and disgrace, and at length be extinct. His hope for heaven, the house on which he leans, shall not stand, but fail in the storm; the deluge that comes will sweep it away. 2. Righteousness is the rise and stability even of mean families: Even <hi type="italic">the tabernacle of the upright,</hi> though movable and despicable as a tent, <hi type="italic">shall flourish,</hi> in outward prosperity if Infinite Wisdom see good, at all events in graces and comfort, which are true riches and honours.

<div eID="gen13835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13836" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof <hi type="italic">are</hi> the ways of death. <div eID="gen13836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13837" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the way and end of a great many self-deluded souls. 1.
