Their way is seemingly fair: It <hi type="italic">seems right</hi> to themselves; they please themselves with a fancy that they are as they should be, that their opinions and practices are good, and such as will bear them out. The way of ignorance and carelessness, the way of worldliness and earthly-mindedness, the way of sensuality and flesh-pleasing, seem right to those that walk in them, much more the way of hypocrisy in religion, external performances, partial reformations, and blind zeal; this they imagine will bring them to heaven; they flatter themselves in their own eyes that all will be well at last. 2. Their end is really fearful, and the more so for their mistake: It is <hi type="italic">the ways of death,</hi> eternal death; their iniquity will certainly be their ruin, and they will perish with a lie in their right hand. Self-deceivers will prove in the end self-destroyers.

<div eID="gen13837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13838" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth <hi type="italic">is</hi> heaviness. <div eID="gen13838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13839" type="x-p"/> This shows the vanity of carnal mirth, and proves what Solomon said of laughter, that <hi type="italic">it is mad;</hi> for, 1. There is sadness under it. Sometimes when sinners are under convictions, or some great trouble, they dissemble their grief by a forced mirth, and put a good face on it, because they will not seem to yield: they cry not when he binds them. Nay, when men really are merry, yet at the same time there is some alloy or other to their mirth, something that casts a damp upon it, which all their gaiety cannot keep from their heart. Their consciences tell them they have no reason to be merry (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.1">Hos. ix. 1</reference>); they cannot but see the vanity of it. Spiritual joy is seated in the soul; the joy of the hypocrite is but from the teeth outward. See <reference osisRef="John.16.22">John xvi. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2 Cor. vi. 10</reference>. 2. There is worse after it: <hi type="italic">The end of that mirth is heaviness.</hi> It is soon over, like the crackling of thorns under a pot; and, if the conscience be awake, all sinful and profane mirth will be reflected upon with bitterness; if not, the heaviness will be so much the greater when <hi type="italic">for all these things God shall bring the</hi> sinner <hi type="italic">into judgment.</hi> The sorrows of the saints will end in everlasting joys (<reference osisRef="Ps.126.5">Ps. cxxvi. 5</reference>), but the laughter of fools will end in endless weeping and wailing.  <div eID="gen13839" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv33"/><title type="x-s3">The Righteous and the Wicked Contrasted.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv33"/> <div sID="gen13840" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways: and a good man <hi type="italic">shall be satisfied</hi> from himself. <div eID="gen13840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13841" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The misery of sinners will be an eternal surfeit upon their sins: The <hi type="italic">backslider in heart,</hi> who for fear of suffering, or in hope of profit or pleasure, forsakes God and his duty, shall be <hi type="italic">filled with his own ways;</hi> God will give him enough of them. They would not leave their brutish lusts and passions, and therefore they shall stick by them, to their everlasting terror and torment. <hi type="italic">He that is filthy shall be filthy still. "Son, remember,</hi>" shall <hi type="italic">fill them with their own ways,</hi> and set their sins in order before them. Backsliding begins in the heart; it is the evil heart of unbelief that departs from God; and of all sinners backsliders will have most terror when they reflect on <hi type="italic">their own ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.11.26">Luke xi. 26</reference>. 2. The happiness of the saints will be an eternal satisfaction in their graces, as tokens of and qualifications for God's peculiar favour: <hi type="italic">A good man shall be</hi> abundantly <hi type="italic">satisfied from himself,</hi> from what God has wrought in him. He has <hi type="italic">rejoicing in himself alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.3">Gal. vi. 3</reference>. As sinners never think they have sin enough till it brings them to hell, so saints never think they have grace enough till it brings them to heaven.

<div eID="gen13841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13842" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The simple believeth every word: but the prudent <hi type="italic">man</hi> looketh well to his going. <div eID="gen13842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13843" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is folly to be credulous, to heed every flying report, to give ear to every man's story, though ever so improbable, to take things upon trust from common fame, to depend upon every man's profession of friendship and give credit to every one that will promise payment; those are <hi type="italic">simple</hi> who thus <hi type="italic">believe every word,</hi> forgetting that all men, in some sense, are liars in comparison with God, all whose words we are to believe with an implicit faith, for he cannot lie. 2. It is wisdom to be cautious: <hi type="italic">The prudent man</hi> will try before he trusts, will weigh both the credibility of the witness and the probability of the testimony, and then give judgment as the thing appears or suspend his judgment till it appears. <hi type="italic">Prove all things,</hi> and <hi type="italic">believe not every spirit.</hi>

<div eID="gen13843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13844" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> A wise <hi type="italic">man</hi> feareth, and departeth from evil: but the fool rageth, and is confident. <div eID="gen13844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13845" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Holy fear is an excellent guard upon every holy thing, and against every thing that is unholy. It is wisdom to depart <hi type="italic">from evil,</hi> from the evil of sin, and thereby from all other evil; and therefore it is wisdom to fear, that is, to be jealous over ourselves with a godly jealousy, to keep up a dread of God's wrath, to be afraid of coming near the borders of sin or dallying with the beginnings of it. A wise man, for fear of harm, keeps out of harm's way, and starts back in a fright when he finds himself entering into temptation. 2. Presumption is folly. He who, when he is warned of his danger, <hi type="italic">rages and is confident,</hi> furiously pushes on, cannot bear to be checked, bids defiance to the wrath and curse of God, and, fearless of danger, persists in his rebellion, makes bold with the occasions of sin, and plays upon the precipice, he is a fool, for he acts against his reason and his interest, and his ruin will quickly be the proof of his folly.

<div eID="gen13845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13846" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is</hi> soon angry dealeth foolishly: and a man of wicked devices is hated. <div eID="gen13846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13847" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Passionate men are justly laughed at. Men who are peevish and touchy, and are <hi type="italic">soon angry</hi> upon every the least provocation, <hi type="italic">deal foolishly;</hi> they say and do that which is ridiculous, and so expose themselves to contempt; they themselves cannot but be ashamed of it when the heat is over. The consideration of this should engage those especially who are in reputation for wisdom and honour with the utmost care to bridle their passion. 2. Malicious men are justly dreaded and detested, for they are much more dangerous and mischievous to all societies: <hi type="italic">A man of wicked devices,</hi> who stifles his resentments till he has an opportunity of being revenged, and is secretly plotting how to wrong his neighbour and to do him an ill turn, as Cain to kill Abel, such a man as this is hated by all mankind. The character of an angry man is pitiable; through the surprise of a temptation he disturbs and disgraces himself, but it is soon over, and he is sorry for it. But that of a spiteful revengeful man is odious; there is no fence against him nor cure for him.

<div eID="gen13847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13848" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> The simple inherit folly: but the prudent are crowned with knowledge. <div eID="gen13848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13849" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Sin is the shame of sinners: <hi type="italic">The simple,</hi> who love simplicity, get nothing by it; they <hi type="italic">inherit folly.</hi> They have it <hi type="italic">by inheritance,</hi> so some. This corruption of nature is derived from our first parents, and all the calamities that attend it we have by kind; it was the inheritance they transmitted to their degenerate race, an hereditary disease. They are as fond of it as a man of his inheritance, hold it as fast, and are as loth to part with it. What they value themselves upon is really foolish; and what will be the issue of their simplicity but folly? They will for ever rue their own foolish choice. 2. Wisdom is the honour of the wise: <hi type="italic">The prudent crown</hi> themselves <hi type="italic">with knowledge,</hi> they look upon it as their brightest ornament, and there is nothing they are so ambitious of; they bind it to their heads as a crown, which they will by no means part with; they press towards the top and perfection of knowledge, which will crown their beginnings and progress. They shall have the praise of it; wise heads shall be respected as if they were crowned heads. They <hi type="italic">crown knowledge</hi> (so some read it); they are a credit to their profession. Wisdom is not only justified, but glorified, of all her children.

<div eID="gen13849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13850" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> The evil bow before the good; and the wicked at the gates of the righteous. <div eID="gen13850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13851" type="x-p"/> That is, 1. The wicked are oftentimes impoverished and brought low, so that they are forced to beg, their wickedness having reduced them to straits; while good men, by the blessing of God, are enriched, and enabled to give, and do give, even to the evil; for where God grants life we must not deny a livelihood. 2. Sometimes God extorts, even from bad men, an acknowledgement of the excellency of God's people. The evil ought always to <hi type="italic">bow before the good,</hi> and sometimes they are made to do it and <hi type="italic">to know that God has loved them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>. They desire their favour (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.7">Esth. vii. 7</reference>), their prayers, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.12">2 Kings iii. 12</reference>. 3. There is a day coming when the upright shall have the dominion (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Ps. xlix. 14</reference>), when the foolish virgins shall come begging to the wise for oil, and shall knock in vain at that gate of the Lord at which the righteous entered.

<div eID="gen13851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13852" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> The poor is hated even of his own neighbour: but the rich <hi type="italic">hath</hi> many friends. <div eID="gen13852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13853" type="x-p"/> This shows, not what should be, but what is the common way of the world—to be shy of the poor and fond of the rich. 1. Few will give countenance to those whom the world frowns upon, though otherwise worthy of respect: <hi type="italic">The poor,</hi> who should be pitied, and encouraged, and relieved, <hi type="italic">is hated,</hi> looked strange upon, and kept at a distance, even <hi type="italic">by his own neighbour,</hi> who, before he fell into disgrace, was intimate with him and pretended to have a kindness for him. Most are swallow-friends, that are gone in winter. It is good having God our friend, for he will not desert us when we are poor. 2. Every one will make court to those whom the world smiles upon, though otherwise unworthy: <hi type="italic">The rich have many friends,</hi> friends to their riches, in hope to get something out of them. There is little friendship in the world but what is governed by self-interest, which is no true friendship at all, nor what a wise man will either value himself on or put any confidence in. Those that make the world their God idolize those that have most of its good things, and seek their favour as if indeed they were Heaven's favourites.

<div eID="gen13853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13854" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy <hi type="italic">is</hi> he. <div eID="gen13854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13855" type="x-p"/> See here how men's character and condition are measured and judged of by their conduct towards their poor neighbours. 1. Those that look upon them with contempt have here assigned them a bad character, and their condition will be accordingly: <hi type="italic">He that despises his neighbour</hi> because he is low in the world, because he is of a mean extraction, rustic education, and makes but a mean figure, that thinks it below him to take notice of him, converse with him, or concern himself about him, and sets him with the dogs of his flock, <hi type="italic">is a sinner,</hi> is guilty of a sin, is in the way to worse, and shall be dealt with as a sinner; unhappy is he. 2. Those that look upon them with compassion are here said to be in a good condition, according to their character: <hi type="italic">He that has mercy on the poor,</hi> is ready to do all the good offices he can to him, and thereby puts an honour upon him, <hi type="italic">happy is he;</hi> he does that which is pleasing to God, which he himself will afterwards reflect upon with great satisfaction, for which the loins of the poor will bless him, and which will be abundantly recompensed in the resurrection of the just.

<div eID="gen13855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13856" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Do they not err that devise evil? but mercy and truth <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> to them that devise good. <div eID="gen13856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13857" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How miserably mistaken those are that not only do evil, but devise it: <hi type="italic">Do they not err?</hi> Yes, certainly they do; every one knows it. They think that by sinning with craft and contrivance, and carrying on their intrigues with more plot and artifice than others, they shall make a better hand of their sins than others do, and come off better. But they are mistaken. God's justice cannot be out-witted. Those that devise evil against their neighbours greatly err, for it will certainly turn upon themselves and end in their own ruin, a fatal error! 2. How wisely those consult their own interest that not only do good but devise it: <hi type="italic">Mercy and truth</hi> shall be to them, not a reward of debt (they will own that they merit nothing), but a reward of mercy, mere mercy, mercy according to the promise, mercy and truth, to which God is pleased to make himself a debtor. Those that are so liberal as to devise liberal things, that seek opportunities of doing good, and contrive how to make their charity most extensive and most acceptable to those that need it, <hi type="italic">by liberal things they shall stand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">Isa. xxxii. 8</reference>.

<div eID="gen13857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13858" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips <hi type="italic">tendeth</hi> only to penury. <div eID="gen13858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13859" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Working, without talking, will make men rich: <hi type="italic">In all labour</hi> of the head, or of the hand, <hi type="italic">there is profit;</hi> it will turn to some good account or other. Industrious people are generally thriving people, and where there is something done there is something to be had. <hi type="italic">The stirring hand gets a penny.</hi> It is good therefore to keep in business, and to keep in action, and what our hand finds to do to do it with all our might. 2. Talking, without working, will make men poor. Those that love to boast of their business and make a noise about it, and that waste their time in tittle-tattle, in telling and hearing new things, like the Athenians, and, under pretence of improving themselves by conversation, neglect the work of their place and day, they waste what they have, and the course they take <hi type="italic">tends to penury,</hi> and will end in it. It is true in the affairs of our souls; those that take pains in the service of God, that strive earnestly in prayer, will find profit in it. But if men's religion runs all out in talk and noise, and their praying is only the labour of the lips, they will be spiritually poor, and come to nothing.

<div eID="gen13859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13860" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> The crown of the wise <hi type="italic">is</hi> their riches: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the foolishness of fools <hi type="italic">is</hi> folly. <div eID="gen13860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13861" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. If men be wise and good, riches make them so much the more honourable and useful: <hi type="italic">The crown of the wise is their riches;</hi> their riches make them to be so much the more respected, and give them the more authority and influence upon others. Those that have wealth, and wisdom to use it, will have a great opportunity of honouring God and doing good in the world. <hi type="italic">Wisdom is good</hi> without <hi type="italic">an inheritance,</hi> but better <hi type="italic">with</hi> it. 2. If men be wicked and corrupt, their wealth will but the more expose them: <hi type="italic">The foolishness of fools,</hi> put them in what condition you will, <hi type="italic">is folly,</hi> and will show itself and shame them; if they have riches, they do mischief with them and are the more hardened in their foolish practices.

<div eID="gen13861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13862" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> A true witness delivereth souls: but a deceitful <hi type="italic">witness</hi> speaketh lies. <div eID="gen13862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13863" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How much praise is due to a faithful witness: He <hi type="italic">delivers the souls</hi> of the innocent, who are falsely accused, and their good names, which are as dear to them as their lives. A man of integrity will venture the displeasure of the greatest, to bring truth to light and rescue those who are injured by falsehood. A faithful minister, who truly witnesses for God against sin, is thereby instrumental to deliver souls from eternal death. 2. How little regard is to be had to a false witness. He forges <hi type="italic">lies,</hi> and yet pours them out with the greatest assurance imaginable for the destruction of the innocent. It is therefore the interest of a nation by all means possible to detect and punish false-witness-bearing, yea, and lying in common conversation; for truth is the cement of society.

<div eID="gen13863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13864" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> In the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge. <hi type="super">27</hi> The fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death. <div eID="gen13864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13865" type="x-p"/> In these two verses we are invited and encouraged to live in the fear of God by the advantages which attend a religious life. The <hi type="italic">fear of the Lord</hi> is here put for all gracious principles, producing gracious practices. 1. Where this reigns it produces a holy security and serenity of mind. There is in it a <hi type="italic">strong confidence;</hi> it enables a man still to hold fast both his purity and his peace, whatever happens, and gives him boldness before God and the world. <hi type="italic">I know that I shall be justified—None of these things move me;</hi> such is the language of this confidence. 2. It entails a blessing upon posterity. The children of those that by faith make God their confidence shall be encouraged by the promise that God will be a God to believers and to their seed to flee to him as their refuge, and they shall find shelter in him. The children of religious parents often do the better for their parents' instructions and example and fare the better for their faith and prayers. "<hi type="italic">Our fathers trusted in thee,</hi> therefore we will." 3. It is an over-flowing ever-flowing spring of comfort and joy; it is <hi type="italic">a fountain of life,</hi> yielding constant pleasure and satisfaction to the soul, joys that are pure and fresh, are life to the soul, and quench its thirst, and can never be drawn dry; it is a <hi type="italic">well of living water,</hi> that is springing up to, and is the earnest of, eternal life. 4. It is a sovereign antidote against sin and temptation. Those that have a true relish of the pleasures of serious godliness will not be allured by the baits of sin to swallow its hook; they know where to obtain better things than any it can pretend to offer, and therefore it is easy to them <hi type="italic">to depart from the snares of death</hi> and to keep their foot from being taken in them.

<div eID="gen13865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13866" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> In the multitude of people <hi type="italic">is</hi> the king's honour: but in the want of people <hi type="italic">is</hi> the destruction of the prince. <div eID="gen13866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13867" type="x-p"/> Here are two maxims in politics, which carry their own evidence with them:—1. That it is much for the honour of a king to have a populous kingdom; it is a sign that he rules well, since strangers are hereby invited to come and settle under his protection and his own subjects live comfortably; it is a sign that he and his kingdom are under the blessing of God, the effect of which is being fruitful and multiplying. It is his strength, and makes him considerable and formidable; happy is the king, the father of his country, who has his <hi type="italic">quiver full of arrows;</hi> he <hi type="italic">shall not be ashamed, but shall speak with his enemy in the gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.127.4-Ps.127.5">Ps. cxxvii. 4, 5</reference>. It is therefore the wisdom of princes, by a mild and gentle government, by encouraging trade and husbandry, and by making all easy under them, to promote the increase of their people. And let all that wish well to the kingdom of Christ, and to his honour, do what they can in their places that many may be added to his church. 2. That when the people are lessened the prince is weakened: <hi type="italic">In the want of people is the leanness of the prince</hi> (so some read it); trade lies dead, the ground lies untilled, the army wants to be recruited, the navy to be manned, and all because there are not hands sufficient. See how much the honour and safety of kings depend upon their people, which is a reason why they should rule by love, and not with rigour. Princes are corrected by those judgments which abate the number of the people, as we find, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.13">2 Sam. xxiv. 13</reference>.

<div eID="gen13867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13868" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is</hi> slow to wrath <hi type="italic">is</hi> of great understanding: but <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> hasty of spirit exalteth folly. <div eID="gen13868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13869" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Meekness is wisdom. <hi type="italic">He</hi> rightly understands himself, and his duty and interest, the infirmities of human nature, and the constitution of human society, who <hi type="italic">is slow to anger,</hi> and knows how to excuse the faults of others as well as his own, how to adjourn his resentments, and moderate them, so as by no provocation to be put out of the possession of his own soul. A mild patient man is really to be accounted an intelligent man, one that learns of Christ, who is Wisdom itself. 2. Unbridled passion is folly proclaimed: <hi type="italic">He that is hasty of spirit,</hi> whose heart is tinder to every spark of provocation, that is all fire and tow, as we say, he thinks hereby to magnify himself and make those about stand in awe of him, whereas really he <hi type="italic">exalts his own folly;</hi> he makes it known, as that which is lifted up is visible to all, and he submits himself to it as to the government of one that is exalted.

<div eID="gen13869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13870" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> A sound heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones. <div eID="gen13870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13871" type="x-p"/> The foregoing verse showed how much our reputation, this how much our health, depends on the good government of our passions and the preserving of the temper of the mind. 1. A healing spirit, made up of love and meekness, a hearty, friendly, cheerful disposition, is <hi type="italic">the life of the flesh;</hi> it contributes to a good constitution of body; people grow fat with good humour. 2. A fretful, envious, discontented spirit, is its own punishment; it consumes the flesh, preys upon the animal spirits, makes the countenance pale, and is the <hi type="italic">rottenness of the bones.</hi> Those that see the prosperity of others and are grieved, let them <hi type="italic">gnash with their teeth and melt away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Ps. cxii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen13871" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen13872"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13873"/>Rumpatur, quisquis rumpitur invidia.<l eID="gen13873" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13874"/>Whoever bursts for envy, let him burst.

<l eID="gen13874" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen13872"/> <div sID="gen13875" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor. <div eID="gen13875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13876" type="x-p"/> God is here pleased to interest himself more than one would imagine in the treatment given to the poor. 1. He reckons himself affronted in the injuries that are done them. Whosoever he be that wrongs a poor man, taking advantage against him because he is poor and cannot help himself, let him know that he puts an affront upon his Maker. God made him, and gave him his being, the same that is the author of our being; we have all one Father, one Maker; see how Job considered this, <reference osisRef="Job.31.15">Job xxxi. 15</reference>. God made him poor, and appointed him his lot, so that, if we deal hardly with any because they are poor, we reflect upon God as dealing hardly with them in laying them low, that they might be trampled upon. 2. He reckons himself honoured in the kindnesses that are done them; he takes them as done to himself, and will show himself accordingly pleased with them. <hi type="italic">I was hungry, and you gave me meat.</hi> Those therefore that have any true honour for God will show it by compassion to the poor, whom he has undertaken in a special manner to protect and patronise.

<div eID="gen13876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13877" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> The wicked is driven away in his wickedness: but the righteous hath hope in his death. <div eID="gen13877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13878" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The desperate condition of a wicked man when he goes out of the world: He <hi type="italic">is driven away in his wickedness.</hi> He cleaves so closely to the world that he cannot find in his heart to leave it, but is driven away out of it; his soul is required, is forced from him, And sin cleaves so closely to him that it is inseparable; it goes with him into another world; he <hi type="italic">is driven away in his wickedness,</hi> dies in his sins, under the guilt and power of them, unjustified, unsanctified. His wickedness is the storm in which he is hurried away, as chaff before the wind, chased out of the world. 2. The comfortable condition of a godly man when he finishes his course: He <hi type="italic">has hope in his death</hi> of a happiness on the other side death, of better things in another world than ever he had in this. <hi type="italic">The righteous</hi> then have the grace of hope in them; though they have pain, and some dread of death, yet they have hope. They have before them the good hoped for, even the blessed hope which God, who cannot lie, has promised.

<div eID="gen13878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13879" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> Wisdom resteth in the heart of him that hath understanding: but <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> in the midst of fools is made known. <div eID="gen13879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13880" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Modesty is the badge of wisdom. He that is truly wise hides his treasure, so as not to boast of it (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Matt. xiii. 44</reference>), though he does not hide his talent, so as not to trade with it. His <hi type="italic">wisdom rests in his heart;</hi> he digests what he knows, and has it ready to him, but does not unseasonably talk of it and make a noise with it. The heart is the seat of the affections, and there wisdom must rest in the practical love of it, and not swim in the head. 2. Openness and ostentation are a mark of folly. If fools have a little smattering of knowledge, they take all occasions, though very foreign, to produce it, and bring it in by head and shoulders. Or the folly that <hi type="italic">is in the midst of fools is made known</hi> by their forwardness to talk. Many a foolish man takes more pains to show his folly than a wise man thinks it worth his while to take to show his wisdom.

<div eID="gen13880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13881" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">34</hi> Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin <hi type="italic">is</hi> a reproach to any people. <div eID="gen13881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13882" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Justice, reigning in a nation, puts an honour upon it. A righteous administration of the government, impartial equity between man and man, public countenance given to religion, the general practice and profession of virtue, the protecting and preserving of virtuous men, charity and compassion to strangers (<hi type="italic">alms</hi> are sometimes called <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi>), these <hi type="italic">exalt a nation;</hi> they uphold the throne, elevate the people's minds, and qualify a nation for the favour of God, which will make them high, as a <hi type="italic">holy nation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.26.19">Deut. xxvi. 19</reference>. 2. Vice, reigning in a nation, puts disgrace upon it: <hi type="italic">Sin is a reproach to any</hi> city or kingdom, and renders them despicable among their neighbours. The people of Israel were often instances of both parts of this observation; they were great when they were good, but when they forsook God all about them insulted them and trampled on them. It is therefore the interest and duty of princes to use their power for the suppression of vice and support of virtue.

<div eID="gen13882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13883" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> The king's favour <hi type="italic">is</hi> toward a wise servant: but his wrath is <hi type="italic">against</hi> him that causeth shame. <div eID="gen13883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13884" type="x-p"/> This shows that in a well-ordered court and government smiles and favours are dispensed among those that are employed in public trusts according to their merits; Solomon lets them know he will go by that rule, 1. That those who behave themselves wisely shall be respected and preferred, whatever enemies they may have that seek to undermine them. No man's services shall be neglected to please a party or a favourite. 2. That those who are selfish and false, who betray their country, oppress the poor, and sow discord, and thus <hi type="italic">cause shame,</hi> shall be displaced and banished the court, whatever friends they may make to speak for them.  <chapter eID="Prov.14"/> <div eID="gen13884" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv34"/><title type="x-s3">The Proper Use of the Tongue.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv34"/> <div sID="gen13886" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger. <div eID="gen13886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13887" type="x-p"/> Solomon, as conservator of the public peace, here tells us, 1. How the peace may be kept, that we may know how in our places to keep it; it is by soft words. If wrath be risen like a threatening cloud, pregnant with storms and thunder, <hi type="italic">a soft answer</hi> will disperse it and turn it away. When men are provoked, speak gently to them, and give them good words, and they will be pacified, as the Ephraimites were by Gideon's mildness (<reference osisRef="Judg.8.1-Judg.8.3">Judg. viii. 1-3</reference>); whereas, upon a like occasion, by Jephthah's roughness, they were exasperated, and the consequences were bad, <reference osisRef="Judg.12.1-Judg.12.3">Judg. xii. 1-3</reference>. Reason will be better spoken, and a righteous cause better pleaded, with meekness then with passion; hard arguments do best with soft words. 2. How the peace will be broken, that we, for our parts, may do nothing towards the breaking of it. Nothing stirs up anger, and sows discord, like <hi type="italic">grievous words,</hi> calling foul names, as <hi type="italic">Raca,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Thou fool,</hi> upbraiding men with their infirmities and infelicities, their extraction or education, or any thing that lessens them and makes them mean; scornful spiteful reflections, by which men affect to show their wit and malice, stir up the anger of others, which does but increase and inflame their own anger. Rather than lose a jest some will lose a friend and make an enemy.

<div eID="gen13887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13888" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> The tongue of the wise useth knowledge aright: but the mouth of fools poureth out foolishness. <div eID="gen13888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13889" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A good heart by the tongue becomes very useful. He that has knowledge is not only to enjoy it, for his own entertainment, but to use it, to use it aright, for the edification of others; and it is <hi type="italic">the tongue</hi> that must make use of it in pious profitable discourse, in giving suitable and seasonable instructions, counsels, and comforts, with all possible expressions of humility and love, and then <hi type="italic">knowledge is used aright;</hi> and to him that has, and thus uses what he has, more shall be given. 2. A wicked heart by the tongue becomes very hurtful; for <hi type="italic">the mouth of fools belches out foolishness,</hi> which is very offensive; and the corrupt communication which proceeds from an evil treasure within (the filthiness, and foolish talking, and jesting) corrupts the good manners of some and debauches them, and grieves the good hearts of others and disturbs them.  <div eID="gen13889" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv35"/><title type="x-s3">The Righteous and the Wicked Contrasted.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv35"/> <div sID="gen13890" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> The eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">are</hi> in every place, beholding the evil and the good. <div eID="gen13890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13891" type="x-p"/> The great truths of divinity are of great use to enforce the precepts of morality, and none more than this—That the eye of God is always upon the children of men. 1. An eye to discern all, not only from which nothing can be concealed, but by which every thing is actually inspected, and nothing overlooked or looked slightly upon: <hi type="italic">The eyes of the Lord are in every place;</hi> for he not only sees all from on high (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.13">Ps. xxxiii. 13</reference>), but he is every where present. Angels are <hi type="italic">full of eyes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Rev. iv. 8</reference>), but God is all eye. It denotes not only his omniscience, that he sees all, but his universal providence, that he upholds and governs all. Secret sins, services, and sorrows, are under his eye. 2. An eye to distinguish both persons and actions. He <hi type="italic">beholds the evil and the good,</hi> is displeased with the evil and approves of the good, and will judge men according to the sight of his eyes, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Ps. i. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">xi. 4</reference>. The wicked shall not go unpunished, nor the righteous unrewarded, for God has his eye upon both and knows their true character; this speaks as much comfort to saints as terror to sinners.

<div eID="gen13891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13892" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> A wholesome tongue <hi type="italic">is</hi> a tree of life: but perverseness therein <hi type="italic">is</hi> a breach in the spirit. <div eID="gen13892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13893" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A good tongue is healing, healing to wounded consciences by comforting them, to sin-sick souls by convincing them, to peace and love when it is broken by accommodating differences, compromising matters in variance, and reconciling parties at variance; this is the healing of the tongue, which <hi type="italic">is a tree of life,</hi> the leaves of which have a sanative virtue, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.2">Rev. xxii. 2</reference>. He that knows how to discourse will make the place he lives in a paradise. 2. An evil tongue is wounding (<hi type="italic">perverseness,</hi> passion, falsehood, and filthiness <hi type="italic">there, are a breach in the spirit</hi>); it wounds the conscience of the evil speaker, and occasions either guilt or grief to the hearers, and both are to be reckoned <hi type="italic">breaches in the spirit.</hi> Hard words indeed break no bones, but many a heart has been broken by them.

<div eID="gen13893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13894" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent. <div eID="gen13894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13895" type="x-p"/> Hence, 1. Let superiors be admonished to give instruction and reproof to those that are under their charge, as they will answer it in the day of account. They must not only instruct with the light of knowledge, but reprove with the heat of zeal; and both these must be done with the authority and affection of a father, and must be continued, though the desired effect be not immediately perceived. If the instruction be despised, give reproof, and rebuke sharply. It is indeed against the grain with good-humoured men to find fault, and make those about them uneasy; but better so than to suffer them to go on undisturbed in the way to ruin. 2. Let inferiors be admonished, not only to submit to instruction and reproof (even hardships must be submitted to), but to value them as favours and not despise them, to make use of them for their direction, and always to have a regard to them; this will be an evidence that they are wise and a means of making them so; whereas he that slights his good education is a fool and is likely to live and die one.

<div eID="gen13895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13896" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> In the house of the righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> much treasure: but in the revenues of the wicked is trouble. <div eID="gen13896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13897" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Where righteousness is riches are, and the comforts of them: <hi type="italic">In the house of the righteous is much treasure.</hi> Religion teaches men to be diligent, temperate, and just, and by these means, ordinarily, the estate is increased. But that is not all: God <hi type="italic">blesses the habitation of the just,</hi> and that blessing makes rich without trouble. Or, if there be not much of this world's goods, yet where there is grace there is true treasure; and those who have but little, if they have a heart to be therewith content, and to enjoy the comfort of that little, it is enough; it is all riches. The righteous perhaps are not themselves enriched, but there is treasure in their house, a blessing in store, which their children after them may reap the benefit of. A wicked worldly man is only for having his belly filled with those treasures, his own sensual appetite gratified (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>); but a righteous man's first care is for his soul and then for his seed, to have treasure in his heart and then in his house, which his relations and those about him may have the benefit of. 2. Where wickedness is, though there may be riches, yet there is vexation of spirit with them: <hi type="italic">In the revenues of the wicked,</hi> the great incomes they have, <hi type="italic">there is trouble;</hi> for there is guilt and a curse; there is pride and passion, and envy and contention; and those are troublesome lusts, which rob them of the joy of their revenues and make them troublesome to their neighbours.

<div eID="gen13897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13898" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The lips of the wise disperse knowledge: but the heart of the foolish <hi type="italic">doeth</hi> not so. <div eID="gen13898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13899" type="x-p"/> This is to the same purport with <reference osisRef="Prov.15.2">v. 2</reference>, and shows what a blessing a wise man is and what a burden a fool is to those about him. Only here observe further, 1. That we then use knowledge aright when we disperse it, not confine it to a few of our intimates, and grudge it to others who would make as good use of it, but <hi type="italic">give a portion</hi> of this spiritual alms <hi type="italic">to seven and also to eight,</hi> not only be communicative, but diffusive, of this good, with humility and prudence. We must take pains to spread and propagate useful knowledge, must teach some that they may teach others, and so it is dispersed. 2. That it is not only a fault to <hi type="italic">pour out foolishness,</hi> but it is a shame not to <hi type="italic">disperse knowledge,</hi> at least not to drop some wise word or other: <hi type="italic">The heart of the foolish does not so;</hi> it has nothing to disperse that is good, or, if it had, has neither skill nor will to do good with it and therefore is little worth.

<div eID="gen13899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13900" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The sacrifice of the wicked <hi type="italic">is</hi> an abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but the prayer of the upright <hi type="italic">is</hi> his delight. <div eID="gen13900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13901" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. God so hates wicked people, whose hearts are malicious and their lives mischievous, that even their <hi type="italic">sacrifices are an abomination to</hi> him. God has sacrifices brought him even by wicked men, to stop the mouth of conscience and to keep up their reputation in the world, as malefactors come to a sanctuary, not because it is a holy place, but because it shelters them from justice; but their sacrifices, though ever so costly, are not accepted of God, because not offered in sincerity nor from a good principle; they dissemble with God, and in their conversations give the lie to their devotions, and for that reason they are <hi type="italic">an abomination</hi> to him, because they are made a cloak for sin, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.14">ch. vii. 14</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa. i. 11</reference>. 2. God has such a love for upright good people that, though they are not at the expense of a sacrifice (he himself has provided that), their <hi type="italic">prayer is a delight</hi> to him. Praying graces are his own gift, and the work of his own Spirit in them, with which he is well pleased. He not only answers their prayers, but delights in their addresses to him, and in doing them good.

<div eID="gen13901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13902" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> The way of the wicked <hi type="italic">is</hi> an abomination unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but he loveth him that followeth after righteousness. <div eID="gen13902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13903" type="x-p"/> This is a reason of what was said in the foregoing verse. 1. <hi type="italic">The sacrifices of the wicked are an abomination to God,</hi> not for want of some nice points of ceremony, but because <hi type="italic">their way,</hi> the whole course and tenour of their conversation, is wicked, and consequently an abomination to him. Sacrifices for sin were not accepted of those that resolved to go on in sin, and were to the highest degree abominable if intended to obtain a connivance at sin and a permission to go on in it. 2. Therefore <hi type="italic">the prayer of the upright is his delight,</hi> because he is a friend of God, and <hi type="italic">he loves him who,</hi> though he have not yet attained, is <hi type="italic">following after righteousness,</hi> aiming at it and pressing towards it, as St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.13">Phil. iii. 13</reference>.

<div eID="gen13903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13904" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Correction <hi type="italic">is</hi> grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that hateth reproof shall die. <div eID="gen13904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13905" type="x-p"/> This shows that those who cannot bear to be corrected must expect to be destroyed. 1. It is common for those who have known the way of righteousness, but have forsaken it, to reckon it a great affront to be reproved and admonished. They are very uneasy at reproof; they cannot, they will not, bear it; nay, because they hate to be reformed, they hate to be reproved, and hate those who deal faithfully and kindly with them. Of all sinners, reproofs are worst resented by apostates. 2. It is certain that those who will not be reproved will be ruined: <hi type="italic">He that hates reproof,</hi> and hardens his heart against it, is joined to his idols; let him alone. He <hi type="italic">shall die,</hi> and perish for ever, in his sins, since he would not be parted from his sins. <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.15">2 Chron. xxv. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">I know that God has determined to destroy thee,</hi> because thou couldst not bear to be reproved; see also <reference osisRef="Prov.29.1">ch. xxix. 1</reference>.

<div eID="gen13905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13906" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Hell and destruction <hi type="italic">are</hi> before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : how much more then the hearts of the children of men? <div eID="gen13906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13907" type="x-p"/> This confirms what was said (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.3">v. 3</reference>) concerning God's omnipresence, in order to his judging of evil and good. 1. God knows all things, even those things that are hidden from the eyes of all living: <hi type="italic">Hell and destruction are before the Lord,</hi> not only the centre of the earth, and its subterraneous caverns, but the grave, and all the dead bodies which are there buried out of our sight; they are all <hi type="italic">before the Lord,</hi> all under his eye, so that none of them can be lost or be to seek when they are to be raised again. He knows where every man lies buried, even Moses, even those that are buried in the greatest obscurity; nor needs he any monument with a <hi type="italic">Hic jacet—Here he lies,</hi> to direct him. The place of the damned in particular, and all their torments, which are inexpressible, the state of separate souls in general, and all their circumstances, are under God's eye. The word here used for <hi type="italic">destruction</hi> is <hi type="italic">Abaddon,</hi> which is one of the devil's names, <reference osisRef="Rev.9.11">Rev. ix. 11</reference>. That destroyer, though he deceives us, cannot evade or elude the divine cognizance. God examines him whence he comes (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job i. 7</reference>), and sees through all his disguises though he is sly, and subtle, and swift, <reference osisRef="Job.26.6">Job xxvi. 6</reference>. 2. He knows particularly <hi type="italic">the hearts of the children of men.</hi> If he sees through the depths and wiles of Satan himself, <hi type="italic">much more</hi> can he search men's hearts, though they be deceitful, since they learned all their fraudulent arts of Satan. <hi type="italic">God is greater than our hearts,</hi> and knows them better than we know them ourselves, and therefore is an infallible Judge of every man's character, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.13">Heb. iv. 13</reference>.

<div eID="gen13907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13908" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> A scorner loveth not one that reproveth him: neither will he go unto the wise. <div eID="gen13908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13909" type="x-p"/> A scorner is one that not only makes a jest of God and religion, but bids defiance to the methods employed for his conviction and reformation, and, as an evidence of that, 1. He cannot endure the checks of his own conscience, nor will he suffer it to deal plainly with him: <hi type="italic">He loves not to reprove him</hi> (so some read it); he cannot endure to retire into his own heart and commune seriously with that, will not admit of any free thought or fair reasoning with himself, nor let his own heart smite him, if he can help it. That man's case is sad who is afraid of being acquainted and of arguing with himself. 2. He cannot endure the advice and admonitions of his friends: <hi type="italic">He will not go unto the wise,</hi> lest they should give him wise counsel. We ought not only to bid the wise welcome when they come to us, but to go to them, as beggars to the rich man's door for an alms; but this the scorner will not do, for fear of being told of his faults and prevailed upon to reform.

<div eID="gen13909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13910" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken. <div eID="gen13910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13911" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. Harmless mirth is recommended to us, as that which contributes to the health of the body, making men lively and fit for business, and to the acceptableness of the conversation, making the face to shine and rendering us pleasant one to another. A cheerful spirit, under the government of wisdom and grace, is a great ornament to religion, puts a further lustre upon the beauty of holiness, and makes men the more capable of doing good. 2. Hurtful melancholy is what we are cautioned against, as a great enemy to us, both in our devotion and in our conversation: <hi type="italic">By sorrow of the heart,</hi> when it has got dominion and plays the tyrant, as it will be apt to do it if be indulged awhile, <hi type="italic">the spirit is broken</hi> and sunk, and becomes unfit for the service of God. <hi type="italic">The sorrow of the world works death.</hi> Let us therefore <hi type="italic">weep as though we wept not,</hi> in justice to ourselves, as well as in conformity to God and his providence.  <div eID="gen13911" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv36"/><title type="x-s3">Wisdom and Folly.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv36"/> <div sID="gen13912" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge: but the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness. <div eID="gen13912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13913" type="x-p"/> Here are two things to be wondered at:—1. A wise man not satisfied with his wisdom, but still seeking the increase of it; the more he has the more he would have: <hi type="italic">The heart of him that has understanding,</hi> rejoices so in the knowledge it has attained to that it is still coveting more, and in the use of the means of knowledge is still labouring for more, <hi type="italic">growing in grace, and in the knowledge of Christ. Si dixisti, Sufficit, periisti—If you say, I have enough, you are undone.</hi> 2. A fool well satisfied with his folly and not seeking the cure of it. While a good man hungers after the solid satisfactions of grace, a carnal mind feasts on the gratifications of appetite and fancy. Vain mirth and sensual pleasures are its delight, and with these it can rest contented, flattering itself in these foolish ways.

<div eID="gen13913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13914" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> All the days of the afflicted <hi type="italic">are</hi> evil: but he that is of a merry heart <hi type="italic">hath</hi> a continual feast. <div eID="gen13914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13915" type="x-p"/> See here what a great difference there is between the condition and temper of some and others of the children of men. 1. Some are much in affliction, and of a sorrowful spirit, and all their days are evil days, like those of old age, and days of which they say they <hi type="italic">have no pleasure in them.</hi> They <hi type="italic">eat in darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.17">Eccl. v. 17</reference>) and never <hi type="italic">eat with pleasure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.25">Job xxi. 25</reference>. How many are the afflictions of the afflicted in this world! Such are not to be censured or despised, but pitied and prayed for, succoured and comforted. It might have been our own lot, or may be yet, merry as we are at present. 2. Others enjoy great prosperity and are of a cheerful spirit; and they have not only good days, but have <hi type="italic">a continual feast;</hi> and if in the abundance of all things they serve God with gladness of heart, and it is oil to the wheels of their obedience (all this, and heaven too), then they serve a good Master. But let not such feast without fear; a sudden change may come; therefore <hi type="italic">rejoice with trembling.</hi>

<div eID="gen13915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13916" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> little with the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> than great treasure and trouble therewith. <hi type="super">17</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith. <div eID="gen13916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13917" type="x-p"/> Solomon had said in the foregoing verse that he who has not a large estate, or a great income, but a cheerful spirit, has <hi type="italic">a continual feast;</hi> Christian contentment, and joy in God, make the life easy and pleasant; now here he tells us what is necessary to that cheerfulness of spirit which will furnish a man with <hi type="italic">a continual feast,</hi> though he has but little in the world—holiness and love. <div eID="gen13917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13918" type="x-p"/> I. Holiness. <hi type="italic">A little,</hi> if we manage it and enjoy it in <hi type="italic">the fear of the Lord,</hi> if we keep a good conscience and go on in the way of duty, and serve God faithfully with the little we have, will be more comfortable, and turn to a better account, <hi type="italic">than great treasure and trouble therewith.</hi> Observe here, 1. It is often the lot of those that fear God to have but a little of this world. <hi type="italic">The poor receive the gospel,</hi> and poor they still are, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">Jam. ii. 5</reference>. 2. Those that have <hi type="italic">great treasure</hi> have often great <hi type="italic">trouble therewith;</hi> it is so far from making them easy that it increases their care and hurry. <hi type="italic">The abundance of the rich will not suffer them to sleep.</hi> 3. If great treasure bring trouble with it, it is for want of the fear of God. If those that have great estates would do their duty with them, and then trust God with them, their treasure would not have so much trouble attending it. 4. It is therefore far better, and more desirable, to have but a little of the world and to have it with a good conscience, to keep up communion with God, and enjoy him in it, and live by faith, than to have the greatest plenty and live without God in the world. <div eID="gen13918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13919" type="x-p"/> II. Love. Next to the fear of God, peace with all men is necessary to the comfort of this life. 1. If <hi type="italic">brethren dwell together in unity,</hi> if they are friendly, and hearty, and pleasant, both in their daily meals and in more solemn entertainments, that will make <hi type="italic">a dinner of herbs</hi> a feast sufficient; though the fare be coarse, and the estate so small that they can afford no better, yet love will sweeten it and they may be as merry over it as if they had all dainties. 2. If there be mutual enmity and strife, though there be a whole ox for dinner, a fat ox, there can be no comfort in it; the leaven of malice, of hating and being hated, is enough to sour it all. Some refer it to him that makes the entertainment; better have a slender dinner and be heartily welcome than a table richly spread with a grudging evil eye. <div eID="gen13919" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen13920"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13921"/>Cum torvo vultu mihi conula nulla placebit,<l eID="gen13921" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13922"/>Cum placido vultu conula ulla placet.<l eID="gen13922" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13923"/>The most sumptuous entertainment, presented with a sullen brow,<l eID="gen13923" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13924"/>would offend me; while the plainest repast, presented kindly,<l eID="gen13924" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13925"/>would delight me.

<l eID="gen13925" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen13920"/> <div sID="gen13926" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> slow to anger appeaseth strife. <div eID="gen13926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13927" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. Passion the great make-bate. Thence <hi type="italic">come wars and fightings.</hi> Anger strikes the fire which sets cities and churches into a flame: <hi type="italic">A wrathful man,</hi> with his peevish passionate reflections, <hi type="italic">stirs up strife,</hi> and sets people together by the ears; he gives occasion to others to quarrel, and takes the occasion that others give, though ever so trifling. When men carry their resentments too far, one quarrel still produces another. 2. Meekness the great peace-maker: <hi type="italic">He that is slow to anger</hi> not only <hi type="italic">prevents</hi> strife, that it be not kindled, but <hi type="italic">appeases</hi> it if it be already kindled, brings water to the flame, unites those again that have fallen out, and by gentle methods brings them to mutual concessions for peace-sake.

<div eID="gen13927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13928" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> The way of the slothful <hi type="italic">man is</hi> as an hedge of thorns: but the way of the righteous <hi type="italic">is</hi> made plain. <div eID="gen13928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13929" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. Whence those difficulties arise which men pretend to meet with in the way of their duty, and to be insuperable; they arise not from any thing in the nature of the duty, but from the slothfulness of those that have really no mind to it. Those that have no heart to their work pretend that their way is hedged up with thorns, and they cannot do their work at all (as if God were a hard Master, reaping where he had not sown), at least that their way is strewed with thorns, that they cannot do their work without a great deal of hardship and danger; and therefore they go about it with as much reluctance as if they were to go barefoot through a thorny hedge. 2. How these imaginary difficulties may be conquered. An honest desire and endeavour to do our duty will, by the grace of God, make it easy, and we shall find it strewed with roses: <hi type="italic">The way of the righteous is made plain;</hi> it is easy to be trodden and not rough, easy to be found, and not intricate.

<div eID="gen13929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13930" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish man despiseth his mother. <div eID="gen13930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13931" type="x-p"/> Observe here, 1. To the praise of good children, that they are the joy of their parents, who ought to have joy of them, having taken so much care and pains about them. And it adds much to the satisfaction of those that are good if they have reason to think that they have been a comfort to their parents in their declining years, when evil days come. 2. To the shame of wicked children, that by their wickedness they put contempt upon their parents, slight their authority, and make an ill requital for their kindness: <hi type="italic">A foolish son despises his mother,</hi> that had most sorrow with him and perhaps had too much indulged him, which makes his sin in despising her the more sinful and her sorrow the more sorrowful.

<div eID="gen13931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13932" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Folly <hi type="italic">is</hi> joy to <hi type="italic">him that is</hi> destitute of wisdom: but a man of understanding walketh uprightly. <div eID="gen13932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13933" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is the character of a wicked man that he takes pleasure in sin; he has an appetite to the bait, and swallows it greedily, and has no dread of the hook, nor feels from it when he has swallowed it: <hi type="italic">Folly is joy to him;</hi> the folly of others is so, and his own much more. He sins, not only without regret, but with delight, not only repents not of it, but makes his boast of it. This is a certain sign of one that is graceless. 2. It is the character of a wise and good man that he makes conscience of his duty. A fool lives at large, walks at all adventures, by no rule, acts with no sincerity or steadiness; <hi type="italic">but a man of understanding,</hi> the eyes of whose understanding are enlightened by the Spirit (and those that have not a good understanding have no understanding), <hi type="italic">walks uprightly,</hi> lives a sober, orderly, regular life, and studies in every thing to conform himself to the will of God; and this is a constant pleasure and <hi type="italic">joy to him.</hi> But what foolishness remains in him, or proceeds from him at any time, is a grief to him, and he is ashamed of it. By these characters we may try ourselves.

<div eID="gen13933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13934" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established. <div eID="gen13934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13935" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. Of what ill consequence it is to be precipitate and rash, and to act without advice: Men's <hi type="italic">purposes are disappointed,</hi> their measures broken, and they come short of their point, gain not their end, because they would not ask counsel about the way. If men will not take time and pains to deliberate with themselves, or are so confident of their own judgment that they scorn to consult with others, they are not likely to bring any thing considerable to pass; circumstances defeat them which, with a little consultation, might have been foreseen and obviated. It is a good rule, both in public and domestic affairs, to do nothing rashly and of one's own head. <hi type="italic">Plus vident oculi quam oculus—Many eyes see more than one.</hi> That often proves best which was least our own doing. 2. How much it will be for our advantage to ask the advice of our friends: <hi type="italic">In the multitude of counsellors</hi> (provided they be discreet and honest, and will not give counsel with a spirit of contradiction) <hi type="italic">purposes are established.</hi> Solomon's son made no good use of this proverb when he acquiesced not in the counsel of the old men, but because he would have a <hi type="italic">multitude of counsellors,</hi> regarding number more than weight, advised with the young men.

<div eID="gen13935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13936" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word <hi type="italic">spoken</hi> in due season, how good <hi type="italic">is it!</hi> <div eID="gen13936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13937" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. We speak wisely when we speak seasonably: <hi type="italic">The answer of the mouth</hi> will be our credit and joy when it is pertinent and to the purpose, and is <hi type="italic">spoken in due season,</hi> when it is needed and will be regarded, and, as we say, hits the joint. Many a good word comes short of doing the good it might have done, for want of being well-timed. Nor is any thing more the beauty of discourse than to have a proper answer ready off-hand, just when there is occasion for it, and it comes in well. 2. If we speak wisely and well, it will redound to our own comfort and to the advantage of others: <hi type="italic">A man has joy by the answer of his mouth;</hi> he may take a pleasure, but may by no means take a pride, in having spoken so acceptably and well that the hearers admire him and say, "<hi type="italic">How good is it,</hi> and how much good does it do!"

<div eID="gen13937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13938" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> The way of life <hi type="italic">is</hi> above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath. <div eID="gen13938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13939" type="x-p"/> The way of wisdom and holiness is here recommended to us, 1. As very safe and comfortable: It is <hi type="italic">the way of life,</hi> the way that leads to eternal life, in which we shall find the joy and satisfaction which will be the life of the soul, and at the end of which we shall find the perfection of blessedness. Be wise and live. It is the way to escape that misery which we cannot but see ourselves exposed to, and in danger of. It is to <hi type="italic">depart from hell beneath,</hi> from the snares of hell, the temptations of Satan, and all his wiles, from the pains of hell, that everlasting destruction which our sins have deserved. 2. As very sublime and honourable: It <hi type="italic">is above.</hi> A good man sets his <hi type="italic">affections on things above,</hi> and deals in those things. His <hi type="italic">conversation is in heaven;</hi> his way leads directly thither; there his treasure is, <hi type="italic">above,</hi> out of the reach of enemies, above the changes of this lower world. A good man is truly noble and great; his desires and designs are high, and he lives above the common rate of other men. It is above the capacity and out of the sight of foolish men.  <div eID="gen13939" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv37"/><title type="x-s3">The Righteous and the Wicked Contrasted.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv37"/> <div sID="gen13940" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will destroy the house of the proud: but he will establish the border of the widow. <div eID="gen13940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13941" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that are elevated God delights to abase, and commonly does it in the course of his providence: <hi type="italic">The proud,</hi> that magnify themselves, bid defiance to the God above them and trample on all about them, are such as God resists and <hi type="italic">will destroy,</hi> not them only, but <hi type="italic">their houses,</hi> which they are proud of and are confident of the continuance and perpetuity of. Pride is the ruin of multitudes. 2. Those that are dejected God delights to support, and often does it remarkably: <hi type="italic">He will establish the border of the poor widow,</hi> which proud injurious men break in upon, and which the poor widow is not herself able to defend and make good. It is the honour of God to protect the weak and appear for those that are oppressed.

<div eID="gen13941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13942" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> The thoughts of the wicked <hi type="italic">are</hi> an abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but <hi type="italic">the words</hi> of the pure <hi type="italic">are</hi> pleasant words. <div eID="gen13942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13943" type="x-p"/> The former part of this verse speaks of thoughts, the latter of words, but they come all to one; for thoughts are words to God, and words are judged of by the thoughts from which they proceed, so that, 1. <hi type="italic">The thoughts</hi> and words <hi type="italic">of the wicked,</hi> which are, like themselves, wicked, which aim at mischief, and have some ill tendency or other, <hi type="italic">are an abomination to the Lord;</hi> he is displeased at them and will reckon for them. The thoughts of wicked men, for the most part, are such as God hates, and are an offence to him, who not only knows the heart and all that passes and repasses there, but requires the innermost and uppermost place in it. 2. The thoughts and <hi type="italic">words of the pure,</hi> being pure like themselves, clean, honest, and sincere, <hi type="italic">are pleasant words</hi> and pleasant thoughts, well-pleasing to the holy God, who delights in purity. It may be understood both of their devotions to God (<hi type="italic">the words of their mouth and the meditations of their heart,</hi> in prayer and praise, are <hi type="italic">acceptable to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.19.14">Ps. xix. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.13">lxix. 13</reference>) and of their discourses with men, tending to edification. Both are pleasant when they come from a pure, a purified, heart.

<div eID="gen13943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13944" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live. <div eID="gen13944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13945" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that are covetous entail trouble upon their families: <hi type="italic">He that is greedy of gain,</hi> and therefore makes himself a slave to the world, rises up early, sits up late, and eats the bread of carefulness, in pursuit of it—he that hurries, and puts himself and all about him upon the stretch, in business, frets and vexes at every loss and disappointment, and quarrels with every body that stands in the way of his profit—he <hi type="italic">troubles his own house,</hi> is a burden and vexation to his children and servants. He that, in his greediness of gain, takes bribes, and uses unlawful ways of getting money, leaves a curse with what he gets to those that come after him, which sooner or later will bring trouble into the house, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.9-Hab.2.10">Hab. ii. 9, 10</reference>. 2. Those that are generous as well as righteous entail a blessing upon their families: <hi type="italic">He that hates gifts,</hi> that shakes his hands from holding the bribes that are thrust into his hand to pervert justice and abhors all sinful indirect ways of getting money—that hates to be paltry and mercenary, and is willing, if there be occasion, to do good gratis—he shall live; he shall have the comfort of life, shall live in prosperity and reputation; his name and family shall live and continue.

<div eID="gen13945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13946" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> The heart of the righteous studieth to answer: but the mouth of the wicked poureth out evil things. <div eID="gen13946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13947" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A good man proved to be a wise man by this, that he governs his tongue well; he that does so <hi type="italic">the same is a perfect man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.3.2">Jam. iii. 2</reference>. It is part of the character of a righteous man that being convinced of the account he must give of his words, and of the good and bad influence of them upon others, he makes conscience of speaking truly (it is his <hi type="italic">heart</hi> that <hi type="italic">answers,</hi> that is, he speaks as he thinks, and dares not do otherwise, he <hi type="italic">speaks the truth in his heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.15.2">Ps. xv. 2</reference>), and of speaking pertinently and profitably, and therefore he <hi type="italic">studies to answer,</hi> that his speech may be with grace, <reference osisRef="Ne.2.4">Neh. ii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="5.7">v. 7</reference>. 2. A wicked man is proved to be a fool by this, that he never heeds what he says, but his <hi type="italic">mouth pours out evil things,</hi> to the dishonour of God and religion, his own reproach, and the hurt of others. Doubtless that is an evil heart which thus overflows with evil.

<div eID="gen13947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13948" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> far from the wicked: but he heareth the prayer of the righteous. <div eID="gen13948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13949" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. God sets himself at a distance from those that set him at defiance: <hi type="italic">The wicked say to the Almighty, Depart from us,</hi> and he is, accordingly, <hi type="italic">far from</hi> them; he does not manifest himself to them, has no communion with them, will not hear them, will not help them, no, not in the time of their need. They shall be for ever banished from his presence and he will behold them afar off. <hi type="italic">Depart from me, you cursed.</hi> 2. He will draw nigh to those in a way of mercy who draw nigh to him in a way of duty: <hi type="italic">He hears the prayer of the righteous,</hi> accepts it, is well pleased with it, and will grant an answer of peace to it. It is <hi type="italic">the prayer of a righteous man</hi> that <hi type="italic">avails much,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.16">Jam. v. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">He is nigh to them,</hi> a present help, <hi type="italic">in all that they call upon him for.</hi>

<div eID="gen13949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13950" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart: <hi type="italic">and</hi> a good report maketh the bones fat. <div eID="gen13950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13951" type="x-p"/> Two things are here pronounced pleasant:— 1. It is pleasant to have a good prospect to see the light of the sun (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.7">Eccl. xi. 7</reference>) and by it to see the wonderful works of God, with which this lower world is beautified and enriched. Those that want the mercy know how to value it; how would <hi type="italic">the light of the eyes rejoice their hearts!</hi> The consideration of this should make us thankful for our eyesight. 2. It is more pleasant to have <hi type="italic">a good name,</hi> a name for good things with God and good people; this <hi type="italic">is as precious ointment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Eccl. vii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">It makes the bones fat;</hi> it gives a secret pleasure, and that which is strengthening. It is also very comfortable to hear (as some understand it) <hi type="italic">a good report</hi> concerning others; a good man has no greater joy than to hear that his friends walk in the truth.

<div eID="gen13951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13952" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise. <div eID="gen13952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13953" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is the character of a wise man that he is very willing to be reproved, and therefore chooses to converse with those that, both by their words and example, will show him what is amiss in him: <hi type="italic">The ear that</hi> can take <hi type="italic">the reproof</hi> will love the reprover. Faithful friendly reproofs are here called <hi type="italic">the reproofs of life,</hi> not only because they are to be given in a lively manner, and with a prudent zeal (and we must reprove by our lives as well as by our doctrine), but because, where they are well-taken, they are means of spiritual life, and lead to eternal life, and (as some think) to distinguish them from rebukes and reproaches for well-doing, which are rather reproofs of death, which we must not regard nor be influenced by. 2. Those that are so wise as to bear reproof well will hereby be <hi type="italic">made wiser</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.9">ch. ix. 9</reference>), and come at length to be numbered among the wise men of the age, and will have both ability and authority to reprove and instruct others. Those that learn well, and obey well, are likely in time to teach well and rule well.

<div eID="gen13953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13954" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding. <div eID="gen13954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13955" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. The folly of those that will not be taught, that <hi type="italic">refuse instruction,</hi> that will not heed it, but turn their backs upon it, or will not hear it, but turn their hearts against it. They <hi type="italic">refuse correction</hi> (margin); they will not <hi type="italic">take it,</hi> no, not from God himself, but kick against the pricks. Those that do so <hi type="italic">despise their own souls;</hi> they show that they have a low and mean opinion of them, and are in little care and concern about them, considered as rational and immortal, instruction being designed to cultivate reason and prepare for the immortal state. The fundamental error of sinners is undervaluing their own souls; therefore they neglect to provide for them, abuse them, expose them, prefer the body before the soul, and wrong the soul to please the body. 2. The wisdom of those that are willing, not only to be taught, but to be reproved: <hi type="italic">He that hears reproof,</hi> and amends the faults he is reproved for, <hi type="italic">gets understanding,</hi> by which his soul is secured from bad ways and directed in good ways, and thereby he both evidences the value he has for his own soul and puts true honour upon it.

<div eID="gen13955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13956" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> The fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> the instruction of wisdom; and before honour <hi type="italic">is</hi> humility. <div eID="gen13956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13957" type="x-p"/> See here how much it is our interest, as well as duty, 1.
