To submit to our God, and keep up a reverence for him: <hi type="italic">The fear of the Lord,</hi> as it is <hi type="italic">the beginning of wisdom,</hi> so it is <hi type="italic">the instruction</hi> and correction <hi type="italic">of wisdom;</hi> the principles of religion, closely adhered to, will improve our knowledge, rectify our mistakes, and be the best and surest guide of our way. An awe of God upon our spirits will put us upon the wisest counsels and chastise us when we say or do unwisely. 2. To stoop to our brethren, and keep up a respect for them. Where there is humility there is a happy presage of honour and preparative for it. Those that humble themselves shall be exalted here and hereafter.  <chapter eID="Prov.15"/> <div eID="gen13957" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv38"/><title type="x-s3">The Sovereignty of Divine Providence.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv38"/> <div sID="gen13959" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, <hi type="italic">is</hi> from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen13959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13960" type="x-p"/> As we read this, it teaches us a great truth, that we are not sufficient of ourselves to <hi type="italic">think or speak any thing of ourselves</hi> that is wise and good, but that all <hi type="italic">our sufficiency is of God,</hi> who is with the heart and with the mouth, and <hi type="italic">works in us both to will and to do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.13">Phil. ii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Ps. x. 17</reference>. But most read it otherwise: <hi type="italic">The preparation of the heart is in man</hi> (he may contrive and design this and the other) but <hi type="italic">the answer of the tongue,</hi> not only the delivering of what he designed to speak, but the issue and success of what he designed to do, <hi type="italic">is of the Lord.</hi> That is, in short, 1. <hi type="italic">Man purposes.</hi> He has a freedom of thought and a freedom of will permitted him; let him form his projects, and lay his schemes, as he thinks best: but, after all, 2. <hi type="italic">God disposes.</hi> Man cannot go on with his business without the assistance and blessing of God, who <hi type="italic">made man's mouth</hi> and teaches us what we shall say. Nay, God easily can, and often does, cross men's purposes, and break their measures. It was a curse that was prepared in Balaam's heart, but the answer of the tongue was a blessing.

<div eID="gen13960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13961" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> All the ways of a man <hi type="italic">are</hi> clean in his own eyes; but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> weigheth the spirits. <div eID="gen13961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13962" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. We are all apt to be partial in judging of ourselves: <hi type="italic">All the ways of a man,</hi> all his designs, all his doings, <hi type="italic">are clean in his own eyes,</hi> and he sees nothing amiss in them, nothing for which to condemn himself, or which should make his projects prove otherwise than well; and therefore he is confident of success, and that the answer of the tongue shall be according to the expectations of the heart; but there is a great deal of pollution cleaving to our ways, which we are not aware of, or do not think so ill of as we ought. 2. The judgment of God concerning us, we are sure, is according to truth: He <hi type="italic">weighs the spirits</hi> in a just and unerring balance, knows what is in us, and passes a judgment upon us accordingly, writing <hi type="italic">Tekel</hi> upon that which passed our scale with approbation—<hi type="italic">weighed in the balance and found wanting;</hi> and by his judgment we must stand or fall. He not only sees men's ways but tries their spirits, and we are as our spirits are.

<div eID="gen13962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13963" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Commit thy works unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and thy thoughts shall be established. <div eID="gen13963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13964" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a very desirable thing to have <hi type="italic">our thoughts established,</hi> and not tossed, and put into a hurry, by disquieting cares and fears,—to go on in an even steady course of honesty and piety, not disturbed, or put out of frame, by any event or change,—to be satisfied that all shall work for good and issue well at last, and therefore to be always easy and sedate. 2. The only way to have our <hi type="italic">thoughts established</hi> is to <hi type="italic">commit our works to the Lord.</hi> The great concerns of our souls must be committed to the grace of God, with a dependence upon and submission to the conduct of that grace (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2 Tim. i. 12</reference>); all our outward concerns must be committed to the providence of God, and to the sovereign, wise, and gracious disposal of that providence. <hi type="italic">Roll thy works upon the Lord</hi> (so the word is); roll the burden of thy care from thyself upon God. Lay the matter before him by prayer. <hi type="italic">Make known thy works unto the Lord</hi> (so some read it), not only the works of thy hand, but the workings of thy heart; and then leave it with him, by faith and dependence upon him, submission and resignation to him. <hi type="italic">The will of the Lord be done.</hi> We may then be easy when we resolve that whatever pleases God shall please us.

<div eID="gen13964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13965" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath made all <hi type="italic">things</hi> for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil. <div eID="gen13965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13966" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. That God is the first cause. He is the former of all things and all persons, the fountain of being; he gave every creature the being it has and appointed it its place. Even the wicked are his creatures, though they are rebels; he gave them those powers with which they fight against him, which aggravates their wickedness, that they will not let him that made them rule them, and therefore, though he made them, he will not save them. 2. That God is the last end. All is of him and from him, and therefore all is to him and for him. He made all according to his will and for his praise; he designed to serve his own purposes by all his creatures, and he will not fail of his designs; all are his servants. The wicked he is not glorified by, but he will be glorified upon. He makes no man wicked, but he made those who he foresaw would be wicked: yet he made them (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.6">Gen. vi. 6</reference>), because he knew how to <hi type="italic">get himself honour upon them.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rom.9.22">Rom. ix. 22</reference>. Or (as some understand it) he made the wicked to be employed by him as the instruments of his wrath in the day of evil, when he brings judgments on the world. He makes some use even of wicked men, as of other things, to be his sword, his hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13-Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 13, 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">flagellum Dei—the scourge of God.</hi> The king of Babylon is called his <hi type="italic">servant.</hi>

<div eID="gen13966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13967" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Every one <hi type="italic">that is</hi> proud in heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> an abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="italic">though</hi> hand <hi type="italic">join</hi> in hand, he shall not be unpunished. <div eID="gen13967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13968" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The pride of sinners sets God against them. He that, being high in estate is proud in heart, whose spirit is elevated with his condition, so that he becomes insolent in his conduct towards God and man, let him know that though he admires himself, and others caress him, yet he is <hi type="italic">an abomination to the Lord.</hi> The great God despises him; the holy God detest him. 2. The power of sinners cannot secure them against God, though they strengthen themselves with body hands. Though they may strengthen one another with their confederacies and combinations, joining forces against God, they shall not escape his righteous judgment. <hi type="italic">Woe unto him that strives with his Maker,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.21">ch. xi. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Isa. xlv. 9</reference>.

<div eID="gen13968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13969" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> By mercy and truth iniquity is purged: and by the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">men</hi> depart from evil. <div eID="gen13969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13970" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How the guilt of sin is taken away from us—by the <hi type="italic">mercy and truth</hi> of God, mercy in promising, truth in performing, the mercy and truth which kiss each other in Jesus Christ the Mediator—by the covenant of grace, in which mercy and truth shine so brightly—by our mercy and truth, as the condition of the pardon and a necessary qualification for it—by these, and not by the legal sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.7-Mic.6.8">Mic. vi. 7, 8</reference>. 2. How the power of sin is broken in us. By the principles of <hi type="italic">mercy and truth</hi> commanding in us the corrupt inclinations are purged out (so we may take the former part); however, <hi type="italic">by the fear of the Lord,</hi> and the influence of that fear, <hi type="italic">men depart from evil;</hi> those will not dare to sin against God who keep up in their minds a holy dread and reverence of him.

<div eID="gen13970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13971" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> When a man's ways please the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him. <div eID="gen13971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13972" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. God can turn foes into friends when he pleases. He that has all hearts in his hand has access to men's spirits and power over them, working insensibly, but irresistibly upon them, can make <hi type="italic">a man's enemies to be at peace with him,</hi> can change their minds, or force them into a feigned submission. He can slay all enemies, and bring those together that were at the greatest distance from each other. 2. He will do it for us when we please him. If we make it our care to be reconciled to God, and to keep ourselves in his love, he will incline those that have been envious towards us, and vexatious to us, to entertain a good opinion of us and to become our friends. God made Esau to be at peace with Jacob, Abimelech with Isaac, and David's enemies to court his favour and desire a league with Israel. The image of God appearing upon the righteous, and his particular lovingkindness to them, are enough to recommend them to the respect of all, even of those that have been most prejudiced against them.

<div eID="gen13972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13973" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a little with righteousness than great revenues without right. <div eID="gen13973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13974" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. It is supposed that an honest good man may have but a little of the wealth of this world (all the righteous are not rich),—that a man may have but little, and yet may be honest (though poverty is a temptation to dishonesty, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">ch. xxx. 9</reference>, yet not an invincible one),—and that a man may grow rich, for a while, by fraud and oppression, may have <hi type="italic">great revenues,</hi> and those got and kept <hi type="italic">without right,</hi> may have no good title to them nor make any good use of them. 2. It is maintained that a small estate, honestly come by, which a man is content with, enjoys comfortably, serves God with cheerfully, and puts to a right use, is much better and more valuable than a great estate ill-got, and then ill-kept or ill-spent. It carries with it more inward satisfaction, a better reputation with all that are wise and good; it will last longer, and will turn to a better account in the great day, when men will be judged, not according to what they had, but what they did.

<div eID="gen13974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13975" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> A man's heart deviseth his way: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> directeth his steps. <div eID="gen13975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13976" type="x-p"/> Man is here represented to us, 1. As a reasonable creature, that has the faculty of contriving for himself: <hi type="italic">His heart devises his way,</hi> designs an end, and projects ways and means leading to that end, which the inferior creatures, who are governed by sense and natural instinct, cannot do. The more shame for him if he do not devise the way how to please God and provide for his everlasting state. 2. But as a depending creature, that is subject to the direction and dominion of his Maker. If men <hi type="italic">devise their way,</hi> so as to make God's glory their end and his will their rule, they may expect that he will <hi type="italic">direct their steps</hi> by his Spirit and grace, so that they shall not miss their way nor come short of their end. But let men devise their worldly affairs ever so politely, and with ever so great a probability of success, yet God has the ordering of the event, and sometimes <hi type="italic">directs their steps</hi> to that which they least intended. The design of this is to teach us to say, <hi type="italic">If the Lord will, we shall live and do this or that</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.14-Jas.4.15">Jam. iv. 14, 15</reference>), and to have our eye to God, not only in the great turns of our lives, but in every step we take. <hi type="italic">Lord, direct my way,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.11">1 Thess. iii. 11</reference>.  <div eID="gen13976" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv39"/><title type="x-s3">The Duties of Kings.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv39"/> <div sID="gen13977" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> A divine sentence <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment. <div eID="gen13977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13978" type="x-p"/> We wish this were always true as a proposition, and we ought to make it our prayer for kings, and all in authority, that a <hi type="italic">divine sentence</hi> may be in their lips, both in giving orders, that they may do that in wisdom, and in giving sentence, that they may do that in equity, both which are included in <hi type="italic">judgment,</hi> and that in neither <hi type="italic">their mouth may transgress,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1 Tim. ii. 1</reference>. But it is often otherwise; and therefore, 1. It may be read as a precept to the kings and judges of the earth to be wise and instructed. Let them be just, and rule in the fear of God; let them act with such wisdom and conscience that there may appear a holy divination in all they say or do, and that they are guided by principles supernatural: let not their mouths transgress in judgment, for the judgment is God's. 2. It may be taken as a promise to all good kings, that if they sincerely aim at God's glory, and seek direction from him, he will qualify them with wisdom and grace above others, in proportion to the eminency of their station and the trusts lodged in their hands. When Saul himself was made king God gave him another spirit. 3. It was true concerning Solomon who wrote this; he had extraordinary wisdom, pursuant to the promise God made him, See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.28">1 Kings iii. 28</reference>.

<div eID="gen13978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13979" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> A just weight and balance <hi type="italic">are</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's: all the weights of the bag <hi type="italic">are</hi> his work. <div eID="gen13979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13980" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The administration of public justice by the magistrate is an ordinance of God; in it the scales are held, and ought to be held by a steady and impartial hand; and we ought to submit to it, for the Lord's sake, and to see his authority in that of the magistrate, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Rom. xiii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.13">1 Pet. ii. 13</reference>. 2. The observance of justice in commerce between man and man is likewise a divine appointment. He taught men discretion to make scales and weights for the adjusting of right exactly between buyer and seller, that neither may be wronged; and all other useful inventions for the preserving of right are from him. He has also appointed by his law that they be just. It is therefore a great affront to him, and to his government, to falsify, and so to do wrong under colour and pretence of doing right, which is <hi type="italic">wickedness in the place of judgment.</hi>

<div eID="gen13980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13981" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness. <div eID="gen13981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13982" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The character of a good king, which Solomon intended not for his own praise, but for instruction to his successors, his neighbours, and the viceroys under him. A good king not only does justice, but it is <hi type="italic">an abomination</hi> to him to do otherwise. He hates the thought of doing wrong and perverting justice; he not only abhors the wickedness done by others, but abhors the wickedness done by others, but abhors to do any himself, though, having power, he might easily and safety do it. 2. The comfort of a good king: His <hi type="italic">throne is established by righteousness.</hi> He that makes conscience of using his power aright shall find that to be the best security of his government, both as it will oblige people, make them easy, and keep them in the interest of it, and as it will obtain the blessing of God, which will be a firm basis to the throne and a strong guard about it.

<div eID="gen13982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13983" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Righteous lips <hi type="italic">are</hi> the delight of kings; and they love him that speaketh right. <div eID="gen13983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13984" type="x-p"/> Here is a further character of good kings, that they <hi type="italic">love</hi> and <hi type="italic">delight</hi> in those that <hi type="italic">speak right.</hi> 1. They hate parasites and those that flatter them, and are very willing that all about them should deal faithfully with them and tell them that which is true, whether it be pleasing or displeasing, both concerning persons and things, that every thing should be set in a true light and nothing disguised, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">ch. xxix. 12</reference>. 2. They not only do righteousness themselves, but take care to employ those under them that do righteousness too, which is of great consequence to the people, who must be subject not only to the king as supreme, but to the governors sent by him, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.14">1 Pet. ii. 14</reference>. A good king will therefore put those in power who are conscientious, and will say that which is righteous and discreet, and know how to speak aright and to the purpose.

<div eID="gen13984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13985" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The wrath of a king <hi type="italic">is as</hi> messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it. <hi type="super">15</hi> In the light of the king's countenance <hi type="italic">is</hi> life; and his favour <hi type="italic">is</hi> as a cloud of the latter rain. <div eID="gen13985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13986" type="x-p"/> These two verses show the power of kings, which is every where great, but was especially so in those eastern countries, where they were absolute and arbitrary. Whom they would they slew and whom they would they kept alive. Their will was a law. We have reason to bless God for the happy constitution of the government we live under, which maintains the prerogative of the prince without any injury to the liberty of the subject. But here it is intimated, 1. How formidable <hi type="italic">the wrath of a king is:</hi> It is <hi type="italic">as messengers of death;</hi> the wrath of Ahasuerus was so to Haman. An angry word from an incensed prince has been to many a <hi type="italic">messenger of death,</hi> and has struck so great a terror upon some as if a sentence of death had been pronounced upon them. He must be a very <hi type="italic">wise man</hi> that knows how to <hi type="italic">pacify</hi> the wrath of a king with a word fitly spoken, as Jonathan once pacified his father's rage against David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.6">1 Sam. xix. 6</reference>. A prudent subject may sometimes suggest that to an angry prince which will cool his resentments. 2. How valuable and desirable the king's favour is to those that have incurred his displeasure; it is life from the dead if the king be reconciled to them. To others it is <hi type="italic">as a cloud of the latter rain,</hi> very refreshing to the ground. Solomon put his subjects in mind of this, that they might not do any thing to incur his wrath, but be careful to recommend themselves to his favour. We ought by it to be put in mind how much we are concerned to escape the wrath and obtain the favour of the King of kings. His frowns are worse than death, and his favour is better than life; and therefore those are fools who to escape the wrath, and obtain the favour, of an earthly prince, will throw themselves out of God's favour, and make themselves obnoxious to his wrath.  <div eID="gen13986" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv40"/><title type="x-s3">Pride and Humility.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv40"/> <div sID="gen13987" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> How much better <hi type="italic">is it</hi> to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver! <div eID="gen13987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13988" type="x-p"/> Solomon here not only asserts that it is better to get wisdom than gold (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.14">ch. iii. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.19">viii. 19</reference>), but he speaks it with assurance, that it is much better, better beyond expression—with admiration (<hi type="italic">How much better!</hi>) as one amazed at the disproportion—with an appeal to men's consciences ("Judge in yourselves how much better it is" )—and with an addition to the same purport, that understanding is <hi type="italic">rather to be chosen than silver</hi> and all the treasures of kings and their favourites. Note, 1. Heavenly wisdom is better than worldly wealth, and to be preferred before it. Grace is more valuable than gold. Grace is the gift of God's peculiar favour; gold only of common providence. Grace is for ourselves; gold for others. Grace is for the soul and eternity; gold only for the body and time. Grace will stand us in stead in a dying hour, when gold will do us no good. 2. The getting of this heavenly wisdom is better than the getting of worldly wealth. Many take care and pains to get wealth, and yet come short of it; but grace was never denied to any that sincerely sought it. There is vanity and vexation of spirit in getting wealth, but joy and satisfaction of spirit in getting wisdom. <hi type="italic">Great peace have those that love it.</hi>

<div eID="gen13988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13989" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> The highway of the upright <hi type="italic">is</hi> to depart from evil: he that keepeth his way preserveth his soul. <div eID="gen13989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13990" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is <hi type="italic">the way of the upright</hi> to avoid sin, and every thing that looks like it and leads towards it; and this is a highway marked out by authority, tracked by many that have gone before us, and in which we meet with many that keep company with us; it is easy to find and safe to be travelled in, like a highway, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">To depart from evil is understanding.</hi> 2. It is the care of the upright to preserve their own souls, that they be not polluted with sin, and that by the troubles of the world they may not be put out of the possession of them, especially that they may not perish for ever, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Matt. xvi. 26</reference>. And it is therefore their care to keep their way, and not turn aside out of it, on either hand, but to press towards perfection. Those that adhere to their duty secure their felicity. Keep thy way and God will keep thee.

<div eID="gen13990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13991" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Pride <hi type="italic">goeth</hi> before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. <div eID="gen13991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13992" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Pride will have a fall. Those that are of a <hi type="italic">haughty spirit,</hi> that think of themselves above what is meet, and look with contempt upon others, that with their pride affront God and disquiet others, will be brought down, either by repentance or by ruin. It is the honour of God to humble the proud, <reference osisRef="Job.40.11-Job.40.12">Job xl. 11, 12</reference>. It is the act of justice that those who have lifted up themselves should be laid low. Pharaoh, Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar, were instances of this. Men cannot punish pride, but either admire it or fear it, and therefore God will take the punishing of it into his own hands. Let him alone to deal with proud men. 2. Proud men are frequently most proud, and insolent, and haughty, just before their destruction, so that it is a certain presage that they are upon the brink of it. When proud men set God's judgments at defiance, and think themselves at the greatest distance from them, it is a sign that they are at the door; witness the case of Benhadad and Herod. <hi type="italic">While the word was in the king's mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.31">Dan. iv. 31</reference>. Therefore let us not fear the pride of others, but greatly fear pride in ourselves.

<div eID="gen13992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13993" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Better <hi type="italic">it is to be</hi> of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud. <div eID="gen13993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13994" type="x-p"/> This is a paradox which the children of this world cannot understand and will not subscribe to, that it is better to be poor and humble than to be rich and proud. 1. Those that <hi type="italic">divide the spoil</hi> are commonly proud; they value themselves and despise others, and their mind rises with their condition; those therefore that are <hi type="italic">rich in this world</hi> have need to be charged that they <hi type="italic">be not high-minded,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1 Tim. vi. 17</reference>. Those that are proud and will put forth themselves, that thrust, and shove, and scramble, for preferment, are the men that commonly <hi type="italic">divide the spoil</hi> and share it among them; they have the world at will and the ball at their foot. 2. It is upon all accounts better to take our lot with those whose condition is low, and their minds brought to it, than to covet and aim to make a figure and a bustle in the world. Humility, though it should expose us to contempt in the world, yet while it recommends us to the favour of God, qualifies us for his gracious visits, prepares us for his glory, secures us from many temptations, and preserves the quiet and repose of our own souls, is much better than that high-spiritedness which, though it carry away the honour and wealth of the world, makes God a man's enemy and the devil his master.  <div eID="gen13994" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv41"/><title type="x-s3">Benefits of Wisdom.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv41"/> <div sID="gen13995" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good: and whoso trusteth in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , happy <hi type="italic">is</hi> he. <div eID="gen13995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13996" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Prudence gains men respect and success: <hi type="italic">He that handles a matter wisely</hi> (that is master of his trade and makes it to appear he understands what he undertakes, that is considerate in his affairs, and, when he speaks or writes on any subject, does it pertinently) shall <hi type="italic">find good,</hi> shall come into good repute, and perhaps may make a good hand of it. 2. But it is piety only that will secure men's true happiness: Those that <hi type="italic">handle a matter wisely,</hi> if they are proud and lean to their own understanding, though they may find some good, yet they will have no great satisfaction in it; but he that <hi type="italic">trusts in the Lord,</hi> and not in his own wisdom, <hi type="italic">happy is he,</hi> and shall speed better at last. Some read the former part of the verse so as to expound it of piety, which is indeed true wisdom: <hi type="italic">He that attends to the word</hi> (the word of God, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.13">ch. xiii. 13</reference>) shall <hi type="italic">find good</hi> in it and good by it. And whoso <hi type="italic">trusts in the Lord,</hi> in his word which he attends to, is happy.

<div eID="gen13996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13997" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> The wise in heart shall be called prudent: and the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning. <div eID="gen13997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13998" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that have solid wisdom will have the credit of it; it will gain them reputation, and they <hi type="italic">shall be called prudent</hi> grave men, and a deference will be paid to their judgment. <hi type="italic">Do that which is wise and good and thou shalt have the praise of the same.</hi> 2. Those that with their wisdom have a happy elocution, that deliver their sentiments easily and with a good grace, are communicative of their wisdom and have words at will, and good language as well as good sense, <hi type="italic">increase learning;</hi> they diffuse and propagate knowledge to others, and do good work with it, and by that means increase their own stock. They add doctrine, improve sciences, and do service to the commonwealth of learning. <hi type="italic">To him that has,</hi> and uses what he has, <hi type="italic">more shall be given.</hi>

<div eID="gen13998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13999" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Understanding <hi type="italic">is</hi> a wellspring of life unto him that hath it: but the instruction of fools <hi type="italic">is</hi> folly. <div eID="gen13999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14000" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. There is always some good to be gotten by a wise and good man: His <hi type="italic">understanding is a well-spring of life to him,</hi> which always flows and can never be drawn dry; he has something to say upon all occasions that is instructive, and of use to those that will make use of it, things new and old to bring out of his treasure; at least, his understanding is a <hi type="italic">spring of life</hi> to himself, yielding him abundant satisfaction; within his own thoughts he entertains and edifies himself, if not others. 2. There is nothing that is good to be gotten by a fool. Even his instruction, his set and solemn discourses, are but folly, like himself, and tending to make others like him. When he does his best it is but folly, in comparison even with the common talk of a wise man, who speaks better at table than a fool in Moses's seat.

<div eID="gen14000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14001" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips. <div eID="gen14001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14002" type="x-p"/> Solomon had commended eloquence, or <hi type="italic">the sweetness of the lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.21">v. 21</reference>), and seemed to prefer it before wisdom; but here he corrects himself, as it were, and shows that unless there be a good treasure within to support the eloquence it is worth little. Wisdom in <hi type="italic">the heart</hi> is the main matter. 1. It is this that directs us in speaking, that <hi type="italic">teaches the mouth</hi> what to speak, and when, and how, so that what is spoken may be proper, and pertinent, and seasonable; otherwise, though the language be ever so fine, it had better be unsaid. 2. It is this that gives weight to what we speak and <hi type="italic">adds learning</hi> to it, strength of reason and force of argument, without which, let a thing be ever so well worded, it will be rejected, when it comes to be considered, as trifling. Quaint expressions please the ear, and humour the fancy, but it is learning in the lips that must convince the judgment, and sway that, to which wisdom in the heart is necessary.

<div eID="gen14002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14003" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Pleasant words <hi type="italic">are as</hi> an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones. <div eID="gen14003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14004" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">pleasant words</hi> here commended must be those which <hi type="italic">the heart of the wise teaches, and adds learning to</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.23">v. 23</reference>), words of seasonable advice, instruction, and comfort, words taken from God's word, for that is it which Solomon had learned from his father to account <hi type="italic">sweeter than honey and the honey-comb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.19.10">Ps. xix. 10</reference>. These words, to those that know how to relish them, 1. Are pleasant. They are like the <hi type="italic">honey-comb, sweet to the soul,</hi> which tastes in them that <hi type="italic">the Lord is gracious;</hi> nothing more grateful and agreeable to the new man than the word of God, and those words which are borrowed from it, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.103">Ps. cxix. 103</reference>. 2. They are wholesome. Many things are pleasant that are not profitable, but these <hi type="italic">pleasant words are health to the bones,</hi> to the inward man, as well as <hi type="italic">sweet to the soul.</hi> They make <hi type="italic">the bones,</hi> which sin has broken and put out of joint, <hi type="italic">to rejoice.</hi> The bones are the strength of the body; and the good word of God is a means of spiritual strength, curing the diseases that weaken us.  <div eID="gen14004" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv42"/><title type="x-s3">Malice and Envy.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv42"/> <div sID="gen14005" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof <hi type="italic">are</hi> the ways of death. <div eID="gen14005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14006" type="x-p"/> This we had before (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.12">ch. xiv. 12</reference>), but here it is repeated, as that which is very necessary to be thought of, 1. By way of caution to us all to take heed of deceiving ourselves in the great concerns of our souls by resting in that which <hi type="italic">seems right</hi> and is not really so, and, for the preventing of a self-delusion, to be impartial in self-examination and keep up a jealousy over ourselves. 2. By way of terror to those whose way is not right, is not as it should be, however it may seem to themselves or others; the end of it will certainly be death; to that it has a direct and certain tendency.

<div eID="gen14006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14007" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> He that laboureth laboureth for himself; for his mouth craveth it of him. <div eID="gen14007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14008" type="x-p"/> This is designed to engage us to diligence, and quicken us, <hi type="italic">what our hand finds to do, to do it with all our might,</hi> both in our worldly business and in the work of religion; for in the original it is, <hi type="italic">The soul that labours labours for itself.</hi> It is heart-work which is here intended, the labour of the soul, which is here recommended to us, 1. As that which will be absolutely needful. Our mouth is continually craving it of us; the necessities both of soul and body are pressing, and require constant relief, so that we must either work or starve. Both call for daily bread, and therefore there must be daily labour; for in the sweat of our face we must eat, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.10">2 Thess. iii. 10</reference>. 2. As that which will be unspeakably gainful. We know on whose errand we go: <hi type="italic">He that labours</hi> shall reap the fruit of his labour; it shall be <hi type="italic">for himself;</hi> he shall rejoice in his own work and <hi type="italic">eat the labour of his hands.</hi> If we make religion our business, God will make it our blessedness.

<div eID="gen14008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14009" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> An ungodly man diggeth up evil: and in his lips <hi type="italic">there is</hi> as a burning fire. <hi type="super">28</hi> A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends. <div eID="gen14009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14010" type="x-p"/> There are those that are not only vicious themselves, but spiteful and mischievous to others, and they are the worst of men; two sorts of such are here described:—1. Such as envy a man the honour of his good name, and do all they can to blast that by calumnies and misrepresentations: They <hi type="italic">dig up evil;</hi> they take a great deal of pains to find out something or other on which to ground a slander, or which may give some colour to it. If none appear above ground, rather than want it they will dig for it, by diving into what is secret, or looking a great way back, or by evil suspicions and surmises, and forced innuendos. In the lips of a slanderer and backbiter <hi type="italic">there is as a fire,</hi> not only to brand his neighbour's reputation, to smoke and sully it, but <hi type="italic">as a burning fire</hi> to consume it. And how great a matter does a little of this fire kindle, and how hardly is it extinguished! <reference osisRef="Jas.3.5-Jas.3.6">James iii. 5, 6</reference>. 2. Such as envy a man the comfort of his friendship, and do all they can to break that, by suggesting that on both sides which will set those at variance that are most nearly related and have been long intimate, or at least cool and alienate their affections one from another: <hi type="italic">A froward man,</hi> that cannot find in his heart to love any body but himself, is vexed to see others live in love, and therefore makes it is his business to <hi type="italic">sow strife,</hi> by giving men base characters one of another, telling lies, and carrying ill-natured stories between <hi type="italic">chief friends,</hi> so as to <hi type="italic">separate</hi> them one from another, and make them angry at or at least suspicious of one another. Those are bad men, and bad women too, that do such ill offices; they are doing the devil's work, and his will their wages be.

<div eID="gen14010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14011" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way <hi type="italic">that is</hi> not good. <hi type="super">30</hi> He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things: moving his lips he bringeth evil to pass. <div eID="gen14011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14012" type="x-p"/> Here is another sort of evil men described to us, that we may neither do like them, nor have any thing to do with them. 1. Such as (like Satan) do all the mischief they can by force and violence, as roaring lions, and not only by fraud and insinuation, as subtle serpents: They are <hi type="italic">violent men,</hi> that do all by rapine and oppression, that <hi type="italic">shut their eyes,</hi> meditating with the closest intention and application of mind <hi type="italic">to devise froward things,</hi> to contrive how they may do the greatest mischief to their neighbour, to do it effectually and yet securely to themselves; and then <hi type="italic">moving their lips,</hi> giving the word of command to their agents, they <hi type="italic">bring the evil to pass,</hi> and accomplish the wicked device, <hi type="italic">biting his lips</hi> (so some read it) for vexation. When <hi type="italic">the wicked plots against the just</hi> he <hi type="italic">gnasheth upon him with his teeth.</hi> 2. Such as (like Satan still) do all they can to <hi type="italic">entice</hi> and draw in others to join with them in doing mischief, <hi type="italic">leading them in a way that is not good,</hi> that is not honest, nor honourable, nor safe, but offensive to God, and which will be in the end pernicious to the sinner. Thus he aims to ruin some in this world by bringing them into trouble, and others in the other world by bringing them into sin.  <div eID="gen14012" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv43"/><title type="x-s3">The Sovereignty of Divine Providence.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv43"/> <div sID="gen14013" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> The hoary head <hi type="italic">is</hi> a crown of glory, <hi type="italic">if</hi> it be found in the way of righteousness. <div eID="gen14013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14014" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It ought to be the great care of old people to <hi type="italic">be found in the way of righteousness,</hi> the way of religion and serious godliness. Both God and man will look for them in that way; it will be expected that those that are old should be good, that the multitude of their years should teach them the best wisdom; let them therefore be found in that way. Death will come; the Judge is coming; <hi type="italic">the Lord is at hand.</hi> That they may <hi type="italic">be found of him in peace,</hi> let them <hi type="italic">be found in the way of righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.14">2 Pet. iii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">found so doing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.46">Matt. xxiv. 46</reference>. Let old people be old disciples; let them persevere to the end <hi type="italic">in the way of righteousness,</hi> which they long since set out in, that they may then be found in it. 2. If old people <hi type="italic">be found in the way of righteousness,</hi> their age will be their honour. Old age, as such, is honourable, and commands respect (<hi type="italic">Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.19.32">Lev. xix. 32</reference>); but, if it be found in the way of wickedness, its honour is forfeited, its crown profaned and laid in the dust, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.20">Isa. lxv. 20</reference>. Old people therefore, if they would preserve their honour, must still hold fast their integrity, and then their gray hairs are indeed <hi type="italic">a crown</hi> to them; they are <hi type="italic">worthy of double honour.</hi> Grace is the glory of old age.

<div eID="gen14014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14015" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is</hi> slow to anger <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city. <div eID="gen14015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14016" type="x-p"/> This recommends the grace of meekness to us, which will well become us all, particularly <hi type="italic">the hoary head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.31">v. 31</reference>. Observe, 1. The nature of it. It is to be <hi type="italic">slow to anger,</hi> not easily put into a passion, nor apt to resent provocation, taking time to consider before we suffer our passion to break out, that it may not transgress due bounds, so slow in our motions towards anger that we may be quickly stopped and pacified. It is to have the rule of our own spirits, our appetites and affections, and all our inclinations, but particularly our passions, our anger, keeping that under direction and check, and the strict government of religion and right reason. We must be <hi type="italic">lords of our anger,</hi> as God is, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">Nah. i. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Æolus sis, affectuum tuorum—Rule your passions, as Æolus rules the winds.</hi> 2. The honour of it. He that gets and keeps the mastery of his passions <hi type="italic">is better than the mighty,</hi> better <hi type="italic">than he that</hi> by a long siege <hi type="italic">takes a city</hi> or by a long war subdues a country. Behold, a greater than Alexander or Cæsar is here. The conquest of ourselves, and our own unruly passions, requires more true wisdom, and a more steady, constant, and regular management, than the obtaining of a victory over the forces of an enemy. A rational conquest is more honourable to a rational creature than a brutal one. It is a victory that does nobody any harm; no lives or treasures are sacrificed to it, but only some base lusts. It is harder, and therefore more glorious, to quash an insurrection at home than to resist an invasion from a broad; nay, such are the gains of meekness that by it <hi type="italic">we are more than conquerors.</hi>

<div eID="gen14016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14017" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof <hi type="italic">is</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14018" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The divine Providence orders and directs those things which to us are perfectly casual and fortuitous. Nothing comes to pass by chance, nor is an event determined by a blind fortune, but every thing by the will and counsel of God. What man has neither eye nor hand in God is intimately concerned in. 2. When solemn appeals are made to Providence by the casting of lots, for the deciding of that matter of moment which could not otherwise be at all, or not so well, decided, God must be eyed in it, by prayer, that it may be disposed aright (<hi type="italic">Give a perfect lot,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.41">1 Sam. xiv. 41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.24">Acts i. 24</reference>), and by acquiescing in it when it is disposed, being satisfied that the hand of God is in it and that hand directed by infinite wisdom. All the disposals of Providence concerning our affairs we must look upon to be the directing of our lot, the determining of what we referred to God, and must be reconciled to them accordingly.  <chapter eID="Prov.16"/> <div eID="gen14018" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv44"/><title type="x-s3">Falsehood and Oppression Reproved.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv44"/> <div sID="gen14020" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices <hi type="italic">with</hi> strife. <div eID="gen14020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14021" type="x-p"/> These words recommend family-love and peace, as conducing very much to the comfort of human life. 1. Those that live in unity and quietness, not only free from jealousies and animosities, but vying in mutual endearments, and obliging to one another, live very comfortably, though they are low in the world, work hard and fare hard, though they have but each of them <hi type="italic">a morsel,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">a dry morsel.</hi> There may be peace and quietness where there are not three meals a day, provided there by a joint satisfaction in God's providence and a mutual satisfaction in each other's prudence. Holy love may be found in a cottage. 2. Those that live in contention, that are always jarring and brawling, and reflecting upon one another, though they have plenty of dainties, <hi type="italic">a house full of sacrifices,</hi> live uncomfortably; they cannot expect the blessing of God upon them and what they have, nor can they have any true relish of their enjoyments, much less any peace in their own consciences. Love will sweeten a <hi type="italic">dry morsel,</hi> but strife will sour and embitter <hi type="italic">a house full of sacrifices.</hi> A little of the leaven of malice will leaven all the enjoyments.

<div eID="gen14021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14022" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> A wise servant shall have rule over a son that causeth shame, and shall have part of the inheritance among the brethren. <div eID="gen14022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14023" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. True merit does not go by dignity. All agree that the son in the family is more worthy than the servant (<reference osisRef="John.8.35">John viii. 35</reference>), and yet sometimes it so happens that the servant is wise, and a blessing and credit to the family, when the son is a fool, and a burden and shame to the family. Eliezer of Damascus, though Abram could not bear to think that he should be his heir, was a stay to the family, when he obtained a wife for Isaac; whereas Ishmael, a son, was a shame to it, when he mocked Isaac. 2. True dignity will go by merit. If a servant be wise, and manage things well, he shall be further trusted, and not only <hi type="italic">have rule</hi> with, but <hi type="italic">rule over a son that causes shame;</hi> for God and nature have designed that <hi type="italic">the fool shall be servant to the wise in heart.</hi> Nay, a prudent servant may perhaps come to have such an interest in his master as to be taken in for a child's share of the estate and to <hi type="italic">have part of the inheritance among the brethren.</hi>

<div eID="gen14023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14024" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> The fining pot <hi type="italic">is</hi> for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> trieth the hearts. <div eID="gen14024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14025" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The hearts of the children of men are subject, not only to God's view, but to his judgment: As <hi type="italic">the fining-pot is for silver,</hi> both to prove it and to improve it so <hi type="italic">the Lord tries the hearts;</hi> he searches whether they are standard or no, and those that are he refines and makes purer, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">Jer. xvii. 10</reference>. God tries the heart by affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.10-Ps.66.11">Ps. lxvi. 10, 11</reference>), and often chooses his people in that furnace (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Isa. xlviii. 10</reference>) and makes them choice. 2. It is God only that <hi type="italic">tries the hearts.</hi> Men may try their <hi type="italic">silver</hi> and <hi type="italic">gold</hi> with <hi type="italic">the fining-pot and the furnace,</hi> but they have no such way of trying one another's hearts; God only does that, who is both the searcher and the sovereign of the heart.

<div eID="gen14025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14026" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> A wicked doer giveth heed to false lips; <hi type="italic">and</hi> a liar giveth ear to a naughty tongue. <div eID="gen14026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14027" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that design to do ill support themselves by falsehood and lying: <hi type="italic">A wicked doer gives</hi> ear, with a great deal of pleasure, <hi type="italic">to false lips,</hi> that will justify him in the ill he does, to those that aim to make public disturbances, catch greedily at libels, and false stories, that defame the government and the administration. 2. Those that take the liberty to tell lies take a pleasure in hearing them told: <hi type="italic">A liar gives</hi> heed to a malicious backbiting tongue, that he may have something to graft his lies upon, and with which to give them some colour of truth and so to support them. Sinners will strengthen one another's hands; and those show that they are bad themselves who court the acquaintance and need the assistance of those that are bad.

<div eID="gen14027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14028" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished. <div eID="gen14028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14029" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What a great sin those are guilty of who trample upon the poor, who ridicule their wants and the meanness of their appearance, upbraid them with their poverty, and take advantage from their weakness to be abusive and injurious to them. They <hi type="italic">reproach their Maker,</hi> put a great contempt and affront upon him, who allotted the poor to the condition they are in, owns them, and takes care of them, and can, when he pleases, reduce us to that condition. Let those that thus reproach their Maker know that they shall be called to an account for it, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.40-Matt.25.41">Matt. xxv. 40, 41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.31">Prov. xiv. 31</reference>. 2. What great danger those are in of falling into trouble themselves who are pleased to see and hear of the troubles of others: <hi type="italic">He that is glad at calamities,</hi> that he may be built up upon the ruins of others, and regales himself with the judgments of God when they are abroad, let him know that he <hi type="italic">shall not go unpunished;</hi> the cup shall be put into his hand, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.6-Ezek.25.7">Ezek. xxv. 6, 7</reference>.  <div eID="gen14029" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv45"/><title type="x-s3">Common Truths.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv45"/> <div sID="gen14030" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Children's children <hi type="italic">are</hi> the crown of old men; and the glory of children <hi type="italic">are</hi> their fathers. <div eID="gen14030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14031" type="x-p"/> They are so, that is, they should be so, and, if they conduct themselves worthily, they are so. 1. It is an honour to parents when they are old to leave children, and <hi type="italic">children's children,</hi> growing up, that tread in the steps of their virtues, and are likely to maintain and advance the reputation of their families. It is an honour to a man to live so long as to see his children's children (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.6">Ps. cxxviii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.50.23">Gen. l. 23</reference>), to see his house built up in them, and to see them likely to serve their generation according to the will of God. This crowns and completes their comfort in this world. 2. It is an honour to children to have wise and godly parents, and to have them continued to them even after they have themselves grown up and settled in the world. Those are unnatural children who reckon their aged parents a burden to them, and think they live too long; whereas, if the children be wise and good, it is as much their honour as can be that thereby they are comforts to their parents in the unpleasant days of their old age.

<div eID="gen14031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14032" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Excellent speech becometh not a fool: much less do lying lips a prince. <div eID="gen14032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14033" type="x-p"/> Two things are here represented as very absurd: 1. That men of no repute should be dictators. What can be more unbecoming than for fools, who are known to have little sense and discretion, to pretend to that which is above them and which they were never cut out for? A fool, in Solomon's proverbs, signifies a wicked man, whom <hi type="italic">excellent speech</hi> does not become, because his conversation gives the lie to his excellent speech. What have those to do to declare God's statutes who <hi type="italic">hate instruction?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.16">Ps. l. 16</reference>. Christ would not suffer the unclean spirits to say that they knew him to be the Son of God. See <reference osisRef="Acts.16.17-Acts.16.18">Acts xvi. 17, 18</reference>. 2. That men of great repute should be deceivers. If it is unbecoming a despicable man to presume to speak as a philosopher or politician, and nobody heeds him, being prejudiced against his character, much more unbecoming is it for a prince, for a man of honour, to take advantage from his character and the confidence that is put in him to lie, and dissemble, and make no conscience of breaking his word. Lying ill becomes any man, but worst a prince, so corrupt is the modern policy, which insinuates that princes ought not to make themselves slaves to their words further than is for their interest, and <hi type="italic">Qui nescit dissimulare nescit regnare—He who knows not how to dissemble knows not how to reign.</hi>

<div eID="gen14033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14034" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> A gift <hi type="italic">is as</hi> a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it: whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth. <div eID="gen14034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14035" type="x-p"/> The design of this observation is to show, 1. That those who have money in their hand think they can do any thing with it. Rich men value a little money as if it were a <hi type="italic">precious stone,</hi> and value themselves on it as if it gave them not only ornament, but power, and every one were bound to be at their beck, even justice itself. Whithersoever they turn this sparkling diamond they expect it should dazzle the eyes of all, and make them do just what they would have them do in hopes of it. The deepest bag will carry the cause. Fee high, and you may have what you will. 2. That those who have money in their eye, and set their hearts upon it, will do any thing for it: <hi type="italic">A bribe is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that takes it;</hi> it has a great influence upon him, and he will be sure to go the way that it leads him, hither and thither, though contrary to justice and not consistent with himself.

<div eID="gen14035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14036" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth <hi type="italic">very</hi> friends. <div eID="gen14036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14037" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The way to preserve peace among relations and neighbours is to make the best of every thing, not to tell others what has been said or done against them when it is not at all necessary to their safety, nor to take notice of what has been said or done against them when it is not at all necessary to their safety, nor to take notice of what has been said or done against ourselves, but to excuse both, and put the best construction upon them. "It was an oversight; therefore overlook it. It was done through forgetfulness; therefore forget it. It perhaps made nothing of you; do you make nothing of it." 2. The ripping up of faults is the ripping out of love, and nothing tends more to the separating of friends, and setting them at variance, than the <hi type="italic">repeating of matters</hi> that have been in variance; for they commonly lose nothing in the repetition, but the things themselves are aggravated and the passions about them revived and exasperated. The best method of peace is by an amnesty or act of oblivion.

<div eID="gen14037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14038" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool. <div eID="gen14038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14039" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A word is enough to the wise. A gentle reproof will enter not only into the head, but into the heart of a wise man, so as to have a strong influence upon him; for, if but a hint be given to conscience, let it alone to carry it on and prosecute it. 2. Stripes are not enough for a fool, to make him sensible of his errors, that he may repent of them, and be more cautious for the future. He that is sottish and wilful is very rarely benefited by severity. David is softened with, <hi type="italic">Thou art the man;</hi> but Pharaoh remains hard under all the plagues of Egypt.

<div eID="gen14039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14040" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> An evil <hi type="italic">man</hi> seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him. <div eID="gen14040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14041" type="x-p"/> Here is the sin and punishment of an evil man. 1. His sin. He is an evil man indeed that seeks all occasions to rebel against God, and the government God has set over him, and to contradict and quarrel with those about him. <hi type="italic">Quærit jurgia—He picks quarrels;</hi> so some. There are some that are actuated by a spirit of opposition, that will contradict for contradiction-sake, that will go on frowardly in their wicked ways in spite of all restraint and check. <hi type="italic">A rebellious man seeks mischief</hi> (so some read it), watches all opportunities to disturb the public peace. 2. His punishment. Because he will not be reclaimed by mild and gentle methods, <hi type="italic">a cruel messenger shall be sent against him,</hi> some dreadful judgment or other, as a messenger from God. Angels, God's messengers, shall be employed as ministers of his justice against him, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.49">Ps. lxxviii. 49</reference>. Satan, the angel of death, shall be let loose upon him, and the <hi type="italic">messengers</hi> of Satan. His prince shall send a sergeant to arrest him, an executioner to cut him off. He that <hi type="italic">kicks against the pricks</hi> is <hi type="italic">waited for of the sword.</hi>  <div eID="gen14041" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv46"/><title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv46"/> <div sID="gen14042" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man, rather than a fool in his folly. <div eID="gen14042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14043" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A passionate man is a brutish man. However at other times he may have some wisdom, take him in his passion ungoverned, and he is a <hi type="italic">fool in his folly;</hi> those are fools in whose bosom anger rests and in whose countenance anger rages. He has put off man, and is become like a bear, a raging bear, <hi type="italic">a bear robbed of her whelps;</hi> he is as fond of the gratifications of his lusts and passions as a bear of her whelps (which, though ugly, are her own), as eager in the pursuit of them as she is in quest of her whelps when they are missing, and as full of indignation if crossed in the pursuit. 2. He is a dangerous man, falls foul of every one that stands in his way, though innocent, though his friend, as a bear robbed of her whelps sets upon the first man she meets as the robber. <hi type="italic">Ira furor brevis est—Anger is temporary madness.</hi> One may more easily stop, escape, or guard against an enraged bear, than an outrageous angry man. Let us therefore watch over our own passions (lest they get head and do mischief) and so consult our own honour; and let us avoid the company of furious men, and get out of their way when they are in their fury, and so consult our own safety. <hi type="italic">Currenti cede furori—Give place unto wrath.</hi>

<div eID="gen14043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14044" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house. <div eID="gen14044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14045" type="x-p"/> A malicious mischievous man is here represented, 1. As ungrateful to his friends. He oftentimes is so absurd and insensible of kindnesses done him that he renders <hi type="italic">evil for good.</hi> David met with those that were his adversaries for his love, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Ps. cix. 4</reference>. To render evil for evil is brutish, but to render evil for good is devilish. He is an ill-natured man who, because he is resolved not to return a kindness, will revenge it. 2. As therein unkind to his family, for he entails a curse upon it. This is a crime so heinous that it shall be punished, not only in his person, but in his posterity, for whom he thus treasures up wrath. <hi type="italic">The sword shall not depart from</hi> David's <hi type="italic">house</hi> because he rewarded Uriah with evil for his good services. The Jews stoned Christ for his good works; therefore is his blood upon them and upon their children.

<div eID="gen14045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14046" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The beginning of strife <hi type="italic">is as</hi> when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with. <div eID="gen14046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14047" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The danger that there is in <hi type="italic">the beginning of strife.</hi> One hot word, one peevish reflection, one angry demand, one spiteful contradiction, begets another, and that a third, and so on, till it proves like the cutting of a dam; when the water has got a little passage it does itself widen the breach, bears down all before it, and there is then no stopping it, no reducing it. 2. A good caution inferred thence, to take heed of the first spark of contention and to put it out as soon as ever it appears. Dread the breaking of the ice, for, if once broken, it will break further; <hi type="italic">therefore leave it off,</hi> not only when you see the worst of it, for then it may be too late, but when you see the first of it. <hi type="italic">Obsta principiis—Resist its earliest display.</hi> Leave it off even <hi type="italic">before it be meddled with;</hi> leave it off, if it were possible, before you begin.

<div eID="gen14047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14048" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both <hi type="italic">are</hi> abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14049" type="x-p"/> This shows what an offence it is to God, 1. When those that are entrusted with the administration of public justice, judges, juries, witnesses, prosecutors, counsel, do either acquit the guilty or condemn those that are not guilty, or in the least contribute to either; this defeats the end of government, which is to protect the good and punish the bad, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.3-Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 3, 4</reference>. It is equally provoking to God to <hi type="italic">justify the wicked,</hi> though it be in pity and <hi type="italic">in favorem vitæ—to safe life,</hi> as to <hi type="italic">condemn the just.</hi> 2. When any private persons plead for sin and sinners, palliate and excuse wickedness, or argue against virtue and piety, and so <hi type="italic">pervert the right ways of the Lord</hi> and confound the eternal distinctions between good and evil.

<div eID="gen14049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14050" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Wherefore <hi type="italic">is there</hi> a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing <hi type="italic">he hath</hi> no heart <hi type="italic">to it?</hi> <div eID="gen14050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14051" type="x-p"/> Two things are here spoken of with astonishment:—1. God's great goodness to foolish man, in putting <hi type="italic">a price into his hand to get wisdom,</hi> to get knowledge and grace to fit him for both worlds. We have rational souls, the means of grace, the strivings of the Spirit, access to God by prayer; we have time and opportunity. He that has a good estate (so some understand it) has advantages thereby of getting wisdom by purchasing instruction. Good parents, relations, ministers, friends, are helps to get wisdom. It is <hi type="italic">a price,</hi> therefore of value, a talent. It is <hi type="italic">a price in the hand,</hi> in possession; <hi type="italic">the word is nigh thee.</hi> It is a price for getting; it is for our own advantage; it is for getting wisdom, the very thing which, being fools, we have most need of. We have reason to wonder that God should so consider our necessity, and should entrust us with such advantages, though he foresaw we should not make a right improvement of them. 2. Man's great wickedness, his neglect of God's favour and his own interest, which is very absurd and unaccountable: <hi type="italic">He has no heart to it,</hi> not to the wisdom that is to be got, nor to the price in the use of which it may be got. <hi type="italic">He has no heart,</hi> no skill, nor will, nor courage, to improve his advantages. He has set his heart upon other things, so that he has no heart to his duty or the great concerns of his soul. Wherefore should a price be thrown away and lost upon one so undeserving of it?  <div eID="gen14051" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv47"/><title type="x-s3">True Friendship.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv47"/> <div sID="gen14052" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity. <div eID="gen14052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14053" type="x-p"/> This intimates the strength of those bonds by which we are bound to each other and which we ought to be sensible of. 1. Friends must be constant to each other <hi type="italic">at all times.</hi> That is not true friendship which is not constant; it will be so if it be sincere, and actuated by a good principle. Those that are fanciful or selfish in their friendship will love no longer than their humour is pleased and their interest served, and therefore their affections turn with the wind and change with the weather. Swallow-friends, that fly to you in summer, but are gone in winter; such friends there is no loss of. But if the friendship be prudent, generous, and cordial, if I love my friend because he is wise, and virtuous, and good, as long as he continues so, though he fall into poverty and disgrace, still I shall love him. Christ is a friend that loves at all times (<reference osisRef="John.13.1">John xiii. 1</reference>) and we must so love him, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.35">Rom. viii. 35</reference>. 2. Relations must in a special manner be careful and tender of one another in affliction: <hi type="italic">A brother is born</hi> to succour a brother or sister in distress, to whom he is joined so closely by nature that he may the more sensibly feel from their burdens, and be the more strongly inclined and engaged, as it were by instinct, to help them. We must often consider what we were <hi type="italic">born for,</hi> not only as men, but as in such a station and relation. <hi type="italic">Who knows but we came</hi> into such a family <hi type="italic">for such a time as this?</hi> We do not answer the end of our relations if we do not do the duty of them. Some take it thus: <hi type="italic">A friend that loves at all times is born</hi> (that is, becomes) <hi type="italic">a brother in adversity,</hi> and is so to be valued.

<div eID="gen14053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14054" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> A man void of understanding striketh hands, <hi type="italic">and</hi> becometh surety in the presence of his friend. <div eID="gen14054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14055" type="x-p"/> Though Solomon had commended friendship in adversity (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">v. 17</reference>), yet let not any, under pretence of being generous to their friends, be unjust to their families and wrong them; one part of our duty must be made to consist with another. Note, 1. It is a piece of wisdom to keep out of debt as much as may be, especially to dread suretiship. There may be a just occasion for a man to pass his word for his friend in his absence, till he come to engage himself; but to be <hi type="italic">surety in the presence of his friend,</hi> when he is upon the spot, supposes that his own word will not be taken, he being deemed insolvent or dishonest, and then who can with safety pass his word for him? 2. Those that are <hi type="italic">void of understanding</hi> are commonly taken in this snare, to the prejudice of their families, and therefore ought not to be trusted too far with their own affairs, but to be under direction.

<div eID="gen14055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14056" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> He loveth transgression that loveth strife: <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that exalteth his gate seeketh destruction. <div eID="gen14056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14057" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that are quarrelsome involve themselves in a great deal of guilt: <hi type="italic">He that loves strife,</hi> that in his worldly business loves to go to law, in religion loves controversies, and in common conversation loves to thwart and fall out, that is never well but when he is in the fire, <hi type="italic">he loves transgression;</hi> for a great deal of sin attends that sin, and the way of it is down-hill. He pretends to stand up for truth, and for his honour and right, but really he loves sin, which God hates. 2. Those that are ambitious and aspiring expose themselves to a great deal of trouble, such as often ends in their ruin: <hi type="italic">He that exalts his gate,</hi> builds a stately house, at least a fine frontispiece, that he may overtop and outshine his neighbours, seeks his own destruction and takes a deal of pains to ruin himself; he makes his gate so large that his house and estate go out at it.  <div eID="gen14057" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv48"/><title type="x-s3">Folly and Wickedness.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv48"/> <div sID="gen14058" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> He that hath a froward heart findeth no good: and he that hath a perverse tongue falleth into mischief. <div eID="gen14058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14059" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Framing ill designs will be of no advantage to us; there is nothing got by them: <hi type="italic">He that has a froward heart,</hi> that sows discord and is full of resentment, cannot promise himself to get by it sufficient to counterbalance the loss of his repose and reputation, nor can he take any rational satisfaction in it; he <hi type="italic">finds no good.</hi> 2. Giving ill language will be a great disadvantage to us: <hi type="italic">He that has a perverse tongue,</hi> spiteful and abusive, scurrilous or backbiting, <hi type="italic">falls into</hi> one <hi type="italic">mischief</hi> or other, loses his friends, provokes his enemies, and pulls trouble upon his own head. Many a one has paid dearly for an unbridled tongue.

<div eID="gen14059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14060" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> He that begetteth a fool <hi type="italic">doeth it</hi> to his sorrow: and the father of a fool hath no joy. <div eID="gen14060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14061" type="x-p"/> This expresses that very emphatically which many wise and good men feel very sensibly, what a grievous vexatious thing it is to have a foolish wicked child. See here, 1. How uncertain all our creature-comforts are, so that we are often not only disappointed in them, but that proves the greatest cross in which we promised ourselves most satisfaction. There was <hi type="italic">joy when a man-child was born into the world,</hi> and yet, if he prove vicious, his own father will wish he had never been born. The name of Absalom signifies his <hi type="italic">father's peace,</hi> but he was his greatest trouble. It should moderate the desire of having children, and the delights of their parents in them, that they may prove a grief to them; yet it should silence the murmurings of the afflicted father in that case that if his son be a fool he is a fool of his own begetting, and therefore he must make the best of him, and take it up as his cross, the rather because Adam begets a son in his own likeness. 2. How unwise we are in suffering one affliction (and that of an untoward child as likely as any other) to drown the sense of a thousand mercies: <hi type="italic">The father of a fool</hi> lays that so much to heart that he <hi type="italic">has no joy</hi> of any thing else. For this he may thank himself; there are joys sufficient to counterbalance even that sorrow.

<div eID="gen14061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14062" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> A merry heart doeth good <hi type="italic">like</hi> a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones. <div eID="gen14062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14063" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is healthful to be cheerful. The Lord is for the body, and has provided for it, not only meat, but medicine, and has here told us that the best medicine is <hi type="italic">a merry heart,</hi> not a heart addicted to vain, carnal, sensual mirth; Solomon himself said of that mirth, It is not medicine, but madness; it is not food, but poison; <hi type="italic">what doth it?</hi> But he means a heart rejoicing in God, and serving him with gladness, and then taking the comfort of outward enjoyments and particularly that of pleasant conversation. It is a great mercy that God gives us leave to be cheerful and cause to be cheerful, especially if by his grace he gives us hearts to be cheerful. This <hi type="italic">does good to a medicine</hi> (so some read it); it will make physic more efficient. Or <hi type="italic">it does good as a medicine</hi> to the body, making it easy and fit for business. But, if mirth be a medicine (understand it of diversion and recreation), it must be used sparingly, only when there is occasion, not turned into food, and it must be used medicinally, <hi type="italic">sub regimine—as a prescribed regimen,</hi> and by rule. 2. The sorrows of the mind often contribute very much to the sickliness of the body: <hi type="italic">A broken spirit,</hi> sunk by the burden of afflictions, and especially a conscience wounded with the sense of guilt and fear of wrath, <hi type="italic">dries the bones,</hi> wastes the radical moisture, exhausts the very marrow, and makes the body a mere skeleton. We should therefore watch and pray against all melancholy dispositions, for they lead us into trouble as well as into temptation.

<div eID="gen14063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14064" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> A wicked <hi type="italic">man</hi> taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment. <div eID="gen14064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14065" type="x-p"/> See here, 1.
