What an evil thing bribery is: He is <hi type="italic">a wicked man</hi> that will <hi type="italic">take a gift</hi> to engage him to give a false testimony, verdict, or judgment; when he does it he is ashamed of it, for he takes it, with all the secresy imaginable, <hi type="italic">out of the bosom</hi> where he knows it is laid ready for him; it is industriously concealed, and so slyly that, if he could, he would hide it from his own conscience. <hi type="italic">A gift is taken out of the bosom of a wicked man</hi> (so some read it); for he is a bad man that gives bribes, as well as he that takes them. 2. What a powerful thing it is. It is of such force that it <hi type="italic">perverts the ways of judgment.</hi> The course of justice is not only obstructed, but turned into injustice; and the greatest wrongs are done under colour of doing right.

<div eID="gen14065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14066" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> before him that hath understanding; but the eyes of a fool <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the ends of the earth. <div eID="gen14066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14067" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. He is to be reckoned an intelligent man that not only has wisdom, but has it ready when he has occasion for it. He lays his <hi type="italic">wisdom before him,</hi> as his card and compass which he steers by, has his eye always upon it, as he that writes has on his copy; and then he has it <hi type="italic">before him;</hi> it is not to seek, but still at hand. 2. He that has a giddy head, a roving rambling fancy, will never be fit for any solid business. He is a fool, and good for nothing, whose <hi type="italic">eyes are in the ends of the earth,</hi> here, and there and every where, any where but where they should be, who cannot fix his thoughts to one subject nor pursue any one purpose with any thing of steadiness. When his mind should be applied to his study and business it is filled with a thousand things foreign and impertinent.

<div eID="gen14067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14068" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> A foolish son <hi type="italic">is</hi> a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bare him. <div eID="gen14068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14069" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Wicked children are an affliction to both their parents. They are an occasion of <hi type="italic">anger</hi> to the father (so the word signifies), because they contemn his authority, but of sorrow and <hi type="italic">bitterness</hi> to the mother, because they abuse her tenderness. The parents, being joint-sufferers, should therefore bring mutual comfort to bear them up under it, and strive to make it as easy as they can, the mother to mollify the father's anger, the father to alleviate the mother's grief. 2. That Solomon often repeats this remark, probably because it was his own case; however, it is a common case.

<div eID="gen14069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14070" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Also to punish the just <hi type="italic">is</hi> not good, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> to strike princes for equity. <div eID="gen14070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14071" type="x-p"/> In differences that happen between magistrates and subjects, and such differences often arise, 1. Let magistrates see to it that they never <hi type="italic">punish the just,</hi> that they be in no case a <hi type="italic">terror to good works,</hi> for that is to abuse their power and betray that great trust which is reposed in them. It is <hi type="italic">not good,</hi> that is, it is a very evil thing, and will end ill, whatever end they may aim at in it. When princes become tyrants and persecutors their thrones will be neither easy nor firm. 2. Let subjects see to it that they do not find fault with the government for doing its duty, for it is a wicked thing <hi type="italic">to strike princes for equity,</hi> by defaming their administration or by any secret attempts against them to strike at them, as the ten tribes that revolted reflected upon Solomon for imposing necessary taxes. Some read it, <hi type="italic">Nor to strike the ingenuous for equity.</hi> Magistrates must take heed that none suffer under them for well doing; nor must parents <hi type="italic">provoke their children to wrath</hi> by unjust rebukes.

<div eID="gen14071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14072" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> He that hath knowledge spareth his words: <hi type="italic">and</hi> a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit. <hi type="super">28</hi> Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that shutteth his lips <hi type="italic">is esteemed</hi> a man of understanding. <div eID="gen14072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14073" type="x-p"/> Two ways a man may show himself to be a wise man:—1. By the good temper, the sweetness and the sedateness, of his mind: <hi type="italic">A man of understanding is of an excellent spirit,</hi> a <hi type="italic">precious spirit</hi> (so the word is); he is one that looks well to his spirit, that it be as it should be, and so keeps it in an even frame, easy to himself and pleasant to others. A gracious spirit is a precious spirit, and renders a man amiable and <hi type="italic">more excellent than his neighbour.</hi> He is of a <hi type="italic">cool spirit</hi> (so some read it), not heated with passion, nor put into any tumult or disorder by the <hi type="italic">impetus</hi> of any corrupt affection, but even and stayed. A cool head with a warm heart is an admirable composition. 2. By the good government of his tongue. (1.) A wise man will be <hi type="italic">of few words,</hi> as being afraid of speaking amiss: <hi type="italic">He that has knowledge,</hi> and aims to do good with it, is careful, when he does speak to speak to the purpose, and says little in order that he may take time to deliberate. He <hi type="italic">spares his words,</hi> because they are better spared than ill-spent. (2.) This is generally taken for such a sure indication of wisdom that a fool may gain the reputation of being a wise man if he have but wit enough to hold his tongue, to hear, and see, and say little. If a fool hold his peace, men of candour will think him wise, because nothing appears to the contrary, and because it will be thought that he is making observations on what others say, and gaining experience, and is consulting with himself what he shall say, that he may speak pertinently. See how easy it is to gain men's good opinion and to impose upon them. But when a <hi type="italic">fool holds his peace</hi> God knows his heart, and the folly that is bound up there; thoughts are words to him, and therefore he cannot be deceived in his judgment of men.  <chapter eID="Prov.17"/> <div eID="gen14073" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv49"/><title type="x-s3">Wisdom and Folly.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv49"/> <div sID="gen14075" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh <hi type="italic">and</hi> intermeddleth with all wisdom. <div eID="gen14075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14076" type="x-p"/> The original here is difficult, and differently understood. 1. Some take it as a rebuke to an affected singularity. When men take a pride in <hi type="italic">separating themselves</hi> from the sentiments and society of others, in contradicting all that has been said before them and advancing new notions of their own, which, though ever so absurd, they are wedded to, it is to gratify a desire or lust of vain-glory, and they are seekers and meddlers with that which does not belong to them. He <hi type="italic">seeks according to his desire, and intermeddles with every business,</hi> pretends to pass a judgment upon every man's matter. He is morose and supercilious. Those generally are so that are opinionative and conceited, and they thus make themselves ridiculous, and are vexatious to others. 2. Our translation seems to take it as an excitement to diligence in the pursuit of wisdom. If we would get knowledge or grace, we must desire it, as that which we need and which will be of great advantage to us, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.31">1 Cor. xii. 31</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">separate ourselves</hi> from all those things which would divert us from or retard us in the pursuit, retire out of the noise of this world's vanities, and then <hi type="italic">seek and intermeddle with all</hi> the means and instructions of <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> be willing to take pains and try all the methods of improving ourselves, be acquainted with a variety of opinions, that we may prove all things and hold fast that which is good.

<div eID="gen14076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14077" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself. <div eID="gen14077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14078" type="x-p"/> A fool may pretend to understanding, and to seek and intermeddle with the means of it, but, 1. He has no true delight in it; it is only to please his friends or save his credit; he does not love his book, nor his business, nor his Bible, nor his prayers; he would rather be playing the fool with his sports. Those who take no pleasure in learning or religion will make nothing to purpose of either. No progress is made in them if they are a task and a drudgery. 2. He has no good design in it, only <hi type="italic">that his heart may discover itself,</hi> that he may have something to make a show with, something wherewith to varnish his folly, that that may pass off the better, because he loves to hear himself talk.

<div eID="gen14078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14079" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> When the wicked cometh, <hi type="italic">then</hi> cometh also contempt, and with ignominy reproach. <div eID="gen14079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14080" type="x-p"/> This may include a double sense:—1. That wicked people are scornful people, and put <hi type="italic">contempt</hi> upon others. <hi type="italic">When the wicked comes</hi> into any company, comes into the schools of wisdom or into the assemblies for religious worship, <hi type="italic">then comes contempt</hi> of God, of his people and ministers, and of every thing that is said and done. You can expect no other from those that are profane than that they will be scoffers; they will be an <hi type="italic">ignominy</hi> and <hi type="italic">reproach;</hi> they will flout and jeer every thing that is serious and grave. But let not wise and good men regard it, for the proverb of the ancients says, such <hi type="italic">wickedness proceeds from the wicked.</hi> 2. That wicked people are shameful people, and bring <hi type="italic">contempt</hi> upon themselves, for God has said that those <hi type="italic">who despise him shall be lightly esteemed.</hi> As soon as ever sin entered shame followed it, and sinners make themselves despicable. Nor do they only draw contempt upon themselves, but they bring <hi type="italic">ignominy</hi> and <hi type="italic">reproach</hi> upon their families, their friends, their ministers, and all that are in any way related to them. Those therefore who would secure their honour must retain their virtue.  <div eID="gen14080" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv50"/><title type="x-s3">The Language of Folly.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv50"/> <div sID="gen14081" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> The words of a man's mouth <hi type="italic">are as</hi> deep waters, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the wellspring of wisdom <hi type="italic">as</hi> a flowing brook. <div eID="gen14081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14082" type="x-p"/> The similitudes here seem to be elegantly transposed. 1. The <hi type="italic">well-spring of wisdom</hi> is <hi type="italic">as deep waters.</hi> An intelligent knowing man has in him a good treasure of useful things, which furnishes him with something to say upon all occasions that is pertinent and profitable. This is as <hi type="italic">deep waters,</hi> which make no noise, but never run dry. 2. The words of such <hi type="italic">a man's mouth are as a flowing brook.</hi> What he sees cause to speak flows naturally from him and with a great deal of ease, and freedom, and natural fluency; it is clean and fresh, it is cleansing and refreshing; from his <hi type="italic">deep waters</hi> there flows what there is occasion for, to water those about him, as the brooks do the low grounds.

<div eID="gen14082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14083" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> not good to accept the person of the wicked, to overthrow the righteous in judgment. <div eID="gen14083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14084" type="x-p"/> This justly condemns those who, being employed in the administration of justice, pervert judgment, 1. By conniving at men's crimes, and protecting and countenancing them in oppression and violence, because of their dignity, or wealth, or some personal kindness they have for them. Whatever excuses men may make for it, certainly <hi type="italic">it is not good</hi> thus to <hi type="italic">accept the person of the wicked;</hi> it is an offence to God, an affront to justice, a wrong to mankind, and a real service done to the kingdom of sin and Satan. The merits of the cause must be regarded, not the person. 2. By giving a cause against justice and equity, because the person is poor and low in the world, or not of the same party or persuasion, or a stranger of another country. This is <hi type="italic">overthrowing the righteous in judgment,</hi> who ought to be supported, and whom God will make to stand.

<div eID="gen14084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14085" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> A fool's lips enter into contention, and his mouth calleth for strokes. <hi type="super">7</hi> A fool's mouth <hi type="italic">is</hi> his destruction, and his lips <hi type="italic">are</hi> the snare of his soul. <div eID="gen14085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14086" type="x-p"/> Solomon has often shown what mischief bad men do to others with their ungoverned tongues; here he shows what mischief they do to themselves. 1. They embroil themselves in quarrels: <hi type="italic">A fool's lips,</hi> without any cause or call, <hi type="italic">enter into contention,</hi> by advancing foolish notions which others find themselves obliged to oppose, and so a quarrel is begun, or by giving provoking language, which will be resented, and satisfaction demanded, or by setting men at defiance, and bidding them <hi type="italic">do if they dare.</hi> Proud, and passionate men, and drunkards, are fools, whose lips <hi type="italic">enter into contention.</hi> A wise man may, against his will, be drawn into a quarrel, but he is a fool that of choice enters into it when he might avoid it, and he will repent it when it is too late. 2. They expose themselves to correction: The <hi type="italic">fool's mouth</hi> does, in effect, <hi type="italic">call for strokes;</hi> he has said that which deserves to be punished with strokes, and is still saying that which needs to be checked, and restrained with strokes, as Ananias unjustly commanded that Paul should be <hi type="italic">smitten on the mouth.</hi> 3. They involve themselves in ruin: A <hi type="italic">fool's mouth,</hi> which has been, or would have been, the destruction of others, proves at length <hi type="italic">his own destruction,</hi> perhaps from men. Shimei's mouth was his own destruction, and Adonijah's, who spoke against his own head. And when a fool, by his foolish speaking, has run himself into a premunire, and thinks to bring himself off by justifying or excusing what he has said, his defence proves his offence, and his lips are still the snare of his soul, entangling him yet more and more. However, when men by their evil words shall be condemned at God's bar their mouths will be their destruction, and it will be such an aggravation of their ruin as will not admit one drop of water, one drop of comfort, to <hi type="italic">cool their tongue,</hi> which is their snare and will be their tormentor.

<div eID="gen14086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14087" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The words of a talebearer <hi type="italic">are</hi> as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly. <div eID="gen14087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14088" type="x-p"/> Tale-bearers are those who secretly carry stories from house to house, which perhaps have some truth in them, but are secrets not fit to be told, or are basely misrepresented, and false colours put upon them, and are all told with design to blast men's reputation, to break their friendship, to make mischief between relations and neighbours, and set them at variance. Now the words of such are here said to be, 1. <hi type="italic">Like as when men are wounded</hi> (so the margin reads it); they pretend to be very much affected with the miscarriages of such and such, and to be in pain for them, and pretend that it is with the greatest grief and reluctance imaginable that they speak of them. They look as if they themselves were wounded by it, whereas really they <hi type="italic">rejoice in iniquity,</hi> are fond of the story, and tell it with pride and pleasure. Thus their words seem; but they <hi type="italic">go down as poison into the innermost parts of the belly,</hi> the pill being thus gilded, thus sugared. 2. <hi type="italic">As wounds</hi> (so the text reads it), as deep wounds, deadly wounds, <hi type="italic">wounds in the innermost parts of the belly;</hi> the <hi type="italic">venter medius vel infimus—the middle or lower belly,</hi> the <hi type="italic">thorax</hi> or the <hi type="italic">abdomen,</hi> in either of which wounds are mortal. The words of the tale-bearer wound him of whom they are spoken, his credit and interest, and him to whom they are spoken, his love and charity. They occasion sin to him, which is a wound to the conscience. Perhaps he seems to slight them, but they would insensibly, by alienating his affections from one he ought to love.  <div eID="gen14088" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv51"/><title type="x-s3">Folly and Pride Exposed.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv51"/> <div sID="gen14089" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster. <div eID="gen14089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14090" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Prodigality is very bad husbandry. Those are not only justly branded as fools among men, but will give an uncomfortable account to God of the talents they are entrusted with, who are wasters of their estates, who live above what they have, spend and give more than they can afford, and so, in effect, throw away what they have, and suffer it to run to waste. 2. Idleness is no better. He that is remiss in his work, whose <hi type="italic">hands hang down</hi> (so the word signifies), that stands, as we may, with his thumbs in his mouth, that neglects his business, does it not at all, or as if he did it not, he is own brother to him that is a prodigal, that is, he is as much a fool and in as sure and ready a way to poverty; one scatters what he has, the other lets it run through his fingers. The observation is too true in the affairs of religion; he that is trifling and careless in praying and hearing is brother to him that does not pray or hear at all; and omissions of duty and in duty are as fatal to the soul as commissions of sin.

<div eID="gen14090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14091" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> The name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe. <div eID="gen14091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14092" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. God's sufficiency for the saints: His <hi type="italic">name is a strong tower</hi> for them, in which they may take rest when they are weary and take sanctuary when they are pursued, where they may be lifted up above their enemies and fortified against them. There is enough in God, and in the discoveries which he has made of himself to us, to make us easy at all times. The wealth laid up in this tower is enough to enrich them, to be a continual feast and a continuing treasure to them. The strength of this tower is enough to protect them; <hi type="italic">the name of the Lord</hi> is all that whereby he has made himself known as God, and our God, not only his titles and attributes, but his covenant and all the promises of it; these make up a tower, a strong tower, impenetrable, impregnable, for all God's people. 2. The saints' security in God. It is a strong tower to those who know how to make use of it as such. <hi type="italic">The righteous,</hi> by faith and prayer, devotion towards God and dependence on him, <hi type="italic">run into it,</hi> as their city of refuge. Having made sure their interest in God's name, they take the comfort and benefit of it; they go out of themselves, retire from the world, live above, dwell in God and God in them, and so they are safe, they think themselves so, and they shall find themselves so.

<div eID="gen14092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14093" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> The rich man's wealth <hi type="italic">is</hi> his strong city, and as an high wall in his own conceit. <div eID="gen14093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14094" type="x-p"/> Having described the firm and faithful defence of the righteous man (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">v. 10</reference>), Solomon here shows what is the false and deceitful defence of the rich man, that has his portion and treasure in the things of this world, and sets his heart upon them. His wealth is as much his confidence, and he expects as much from it, as a godly man from his God. See, 1. How he supports himself. He makes his <hi type="italic">wealth his city,</hi> where he dwells, where he rules, with a great deal of self-complacency, as if he had a whole city under his command. It <hi type="italic">is his strong city,</hi> in which he intrenches himself, and then sets danger at defiance, as if nothing could hurt him. <hi type="italic">His scales are his pride;</hi> his wealth is his wall in which he encloses himself, and he thinks it a <hi type="italic">high wall,</hi> which cannot be scaled or got over, <reference osisRef="Job.31.24">Job xxxi. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.7">Rev. xviii. 7</reference>. 2. How herein he cheats himself. It is a <hi type="italic">strong city,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">high wall,</hi> but it is so only <hi type="italic">in his own conceit;</hi> it will not prove to be really so, but like the house built on the sand, which will fail the builder when he most needs it.

<div eID="gen14094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14095" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and before honour <hi type="italic">is</hi> humility. <div eID="gen14095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14096" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Pride is the presage of ruin, and ruin will at last be the punishment of pride; for <hi type="italic">before destruction</hi> men are commonly so infatuated by the just judgment of God that they are more haughty than ever, that their ruin may be the sorer and the more surprising. Of, if that do not always hold, yet after the heart has been lifted up with pride, a fall comes, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.18">ch. xvi. 18</reference>. 2. Humility is the presage of honour and prepares men for it, and honour shall at length be the reward of humility, as he had said before, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.33">ch. xv. 33</reference>. That has need to be often said which men are so loth to believe.

<div eID="gen14096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14097" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> He that answereth a matter before he heareth <hi type="italic">it,</hi> it <hi type="italic">is</hi> folly and shame unto him. <div eID="gen14097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14098" type="x-p"/> See here how men often expose themselves by that very thing by which they hope to gain applause. 1. Some take a pride in being quick. They <hi type="italic">answer a matter before they hear it,</hi> hear it out, nay, as soon as they but hear of it. They think it is their honour to take up a cause suddenly; and, when they have heard one side, they think the matter so plain that they need not trouble themselves to hear the other; they are already apprized of it, and masters of all the merits of the cause. Whereas, though a ready wit is an agreeable thing to play with, it is solid judgment and sound wisdom that do business. 2. Those that take a pride in being quick commonly fall under the just reproach of being impertinent. It is folly for a man to go about to speak to a thing which he does not understand, or to pass sentence upon a matter which he is not truly and fully informed of, and has not patience to make a strict enquiry into; and, if it be folly, it is and will be shame.  <div eID="gen14098" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv52"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv52"/> <div sID="gen14099" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear? <div eID="gen14099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14100" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Outward grievances are tolerable as long as the mind enjoys itself and is at ease. Many infirmities, many calamities, we are liable to in this world, in body, name, and estate, which a man may bear, and bear up under, if he have but good conduct and courage, and be able to act with reason and resolution, especially if he have a good conscience, and the testimony of that be for him; and, if the <hi type="italic">spirit of a man</hi> will <hi type="italic">sustain the infirmity,</hi> much more will the spirit of a Christian, or rather the Spirit of God witnessing and working with our spirits in a day of trouble. 2. The grievances of the spirit are of all others most heavy, and hardly to be borne; these make sore the shoulders which should sustain the other infirmities. If the spirit be wounded by the disturbance of the reason, dejection under the trouble, whatever it is, and despair of relief, if the spirit be wounded by the amazing apprehensions of God's wrath for sin, and the fearful expectations of judgment and fiery indignation, <hi type="italic">who can bear</hi> this? Wounded spirits cannot help themselves, nor do others know how to help them. It is therefore wisdom to keep conscience void of offence.

<div eID="gen14100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14101" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge. <div eID="gen14101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14102" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that are prudent will seek knowledge, and apply their ear and heart to the pursuit of it, their ear to attend to the means of knowledge and their heart to mix faith with what they hear and make a good improvement of it. Those that are prudent do not think they have prudence enough, but still see they have need of more; and the more prudent a man is the more inquisitive will he be after knowledge, the knowledge of God and his duty, and the way to heaven, for that is the best knowledge. 2. Those that prudently seek knowledge shall certainly get knowledge, for God never said to such, <hi type="italic">Seek in vain,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">Seek and you shall find.</hi> If the ear seeks it, the heart gets it, and keeps it, and is enriched by it. We must get knowledge, not only into our heads, but into our hearts, get the savour and relish of it, apply what we know to ourselves and experience the power and influence of it.

<div eID="gen14102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14103" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> A man's gift maketh room for him, and bringeth him before great men. <div eID="gen14103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14104" type="x-p"/> Of what great force gifts (that is, bribes) are he had intimated before, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.8">ch. xvii. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.23">23</reference>. Here he shows the power of gifts, that is, presents made even by inferiors to those that are above them and have much more than they have. A good present will go far, 1. Towards a man's liberty: <hi type="italic">A man's gift,</hi> if he be in prison, may procure his enlargement; there are courtiers, who, if they use their interest even for oppressed innocency, expect to receive a gratuity for it. Or, if a mean man know not how to get access to a great man, he may do it by a fee to his servants or a present to himself; those will make room for him. 2. Towards his preferment. It will bring him to sit among <hi type="italic">great men,</hi> in honour and power. See how corrupt the world is when men's gifts will not do, though ever so great; nay, will gain that for them which they are unworthy of and unfit for; and no wonder that those take bribes in their offices who gave bribes for them. <hi type="italic">Vendere jura potest, emerat ille prius—He that bought law can sell it.</hi>

<div eID="gen14104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14105" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is</hi> first in his own cause <hi type="italic">seemeth</hi> just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him. <div eID="gen14105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14106" type="x-p"/> This shows that one tale is good till another is told. 1. He that speaks first will be sure to tell a straight story, and relate that only which makes for him, and put the best colour he can upon it, so that his cause shall appear good, whether it really be so or no. 2. The plaintiff having done his evidence, it is fit that the defendant should be heard, should have leave to confront the witnesses and cross-examine them, and show the falsehood and fallacy of what has been alleged, which perhaps may make the matter appear quite otherwise than it did. We must therefore remember that we have two ears, to hear both sides before we give judgment.

<div eID="gen14106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14107" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> The lot causeth contentions to cease, and parteth between the mighty. <div eID="gen14107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14108" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Contentions commonly happen among the mighty, that are jealous for their honour and right and stand upon the punctilios of both, that are confident of their being able to make their part good and therefore will hardly condescend to the necessary terms of an accommodation; whereas those that are poor are forced to be peaceable, and sit down losers. 2. Even the contentions of the mighty may be ended by lot if they cannot otherwise be compromised, and sometimes better so than by arguments which are endless, or concessions which they are loth to stoop to, whereas it is no disparagement to a man to acquiesce in the determination of the lot when once it is referred to that. To prevent quarrels Canaan was divided by lot; and, if lusory lots had not profaned this way of appeal to Providence, perhaps it might be very well used now for the deciding of many controversies, both to the honour of God and the satisfaction of the parties, provided it were done with prayer and due solemnity, this and some other scriptures seeming to direct to it, especially <reference osisRef="Acts.1.26">Acts i. 26</reference>. If the law be a lottery (as some have called it), it were as well that a lottery were the law.

<div eID="gen14108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14109" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> A brother offended <hi type="italic">is harder to be won</hi> than a strong city: and <hi type="italic">their</hi> contentions <hi type="italic">are</hi> like the bars of a castle. <div eID="gen14109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14110" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Great care must be taken to prevent quarrels among relations, and those that are under special obligation to each other, not only because they are most unnatural and unbecoming, but because between such things are commonly taken most unkindly, and resentments are apt to be carried too far. Wisdom and grace would indeed make it most easy to us to forgive our relations and friends if they offend us, but corruption makes it most difficult to forgive them; let us therefore take heed of disobliging a brother, or one that has been as a brother; ingratitude is very provoking. 2. Great pains must be taken to compromise matters in variance between relations, with all speed, because it is a work of so much difficulty, and consequently the more honourable if it be done. Esau was a <hi type="italic">brother offended,</hi> and seemed <hi type="italic">harder to be won than a strong city,</hi> yet by a work of God upon his heart, in answer to Jacob's prayer, he was won.

<div eID="gen14110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14111" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> A man's belly shall be satisfied with the fruit of his mouth; <hi type="italic">and</hi> with the increase of his lips shall he be filled. <div eID="gen14111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14112" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Our comfort depends very much upon the testimony of our own consciences, for us or against us. The <hi type="italic">belly</hi> is here put for the conscience, as <reference osisRef="Prov.20.27">ch. xx. 27</reference>. Now it is of great consequence to us whether that be satisfied, and what that is filled with, for, accordingly, will our satisfaction be and our inward peace. 2. The testimony of our consciences will be for us, or against us, according as we have or have not governed our tongues well. According as <hi type="italic">the fruit of the mouth</hi> is good or bad, unto iniquity or unto righteousness, so the character of the man is, and consequently the testimony of his conscience concerning him. "We ought to take as great care about the words we speak as we do about the fruit of our trees or the increase of the earth, which we are to eat; for, according as they are wholesome or unwholesome, so will the pleasure or the pain be wherewith we shall be filled." So bishop Patrick.

<div eID="gen14112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14113" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Death and life <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof. <div eID="gen14113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14114" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A man may do a great deal of good, or a great deal of hurt, both to others and to himself, according to the use he makes of his tongue. Many a one has been his own death by a foul tongue, or the death of others by a false tongue; and, on the contrary, many a one has saved his own life, or procured the comfort of it, by a prudent gentle tongue, and saved the lives of others by a seasonable testimony or intercession for them. And, if by our words we must be justified or condemned, <hi type="italic">death and life are,</hi> no doubt, <hi type="italic">in the power of the tongue.</hi> Tongues were Æsop's best meat, and his worst. 2. Men's words will be judged of by the affections with which they speak; he that not only speaks aright (which a bad man may do to save his credit or please his company), but loves to speak so, speaks well of choice, and with delight, to him it will be life; and he that not only speaks amiss (which a good man may do through inadvertency), but loves to speak so (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.4">Ps. lii. 4</reference>), to him it will be death. As men <hi type="italic">love it</hi> they shall <hi type="italic">eat the fruit of it.</hi>

<div eID="gen14114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14115" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> <hi type="italic">Whoso</hi> findeth a wife findeth a good <hi type="italic">thing,</hi> and obtaineth favour of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14116" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A good wife is a great blessing to a man. He that <hi type="italic">finds a wife</hi> (that is, a wife indeed; a bad wife does not deserve to be called by a name of so much honour), that finds a help meet for him (that is a wife in the original acceptation of the word), that sought such a one with care and prayer and has found what he sought, he has found a <hi type="italic">good thing,</hi> a jewel of great value, a rare jewel; he has found that which will not only contribute more than any thing to his comfort in this life, but will forward him in the way to heaven. 2. God is to be acknowledged in it with thankfulness; it is a token of his favour, and a happy pledge of further favours; it is a sign that God delights in a man to do him good and has mercy in store for him; for this, therefore, God must be sought unto.

<div eID="gen14116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14117" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> The poor useth intreaties; but the rich answereth roughly. <div eID="gen14117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14118" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Poverty, though many inconveniences to the body attend it, has often a good effect upon the spirit, for it makes men humble and submissive, and mortifies their pride. It teaches them to <hi type="italic">use entreaties.</hi> When necessity forces men to beg it tells them they must not prescribe or demand, but take what is given them and be thankful. At the throne of God's grace we are all poor, and must use entreaties, not answer, but make application, must sue <hi type="italic">sub forma pauperis—as a pauper.</hi> 2. A prosperous condition, though it has many advantages, has often this mischief attending it, that it makes men proud, haughty, and imperious: <hi type="italic">The rich answers the entreaties of the poor roughly,</hi> as Nabal answered David's messengers with railing. It is a very foolish humour of some rich men, especially those who have risen from little, that they think their riches will warrant them to give hard words, and, even where they not design any rough dealing, that it becomes them to answer roughly, whereas gentlemen ought to be gentle, <reference osisRef="Jas.3.17">Jam. iii. 17</reference>.

<div eID="gen14118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14119" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> A man <hi type="italic">that hath</hi> friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend <hi type="italic">that</hi> sticketh closer than a brother. <div eID="gen14119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14120" type="x-p"/> Solomon here recommends friendship to us, and shows, 1. What we must do that we may contract and cultivate friendship; we must <hi type="italic">show ourselves friendly.</hi> Would we have friends and keep them, we must not only not affront them, or quarrel with them, but we must love them, and make it appear that we do so by all expressions that are endearing, by being free with them, pleasing to them, visiting them and bidding them welcome, and especially by doing all the good offices we can and serving them in every thing that lies in our power; that is <hi type="italic">showing ourselves friendly.</hi> <div eID="gen14120" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen14121"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14122"/>Si vis amari, ama—<l eID="gen14122" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14123"/>If you wish to gain affection, bestow it.—Sen.<l eID="gen14123" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14124"/>Ut ameris, amabilis esto—<l eID="gen14124" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14125"/>The way to be beloved is to be lovely.—Ovid.<l eID="gen14125" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen14121"/> <div sID="gen14126" type="x-p"/> 2. That it is worth while to do so, for we may promise ourselves a great deal of comfort in a true friend. A <hi type="italic">brother</hi> indeed <hi type="italic">is born for adversity,</hi> as he had said, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">ch. xvii. 17</reference>. In our troubles we expect comfort and relief from our relations, but sometimes <hi type="italic">there is a friend,</hi> that is nothing akin to us, the bonds of whose esteem and love prove stronger than those of nature, and, when it comes to the trial, will do more for us than a brother will. Christ is a friend to all believers that <hi type="italic">sticks closer than a brother;</hi> to him therefore let them show themselves friendly.  <chapter eID="Prov.18"/> <div eID="gen14126" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv53"/><title type="x-s3">The Disadvantages of Poverty.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv53"/> <div sID="gen14128" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> the poor that walketh in his integrity, than <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> perverse in his lips, and is a fool. <div eID="gen14128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14129" type="x-p"/> Here see, 1. What will be the credit and comfort of a poor man, and make him more excellent than his neighbour, though his poverty may expose him to contempt and may dispirit him. Let him be honest and <hi type="italic">walk in integrity,</hi> let him keep a good conscience and make it appear that he does so, let him always speak and act with sincerity when he is under the greatest temptations to dissemble and break his word, and then let him value himself upon that, for all wise and good men will value him. He is better, has a better character, is in a better condition, is better beloved, and lives to better purpose, than many a one that looks great and makes a figure. 2. What will be the shame of a rich man, notwithstanding all his pomp. If he have a shallow head and an evil tongue, if he is <hi type="italic">perverse in his lips and is a fool,</hi> if he is a wicked man and gets what he has by fraud and oppression, he <hi type="italic">is a fool,</hi> and an honest poor man is to be preferred far before him.

<div eID="gen14129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14130" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> Also, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the soul <hi type="italic">be</hi> without knowledge, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> not good; and he that hasteth with <hi type="italic">his</hi> feet sinneth. <div eID="gen14130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14131" type="x-p"/> Two things are here declared to be of bad consequence:—1. Ignorance: <hi type="italic">To be without the knowledge of the soul is not good,</hi> so some read it. Know we not our own selves, our own hearts? <hi type="italic">A soul without knowledge is not good;</hi> it is a great privilege that we have souls, but, if these souls have not knowledge, what the better are we? If man <hi type="italic">has not understanding, he is as the beasts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.20">Ps. xlix. 20</reference>. An ignorant soul cannot be a good soul. That the soul be without knowledge is not safe, nor pleasant; what good can the soul do, of what is it good for, if it be without knowledge? 2. Rashness. <hi type="italic">He that hastes with his feet</hi> (that does things inconsiderately and with precipitation, and will not take time to ponder the path of his feet) <hi type="italic">sins;</hi> he cannot but often miss the mark and take many a false step, which those prevent that consider their ways. As good not know as not consider.

<div eID="gen14131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14132" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14133" type="x-p"/> We have here two instances of men's folly:—1. That they bring themselves into straits and troubles, and run themselves a-ground, and embarrass themselves: <hi type="italic">The foolishness of man perverts his way.</hi> Men meet with crosses and disappointments in their affairs, and things do not succeed as they expected and wished, and it is owing to themselves and their own folly; it is their own iniquity that corrects them. 2. That when they have done so they lay the blame upon God, and their hearts fret against him, as if he had done them wrong, whereas really they wrong themselves. In fretting, we are enemies to our own peace, and become self-tormentors; in <hi type="italic">fretting against the Lord</hi> we affront him, his justice, goodness, and sovereignty; and it is very absurd to take occasion from the trouble which we pull upon our own heads by our wilfulness, or neglect, to quarrel with him, when we ought to blame ourselves, for it is our own doing. See <reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Isa. l. 1</reference>.

<div eID="gen14133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14134" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Wealth maketh many friends; but the poor is separated from his neighbour. <div eID="gen14134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14135" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. We may see how strong men's love of money is, that they will love any man, how undeserving soever he be otherwise, if he has but a deal of money and is free with it, so that they may hope to be the better for it. Wealth enables a man to send many presents, make many entertainments, and do many good offices, and so gains him many friends, who pretend to love him, for they flatter him and make their court to him, but really love what he has, or rather love themselves, hoping to get by him. 2. We may see how weak men's love of one another is. He who, while he prospered, was beloved and respected, if he fall into poverty is <hi type="italic">separated from his neighbour,</hi> is not owned nor looked upon, not visited nor regarded, is bidden to keep his distance and told he is troublesome. Even one that has been his neighbour and acquaintance will turn his face from him and pass by on the other side. Because men's consciences tell them they ought to relieve and succour such, they are willing to have this excuse, that they did not see them.

<div eID="gen14135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14136" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> A false witness shall not be unpunished, and <hi type="italic">he that</hi> speaketh lies shall not escape. <div eID="gen14136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14137" type="x-p"/> Here we have, 1. The sins threatened—bearing <hi type="italic">false witness</hi> in judgment and <hi type="italic">speaking lies</hi> in common conversation. Men could not arrive at such a pitch of impiety as to bear false witness (where to the guilt of a lie is added that of perjury and injury) if they had not advanced to it by allowing themselves to speak untruths in jest and banter, or under pretence of doing good. Thus men <hi type="italic">teach their tongues to speak lies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.9.5">Jer. ix. 5</reference>. Those that will take a liberty to tell lies in discourse are in a fair way to be guilty of the greater wickedness of false-witness-bearing, whenever they are tempted to it, though they seemed to detest it. Those that can swallow a false word debauch their consciences, so that a false oath will not choke them. 2. The threatening itself: They <hi type="italic">shall not go unpunished;</hi> they <hi type="italic">shall not escape.</hi> This intimates that that which emboldens them in the sin is the hope of impunity, it being a sin which commonly escapes punishment from men, though the law is strict, <reference osisRef="Deut.19.18-Deut.19.19">Deut. xix. 18, 19</reference>. But it <hi type="italic">shall not escape</hi> the righteous judgment of God, who is jealous, and will not suffer his name to be profaned; we know where all liars will have their everlasting portion.

<div eID="gen14137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14138" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Many will intreat the favour of the prince: and every man <hi type="italic">is</hi> a friend to him that giveth gifts. <hi type="super">7</hi> All the brethren of the poor do hate him: how much more do his friends go far from him? he pursueth <hi type="italic">them with</hi> words, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> they <hi type="italic">are</hi> wanting <hi type="italic">to him.</hi> <div eID="gen14138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14139" type="x-p"/> These two verses are a comment upon <reference osisRef="Prov.18.4">v. 4</reference>, and show, 1. How those that are rich and great are courted and caressed, and have suitors and servants in abundance. The prince that has power in his hand, and preferments at his disposal, has his gate and his ante-chamber thronged with petitioners, that are ready to adore him for what they can get. <hi type="italic">Many will entreat his favour,</hi> and think themselves happy in it. Even great men are humble suppliants to the prince. How earnest then should we be for the favour of God, which is far beyond that of any earthly prince. But, it should seem, liberality will go further than majesty itself to gain respect, for there are many that court the prince, but <hi type="italic">every man is a friend to him that gives gifts;</hi> not only those that have received, or do expect, gifts from him, will, as friends, be ready to serve him, but others also will, as friends, give him their good word. Prodigals, who are foolishly free of what they have, will have many hangers-on who will cry them up as long as it lasts, but will leave them when it is done. Those that are prudently generous make an interest by it which may stand them in good stead; those that are accounted benefactors exercise an authority which may give them an opportunity of doing good, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.25">Luke xxii. 25</reference>. 2. How those that are poor and low are slighted and despised. Men may, if they please, court the prince, and the princely, but they may not trample upon the poor and look at them with disdain. Yet so it often is: <hi type="italic">All the brethren of the poor do hate him;</hi> even his own relations are shy of him, because he is needy and craving, and expects something from them, and because they look upon him as a blemish to their family; and then no marvel if others of his friends, that were nothing akin to him, <hi type="italic">go far from him,</hi> to get out of his way. <hi type="italic">He pursues them with words,</hi> hoping to prevail with them by his importunity to be kind to him, but all in vain; they have nothing for him. <hi type="italic">They pursue him with words</hi> (so some understand it), to excuse themselves from giving him any thing; they tell him that he is idle and impertinent, that he has brought himself into poverty, and therefore ought not to be relieved; as Nabal said to David's messengers: "<hi type="italic">There are many servants now a days that run away from their masters;</hi> and how do I know but that David may be one of them?" Let poor people therefore make God their friend, pursue him with their prayers, and he will not be wanting to them.  <div eID="gen14139" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv54"/><title type="x-s3">Domestic Grievances.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv54"/> <div sID="gen14140" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> He that getteth wisdom loveth his own soul: he that keepeth understanding shall find good. <div eID="gen14140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14141" type="x-p"/> Those are here encouraged, 1. That take pains to <hi type="italic">get wisdom,</hi> to get knowledge, and grace, and acquaintance with God; those that do so show that they <hi type="italic">love their own souls,</hi> and will be found to have done themselves the greatest kindness imaginable. No man ever <hi type="italic">hated his own flesh,</hi> but loves that, yet many are wanting in love to their own souls, for only those love their souls, and consequently love themselves, aright, that <hi type="italic">get wisdom,</hi> true wisdom. 2. That take care to keep it when they have got it; it is health, and wealth, and honour, and all, to the soul, and therefore he that <hi type="italic">keeps understanding,</hi> as he shows that he <hi type="italic">loves his own soul,</hi> so he shall certainly <hi type="italic">find good,</hi> all good. He that retains the good lessons he has learnt, and orders his conversation according to them, shall find the benefit and comfort of it in his own soul and shall be happy here and for ever.

<div eID="gen14141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14142" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> A false witness shall not be unpunished, and <hi type="italic">he that</hi> speaketh lies shall perish. <div eID="gen14142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14143" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A repetition of what was said before (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.5">v. 5</reference>), for we have need to be again and again warned of the danger of the sin of lying and false-witness-bearing, since nothing is of more fatal consequence. 2. An addition to it in one word; there it was said, <hi type="italic">He that speaks lies shall not escape,</hi> and intimated that he shall be punished. Here it is said, His punishment shall be such as will be his destruction: he <hi type="italic">shall perish;</hi> the lies he forged against others will be his own ruin. It is a damning destroying sin.

<div eID="gen14143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14144" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Delight is not seemly for a fool; much less for a servant to have rule over princes. <div eID="gen14144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14145" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Pleasure and liberty ill become a fool: <hi type="italic">Delight is not seemly for</hi> such a one. A man that has not wisdom and grace has no right nor title to true joy, and therefore it is unseemly. It ill becomes those that do not delight in God to delight in any thing, nor how to manage themselves, and therefore they do but expose themselves. It becomes ungracious fools to be afflicted, and mourn, and weep, not to laugh and be merry; rebukes are more proper for them than delights. Delight is seemly for a man of business, to refresh him when he is fatigued, but not <hi type="italic">for a fool,</hi> that lives an idle life and abuses his recreations. <hi type="italic">The prosperity of fools</hi> discovers their folly and <hi type="italic">destroys them.</hi> 2. Power and honour ill become a man of a servile spirit. Nothing is more unseemly than <hi type="italic">for a servant to have rule over princes;</hi> it is absurd in itself, and very preposterous, for none are so insolent and intolerable as a beggar on horseback, <hi type="italic">a servant when he reigns,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.22">ch. xxx. 22</reference>. It is very unseemly for one that is a servant to sin and his lusts to rule over and oppress those that are God's freemen and made kings and priests to him.

<div eID="gen14145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14146" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and <hi type="italic">it is</hi> his glory to pass over a transgression. <div eID="gen14146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14147" type="x-p"/> A wise man will observe these two rules about his anger: 1. Not to be over-hasty in his resentments: <hi type="italic">Discretion</hi> teaches us to <hi type="italic">defer our anger,</hi> to defer the admission of it till we have thoroughly considered all the merits of the provocation, seen them in a true light and weighed them in a just balance; and then to defer the prosecution of it till there be no danger of running into any indecencies. Plato said to his servant, "I would beat thee, but that I am angry." Give it time, and it will cool. 2. Not to be over-critical in his resentments. Whereas it is commonly looked upon as a piece of ingenuity to apprehend an affront quickly, it is here made a man's <hi type="italic">glory to pass over a transgression,</hi> to appear as if he did not see it (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.13">Ps. xxxviii. 13</reference>), or, if he sees fit to take notice of it, yet to forgive it and meditate no revenge.

<div eID="gen14147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14148" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The king's wrath <hi type="italic">is</hi> as the roaring of a lion; but his favour <hi type="italic">is</hi> as dew upon the grass. <div eID="gen14148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14149" type="x-p"/> This is to the same purport with what we had <reference osisRef="Prov.16.14-Prov.16.15">ch. xvi. 14, 15</reference>, and the design of it is, 1. To make kings wise and considerate in dispensing their frowns and smiles. They are not like those of common persons; their frowns are very terrible and their smiles very comfortable, and therefore it concerns them to be very careful that they never frighten a good man from doing well with their frowns, nor ever give countenance to a wicked man in doing ill with their smiles, for then they abuse their influence, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.3">Rom. xiii. 3</reference>. 2. To make subjects faithful and dutiful to their princes. Let them be restrained from all disloyalty by the consideration of the dreadful consequence of having the government against them; and let them be encouraged in all good services to the public by the hopes of the favour of their prince. Christ is a King whose wrath against his enemies will be <hi type="italic">as the roaring of a lion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.3">Rev. x. 3</reference>) and his favour to his own people as the refreshing dew, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Ps. lxxii. 6</reference>.

<div eID="gen14149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14150" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> A foolish son <hi type="italic">is</hi> the calamity of his father: and the contentions of a wife <hi type="italic">are</hi> a continual dropping. <div eID="gen14150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14151" type="x-p"/> It is an instance of the vanity of the world that we are liable to the greatest grief in those things wherein we promise ourselves the greatest comfort. It is as it proves. What greater temporal comfort can a man have than a good wife and good children? Yet, 1. <hi type="italic">A foolish son is</hi> a great affliction, and may make a man wish a thousand times he had been written childless. A son that will apply himself to no study or business, that will take no advice, that lives a lewd, loose, rakish life, and spends what he has extravagantly, games it away and wastes it in the excess of riot, or that is proud, foppish, and conceited, such a one is the grief <hi type="italic">of his father,</hi> because he is the disgrace, and is likely to be the ruin, of his family. He hates all his labour, when he sees to whom he must leave the fruit of it. 2. A cross peevish wife is as great an affliction: Her <hi type="italic">contentions are continual;</hi> every day, and every hour in the day, she finds some occasion to make herself and those about her uneasy. Those that are accustomed to chide never want something or other to chide at; but it is <hi type="italic">a continual dropping,</hi> that is, a continual vexation, as it is to have a house so much out of repair that it rains in and a man cannot lie dry in it. That man has an uncomfortable life, and has need of a great deal of wisdom and grace to enable him to bear his affliction and do his duty, who has a sot for his son and a scold for his wife.

<div eID="gen14151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14152" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> House and riches <hi type="italic">are</hi> the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife <hi type="italic">is</hi> from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14153" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A discreet and virtuous wife is a choice gift of God's providence to a man—a wife that is <hi type="italic">prudent,</hi> in opposition to one that is contentious, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.13">v. 13</reference>. For, though a wife that is continually finding fault may think it is her wit and wisdom to be so, it is really her folly; <hi type="italic">a prudent wife</hi> is meek and quiet, and makes the best of every thing. If a man has such a wife, let him not ascribe it to the wisdom of his own choice or his own management (for the wisest have been deceived both in and by a woman), but let him ascribe it to the goodness of God, who made him a help meet for him, and perhaps by some hits and turns of providence that seemed casual brought her to him. Every creature is what he makes it. Happy marriages, we are sure, are made in heaven; Abraham's servant prayed in the belief of this, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.12">Gen. xxiv. 12</reference>. 2. It is a more valuable gift than <hi type="italic">house and riches,</hi> contributes more to the comfort and credit of a man's life and the welfare of his family, is a greater token of God's favour, and about which the divine providence is in a more especial manner conversant. A good estate may be <hi type="italic">the inheritance of fathers,</hi> which, by the common direction of Providence, comes in course to a man; but no man has a good wife by descent or entail. Parents that are worldly, in disposing of their children, look no further than to match them to <hi type="italic">house and riches,</hi> but, if withal it be to <hi type="italic">a prudent wife,</hi> let God have the glory.  <div eID="gen14153" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv55"/><title type="x-s3">Circumspection and Charity.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv55"/> <div sID="gen14154" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger. <div eID="gen14154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14155" type="x-p"/> See here the evil of a sluggish slothful disposition. 1. It stupefies men, and makes them senseless, and mindless of their own affairs, as they were <hi type="italic">cast into a deep sleep,</hi> dreaming much, but doing nothing. Slothful people doze away their time, bury their talents, live a useless life, and are the unprofitable burdens of the earth; for any service they do when they are awake they might as well be always asleep. Even their souls are idle and lulled asleep, their rational powers chilled and frozen. 2. It impoverishes men and brings them to want. Those that will not labour cannot expect to eat, but must <hi type="italic">suffer hunger: An idle soul,</hi> one that is idle in the affairs of his soul, that takes no care or pains to work out his salvation, shall perish for want of that which is necessary to the life and happiness of the soul.

<div eID="gen14155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14156" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> He that keepeth the commandment keepeth his own soul; <hi type="italic">but</hi> he that despiseth his ways shall die. <div eID="gen14156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14157" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The happiness of those that walk circumspectly. Those that make conscience of <hi type="italic">keeping the commandment</hi> in every thing, that live by rule, as becomes servants and patients, <hi type="italic">keep their own souls;</hi> they secure their present peace and future bliss, and provide every way well for themselves. If we keep God's word, God's word will keep us from every thing really hurtful. 2. The misery of those that live at large and never mind what they do: Those <hi type="italic">that despair their ways shall die,</hi> shall perish eternally; they are in the high road to ruin. With respect to those that are careless about the end of their ways, and never consider whither they are going, and about the rule of their ways, that will walk in the way of their hearts and after the course of the world (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Eccl. xi. 9</reference>), that never consider what they have done nor what they are concerned to do, but <hi type="italic">walk at all adventures</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.21">Lev. xxvi. 21</reference>), right or wrong, it is all one to them—what can come of this but the greatest mischief?

<div eID="gen14157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14158" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and that which he hath given will he pay him again. <div eID="gen14158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14159" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The duty of charity described. It includes two things:—1. Compassion, which is the inward principle of charity in the heart; it is to <hi type="italic">have pity on the poor.</hi> Those that have not a penny for the poor, yet may have pity for them, a charitable concern and sympathy; and, if a man <hi type="italic">give all his goods to feed the poor</hi> and have not this charity in his heart, <hi type="italic">it is nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.3">1 Cor. xiii. 3</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">draw out our souls to the hungry,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.10">Isa. lviii. 10</reference>. 2. Bounty and liberality. We must not only pity the poor, but give, according to their necessity and our ability, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.15-Jas.2.16">Jam. ii. 15, 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">That which he has given.</hi> Margin, <hi type="italic">His deed.</hi> It is charity to do for the poor, as well as to give; and thus, if they have their limbs and senses, they may be charitable to one another. <div eID="gen14159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14160" type="x-p"/> II. The encouragement of charity. 1. A very kind construction shall be put upon it. What is given to the poor, or done for them, God will place it to account as lent to him, <hi type="italic">lent upon interest</hi> (so the word signifies); he takes it kindly, as if it were done to himself, and he would have us take the comfort of it and to be as well pleased as ever any usurer was when he had let out a sum of money into good hands. 2. A very rich recompence shall be made for it: <hi type="italic">He will pay him again,</hi> in temporal, spiritual, and eternal blessings. Almsgiving is the surest and safest way of thriving.  <div eID="gen14160" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv56"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv56"/> <div sID="gen14161" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Chasten thy son while there is hope, and let not thy soul spare for his crying. <div eID="gen14161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14162" type="x-p"/> Parents are here cautioned against a foolish indulgence of their children that are untoward and viciously inclined, and that discover such an ill temper of mind as is not likely to be cured but by severity. 1. Do not say that it is all in good time to correct them; no, as soon as ever there appears a corrupt disposition in them check it immediately, before it gets head, and takes root, and is hardened into a habit: <hi type="italic">Chasten thy son while there is hope,</hi> for perhaps, if he be let alone awhile, he will be past hope, and a much greater chastening will not do that which now a less would effect. It is easiest plucking up weeds as soon as they spring up, and the bullock that is designed for the yoke should be betimes accustomed to it. 2. Do not say that it is a pity to correct them, and that, because they cry and beg to be forgiven, you cannot find in your heart to do it. If the point can be gained without correction, well and good; but if you find, as it often proves, that your forgiving them once, upon a dissembled repentance and promise of amendment, does but embolden them to offend again, especially if it be a thing that is in itself sinful (as lying, swearing, ribaldry, stealing, or the like), in such a case put on resolution, <hi type="italic">and let not thy soul spare for his crying.</hi> It is better that he should cry under thy rod than under the sword of the magistrate, or, which is more fearful, that of divine vengeance.

<div eID="gen14162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14163" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> A man of great wrath shall suffer punishment: for if thou deliver <hi type="italic">him,</hi> yet thou must do it again. <div eID="gen14163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14164" type="x-p"/> 1. As we read this, it intimates, in short, that angry men never want woe. Those that are of strong, or rather headstrong, passions, commonly bring themselves and their families into trouble by vexatious suits and quarrels and the provocations they give; they are still smarting, in one instance or other, for their ungoverned heats; and, if their friends deliver them out of one trouble, they will quickly involve themselves in another, and they <hi type="italic">must do it again,</hi> all which troubles to themselves and others would be prevented if they would mortify their passions and get the rule of their own spirits. 2. It may as well be read, <hi type="italic">He that is of great wrath</hi> (meaning the child that is to be corrected and is impatient of rebuke, cries and makes a noise, even that wrath of his against the rod of correction) <hi type="italic">deserves to be punished; for, if thou deliver him</hi> for the sake of that, thou wilt be forced to punish him so much the more next time. A stomachful high-spirited child must be subdued betimes, or it will be the worse for it.

<div eID="gen14164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14165" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end. <div eID="gen14165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14166" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is well with those that are <hi type="italic">wise in their latter end,</hi> wise for their latter end, for their future state, wise for another world, that are found wise when their latter end comes, wise virgins, wise builders, wise stewards, that are wise at length, and <hi type="italic">understand the things that belong to their peace, before they be hidden from their eyes.</hi> A carnal worldling <hi type="italic">at his end shall be a fool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.11">Jer. xvii. 11</reference>), but godliness will prove wisdom at last. 2. Those that would <hi type="italic">be wise in their latter end</hi> must <hi type="italic">hear counsel</hi> and <hi type="italic">receive instruction,</hi> in their beginnings must be willing to be taught and ruled, willing to be advised and reproved, when they are young. Those that would be stored in winter must gather in summer.

<div eID="gen14166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14167" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> <hi type="italic">There are</hi> many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that shall stand. <div eID="gen14167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14168" type="x-p"/> Here we have, 1. Men projecting. They keep their designs to themselves, but they cannot hide them from God; he knows the <hi type="italic">many devices that are in men's hearts,</hi>—devices against his counsels (as those, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.3">Ps. ii. 1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11">Micah iv. 11</reference>),— devices without his counsel (no regard had to his providence, as those <reference osisRef="Jas.4.13">Jam. iv. 13</reference>, this and the other they will do, and not take God along with them),—devices unlike God's counsels; men are wavering in their devices, and often absurd and unjust, but God's counsels are wise and holy, steady and uniform. 2. God overruling. Various men have various designs, according as their inclination or interest leads them, but <hi type="italic">the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand,</hi> whatever becomes of the devices of men. His counsel often breaks men's measures and baffles their devices; but their devices cannot in the least alter his counsel, not disturb the proceedings of it, nor put him upon new counsels, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.24">Isa. xiv. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.11">xlvi. 11</reference>. What a check does this give to politic designing men, who think they can outwit all mankind, that there is a God in heaven that laughs at them! <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Ps. ii. 4</reference>. What comfort does this speak to all God's people, that all God's purposes, which we are sure are right and good, shall be accomplished in due time!

<div eID="gen14168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14169" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> The desire of a man <hi type="italic">is</hi> his kindness: and a poor man <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than a liar. <div eID="gen14169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14170" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The honour of doing good is what we may laudably be ambitious of. It cannot but be <hi type="italic">the desire of man,</hi> if he have any spark of virtue in him, to be kind; one would not covet an estate for any thing so much as thereby to be put into a capacity of relieving the poor and obliging our friends. 2. It is far better to have a heart to do good and want ability for it than have ability for it and want a heart to it: <hi type="italic">The desire of a man</hi> to be kind, and charitable, and generous, <hi type="italic">is his kindness,</hi> and shall be so construed; both God and man will accept his good-will, <hi type="italic">according to what he has,</hi> and will not expect more. <hi type="italic">A poor man,</hi> who wishes you well, but can promise you nothing, because he has nothing to be kind with, <hi type="italic">is better than a liar,</hi> than a rich man who makes you believe he will do mighty things, but, when it comes to the setting to, will do nothing. The character of the men of low degree, that they <hi type="italic">are vanity,</hi> from whom nothing is expected, is better than that of men of high degree, that they <hi type="italic">are a lie,</hi> they deceive those whose expectations they raised.

<div eID="gen14170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14171" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> The fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">tendeth</hi> to life: and <hi type="italic">he that hath it</hi> shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited with evil. <div eID="gen14171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14172" type="x-p"/> See what those that get by it that live in the fear of God, and always make conscience of their duty to him. 1. Safety: They <hi type="italic">shall not be visited with evil;</hi> they may be visited with sickness or other afflictions, but there shall be no evil in them, nothing to hurt them, because nothing to separate them <hi type="italic">from the love of God,</hi> or hurt to the soul. 2. Satisfaction: They <hi type="italic">shall abide satisfied;</hi> they shall have those comforts which are satisfying, and shall have a constant contentment and complacency in them. It is a satisfaction which will abide, whereas all the satisfactions of sense are transient and soon gone. <hi type="italic">Satur pernoctabit, non cubabit incoenatus</hi>—<hi type="italic">He shall not go supperless to bed;</hi> he shall have that which will make him easy and be an entertainment to him in his silent and solitary hours, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.6-Ps.16.7">Ps. xvi. 6, 7</reference>. 3. True and complete happiness. Serious godliness has a direct tendency <hi type="italic">to life;</hi> to all good, to eternal life; it is the sure and ready way to it; there is something in the nature of it fitting men for heaven and so leading them to it.

<div eID="gen14172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14173" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> A slothful <hi type="italic">man</hi> hideth his hand in <hi type="italic">his</hi> bosom, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth again. <div eID="gen14173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14174" type="x-p"/> A sluggard is here exposed as a fool, for, 1. All his care is to save himself from labour and cold. See his posture: He <hi type="italic">hides his hand in his bosom,</hi> pretends he is lame and cannot work; his hands are cold, and he must warm them in his bosom; and, when they are warm there, he must keep them so. He hugs himself in his own ease and is resolved against labour and hardship. Let those work that love it; for his part he thinks there is no such fine life as sitting still and doing nothing. 2. He will not be at the pains to feed himself, an elegant hyperbole; as we say, A man is so lazy that he would not shake fire off him, so here, He cannot find in his heart to take his hand out of his bosom, no, not to put meat into his own mouth. If the law be so that those that will not labour must not eat, he will rather starve than stir. Thus his sin is his punishment, and therefore is egregious folly.

<div eID="gen14174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14175" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> Smite a scorner, and the simple will beware: and reprove one that hath understanding, <hi type="italic">and</hi> he will understand knowledge. <div eID="gen14175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14176" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The punishment of scorners will be a means of good to others. When men are so hardened in wickedness that they will not themselves be wrought upon by the severe methods that are used to reclaim and reform them, yet such methods must be used for the sake of others, that <hi type="italic">they may hear and fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.19.20">Deut. xix. 20</reference>. If the <hi type="italic">scorner</hi> will not be recovered from his sin, the disease being inveterate, yet <hi type="italic">the simple will beware</hi> of venturing upon the sin which exposes men thus. If it cure not the infected, it may prevent the spreading of the infection. 2. The reproof of wise men will be a means of good to themselves. They need not be smitten; a word to the wise is enough. Do but <hi type="italic">reprove one that has understanding and he will</hi> so far understand himself and his own interest that he will <hi type="italic">understand knowledge</hi> by it, and not miss it again through ignorance and inadvertency when once he has been told of it; so kindly does he take reproof and so wisely improve it.

<div eID="gen14176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14177" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> He that wasteth <hi type="italic">his</hi> father, <hi type="italic">and</hi> chaseth away <hi type="italic">his</hi> mother, <hi type="italic">is</hi> a son that causeth shame, and bringeth reproach. <div eID="gen14177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14178" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The sin of a prodigal son. Besides the wrong he does to himself, he is injurious to his good parents, and basely ungrateful to those that were instruments of his being and have taken so much care and pains about him, which is a great aggravation of his sin and renders it exceedingly sinful in the eyes of God and man: <hi type="italic">He wastes is father,</hi> wastes his estate which he should have to support him in his old age, wastes his spirits, and breaks his heart, and brings his gray head <hi type="italic">with sorrow to the grave.</hi> He <hi type="italic">chases away his mother,</hi> alienates her affections from him, which cannot be done without a great deal of regret and uneasiness to her; he makes her weary of the house, with his rudeness and insolence, and glad to retire for a little quietness; and, when he has spent all, he turns her out of doors. 2. The shame of a prodigal son. It is a shame to himself that he should be so brutish and unnatural. He makes himself odious to all mankind. It is a shame to his parents and family, who are reflected upon, though, perhaps, without just cause, for teaching him no better, or being in some way wanting to him.
