<div eID="gen14178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14179" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Cease, my son, to hear the instruction <hi type="italic">that causeth</hi> to err from the words of knowledge. <div eID="gen14179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14180" type="x-p"/> This is a good caution to those that have had a good education to take heed of hearkening to those who, under pretence of instructing them, draw them off from those good principles under the influence of which they were trained up. Observe, 1. There is that which seems designed for instruction, but really tends to the destruction of young men. The factors for vice will undertake to teach them free thoughts and a fashionable conversation, how to palliate the sins they have a mind to and stop the mouth of their own consciences, how to get clear of the restraints of their education and to set up for wits and beaux. This is <hi type="italic">the instruction</hi> which <hi type="italic">causes to err from the</hi> forms of sound words, which should be held fast in faith and love. 2. It is the wisdom of young men to turn a deaf ear to such instructions, as the adder does to the charms that are designed to ensnare her. "Dread hearing such talk as tends top instil loose principles into the mind; and, if thou art linked in with such, break off from them; thou hast heard enough, or too much, and therefore hear no more of the evil communication which corrupts good manners."

<div eID="gen14180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14181" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> An ungodly witness scorneth judgment: and the mouth of the wicked devoureth iniquity. <div eID="gen14181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14182" type="x-p"/> Here is a description of the worst of sinners, whose <hi type="italic">hearts are fully set in them to do evil.</hi> 1. They set that at defiance which would deter and detain them from sin: <hi type="italic">An ungodly witness</hi> is one that bears false witness against his neighbour, and will forswear himself to do another a mischief, in which there is not only great injustice, but great impiety; this is one of the worst of men. Or <hi type="italic">an ungodly witness</hi> is one that profanely and atheistically witnesses against religion and godliness, whose instructions seduce <hi type="italic">from the words of knowledge</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.27">v. 27</reference>); such a one <hi type="italic">scorns judgment,</hi> laughs at the terrors of the Lord, mocks at that fear, <reference osisRef="Job.15.26">Job xv. 26</reference>. Tell him of law and equity, that the scriptures and an oath are sacred things, and not to be jested with, that there will come a reckoning day; he laughs at it all, and scorns to heed it. 2. They are greedy, and glad of that which gives them an opportunity to sin: <hi type="italic">The mouth of the wicked</hi> eagerly <hi type="italic">devours iniquity, drinks it in like water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.16">Job xv. 16</reference>.

<div eID="gen14182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14183" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> Judgments are prepared for scorners, and stripes for the back of fools. <div eID="gen14183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14184" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Scorners are fools. Those that ridicule things sacred and serious do but make themselves ridiculous. <hi type="italic">Their folly shall be manifest unto all men.</hi> 2. Those that scorn judgments cannot escape them, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.28">v. 28</reference>. The unbelief of man shall not make God's threatenings of no effect; those that <hi type="italic">devour iniquity</hi> swallow the hook with the bait. The civil magistrate has <hi type="italic">judgments prepared for scorners,</hi> for otherwise he would <hi type="italic">bear the sword in vain;</hi> but if he be remiss, and connive at sin, yet God's judgments slumber not; they are prepared, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.41">Matt. xxv. 41</reference>.  <chapter eID="Prov.19"/> <div eID="gen14184" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv57"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv57"/> <div sID="gen14186" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Wine <hi type="italic">is</hi> a mocker, strong drink <hi type="italic">is</hi> raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise. <div eID="gen14186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14187" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The mischief of drunkenness: <hi type="italic">Wine is a mocker; strong drink is raging.</hi> It is so to the sinner himself; it mocks him, makes a fool of him, promises him that satisfaction which it can never give him. It smiles upon him at first, but <hi type="italic">at the last it bites.</hi> In reflection upon it, it rages in his conscience. It is raging in the body, puts the humours into a ferment. <hi type="italic">When the wine is in the wit is out,</hi> and then the man, according as his natural temper is, either mocks like a fool or rages like a madman. Drunkenness, which pretends to be a sociable thing, renders men unfit for society, for it makes them abusive with their tongues and outrageous in their passions, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.29">ch. xxiii. 29</reference>. 2. The folly of drunkards is easily inferred thence. He that <hi type="italic">is deceived thereby,</hi> that suffers himself to be drawn into this sin when he is so plainly warned of the consequences of it, <hi type="italic">is not wise;</hi> he shows that he has no right sense or consideration of things; and not only so, but he renders himself incapable of getting wisdom; for it is a sin that infatuates and besots men, and takes away their heart. A drunkard is a fool, and a fool he is likely to be.

<div eID="gen14187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14188" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> The fear of a king <hi type="italic">is</hi> as the roaring of a lion: <hi type="italic">whoso</hi> provoketh him to anger sinneth <hi type="italic">against</hi> his own soul. <div eID="gen14188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14189" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How formidable kings are, and what a terror they strike upon those they are angry with. Their <hi type="italic">fear,</hi> with which (especially when they are absolute and their will is a law) they keep their subjects in awe, <hi type="italic">is as the roaring of a lion,</hi> which is very dreadful to the creatures he preys upon, and makes them tremble so that they cannot escape from him. Those princes that rule by wisdom and love rule like God himself, and bear his image; but those that rule merely by terror, and with a high hand, do but rule like a lion in the forest, with a brutal power. <hi type="italic">Oderint, dum metuant</hi>—<hi type="italic">Let them hate, provided they fear.</hi> 2. How unwise therefore those are that quarrel with them, that are angry at them, and so <hi type="italic">provoke them to anger.</hi> They <hi type="italic">sin against their own lives.</hi> Much more do those do so that provoke the King of kings to anger. <hi type="italic">Nemo me impune lacesset</hi>—<hi type="italic">No one shall provoke me with impunity.</hi>

<div eID="gen14189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14190" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling. <div eID="gen14190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14191" type="x-p"/> This is designed to rectify men's mistakes concerning strife. 1. Men think it is their wisdom to engage in quarrels; whereas it is the greatest folly that can be. He thinks himself a wise man that is quick in resenting affronts, that stands upon every nicety of honour and right, and will not abate an ace of either, that prescribes, and imposes, and gives law, to every body; but he that thus meddles is a fool, and creates a great deal of needless vexation to himself. 2. Men think, when they are engaged in quarrels, that it would be a shame to them to go back and let fall the weapon; whereas really <hi type="italic">it is an honour for a man to cease from strife,</hi> an honour to withdraw an action, to drop a controversy, to forgive an injury, and to be friends with those that we have fallen out with. It is the honour of a man, a wise man, a man of spirit, to show the command he has of himself by <hi type="italic">ceasing from strife,</hi> yielding, and stooping, and receding from his just demands, for peace-sake, as Abraham, the better man, <reference osisRef="Gen.13.8">Gen. xiii. 8</reference>.

<div eID="gen14191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14192" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> shall he beg in harvest, and <hi type="italic">have</hi> nothing. <div eID="gen14192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14193" type="x-p"/> See here the evil of slothfulness and the love of ease. 1. It keeps men from the most necessary business, from ploughing and sowing when the season is: <hi type="italic">The sluggard</hi> has ground to occupy, and has ability for it; he can plough, but he <hi type="italic">will not;</hi> some excuse or other he has to shift it off, but the true reason is that it is <hi type="italic">cold</hi> weather. Though ploughing time is not in the depth of winter, it is in the borders of winter, when he thinks it too cold for him to be abroad. Those are scandalously sluggish who, in the way of their business, cannot find in their hearts to undergo so little toil as that of ploughing and so little hardship as that of a cold blast. Thus careless are many in the affairs of their souls; a trifling difficulty will frighten them from the most important duty; but good soldiers must endure hardness. 2. Thereby it deprives them of the most necessary supports: Those that <hi type="italic">will not plough</hi> in seed-time cannot expect to reap in harvest; and therefore they must beg their bread with astonishment when the diligent are bringing home their sheaves with joy. He that will not submit to the labour of ploughing must submit to the shame of begging. They <hi type="italic">shall beg in harvest, and</hi> yet <hi type="italic">have nothing;</hi> no, not then when there is great plenty. Though it may be charity to relieve sluggards, yet a man may, in justice, not relieve them; they deserve to be left to starve. Those that would not provide oil in their vessels begged when the bridegroom came, and were denied.

<div eID="gen14193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14194" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Counsel in the heart of man <hi type="italic">is like</hi> deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out. <div eID="gen14194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14195" type="x-p"/> A man's wisdom is here said to be of use to him for the pumping of other people, and diving into them, 1. To get the knowledge of them. Though men's counsels and designs are ever so carefully concealed by them, so that they are as <hi type="italic">deep water</hi> which one cannot fathom, yet there are those who by sly insinuations, and questions that seem foreign, will get out of them both what they have done and what they intend to do. Those therefore who would keep counsel must not only put on resolution, but stand upon their guard. 2. To get knowledge by them. Some are very able and fit to give counsel, having an excellent faculty of cleaving a hair, hitting the joint of a difficulty, and advising pertinently, but they are modest, and reserved, and not communicative; they have a great deal in them, but it is loth to come out. In such a case <hi type="italic">a man of understanding will draw it out,</hi> as wine out of a vessel. We lose the benefit we might have by the conversation of wise men for want of the art of being inquisitive.

<div eID="gen14195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14196" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Most men will proclaim every one his own goodness: but a faithful man who can find? <div eID="gen14196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14197" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is easy to find those that will pretend to be kind and liberal. Many a man will call himself a man of mercy, will boast what good he has done and what good he designs to do, or, at least, what an affection he has to well-doing. Most men will talk a great deal of their charity, generosity, hospitality, and piety, will sound a trumpet to themselves, as the Pharisees, and what little goodness they have will proclaim it and make a mighty matter of it. 2. But it is hard to find those that really are kind and liberal, that have done and will do more than either they speak of or care to hear spoken of, that will be true friends in a strait; such a one as one may trust to is like a black swan.

<div eID="gen14197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14198" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The just <hi type="italic">man</hi> walketh in his integrity: his children <hi type="italic">are</hi> blessed after him. <div eID="gen14198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14199" type="x-p"/> It is here observed to the honour of a good man, 1. That he does well for himself. He has a certain rule, which with an even steady hand he governs himself by: He <hi type="italic">walks in his integrity;</hi> he keeps good conscience, and he has the comfort of it, for <hi type="italic">it is his rejoicing.</hi> He is not liable to those uneasinesses, either in contriving what he shall do or reflecting on what he has done, which those are liable to that walk in deceit. 2. That he does well for his family: <hi type="italic">His children are blessed after him,</hi> and fare the better for his sake. God has mercy in store for the seed of the faithful.

<div eID="gen14199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14200" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes. <div eID="gen14200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14201" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The character of a good governor: He is <hi type="italic">a king</hi> that deserves to be called so who <hi type="italic">sits in the throne,</hi> not as a throne of honour, to take his ease, and take state upon him, and oblige men to keep their distance, but as a <hi type="italic">throne of judgment,</hi> that he may do justice, give redress to the injured and punish the injurious, who makes his business his delight and loves no pleasure comparably to it, who does not devolve the whole care and trouble upon others, but takes cognizance of affairs himself and sees with his own eyes as much as may be, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.9">1 Kings x. 9</reference>. 2. The happy effect of a good government. The presence of the prince goes far towards the putting of wickedness out of countenance; if he inspect his affairs himself, those that are employed under him will be kept in awe and restrained from doing wrong. If great men be good men, and will use their power as they may and ought, what good may they do and what evil may they prevent!

<div eID="gen14201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14202" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin? <div eID="gen14202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14203" type="x-p"/> This question is not only a challenge to any man in the world to prove himself sinless, whatever he pretends, but a lamentation of the corruption of mankind, even that which remains in the best. Alas! <hi type="italic">Who can say,</hi> "I am sinless?" Observe, 1. Who the persons are that are excluded from these pretensions—all, one as well as another. Here, in this imperfect state, no person whatsoever can pretend to be without sin. Adam could say so in innocency, and saints can say so in heaven, but none in this life. Those that think themselves as good as they should be cannot, nay, and those that are really good will not, dare not, say this. 2. What the pretension is that is excluded. We cannot say, We <hi type="italic">have made our hearts clean.</hi> Though we can say, through grace, "We are cleaner than we have been," yet we cannot say, "We are clean and pure from all remainders of sin." Or, though we are clean from the gross acts of sin, yet we cannot say, "Our hearts are clean." Or, though we are washed and cleansed, yet we cannot say, "We ourselves made our own hearts clean;" it was the work of the Spirit. Or, though we are pure from the sins of many others, yet we cannot say, "We are <hi type="italic">pure from our sin, the sin that easily besets us,</hi> the <hi type="italic">body of death</hi> which Paul complained of," <reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">Rom. vii. 24</reference>.

<div eID="gen14203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14204" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Divers weights, <hi type="italic">and</hi> divers measures, both of them <hi type="italic">are</hi> alike abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14205" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. The various arts of deceiving that men have, all which evils the <hi type="italic">love of money</hi> is the root of. In paying and receiving money, which was then commonly done by the scale, they had <hi type="italic">divers weights,</hi> an under-weight for what they paid and an over-weight for what they received; in delivering out and taking in goods they had <hi type="italic">divers measures,</hi> a scanty measure to sell by and a large measure to buy by. This was done wrong with plot and contrivance, and under colour of doing right. Under these is included all manner of fraud and deceit in commerce and trade. 2. The displeasure of God against them. Whether they be about the money or the goods, in the buyer or in the seller, they are all <hi type="italic">alike an abomination to the Lord.</hi> He will not prosper the trade that is thus driven, nor bless what is thus got. He hates those that thus break the common faith by which justice is maintained, and will be <hi type="italic">the avenger of all such.</hi>

<div eID="gen14205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14206" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work <hi type="italic">be</hi> pure, and whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> right. <div eID="gen14206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14207" type="x-p"/> The tree is known by its fruits, a man <hi type="italic">by his doings,</hi> even a young tree by its first fruits, <hi type="italic">a child by his</hi> childish things, <hi type="italic">whether his work be clean</hi> only, appearing good (the word is used <reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">ch. xvi. 2</reference>), or <hi type="italic">whether it be right,</hi> that is, really good. This intimates, 1. That children will discover themselves. One may soon see what their temper is, and which way their inclination leads them, according as their constitution is. Children have not learned the art of dissembling and concealing their bent as grown people have. 2. That parents should observe their children, that they may discover their disposition and genius, and both manage and dispose of them accordingly, drive the nail that will go and draw out that which goes amiss. <hi type="italic">Wisdom is</hi> herein <hi type="italic">profitable to direct.</hi>

<div eID="gen14207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14208" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath made even both of them. <div eID="gen14208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14209" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. God is the God of nature, and all the powers and faculties of nature are derived from him and depend upon him, and therefore are to be employed for him. It was he that <hi type="italic">formed the eye</hi> and <hi type="italic">planted the ear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Ps. xciv. 9</reference>), and the structure of both is admirable; and it is he that preserves to us the use of both; to his providence we owe it that our eyes are <hi type="italic">seeing eyes</hi> and our ears <hi type="italic">hearing ears.</hi> Hearing and seeing are the learning senses, and must particularly own God's goodness in them. 2. God is the God of grace. It is he that gives the ear that hears God's voice, the eye that sees his beauty, for it is he that opens the understanding.

<div eID="gen14209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14210" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Love not sleep, lest thou come to poverty; open thine eyes, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thou shalt be satisfied with bread. <div eID="gen14210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14211" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that indulge themselves in their ease may expect to want necessaries, which should have been gotten by honest labour. "Therefore, though thou must sleep (nature requires it), yet <hi type="italic">love not sleep,</hi> as those do that hate business. Love not sleep for its own sake, but only as it fits for further work. Love not much sleep, but rather grudge the time that is spent in it, and wish thou couldst live without it, that thou mightest always be employed in some good exercise." We must allow it to our bodies as men allow it to their servants, because they cannot help it and otherwise they shall have no good of them. Those that love sleep are likely to <hi type="italic">come to poverty,</hi> not only because they lose the time they spend in excess of sleep, but because they contract a listless careless disposition, and are still half asleep, never well awake. 2. Those that stir up themselves to their business may expect to have conveniences: "<hi type="italic">Open thy eyes,</hi> awake and shake off sleep, see how far in the day it is, how thy work wants thee, and how busy others are about thee! And, when thou art awake, look up, look to thy advantages, and do not let slip thy opportunities; apply thy mind closely to thy business and be in care about it. It is the easy condition of a great advantage: <hi type="italic">Open thy eyes and thou shalt be satisfied with bread;</hi> if thou dost not grow rich, yet though shalt have enough, and that is as good as a feast."

<div eID="gen14211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14212" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> naught, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> naught, saith the buyer: but when he is gone his way, then he boasteth. <div eID="gen14212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14213" type="x-p"/> See here 1. What arts men use to get a good bargain and to buy cheap. They not only cheapen carelessly, as if they had no need, no mind for the commodity, when perhaps they cannot go without it (there may be prudence in that), but they vilify and run down that which yet they know to be of value; they cry, "<hi type="italic">It is naught, it is naught;</hi> it has this and the other fault, or perhaps may have; it is not good of the sort; and it is too dear; we can have better and cheaper elsewhere, or have bought better and cheaper." This is the common way of dealing; and after all, it may be, they know the contrary of what they affirm; but the buyer, who may think he has no other way of being even with the seller, does as extravagantly commend his goods and justify the price he sets on them, and so there is a fault on both sides; whereas the bargain would be made every jot as well if both buyer and seller would be modest and speak as they think. 2. What pride and pleasure men take in a good bargain when they have got it, though therein they contradict themselves, and own they dissembled when they were driving the bargain. When the buyer has beaten down the seller, who was content to lower his price rather than lose a customer (as many poor tradesmen are forced to do—small profit is better than none), then he goes his way, and boasts what excellent goods he has got at his own price, and takes it as an affront and a reflection upon his judgment if any body disparages his bargain. Perhaps he knew the worth of the good better than the seller himself did and knows how to get a great deal by them. See how apt men are to be pleased with their gettings and proud of their tricks; whereas a fraud and a lie are what a man ought to be ashamed of, though he have gained ever so much by them.

<div eID="gen14213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14214" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> There is gold, and a multitude of rubies: but the lips of knowledge <hi type="italic">are</hi> a precious jewel. <div eID="gen14214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14215" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">lips of knowledge</hi> (a good understanding to guide the lips and a good elocution to diffuse the knowledge) are to be preferred far before gold, and pearl, and rubies; for, 1. They are more rare in themselves, more scarce and hard to be got. <hi type="italic">There is gold</hi> in many a man's pocket that has no grace in his heart. In Solomon's time there was plenty of gold (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.21">1 Kings x. 21</reference>) and <hi type="italic">abundance of rubies;</hi> every body wore them; they were to be bought in every town. But wisdom is a rare thing, a precious jewel; few have it so as to do good with it, nor is it to be purchased of the merchants. 2. They are more enriching to us and more adorning. They make us rich towards God, rich in good works, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9-1Tim.2.10">1 Tim. ii. 9, 10</reference>. Most people are fond of gold, and a ruby or two will not serve, they must have a multitude of them, a cabinet of jewels; but he that has the lips of knowledge despises these, because he knows and possesses better things.

<div eID="gen14215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14216" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Take his garment that is surety <hi type="italic">for</hi> a stranger: and take a pledge of him for a strange woman. <div eID="gen14216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14217" type="x-p"/> Two sorts of persons are here spoken of that are ruining their own estates, and will be beggars shortly, and therefore are not to be trusted with any good security:—1. Those that will be bound for any body that will ask them, that entangle themselves in rash suretiship to oblige their idle companions; they will break at last, nay, they cannot hold out long; these waste by wholesale. 2. Those that are in league with abandoned women, that treat them, and court them, and keep company with them. They will be beggars in a little time; never give them credit without good pledge. Strange women have strange ways of impoverishing men to enrich themselves.

<div eID="gen14217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14218" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Bread of deceit <hi type="italic">is</hi> sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel. <div eID="gen14218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14219" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Sin may possibly be pleasant in the commission: <hi type="italic">Bread of deceit,</hi> wealth gotten by fraud, by lying and oppression, may be <hi type="italic">sweet to a man,</hi> and the more sweet for its being ill-gotten, such pleasure does the carnal mind take in the success of its wicked projects. All the pleasures and profits of sin are <hi type="italic">bread of deceit.</hi> They are stolen, for they are forbidden fruit; and they will deceive men, for they are not what they promise. For a time, however, they are <hi type="italic">rolled under the tongue as a sweet morsel,</hi> and the sinner blesses himself in them. But, 2. It will be bitter in reflection. Afterwards the sinner's <hi type="italic">mouth shall be filled with gravel.</hi> When his conscience is awakened, when he sees himself cheated, and becomes apprehensive of the wrath of God against him for his sin, how painful and uneasy then is the thought of it! The pleasures of sin are but for a season, and are succeeded with sorrow. Some nations have punished malefactors by mingling gravel with their bread.

<div eID="gen14219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14220" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">Every</hi> purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war. <div eID="gen14220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14221" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is good in every thing to act with deliberation, and to consult with ourselves at least, and, in matters of moment, with our friends, too, before we determine, but especially to ask counsel of God, and beg direction from him, and observe the guidance of this eye. This is the way to have both our minds and our purposes established, and to succeed well in our affairs; whereas what is done hastily and with precipitation is repented of at leisure. Take time, and you will have done the sooner. <hi type="italic">Deliberandum est diu, quod statuendum est semel</hi>—<hi type="italic">A final decision should be preceded by mature deliberation.</hi> 2. It is especially our wisdom to be cautious in making war. Consider, and take advice, whether the war should be begun or no, whether it be just, whether it be prudent, whether we be a match for the enemy, and able to carry it on when it is too late to retreat (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.31">Luke xiv. 31</reference>); and, when it is begun, consider how and by what arts it may be prosecuted, for management is as necessary as courage. Going to law is a kind of going to war, and therefore must be done with good advice, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.8">Prov. xxv. 8</reference>. The rule among the Romans was <hi type="italic">nec sequi bellum, nec fugere</hi>—<hi type="italic">neither to urge war nor yet to shun it.</hi>

<div eID="gen14221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14222" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> He that goeth about <hi type="italic">as</hi> a talebearer revealeth secrets: therefore meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips. <div eID="gen14222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14223" type="x-p"/> Two sorts of people are dangerous to be conversed with:—1. Tale-bearers, though they are commonly flatterers, and by fair speeches insinuate themselves into men's acquaintance. Those are unprincipled people that go about carrying stories, that make mischief among neighbours and relations, that sow in the minds of people jealousies of their governors, of their ministers, and of one another, that reveal secrets which they are entrusted with or which by unfair means they come to the knowledge of, under pretence of guessing at men's thoughts and intentions, tell that of them which is really false. "Be not familiar with such; do not give them the hearing when they tell their tales and reveal secrets, for you may be sure that they will betray your secrets too and tell tales of you." 2. Flatterers, for they are commonly tale-bearers. If a man fawn upon you, compliment and commend you, suspect him to have some design upon you, and stand upon your guard; he would pick that out of you which will serve him to make a story of to somebody else to your prejudice; therefore <hi type="italic">meddle not with him that flatters with his lips.</hi> Those too dearly love, and too dearly buy, their own praise, that will put confidence in a man and trust him with a secret or business because he flatters them.

<div eID="gen14223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14224" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness. <div eID="gen14224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14225" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. An undutiful child become very wicked by degrees. He began with despising his father and mother, slighting their instructions, disobeying their commands, and raging at their rebukes, but at length he arrives at such a pitch of impudence and impiety as to curse them, to give them scurrilous and opprobrious language, and to wish mischief to those that were instruments of his being and have taken so much care and pains about him, and this in defiance of God and his law, which had made this a capital crime (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.17">Exod. xxi. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.4">Matt. xv. 4</reference>), and in violation of all the bonds of duty, natural affection, and gratitude. 2. An undutiful child become very miserable at last: <hi type="italic">His lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness;</hi> all his honour shall be laid in the dust, and he shall for ever lose his reputation. Let him never expect any peace or comfort in his own mind, no, nor to prosper in this world. His days shall be shortened, and the lamp of his life extinguished, according to the reverse of the promise of the fifth commandment. His family shall be cut off and his posterity be a curse to him. And it will be his eternal ruin; the lamp of his happiness shall be <hi type="italic">put out in the blackness of darkness</hi> (so the word is), even that which is <hi type="italic">for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.13">Jude 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.13">Matt. xxii. 13</reference>.

<div eID="gen14225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14226" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> An inheritance <hi type="italic">may be</hi> gotten hastily at the beginning; but the end thereof shall not be blessed. <div eID="gen14226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14227" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is possible that an estate may be suddenly raised. There are those that will be rich, by right or wrong, who make no conscience of what they say or do if they can but get money by it, who, when it is in their power, will cheat their own father, and who sordidly spare and hoard up what they get, grudging themselves and their families food convenient and thinking all lost but what they buy land with or put out to interest. By such ways as these a man may grow rich, may grow very rich, in a little time, at his first setting out. 2. An estate that is suddenly raised is often as suddenly ruined. It was raised hastily, but, not being raised honestly, it proves <hi type="italic">soon ripe and soon rotten: The end thereof shall not be blessed</hi> of God, and, if he do not bless it, it can neither be comfortable nor of any continuance; so that he who got it at the end will be a fool. He had better have taken time and built firmly.

<div eID="gen14227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14228" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Say not thou, I will recompense evil; <hi type="italic">but</hi> wait on the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he shall save thee. <div eID="gen14228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14229" type="x-p"/> Those that live in this world must expect to have injuries done them, affronts given them, and trouble wrongfully created them, for we dwell among briers. Now here we are told what to do when we have wrong done us. 1. We must not avenge ourselves, no, nor so much as think of revenge, or design it: "<hi type="italic">Say not thou,</hi> no, not in thy heart, <hi type="italic">I will recompense evil</hi> for evil. Do not please thyself with the thought that some time or other thou shalt have an opportunity of being quits with him. Do not wish revenge, or hope for it, much less resolve upon it, no, not when the injury is fresh and the resentment of it most deep. Never say that thou wilt do a thing which thou canst not in faith pray to God to assist thee in, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou canst not do in mediating revenge." 2. We must refer ourselves to God, and leave it to him to plead our cause, to maintain our right, and reckon with those that do us wrong in such a way and manner as he thinks fit and in his own due time: "<hi type="italic">Wait on the Lord,</hi> and attend his pleasure, acquiesce in his will, and he does not say that he will punish him that has injured thee (instead of desiring that thou must forgive him and pray for him), but <hi type="italic">he will save thee,</hi> and that is enough. He will protect thee, so that thy passing by one injury shall not (as is commonly feared) expose thee to another; nay, he will recompense good to thee, to balance thy trouble and encourage thy patience," as David hoped, when Shimei cursed him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.12">2 Sam. xvi. 12</reference>.

<div eID="gen14229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14230" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Divers weights <hi type="italic">are</hi> an abomination unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and a false balance <hi type="italic">is</hi> not good. <div eID="gen14230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14231" type="x-p"/> This is to the same purport with what was said <reference osisRef="Prov.20.20">v. 20</reference>. 1. It is here repeated, because it is a sin that God doubly hates (as lying, which is of the same nature with this sin, is mentioned twice among the seven things that God hates, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.17">ch. vi. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.19">19</reference>), and because it was probably a sin very much practised at that time in Israel, and therefore made light of as if there were no harm in it, under pretence that, being commonly used, there was no trading without it. 2. It is here added, <hi type="italic">A false balance is not good,</hi> to intimate that it is not only abominable to God, but unprofitable to the sinner himself; there is really no good to be got by it, no, not a good bargain, for a bargain made by fraud will prove a losing bargain in the end.

<div eID="gen14231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14232" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Man's goings <hi type="italic">are</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; how can a man then understand his own way? <div eID="gen14232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14233" type="x-p"/> We are here taught that in all our affairs, 1. We have a necessary and constant dependence upon God. All our natural actions depend upon his providence, all our spiritual actions upon his grace. The best man is no better than God makes him; and every creature is that to us which it is the will of God that it should be. Our enterprises succeed, not as we desire and design, but as God directs and disposes. The goings even of a strong man (so the word signifies) <hi type="italic">are of the Lord,</hi> for his strength is weakness without God, nor is the battle always to the strong. 2. We have no foresight of future events, and therefore know not how to forecast for them: <hi type="italic">How can a man understand his own way?</hi> How can he tell what will befal him, since God's counsels concerning him are secret, and therefore how can he of himself contrive what to do without divine direction? We so little understand our own way that we know not what is good for ourselves, and therefore we must make a virtue of necessity, and commit our way unto the Lord, in whose hand it is, follow the guidance and submit to the disposal of Providence.

<div eID="gen14233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14234" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> a snare to the man <hi type="italic">who</hi> devoureth <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> holy, and after vows to make enquiry. <div eID="gen14234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14235" type="x-p"/> Two things, by which God is greatly affronted, men are here said to be ensnared by, and entangled not only in guilt, but in trouble and ruin at length:—1. Sacrilege, men's alienating holy things and converting them to their own use, which is here called <hi type="italic">devouring</hi> them. What is devoted in any way to the service and honour of God, for the support of religion and divine worship or the relief of the poor, ought to be conscientiously preserved to the purposes designed; and those that directly or indirectly embezzle it, or defeat the purpose for which it was given, will have a great deal to answer for. <hi type="italic">Will a man rob God in tithes and offerings?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.8">Mal. iii. 8</reference>. Those that hurry over religious offices (their praying and preaching) and huddle them up in haste, as being impatient to get done, may be said to <hi type="italic">devour that which is holy.</hi> 2. Covenant-breaking. <hi type="italic">It is a snare to a man, after</hi> he has made <hi type="italic">vows</hi> to God, to <hi type="italic">enquire</hi> how he may evade them or get dispensed with, and to contrive excuses for the violating of them. If the matter of them was doubtful, and the expressions were ambiguous, that was his fault; he should have made them with more caution and consideration, for it will involve his conscience (if it be tender) in great perplexities, if he be to enquire concerning them afterwards (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Eccl. v. 6</reference>); for, when we have opened our mouth to the Lord, it is too late to think of going back, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.4">Acts v. 4</reference>.

<div eID="gen14235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14236" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> A wise king scattereth the wicked, and bringeth the wheel over them. <div eID="gen14236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14237" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What is the business of magistrates. They are to be a terror to evil-doers. They must <hi type="italic">scatter the wicked,</hi> who are linked in confederacies to assist and embolden one another in doing mischief; and there is no doing this but by <hi type="italic">bringing the wheel over them,</hi> that is, putting the laws in execution against them, crushing their power and quashing their projects. Severity must sometimes be used to rid the country of those that are openly vicious and mischievous, debauched and debauching. 2. What is the qualification of magistrates, which is necessary in order to do this. They have need to be both pious and prudent, for it is the wise king, who is both religious and discreet, that is likely to effect the suppression of vice and reformation of manners.

<div eID="gen14237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14238" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> The spirit of man <hi type="italic">is</hi> the candle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , searching all the inward parts of the belly. <div eID="gen14238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14239" type="x-p"/> We have here the dignity of the soul, the great soul of man, that light which lighteth every man. 1. It is a divine light; it is the <hi type="italic">candle of the Lord,</hi> a candle of his lighting, for it is <hi type="italic">the inspiration of the Almighty</hi> that <hi type="italic">gives us understanding.</hi> He <hi type="italic">forms the spirit of man within him.</hi> It is after the image of God that man is created in knowledge. Conscience, that noble faculty, is God's deputy in the soul; it is a candle not only lighted by him, but lighted for him. The Father of spirits is therefore called the <hi type="italic">Father of lights.</hi> 2. It is a discovering light. By the help of reason we come to know men, to judge of their characters, and dive into their designs; by the help of conscience we come to know ourselves. The spirit of a man has a self-consciousness (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.11">1 Cor. ii. 11</reference>); it searches into the dispositions and affections of the soul, praises what is good, condemns what is otherwise, and judges of the thoughts and intents of the heart. This is the office, this the power, of conscience, which we are therefore concerned to get rightly informed and to keep void of offence.

<div eID="gen14239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14240" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy. <div eID="gen14240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14241" type="x-p"/> Here we have, 1. The virtues of a good king. Those are <hi type="italic">mercy and truth,</hi> especially mercy, for that is mentioned twice here. He must be strictly faithful to his word, must be sincere, and abhor all dissimulation, must religiously discharge all the trusts reposed in him, must support and countenance truth. He must likewise rule with clemency, and by all acts of compassion gain the affections of his people. <hi type="italic">Mercy and truth</hi> are the glories of God's throne, and kings are called <hi type="italic">gods.</hi> 2. The advantages he gains thereby. These virtues will preserve his person and support his government, will make him easy and safe, beloved by his own people and feared by his enemies, if it be possible that he should have any.

<div eID="gen14241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14242" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> The glory of young men <hi type="italic">is</hi> their strength: and the beauty of old men <hi type="italic">is</hi> the gray head. <div eID="gen14242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14243" type="x-p"/> This shows that both young and old have their advantages, and therefore must each of them be, according to their capacities, serviceable to the public, and neither of them despise nor envy the other. 1. Let not old people despise the young, for they are strong and fit for action, able to go through business and break through difficulties, which the aged and weak cannot grapple with. The <hi type="italic">glory of young men is their strength,</hi> provided they use it well (in the service of God and their country, not of their lusts), and that they be not proud of it nor trust to it. 2. Let not young people despise the old, for they are grave, and fit for counsel, and, though they have not the strength that young men have, yet they have more wisdom and experience. <hi type="italic">Juniores ad labores, seniores ad honores</hi>—<hi type="italic">Labour is for the young, honour for the aged.</hi> God has put honour upon the old man; for his <hi type="italic">gray head</hi> is his beauty. See <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">Dan. vii. 9</reference>.

<div eID="gen14243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14244" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil: so <hi type="italic">do</hi> stripes the inward parts of the belly. <div eID="gen14244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14245" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Many need severe rebukes. Some children are so obstinate that their parents can do no good with them without sharp correction; some criminals must feel the rigour of the law and public justice; gentle methods will not work upon them; they must be beaten black and blue. And the wise God sees that his own children sometimes need very sharp afflictions. 2. Severe rebukes sometimes do a great deal of good, as corrosives contribute to the cure of a wound, eating out the proud flesh. The rod drives out even that foolishness which was bound up in the heart, and cleanses away the evil there. 3. Frequently those that most need severe rebukes can worse bear them. Such is the corruption of nature that men are as loth to be rebuked sharply for their sins as to be beaten till their bones ache. <hi type="italic">Correction is grievous to him that forsakes the way,</hi> and yet it is good for him, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">Heb. xii. 11</reference>.  <chapter eID="Prov.20"/> <div eID="gen14245" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv58"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv58"/> <div sID="gen14247" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The king's heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">as</hi> the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will. <div eID="gen14247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14248" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Even the <hi type="italic">hearts</hi> of men are in God's hand, and not only their <hi type="italic">goings,</hi> as he had said, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.24">ch. xx. 24</reference>. God can change men's minds, can, by a powerful insensible operation under their spirits, turn them from that which they seemed most intent upon, and incline them to that which they seemed most averse to, as the husbandman, by canals and gutters, turns the water through his grounds as he pleases, which does not alter the nature of the water, nor put any force upon it, any more than God's providence does upon the native freedom of man's will, but directs the course of it to serve his own purpose. 2. Even kings' hearts are so, notwithstanding their powers and prerogatives, as much as the hearts of common persons. The <hi type="italic">hearts of kings are unsearchable</hi> to us, much more unmanageable by us; as they have their <hi type="italic">arcana imperii</hi>—<hi type="italic">state secrets,</hi> so that they have great prerogatives of their crown; but the great God has them not only under his eye, but in his hand. Kings are what he makes them. Those that are most absolute are under God's government; he <hi type="italic">puts things into their hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.17.17">Rev. xvii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.27">Ezra vii. 27</reference>.

<div eID="gen14248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14249" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> Every way of a man <hi type="italic">is</hi> right in his own eyes: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> pondereth the hearts. <div eID="gen14249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14250" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. We are all apt to be partial in judging of ourselves and our own actions, and to think too favourably of our own character, as if there was nothing amiss in it: <hi type="italic">Every way of a man,</hi> even his by-way, <hi type="italic">is right in his own eyes.</hi> The proud heart is very ingenious in putting a fair face upon a foul matter, and in making that appear right to itself which is far from being so, to stop the mouth of conscience. 2. We are sure that the judgment of God concerning us is according to truth. Whatever our judgment is concerning ourselves, <hi type="italic">the Lord ponders the heart.</hi> God looks at the heart, and judges of men according to that, of their actions according to their principles and intentions; and his judgment of that is as exact as ours is of that which we ponder most, and more so; he weighs it in an unerring balance, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">ch. xvi. 2</reference>.

<div eID="gen14250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14251" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> To do justice and judgment <hi type="italic">is</hi> more acceptable to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> than sacrifice. <div eID="gen14251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14252" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. It is implied that many deceive themselves with a conceit that, if they offer sacrifice, that will excuse them from doing justice, and procure them a dispensation for their unrighteousness; and this makes their way <hi type="italic">seem right,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.2">v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">We have fasted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">Isa. lviii. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">I have peace-offerings with me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.7.14">Prov. vii. 14</reference>. 2. It is plainly declared that living a good life (doing justly and loving mercy) is more pleasing to God than the most pompous and expensive instances of devotion. Sacrifices were of divine institution, and were acceptable to God if they were offered in faith and with repentance, otherwise not, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa. i. 11</reference>, &c. But even then moral duties were preferred before them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1 Sam. xv. 22</reference>), which intimates that their excellency was not innate nor the obligation to them perpetual, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8">Mic. vi. 6-8</reference>. Much of religion lies in doing judgment and justice from a principle of duty to God, contempt of the world, and love to our neighbour; and this is more pleasing to God than all burnt-offerings and sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.33">Mark xii. 33</reference>.

<div eID="gen14252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14253" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> An high look, and a proud heart, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the plowing of the wicked, <hi type="italic">is</hi> sin. <div eID="gen14253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14254" type="x-p"/> This may be taken as showing us, 1. The marks of a wicked man. He that has a <hi type="italic">high look and a proud heart,</hi> that carries himself insolently and scornfully towards both God and man, and that is always ploughing and plotting, designing and devising some mischief or other, is indeed a wicked man. <hi type="italic">The light of the wicked is sin.</hi> Sin is <hi type="italic">the pride, the ambition, the glory and joy,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the business of wicked men.</hi> 2. The miseries of wicked man. His raised expectations, his high designs, and most elaborate contrivances and projects, are sin to him; he contracts guilt in them and so prepares trouble for himself. The very business of all wicked men, as well as their pleasure, is nothing but sin; so Bishop Patrick. They do all to serve their lusts, and have no regard to the glory of God in it, and therefore <hi type="italic">their ploughing is sin,</hi> and no marvel when their sacrificing is so, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">ch. xv. 8</reference>.

<div eID="gen14254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14255" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> The thoughts of the diligent <hi type="italic">tend</hi> only to plenteousness; but of every one <hi type="italic">that is</hi> hasty only to want. <div eID="gen14255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14256" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The way to be rich. If we would live plentifully and comfortably in the world, we must be diligent in our business, and not shrink from the toil and trouble of it, but prosecute it closely, improving all advantages and opportunities for it, and doing what we do with all our might; yet we must not be hasty in it, nor hurry ourselves and others with it, but keep doing fair and softly, which, we say, goes far in a day. With diligence there must be contrivance. The <hi type="italic">thoughts of the diligent</hi> are as necessary as the hand of the diligent. Forecast is as good as work. Seest thou a man thus prudent and diligent? He will have enough to live on. 2. The way to be poor. Those that are hasty, that are rash and inconsiderate in their affairs, and will not take time to think, that are greedy of gain, by right or wrong, and make haste to be rich by unjust practices or unwise projects, are in the ready road to poverty. Their thoughts and contrivances, by which they hope to raise themselves, will ruin them.

<div eID="gen14256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14257" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> The getting of treasures by a lying tongue <hi type="italic">is</hi> a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death. <div eID="gen14257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14258" type="x-p"/> This shows the folly of those that hope to enrich themselves by dishonest practices, by oppressing and over-reaching those with whom they deal, by false-witness-bearing, or by fraudulent contracts, of those that make no scruples of lying when there is any thing to be got by it. They may perhaps heap up treasures by these means, that which they make their treasure; but, 1. They will not meet with the satisfaction they expect. It is a <hi type="italic">vanity tossed to and fro;</hi> it will be disappointment and vexation of spirit to them; they will not have the comfort of it, nor can they put any confidence in it, but will be perpetually uneasy. It will be <hi type="italic">tossed to and fro</hi> by their own consciences, and by the censures of men; let them expect to be in a constant hurry. 2. They will meet with destruction they do not expect. While they are seeking wealth by such unlawful practices they are really seeking death; they lay themselves open to the envy and ill-will of men by the treasures they get, and to the wrath and curse of God, by the lying tongue wherewith they get them, which he will make to fall upon themselves and sink them to hell.

<div eID="gen14258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14259" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The robbery of the wicked shall destroy them; because they refuse to do judgment. <div eID="gen14259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14260" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. The nature of injustice. Getting money by lying (<reference osisRef="Prov.21.6">v. 6</reference>) is no better than downright robbery. Cheating is stealing; you might as well pick a man's pocket as impose upon him by a lie in making a bargain, which he had no fence against but by not believing you; and it will be no excuse from the guilt of robbery to say that he might choose whether he would believe you, for that is a debt we should owe to all men. 2. The cause of injustice. Men <hi type="italic">refuse to do judgment;</hi> they will not render to all their due, but withhold it, and omissions make way for commissions; they come at length to robbery itself. Those that refuse to do justice will choose to do wrong. 3. The effects of injustice; it will return upon the sinner's own head. The robbery of the wicked will <hi type="italic">terrify them</hi> (so some); their consciences will be filled with horror and amazement, will cut them, will <hi type="italic">saw them asunder</hi> (so others); it will <hi type="italic">destroy them</hi> here and for ever, therefore he had said (<reference osisRef="Prov.21.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">They seek death.</hi>

<div eID="gen14260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14261" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The way of man <hi type="italic">is</hi> froward and strange: but <hi type="italic">as for</hi> the pure, his work <hi type="italic">is</hi> right. <div eID="gen14261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14262" type="x-p"/> This shows that as men are so is their way. 1. Evil men have evil ways. If the man be <hi type="italic">froward,</hi> his way also is <hi type="italic">strange;</hi> and this is the way of most men, such is the general corruption of mankind. <hi type="italic">They have all gone aside</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.2-Ps.14.3">Ps. xiv. 2, 3</reference>); all flesh have perverted their way. But the froward man, the man of deceit, that acts by craft and trick in all he does, his way is strange, contrary to all the rules of honour and honesty. It is strange, for you know not where to find him nor when you have him; it is strange, for it is alienated from all good and estranges men from God and his favour. It is what he behold afar off, and so do all honest men. 2. Men that are pure are proved to be such by their work, for it <hi type="italic">is right,</hi> it is just and regular; and they are accepted of God and approved of men. The way of mankind in their apostasy is froward and strange; but as for the pure, those that by the grace of God are recovered out of that state, of which there is here and there one, <hi type="italic">their work is right,</hi> as Noah's was in the old world, <reference osisRef="Gen.7.1">Gen. vii. 1</reference>.

<div eID="gen14262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14263" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house. <div eID="gen14263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14264" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What a great affliction it is to a man to have a brawling scolding woman for his wife, who upon every occasion, and often upon no occasion, breaks out into a passion, and chides either him or those about her, is fretful to herself and furious to her children and servants, and, in both, vexatious to her husband. If a man has a wide house, spacious and pompous, this will embitter the comfort of it to him—<hi type="italic">a house of society</hi> (so the word is), in which a man may be sociable, and entertain his friends; this will make both him and his house unsociable, and unfit for enjoyments of true friendship. It makes a man ashamed of his choice and his management, and disturbs his company. 2. What many a man is forced to do under such an affliction. He cannot keep up his authority. He finds it to no purpose to contradict the most unreasonable passion, for it is unruly and rages so much the more; and his wisdom and grace will not suffer him to render railing for railing, nor his conjugal affection to use any severity, and therefore he finds it his best way to retire <hi type="italic">into a corner of the house-top,</hi> and sit alone there, out of the hearing of her clamour; and if he employ himself well there, as he may do, it is the wisest course he can take. Better do so than quit the house, and go into bad company, for diversion, as many, who, like Adam, make their wife's sin the excuse of their own.

<div eID="gen14264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14265" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> The soul of the wicked desireth evil: his neighbour findeth no favour in his eyes. <div eID="gen14265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14266" type="x-p"/> See here the character of a very wicked man. 1. The strong inclination he has to do mischief. His very <hi type="italic">soul desires evil,</hi> desires that evil may be done and that he may have the pleasure, not only of seeing it, but of having a hand in it. The root of wickedness lies in the soul; the desire that men have to do evil, that is the lust which conceives and brings forth sin. 2. The strong aversion he has to do good: <hi type="italic">His neighbour,</hi> his friend, his nearest relation, <hi type="italic">finds no favour in his eyes,</hi> cannot gain from him the least kindness, though he be in the greatest need of it. And, when he is in the pursuit of the evil his heart is so much upon, he will spare no man that stands in his way; his next neighbour shall be used no better than a stranger, than an enemy.

<div eID="gen14266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14267" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> When the scorner is punished, the simple is made wise: and when the wise is instructed, he receiveth knowledge. <div eID="gen14267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14268" type="x-p"/> This we had before (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.25">ch. xix. 25</reference>), and it shows that there are two ways by which the simple may be made wise:—1. By the punishments that are inflicted on those that are incorrigibly wicked. Let the law be executed upon a scorner, and even he that is simple will be awakened and alarmed by it, and will discern, more than he did, the evil of sin, and will take warning by it and take heed. 2. By the instructions that are given to those that are wise and willing to be taught: <hi type="italic">When the wise is instructed</hi> by the preaching of the word <hi type="italic">he</hi> (not only the wise himself, but the simple that stands by) <hi type="italic">receives knowledge.</hi> It is no injustice at all to take a good lesson to ourselves which was designed for another.

<div eID="gen14268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14269" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The righteous <hi type="italic">man</hi> wisely considereth the house of the wicked: <hi type="italic">but God</hi> overthroweth the wicked for <hi type="italic">their</hi> wickedness. <div eID="gen14269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14270" type="x-p"/> 1. As we read this verse, it shows why good men, when they come to understand things aright, will not envy the prosperity of evil-doers. When they see <hi type="italic">the house of the wicked,</hi> how full it is perhaps of all the good things of this life, they are tempted to envy; but when they <hi type="italic">wisely consider</hi> it, when they look upon it with an eye of faith, when they see <hi type="italic">God overthrowing the wicked for their wickedness,</hi> that there is a curse upon their habitation which will certainly be the ruin of it ere long, they see more reason to despise them, or pity them, than to fear or envy them. 2. Some give another sense of it: <hi type="italic">The righteous man</hi> (the judge or magistrate, that is entrusted with the execution of justice, and the preservation of public peace) <hi type="italic">examines the house of the wicked,</hi> searches it for arms or for stolen goods, makes a diligent enquiry concerning his family and the characters of those about him, that he may by his power <hi type="italic">overthrow the wicked for their wickedness</hi> and prevent their doing any further mischief, that he may fire the nests where the birds of prey are harboured or the unclean birds.

<div eID="gen14270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14271" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard. <div eID="gen14271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14272" type="x-p"/> Here we have the description and doom of an uncharitable man. 1. His description: He <hi type="italic">stops his ears at the cry of the poor,</hi> at the cry of their wants and miseries (he resolves to take no cognizance of them), at the cry of their requests and supplications—he resolves he will not so much as give them the hearing, turns them away from his door, and forbids them to come near him, or, if he cannot avoid hearing them, he will not need them, nor be moved by their complaints, no be prevailed with by their importunities; he <hi type="italic">shuts up the bowels of his compassion,</hi> and that is equivalent to the stopping of his ears, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.57">Acts vii. 57</reference>. 2. His doom. He shall himself be reduced to straits, which will make him <hi type="italic">cry,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">he shall not be heard.</hi> Men will not hear him, but reward him as he has rewarded others. God will not hear him; for he that <hi type="italic">showed no mercy shall have judgment without mercy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.13">Jam. ii. 13</reference>), and he that on earth denied a crumb of bread in hell was denied a drop of water. God will be deaf to the prayers of those who are deaf to the cries of the poor, which, if they be not heard by us, will be heard against us, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.23">Exod. xxii. 23</reference>.

<div eID="gen14272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14273" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> A gift in secret pacifieth anger: and a reward in the bosom strong wrath. <div eID="gen14273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14274" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The power that is commonly found to be in gifts. Nothing is more violent than <hi type="italic">anger.</hi> O the force of <hi type="italic">strong wrath!</hi> And yet a handsome present, prudently managed, will turn away some men's wrath when it seemed implacable, and disarm the keenest and most passionate resentments. Covetousness is commonly a master-sin and has the command of other lusts. <hi type="italic">Pecuniæ obediunt omnia</hi>—<hi type="italic">Money commands all things.</hi> Thus Jacob pacified Esau and Abigail David. 2. The policy that is commonly used in giving and receiving bribes. It must be a <hi type="italic">gift in secret and a reward in the bosom,</hi> for he that takes it would not be thought to covet it, nor known to receive it, nor would he willingly be beholden to him whom he has been offended with; but, if it be done privately, all is well. No man should be too open in giving any gift, nor boast of the presents he sends; but, if it be a bribe to pervert justice, that is so scandalous that those who are fond of it are ashamed of it.

<div eID="gen14274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14275" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> joy to the just to do judgment: but destruction <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> to the workers of iniquity. <div eID="gen14275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14276" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a pleasure and satisfaction to good men both to see justice administered by the government they live under, right taking place and iniquity suppressed, and also to practise it themselves, according as their sphere is. They not only do justice, but do it with pleasure, not only for fear of shame, but for love of virtue. 2. It is a terror to wicked men to see the laws put in execution against vice and profaneness. It is destruction to them; as it is also a vexation to them to be forced, either for the support of their credit or for fear of punishment, <hi type="italic">to do judgment</hi> themselves. Or, if we take it as we read it, the meaning is, There is true pleasure in the practice of religion, but certain destruction at the end of all vicious courses.

<div eID="gen14276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14277" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> The man that wandereth out of the way of understanding shall remain in the congregation of the dead. <div eID="gen14277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14278" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The sinner upon his ramble: He <hi type="italic">wanders out of the way of understanding,</hi> and when once he has left that good way he wanders endlessly. The way of religion is <hi type="italic">the way of understanding;</hi> those that are not truly pious are not truly intelligent; those <hi type="italic">that wander out of this way</hi> break the hedge which God has set, and follow the conduct of the world and the flesh; and they go astray like lost sheep. 2. The sinner at his rest, or rather his ruin: He <hi type="italic">shall remain</hi> (<hi type="italic">quiescet</hi>—<hi type="italic">he shall rest,</hi> but not <hi type="italic">in pace</hi>—<hi type="italic">in peace</hi>) <hi type="italic">in the congregation of the giants,</hi> the sinners of the old world, that were swept away by the deluge; to that destruction the damnation of sinners is compared, as sometimes to the destruction of Sodom, when they are said to have their portion in fire and brimstone. Or <hi type="italic">in the congregation of the damned,</hi> that are under the power of the second death. There is a vast congregation of damned sinners, bound in bundles for the fire, and in that those shall remain, remain for ever, who are shut out from the congregation of the righteous. He that forsakes the way to heaven, if he return not to it, will certainly sink into the depths of hell.

<div eID="gen14278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14279" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> He that loveth pleasure <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a poor man: he that loveth wine and oil shall not be rich. <div eID="gen14279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14280" type="x-p"/> Here is an argument against a voluptuous luxurious life, taken from the ruin it brings upon men's temporal interests. Here is 1. The description of an epicure: <hi type="italic">He loves pleasure.</hi> God allows us to use the delights of sense soberly and temperately, <hi type="italic">wine to make glad the heart</hi> and put vigour into the spirits, and <hi type="italic">oil to make the face to shine</hi> and beautify the countenance; but he that loves these, that sets his heart upon them, covets them earnestly, is solicitous to have all the delights of sense wound up to the height of pleasurableness, is impatient of every thing that crosses him in his pleasures, relishes these as the best pleasures, and has his mouth by them put out of taste for spiritual delights, he is an epicure, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.4">2 Tim. iii. 4</reference>. 2. The punishment of an epicure in this world: <hi type="italic">He shall be a poor man;</hi> for the lusts of sensuality are not maintained but at great expense, and there are instances of those who want necessaries, and live upon alms, who once could not live without dainties and varieties. Many a beau becomes a beggar.

<div eID="gen14280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14281" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> The wicked <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a ransom for the righteous, and the transgressor for the upright. <div eID="gen14281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14282" type="x-p"/> This intimates, 1. What should be done by the justice of men: <hi type="italic">The wicked,</hi> that are the troublers of a land, ought to be punished, for the preventing and turning away of those national judgments which otherwise will be inflicted and in which even the righteous are many times involved. Thus when Achan was stoned he was <hi type="italic">a ransom for the</hi> camp of <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> Israel; and the seven sons of Saul, when they were hanged, were <hi type="italic">a ransom for the</hi> kingdom of <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> David. 2. What is often done by the providence of God: <hi type="italic">The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked comes in his stead,</hi> and so seems as if he were <hi type="italic">a ransom for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.8">ch. xi. 8</reference>. God will rather leave many wicked people to be cut off than abandon his own people. <hi type="italic">I will give men for thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.3-Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 3, 4</reference>.

<div eID="gen14282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14283" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> better to dwell in the wilderness, than with a contentious and an angry woman. <div eID="gen14283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14284" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Unbridled passions embitter and spoil the comfort of all relations. A peevish angry wife makes her husband's life uneasy, to whom she should be a comfort and a meet help. Those cannot dwell in peace and happiness that cannot dwell in peace and love. Even those that are one flesh, if they be not withal one spirit, have no joy of their union. 2. It is better to have no company than bad company. The wife of thy covenant is thy companion, and yet, if she be peevish and provoking, <hi type="italic">it is better to dwell in</hi> a solitary <hi type="italic">wilderness,</hi> exposed to wind and weather, than in company with her. A man may better enjoy God and himself in a wilderness than among quarrelsome relations and neighbours. See <reference osisRef="Prov.21.9">v. 9</reference>.

<div eID="gen14284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14285" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up. <div eID="gen14285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14286" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that are wise will increase what they have and live plentifully; their wisdom will teach them to proportion their expenses to their income and to lay up for hereafter; so that <hi type="italic">there is a treasure</hi> of things <hi type="italic">to be desired,</hi> and as much as needs be desired, a good stock of all things convenient, laid up in season, and particularly of <hi type="italic">oil,</hi> one of the staple commodities of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.8">Deut. viii. 8</reference>. This is <hi type="italic">in the habitation,</hi> or cottage, <hi type="italic">of the wise;</hi> and it is better to have an old-fashioned house, and have it well furnished, than a fine modern one, with sorry housekeeping. God blesses the endeavors of the wise and then their houses are replenished. 2. Those that are foolish will misspend what they have upon their lusts, and so bring the stock they have to nothing. Those manage wretchedly that are in haste to spend what they had, but not in care which way to get more. Foolish children spend what their wise parents have laid up. <hi type="italic">One sinner destroys much good,</hi> as the prodigal son.

<div eID="gen14286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14287" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> He that followeth after righteousness and mercy findeth life, righteousness, and honour. <div eID="gen14287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14288" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What it is to make religion our business; it is to <hi type="italic">follow after righteousness and mercy,</hi> not to content ourselves with easy performances, but to do our duty with the utmost care and pains, as those that are pressing forward and in fear of coming short. We must both do justly and love mercy, and must proceed and persevere therein; and, though we cannot attain to perfection, yet it will be a comfort to us if we aim at it and follow after it. 2. What will be the advantage of doing so: Those that do <hi type="italic">follow after righteousness</hi> shall <hi type="italic">find righteousness;</hi> God will give them grace to do good, and they shall have the pleasure and comfort of doing it; those that make conscience of being just to others shall have the pleasure and comfort of doing it; those that make conscience of being just to others shall be justly dealt with by others and others shall be kind to them. The Jews <hi type="italic">followed after righteousness,</hi> and did not find it, because they sought amiss, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.31">Rom. ix. 31</reference>. Otherwise, <hi type="italic">Seek and you shall find,</hi> and with it shall find both <hi type="italic">life and honour,</hi> everlasting life and honour, the <hi type="italic">crown of righteousness.</hi>

<div eID="gen14288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14289" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> A wise <hi type="italic">man</hi> scaleth the city of the mighty, and casteth down the strength of the confidence thereof. <div eID="gen14289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14290" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that have power are apt to promise themselves great things from their power. <hi type="italic">The city of the mighty</hi> thinks itself impregnable, and therefore its strength is <hi type="italic">the confidence thereof,</hi> what it boasts of and trust in, bidding defiance to danger. 2. Those that have wisdom, though they are so modest as not to promise much, often perform great things, even against those that are so confident of their strength, by their wisdom. Good conduct will go far even against great force; and a stratagem, well managed, may effectually <hi type="italic">scale the city of the mighty and cast down the strength</hi> it had such a confidence in. <hi type="italic">A wise man</hi> will gain upon the affections of people and conquer them by strength of reason, which is a more noble conquest than that obtained by strength of arms. Those that understand their interest will willingly submit themselves to a wise and good man, and the strongest walls shall not hold out against him.

<div eID="gen14290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14291" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Whoso keepeth his mouth and his tongue keepeth his soul from troubles. <div eID="gen14291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14292" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is our great concern to keep our souls from straits, being entangled in snares and perplexities, and disquieted with troubles, that we may preserve the possession and enjoyment of ourselves and that our souls may be in frame for the service of God. 2. Those that would keep their souls must keep a watch before the door of their lips, must <hi type="italic">keep the mouth</hi> by temperance, that no forbidden fruit go into it, no stolen waters, that nothing be eaten or drunk to excess; they must <hi type="italic">keep the tongue</hi> also, that no forbidden word go out of the door of the lips, no corrupt communication. By a constant watchfulness over our words we shall prevent abundance of mischiefs which an ungoverned tongue runs men into. Keep thy heart, and that will keep thy tongue from sin; keep thy tongue, and that will keep thy heart from trouble.

<div eID="gen14292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14293" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Proud <hi type="italic">and</hi> haughty scorner <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name, who dealeth in proud wrath. <div eID="gen14293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14294" type="x-p"/> See here the mischief of pride and haughtiness. 1. It exposes men to sin; it makes them passionate, and kindles in them the fire of <hi type="italic">proud wrath.</hi> They are continually dealing in it, as if it were their trade to be angry, and they had nothing so much to do as to barter passions and exchange bitter words. Most of the wrath that inflames the spirits and societies of men is <hi type="italic">proud wrath.</hi> Men cannot bear the least slight, nor in any thing to be crossed or contradicted, but they are out of humour, nay, in a heat, immediately.
