It likewise makes them scornful when they are angry, very abusive with their tongues, insolent towards those above them and imperious towards all about them. <hi type="italic">Only by pride</hi> comes all this. 2. It exposes men to shame. They get a bad name by it, and every one calls them <hi type="italic">proud and haughty scorners,</hi> and therefore nobody cares for having any thing to do with them. If men would but consult their reputation a little and the credit of their profession, which suffers with it, they would not indulge their pride and passion as they do.

<div eID="gen14294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14295" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> The desire of the slothful killeth him; for his hands refuse to labour. <hi type="super">26</hi> He coveteth greedily all the day long: but the righteous giveth and spareth not. <div eID="gen14295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14296" type="x-p"/> Here we have, 1. The miseries of the slothful, whose <hi type="italic">hands refuse to labour</hi> in an honest calling, by which they might get an honest livelihood. They are as fit for labour as other men, and business offers itself, to which they might lay their hands and apply their minds, but they will not; herein they fondly think they do well for themselves, see <reference osisRef="Prov.26.16">ch. xxvi. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Soul, take thy ease.</hi> But really they are enemies to themselves; for, besides that their slothfulness starves them, depriving them of their necessary supports, their desires at the same time stab them. Though their hands refuse to labour, their hearts cease not to covet riches, and pleasures, and honours, which yet cannot be obtained without labour. Their desires are impetuous and insatiable; they <hi type="italic">covet greedily all the day long,</hi> and cry, <hi type="italic">Give, give;</hi> they expect every body should do for them, though they will do nothing for themselves, much less for any body else. Now these <hi type="italic">desires kill them;</hi> they are a perpetual vexation to them, fret them to death, and perhaps put them upon such dangerous courses for the satisfying of their craving lusts as hasten them to an untimely end. Many that must have money with which to make provision for the flesh, and would not be at the pains to get it honestly, have turned highwaymen, and that has killed them. Those that are slothful in the affairs of their souls, and yet have desires towards that which would be the happiness of their souls, those <hi type="italic">desires kill them,</hi> will aggravate their condemnation and be witnesses against them that were convinced of the worth of spiritual blessings, but refused to be at the pains that were necessary to the obtaining of them. 2. The honours of the honest and diligent. The righteous and industrious have their desires satisfied, and enjoy not only that satisfaction, but the further satisfaction of doing good to others. The slothful are always craving and gaping to receive, <hi type="italic">but the righteous</hi> are always full and contriving to give; and <hi type="italic">it is more blessed to give than to receive.</hi> They <hi type="italic">give and spare not,</hi> give liberally and upbraid not; they <hi type="italic">give a portion to seven and also to eight,</hi> and do not spare for fear of wanting.

<div eID="gen14296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14297" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> The sacrifice of the wicked <hi type="italic">is</hi> abomination: how much more, <hi type="italic">when</hi> he bringeth it with a wicked mind? <div eID="gen14297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14298" type="x-p"/> Sacrifices were of divine institution; and when they were offered in faith, and with repentance and reformation, God was greatly honoured by them and well-pleased in them. But they were often not only unacceptable, but an <hi type="italic">abomination,</hi> to God, and he declared so, which was an indication both that they were not required for their own sakes and that there were better things, and for effectual, in reserve, when sacrifice and offering should be done away. They were an <hi type="italic">abomination,</hi> 1. When they were brought by wicked men, who did not, according to the true intent and meaning of sacrificing, repent of their sins, mortify their lusts, and amend their lives. Cain brought his offering. Even wicked men may be found in the external performances of religious worship. Many can freely give God their beasts, their lips, their knees, who would not give him their hearts; the Pharisees gave alms. But when the person is an <hi type="italic">abomination,</hi> as every wicked man is to God, the performance cannot but be so; <hi type="italic">even when he brings it diligently;</hi> so some read the latter part of the verse. Though their offerings are continually before God (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Ps. l. 8</reference>), yet they are an abomination to him. 2. <hi type="italic">Much more when</hi> they were brought with <hi type="italic">wicked minds,</hi> when their sacrifices were made, not only consistent with, but serviceable to, their wickedness, as Absalom's vow, Jezebel's fast, and the Pharisees' long prayers. When men make a show of devotion, that they may the more easily and effectually compass some covetous or malicious design, when holiness is pretended, but some wickedness intended, then especially the performance is an abomination, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Isa. lxvi. 5</reference>.

<div eID="gen14298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14299" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> A false witness shall perish: but the man that heareth speaketh constantly. <div eID="gen14299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14300" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The doom of <hi type="italic">a false witness.</hi> He who, for favour to one side or malice to the other, gives in a false evidence, or makes an affidavit of that which he knows to be false, or at least does not know to be true, if it be discovered, his reputation will be ruined. A man may tell a lie perhaps in his haste; but he that gives a false testimony does it with deliberation and solemnity, and it cannot but be a presumptuous sin, and a forfeiture of man's credit. But, though he should not be discovered, he himself shall be ruined; the vengeance he imprecated upon himself, when he took the false oath, will come upon him. 2. The praise of him that is conscientious: He <hi type="italic">who hears</hi> (that is, obeys) the command of God, which is to <hi type="italic">speak every man truth with his neighbour,</hi> he who testifies nothing but what he has heard and knows to be true, <hi type="italic">speaks constantly</hi> (that is, consistently with himself); he is always in the same story; he speaks <hi type="italic">in finem</hi>—<hi type="italic">to the end;</hi> people will give credit to him and hear him out; he speaks unto victory; he carries the cause, which the <hi type="italic">false witness</hi> shall lose; he shall speak to eternity. What is true is true eternally. <hi type="italic">The lip of truth is established for ever.</hi>

<div eID="gen14300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14301" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> A wicked man hardeneth his face: but <hi type="italic">as for</hi> the upright, he directeth his way. <div eID="gen14301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14302" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The presumption and impudence of a wicked man: He <hi type="italic">hardens his face</hi>—brazens it, that he may not blush—steels it, that he may not tremble when he commits the greatest crimes; he bids defiance to the terrors of the law and the checks of his own conscience, the reproofs of the word and the rebukes of Providence; he will have his way and nothing shall hinder him, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.17">Isa. lvii. 17</reference>. 2. The caution and circumspection of a good man: <hi type="italic">As for the upright,</hi> he does not say, What <hi type="italic">would</hi> I do? What have I a mind to? and that will I have; but, What <hi type="italic">should</hi> I do? What does God require of me? What is duty? What is prudence? What is for edification? And so he does not force his way, but <hi type="italic">direct his way</hi> by a safe and certain rule.

<div eID="gen14302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14303" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">31</hi> The horse <hi type="italic">is</hi> prepared against the day of battle: but safety <hi type="italic">is</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14304" type="x-p"/> The designing busy part of mankind are directed, in all their counsels and undertakings, to have their eye to God, and to believe, 1. That there can be no success against God, and therefore they must never act in opposition to him, in contempt of his commands, or in contradiction to his counsels. Though they think they have <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> and <hi type="italic">understanding,</hi> and <hi type="italic">counsel,</hi> the best politics and politicians, on their side, yet, if it be <hi type="italic">against the Lord,</hi> it cannot prosper long; it shall not prevail at last. He that sits in heaven laughs at men's projects against him and his anointed, and will carry his point in spite of them, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 1-6</reference>. Those that fight against God are preparing shame and ruin for themselves; whoever <hi type="italic">make war with the Lamb,</hi> he will certainly <hi type="italic">overcome them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.17.14">Rev. xvii. 14</reference>. 2. That there can be no success without God, and therefore they must never act but in dependence on him. Be the cause ever so good, and the patrons of it ever so strong, and wise, and faithful, and the means of carrying it on, and gaining the point, ever so probable, still they must acknowledge God and take him along with them. Means indeed are to be used; <hi type="italic">the horse</hi> must be <hi type="italic">prepared against the day of battle,</hi> and the foot too; they must be armed and disciplined. In Solomon's time even Israel's kings used horses in war, though they were forbidden to multiply them. <hi type="italic">But,</hi> after all, <hi type="italic">safety</hi> and salvation <hi type="italic">are of the Lord;</hi> he can save without armies, but armies cannot save without him; and therefore he must be sought to and trusted in for success, and when success is obtained he must have all the glory. When we are preparing for <hi type="italic">the day of battle</hi> our great concern must be to make God our friend and secure his favour.  <chapter eID="Prov.21"/> <div eID="gen14304" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv59"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv59"/> <div sID="gen14306" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> A <hi type="italic">good</hi> name <hi type="italic">is</hi> rather to be chosen than great riches, <hi type="italic">and</hi> loving favour rather than silver and gold. <div eID="gen14306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14307" type="x-p"/> Here are two things which are more valuable and which we should covet more than great riches:—1. To be well spoken of: <hi type="italic">A name</hi> (that is, <hi type="italic">a good name,</hi> a name for good things with God and good people) <hi type="italic">is rather to be chosen than great riches;</hi> that is, we should be more careful to do that by which we may get and keep a good name than that by which we may raise and increase a great estate. Great riches bring great cares with them, expose men to danger, and add no real value to a man. A fool and a knave may have <hi type="italic">great riches,</hi> but <hi type="italic">a good name</hi> makes a man easy and safe, supposes a man wise and honest, redounds to the glory of God, and gives a man a greater opportunity of doing good. By great riches we may relieve the bodily wants of others, but by a good name we may recommend religion to them. 2. To be well beloved, to have an interest in the esteem and affections of all about us; this is better <hi type="italic">than silver and gold.</hi> Christ has neither silver nor gold, but he <hi type="italic">grew in favour with God and man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.52">Luke ii. 52</reference>. This should teach us to look with a holy contempt upon the wealth of this world, not to set our hearts upon that, but with all possible care to <hi type="italic">think of those things that are lovely and of good report,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Phil. iv. 8</reference>.

<div eID="gen14307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14308" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> The rich and poor meet together: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> the maker of them all. <div eID="gen14308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14309" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Among the children of men divine Providence has so ordered it that some are <hi type="italic">rich</hi> and others <hi type="italic">poor,</hi> and these are intermixed in societies: <hi type="italic">The Lord is the Maker of both,</hi> both the author of their being and the disposer of their lot. The greatest man in the world must acknowledge God to be his Maker, and is under the same obligations to be subject to him that the meanest is; and the poorest has the honour to be the work of God's hands as much as the greatest. <hi type="italic">Have they not all one Father?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.10">Mal. ii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.15">Job xxxi. 15</reference>. God makes some rich, that they may be charitable to the poor, and others poor, that they may be serviceable to the rich; and they have need of one another, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.21">1 Cor. xii. 21</reference>. He make some poor, to exercise their patience, and contentment, and dependence upon God, and others rich, to exercise their thankfulness and beneficence. Even <hi type="italic">the poor</hi> we <hi type="italic">have always with</hi> us; they shall never cease out of the land, nor the rich neither. 2. Notwithstanding the distance that is in many respects between <hi type="italic">rich and poor,</hi> yet in most things they <hi type="italic">meet together,</hi> especially before <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi> who <hi type="italic">is the Maker of them all,</hi> and <hi type="italic">regards not the rich more than the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.34.19">Job xxxiv. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">Rich and poor meet together</hi> at the bar of God's justice, all guilty before God, concluded under sin, and shapen in iniquity, the rich as much as the poor; and they meet at the throne of God's grace; the poor are as welcome there as the rich. There is the same Christ, the same scripture, the same Spirit, the same covenant of promises, for them both. There is the same heaven for poor saints that there is for rich: Lazarus is in the bosom of Abraham. And there is the same hell for rich sinners that there is for poor. All stand upon the same level before God, as they do also in the grave. <hi type="italic">The small and great are there.</hi>

<div eID="gen14309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14310" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> A prudent <hi type="italic">man</hi> foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished. <div eID="gen14310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14311" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. The benefit of wisdom and consideration: <hi type="italic">A prudent man,</hi> by the help of his prudence, will <hi type="italic">foresee an evil,</hi> before it comes, <hi type="italic">and hide himself;</hi> he will be aware when he is entering into a temptation and will put on his armour and stand on his guard. When the clouds are gathering for a storm he takes the warning, and flies to the name of the Lord as his strong tower. Noah foresaw the deluge, Joseph the years of famine, and provided accordingly. 2. The mischief of rashness and inconsideration. <hi type="italic">The simple,</hi> who believe every word that flatters them, will believe none that warns them, and so they <hi type="italic">pass on and are punished.</hi> They venture upon sin, though they are told what will be in the end thereof; they throw themselves into trouble, notwithstanding the fair warning given them, and they repent their presumption when it is too late. See an instance of both these, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.20-Exod.9.21">Exod. ix. 20, 21</reference>. Nothing is so fatal to precious souls as this, they will not take warning.

<div eID="gen14311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14312" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> By humility <hi type="italic">and</hi> the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">are</hi> riches, and honour, and life. <div eID="gen14312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14313" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. Wherein religion does very much consist—in <hi type="italic">humility and the fear of the Lord;</hi> that is, walking humbly with God. We must so reverence God's majesty and authority as to submit with all humility to the commands of his word and the disposals of his providence. We must have such low thoughts of ourselves as to behave humbly towards God and man. Where the fear of God is there will be humility. 2. What is to be gotten by it—<hi type="italic">riches, and honour,</hi> and comfort, <hi type="italic">and</hi> long life, in this world, as far as God sees good, at least spiritual <hi type="italic">riches and honour</hi> in the favour of God, and the promises and privileges of the covenant of grace, <hi type="italic">and</hi> eternal <hi type="italic">life</hi> at last.

<div eID="gen14313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14314" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Thorns <hi type="italic">and</hi> snares <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the way of the froward: he that doth keep his soul shall be far from them. <div eID="gen14314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14315" type="x-p"/> Note 1. The way of sin is vexatious and dangerous: <hi type="italic">In the way of the froward,</hi> that crooked way, which is contrary to the will and word of God, <hi type="italic">thorns and snares are</hi> found, thorns of grief for past sins and snares entangling them in further sin. He that makes no conscience of what he says and does will find himself hampered by that imaginary liberty, and tormented by his pleasures. Froward people, who are soon angry, expose themselves to trouble at every step. Every thing will fret and vex him that will fret and vex at every thing. 2. The way of duty is safe and easy: <hi type="italic">He that keeps his soul,</hi> that watches carefully over his own heart and ways, is <hi type="italic">far from</hi> those <hi type="italic">thorns and snares,</hi> for his way is both plain and pleasant.

<div eID="gen14315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14316" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it. <div eID="gen14316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14317" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A great duty enjoined, particularly to those that are the parents and instructors of children, in order to the propagating of wisdom, that it may not die with them: <hi type="italic">Train up children</hi> in that age of vanity, to keep them from the sins and snares of it, in that learning age, to prepare them for what they are designed for. <hi type="italic">Catechise</hi> them; initiate them; keep them under discipline. <hi type="italic">Train</hi> them as soldiers, who are taught to handle their arms, keep rank, and observe the word of command. <hi type="italic">Train</hi> them up, not in the way they would go (the bias of their corrupt hearts would draw them aside), but <hi type="italic">in the way they should go,</hi> the way in which, if you love them, you would have them go. <hi type="italic">Train up a child according as he is capable</hi> (as some take it), with a gentle hand, as nurses feed children, little and often, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">Deut. vi. 7</reference>. 2. A good reason for it, taken from the great advantage of this care and pains with children: When they <hi type="italic">grow up,</hi> when they <hi type="italic">grow old,</hi> it is to be hoped, they <hi type="italic">will not depart from it.</hi> Good impressions made upon them then will abide upon them all their days. Ordinarily the vessel retains the savour with which it was first seasoned. Many indeed have departed from the good way in which they were trained up; Solomon himself did so. But early training may be a means of their recovering themselves, as it is supposed Solomon did. At least the parents will have the comfort of having done their duty and used the means.

<div eID="gen14317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14318" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower <hi type="italic">is</hi> servant to the lender. <div eID="gen14318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14319" type="x-p"/> He had said (<reference osisRef="Prov.22.2">v. 2</reference>.), <hi type="italic">Rich and poor meet together;</hi> but here he finds, here he shows, that, as to the things of this life, there is a great difference; for, 1. Those that have little will be in subjection to those that have much, because they have dependence upon them, they have received, and expect to receive, support from them: <hi type="italic">The rich rule over the poor,</hi> and too often more than becomes them, with pride and rigour, unlike to God, who, though he be great, yet despises not any. It is part of the affliction of the poor that they must expect to be trampled upon, and part of their duty to be serviceable, as far as they can, to those that are kind to them, and study to be grateful. 2. Those that are but going behindhand find themselves to lie much at the mercy of those that are before hand: <hi type="italic">The borrower is servant to the lender,</hi> is obliged to him, and must sometimes beg, <hi type="italic">Have patience with me.</hi> Therefore it is part of Israel's promised happiness that they should lend and borrow, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.12">Deut. xxviii. 12</reference>. And it should be our endeavour to keep as much as may be out of debt. Some sell their liberty to gratify their luxury.

<div eID="gen14319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14320" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity: and the rod of his anger shall fail. <div eID="gen14320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14321" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Ill-gotten gains will not prosper: <hi type="italic">He that sows iniquity,</hi> that does an unjust thing in hopes to get by it, <hi type="italic">shall reap vanity;</hi> what he gets will never do him any good nor give him any satisfaction. He will meet nothing but disappointment. Those that create trouble to others do but prepare trouble for themselves. Men shall reap as they sow. 2. Abused power will not last. If the rod of authority turn into a <hi type="italic">rod of anger,</hi> if men rule by passion instead of prudence, and, instead of the public welfare, aim at nothing so much as the gratifying of their own resentments, it <hi type="italic">shall fail</hi> and be broken, and their power shall not bear them out in their exorbitances, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.24-Isa.10.25">Isa. x. 24, 25</reference>.

<div eID="gen14321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14322" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor. <div eID="gen14322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14323" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The description of a charitable man; he has a <hi type="italic">bountiful eye,</hi> opposed to the evil eye (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.6">ch. xxiii. 6</reference>) and the same with the <hi type="italic">single eye</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.22">Matt. vi. 22</reference>),—an eye that seeks out objects of charity, besides those that offer themselves,—an eye that, upon the sight of one in want and misery, affects the heart with compassion,—an eye that with the alms gives a pleasant look, which makes the alms doubly acceptable. He has also a liberal hand: <hi type="italic">He gives of his bread</hi> to those that need—<hi type="italic">his bread,</hi> the bread appointed for his own eating. He will rather abridge himself than see the poor perish for want; yet he does not give all <hi type="italic">his bread,</hi> but <hi type="italic">of his bread;</hi> the poor shall have their share with his own family. 2. The blessedness of such a man. The loins of the poor will bless them, all about him will speak well of him, and God himself will bless him, in answer to many a good prayer put up for him, and he <hi type="italic">shall be blessed.</hi>

<div eID="gen14323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14324" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea, strife and reproach shall cease. <div eID="gen14324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14325" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What <hi type="italic">the scorner</hi> does. It is implied that he sows discord and makes mischief wherever he comes. Much of the <hi type="italic">strife and contention</hi> which disturb the peace of all societies is owing to <hi type="italic">the evil interpreter</hi> (as some read it), that construes every thing into the worst, to those that despise and deride every one that comes in their way and take a pride in bantering and abusing all mankind. 2. What is to be done with the scorner that will not be reclaimed: <hi type="italic">Cast</hi> him <hi type="italic">out</hi> of your society, as Ishmael, when he mocked Isaac, was thrust out of Abraham's family. Those that would secure the peace must exclude the scorner.

<div eID="gen14325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14326" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> He that loveth pureness of heart, <hi type="italic">for</hi> the grace of his lips the king <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> his friend. <div eID="gen14326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14327" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The qualification of an accomplished, a complete gentleman, that is fit to be employed in public business. He must be an honest man, a man <hi type="italic">that loves pureness of heart</hi> and hates all impurity, not only pure from all fleshly lusts, but from all deceit and dissimulation, from all selfishness and sinister designs, that takes care to approve himself a man of sincerity, is just and fair from principle, and delights in nothing more than in keeping his own conscience clean and void of offence. He must also be able to speak with a good grace, not to daub and flatter, but to deliver his sentiments decently and ingeniously, in language clean and smooth as his spirit. 2. The preferment such a man stands fair for: <hi type="italic">The king,</hi> if he be wise and good, and understand his own and his people's interest, <hi type="italic">will be his friend,</hi> will make him of his cabinet-council, as there was one in David's court, and another in Solomon's, that was called the <hi type="italic">king's friend;</hi> or, in any business that he has, the king will befriend him. Some understand it of the King of kings. A man <hi type="italic">in whose spirit there is no guile,</hi> and whose speech is always with grace, God will be his friend, Messiah, the Prince, will be his friend. <hi type="italic">This honour have all the saints.</hi>

<div eID="gen14327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14328" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> The eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> preserve knowledge, and he overthroweth the words of the transgressor. <div eID="gen14328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14329" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The special care God takes to <hi type="italic">preserve knowledge,</hi> that is, to keep up religion in the world by keeping up among men the knowledge of himself and of good and evil, notwithstanding the corruption of mankind, and the artifices of Satan to blind men's minds and keep them in ignorance. It is a wonderful instance of the power and goodness of <hi type="italic">the eyes of the Lord,</hi> that is, his watchful providence. He preserves <hi type="italic">men of knowledge,</hi> wise and good men (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 9</reference>), particularly faithful witnesses, who speak what they know; God protects such, and prospers their counsels. He does by his grace <hi type="italic">preserve knowledge</hi> in such, secures his own work and interest in them. See <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7-Prov.2.8">Prov. ii. 7, 8</reference>. 2. The just vengeance God takes on those that speak and act against knowledge and against the interests of knowledge and religion in the world: <hi type="italic">He overthrows the words of the transgressor,</hi> and <hi type="italic">preserves knowledge</hi> in spite of him. He defeats all the counsels and designs of false and treacherous men, and turns them to their own confusion.

<div eID="gen14329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14330" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> The slothful <hi type="italic">man</hi> saith, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a lion without, I shall be slain in the streets. <div eID="gen14330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14331" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that have no love for their business will never want excuses to shake it off. Multitudes are ruined, both for soul and body, by their slothfulness, and yet still they have something or other to say for themselves, so ingenious are men in putting a cheat upon their own souls. And who, I pray, will be the gainer at last, when the pretences will be all rejected as vain and frivolous? 2. Many frighten themselves from real duties by imaginary difficulties: <hi type="italic">The slothful man</hi> has work to do <hi type="italic">without</hi> in the fields, but he fancies <hi type="italic">there is a lion</hi> there; nay, he pretends he dares not go along the streets for fear somebody or other should meet him and kill him. He does not himself think so; he only says so to those that call him up. He talks of <hi type="italic">a lion without,</hi> but considers not his real danger from the devil, that <hi type="italic">roaring lion,</hi> which is in bed with him, and from his own slothfulness, which kills him.

<div eID="gen14331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14332" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The mouth of strange women <hi type="italic">is</hi> a deep pit: he that is abhorred of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall fall therein. <div eID="gen14332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14333" type="x-p"/> This is designed to warn all young men against the lusts of uncleanness. As they regard the welfare of their souls, let them take heed of <hi type="italic">strange women,</hi> lewd women, whom they ought to be strange to, of <hi type="italic">the mouth of strange women,</hi> of the kisses of their lips (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.13">ch. vii. 13</reference>), of the words of their lips, their charms and enticements. Dread them; have nothing to do with them; for, 1. Those who abandon themselves to that sin give proof that they are abandoned of God: it <hi type="italic">is a deep pit,</hi> which those <hi type="italic">fall</hi> into that are <hi type="italic">abhorred of the Lord,</hi> who leaves them to themselves to enter into that temptation, and takes off the bridle of his restraining grace, to punish them for other sins. Value not thyself upon thy being in favour with such women, when it proclaims thee under the wrath of God. 2. It is seldom that they recover themselves, for it <hi type="italic">is a deep pit;</hi> it will be hard getting out of it, it so besots the mind and debauches the conscience, by pleasing the flesh.

<div eID="gen14333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14334" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Foolishness <hi type="italic">is</hi> bound in the heart of a child; <hi type="italic">but</hi> the rod of correction shall drive it far from him. <div eID="gen14334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14335" type="x-p"/> We have here two very sad considerations:— 1. That corruption is woven into our nature. Sin is <hi type="italic">foolishness;</hi> it is contrary both to our right reason and to our true interest. It <hi type="italic">is in the heart;</hi> there is an inward inclination to sin, to speak and act foolishly. It <hi type="italic">is in the heart of children;</hi> they bring it into the world with them; it is what they were shapen and conceived in. It is not only <hi type="italic">found</hi> there, but it is <hi type="italic">bound</hi> there; it is annexed to the heart (so some); vicious dispositions cleave closely to the soul, are bound to it as the cion to the stock into which it is grafted, which quite alters the property. There is a knot tied between the soul and sin, a true lover's knot; they two became one flesh. It is true of ourselves, it is true of our children, whom we have begotten in our own likeness. <hi type="italic">O God! thou knowest</hi> this <hi type="italic">foolishness.</hi> 2. That correction is necessary to the cure of it. It will not be got out by fair means and gentle methods; there must be strictness and severity, and that which will cause grief. Children need to be corrected, and kept under discipline, by their parents; and we all need to be corrected by our heavenly Father (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.6-Heb.12.7">Heb. xii. 6, 7</reference>), and under the correction we must stroke down folly and kiss the rod.

<div eID="gen14335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14336" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> He that oppresseth the poor to increase his <hi type="italic">riches, and</hi> he that giveth to the rich, <hi type="italic">shall</hi> surely <hi type="italic">come</hi> to want. <div eID="gen14336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14337" type="x-p"/> This shows what evil courses rich men sometimes take, by which, in the end, they will impoverish themselves and provoke God, notwithstanding their abundance, to bring them to want; they <hi type="italic">oppress the poor and give to the rich.</hi> 1. They will not in charity relieve the poor, but withhold from them, that by saving that which is really the best, but which they think the most needless part of their expenses, they may <hi type="italic">increase their riches;</hi> but they will make presents <hi type="italic">to the rich,</hi> and give them great entertainments, either in pride and vain-glory, that they may look great, or in policy, that they may receive it again with advantage. Such <hi type="italic">shall surely come to want.</hi> Many have been beggared by a foolish generosity, but never any by a prudent charity. Christ bids us to invite the poor, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.12-Luke.14.13">Luke xiv. 12, 13</reference>. 2. They not only will not relieve <hi type="italic">the poor,</hi> but they <hi type="italic">oppress</hi> them, rob the spital, extort from their poor tenants and neighbours, invade the rights of those who have not wherewithal to defend themselves, and then <hi type="italic">give</hi> bribes <hi type="italic">to the rich,</hi> to protect and countenance them in it. But it is all in vain; they <hi type="italic">shall come to want.</hi> Those that rob God, and so make him the enemy, cannot secure themselves by <hi type="italic">giving to the rich,</hi> to make them their friends.  <div eID="gen14337" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv60"/><title type="x-s3">Serious Attention Inculcated.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv60"/> <div sID="gen14338" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Bow down thine ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply thine heart unto my knowledge. <hi type="super">18</hi> For <hi type="italic">it is</hi> a pleasant thing if thou keep them within thee; they shall withal be fitted in thy lips. <hi type="super">19</hi> That thy trust may be in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , I have made known to thee this day, even to thee. <hi type="super">20</hi> Have not I written to thee excellent things in counsels and knowledge, <hi type="super">21</hi> That I might make thee know the certainty of the words of truth; that thou mightest answer the words of truth to them that send unto thee? <div eID="gen14338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14339" type="x-p"/> Solomon here changes his style and manner of speaking. Hitherto, for the most part, since the beginning of <reference osisRef="Prov.10.1">ch. x.</reference>, he had laid down doctrinal truths, and but now and then dropped a word of exhortation, leaving us to make the application as we went along; but here, to the end of <reference osisRef="Prov.22.17-Prov.24.34">ch. xxiv.</reference>, he directs his speech to his son, his pupil, his reader, his hearer, speaking as to a particular person. Hitherto, for the most part, his sense was comprised in one verse, but here usually it is drawn out further. See how Wisdom tries variety of methods with us, lest we should be cloyed with any one. To awaken attention and to assist our application the method of direct address is here adopted. Ministers must not think it enough to preach before their hearers, but must preach to them, nor enough to preach to them all in general, but should address themselves to particular persons, as here: Do <hi type="italic">thou</hi> do so and so. Here is, <div eID="gen14339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14340" type="x-p"/> I. An earnest exhortation to get wisdom and grace, by attending to <hi type="italic">the words of the wise</hi> men, both written and preached, the words of the prophets and priests, and particularly to that <hi type="italic">knowledge</hi> which Solomon in this book gives men of good and evil, sin and duty, rewards and punishments. To these <hi type="italic">words,</hi> to this <hi type="italic">knowledge,</hi> the ear must be <hi type="italic">bowed down</hi> in humility and serious attention and the heart <hi type="italic">applied</hi> by faith, and love, and close consideration. The ear will not serve without the heart. <div eID="gen14340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14341" type="x-p"/> II. Arguments to enforce this exhortation. Consider, <div eID="gen14341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14342" type="x-p"/> 1. The worth and weight of the things themselves which Solomon in this book gives us the <hi type="italic">knowledge</hi> of. They are not trivial things, for amusements and diversion, not jocular proverbs, to be repeated in sport and in order to pass away time. No; they are <hi type="italic">excellent things,</hi> which concern the glory of God, the holiness and happiness of our souls, the welfare of mankind and all communities; they are <hi type="italic">princely things</hi> (so the word is), fit for kings to speak and senates to hear; they are things that concern <hi type="italic">counsels and knowledge,</hi> that is, wise counsels, relating to the most important concerns; things which will not only make us knowing ourselves, but enable us to advise others. <div eID="gen14342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14343" type="x-p"/> 2. The clearness of the discovery of these things and the directing of them to us in particular. "They are <hi type="italic">made known,</hi> publicly known, that all may read,—plainly known, that he that runs may read,—<hi type="italic">made known this day</hi> more fully than ever before, in this day of light and knowledge,—<hi type="italic">made known in this thy day.</hi> But it is only a little while that this light is with thee; perhaps the things that are <hi type="italic">this day made known to thee,</hi> if thou improve not the day of thy visitation, may, before to-morrow, be <hi type="italic">hidden from thy eyes.</hi> They are <hi type="italic">written,</hi> for the greater certainty, and that they may be received and the more safely transmitted pure and entire to posterity. But that which the emphasis is here most laid upon is that they are <hi type="italic">made known to thee, even to thee,</hi> and <hi type="italic">written to thee,</hi> as if it were a letter directed to thee by name. It is suited to thee and to thy case; thou mayest in this glass see thy own face; it is intended for thee, to be a rule to thee, and by it thou must be judged." We cannot say of these things, "They are good things, but they are nothing to us;" no, they are of the greatest concern imaginable to us. <div eID="gen14343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14344" type="x-p"/> 3. The agreeableness of these things to us, in respect both of comfort and credit. (1.) If we hide them in our hearts, they will be very pleasing and yield us an abundant satisfaction (<reference osisRef="Prov.22.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">It is a pleasant thing,</hi> and will be thy constant entertainment, <hi type="italic">if thou keep them within thee;</hi> if thou digest them, and be actuated and governed by them, and delivered into them as into a mould." The form of godliness, when that is rested in, is but a force put upon a man, and he does but do penance in that white clothing; those only that submit to the power of godliness, and make heart-work of it, find the pleasure of it, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10">ch. ii. 10</reference>. (2.) If we make use of them in our discourse, they will be very becoming, and gain us a good reputation. <hi type="italic">They shall be fitted in thy lips.</hi> "Speak of these things, and thou speakest like thyself, and as is fit for thee to speak considering thy character; thou wilt also have pleasure in speaking of these things as well as in thinking of them." <div eID="gen14344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14345" type="x-p"/> 4. The advantage designed us by them. The <hi type="italic">excellent things</hi> which God has <hi type="italic">written to</hi> us are not like the commands which the master gives his servant, which are all intended for the benefit of the master, but like those which the master gives his scholar, which are all intended for the benefit of the scholar. These things must be kept by us, for they are written to us, (1.) That we may have a confidence in him and communion with him. <hi type="italic">That thy trust may be in the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.22.19">v. 19</reference>. We cannot trust in God except in the way of duty; we are <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> taught our duty, that we may have reason to trust in God. Nay, this is itself one great duty we are to learn, and a duty that is the foundation of all practical religion, to live a life of delight in God and dependence on him. (2.) That we may have a satisfaction in our own judgment: "<hi type="italic">That I might make thee know the certainty of the words of truth;</hi> that thou mayest know what is truth, mayest plainly distinguish between it and falsehood, and mayest know upon what grounds thou receivest and believest the truths of God." Note, [1.] It is a desirable thing to know, not only <hi type="italic">the words of truth,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the certainty of</hi> them, that our faith may be intelligent and rational, and may grow up to a full assurance. [2.] The way to <hi type="italic">know the certainty of the words of truth</hi> is to make conscience of our duty; for, <hi type="italic">if any man do his will, he shall know</hi> for certain that the doctrine is of God, <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. (3.) That we may be useful and serviceable to others for their instruction: "<hi type="italic">That thou mayest</hi> give a good account <hi type="italic">of the words of truth to those that send to thee</hi> to consult thee as an oracle," or (as the margin reads it) "<hi type="italic">to those that send thee,</hi> that employ thee as an agent or ambassador in any business." Knowledge is given us to do good with, that others may light their candle at our lamp, and that we may in our place serve our generation according to the will of God; and those who make conscience of keeping God's commandments will be best able to <hi type="italic">give a reason of the hope that is in</hi> them.  <div eID="gen14345" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv61"/><title type="x-s3">Caution against Oppressing the Poor.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv61"/> <div sID="gen14346" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Rob not the poor, because he <hi type="italic">is</hi> poor: neither oppress the afflicted in the gate: <hi type="super">23</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will plead their cause, and spoil the soul of those that spoiled them. <div eID="gen14346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14347" type="x-p"/> After this solemn preface, one would have expected something new and surprising; but no; here is a plain and common, but very needful caution against the barbarous and inhuman practices of oppressing poor people. Observe, <div eID="gen14347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14348" type="x-p"/> I. The sin itself, and that is <hi type="italic">robbing the poor</hi> and making them poorer, taking from those that have but little to lose and so leaving them nothing. It is bad to rob any man, but most absurd to rob the poor, whom we should relieve,—to squeeze those with our power whom we should water with our bounty,—<hi type="italic">to oppress the afflicted,</hi> and so to add affliction to them,—to give judgment against them, and so to patronise those that do rob them, which is as bad as if we robbed them ourselves. Rich men will not suffer themselves to be wronged; poor men cannot help themselves, and therefore we ought to be the more careful not to wrong them. <div eID="gen14348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14349" type="x-p"/> II. The aggravations of the sin. 1. If their inability, by reason of their poverty, to right themselves, embolden us to rob them, it is so much the worse; this is <hi type="italic">robbing the poor because he is poor;</hi> this is not only a base and cowardly thing, to take advantage against a man because he is helpless, but it is unnatural, and proves men worse than beasts. 2. Or, if it be done under the colour of law and justice, that is oppressing <hi type="italic">the afflicted in the gate,</hi> where they ought to be protected from wrong and to have justice done them against those that oppress them. <div eID="gen14349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14350" type="x-p"/> III. The danger that attends this sin. He that robs and oppresses the poor does it at his peril; for, 1. The oppressed will find God their powerful patron. He <hi type="italic">will plead their cause,</hi> and not suffer them to be run down and trampled upon. If men will not appear for them, God will. 2. The oppressors will find him a just avenger. He will make reprisals upon them, will <hi type="italic">spoil the souls of those that spoil them;</hi> he will repay them in spiritual judgments, in curses to their souls. He that robs the poor will be found in the end a murderer of himself.  <div eID="gen14350" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv62"/><title type="x-s3">Prudential Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv62"/> <div sID="gen14351" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: <hi type="super">25</hi> Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul. <div eID="gen14351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14352" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A good caution against being intimate with a passionate man. It is the law of friendship that we accommodate ourselves to our friends and be ready to serve them, and therefore we ought to be wise and wary in the choice of a friend, that we come not under the sacred tie to any one whom it would be our folly to accommodate ourselves to. Thought we must be civil to all, yet we must be careful whom we lay in our bosoms and contract a familiarity with. And, among others, a man who is easily provoked, touchy, and apt to resent affronts, who, when he is in a passion, cares not what he says or does, but grows outrageous, such a one is not fit to be made a friend or companion, for he will be ever and anon angry with us and that will be our trouble, and he will expect that we should, like him, be angry with others, and that will be our sin. 2. Good cause given for this caution: <hi type="italic">Lest thou learn his way.</hi> Those we go with we are apt to grow like. Our corrupt hearts have so much tinder in them that it is dangerous conversing with those that throw about the sparks of their passion. We shall thereby <hi type="italic">get a snare to our souls,</hi> for a disposition to anger is a great snare to any man, and an occasion of much sin. He does not say, "Lest thou have ill language given thee or get a broken head," but, which is must worse, "Lest thou imitate him, to humour him, and so contract an ill habit."

<div eID="gen14352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14353" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Be not thou <hi type="italic">one</hi> of them that strike hands, <hi type="italic">or</hi> of them that are sureties for debts. <hi type="super">27</hi> If thou hast nothing to pay, why should he take away thy bed from under thee? <div eID="gen14353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14354" type="x-p"/> We have here, as often before, a caution against suretiship, as a thing both imprudent and unjust. 1. We must not associate ourselves, nor contract an intimacy, with men of broken fortunes, and reputations, who need and will urge their friends to be bound for them, that they may cheat their neighbours to feed their lusts, and by keeping up a little longer may do the more damage at last to those that give them credit. Have nothing to do with such; be not thou among them. 2. We must not cheat people of their money, by <hi type="italic">striking hands</hi> ourselves, or <hi type="italic">becoming surety for others,</hi> when we <hi type="italic">have not to pay.</hi> If a man by the divine providence is disabled to pay his debts, he ought to be pitied and helped; but he that takes up money or goods himself, or is bound for another, when he knows that he has not wherewithal to pay, or that what he has is so settled that the creditors cannot come at it, does in effect pick his neighbour's pocket, and though, in all cases, compassion is to be used, yet he may thank himself if the law have its course and his <hi type="italic">bed</hi> be <hi type="italic">taken from under him,</hi> which might be taken for a pledge to secure a debt, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.26-Exod.22.27">Exod. xxii. 26, 27</reference>. For, if a man appeared to be so poor that he had nothing else to give for security, he ought to be relieved, and it was honestly done to own it; but, for the recovery of a debt, it seems it might be taken by the <hi type="italic">summum jus</hi>—<hi type="italic">the strict operation of law.</hi> 3. We must not ruin our own estates and families. Every man ought to be just to himself and to his wife and children; those are not so who live above what they have, who by the mismanagement of their own affairs, or by encumbering themselves with debts of others, waste what they have and bring themselves to poverty. We may <hi type="italic">take joyfully the spoiling of our goods</hi> if it be for the testimony of a good conscience; but, if be for our own rashness and folly, we cannot but take it heavily.

<div eID="gen14354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14355" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set. <div eID="gen14355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14356" type="x-p"/> 1. We are here taught not to invade another man's right, though we can find ways of doing it ever so secretly and plausibly, clandestinely and by fraud, without any open force. Let not property in general be entrenched upon, by robbing men of their liberties and privileges, or of any just ways of maintaining them. Let not the property of particular persons be encroached upon. The land-marks, or meer-stones, are standing witnesses to every man's right; let not those be removed quite away, for thence come wars, and fightings, and endless disputes; let them not be removed so as to take from thy neighbour's lot to thy own, for that is downright robbing him and entailing the fraud upon posterity. 2. We may infer hence that a deference is to be paid, in all civil matters, to usages that have prevailed time out of mind and the settled constitutions of government, in which it becomes us to acquiesce, lest an attempt to change it, under pretence of changing it for the better, prove of dangerous consequence.

<div eID="gen14356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14357" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean <hi type="italic">men.</hi> <div eID="gen14357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14358" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A plain intimation what a hard thing it is to find a truly ingenious industrious man: "<hi type="italic">Seest thou a man diligent in his business?</hi> Thou wilt not see many such, so epidemical are dulness and slothfulness." He is here commended who lays out himself to get business, though it be but in a very low and narrow sphere, and is not easy when he is out of business, who loves business, is quick and active in it, and goes through it, not only with constancy and resolution, but with dexterity and expedition, a man of despatch, who knows how to bring a deal of business into a little compass. 2. A moral prognostication of the preferment of such a man; though now he <hi type="italic">stands before mean men,</hi> is employed by them and attends upon them, yet he will rise, and is likely enough to <hi type="italic">stand before kings,</hi> as an ambassador to foreign kings or prime-minister of state to his own. <hi type="italic">Seest thou a man diligent</hi> in the business of religion? He is likely to excel in virtue, and shall stand before the King of kings.  <chapter eID="Prov.22"/> <div eID="gen14358" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv63"/><title type="x-s3">Cautions against Luxury and Covetousness.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv63"/> <div sID="gen14360" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what <hi type="italic">is</hi> before thee: <hi type="super">2</hi> And put a knife to thy throat, if thou <hi type="italic">be</hi> a man given to appetite. 3 Be not desirous of his dainties: for they <hi type="italic">are</hi> deceitful meat. <div eID="gen14360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14361" type="x-p"/> The sin we are here warned against is luxury and sensuality, and the indulgence of the appetite in eating and drinking, a sin that most easily besets us. 1. We are here told when we enter into temptation, and are in most danger of falling into this sin: "<hi type="italic">When thou sittest to eat with a ruler</hi> thou has great plenty before thee, varieties and dainties, such a table spread as thou has seldom seen; thou are ready to think, as Haman did, of nothing but the honour hereby done thee (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.12">Esth. v. 12</reference>), and the opportunity thou hast of pleasing thy palate, and forgettest that there is a snare laid for thee." Perhaps the temptation may be stronger, and more dangerous, to one that is not used to such entertainments, than to one that always sits down to a good table. 2. We are here directed to double our guard at such a time. We must, (1.) Apprehend ourselves to be in danger: "<hi type="italic">Consider diligently what is before thee,</hi> what meat and drink are before thee, that thou mayest choose that which is safest for thee and which thou art least likely to eat and drink of to excess. Consider what company is before thee, the ruler himself, who, if he be wise and good, will take it as an affront for any of his guests to disorder themselves at his table." And, if when we sit to eat with a ruler, much more when we sit to eat with the ruler of rulers at the Lord's table, must we <hi type="italic">consider diligently what is before us,</hi> that we may not in any respect <hi type="italic">eat and drink unworthily,</hi> unbecomingly, lest that table become a snare. (2.) We must alarm ourselves into temperance and moderation: "<hi type="italic">Put a knife to thy throat,</hi> that is, restrain thyself, as it were with a sword hanging over thy head, from all excess. Let these words, <hi type="italic">Take heed lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness, and so that day come upon you unawares</hi>—or those, <hi type="italic">For all these things, God shall bring thee into judgment</hi>—or those, <hi type="italic">Drunkards, shall not inherit the kingdom of God,</hi> be a knife to the throat." The Latins call luxury <hi type="italic">gula</hi>—<hi type="italic">the throat.</hi> "Take up arms against that sin. Rather be so abstemious that thy craving appetite will begin to think thy throat cut than indulge thyself in voluptuousness." We must never <hi type="italic">feed ourselves without fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.12">Jude 12</reference>), but we must in a special manner fear when temptation is before us. (3.) We must reason ourselves into a holy contempt of the gratifications of sense: "<hi type="italic">If thou be a man given to appetite,</hi> thou must, by a present solution, and an application of the terrors of the Lord, restrain thyself. When thou art in danger of falling into any excess <hi type="italic">put a knife to thy throat;</hi> that may serve for once. But that is not enough: lay the axe to the root; mortify that appetite which has such a power over thee: <hi type="italic">Be not desirous of dainties.</hi>" Note, We ought to observe what is our own iniquity, and, if we find ourselves addicted to flesh-pleasing, we must not only stand upon our guard against temptations from without, but subdue the corruption within. Nature is desirous of food, and we are taught to pray for it, but it is lust that is desirous of dainties, and we cannot in faith pray for them, for frequently they are not food convenient for mind, body, or estate. They are deceitful meat, and therefore David, instead of praying for them, prays against them, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.4">Ps. cxli. 4</reference>. They are pleasant to the palate, but perhaps rise in the stomach, turn sour there, upbraid a man, and make him sick. They do not yield men the satisfaction they promised themselves from them; for those that are given to appetite, when they have that which is very dainty, are not pleased; they are soon weary of it; they must have something else more dainty. The more a luxurious appetite is humoured and indulged the more humour some and troublesome it grows, and the more hard to please; dainties will surfeit, but never satisfy. But especially they are upon <hi type="italic">this</hi> account deceitful meat, that, while they please the body, they prejudice the soul, they overcharge the heart, and unfit it for the service of God, nay, they take away the heart, and alienate the mind from spiritual delights, and spoil its relish of them. Why then should we covet that which will certainly cheat us?

<div eID="gen14361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14362" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom. <hi type="super">5</hi> Wilt thou set thine eyes upon that which is not? for <hi type="italic">riches</hi> certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven. <div eID="gen14362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14363" type="x-p"/> As some are given to appetite (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.2">v. 2</reference>) so others to covetousness, and those Solomon here takes to task. Men cheat themselves as much by setting their hearts on money (though it seems most substantial) as by setting them on dainties. Observe, <div eID="gen14363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14364" type="x-p"/> I. How he dissuades the covetous man from toiling and tormenting himself (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.4">v. 4</reference>). "Do not <hi type="italic">aim to be rich,</hi> to raise an estate, and to make what thou hast in abundance more than it is." We must endeavor to live comfortably, and provide for our children and families, according as our rank and condition are, but we must not seek great things. Be not of those that will be rich, that desire it as their chief good and design it as their highest end, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.9">1 Tim. vi. 9</reference>. Covetous men think it is their wisdom, imagining that if they be rich to such a degree they shall be completely happy. <hi type="italic">Cease from that wisdom,</hi> for it is a mistake; <hi type="italic">a man's life consists not in the abundance of the things which he possesses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.15">Luke xii. 15</reference>. 1. Those that aim at great things fill their hands with business more than they can grasp, so that their life is both a perfect drudgery and a perpetual hurry; but be not thou such a fool; <hi type="italic">labour not to be rich.</hi> What thou hast, or doest, be master of it, and not a slave to it as those that <hi type="italic">rise up early, sit up late,</hi> and <hi type="italic">eat the bread of carefulness,</hi> and all to be rich. Moderate labour, <hi type="italic">that we may have to give,</hi> is our wisdom and duty, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>. Immoderate labour, that we may have to hoard, is our sin and folly. 2. They fill their heads with projects more than they understand, so that their life is a constant toss of care and fear; but do not thou thus vex thyself: <hi type="italic">Cease from thy own wisdom;</hi> go on quietly in the way of thy business, not contriving new ways and setting thy wits to work to find out new inventions. Acquiesce in God's wisdom, and cease from thy own, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.5-Prov.3.6">ch. iii. 5, 6</reference>. <div eID="gen14364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14365" type="x-p"/> II. How he dissuades the covetous man from cheating and deceiving himself by an inordinate love and pursuit of that which is vanity and vexation of spirit; for, <div eID="gen14365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14366" type="x-p"/> 1. It is not substantial and satisfying: "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou</hi> be such a fool as to <hi type="italic">set thy eyes,</hi> to cause thy eyes to fly with eagerness and violence, <hi type="italic">upon that which is not?</hi>" Note, (1.) The things of this world are things that are not. They have a real existence in nature and are the real gifts of Providence, but in the kingdom of grace they are things that are not; they are not a happiness and portion for a soul, are not what they promise to be nor what we expect them to be; they are a show, a shadow, a sham upon the soul that trusts to them. They are not, for in a little while they will not be, they will not be ours; they perish in the using; the fashion of them passes away. (2.) It is therefore folly for us to set our eyes upon them, to admire them as the best things, to appropriate them to ourselves as our good things, and to aim at them as our mark at which all our actions are levelled, to fly upon them as the eagle upon her prey. "Wilt thou do a thing so absurd in itself? What thou, a reasonable creature, wilt thou dote upon shadows? The eyes are put for rational and intellectual powers; wilt thou throw those away upon such undeserving objects? To set the hands and feet upon the world is well enough, but not the eyes, the eyes of the mind; those were made to contemplate better things. Wilt thou, my son, that professest religion, put such an affront upon God (towards whom the eyes should ever be) and such an abuse upon thy soul?" <div eID="gen14366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14367" type="x-p"/> 2. It is not durable and abiding. Riches are very uncertain things; certainly they are so: <hi type="italic">They make themselves wings, and fly away.</hi> The more we cause our eyes to fly upon them the more likely they are to fly away from us. (1.) Riches will leave us. Those that hold them ever so fast cannot hold them long; either they must be taken from us or we must be taken from them. The goods are said to flow away as a stream (<reference osisRef="Job.20.28">Job xx. 28</reference>), here to flee as a bird. (2.) Perhaps they may leave us suddenly, when we have taken a great deal of pains for them and begin to take a great deal of pride and pleasure in them. The covetous man sits hatching upon his wealth, and brooding over it, till it is fledged, as the young ones under the hen, and then it is gone. Or, as if a man should be fond of a flight of wild-fowl that light in his field, and call them his own because they are upon his ground, whereas, if he offers to come near them, they take wing immediately and are gone to another man's field. (3.) The wings they fly away upon are of their own making. They have in themselves the principles of their own corruption, their own moth and rust. They are wasting in their own nature, and like a handful of dust, which, if it be grasped, slips through the fingers. Snow will last awhile, and look pretty, if it be left to lie on the ground where it fell, but, if gathered up and laid in the bosom, it is dissolved and gone immediately. (4.) They go irresistibly and irrecoverably, as <hi type="italic">an eagle toward heaven,</hi> that flies strongly (there is no stopping her), and flies out of sight and out of call (there is no bringing her back); thus do riches leave men, and leave them in grief and vexation if they set their hearts upon them.

<div eID="gen14367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14368" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Eat thou not the bread of <hi type="italic">him that hath</hi> an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats: <hi type="super">7</hi> For as he thinketh in his heart, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> he: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> not with thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> The morsel <hi type="italic">which</hi> thou hast eaten shalt thou vomit up, and lose thy sweet words. <div eID="gen14368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14369" type="x-p"/> Those that are voluptuous and given to appetite (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.2">v. 2</reference>) are glad to be where there is good cheer stirring, and those that are covetous and saving, that they may spare at home, will be glad to get a dinner at another man's table; and therefore both are here advised not to be forward to accept of every man's invitation, but especially not to thrust themselves in uninvited. Observe, 1. There are those that pretend to bid their friends welcome that are not hearty and sincere in it. They have a fair tongue, and know what they should say: <hi type="italic">Eat and drink, saith he,</hi> because it is expected that the master of the feast should so compliment his guests; but they have <hi type="italic">an evil eye,</hi> and grudge their guests every bit they eat, especially if the eat freely. They would seem to be liberal in making the entertainment, and would have the credit of it, but they have so great a love to their money, and so little to their friends, that they cannot have the comfort of it, nor any enjoyment of themselves or their friends. The miser's feast is his penance. If a man be so very selfish, and sordid, and mean that he cannot find in his heart to bid his friends welcome to what he has, he ought not to add to that the guilt of dissimulation by inviting them, but let him own himself to be what he is, that <hi type="italic">the vile person may not be called liberal nor the churl bountiful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">Isa. xxxii. 5</reference>. 2. One can have no comfort in accepting the entertainments that are given grudgingly: "<hi type="italic">Eat not thou the bread</hi> of such a man; let him keep it to himself. Do not sponge upon those that are bountiful, nor make thyself burdensome to any; but especially scorn to be beholden to those that are paltry and not sincere. Better have a dinner of herbs, and true welcome, than <hi type="italic">dainty meats</hi> without it. Therefore," (1.) "Judge of the man as his mind is. Thou thinkest to pay thy respect to him as a friend, so thou takest him to be, because he compliments thee, but <hi type="italic">as he thinks in his heart so is he,</hi> not as he speaks with his tongue." We are that really, both to God and man, which we are inwardly; and neither religion nor friendship is worth any thing further than as it is sincere. (2.) "Judge of the meat as the digestion is and as it agrees with thee. He bids thee eat freely, but, first or last, he will discover his sordid covetous humour, and <hi type="italic">as he thinks in his heart</hi> so will he look, and give thee to understand that thou art not welcome, and then <hi type="italic">the morsel thou hast eaten thou shalt vomit up;</hi> the very thought of that will make thee even to vomit the meat thou hast eaten, and eat the words thou has spoken in returning his compliments and giving him thanks for his civilities. Thou shalt <hi type="italic">lose thy sweet words,</hi> which he has given thee and thou has given him."

<div eID="gen14369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14370" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words. <div eID="gen14370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14371" type="x-p"/> We are here directed not to <hi type="italic">cast pearls before swine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Matt. vii. 6</reference>) and not to expose things sacred to the contempt and ridicule of profane scoffers. It is our duty to take all fit occasions to speak of divine things; but, 1. There are some that will make a jest of every thing, though it be ever so prudently and pertinently spoken, that will not only despise a wise man's words, but despise even the wisdom of them, that in them which is most improvable for their own edification; they will particularly reproach that, as if it had an ill design upon them, which they must guard against. 2. Those that do so forfeit the benefit of good advice and instruction, and a wise man is not only allowed, but advised, not to <hi type="italic">speak in the ears</hi> of such fools; let them be foolish still, and let not precious breath be thrown away upon them. If what a wise man says in his wisdom will not be heard, let him hold his peace, and try whether the wisdom of that will be regarded.

<div eID="gen14371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14372" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless: <hi type="super">11</hi> For their redeemer <hi type="italic">is</hi> mighty; he shall plead their cause with thee. <div eID="gen14372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14373" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The fatherless are taken under God's special protection; with him they not only find mercy shown to them (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.3">Hos. xiv. 3</reference>) but justice done for them. He is <hi type="italic">their Redeemer,</hi> their <hi type="italic">Go&#235;l,</hi> their near kinsman, that will take their part and stand up for them with jealousy, as taking himself affronted in the injuries done to them. As their Redeemer <hi type="italic">he will plead their cause</hi> against those that do them any injury, and, one way or other, will not only defend their right, and recover it for them, but avenge the wrongs done to them. And he <hi type="italic">is mighty,</hi> almighty; his omnipotence is engaged and employed for their protection, and their proudest and most powerful oppressors will not only find themselves an unequal match for this, but will find that it is at their peril to contend with it. 2. Every man therefore must be careful not to injure them in any thing, or to invade their rights, either by a clandestine removal of the old land-marks or by a forcible entry into their fields. Being fatherless, they have none to redress their wrongs, and, being in their childhood, they do not so much as apprehend the wrong that is done them. Sense of honour, and much more the fear of God, would restrain men from offering injury to children, especially fatherless children.  <div eID="gen14373" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv64"/><title type="x-s3">Parental Duties.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv64"/> <div sID="gen14374" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge. <hi type="super">13</hi> Withhold not correction from the child: for <hi type="italic">if</hi> thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die. <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell. <hi type="super">15</hi> My son, if thine heart be wise, my heart shall rejoice, even mine. <hi type="super">16</hi> Yea, my reins shall rejoice, when thy lips speak right things. <div eID="gen14374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14375" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A parent instructing his child. He is here brought in persuading him to give his mind to his book, and especially to the scriptures and his catechism, to attend <hi type="italic">to the words of knowledge,</hi> by which he might come to know his duty, and danger, and interest, and not to think it enough to give them the hearing, but to apply his heart to them, to delight in them, and bow his will to the authority of them. The heart is <hi type="italic">then</hi> applied to the instruction when the instruction is applied to the heart. 2. A parent correcting his child. A tender parent can scarcely find in his heart to do this; it goes much against the grain. But he finds it is necessary; it is his duty, and therefore he dares not <hi type="italic">withhold correction</hi> when there is occasion for it (<hi type="italic">spare the rod and spoil the child</hi>); he <hi type="italic">beats him with the rod,</hi> gives him a gentle correction, the <hi type="italic">stripes of the sons of men,</hi> not such as we give to beasts. <hi type="italic">Beat him with the rod and he shall not die.</hi> The rod will not kill him; nay, it will prevent his killing himself by those vicious courses which the rod will be necessary to restrain him from. For the present <hi type="italic">it is not joyous, but grievous,</hi> both to the parent and to the child; but when it is given with wisdom, designed for good, accompanied with prayer, and blessed of God, it may prove a happy means of preventing his utter destruction and <hi type="italic">delivering his soul from hell.</hi> Our great care must be about our children's souls; we must not see them in danger of hell without using all possible means, with the utmost care and concern, to snatch them as brands out of everlasting burnings. Let the body smart, so that the spirit be <hi type="italic">saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.</hi> 3. A parent encouraging his child, telling him, (1.) What was all he expected, nothing but what would be for his own good, that <hi type="italic">his heart be wise</hi> and that his <hi type="italic">lips speak right things,</hi> that he be under the government of good principles, and that by those principles he particularly maintain a good environment of his tongue. It is to be hoped that those will do <hi type="italic">right things</hi> when they grow up who learn to <hi type="italic">speak right things</hi> when they are young, and dare not speak any bad words. (2.) What a comfort it would be to him if herein he answered his expectation: "<hi type="italic">If thy heart be wise, my heart shall rejoice,</hi> shall rejoice in thee, <hi type="italic">even mine,</hi> who have taken so much care and pains about thee, my heart, that has many a time ached for thee, for which thou shouldst study thus to make a grateful requital." Note, The wisdom of children will be the joy of their parents and teachers, who have no greater joy than to see them <hi type="italic">walk in the truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="3John.1.4">3 John 4</reference>. "Children, if you be wise and good, devout and conscientious, God will be pleased with you, and that will be our joy: we shall think our labour in instructing you well bestowed; it will be a comfortable answer for the many prayers we have put up for you; we shall be eased of a great deal of care, shall not need to be so strict and severe in watching over you, and shall consequently be the easier both to you and to ourselves. We shall rejoice in hope that you will be a credit and comfort to us, if we should live to be old, that you will bear up the name of Christ in your generation, that you will live comfortably in this world and happily in another."  <div eID="gen14375" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv65"/><title type="x-s3">Parental Advice.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv65"/> <div sID="gen14376" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Let not thine heart envy sinners: but <hi type="italic">be thou</hi> in the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> all the day long. <hi type="super">18</hi> For surely there is an end; and thine expectation shall not be cut off. <div eID="gen14376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14377" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A necessary caution against entertaining any favourable thoughts of prospering profaneness: "<hi type="italic">Let not thy heart envy sinners;</hi> do not grudge them either the liberty they take to sin or the success they are to be pitied rather than envied. Their prosperity is their portion (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.14">Ps. xii. 14</reference>), nay, it is their poison," <reference osisRef="Prov.1.32">Prov. i. 32</reference>. We must not harbour in our hearts any secret discontent at the providence of God, though it seem to smile upon them, nor wish ourselves in their condition. "<hi type="italic">Let not thy heart imitate sinners</hi>" (so some read it); do not as they do; walk not in the way with them; use not the methods they take to enrich themselves, though they thrive by them. 2. An excellent direction to maintain high thoughts of God in our minds at all times: <hi type="italic">Be thou in the fear of the Lord</hi> every day and <hi type="italic">all the day long.</hi> We must be in the fear of the Lord as in our employment, exercising ourselves in holy adorings of God, in subjection to his precepts, submission to his providences, and a constant care to please him; we must be in it as in our element, taking a pleasure in contemplating God's glory and complying with his will. We must be <hi type="italic">devoted to his fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.38">Ps. cxix. 38</reference>); and governed by it as our commanding principle in all we say and do. All the days of our life we must constantly keep up an awe of God upon our spirits, must pay a deference to his authority, and have a dread of his wrath. We must be always so in his fear as never to be out of it. 3.
