A good reason for both of these (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Surely there is an end,</hi> an end and expectation, as <reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">Jer. xxix. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">There will be an end of the prosperity of the wicked,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">do not envy them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Ps. lxxiii. 17</reference>); there will be an end of thy afflictions, therefore be not weary of them, an end of thy services, thy work and warfare will be accomplished, <hi type="italic">perfect love will shortly cast out fear,</hi> and <hi type="italic">thy expectation</hi> of the reward not only will be <hi type="italic">not cut off,</hi> or disappointed, but it will be infinitely outdone. The consideration of the end will help to reconcile us to all the difficulties and discouragements of the way.

<div eID="gen14377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14378" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Hear thou, my son, and be wise, and guide thine heart in the way. <hi type="super">20</hi> Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh: <hi type="super">21</hi> For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe <hi type="italic">a man</hi> with rags. <hi type="super">22</hi> Hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old. <hi type="super">23</hi> Buy the truth, and sell <hi type="italic">it</hi> not; <hi type="italic">also</hi> wisdom, and instruction, and understanding. <hi type="super">24</hi> The father of the righteous shall greatly rejoice: and he that begetteth a wise <hi type="italic">child</hi> shall have joy of him. <hi type="super">25</hi> Thy father and thy mother shall be glad, and she that bare thee shall rejoice. <hi type="super">26</hi> My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways. <hi type="super">27</hi> For a whore <hi type="italic">is</hi> a deep ditch; and a strange woman <hi type="italic">is</hi> a narrow pit. 28 She also lieth in wait as <hi type="italic">for</hi> a prey, and increaseth the transgressors among men. <div eID="gen14378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14379" type="x-p"/> Here is good advice for parents to give to their children; words are put into their mouths, that they may <hi type="italic">train them up in the way they should go.</hi> Here we have, <div eID="gen14379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14380" type="x-p"/> I. An earnest call to young people to attend to the advice of their godly parents, not only to this that is here given, but to all other profitable instructions: "<hi type="italic">Here, my son, and be wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.19">v. 19</reference>. This will be an evidence that thou art wise and a means to make thee wiser." Wisdom, as <hi type="italic">faith, comes by hearing.</hi> And again (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hearken unto thy father who begot thee,</hi> and who therefore has an authority over thee and an affection for thee, and, thou mayest be sure, can have no other design than thy own good." We ought to <hi type="italic">give reverence to the fathers of our flesh,</hi> who begot us, and were the instruments of our being; much more ought we to obey and be in subjection to the <hi type="italic">Father of our spirits,</hi> who made us and is the author of our being. And since <hi type="italic">the mother</hi> also, from a sense of duty to God and from love to her child, gives him good instructions, let him not <hi type="italic">despise her,</hi> nor her advice, <hi type="italic">when she is old.</hi> When the mother was grown old we may suppose the children to be grown up; but let them not think themselves past being taught, even by her, but rather respect her the more for the multitude of her years and the wisdom which they teach. Scornful and insolent young men will make a jest, it may be, of the good advice of an aged mother, and think themselves not concerned to heed what an old woman says; but such will have a great deal to answer for another day, not only as having set at nought good counsel, but as having slighted and grieved a good mother, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.17">ch. xxx. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen14380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14381" type="x-p"/> II. An argument to enforce this call, taken from the great comfort which this will be to their parents, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.24-Prov.23.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. Note, 1. It is the duty of children to study how they may gladden the hearts of their good parents, and do it yet more and more, so that they may <hi type="italic">greatly rejoice</hi> in them, even when the <hi type="italic">evil days come and the years of which they say they have no pleasure in them</hi> but this, to see their children do well, as <hi type="italic">Barzillai</hi> to see <hi type="italic">Chimham</hi> preferred. 2. Children will be a joy to their parents if they be <hi type="italic">righteous and wise.</hi> Righteousness is true wisdom; those who do good so well for themselves. Those are completely such as they should be who are not only <hi type="italic">wise</hi> (that is, knowing and learned), but <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> (that is, honest and good), and not only <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> (that is, conscientious and well-meaning), but <hi type="italic">wise</hi> (that is, prudent and discreet) in the management of themselves. If such the children be, especially all the children, the father and mother will be glad, and think nothing too much that they have done, or do, for them; they will please themselves in them, and give God thanks for them; particularly she that bore them with pain, and nursed them with pains, will rejoice in them, and reckon herself well requited, and the sorrow more than forgotten, because a wise and good man is the product of it, who is a blessing to the world he was born into. <div eID="gen14381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14382" type="x-p"/> III. Some general precepts of wisdom and virtue. <div eID="gen14382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14383" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Guide thy heart in the way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.19">v. 19</reference>. It is the heart that must be taken care of and directed aright; the motions and affections of the soul must be towards right objects and under a steady guidance. If the heart be guided in the way, the steps will be guided and the conversation well ordered. <div eID="gen14383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14384" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">Buy the truth and sell it not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.23">v. 23</reference>. Truth is that by which the heart must be guided and governed, for without truth there is no goodness; no regular practices without right principles. It is by the power of truth, known and believed, that we must be kept back from sin and constrained to duty. The understanding must be well-informed with wisdom and instruction, and therefore, (1.) We must buy it, that is, be willing to part with any thing for it. He does not say at what rate we must buy it, because we cannot buy it too dear, but must have it at any rate; whatever it costs us, we shall not repent the bargain. When we are at expense for the means of knowledge, and resolved not to starve so good a cause, then we <hi type="italic">buy the truth.</hi> Riches should be employed for the getting of knowledge, rather than knowledge for the getting of riches. When we are at pains in searching after truth, that we may come to the knowledge of it and may distinguish between it and error, then we buy it. <hi type="italic">Dii laboribus omnia vendunt—Heaven concedes every thing to the laborious.</hi> When we choose rather to suffer loss in our temporal interest than to deny or neglect the truth they we buy it; and it is a pearl of such great price that we must be willing to part with all to purchase it, must make shipwreck of estate, trade, preferment, rather than of faith and a good conscience. (2.) We must not sell it. Do not part with it for pleasures, honours, riches, any things in this world. Do not neglect the study of it, nor throw off the profession of it, nor revolt from under the dominion of it, for the getting or saving of any secular interest whatsoever. <hi type="italic">Hold fast the form of sound words,</hi> and never let it go upon any terms. <div eID="gen14384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14385" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">Give me thy heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.26">v. 26</reference>. God in this exhortation, speaks to us as unto children: "Son, Daughter, <hi type="italic">Give my thy heart.</hi>" The heart is that which the great God requires and calls for from every one of us; whatever we give, if we do not give him our hearts, it will not be accepted. We must set our love upon him. Our thoughts must converse much with him, and on him, as our highest end. <hi type="italic">The intents of our hearts</hi> must be fastened. We must make it our own act and deed to devote ourselves to the Lord, and we must be free and cheerful in it. We must not think to divide the heart between God and the world; he will have all or none. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart.</hi> To this call we must readily answer, "<hi type="italic">My father, take my heart,</hi> such as it is, and make it such as it should be; take possession of it, and set up thy throne in it." <div eID="gen14385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14386" type="x-p"/> 4. <hi type="italic">Let thy eyes observe my ways;</hi> have an eye to the rule of God's word, the conduct of his providence, and the good examples of his people. Our eyes must observe these, as he that writes observes his copy, that we may keep in the right paths and may proceed and persevere in them. <div eID="gen14386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14387" type="x-p"/> IV. Some particular cautions against those sins which are, of all sins, the most destructive to the seeds of wisdom and grace in the soul, which impoverish and ruin it. 1. Gluttony and drunkenness, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.20-Prov.23.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. The world is full of examples of this sin and temptations to it, which all young people are concerned to stand upon their guard against and keep at a distance from <hi type="italic">Be not a wine-bibber;</hi> we are allowed to drink <hi type="italic">a little wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1 Tim. v. 23</reference>), but not much, not to make a trade of it, never to drink to excess. <hi type="italic">Be not a riotous eater of flesh,</hi> as the Israelites were, who lusted exceedingly after it, saying, <hi type="italic">Who will give us flesh to eat?</hi> Whereas Paul, though he is free to eat flesh, yet resolves that <hi type="italic">he will eat no flesh while the world stands rather than make his brother to offend;</hi> so indifferent is he to it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.13">1 Cor. viii. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Be not an</hi> excessive <hi type="italic">eater of flesh.</hi> Intemperance must be avoided in meat as well as drink. <hi type="italic">Be not a</hi> luxurious <hi type="italic">eater of flesh,</hi> not pleased with any thing but what is very nice and delicate, savoury dishes, and forced meat. Some take not only a pleasure, but a pride, in being curious about their diet, and, as they call it, eating well; as if that were the ornament of a gentleman, which is really the shame of a Christian, making a God of the belly. "<hi type="italic">Be not a wine bibber,</hi> and <hi type="italic">be not a riotous eater;</hi> and therefore, <hi type="italic">be not among wine-bibbers</hi> nor <hi type="italic">among riotous eaters;</hi> do not give them countenance, lest thou learn their ways and insensibly fall into those sins, or at least lose the dread and detestation of them. They covet to have thee among them; for those that are debauched themselves are very desirous to debauch others; therefore do not gratify them, lest thou endanger thyself." He fetches an argument against this sin from the expensiveness of it and its tendency to impoverish men: and if men will not be deterred from it by the ruin it brings on their secular interests, which lie nearest their hearts, no marvel that they are not frightened from it by what they are told out of the word of God of the mischief it does them in their spiritual and eternal concerns. <hi type="italic">The drunkard and the glutton</hi> hate to be reformed, though they are told they <hi type="italic">shall come to poverty,</hi> nay, though they are told they shall come to hell. Drunkenness is the cause of <hi type="italic">drowsiness;</hi> it stupefies men, and makes them inattentive to business, and then all goes to wreck and ruin: thus men that have lived creditably come to be <hi type="italic">clothed with rags.</hi> 2. Whoredom. This is another sin which <hi type="italic">takes away the heart</hi> that should be given to God, <reference osisRef="Hos.4.11">Hos. iv. 11</reference>. He shows the danger which attends that sin, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.27-Prov.23.28">v. 27, 28</reference>, (1.) It is a sin from which few recover themselves when once they are entangled in it. It is like <hi type="italic">a deep ditch</hi> and <hi type="italic">a narrow pit,</hi> which it is almost impossible to get out of; and therefore it is wisdom to keep far enough from the brink of it. Take heed of making any approaches towards this sin, because it is so hard to make a retreat from it, conscience, which should head the retreat, being debauched by it, and divine grace forfeited. (2.) It is a sin which bewitches men to their ruin: <hi type="italic">The adulteress lies in wait as a robber,</hi> pretending friendship, but designing the greatest mischief, to rob them of all they have that is valuable, to strip them both of their armour and of their ornaments. Even those who, being virtuously educated, endeavour to shun the adulteress, she will <hi type="italic">lie in wait</hi> for, that she may assault them when they are off their guard and she has them at an advantage. Let none therefore be at any time secure. (3.) It is a sin that contributes more than any other to the spreading of vice and immorality in a kingdom: It <hi type="italic">increases the transgressors among men.</hi> One adulteress may be the ruin of many a precious soul and may help to debauch a whole town. It increases the treacherous or perfidious ones; it not only occasions husbands to be false to their wives and servants to their masters, but many that have professed religion to throw off their profession and break their covenants with God. Houses of uncleanness are therefore such pest-houses as ought to be suppressed by those whose office it is to take care of the public welfare.  <div eID="gen14387" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv66"/><title type="x-s3">Cautions against Intemperance.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv66"/> <div sID="gen14388" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath babbling? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes? <hi type="super">30</hi> They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine. <hi type="super">31</hi> Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, <hi type="italic">when</hi> it moveth itself aright. <hi type="super">32</hi> At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder. <hi type="super">33</hi> Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things. <hi type="super">34</hi> Yea, thou shalt be as he that lieth down in the midst of the sea, or as he that lieth upon the top of a mast. <hi type="super">35</hi> They have stricken me, <hi type="italic">shalt thou say, and</hi> I was not sick; they have beaten me, <hi type="italic">and</hi> I felt <hi type="italic">it</hi> not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again. <div eID="gen14388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14389" type="x-p"/> Solomon here gives fair warning against the sin of drunkenness, to confirm what he had said, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.20">v. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen14389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14390" type="x-p"/> I. He cautions all people to keep out of the way of temptations to this sin (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Look not thou upon the wine when it is red.</hi> Red wine was in Canaan looked upon as the best wine, it is therefore called <hi type="italic">the blood of the grape.</hi> Critics judge of wine, among other indications, by the colour of it; some wine, they say, looks charmingly, looks so well that it even says, "Come and drink me;" <hi type="italic">it moves itself aright,</hi> goes down very smoothly, or perhaps the roughness of it is grateful. It is said of generous strong-bodied wine that it even <hi type="italic">causes the lips of those that are asleep to speak,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.7.9">Cant. vii. 9</reference>. But <hi type="italic">look not thou upon it.</hi> 1. "Be not ruled by sense, but by reason and religion. Covet not that which pleases the eye, in hopes that it will please the taste; but let thy serious thoughts correct the errors of thy senses and convince thee that that which seems delightful is really hurtful, and resolve against it accordingly. Let not the heart walk after the eye, for it is a deceitful guide." 2. "Be not too bold with the charms of this or any other sin; <hi type="italic">look not,</hi> lest thou lust, lest thou take the forbidden fruit." Note Those that would be kept from any sin must keep themselves from all the occasions and beginnings of it, and be afraid of coming within the reach of its allurements, lest they be overcome by them. <div eID="gen14390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14391" type="x-p"/> II. He shows the many pernicious consequences of the sin of drunkenness, for the enforcement of this caution. Take heed of the bait, for fear of the hook: <hi type="italic">At the last it bites,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.32">v. 32</reference>. All sin will be bitterness in the end, and this sin particularly. <hi type="italic">It bites like a serpent,</hi> when the drunkard is made sick by his surfeit, thrown by it into a dropsy or some fatal disease, beggared and ruined in his estate, especially when his conscience is awakened and he cannot reflect upon it without horror and indignation at himself, but worst of all, at last, when the cup of drunkenness shall be turned into a cup of trembling, the cup of the Lord's wrath, the dregs of which he must be for ever drinking, and shall not have a drop of water to cool his inflamed tongue. To take off the force of the temptation that there is in the pleasure of the sin, foresee the punishment of it, and what it will at last end in if repentance prevent not. In <hi type="italic">its latter end it bites</hi> (so the word is); think therefore what will be <hi type="italic">in the end thereof.</hi> But the inspired writer chooses to specify those pernicious consequences of this sin which are present and sensible. <div eID="gen14391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14392" type="x-p"/> 1. It embroils men in quarrels, makes them quarrel with others, and say and do that which gives others occasion to quarrel with them, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.29">v. 29</reference>. He asks, <hi type="italic">Who hath woe? Who hath sorrow?</hi> Who has not, in this world? Many have woe and sorrow, and cannot help it; but drunkards wilfully create woe and sorrow to themselves. Those that have <hi type="italic">contentions</hi> have <hi type="italic">woe and sorrow;</hi> and drunkards are the fools whose <hi type="italic">lips enter into contention.</hi> When the wine is in the wit is out and the passions are up; and thence come drunken scuffles, and drunken frays, and drunken disputes over the cups; many a vexatious ruining law-suit has begun thus. There is <hi type="italic">babbling,</hi> quarrels in word and the exchanging of scurrilous language; yet it rests not there: you shall have <hi type="italic">wounds without cause,</hi> for causes are things which drunkards are in no capacity to judge of, and therefore they deal blows about without the least consideration why or wherefore, and must expect to be in like manner treated themselves. The wounds which men receive in defence of their country and its just rights are their honour; but <hi type="italic">wounds without cause,</hi> received in the service of their lusts, are marks of their infamy. Nay, drunkards wound themselves in a tender part, for they have <hi type="italic">redness of eyes,</hi> symptoms of an inward inflammation; their sight is weakened by it, and their looks are deformed. This comes, (1.) Of drinking long, <hi type="italic">tarrying long at the wine,</hi> and spending that time in drunken company which should be spent in useful business, or in sleep, which should fit for business, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.30">v. 30</reference>. O the precious hours which thousands throw away thus, every one of which will be brought into the account at the great day! (2.) Of drinking that which is strong and intoxicating. <hi type="italic">They go</hi> up and down <hi type="italic">to seek wine</hi> that will please them; their great enquiry is, "Where is the best liquor?" <hi type="italic">They seek mixed wine,</hi> which is most palatable, but most heady, so willingly do they sacrifice their reason to please their palate! <div eID="gen14392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14393" type="x-p"/> 2. It makes men impure and insolent, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.33">v. 33</reference>. (1.) The <hi type="italic">eyes</hi> grow unruly and <hi type="italic">behold strange women</hi> to lust after them, and so let in adultery into the heart. <hi type="italic">Est Venus in vinis—Wine is oil to the fire of lust. Thy eyes shall behold strange things</hi> (so some read it); when men are drunk the house turns round with them, and every thing looks strange to them, so that them they cannot trust their own eyes. (2.) The tongue also grows unruly and talks extravagantly; by it the <hi type="italic">heart utters perverse things,</hi> things contrary to reason, religion, and common civility, which they would be ashamed to speak if they were sober. What ridiculous incoherent nonsense men will talk when they are drunk who at another time will speak admirably well and to the purpose! <div eID="gen14393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14394" type="x-p"/> 3. It stupefies and besots men, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.34">v. 34</reference>. When men are drunk they know not where they are nor what they say and do. (1.) Their heads are giddy, and when they lie down to sleep they are as if they were tossed by the rolling waves <hi type="italic">of the sea,</hi> or <hi type="italic">upon the top of a mast;</hi> hence they complain that their heads swim; their sleep is commonly unquiet and not refreshing, and their dreams are tumultuous. (2.) Their judgments are clouded, and they have no more steadiness and consistency than he that sleeps <hi type="italic">upon the top of a mast:</hi> they <hi type="italic">drink and forget the law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">ch. xxxi. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">they err through wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa. xxviii. 7</reference>), and think as extravagantly as they talk. (3.) They are heedless and fearless of danger, and senseless of the rebukes they are under either from God or man. They are in imminent danger of death, of damnation, lie as much exposed as if they slept <hi type="italic">upon the top of a mast,</hi> and yet are secure and sleep on. They fear no peril when the terrors of the Lord are laid before them; nay, they feel no pain when the judgments of God are actually upon them; they cry not when he binds them. Set a drunkard in the stocks, and he is not sensible of the punishment. "<hi type="italic">They have stricken me, and I was not sick; I felt it not:</hi> it made no impression at all upon me." Drunkenness turns me into stocks and stones; they are scarcely to be reckoned animals; they are dead while they live. <div eID="gen14394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14395" type="x-p"/> 4. Worst of all, the heart is hardened in the sin, and the sinner, notwithstanding all these present mischiefs that attend it, obstinately persist in it, and hates to be reformed: <hi type="italic">When shall I awake?</hi> Much ado he has to shake off the chains of his drunken sleep; he can hardly get clear of the fumes of the wine, though he strives with them, that (being thirsty in the morning) he may return to it again. So perfectly lost is he to all sense of virtue and honour, and so wretchedly is his conscience seared, that he is not ashamed to say, <hi type="italic">I will seek it yet again. There is no hope; no, they have loved</hi> drunkards, and <hi type="italic">after them they will go,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jer. ii. 25</reference>. This is <hi type="italic">adding drunkenness to thirst,</hi> and <hi type="italic">following strong drink;</hi> those that do so may read their doom <reference osisRef="Deut.29.19-Deut.29.20">Deut. xxix. 19, 20</reference>, their <hi type="italic">woe</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Isa. v. 11</reference>, and, if this be the end of the sin, with good reason were we directed to stop at the beginning of it: <hi type="italic">Look not upon the wine when it is red.</hi>  <chapter eID="Prov.23"/> <div eID="gen14395" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv67"/><title type="x-s3">The Excellence of Wisdom.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv67"/> <div sID="gen14397" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Be not thou envious against evil men, neither desire to be with them. <hi type="super">2</hi> For their heart studieth destruction, and their lips talk of mischief. <div eID="gen14397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14398" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The caution given is much the same with that which we had before (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.17">ch. xxiii. 17</reference>), not to envy sinners, not to think them happy, nor to wish ourselves in their condition, though they prosper ever so much in this world, and are ever so merry and ever so secure. "Let not such a thought ever come into thy mind, O that I could shake off the restraints of religion and conscience, and take as great a liberty to indulge the sensual appetite, as I see such and such do! No; <hi type="italic">desire not to be with them,</hi> to do as they do and fare as they fare, and to <hi type="italic">cast in thy lot among</hi> them." 2. Here is another reason given for this caution: "<hi type="italic">Be not envious against</hi> them, not only because their end will be had, but because their way is so, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.2">v. 2</reference>. Do not think with them, <hi type="italic">for their heart studies destruction</hi> to others, but it will prove destruction to themselves. Do not speak like them, for <hi type="italic">their lips talk of their mischief.</hi> All they say has an ill tendency, to dishonour God, reproach religion, or wrong their neighbour; but it will be mischief to themselves at last. It is therefore thy wisdom to have nothing to do with them. Nor hast thou any reason to look upon them with envy, but with pity rather, or a just indignation at their wicked practices."

<div eID="gen14398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14399" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established: <hi type="super">4</hi> And by knowledge shall the chambers be filled with all precious and pleasant riches. 5 A wise man <hi type="italic">is</hi> strong; yea, a man of knowledge increaseth strength. <hi type="super">6</hi> For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war: and in multitude of counsellors <hi type="italic">there is</hi> safety. <div eID="gen14399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14400" type="x-p"/> We are tempted to envy those that grow rich, and raise their estates and families, by such unjust courses as our consciences will by no means suffer us to use. But, to set aside that temptation, Solomon here shows that a man, with prudent management, may raise his estate and family by lawful and honest means, with a good conscience, and a good name, and the blessing of God upon his industry; and, if the other be raised a little sooner, yet these will last a great deal longer. 1. That which is here recommended to us as having the best influence upon our outward prosperity is <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> and <hi type="italic">understanding,</hi> and <hi type="italic">knowledge;</hi> that is, both piety towards God (for that is true wisdom) and prudence in the management of our outward affairs. We must govern ourselves in every thing by the rules of religion first and then of discretion. Some that are truly pious do not thrive in the world, for want of prudence; and some that are prudent enough, yet do not prosper, because they lean to their own understanding and do not acknowledge God in their ways; therefore both must go together to complete a wise man. 2. That which is here set before us as the advantage of true wisdom is that it will make men's outward affairs prosperous and successful. (1.) it will <hi type="italic">build a house and establish it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.24.3">v. 3</reference>. Men may by unrighteous practices build their houses, but they cannot establish them, for the foundation is rotten (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.9-Hab.2.10">Hab. ii. 9, 10</reference>); whereas what is honestly got will wear like steel and be an inheritance to children's children. (2.) It will enrich a house and furnish it, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.4">v. 4</reference>. Those that manage their affairs with wisdom and equity, that are diligent in the use of lawful means for increasing what they have that spare from luxury and spend in charity, are in a fair way to have their shops, their warehouses, their <hi type="italic">chambers, filled with all precious and pleasant riches—precious</hi> because got by honest labour, and <hi type="italic">the substance of a diligent man is precious—pleasant</hi> because enjoyed with holy cheerfulness. Some think this is to be understood chiefly of spiritual riches. <hi type="italic">By knowledge the chambers</hi> of the soul are filled with the graces and comforts of the Spirit, those <hi type="italic">precious and pleasant riches;</hi> for the Spirit, by enlightening the understanding, performs all his other operations on the soul. (3.) It will fortify a house and turn it into a castle: <hi type="italic">Wisdom is better than weapons of war,</hi> offensive or defensive. <hi type="italic">A wise man is in strength,</hi> is in a strong-hold, <hi type="italic">yea, a man of knowledge strengthens might,</hi> that is, increases it, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.5">v. 5</reference>. As we grow in knowledge we grow in all grace, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.18">2 Pet. iii. 18</reference>. Those that <hi type="italic">increase in wisdom</hi> are <hi type="italic">strengthened with all might,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.9">Col. i. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.1.11">11</reference>. A wise man will compass that by his wisdom which a strong man cannot effect by force of arms. The spirit is strengthened both for the spiritual work and the spiritual warfare by true wisdom. (4.) It will govern a house and a kingdom too, and the affairs of both, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.6">v. 6</reference>. Wisdom will erect a college, or council of state. Wisdom will be of use, [1.] For the managing of the public quarrels, so as not to engage in them but for an honest cause and with some probability of success, and, when they are engaged in, to manage them well, and so as to make either an advantageous peace or an honourable retreat: <hi type="italic">By wise counsel thou shalt make war,</hi> which is a thing that may prove of ill consequence if not done by wise counsel. [2.] For the securing of the public peace: <hi type="italic">In the multitude of counsellors there is safety,</hi> for one may foresee the danger, and discern the advantages, which another cannot. In our spiritual conflicts we need wisdom, for our enemy is subtle.  <div eID="gen14400" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv68"/><title type="x-s3">The Malicious and the Scornful.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv68"/> <div sID="gen14401" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> too high for a fool: he openeth not his mouth in the gate. <hi type="super">8</hi> He that deviseth to do evil shall be called a mischievous person. <hi type="super">9</hi> The thought of foolishness <hi type="italic">is</hi> sin: and the scorner <hi type="italic">is</hi> an abomination to men. <div eID="gen14401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14402" type="x-p"/> Here is the description, 1. Of a weak man: <hi type="italic">Wisdom is too high</hi> for him; he thinks it so, and therefore, despairing to attain it, he will take no pains in the pursuit of it, but sit down content without it. And really it is so; he has not capacity for it, and therefore the advantages he has for getting it are all in vain to him. It is no easy thing to get wisdom; those that have natural parts good enough, yet if they be foolish, that is, if they be slothful and will not take pains, if they be playful and trifling, and given to their pleasures, if they be viciously inclined and keep bad company, it <hi type="italic">is too high</hi> for them; they are not likely to reach it. And, for want of it, they are unfit for the service of their country: They <hi type="italic">open not their mouth in the gate;</hi> they are not admitted into the council or magistracy, or, if they are, they are dumb statues, and stand for cyphers; they say nothing, because they have nothing to say, and they know that if they should offer any thing it would not be heeded, nay, it would be hissed at. Let young men take pains to get wisdom, that they may be qualified for public business, and do it with reputation. 2. Of a wicked man, who is not only despised as a fool is, but detested. Two sorts of wicked men are so:—(1.) Such as are secretly malicious. Though they speak courteously and conduct themselves plausibly, they <hi type="italic">devise to do evil,</hi> are contriving to do an ill turn to those they bear a grudge to, or have an envious eye at. He that does so <hi type="italic">shall be called a mischievous person,</hi> or <hi type="italic">a master of mischief,</hi> which perhaps was then a common name of reproach; he shall be branded as an <hi type="italic">inventor of evil things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.30">Rom. i. 30</reference>), or if any mischief be done, he shall be suspected as the author of it, or at least accessory to it. This <hi type="italic">devising evil is the thought of foolishness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.24.9">v. 9</reference>. It is made light of, and turned off with a jest, as only a foolish thing, but really it <hi type="italic">is sin,</hi> it is exceedingly sinful; you cannot call it by a worse name than to call it <hi type="italic">sin.</hi> It is bad to do evil, but it is worse to devise it; for that has in it the subtlety and poison of the old serpent. But it may be taken more generally. We contract guilt, not only by the act of foolishness, but by the thought of it, though it go no further; the first risings of sin in the heart are sin, offensive to God, and must be repented of or we are undone. Not only malicious, unclean, proud thoughts, but even foolish thoughts, are sinful thoughts. If <hi type="italic">vain thoughts lodge in the heart,</hi> they defile it (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.14">Jer. iv. 14</reference>), which is a reason why we should <hi type="italic">keep our hearts with all diligence,</hi> and harbour no thoughts there which cannot give a good account of themselves, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.5">Gen. vi. 5</reference>. (2.) Such as are openly abusive: <hi type="italic">The scorner,</hi> who gives ill-language to every body, takes a pleasure in affronting people and reflecting upon them, <hi type="italic">is an abomination to men;</hi> none that have any sense of honour and virtue will care to keep company with him. <hi type="italic">The seat of the scornful</hi> is the <hi type="italic">pestilential chair</hi> (as the LXX. calls it, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Ps. i. 1</reference>), which no wise man will come near, for fear of taking the infection. Those that strive to make others odious do but make themselves so.

<div eID="gen14402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14403" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> <hi type="italic">If</hi> thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength <hi type="italic">is</hi> small. <div eID="gen14403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14404" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. In <hi type="italic">the day of adversity</hi> we are apt to <hi type="italic">faint,</hi> to droop and be discouraged, to desist from our work, and to despair of relief. Our spirits sink, and then our hands hang down and our knees grow feeble, and we become unfit for anything. And often those that are most cheerful when they are well droop most, and are most dejected, when any thing ails them. 2. This is an evidence that our <hi type="italic">strength is small,</hi> and is a means of weakening it more. "It is a sign that thou art not a man of any resolution, any firmness of thought, any consideration, any faith (for that is the strength of a soul), if thou canst not bear up under an afflictive change of thy condition." Some are so feeble that they can bear nothing; if a trouble does but <hi type="italic">touch</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Job.4.5">Job iv. 5</reference>), nay, if it does but threaten them, they faint immediately and are ready to give up all for gone; and by this means they render themselves unfit to grapple with their trouble and unable to help themselves. <hi type="italic">Be of good courage</hi> therefore, <hi type="italic">and God shall strengthen thy heart.</hi>  <div eID="gen14404" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv69"/><title type="x-s3">Pleasure and Advantages of Wisdom.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv69"/> <div sID="gen14405" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> If thou forbear to deliver <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> drawn unto death, and <hi type="italic">those that are</hi> ready to be slain; <hi type="super">12</hi> If thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider <hi type="italic">it?</hi> and he that keepeth thy soul, doth <hi type="italic">not</hi> he know <hi type="italic">it?</hi> and shall <hi type="italic">not</hi> he render to <hi type="italic">every</hi> man according to his works? <div eID="gen14405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14406" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A great duty required of us, and that is to appear for the relief of oppressed innocency. If we see the lives or livelihoods of any in danger of being taken away unjustly, we ought to bestir ourselves all we can to save them, by disproving the false accusations on which they are condemned and seeking out proofs of their innocency. Though the persons be not such as we are under any particular obligation to, we must help them, out of a general zeal for justice. If any be set upon by force and violence, and it be in our power to rescue them, we ought to do it. Nay, if we see any through ignorance exposing themselves to danger, or fallen in distress, as travellers upon the road, ships at sea, or any the like, it is our duty, though it be with peril to ourselves, to hasten with help to them and not <hi type="italic">forbear to deliver them,</hi> not to be slack, or remiss, or indifferent, in such a case. 2. An answer to the excuse that is commonly make for the omission of this duty. Thou wilt say, "<hi type="italic">Behold, we knew it not;</hi> we were not aware of the imminency of the danger the person was in; we could not be sure that he was innocent, nor did we know how to prove his innocence, nor which way to do any thing in favour of him, else we would have helped him." Now, (1.) It is easy to make such an excuse as this, sufficient to avoid the censures of men, for perhaps they cannot disprove us when we say, <hi type="italic">We knew it not,</hi> or, <hi type="italic">We forgot;</hi> and the temptation to tell a lie for the excusing of a fault is very strong when we know that it is impossible to be disproved, the truth lying wholly in our own breast, as when we say, <hi type="italic">We thought so and so, and really designed it,</hi> which no one is conscious of but ourselves. (2.) It is not so easy with such excuses to evade the judgment of God; and to the discovery of that we lie open and by the determination of that we must abide. Now, [1.] God <hi type="italic">ponders the heart and keeps the soul;</hi> he keeps an eye upon it, observes all the motions of it; its most secret thoughts and intents are all naked and open before him. It is his prerogative to do so, and that in which he glories. <reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">Jer. xvii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">I the Lord search the heart.</hi> He <hi type="italic">keeps the soul,</hi> holds it in life. This is a good reason why we should be tender of the lives of others, and do all we can to preserve them, because our lives have been precious in the sight of God and he has graciously kept them. [2.] He knows and considers whether the excuse we make be true or no, whether it was because we did not know it or whether the true reason was not because we did not love our neighbour as we ought, but were selfish, and regardless both of God and man. Let this serve to silence all our frivolous pleas, by which we think to stop the mouth of conscience when it charges us with the omission of plain duty: <hi type="italic">Does not he that ponders the heart consider it?</hi> [3.] He will judge us accordingly. As his knowledge cannot be imposed upon, so his justice cannot be biassed, but he will <hi type="italic">render to every man according to his works,</hi> not only the commission of evil works, but the omission of good works.

<div eID="gen14406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14407" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> My son, eat thou honey, because <hi type="italic">it is</hi> good; and the honeycomb, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> sweet to thy taste: <hi type="super">14</hi> So <hi type="italic">shall</hi> the knowledge of wisdom <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto thy soul: when thou hast found <hi type="italic">it,</hi> then there shall be a reward, and thy expectation shall not be cut off. <div eID="gen14407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14408" type="x-p"/> We are here quickened to the study of wisdom by the consideration both of the pleasure and the profit of it. 1. It will be very pleasant. We <hi type="italic">eat honey because it is sweet to the taste,</hi> and upon that account we call it <hi type="italic">good,</hi> especially that which runs first from the <hi type="italic">honey-comb.</hi> Canaan was said to flow with milk and honey, and honey was the common food of the country (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.41-Luke.24.42">Luke xxiv. 41, 42</reference>), even for children, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.15">Isa. vii. 15</reference>. Thus should we feed upon wisdom, and relish the good instructions of it. Those that have tasted honey need no further proof that it is sweet, nor can they by any argument be convinced of the contrary; so those that have experienced the power of truth and godliness are abundantly satisfied of the pleasure of both; they have tasted the sweetness of them, and all the atheists in the world with their sophistry, and the profane with their banter, cannot alter their sentiments. 2. It will be very profitable. Honey may be <hi type="italic">sweet to the taste</hi> and yet not wholesome, but wisdom has a future recompence attending it, as well as a present sweetness in it. "Thou art permitted to <hi type="italic">eat honey,</hi> and the agreeableness of it to thy taste invites thee to it; but thou hast much more reason to relish and digest the precepts <hi type="italic">of wisdom,</hi> for <hi type="italic">when thou hast found</hi> that, <hi type="italic">there shall be a reward;</hi> thou shalt be paid for thy pleasure, while the servants of sin pay dearly for their pains. Wisdom does indeed set thee to work, but <hi type="italic">there shall be a reward;</hi> it does indeed raise great expectations in thee, but as thy labour, so thy hope, shall not be in vain; <hi type="italic">thy expectation shall not be cut off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.18">ch. xxiii. 18</reference>), nay, it shall be infinitely outdone."  <div eID="gen14408" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv70"/><title type="x-s3">Cautions against Envy.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv70"/> <div sID="gen14409" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Lay not wait, O wicked <hi type="italic">man,</hi> against the dwelling of the righteous; spoil not his resting place: <hi type="super">16</hi> For a just <hi type="italic">man</hi> falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief. <div eID="gen14409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14410" type="x-p"/> This is spoken, not so much by way of counsel to wicked men (they will not receive instruction, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.9">ch. xxiii. 9</reference>), but rather in defiance of them, for the encouragement of good people that are threatened by them. See here, 1. The designs of the wicked against the righteous, and the success they promise themselves in those designs. The plot is laid deeply: They <hi type="italic">lay wait against the dwelling of the righteous,</hi> thinking to charge some iniquity upon it, or compass some design against it; they lie in wait at the door, to catch him when he stirs out, as David's persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.1">Ps. lix.</reference> <hi type="italic">title.</hi> The hope is raised high; they doubt not but to <hi type="italic">spoil his dwelling-place</hi> because he is weak and cannot support it, because his condition is low and distressed, and he is almost down already. All this is a fruit of the old enmity in the seed of the serpent against the seed of the woman. <hi type="italic">The blood-thirsty hate the upright.</hi> 2. The folly and frustration of these designs (1.) The righteous man, whose ruin was expected, recovers himself. He <hi type="italic">falls seven times</hi> into trouble, but, by the blessing of God upon his wisdom and integrity, he <hi type="italic">rises again,</hi> sees through his troubles and sees better times after them. The <hi type="italic">just man falls,</hi> sometimes <hi type="italic">falls seven times</hi> perhaps, into sin, sins of infirmity, through the surprise of temptation; but he <hi type="italic">rises again</hi> by repentance, finds mercy with God, and regains his peace. (2.) <hi type="italic">The wicked</hi> man, who expected to see his ruin and to help it forward, is undone. He <hi type="italic">falls into mischief;</hi> his sins and his troubles are his utter destruction.

<div eID="gen14410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14411" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth: <hi type="super">18</hi> Lest the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> see <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him. <div eID="gen14411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14412" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The pleasure we are apt to take in the troubles of an enemy is forbidden us. If any have done us an ill turn, or if we bear them ill-will only because they stand in our light or in our way, when any damage comes to them (suppose they fall), or any danger (suppose they stumble), our corrupt hearts are too apt to conceive a secret delight and satisfaction in it—<hi type="italic">Aha! so would we have it; they are entangled; the wilderness has shut them in</hi>—or, as Tyrus said concerning Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.2">Ezek. xxvi. 2</reference>) <hi type="italic">I shall be replenished, now she is laid waste.</hi> "Men hope in the ruin of their enemies or rivals to wreak their revenge or to find their account; but be not thou so inhuman; <hi type="italic">rejoice not when</hi> the worst <hi type="italic">enemy</hi> thou hast <hi type="italic">falls.</hi>" There may be a holy joy in the destruction of God's enemies, as it tends to the glory of God and the welfare of the church (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.10">Ps. lviii. 10</reference>); but in the ruin of our enemies, as such, we must by no means rejoice; on the contrary, we must weep even with them when they weep (as David, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.13-Ps.35.14">Ps. xxxv. 13, 14</reference>), and that in sincerity, not so much as letting our hearts be secretly glad at their calamities. 2. The provocation which that pleasure gives to God is assigned as the reason of that prohibition: <hi type="italic">The Lord</hi> will <hi type="italic">see it,</hi> though it be hidden in the heart only, <hi type="italic">and it</hi> will <hi type="italic">displease him,</hi> as it will displease a prudent father to see one child triumph in the correction of another, which he ought to tremble at, and take warning by, not knowing how soon it may be his own case, he having so often deserved it. Solomon adds an argument <hi type="italic">ad hominem—addressed to the individual:</hi> "Thou canst not do a greater kindness to <hi type="italic">thy enemy,</hi> when he has fallen, than to rejoice in it; for them, to cross thee and vex thee, God will <hi type="italic">turn his wrath from him;</hi> for, as <hi type="italic">the wrath of man works not the righteousness of God,</hi> so the righteousness of God was never intended to gratify the wrath of man, and humour his foolish passions; rather than seem to do that he will adjourn the execution of his wrath: nay, it is implied that when he <hi type="italic">turns his wrath from him</hi> he will turn it against thee and the cup of trembling shall be put into thy hand."

<div eID="gen14412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14413" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Fret not thyself because of evil <hi type="italic">men,</hi> neither be thou envious at the wicked; <hi type="super">20</hi> For there shall be no reward to the evil <hi type="italic">man;</hi> the candle of the wicked shall be put out. <div eID="gen14413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14414" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. He repeats the caution he had before given against envying the pleasures and successes of wicked man in their wicked ways. This he quotes from his father David, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1">Ps. xxxvii. 1</reference>. We must not in any case <hi type="italic">fret</hi> ourselves, or make ourselves uneasy, whatever God does in his providence how disagreeable soever it is to our sentiments, interests, and expectations, we must acquiesce in it. Even that which grieves us must not <hi type="italic">fret</hi> us; nor must our eye be evil against any because God is good. Are we more wise or just than he? If wicked people prosper, we must not therefore incline to do as they do. 2. He gives a reason for this caution, taken from the end of that way which wicked man walk in. Envy not their prosperity; for, (1.) There is no true happiness in it: <hi type="italic">Thee shall be no reward to the evil man;</hi> his prosperity only serves for his present subsistence; these are all the good things he must ever expect: there is none intended him in the world of retribution. <hi type="italic">He has his reward,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.6.2">Matt. vi. 2</reference>. He shall have none. Those are not to be envied that have their portion in this life and must out-live it, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>. (2.) There is no continuance in it; their <hi type="italic">candle</hi> shines brightly, but it shall presently <hi type="italic">be put out,</hi> and a final period put to all their comforts, <reference osisRef="Job.21.14">Job xxi. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1-Ps.37.2">Ps. xxxvii. 1, 2</reference>.  <div eID="gen14414" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv71"/><title type="x-s3">Counsel to Magistrates.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv71"/> <div sID="gen14415" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> My son, fear thou the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> and the king: <hi type="italic">and</hi> meddle not with them that are given to change: <hi type="super">22</hi> For their calamity shall rise suddenly; and who knoweth the ruin of them both? <div eID="gen14415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14416" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Religion and loyalty must go together. As men, it is our duty to honour our Creator, to worship and reverence him, and to be always in his fear; as members of a community, incorporated for mutual benefit, it is our duty to be faithful and dutiful to the government God has set over us, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1-Rom.13.2">Rom. xiii. 1, 2</reference>. Those that are truly religious will be loyal, in conscience towards God; the godly in the land will be the <hi type="italic">quiet in the land;</hi> and those are not truly loyal, or will be so no longer than is for their interest, that are not religious. How should he be true to his prince that is false to his God? And, if they come in competition, it is an adjudged case, we must <hi type="italic">obey God rather than men.</hi> 2. Innovations in both are to be dreaded. Have nothing to do, he does not say, with those that <hi type="italic">change,</hi> for there may be cause to change for the better, but <hi type="italic">those that are given to change,</hi> that affect change for change-sake, out of a peevish discontent with that which is and a fondness for novelty, or a desire to fish in troubled waters: <hi type="italic">Meddle not with those that are given to change</hi> either in religion or in a civil government; <hi type="italic">come not into their secret;</hi> join not with them in their cabals, nor enter into the mystery of their iniquity. 3. Those that are of restless, factious, turbulent spirits, commonly pull mischief upon their own heads ere they are aware: <hi type="italic">Their calamity shall rise suddenly.</hi> Though they carry on their designs with the utmost secresy, they will be discovered, and brought to condign punishment, when they little think of it. <hi type="italic">Who knows</hi> the time and manner of <hi type="italic">the ruin</hi> which both God and the king will bring on their contemners, <hi type="italic">both</hi> on them and those that meddle with them?

<div eID="gen14416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14417" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> These <hi type="italic">things</hi> also <hi type="italic">belong</hi> to the wise. <hi type="italic">It is</hi> not good to have respect of persons in judgment. 24 He that saith unto the wicked, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> righteous; him shall the people curse, nations shall abhor him: <hi type="super">25</hi> But to them that rebuke <hi type="italic">him</hi> shall be delight, and a good blessing shall come upon them. <hi type="super">26</hi> <hi type="italic">Every man</hi> shall kiss <hi type="italic">his</hi> lips that giveth a right answer. <div eID="gen14417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14418" type="x-p"/> Here are lessons for <hi type="italic">wise</hi> men, that is, judges and princes. As subjects must do their duty, and be obedient to magistrates, so magistrates must do their duty in administering justice to their subjects, both in pleas of the crown and causes between party and party. These are lessons for them. 1. They must always weigh the merits of a cause, and not be swayed by any regard, one way or other, to the parties concerned: <hi type="italic">It is not good</hi> in itself, nor can it ever do well, <hi type="italic">to have respect of persons in judgment;</hi> the consequences of it cannot but be the perverting of justice and doing wrong under colour of law and equity. A good judge will know the truth, not know faces, so as to countenance a friend and help him out in a bad cause, or so much as omit any thing that can be said or done in favour of a righteous cause, when it is the cause of an enemy. 2. They must never connive at or encourage wicked people in their wicked practices. Magistrates in their places, and ministers in theirs, are to deal faithfully and the wicked man, though he be a great man or a particular friend, to convict him of his wickedness, to show him what will be in the end thereof, to discover him to others, that they may avoid him. But if those whose office it is thus to show people their transgressions palliate them and connive at them, if they excuse the wicked man, much more if they prefer him and associate with him (which is, in effect, to say, <hi type="italic">Thou art righteous</hi>), they shall justly be looked upon as enemies to the public peace and welfare, which they ought to advance, and <hi type="italic">the people shall curse them</hi> and cry out shame on them; and even those of other <hi type="italic">nations shall abhor them,</hi> as base betrayers of their trust. 3. They must discountenance and give check to all fraud, violence, injustice, and immorality; and, though thereby they may disoblige a particular person, yet they will recommend themselves to the favour of God and man. Let magistrates and ministers, and private persons too that are capable of doing it, <hi type="italic">rebuke</hi> the wicked, that they may bring them to repentance or put them to shame, and they shall have the comfort of it in their own bosoms: <hi type="italic">To them shall be delight,</hi> when their consciences witness for them that they have been witnesses for God; <hi type="italic">and a good blessing shall come upon them,</hi> the blessing of God and good men; they shall be deemed religion's patrons and their country's patriots. See <reference osisRef="Prov.28.23">ch. xxviii. 23</reference>. 4. They must always give judgment according to equity (<reference osisRef="Prov.24.26">v. 26</reference>); they must <hi type="italic">give a right answer,</hi> that is, give their opinion and pass sentence according to law and them true merits of the cause; and <hi type="italic">every one shall kiss his lips that</hi> does so, that is, shall love and honour him, and be subject to his orders, for there is a kiss of allegiance as well as of affection. He that in common conversation likewise speaks pertinently and with sincerity recommends himself to his company and is beloved and respected by all.

<div eID="gen14418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14419" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house. <div eID="gen14419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14420" type="x-p"/> This is a rule of prudence in the management of household affairs; for all good men should be good husbands, and manage with discretion, which would prevent a great deal of sin, and trouble, and disgrace to their profession. 1. We must prefer necessaries before conveniences, and not lay that out for show which should be expended for the support of the family. We must be contented with a mean cottage for a habitation, rather than want, or go in debt for, food convenient. 2. We must not think of building till we can afford it: "First apply thyself to <hi type="italic">thy work without in the field;</hi> let thy ground be put into good order; look after thy husbandry, for it is that by which thou must get; and, when thou hast got well by that, then, and not till then, thou mayest think of rebuilding and beautifying <hi type="italic">thy house,</hi> for that is it upon which, and in which, thou wilt have occasion to spend." Many have ruined their estates and families by laying out money on that which brings nothing in, beginning <hi type="italic">to build</hi> when they were <hi type="italic">not able to finish.</hi> Some understand it as advice to young men not to marry (for by that the house is built) till they have set up in the world, and not wherewith to maintain a wife and children comfortably. 3. When we have any great design on foot it is wisdom to take it before us, and make the necessary preparations, before we fall to work, that, when it is begun, it may not stand still for want of materials. Solomon observed this rule himself in building the house of God; all was made ready <hi type="italic">before it was brought to the ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.7">1 Kings vi. 7</reference>.

<div eID="gen14420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14421" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Be not a witness against thy neighbour without cause; and deceive <hi type="italic">not</hi> with thy lips. <hi type="super">29</hi> Say not, I will do so to him as he hath done to me: I will render to the man according to his work. <div eID="gen14421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14422" type="x-p"/> We are here forbidden to be in any thing injurious to our neighbour, particularly in and by the forms of law, either, 1. As <hi type="italic">a witness:</hi> "Never bear a testimony against any man <hi type="italic">without cause,</hi> unless what thou sayest thou knowest to be punctually true and thou hast a clear call to testify it. Never bear a false testimony against any one;" for it follows, "<hi type="italic">Deceive not with thy lips;</hi> deceive not the judge and jury, deceive not those whom thou conversest with, into an ill opinion of thy neighbour. When thou speakest of thy neighbour do not only speak that which is true, but take heed lest, in the manner of thy speaking, thou insinuate any thing that is otherwise and so shouldst deceive by innuendos or hyperboles." Or, 2. As a plaintiff or prosecutor. If there be occasion to bring an action or information against thy neighbour, let it not be from a spirit of revenge. "<hi type="italic">Say not,</hi> I am resolved I will be even with him: <hi type="italic">I will do so to him as he had done to me.</hi>" Even a righteous cause becomes unrighteous when it is thus prosecuted with malice. <hi type="italic">Say not, I will render to the man according to his work,</hi> and make him pay dearly for it; for it is God's prerogative to do so, and we must leave it to him, and not step into his throne, or take his work out of his hands. If we will needs be our own carvers, and judges in our own cause, we forfeit the benefit of an appeal to God's tribunal; therefore we must not avenge ourselves, because he has said, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine.</hi>  <div eID="gen14422" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv72"/><title type="x-s3">The Vineyard of the Slothful.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv72"/> <div sID="gen14423" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> I went by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding; <hi type="super">31</hi> And, lo, it was all grown over with thorns, <hi type="italic">and</hi> nettles had covered the face thereof, and the stone wall thereof was broken down. 32 Then I saw, <hi type="italic">and</hi> considered <hi type="italic">it</hi> well: I looked upon <hi type="italic">it, and</hi> received instruction. 33 <hi type="italic">Yet</hi> a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: <hi type="super">34</hi> So shall thy poverty come <hi type="italic">as</hi> one that travelleth; and thy want as an armed man. <div eID="gen14423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14424" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The view which Solomon took of <hi type="italic">the field and vineyard of the slothful</hi> man. He did not go on purpose to see it, but, as he passed by, observing the fruitfulness of the ground, as it is very proper for travellers to do, and his subjects' management of their land, as it is very proper for magistrates to do, he cast his eye upon a <hi type="italic">field</hi> and a <hi type="italic">vineyard</hi> unlike all the rest; for, though the soil was good, yet there was nothing growing in them but <hi type="italic">thorns and nettles,</hi> not here and there one, but they were all overrun with weeds; and, if there had been any fruit, it would have been eaten up by the beasts, for there was no fence: <hi type="italic">The stone-wall was broken down</hi> See the effects of that curse upon the ground (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.18">Gen. iii. 18</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth unto thee,</hi> and nothing else unless thou take pains with it." See what a blessing to the world the husbandman's calling is, and what a wilderness this earth, even Canaan itself, would be without it. <hi type="italic">The king himself is served of the field,</hi> but he would be ill served if God did not teach the husbandman discretion and diligence to clear the ground, plant it, sow it, and fence it. See what a great difference there is between some and others in the management even of their worldly affairs, and how little some consult their reputation, not caring though they proclaim their slothfulness, in the manifest effects of it, to all that pass by, shamed by their neighbour's diligence. 2. The reflections which he made upon it. He paused a little <hi type="italic">and considered it, looked</hi> again <hi type="italic">upon it, and received instruction.</hi> He did not break out into any passionate censures of the owner, did not call him any ill names, but he endeavoured himself to get good by the observation and to be quickened by it to diligence. Note, Those that are to give instruction to others must receive instruction themselves, and instruction may be received, not only from what we read and hear, but from what we see, not only from what we see of the works of God, but from what we see of the manners of man, not only from men's good manners, but from their evil manners. Plutarch relates a saying of Cato Major, "That wise men profit more by fools than fools by wise men; for wise men will avoid the faults of fools, but fools will not imitate the virtues of wise men." Solomon reckoned that he <hi type="italic">received instruction</hi> by this sight, though it did not suggest to him any new notion or lesson, but only put him in mind of an observation he himself had formerly made, both of the ridiculous folly of the sluggard (who, when he has needful work to do, lies dozing in bed and cries, <hi type="italic">Yet a little sleep, a little slumber,</hi> and still it will be a little more, till he has slept his eyes out, and, instead of being fitted by sleep for business, as wise men are, he is dulled, and stupefied, and made good for nothing) and of certain misery that attends him: his <hi type="italic">poverty comes as one that travels;</hi> it is constantly coming nearer and nearer to him, and will be upon him speedily, and want seizes him as irresistibly <hi type="italic">as an armed man,</hi> a highwayman that will strip him of all he has. Now this is applicable, not only to our worldly business, to show what a scandalous thing slothfulness in that is, and how injurious to the family, but to the affairs of our souls. Note, (1.) Our souls are our fields and vineyards, which we are every one of us to take care of, to dress, and to keep. They are capable of being improved with good husbandry; that may be got out of them which will be fruit abounding to our account. We are charged with them, to occupy them till our Lord come; and a great deal of care and pains it is requisite that we should take about them. (2.) These fields and vineyards are often in a very bad state, not only no fruit brought forth, but all overgrown with <hi type="italic">thorns</hi> and <hi type="italic">nettles</hi> (scratching, stinging, inordinate lusts and passions, pride, covetousness, sensuality, malice, those are the thorns and nettles, the wild grapes, which the unsanctified heart produces), no guard kept against the enemy, but the <hi type="italic">stone-wall broken down,</hi> and all lies in common, all exposed. (3.) Where it is thus it is owing to the sinner's own slothfulness and folly. He is a sluggard, loves sleep, hates labour; and he is void of understanding, understands neither his business nor his interest; he is perfectly besotted. (4.) The issue of it will certainly be the ruin of the soul and all its welfare. It is everlasting want that thus comes upon it as an armed man. We know the place assigned to the wicked and slothful servant.  <chapter eID="Prov.24"/> <div eID="gen14424" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv73"/><title type="x-s3">Pleasures and Advantages of Wisdom.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv73"/> <div sID="gen14426" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out. <div eID="gen14426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14427" type="x-p"/> This verse is the title of this latter collection of Solomon's proverbs, for he <hi type="italic">sought out and set in order many proverbs,</hi> that by them he might be still <hi type="italic">teaching the people knowledge,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.9">Eccl. xii. 9</reference>. Observe, 1. The proverbs were Solomon's, who was divinely inspired to deliver, for the use of the church, these wise and weighty sentences; we have had many, but still there are more. Yet herein Christ is greater than Solomon, for if we had all upon record that Christ said, and did, that was instructive, <hi type="italic">the world could not contain the books that would be written,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.21.25">John xxi. 25</reference>. 2. The publishers were Hezekiah's servants, who, it is likely, herein acted as his servants, being appointed by him to do this good service to the church, among other good offices that he did <hi type="italic">in the law and in the commandments,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.21">2 Chron. xxxi. 21</reference>. Whether he employed the prophets in this work, as Isaiah, Hosea, or Micah, who lived in his time, or some that were trained up in the schools of the prophets, or some of the priests and Levites, to whom we find him giving a charge concerning divine things (<reference osisRef="2Chr.29.4">2 Chron. xxix. 4</reference>), or (as the Jews think) his princes and ministers of state, who were more properly called his <hi type="italic">servants,</hi> is not certain; if the work was done by Eliakim, and Joah, and Shebna, it was no diminution to their character. They copied out these proverbs from the records of Solomon's reign, and published them as an appendix to the former edition of this book. It may be a piece of very good service to the church to publish other man's works that have lain hidden in obscurity, perhaps a great while. Some think they culled these out of the 3000 proverbs which Solomon spoke (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.32">1 Kings iv. 32</reference>), leaving out those that were physical, and that pertained to natural philosophy, and preserving such only as were divine and moral; and in this collection some observe that special regard was had to those observations which concern kings and their administration.  <div eID="gen14427" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv74"/><title type="x-s3">Prudential Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv74"/> <div sID="gen14428" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings <hi type="italic">is</hi> to search out a matter. 3 The heaven for height, and the earth for depth, and the heart of kings <hi type="italic">is</hi> unsearchable. <div eID="gen14428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14429" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. An instance given of the honour of God: <hi type="italic">It is his glory to conceal a matter.</hi> He needs not search into any thing, for he perfectly knows every thing by a clear and certain view, and nothing can be hidden from him; and yet his own <hi type="italic">way is in the sea</hi> and his <hi type="italic">path in the great waters.</hi> There is an unfathomable depth in his counsels, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Rom. xi. 33</reference>. It is but a little portion that is heard of him. <hi type="italic">Clouds and darkness are round about him.</hi> We see what he does, but we know not the reasons. Some refer it to the sins of men; it is his glory to pardon sin, which is covering it, not remembering it, not mentioning it; his forbearance, which he exercises towards sinners, is likewise his honour, in which he seems to keep silence and take no notice of the matter. 2. A double instance of the honour of kings:—(1.) It is God's glory that he needs not <hi type="italic">search into a matter,</hi> because he knows it without search; but it is the honour of kings, with a close application of mind, and by all the methods of enquiry, to search out the matters that are brought before them, to take pains in examining offenders, that they may discover their designs and bring to light the hidden works of darkness, not to give judgment hastily or till they have weighed things, nor to leave it wholly to others to examine things, but to see with their own eyes. (2.) It is God's glory that he cannot himself be found out by searching, and some of that honour is devolved upon kings, wise kings, that <hi type="italic">search out matters;</hi> their <hi type="italic">hearts</hi> are <hi type="italic">unsearchable,</hi> like the <hi type="italic">height of heaven</hi> or the <hi type="italic">depth of the earth,</hi> which we may guess at, but cannot measure. Princes have their <hi type="italic">arcana imperii—state secrets,</hi> designs which are kept private, and reasons of state, which private persons are not competent judges of, and therefore ought not to pry into. Wise princes, when they <hi type="italic">search into a matter,</hi> have reaches which one would not think of, as Solomon, when he called of a sword to divide the living child with, designing thereby to discover the true mother.

<div eID="gen14429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14430" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer. <hi type="super">5</hi> Take away the wicked <hi type="italic">from</hi> before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness. <div eID="gen14430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14431" type="x-p"/> This shows that the vigorous endeavour of a prince to suppress vice, and reform the manners of his people, is the most effectual way to support his government. Observe, 1. What the duty of magistrates is: To <hi type="italic">take away the wicked,</hi> to use their power for the terror of evil works and evil workers, not only to banish those that are vicious and profane from their presence, and forbid them the court, but so to frighten them and restrain them that they may not spread the infection of their wickedness among their subjects. This is called <hi type="italic">taking away the dross from the silver,</hi> which is done by the force of fire. Wicked people are the dross of a nation, the scum of the country, and, as such, to be taken away. If men will not take them away, God will, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.119">Ps. cxix. 119</reference>. If the <hi type="italic">wicked be taken away from before the king,</hi> if he abandon them and show his detestation of their wicked courses, it will go far towards the disabling of them to do mischief. The reformation of the court will promote the reformation of the kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.3">Ps. ci. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.101.8">8</reference>. 2. What the advantage will be of their doing this duty. (1.) It will be the bettering of the subjects; they shall be made like silver refined, fit to be made <hi type="italic">vessels of honour.</hi> (2.) It will be the settling of the prince. <hi type="italic">His throne shall be established in</hi> this <hi type="italic">righteousness,</hi> for God will bless his government, the people will be pliable to it, and so it will become durable.

<div eID="gen14431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14432" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king, and stand not in the place of great <hi type="italic">men:</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> For better <hi type="italic">it is</hi> that it be said unto thee, Come up hither; than that thou shouldest be put lower in the presence of the prince whom thine eyes have seen. <div eID="gen14432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14433" type="x-p"/> Here we see, 1. That religion is so far from destroying good manners that it reaches us to behave ourselves lowly and reverently towards our superiors, to keep our distance, and give place to those to whom it belongs "<hi type="italic">Put not forth thyself</hi> rudely and carelessly <hi type="italic">in the king's presence,</hi> or in the presence of great men; do not <hi type="italic">compare with them</hi>" (so some understand it); "do not vie with them in apparel, furniture, gardens, house-keeping, or retinue, for that is an affront to them and will waste thy own estate." 2. That religion teaches us humility and self-denial, which is a better lesson than that of good manners: "Deny thyself the place thou art entitled to; covet not to make a fair show, nor air at preferment, nor thrust thyself into the company of those that are above thee; be content in a low sphere if that is it which God has allotted to thee." The reason he gives is because this is really the way to advancement, as our Saviour shows in a parable that seems to be borrowed from this, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.9">Luke xiv. 9</reference>. Not that we must <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> pretend modesty and humility, and make a stratagem of it, for the courting of honour, but <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> we must really be modest and humble, because God will put honour on such and so will men too. It is better, more for a man's satisfaction and reputation, to be advanced above his pretensions and expectations, than to be thrust down below them, <hi type="italic">in the presence of the prince,</hi> whom it was a great piece of honour to be admitted to the sight of and a great piece of presumption to look upon without leave.

<div eID="gen14433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14434" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Go not forth hastily to strive, lest <hi type="italic">thou know not</hi> what to do in the end thereof, when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame. <hi type="super">9</hi> Debate thy cause with thy neighbour <hi type="italic">himself;</hi> and discover not a secret to another: <hi type="super">10</hi> Lest he that heareth <hi type="italic">it</hi> put thee to shame, and thine infamy turn not away. <div eID="gen14434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14435" type="x-p"/> I. Here is good counsel given about going to law:—1.
