"Be not hasty in bringing an action, before thou hast thyself considered it, and consulted with thy friends about it: <hi type="italic">Go not forth hastily to strive;</hi> do not send for a writ in a passion, or upon the first appearance of right on thy side, but weigh the matter deliberately, because we are apt to be partial in our own cause; consider the certainty of the expenses and the uncertainty of the success, how much care and vexation it will be the occasion of, and, after all, the cause may go against thee; surely then thou shouldst not <hi type="italic">go forth hastily to strive.</hi>" 2. "Bring not an action before thou hast tried to end the matter amicably ( <reference osisRef="Prov.25.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Debate thy cause with thy neighbour</hi> privately, and perhaps you will understand one another better and see that there is no occasion to go to law." In public quarrels the war that must at length end might better have been prevented by a treaty of peace, and a great deal of blood and treasure spared. It is so in private quarrels: "Sue not thy neighbour as a <hi type="italic">heathen man and a publican</hi> until thou hast told him his fault between thee and him alone, and he has refused to refer the matter, or to come to an accommodation. Perhaps the matter in variance is a secret, not fit to be divulged to any, much less to be brought upon the stage before the country; and therefore end it privately, that it may not be discovered." <hi type="italic">Reveal not the secret of another,</hi> so some read it. "Do not, in revenge, to disgrace thy adversary, disclose that which should be kept private and which does not at all belong to the cause." <div eID="gen14435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14436" type="x-p"/> II. Two reasons he gives why we should be thus cautious in going to law:—1. "Because otherwise the cause will be in danger of going against thee, and thou wilt <hi type="italic">not know what to do</hi> when the defendant has justified himself in what thou didst charge upon him, and made it out that thy complaint was frivolous and vexatious and that thou hadst no just cause of action, and so <hi type="italic">put thee to shame,</hi> non-suit thee, and force thee to pay costs, all which might have been prevented by a little consideration." 2. "Because it will turn very much to thy reproach if thou fall under the character of being litigious. Not only the defendant himself (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.8">v. 8</reference>), but he that hears the cause tried will <hi type="italic">put thee to shame,</hi> will expose thee as a man of no principle, and <hi type="italic">thy infamy will not turn away;</hi> thou wilt never retrieve thy reputation."  <div eID="gen14436" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv75"/><title type="x-s3">Instructive Similes.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv75"/> <div sID="gen14437" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> A word fitly spoken <hi type="italic">is like</hi> apples of gold in pictures of silver. <hi type="super">12</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, <hi type="italic">so is</hi> a wise reprover upon an obedient ear. <div eID="gen14437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14438" type="x-p"/> Solomon here shows how much it becomes a man, 1. To speak pertinently: <hi type="italic">A word upon the wheels,</hi> that runs well, is well-circumstanced, in proper time and place—instruction, advice, or comfort, given seasonably, and in apt expressions, adapted to the case of the person spoken to and agreeing with the character of the person speaking—<hi type="italic">is like golden</hi> balls resembling <hi type="italic">apples,</hi> or like true apples of a golden colour (golden rennets), or perhaps gilded, as sometimes we have gilded laurels, and those embossed <hi type="italic">in pictures of silver,</hi> or rather brought to table in a silver network basket, or in a silver box of that which we call <hi type="italic">filigree</hi>—work, through which the golden apples might be seen. Doubtless in was some ornament of the table, then well known. As that was very pleasing to the eye, so is <hi type="italic">a word fitly spoken</hi> to the ear. 2. Especially to give a reproof with discretion, and so as to make it acceptable. If it be well given, by <hi type="italic">a wise reprover,</hi> and well taken, by an <hi type="italic">obedient ear,</hi> it is an <hi type="italic">earring of gold</hi> and an <hi type="italic">ornament of fine gold,</hi> very graceful and well becoming both the reprover and the reproved; both will have their praise, the reprover for giving it so prudently and the reproved for taking it so patiently and making a good use of it. Others will commend them both, and they will have satisfaction in each other; he who gave the reproof is pleased that it had the desired effect, and he to whom it was given has reason to be thankful for it as a kindness. <hi type="italic">That is well given,</hi> we say, <hi type="italic">that is well taken;</hi> yet it does not always prove that that is well taken which is well given. It were to be wished that a <hi type="italic">wise reprover</hi> should always meet with an <hi type="italic">obedient ear,</hi> but often it is not so.

<div eID="gen14438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14439" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, <hi type="italic">so is</hi> a faithful messenger to them that send him: for he refresheth the soul of his masters. <div eID="gen14439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14440" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What ought to be the care of a servant, the meanest that is sent on an errand and entrusted with any business, much more the greatest, the agent and ambassador of a prince; he ought to be <hi type="italic">faithful to him that sends him,</hi> and to see to it that he do not, by mistake or with design, falsify his trust, and that he be in nothing that lies in his power wanting to his master's interest. Those that act as factors, by commission, ought to act as carefully as for themselves. 2. How much this will be the satisfaction of the master; it will <hi type="italic">refresh his soul</hi> as much as ever the <hi type="italic">cold of snow</hi> (which is hot countries they preserve by art all the year round) refreshed the labourers in the harvest, that <hi type="italic">bore the burden and heat of the day.</hi> The more important the affair was, and the more fear of its miscarrying, the more acceptable is the messenger, if he have managed it successfully and well. A faithful minister, Christ's messenger, should be thus acceptable to us (<reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job xxxiii. 23</reference>); however, he will be a <hi type="italic">sweet savour to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">2 Cor. ii. 15</reference>.

<div eID="gen14440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14441" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Whoso boasteth himself of a false gift <hi type="italic">is like</hi> clouds and wind without rain. <div eID="gen14441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14442" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">He</hi> may be said to boast of a false gift, 1. Who pretends to have received or given that which he never had, which he never gave, makes a noise of his great accomplishments and his good services, but it is all false; he is not what he pretends to be. Or, 2. Who promises what he will give and what he will do, but performs nothing, who raises people's expectations of the mighty things he will do for his country, for his friends, what noble legacies he will leave, but either he has not wherewithal to do what he says or he never designs it. Such a one is like the morning-cloud, that passes away, and disappoints those who looked for rain from it to water the parched ground (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.12">Jude 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">clouds without water.</hi>  <div eID="gen14442" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv76"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv76"/> <div sID="gen14443" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone. <div eID="gen14443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14444" type="x-p"/> Two things are here recommended to us, in dealing with others, as likely means to gain our point:—1. Patience, to bear a present heat without being put into a heat by it, and to wait for a fit opportunity to offer our reasons and to give persons time to consider them. By this means even a <hi type="italic">prince</hi> may be <hi type="italic">persuaded</hi> to do a thing which he seemed very averse to, much more a common person. That which is justice and reason now will be so another time, and therefore we need not urge them with violence now, but wait for a more convenient season. 2. Mildness, to speak without passion or provocation: <hi type="italic">A soft tongue breaks the bone;</hi> it mollifies the roughest spirits and overcomes those that are most morose, like lightning, which, they say, has sometimes broken the bone, and yet not pierced the flesh. Gideon with a soft tongue pacified the Ephraimites and Abigail turned away David's wrath. <hi type="italic">Hard words,</hi> we say, <hi type="italic">break no bones,</hi> and therefore we should bear them patiently; but, it seems, <hi type="italic">soft words</hi> do, and therefore we should, on all occasions, give them prudently.

<div eID="gen14444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14445" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it. <div eID="gen14445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14446" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. We are allowed a sober and moderate use of the delights of sense: <hi type="italic">Hast thou found honey?</hi> It is not forbidden fruit to thee, as it was to Jonathan; thou mayest eat of it with thanksgiving to God, who, having created things grateful to our senses, has given us leave to make use of them. <hi type="italic">Eat as much as is sufficient,</hi> and no more. <hi type="italic">Enough is as good as a feast.</hi> 2. We are cautioned to take heed of excess. We must use all pleasures as we do honey, with a check upon our appetite, lest we take more than does us good and make ourselves sick with it. We are most in danger of surfeiting upon that which is most sweet, and therefore those that fare sumptuously every day have need to watch over themselves, <hi type="italic">lest their hearts be at any time overcharged.</hi> The pleasures of sense lose their sweetness by the excessive use of them and become nauseous, as honey, which turns sour in the stomach; it is therefore our interest, as well as our duty, to use them with sobriety.

<div eID="gen14446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14447" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Withdraw thy foot from thy neighbour's house; lest he be weary of thee, and <hi type="italic">so</hi> hate thee. <div eID="gen14447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14448" type="x-p"/> Here he mentions another pleasure which we must not take too much of, that of visiting our friends, the former for fear of surfeiting ourselves, this for fear of surfeiting our neighbour. 1. It is a piece of civility to visit our neighbours sometimes, to show our respect to them and concern for them, and to cultivate and improve mutual acquaintance and love, and that we may have both the satisfaction and advantage of their conversation. 2. It is wisdom, as well as good manners, not to be troublesome to our friends in our visiting them, not to visit too often, nor stay too long, nor contrive to come at meal-time, nor make ourselves busy in the affairs of their families; hereby we make ourselves cheap, mean, and burdensome. Thy neighbour, who is thus plagued and haunted with thy visits, will be <hi type="italic">weary of thee and hate thee,</hi> and <hi type="italic">that</hi> will be the destruction of friendship which should have been the improvement of it. <hi type="italic">Post tres sæpe dies piscis vilescit et hospes—After the third day fish and company become distasteful.</hi> Familiarity breeds contempt. <hi type="italic">Nulli te facias nimis sodalem—Be not too intimate with any.</hi> He that sponges upon his friend loses him. How much better a friend then is God than any other friend; for we need not withdraw our foot from his house, the throne of his grace (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.34">ch. viii. 34</reference>); the oftener we come to him the better and the more welcome.

<div eID="gen14448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14449" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour <hi type="italic">is</hi> a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow. <div eID="gen14449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14450" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The sin condemned is <hi type="italic">bearing false witness against our neighbour,</hi> either in judgment or in common conversation, contrary to the law of the ninth commandment. 2. That which it is here condemned for is the mischievousness of it; it is in its power to ruin not only men's reputation, but their lives, estates, families, all that is dear to them. A false testimony is every thing that is dangerous; it <hi type="italic">is a maul</hi> (or <hi type="italic">club</hi> to knock a man's brains out with), a flail, which there is no fence against; it is <hi type="italic">a sword</hi> to wound near at hand and a <hi type="italic">sharp arrow</hi> to wound at a distance; we have therefore need to pray, <hi type="italic">Deliver my soul, O Lord! from lying lips,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.120.2">Ps. cxx. 2</reference>.

<div eID="gen14450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14451" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble <hi type="italic">is like</hi> a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint. <div eID="gen14451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14452" type="x-p"/> 1. The <hi type="italic">confidence of an unfaithful man</hi> (so some read it) will be <hi type="italic">like a broken tooth;</hi> his policy, his power, his interest, all that which he trusted in to support him in his wickedness, will fail him in time of trouble, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">Ps. lii. 7</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">Confidence in an unfaithful man</hi> (so we read it), in a man whom we thought trusty and therefore depended on, but who proves otherwise; it proves not only unserviceable, but painful and vexatious, like a <hi type="italic">broken tooth, or a foot out of joint,</hi> which, when we put any stress upon it, not only fails us, but makes us feel from it, especially <hi type="italic">in time of trouble,</hi> when we most expect help from it; it is like a broken reed, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.6">Isa. xxxvi. 6</reference>. Confidence in a faithful God, in time of trouble, will not prove thus; on him we may rest and in him dwell at ease.

<div eID="gen14452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14453" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, <hi type="italic">and as</hi> vinegar upon nitre, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that singeth songs to an heavy heart. <div eID="gen14453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14454" type="x-p"/> 1. The absurdity here censured is <hi type="italic">singing songs to a heavy heart.</hi> Those that are in great sorrow are to be comforted by sympathizing with them, condoling with them, and concurring in their lamentation. If we take that method, the <hi type="italic">moving of our lips may assuage their grief</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.16.5">Job xvi. 5</reference>); but we take a wrong course with them if we think to relieve them by being merry with them, and endeavouring to make them merry; for it adds to their grief to see their friends so little concerned for them; it puts them upon ripping up the causes of their grief, and aggravating them, and makes them harden themselves in sorrow against the assaults of mirth. 2. The absurdities this is compared to are, <hi type="italic">taking away a garment</hi> from a man in <hi type="italic">cold weather,</hi> which makes him colder, and pouring <hi type="italic">vinegar upon nitre,</hi> which, like water upon lime, puts it into a ferment; so improper, so incongruous, is it to sing pleasant songs to one that is of a sorrowful spirit. Some read it in a contrary sense: <hi type="italic">As he that puts on a garment in cold weather</hi> warms the body, or as <hi type="italic">vinegar upon nitre</hi> dissolves it, so he that <hi type="italic">sings songs</hi> of comfort to a person in sorrow refreshes him and dispels his grief.  <div eID="gen14454" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv77"/><title type="x-s3">Forgiveness of Enemies.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv77"/> <div sID="gen14455" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: <hi type="super">22</hi> For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall reward thee. <div eID="gen14455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14456" type="x-p"/> By this it appears that, however the scribes and Pharisees had corrupted the law, not only the commandment of loving our brethren, but even that of loving our enemies, was not only a new, but also an old commandment, an Old-Testament commandment, though our Saviour has given it to us with the new enforcement of his own great example in loving us when we were enemies. Observe, 1. How we must express our love to our enemies by the real offices of kindness, even those that are expensive to ourselves and most acceptable to them: "If they be <hi type="italic">hungry</hi> and <hi type="italic">thirsty,</hi> instead of pleasing thyself with their distress and contriving how to cut off supplies from them, relieve them, as Elisha did the Syrians that came to apprehend him," <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.22">2 King vi. 22</reference>. 2. What encouragement we have to do so. (1.) It will be a likely means to win upon them, and bring them over to be reconciled to us; we shall mollify them as the refiner melts the metal in the crucible, not only by putting it over the fire, but by heaping coals of fire upon it. The way to turn an enemy into a friend is, to act towards him in a friendly manner. If it do not gain him, it will aggravate his sin and punishment, and heap the burning coals of God's wrath upon his head, as rejoicing in his calamity may be an occasion of God's turning his wrath from him, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.17">ch. xxiv. 17</reference>. (2.) However, we shall be no losers by our self-denial: "Whether he relent towards thee or no, <hi type="italic">the Lord shall reward thee;</hi> he shall forgive thee who thus showest thyself to be of a forgiving spirit. He shall provide for thee when thou art in distress (though thou hast been evil and ungrateful), as thou dost for thy enemy; at least it shall be recompensed in the resurrection of the just, when kindnesses done to our enemies shall be remembered as well as those shown to God's friends."  <div eID="gen14456" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv78"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv78"/> <div sID="gen14457" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> The north wind driveth away rain: so <hi type="italic">doth</hi> an angry countenance a backbiting tongue. <div eID="gen14457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14458" type="x-p"/> Here see, 1. How we must discourage sin and witness against it, and particularly the sin of slandering and backbiting; we must frown upon it, and, by giving it an angry countenance, endeavour to put it out of countenance. Slanders would not be so readily spoken as they are if they were not readily heard; but good manners would silence the slanderer if he saw that his tales displeased the company. We should show ourselves uneasy if we heard a dear friend, whom we value, evil-spoken of; the same dislike we should show of evil-speaking in general. If we cannot otherwise reprove, we may do it by our looks. 2. The good effect which this might probably have; who knows but it may silence and drive away a <hi type="italic">backbiting tongue?</hi> Sin, if it be countenanced, becomes daring, but, if it receive any check, it is so conscious of its own shame that it becomes cowardly, and this sin in particular, for many abuse those they speak of only in hopes to curry favour with those they speak to.

<div eID="gen14458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14459" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> better to dwell in the corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman and in a wide house. <div eID="gen14459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14460" type="x-p"/> This is the same with what he had said, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.9">ch. xxi. 9</reference>. Observe, 1. How those are to be pitied that are unequally yoked, especially with such as are brawling and contentious, whether husband or wife; for it is equally true of both. It is better to be alone than to be joined to one who, instead of being a meet-help, is a great hindrance to the comfort of life. 2. How those may sometimes be envied that live in solitude; as they want the comfort of society, so they are free from the vexation of it. And as there are cases which give occasion to say, "Blessed is the womb that has not borne," so there are which give occasion to say, "Blessed is the man who was never married, but who lies like a servant in <hi type="italic">a corner of the house-top.</hi>"

<div eID="gen14460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14461" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> cold waters to a thirsty soul, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> good news from a far country. <div eID="gen14461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14462" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How natural it is to us to desire to hear good news from our friends, and concerning our affairs at a distance. It is sometimes with impatience that we expect to hear from abroad; our souls thirst after it. But we should check the inordinateness of that desire; if it be bad news, it will come too soon, if good, it will be welcome at any time. 2. How acceptable such good news will be when it does come, as refreshing as cold water to one that is thirsty. Solomon himself had much trading abroad, as well as correspondence by his ambassadors with foreign courts; and how pleasant it was to hear of the good success of his negotiations abroad he well knew by experience. Heaven is a country afar off; how refreshing is it to hear good news thence, both in the everlasting gospel, which signified glad tidings, and in the witness of the Spirit with our spirits that we are God's children.

<div eID="gen14462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14463" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> A righteous man falling down before the wicked <hi type="italic">is as</hi> a troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring. <div eID="gen14463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14464" type="x-p"/> It is here represented as a very lamentable thing, and a public grievance, and of ill consequence to many, like the <hi type="italic">troubling</hi> of a <hi type="italic">fountain</hi> and the <hi type="italic">corrupting</hi> of a <hi type="italic">spring,</hi> for the righteous to <hi type="italic">fall down before the wicked,</hi> that is, 1. For the righteous to fall into sin in the sight of the wicked—for them to do any thing unbecoming their profession, which is <hi type="italic">told in Gath,</hi> and <hi type="italic">published in the streets of Ashkelon,</hi> and in which the <hi type="italic">daughters of the Philistines rejoice.</hi> For those that have been <hi type="italic">in reputation for wisdom and honour</hi> to fall from their excellency, this <hi type="italic">troubles the fountains</hi> by grieving some, and <hi type="italic">corrupts the springs</hi> by infecting others and emboldening them to do likewise. 2. For the righteous to be oppressed, and run down, and trampled upon, by the violence or subtlety of evil men, to be displaced and thrust into obscurity, this is the troubling of the fountains of justice and corrupting the very springs of government, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.12 Prov.28.28">ch. xxviii. 12, 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.29.2">xxix. 2</reference>. 3. For the righteous to be cowardly, to truckle to the wicked, to be afraid of opposing his wickedness and basely to yield to him, this is a reflection upon religion, a discouragement to good men, and strengthens the hands of sinners in their sins, and so is like a <hi type="italic">troubled fountain</hi> and a <hi type="italic">corrupt spring.</hi>

<div eID="gen14464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14465" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> not good to eat much honey: so <hi type="italic">for men</hi> to search their own glory <hi type="italic">is not</hi> glory. <div eID="gen14465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14466" type="x-p"/> I. Two things we must be graciously dead to:—1. To the pleasures of sense, for <hi type="italic">it is not good to eat much honey;</hi> though it pleases the taste, and, if eaten with moderation, is very wholesome, yet, if eaten to excess, it becomes nauseous, creates bile, and is the occasion of many diseases. It is true of all the delights of the children of men that they will surfeit, but never satisfy, and they are dangerous to those that allow themselves the liberal use of them. 2. To the praise of man. We must not be greedy of that any more than of pleasure, because, <hi type="italic">for men to search their own glory,</hi> to court applause and covet to make themselves popular, is not their glory, but their shame; every one will laugh at them for it; and the glory which is so courted <hi type="italic">is not glory</hi> when it is got, for it is really no true honour to a man. <div eID="gen14466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14467" type="x-p"/> II. Some give another sense of this verse: <hi type="italic">To eat much honey is not good,</hi> but to search into glorious and excellent things is a great commendation, it is true glory; we cannot therein offend by excess. Others thus: "As honey, though pleasant to the taste, if used immoderately, oppresses the stomach, so an over-curious search into things sublime and glorious, though pleasant to us, if we pry too far, will overwhelm our capacities with a greater glory and lustre than they can bear." Or thus: "You may be surfeited with eating too much honey, but the last of glory, of their glory, the glory of the blessed, is glory; it will be ever fresh, and never pall the appetite."

<div eID="gen14467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14468" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> He that <hi type="italic">hath</hi> no rule over his own spirit <hi type="italic">is like</hi> a city <hi type="italic">that is</hi> broken down, <hi type="italic">and</hi> without walls. <div eID="gen14468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14469" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The good character of a wise and virtuous man implied. He is one that has <hi type="italic">rule over his own spirit;</hi> he maintains the government of himself, and of his own appetites and passions, and does not suffer them to rebel against reason and conscience. He has the rule of his own thoughts, his desires, his inclinations, his resentments, and keeps them all in good order. 2. The bad case of a vicious man, who has not this rule over his own spirit, who, when temptations to excess in eating or drinking are before him, has no government of himself, when he is provoked breaks out into exorbitant passions, such a one is <hi type="italic">like a city that is broken down and without walls.</hi> All that is good goes out, and forsakes him; all that is evil breaks in upon him. He lies exposed to all the temptations of Satan and becomes an easy prey to that enemy; he is also liable to many troubles and vexations; it is likewise as much a reproach to him as it is to a city to have its walls ruined, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.3">Neh. i. 3</reference>.  <chapter eID="Prov.25"/> <div eID="gen14469" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv79"/><title type="x-s3">Proper Treatment of Fools.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv79"/> <div sID="gen14471" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> As snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honour is not seemly for a fool. <div eID="gen14471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14472" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is too common a thing for honour to be given to fools, who are utterly unworthy of it and unfit for it. Bad men, who have neither wit nor grace, are sometimes preferred by princes, and applauded and cried up by the people. <hi type="italic">Folly is set in great dignity,</hi> as Solomon observed, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.6">Eccl. x. 6</reference>. 2. It is very absurd and unbecoming when it is so. It is an incongruous <hi type="italic">as snow in summer,</hi> and as great a disorder in the commonwealth as that is in the course of nature and in the seasons of the year; nay, it is as injurious <hi type="italic">as rain in harvest,</hi> which hinders the labourers and spoils the fruits of the earth when they are ready to be gathered. When bad men are in power they commonly abuse their power, in discouraging virtue, and giving countenance to wickedness, for want of wisdom to discern it and grace to detest it.

<div eID="gen14472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14473" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> As the bird by wandering, as the swallow by flying, so the curse causeless shall not come. <div eID="gen14473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14474" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The folly of passion. It makes men scatter <hi type="italic">causeless curses,</hi> wishing ill to others upon presumption that they are bad and have done ill, when either they mistake the person or misunderstand the fact, or they call evil good and good evil. Give honour to a fool, and he thunders out his anathemas against all that he is disgusted with, right or wrong. Great men, when wicked, think they have a privilege to keep those about them in awe, by cursing them, and swearing at them, which yet is an expression of the most impotent malice and shows their weakness as much as their wickedness. 2. The safety of innocency. He that is cursed without cause, whether by furious imprecations or solemn anathemas, the curse shall do him no more harm than the bird that flies over his head, than Goliath's curses did to David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.43">1 Sam. xvii. 43</reference>. It will fly away like the sparrow or the wild dove, which go nobody knows where, till they return to their proper place, as the curse will at length return upon the head of him that uttered it.

<div eID="gen14474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14475" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool's back. <div eID="gen14475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14476" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. Wicked men are compared to <hi type="italic">the horse</hi> and <hi type="italic">the ass,</hi> so brutish are they, so unreasonable, so unruly, and not to be governed but by force or fear, so low has sin sunk men, so much below themselves. Man indeed is <hi type="italic">born like the wild ass's colt,</hi> but as some by the grace of God are changed, and become rational, so others by custom in sin are hardened, and become more and more sottish, <hi type="italic">as the horse and the mule,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Ps. xxxii. 9</reference>. 2. Direction is given to use them accordingly. Princes, instead of giving <hi type="italic">honour to a fool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.1">v. 1</reference>), must put disgrace upon him—instead of putting power into his hand, must exercise power over him. A <hi type="italic">horse</hi> unbroken needs <hi type="italic">a whip</hi> for correction, and an <hi type="italic">ass a bridle</hi> for direction and to check him when he would turn out of the way; so a vicious man, who will not be under the guidance and restraint of religion and reason, ought to be whipped and bridled, to be rebuked severely, and made to smart for what he has done amiss, and to be restrained from offending any more.

<div eID="gen14476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14477" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him. <hi type="super">5</hi> Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit. <div eID="gen14477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14478" type="x-p"/> See here the noble security of the scripture-style, which seems to contradict itself, but really does not. Wise men have need to be directed how to deal with fools; and they have never more need of wisdom than in dealing with such, to know when to keep silence and when to speak, for there may be a time for both. 1. In some cases a wise man will not set his wit to that of a fool so far as to <hi type="italic">answer him according to his folly</hi> "If he boast of himself, do not answer him by boasting of thyself. If he rail and talk passionately, do not thou rail and talk passionately too. If he tell one great lie, do not thou tell another to match it. If he calumniate thy friends, do not thou calumniate his. If he banter, do not answer him in his own language, <hi type="italic">lest thou be like him,</hi> even thou, who knowest better things, who hast more sense, and hast been better taught." 2. Yet, in other cases, a wise man will use his wisdom for the conviction of a fool, when, by taking notice of what he says, there may be hopes of doing good, or at least preventing further, mischief, either to himself or others. "If thou have reason to think that thy silence will be deemed an evidence of the weakness of thy cause, or of thy own weakness, in such a case <hi type="italic">answer him,</hi> and let it be an answer <hi type="italic">ad hominem—to the man,</hi> beat him at his own weapons, and that will be an answer <hi type="italic">ad rem—to the point,</hi> or as good as one. If he offer any thing that looks like an argument, an answer that, and suit thy answer to his case. If he think, because thou dost not answer him, that what he says is unanswerable, then give him an answer, <hi type="italic">lest he be wise in his own conceit</hi> and boast of a victory." For (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.35">Luke vii. 35</reference>) Wisdom's children must justify her.

<div eID="gen14478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14479" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet, <hi type="italic">and</hi> drinketh damage. <hi type="super">7</hi> The legs of the lame are not equal: so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a parable in the mouth of fools. <hi type="super">8</hi> As he that bindeth a stone in a sling, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that giveth honour to a fool. <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> a thorn goeth up into the hand of a drunkard, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a parable in the mouth of fools. <div eID="gen14479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14480" type="x-p"/> To recommend wisdom to us, and to quicken us to the diligent use of all the means for the getting of wisdom, Solomon here shows that fools are fit for nothing; they are either sottish men, who will never think and design at all, or vicious men, who will never think and design well. 1. They are not fit to be entrusted with any business, not fit to go on an errand (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that</hi> does but <hi type="italic">send a message by the hand of a fool,</hi> of a careless heedless person, one who is so full of his jests and so given to his pleasures that he cannot apply his mind to any thing that is serious, will find his message misunderstood, the one half of it forgotten, the rest awkwardly delivered, and so many blunders made about it that he might as well have <hi type="italic">cut off his legs,</hi> that is, never have sent him. Nay, he will <hi type="italic">drink damage;</hi> it will be very much to his prejudice to have employed such a one, who, instead of bringing him a good account of his affairs, will abuse him and put a trick upon him; for, in Solomon's language, a knave and a fool are of the same signification. It will turn much to a man's disgrace to make use of the service of a fool, for people will be apt to judge of the master by his messenger. 2. They are not fit to have any honour put upon them. He had said (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Honour is not seemly for a fool;</hi> here he shows that it is lost and thrown away upon him, as if a man should throw a precious stone, or a stone fit to be used in weighing, into a heap of common stones, where it would be buried and of no use; it is as absurd as if a man should <hi type="italic">dress up a stone in purple</hi> (so others); nay, it is dangerous, it is like <hi type="italic">a stone bound in a sling,</hi> with which a man will be likely to do hurt. To <hi type="italic">give honour to a fool</hi> is to put a sword in a madman's hand, with which we know not what mischief he may do, even to those that put it into his hand. 3. They are not fit to deliver wise sayings, nor should they undertake to handle any matter of weight, though they should be instructed concerning it, and be able to say something to it. Wise sayings, as a foolish man delivers them and applies them (in such a manner that one may know he does not rightly understand them), lose their excellency and usefulness: <hi type="italic">A parable in the mouth of fools</hi> ceases to be a parable, and becomes a jest. If a man who lives a wicked life, yet speaks religiously and takes God's covenant into his mouth, (1.) He does but shame himself and his profession: As <hi type="italic">the legs of the lame are not equal,</hi> by reason of which their going is unseemly, so unseemly is it for a fool to pretend to speak apophthegms, and give advice, and for a man to talk devoutly whose conversation is a constant contradiction to his talk and gives him the lie. His good words raise him up, but then his bad life takes him down, and so his <hi type="italic">legs are not equal.</hi> "A wise saying," (says bishop Patrick) "doth as ill become a fool as dancing doth a cripple; for, as his lameness never so much appears as when he would seem nimble, so the other's folly is never so ridiculous as when he would seem wise." As therefore it is best for a lame man to keep his seat, so it is best for a silly man, or a bad man, to hold his tongue. (2.) He does but do mischief with it to himself and others, as a drunkard does with a thorn, or any other sharp thing which he takes in his hand, with which he tears himself and those about him, because he knows not how to manage it. Those that talk well and do not live well, their good words will aggravate their own condemnation and others will be hardened by their inconsistency with themselves. Some give this sense of it: The sharpest saying, by which a sinner, one would think, should be pricked to the heart, makes no more impression upon a fool, no, though it come out of his own mouth, than the scratch of a thorn does upon the hand of a man when he is drunk, who then feels it not nor complains of it, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.35">ch. xxiii. 35</reference>.  <div eID="gen14480" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv80"/><title type="x-s3">The Conduct of Fools.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv80"/> <div sID="gen14481" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> The great <hi type="italic">God</hi> that formed all <hi type="italic">things</hi> both rewardeth the fool, and rewardeth transgressors. <div eID="gen14481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14482" type="x-p"/> Our translation gives this verse a different reading in the text and in the margin; and accordingly it expresses either, 1. The equity of a good God. The <hi type="italic">Master,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> (so <hi type="italic">Rab</hi> signifies), or, as we read it, <hi type="italic">The great God that formed all things</hi> at first, and still governs them in infinite wisdom, renders to every man according to his work. He <hi type="italic">rewards the fool,</hi> who sinned through ignorance, <hi type="italic">who knew not his Lord's will, with few stripes;</hi> and he <hi type="italic">rewards the transgressor,</hi> who sinned presumptuously and with a high hand, who <hi type="italic">knew his Lord's will and would not do it, with many stripes.</hi> Some understand it of the goodness of God's common providence even to fools and transgressors, on whom <hi type="italic">he causes his sun to shine</hi> and <hi type="italic">his rain to fall.</hi> Or, 2. The iniquity of a bad prince (so the margin reads it): <hi type="italic">A great man grieves all, and he hires the fool; he hires also the transgressors.</hi> When a wicked man gets power in his hand, by himself, and by the fools and knaves whom he employs under him, whom he hires and chooses to make use of, he grieves all who are under him and is vexatious to them. We should therefore <hi type="italic">pray for kings and all in authority,</hi> that, under them, our lives may be quiet and peaceable.

<div eID="gen14482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14483" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> As a dog returneth to his vomit, <hi type="italic">so</hi> a fool returneth to his folly. <div eID="gen14483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14484" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What an abominable thing sin is, and how hateful sometimes it is made to appear, even to the sinner himself. When his conscience is convinced, or he feels smart from his sin, he is sick of it, and vomits it up; he seems then to detest it and to be willing to part with it. It is in itself, and, first or last, will be to the sinner, more loathsome than the vomit of a dog, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.2">Ps. xxxvi. 2</reference>. 2. How apt sinners are to relapse into it notwithstanding. As the dog, after he has gained ease by vomiting that which burdened his stomach, yet goes and licks it up again, so sinners, who have been convinced only and not converted, return to sin again, forgetting how sick it made them. The apostle (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.22">2 Pet. ii. 22</reference>) applies this proverb to those that <hi type="italic">have known the way of righteousness</hi> but are <hi type="italic">turned from it;</hi> but God will <hi type="italic">spue them out of his mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.16">Rev. iii. 16</reference>.

<div eID="gen14484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14485" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? <hi type="italic">there is</hi> more hope of a fool than of him. <div eID="gen14485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14486" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A spiritual disease supposed, and that is self-conceit: <hi type="italic">Seest thou a man?</hi> Yes, we see many a one, <hi type="italic">wise in his own conceit,</hi> who has some little sense, but is proud of it, thinks it much more than it is, more than any of his neighbours, have, and enough, so that he needs no more, has such a conceit of his own abilities as makes him opinionative, dogmatical, and censorious; and all the use he makes of his knowledge is that it puffs him up. Or, if by a wise man we understand a religious man, it describes the character of those who, making some show of religion, conclude their spiritual state to be good when really it is very bad, like Laodicea, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.17">Rev. iii. 17</reference>. 2. The danger of this disease. It is in a manner desperate: <hi type="italic">There is more hope of a fool,</hi> that knows and owns himself to be such, <hi type="italic">than of</hi> such a one. Solomon was not only a wise man himself, but a teacher of wisdom; and this observation he made upon his pupils, that he found his work most difficult and least successful with those that had a good opinion of themselves and were not sensible that they needed instruction. Therefore he that <hi type="italic">seems</hi> to himself <hi type="italic">to be wise</hi> must <hi type="italic">become a fool, that he may be wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18">1 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. There is more hope of a publican than of a proud Pharisee, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.32">Matt. xxi. 32</reference>. Many are hindered from being truly wise and religious by a false and groundless conceit that they are so, <reference osisRef="John.9.40-John.9.41">John ix. 40, 41</reference>.  <div eID="gen14486" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv81"/><title type="x-s3">The Disgrace of Slothfulness.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv81"/> <div sID="gen14487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> The slothful <hi type="italic">man</hi> saith, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a lion in the way; a lion <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the streets. <div eID="gen14487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14488" type="x-p"/> When a man talks foolishly we say, He talks idly; for none betray their folly more than those who are idle and go about to excuse themselves in their idleness. As men's folly makes them slothful, so their slothfulness makes them foolish. Observe, 1. What <hi type="italic">the slothful man</hi> really dreads. He dreads <hi type="italic">the way, the streets,</hi> the place where work is to be done and a journey to be gone; he hates business, hates every thing that requires care and labour. 2. What he dreams of, and pretends to dread—<hi type="italic">a lion in the way.</hi> When he is pressed to be diligent, either in his worldly affairs or in the business of religion, this is his excuse (and a sorry excuse it is, as bad as none), <hi type="italic">There is a lion in the way,</hi> some insuperable difficulty or danger which he cannot pretend to grapple with. Lions frequent woods and deserts; and, in the day-time, when man has business to do, they are in their dens, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.22-Ps.104.23">Ps. civ. 22, 23</reference>. But the sluggard fancies, or rather pretends to fancy, <hi type="italic">a lion in the streets,</hi> whereas the lion is only in his own fancy, nor is he so fierce as he is painted. Note, It is a foolish thing to frighten ourselves from real duties by fancied difficulties, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Eccl. xi. 4</reference>.

<div eID="gen14488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14489" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> the door turneth upon his hinges, so <hi type="italic">doth</hi> the slothful upon his bed. <div eID="gen14489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14490" type="x-p"/> Having seen the slothful man in fear of his work, here we find him in love with his ease; he lies in his bed on one side till he is weary of that, and then turns to the other, but still in his bed, when it is far in the day and work is to be done, as the door is moved, but not removed; and so his business is neglected and his opportunities are let slip. See the sluggard's character. 1. He is one that does not care to get out of his bed, but seems to be hung upon it, <hi type="italic">as the door upon the hinges.</hi> Bodily ease, too much consulted, is the sad occasion of many a spiritual disease. Those that love sleep will prove in the end to have loved death. 2. He does not care to get forward with his business; in that he stirs to and fro a little, but to no purpose; he is where he was. Slothful professors turn, in profession, like <hi type="italic">the door upon the hinges.</hi> The world and the flesh are the two hinges on which they are hung, and though they move in a course of external services, have got into road of duties, and tread around in them like the horse in the mill, yet they get no good, they get no ground, they are never the nearer heaven—sinners unchanged, saints unimproved.

<div eID="gen14490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14491" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The slothful hideth his hand in <hi type="italic">his</hi> bosom; it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth. <div eID="gen14491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14492" type="x-p"/> The sluggard has now, with much ado, got out of his bed, but he might as well have lain there still for any thing he is likely to bring to pass in his work, so awkwardly does he go about it. Observe, 1. The pretence he makes for his slothfulness: He <hi type="italic">hides his hand in his bosom</hi> for fear of cold; next to his warm bed in his warm bosom. Or he pretends that he is lame, as some do that make a trade of begging; something ails his hand; he would have it thought that it is blistered with yesterday's hard work. Or it intimates, in general, his aversion to business; he has tried, and his hands are not used to labour, and therefore he hugs himself in his own ease and cares for nobody. Note, It is common for those that will not do their duty to pretend they cannot. <hi type="italic">I cannot dig,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.3">Luke xvi. 3</reference>. 2. The prejudice he sustains by his slothfulness. He himself is the loser by it, for he starves himself: <hi type="italic">It grieves him to bring his hand to his mouth,</hi> that is, he cannot find in his heart to feed himself, but dreads, as if it were a mighty toil, to lift his hand to his head. It is an elegant hyperbole, aggravating his sin, that he cannot endure to take the least pains, no, not for the greatest profit, and showing how his sin is his punishment. Those that are slothful in the business of religion will not be at the pains to feed their own souls with the word of God, the bread of life, nor to fetch in promised blessings by prayer, though they might have them for the fetching.

<div eID="gen14492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14493" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> The sluggard <hi type="italic">is</hi> wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason. <div eID="gen14493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14494" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. The high opinion which the sluggard has of himself, notwithstanding the gross absurdity and folly of his slothfulness: He thinks himself <hi type="italic">wiser than seven men,</hi> than seven wise men, for they are such as <hi type="italic">can render a reason.</hi> It is the wisdom of a man to be able to <hi type="italic">render a reason,</hi> of a good man to be able to give <hi type="italic">a reason of the hope that is in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1 Pet. iii. 15</reference>. What we do we should be able to <hi type="italic">render a reason</hi> for, though perhaps we may not have wit enough to show the fallacy of every objection against it. He that takes pains in religion can render a good reason for it; he knows that he is working for a good Master and that <hi type="italic">his labour shall not be in vain.</hi> But <hi type="italic">the sluggard</hi> thinks himself <hi type="italic">wiser than seven</hi> such; for let seven such persuade him to be diligent, with all the reasons they can render for it, it is to no purpose; his own determination, he thinks, answer enough to them and all their reasons. 2. The reference that this has to his slothfulness. It is <hi type="italic">the sluggard,</hi> above all men, that is thus self-conceited; for, (1.) His good opinion of himself is the cause of his slothfulness; he will not take pains to get wisdom because he thinks he is wise enough already. A conceit of the sufficiency of our attainments is a great enemy to our improvement. (2.) His slothfulness is the cause of his good opinion of himself. If he would but take pains to examine himself, and compare himself with the laws of wisdom, he would have other thoughts of himself. Indulged slothfulness is at the bottom of prevailing self-conceitedness. Nay, (3.) So wretchedly besotted is he that he takes his slothfulness to be his wisdom; he thinks it is his wisdom to make much of himself, and take all the ease he can get, and do no more in religion than he needs must, to avoid suffering, to sit still and see what other people do, that he may have the pleasure of finding fault with them. Of such sluggards, who are proud of that which is their shame, their is little hope, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.12">v. 12</reference>.  <div eID="gen14494" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv82"/><title type="x-s3">Hatred and Strife.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv82"/> <div sID="gen14495" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> He that passeth by, <hi type="italic">and</hi> meddleth with strife <hi type="italic">belonging</hi> not to him, <hi type="italic">is like</hi> one that taketh a dog by the ears. <div eID="gen14495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14496" type="x-p"/> 1. That which is here condemned is <hi type="italic">meddling with strife that belongs not to us.</hi> If we must not be hasty to strive in our own cause (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.8">ch. xxv. 8</reference>), much less in other people's, especially theirs that we are no way related to or concerned in, but light on accidentally as we pass by. If we can be instrumental to make peace between those that are at variance we must do it, though we should thereby get the ill-will of both sides, at least while they are in their heat; but to make ourselves busy in other men's matters, and parties in other men's quarrels, is not only to court our own trouble, but to thrust ourselves into temptation. <hi type="italic">Who made</hi> me <hi type="italic">a judge?</hi> Let them end it, as they began it, between themselves. 2. We are cautioned against it because of the danger it exposes us to; it is like taking a snarling cur <hi type="italic">by the ears,</hi> that will snap at you and bite you; you had better have let him alone, for you cannot get clear of him when you would, and must thank yourselves if you come off with a wound and dishonour. He that has got <hi type="italic">a dog by the ears,</hi> if he lets him go he flies at him, if he keeps his hold, he has his hands full, and can do nothing else. Let every one <hi type="italic">with quietness work and mind his own business,</hi> and not with unquietness quarrel and meddle with other people's business.

<div eID="gen14496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14497" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> As a mad <hi type="italic">man</hi> who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, <hi type="super">19</hi> So <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man <hi type="italic">that</hi> deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport? <div eID="gen14497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14498" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How mischievous those are that make no scruple of <hi type="italic">deceiving their neighbours;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">as madmen that cast firebrands, arrows, and death,</hi> so much hurt may they do by their deceits. They value themselves upon it as polite cunning men, but really they are <hi type="italic">as madmen.</hi> There is not a greater madness in the world than a wilful sin. It is not only the passionate furious man, but the malicious deceitful man, that is <hi type="italic">a madman;</hi> he does in effect <hi type="italic">cast fire-brands, arrows, and death;</hi> he does more mischief than he can imagine. Fraud and falsehood burn like fire-brands, kill, even at a distance, like arrows. 2. See how frivolous the excuse is which men commonly make for the mischief they do, that they did it in a jest; with this they think to turn it off when they are reproved for it, <hi type="italic">Am not I in sport?</hi> But it will prove dangerous playing with fire and jesting with edge-tools. Not that those are to be commended who are captious, and can take no jest (those that themselves are <hi type="italic">wise must suffer fools,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.19-2Cor.11.20">2 Cor. xi. 19, 20</reference>), but those are certainly to be condemned who are any way abusive to their neighbours, impose upon their credulity, cheat them in their bargains with them, tell lies to them or tell lies of them, give them ill language, or sully their reputation, and then think to excuse it by saying that they did but jest. <hi type="italic">Am not I in sport?</hi> He that sins in just must repent in earnest, or his sin will be his ruin. Truth is too valuable a thing to be sold for a jest, and so is the reputation of our neighbour. By lying and slandering in jest men learn themselves, and teach others, to lie and slander in earnest; and a false report, raised in mirth, may be spread in malice; besides, if a man may tell a lie to make himself merry, why not to make himself rich, and so <hi type="italic">truth quite perishes,</hi> and men <hi type="italic">teach their tongues to tell lies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.9.5">Jer. ix. 5</reference>. If men would consider that a lie comes from the devil, and brings to hell-fire, surely that would spoil the sport of it; it is <hi type="italic">casting arrows and death</hi> to themselves.

<div eID="gen14498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14499" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Where no wood is, <hi type="italic">there</hi> the fire goeth out: so where <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no talebearer, the strife ceaseth. 21 <hi type="italic">As</hi> coals <hi type="italic">are</hi> to burning coals, and wood to fire; so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a contentious man to kindle strife. <hi type="super">22</hi> The words of a talebearer <hi type="italic">are</hi> as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly. <div eID="gen14499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14500" type="x-p"/> Contention is as a fire; it heats the spirit, burns up all that is good, and puts families and societies into a flame. Now here we are told how that fire is commonly kindled and kept burning, that we may avoid the occasions of strife and so prevent the mischievous consequences of it. If then we would keep the peace, 1. We must not give ear to <hi type="italic">talebearers,</hi> for they feed the fire of contention with fuel; nay, they spread it with combustible matter; the tales they carry are fireballs. Those who by insinuating base characters, revealing secrets, and misrepresenting words and actions, do what they can to make relations, friends, and neighbours, jealous one of another, to alienate them one from another, and sow discord among them, are to be banished out of families and all societies, and then strife will as surely cease as the fire will go out when it has no fuel; the contenders will better understand one another and come to a better temper; old stories will soon be forgotten when there are no new ones told to keep up the remembrance of them, and both sides will see how they have been imposed upon by a common enemy. Whisperers and backbiters are incendiaries not to be suffered. To illustrate this, he repeats (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.22">v. 22</reference>) what he had said before (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.8">ch. xviii. 8</reference>), that <hi type="italic">the words of a tale-bearer are as wounds,</hi> deep and dangerous wounds, wounds in the vitals. They wound the reputation of him who is belied, and perhaps the wound proves incurable, and even the plaster of a recantation (which yet can seldom be obtained) may not prove wide enough for it. They wound the love and charity which he to whom they are spoken ought to have for his neighbour and give a fatal stab to friendship and Christian fellowship. We must therefore not only not be tale-bearers ourselves at any time, nor ever do any ill offices, but we should not give the least countenance to those that are. 2. We must not associate with peevish passionate people, that are exceptions, and apt to put the worst constructions upon everything, that pick quarrels upon the least occasion, and are quick, and high, and hot, in resenting affronts. These are <hi type="italic">contentious men,</hi> that <hi type="italic">kindle strife,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.21">v. 21</reference>. The less we have to do with such the better, for it will be very difficult to avoid quarrelling with those that are quarrelsome.

<div eID="gen14500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14501" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Burning lips and a wicked heart <hi type="italic">are like</hi> a potsherd covered with silver dross. <div eID="gen14501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14502" type="x-p"/> This may be meant either, 1. Of <hi type="italic">a wicked heart</hi> showing itself in <hi type="italic">burning lips,</hi> furious, passionate, outrageous words, burning in malice, and persecuting those to whom, or of whom, they are spoken; ill words and ill-will agree as well together as <hi type="italic">a potsherd</hi> and the <hi type="italic">dross of silver,</hi> which, now that the pot is broken and the dross separated from the silver, are fit to be thrown together to the dunghill. 2. Or of <hi type="italic">a wicked heart</hi> disguising itself with <hi type="italic">burning lips,</hi> burning with the professions of love and friendship, and even persecuting a man with flatteries; this is <hi type="italic">like a potsherd covered with</hi> the scum or <hi type="italic">dross of silver,</hi> with which one that is weak may be imposed upon, as if it were of some value, but a wise man is soon aware of the cheat. This sense agrees with the following verses.

<div eID="gen14502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14503" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him; <hi type="super">25</hi> When he speaketh fair, believe him not: for <hi type="italic">there are</hi> seven abominations in his heart. <hi type="super">26</hi> <hi type="italic">Whose</hi> hatred is covered by deceit, his wickedness shall be shewed before the <hi type="italic">whole</hi> congregation. <div eID="gen14503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14504" type="x-p"/> There is cause to complain, not only of the want of sincerity in men's profession of friendship, and that they do not love so well as they pretend nor will serve their friends so much as they promise, but, which is much worse, of wicked designs in the profession of friendship, and the making of it subservient to the most malicious intentions. This is here spoken of as a common thing (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that hates</hi> his neighbour, and is contriving to do him a mischief, yet <hi type="italic">dissembles with his lips,</hi> professes to have a respect for him and to be ready to serve him, talks kindly with him, as Cain with Abel, asks, <hi type="italic">Art thou in health, my brother?</hi> as Joab to Amasa, that his malice may not be suspected and guarded against, and so he may have the fairer opportunity to execute the purposes of it, this man <hi type="italic">lays up deceit within him,</hi> that is, he keeps in his mind the mischief he intends to do his neighbour till he catches him at an advantage. This is malice which has no less of the subtlety than it has of the venom of the old serpent in it. Now, as to this matter, we are here cautioned, 1. Not to be so foolish as to suffer ourselves to be imposed upon by the pretensions of friendship. Remember to distrust when a man <hi type="italic">speaks fair;</hi> be not too forward to <hi type="italic">believe him</hi> unless you know him well, for it is possible there may be <hi type="italic">seven abominations in his heart,</hi> a great many projects of mischief against you, which he is labouring so industriously to conceal with his fair speech. Satan is an enemy that hates us, and yet in his temptations speaks fair, as he did to Eve, but it is madness to give credit to him, <hi type="italic">for there are seven abominations in his heart; seven other spirits</hi> does one unclean spirit bring <hi type="italic">more wicked than himself.</hi> 2. Not to be so wicked as to impose upon any with a profession of friendship; for, though the fraud may be carried on plausibly awhile, it will be brought to light, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.26">v. 26</reference>. He <hi type="italic">whose hatred is covered by deceit</hi> will one time or other be discovered, and <hi type="italic">his wickedness shown,</hi> to his shame and confusion, <hi type="italic">before the whole congregation;</hi> and nothing will do more to make a man odious to all companies. Love (says one) is the best armour, but the worst cloak, and will serve dissemblers as the disguise which Ahab put on and perished in.

<div eID="gen14504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14505" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him. <div eID="gen14505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14506" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What pains men take to do mischief to others. As they put a force upon themselves by concealing their design with a profession of friendship, so they put themselves to a great deal of labour to bring it about; it is <hi type="italic">digging a pit,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">rolling a stone,</hi> hard work, and yet men will not stick at it to gratify their passion and revenge. 2. What preparation they hereby make of mischief to themselves. Their violent dealing will return upon their own heads; they shall themselves <hi type="italic">fall into the pit they digged,</hi> and the stone they rolled <hi type="italic">will return upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.7.15-Ps.7.16">Ps. vii. 15, 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.15-Ps.9.16">ix. 15, 16</reference>. The righteous God will take the wise, not only <hi type="italic">in their own craftiness,</hi> but in their own cruelty. It is the plotter's doom. Haman is hanged on a gallows of his own preparing. <div eID="gen14506" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen14507"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14508"/>—————nec lex est justior ulla<l eID="gen14508" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14509"/>Quam necis artifices arte perire sua—<l eID="gen14509" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14510"/>Nor is there any law more just than that the contrivers<l eID="gen14510" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14511"/>of destruction should perish by their own arts.

<l eID="gen14511" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen14507"/> <div sID="gen14512" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> A lying tongue hateth <hi type="italic">those that are</hi> afflicted by it; and a flattering mouth worketh ruin. <div eID="gen14512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14513" type="x-p"/> There are two sorts of lies equally detestable:—1. A slandering lie, which avowedly hates those it is spoken of: <hi type="italic">A lying tongue hates those that are afflicted by it;</hi> it afflicts them by calumnies and reproaches because it hates them, and can thus smite them secretly where they are without defence; and it hates them because it has afflicted them and made them its enemies. The mischief of this is open and obvious; it afflicts, it hates, and owns it, and every body sees it. 2. A flattering lie, which secretly works the ruin of those it is spoken to. In the former the mischief is plain, and men guard against it as well as they can, but in this it is little suspected, and men betray themselves by being credulous of their own praises and the compliments that are passed upon them. A wise man therefore will be more afraid of a flatterer that kisses and kills than of a slanderer that proclaims war.  <chapter eID="Prov.26"/> <div eID="gen14513" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv83"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv83"/> <div sID="gen14515" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth. <div eID="gen14515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14516" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A good caution against presuming upon time to come: <hi type="italic">Boast not thyself,</hi> no, not <hi type="italic">of to-morrow,</hi> much less of many days or years to come. This does not forbid preparing for to-morrow, but presuming upon to-morrow. We must not promise ourselves the continuance of our lives and comforts till to-morrow, but speak of it with submission to the will of God and as those who with good reason are kept at uncertainty about it. We must not <hi type="italic">take thought for the morrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.34">Matt. vi. 34</reference>), but we must cast our care concerning it upon God. See <reference osisRef="Jas.4.13-Jas.4.15">James iv. 13-15</reference>. We must not put off the great work of conversion, that one thing needful, till to-morrow, as if we were sure of it, <hi type="italic">but to-day, while it is called to-day,</hi> hear God's voice. 2. A good consideration, upon which this caution is grounded: <hi type="italic">We know not what a day may bring forth,</hi> what event may be in the teeming womb, of time; it is a secret till it is born, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Eccl. xi. 5</reference>. A little time may produce considerable changes, and such as we little think of. We <hi type="italic">know not what</hi> the present <hi type="italic">day may bring forth;</hi> the evening must commend it. <hi type="italic">Nescis quid serus vesper vehat—Thou knowest not what the close of evening may bring with it.</hi> God has wisely kept us in the dark concerning future events, and reserved to himself the knowledge of them, as a flower of the crown, that he may train us up in a dependence upon himself and a continued readiness for every event, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Acts i. 7</reference>.

<div eID="gen14516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14517" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips. <div eID="gen14517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14518" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. We must do that which is commendable, for which even strangers may praise us. Our <hi type="italic">light</hi> must <hi type="italic">shine before men,</hi> and we must do good works that may be seen, though we must not do them on purpose that they may be seen. Let our own works be such as will praise us, even <hi type="italic">in the gates,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Phil. iv. 8</reference>. 2. When we have done it we must not commend ourselves, for that is an evidence of pride, folly, and self-love, and a great lessening to a man's reputation. Every one will be forward to run him down that cries himself up. There may be a just occasion for us to vindicate ourselves, but it does not become us to applaud ourselves. <hi type="italic">Proprio laus sordet in ore—Self-praise defiles the mouth.</hi>

<div eID="gen14518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14519" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> A stone <hi type="italic">is</hi> heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath <hi type="italic">is</hi> heavier than them both. <hi type="super">4</hi> Wrath <hi type="italic">is</hi> cruel, and anger <hi type="italic">is</hi> outrageous; but who <hi type="italic">is</hi> able to stand before envy? <div eID="gen14519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14520" type="x-p"/> These two verses show the intolerable mischief, 1. Of ungoverned passion. The wrath of a fool, who when he is provoked cares not what he says and does, is more grievous than a great stone or a load of sand. It lies heavily upon himself. Those who have no command of their passions do themselves even sink under the load of them. The wrath of a fool lies heavily upon those he is enraged at, to whom, in his fury, he will be in danger of doing some mischief. It is therefore our wisdom not to give provocation to a fool, but, if he be in a passion, to get out of his way. 2. Of rooted malice, which is as much worse than the former as coals of juniper are worse than a fire of thorns. <hi type="italic">Wrath</hi> (it is true) <hi type="italic">is cruel,</hi> and does many a barbarous thing, <hi type="italic">and anger is outrageous;</hi> but a secret enmity at the person of another, an envy at his prosperity, and a desire of revenge for some injury or affront, are much more mischievous. One may avoid a sudden heat, as David escaped Saul's javelin, but when it grows, as Saul's did, to a settled envy, there is no <hi type="italic">standing before it;</hi> it will pursue; it will overtake. He that grieves at the good of another will be still contriving to do him hurt, and will keep his anger for ever.

<div eID="gen14520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14521" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Open rebuke <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than secret love. 6 Faithful <hi type="italic">are</hi> the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy <hi type="italic">are</hi> deceitful. <div eID="gen14521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14522" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is good for us to be reproved, and told of our faults, by our friends. If true love in the heart has but zeal and courage enough to show itself in dealing plainly with our friends, and reproving them for what they say and do amiss, this is really <hi type="italic">better,</hi> not only than secret hatred (as <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">Lev. xix. 17</reference>), but <hi type="italic">than secret love,</hi> that love to our neighbours which does not show itself in this good fruit, which compliments them in their sins, to the prejudice of their souls. <hi type="italic">Faithful are the reproofs of a friend,</hi> though for the present they are painful as <hi type="italic">wounds.</hi> It is a sign that our friends are faithful indeed if, in love to our souls, they will not suffer sin upon us, nor let us alone in it. The physician's care is to cure the patient's disease, not to please his palate. 2. It is dangerous to be caressed and flattered by <hi type="italic">an enemy,</hi> whose <hi type="italic">kisses are deceitful</hi> We can take no pleasure in them because we can put no confidence in them (Joab's kiss and Judas's were deceitful), and therefore we have need to stand upon our guard, that we be not deluded by them; they are to be deprecated. Some read it: <hi type="italic">The Lord deliver us from an enemy's kisses, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue.</hi>

<div eID="gen14522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14523" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet. <div eID="gen14523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14524" type="x-p"/> Solomon here, as often in this book, shows that the poor have in some respects the advantage of the rich; for, 1. They have a better relish of their enjoyments than the rich have. Hunger is the best sauce. Coarse fare, with a good appetite to it has a sensible pleasantness in it, which those are strangers to whose hearts are <hi type="italic">overcharged with surfeiting.</hi> Those that fare sumptuously every day nauseate even delicate food, as the Israelites did the quails; whereas those that have no more than their necessary food, though it be such as <hi type="italic">the full soul</hi> would call <hi type="italic">bitter,</hi> to them it <hi type="italic">is sweet;</hi> they eat it with pleasure, digest it, and are refreshed by it. 2. They are more thankful for their enjoyments: <hi type="italic">The hungry</hi> will bless God for bread and water, while those that are <hi type="italic">full</hi> think the greatest dainties and varieties scarcely worth giving thanks for. The virgin Mary seems to refer to this when she says (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.53">Luke i. 53</reference>), <hi type="italic">The hungry,</hi> who know how to value God's blessings, <hi type="italic">are filled with good things,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the rich,</hi> who despise them, are justly <hi type="italic">sent empty away.</hi>

<div eID="gen14524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14525" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a man that wandereth from his place. <div eID="gen14525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14526" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. There are many that do not know when they are well off, but are uneasy with their present condition, and given to change. God, in his providence, has appointed them a place fit for them and has made it comfortable to them; but they affect unsettledness; they love to wander; they are glad of a pretence to go abroad, and do not care for staying long at a place; they needlessly absent themselves from their own work and care, and meddle with that which belongs not to them. 2. Those that thus desert the post assigned to them are like <hi type="italic">a bird that wanders from her nest.</hi> It is an instance of their folly; they are like a silly bird; they are always wavering, like the wandering bird that hops from bough to bough and rests nowhere. It is unsafe; the bird that wanders is exposed; a man's place is his castle; he that quits it makes himself an easy prey to the fowler. When the bird wanders from her nest the eggs and young ones there are neglected. Those that love to be abroad leave their work at home undone. <hi type="italic">Let every man therefore, in the calling wherein he is called, therein abide,</hi> therein abide <hi type="italic">with God.</hi>

<div eID="gen14526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14527" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so <hi type="italic">doth</hi> the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel. 10 Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother's house in the day of thy calamity: <hi type="italic">for</hi> better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a neighbour <hi type="italic">that is</hi> near than a brother far off. <div eID="gen14527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14528" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A charge given to be faithful and constant to our friends, our old friends, to keep up an intimacy with them, and to be ready to do them all the offices that lie in our power. It is good to have a friend, a bosom-friend, whom we can be free with, and with whom we may communicate counsels. It is not necessary that this friend should be a relation, or any way akin to us, though it is happiest when, among those who are so, we find one fit to make a friend of. Peter and Andrew were brethren, so were James and John; yet Solomon frequently distinguishes between a friend and a brother. But it is advisable to choose a friend among our neighbours who live near us, that acquaintance may be kept up and kindnesses the more frequently interchanged. It is good also to have a special respect to those who have been friends to our family: "<hi type="italic">Thy own friend,</hi> especially if he have been <hi type="italic">thy father's friend, forsake not;</hi> fail not both to serve him and to use him, as there is occasion. He is a tried friend; he knows thy affairs; he has a particular concern for thee; therefore be advised by him." It is a duty we owe to our parents, when they are gone, to love their friends and consult with them. Solomon's son undid himself by forsaking the counsel of his father's friends. 2. A good reason given why we should thus value true friendship and be choice of it. (1.) Because of the pleasure of it. There is a great deal of <hi type="italic">sweetness</hi> in conversing and consulting with a cordial friend. It is like <hi type="italic">ointment and perfume,</hi> which are very grateful to the smell, and exhilarate the spirits.
