It <hi type="italic">rejoices the heart;</hi> the burden of care is made lighter by unbosoming ourselves to our friend, and it is a great satisfaction to us to have his sentiments concerning our affairs. <hi type="italic">The sweetness of</hi> friendship lies not in hearty mirth, and hearty laughter, but in <hi type="italic">hearty counsel,</hi> faithful advice, sincerely given and without flattery, <hi type="italic">by counsel of the soul</hi> (so the word is), counsel which reaches the case, and comes to the heart, counsel about soul-concerns, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>. We should reckon that the most pleasant conversation which is about spiritual things, and promotes the prosperity of the soul. (2.) Because of the profit and advantage of it, especially in a <hi type="italic">day of calamity.</hi> We are here advised not to go into a <hi type="italic">brother's house,</hi> not to expect relief from a kinsman merely for kindred-sake, for the obligation of that commonly goes little further than calling cousin and fails when it comes to the trial of a real kindness, but rather to apply ourselves to our neighbours, who are at hand, and will be ready to help us at an exigence. It is wisdom to oblige them by being neighbourly, and we shall have the benefit of it in distress, by finding them so to us, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.24">ch. xviii. 24</reference>.

<div eID="gen14528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14529" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> My son, be wise, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him that reproacheth me. <div eID="gen14529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14530" type="x-p"/> Children are here exhorted to be wise and good, 1. That they may be a comfort to their parents and may <hi type="italic">make their hearts glad,</hi> even when <hi type="italic">the evil days come,</hi> and so recompense them for their care, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.15">ch. xxiii. 15</reference>. 2. That they may be a credit to them: "<hi type="italic">That I may answer him that reproaches me</hi> with having been over-strict and severe in bringing up my children, and having taken a wrong method with them in restraining them from the liberties which other young people take. <hi type="italic">My son, be wise,</hi> and then it will appear, in the effect, that I went the wisest way to work with my children." Those that have been blessed with a religious education should in every thing conduct themselves so as to be a credit to their education and to silence those who say, <hi type="italic">A young saint, an old devil;</hi> and to prove the contrary, <hi type="italic">A young saint, an old angel.</hi>

<div eID="gen14530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14531" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> A prudent <hi type="italic">man</hi> foreseeth the evil, <hi type="italic">and</hi> hideth himself; <hi type="italic">but</hi> the simple pass on, <hi type="italic">and</hi> are punished. <div eID="gen14531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14532" type="x-p"/> This we had before, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.3">ch. xxii. 3</reference>. Note, 1. Evil may be foreseen. Where there is temptation, it is easy to foresee that if we thrust ourselves into it there will be sin, and as easy to foresee that if we venture upon the evil of sin there will follow the evil of punishment; and, commonly, God warns before he wounds, having <hi type="italic">set watchmen over us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">Jer. vi. 17</reference>. 2. It will be well or ill with us according as we do or do not improve the foresight we have of evil before us: The <hi type="italic">prudent man, foreseeing the evil,</hi> forecasts accordingly, <hi type="italic">and hides himself, but the simple</hi> is either so dull that he does not foresee it or so wilful and slothful that he will take no care to avoid it, and so he <hi type="italic">passes on</hi> securely <hi type="italic">and is punished.</hi> We do well for ourselves when we provide for hereafter.

<div eID="gen14532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14533" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Take his garment that is surety for a stranger, and take a pledge of him for a strange woman. <div eID="gen14533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14534" type="x-p"/> This also we had before, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.16">ch. xx. 16</reference>. 1. It shows who those are that are hastening to poverty, those that have so little consideration as to be bound for every body that will ask them and those that are given to women. Such as these will take up money as far as ever their credit will go, but they will certainly cheat their creditors at last, nay, they are cheating them all along. An honest man may be made a beggar, but he is not honest that makes himself one. 2. It advises us to be so discreet in ordering our affairs as not to lend money to those who are manifestly wasting their estates, unless they give very good security for it. Foolish lending is injustice to our families. He does not say, "Get another to be bound with him," for he that makes himself a common voucher will have those to be his security who are as insolvent as himself; therefore <hi type="italic">take his garment.</hi>

<div eID="gen14534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14535" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him. <div eID="gen14535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14536" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a great folly to be extravagant in praising even the best of our friends and benefactors. It is our duty to give every one his due praise, to applaud those who excel in knowledge, virtue, and usefulness, and to acknowledge the kindnesses we have received with thankfulness; but to do this <hi type="italic">with a loud voice, rising early in the morning,</hi> to be always harping on this string, in all companies, even to our friend's face, or so as that he may be sure to hear it, to do it studiously, as we do that which we rise early to, to magnify the merits of our friend above measure and with hyperboles, is fulsome, and nauseous, and savours of hypocrisy and design. Praising men for what they have done is only to get more out of them; and every body concludes the parasite hopes to be well paid for his panegyric or epistle dedicatory. We must not give that praise to our friend which is due to God only, as some think is intimated in <hi type="italic">rising early</hi> to do it; for in the morning God is to be praised. We must not <hi type="italic">make too much haste to praise men</hi> (so some understand it), not cry up men too soon for their abilities and performances, but let them first be proved; lest they be lifted up with pride, and laid to sleep in idleness. 2. It is a greater folly to be fond of being ourselves extravagantly praised. A wise man rather counts it <hi type="italic">a curse,</hi> and a reflection upon him, not only designed to pick his pocket, but which may really turn to his prejudice. Modest praises (as a great man observes) invite such as are present to add to the commendation, but immodest immoderate praises tempt them to detract rather, and to censure one that they hear over-commended. And, besides, over-praising a man makes him the object of envy; every man puts in for a share of reputation, and therefore reckons himself injured if another monopolize it or have more given him than his share. And the greatest danger of all is that it is a temptation to pride; men are apt to think of themselves above what is meet when others speak of them above what is meet. See how careful blessed Paul was not to be over-valued, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.6">2 Cor. xii. 6</reference>.

<div eID="gen14536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14537" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike. <hi type="super">16</hi> Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and the ointment of his right hand, <hi type="italic">which</hi> bewrayeth <hi type="italic">itself.</hi> <div eID="gen14537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14538" type="x-p"/> Here, as before, Solomon laments the case of him that has a peevish passionate wife, that is continually chiding, and making herself and all about her uneasy. 1. It is a grievance that there is no avoiding, for it is like <hi type="italic">a continual dropping in a very rainy day.</hi> The contentions of a neighbour may be like a sharp shower, troublesome for the time, yet, while it lasts, one may take shelter; but <hi type="italic">the contentions of a wife</hi> are like a constant soaking rain, for which there is no remedy but patience See <reference osisRef="Prov.19.13">ch. xix. 13</reference>. 2. It is a grievance that there is no concealing. A wise man would hide it if he could, for the sake both of his own and his wife's reputation, but he cannot, any more than he can conceal the noise of the wind when it blows or the smell of a strong perfume. Those that are froward and brawling will proclaim their own shame, even when their friends, in kindness to them, would cover it.

<div eID="gen14538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14539" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend. <div eID="gen14539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14540" type="x-p"/> This intimates both the pleasure and the advantage of conversation. One man is nobody; nor will poring upon a book in a corner accomplish a man as the reading and studying of men will. Wise and profitable discourse sharpens men's wits; and those that have ever so much knowledge may by conference have something added to them. It sharpens men's looks, and, by cheering the spirits, puts a briskness and liveliness into the countenance, and gives a man such an air as shows he is pleased himself and makes him pleasing to those about him. Good men's graces are sharpened by converse with those that are good, and bad men's lusts and passions are sharpened by converse with those that are bad, as iron is sharpened by its like, especially by the file. Men are filed, made smooth, and bright, and fit for business (who were rough, and dull, and inactive), by conversation. This is designed, 1. To recommend to us this expedient for sharpening ourselves, but with a caution to take heed whom we choose to converse with, because the influence upon us is so great either for the better or for the worse. 2. To direct us what we must have in our eye in conversation, namely to improve both others and ourselves, not to pass away time or banter one another, but to <hi type="italic">provoke one another to love and to good works</hi> and so to make one another wiser and better.

<div eID="gen14540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14541" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Whoso keepeth the fig tree shall eat the fruit thereof: so he that waiteth on his master shall be honoured. <div eID="gen14541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14542" type="x-p"/> This is designed to encourage diligence, faithfulness, and constancy, even in mean employments. Though the calling be laborious and despicable, yet those who keep to it will find there is something to be got by it. 1. Let not a poor gardener, who <hi type="italic">keeps the fig-tree,</hi> be discouraged; though it require constant care and attendance to nurse up fig-trees, and, when they have grown to maturity, to keep them in good order, and gather the figs in their season, yet he shall be paid for his pains: He <hi type="italic">shall eat the fruit</hi> of it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1 Cor. ix. 7</reference>. 2. Nay, let not a poor servant think himself incapable of thriving and being preferred; for if he be diligent in <hi type="italic">waiting on his master,</hi> observant of him and obedient to him, if <hi type="italic">he keep his master</hi> (so the word is), if he do all he can for the securing of his person and reputation and take care that his estate be not wasted or damaged, such a one <hi type="italic">shall be honoured,</hi> shall not only get a good word, but be preferred and rewarded. God is a Master who has engaged to put an honour on those that serve him faithfully, <reference osisRef="John.12.26">John xii. 26</reference>.

<div eID="gen14542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14543" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> As in water face <hi type="italic">answereth</hi> to face, so the heart of man to man. <div eID="gen14543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14544" type="x-p"/> This shows us that there is a way, 1. Of knowing ourselves. As the water is a looking-glass in which we may see our faces by reflection, so there are mirrors by which the <hi type="italic">heart of a man</hi> is discovered to <hi type="italic">a man,</hi> that is, to himself. Let a man examine his own conscience, his thoughts, affections, and intentions. Let him behold his <hi type="italic">natural face in the glass</hi> of the divine law (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.23">Jam. i. 23</reference>), and he may discern what kind of man he is and what is his true character, which it will be of great use to every man rightly to know. 2. Of knowing one another by ourselves; for, as there is a similitude between the face of a man and the reflection of it in the water, so there is between one man's heart and another's for God has fashioned men's hearts alike; and in many cases we may judge of others by ourselves, which is one of the foundations on which that rule is built of doing to others as we would be done by, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.9">Exod. xxiii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Nihil est unum uni tam simile, tam par, quam omnes inter nosmet ipsos sumus. Sui nemo ipse tam similis quam omnes sunt omnium—No one thing is so like another as man is to man. No person is so like himself as each person is to all besides. Cic. de Legib. lib.</hi> 1. One corrupt heart is like another, and so is one sanctified heart, for the former bears the same image of the earthy, the latter the same image of the heavenly.

<div eID="gen14544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14545" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied. <div eID="gen14545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14546" type="x-p"/> Two things are here said to be insatiable, and they are two things near of kin—death and sin. 1. Death is insatiable. The first death, the second death, both are so. The grave is not clogged with the multitude of dead bodies that are daily thrown into it, but is still an <hi type="italic">open sepulchre,</hi> and cries, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi> Hell also has enlarged itself, and still has room for the damned spirits that are committed to that prison. <hi type="italic">Tophet is deep and large,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>. 2. Sin is insatiable: <hi type="italic">The eyes of man are never satisfied,</hi> nor the appetites of the carnal mind towards profit or pleasure. The <hi type="italic">eye is not satisfied with seeing,</hi> nor is he the <hi type="italic">loves silver satisfied with silver.</hi> Men labour for that which surfeits, but satisfies not; nay, it is dissatisfying; but satisfies not; nay, it is dissatisfying; such a perpetual uneasiness have men justly been doomed to ever since our first parents were not satisfied with all the trees of Eden, but they must meddle with the forbidden tree. Those whose eyes are ever toward the Lord in him are satisfied, and shall for ever be so.

<div eID="gen14546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14547" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> the fining pot for silver, and the furnace for gold; so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a man to his praise. <div eID="gen14547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14548" type="x-p"/> This gives us a touchstone by which we may try ourselves. Silver and gold are tried by putting them into the furnace and fining-pot; so is man tried by praising him. Let him be extolled and preferred, and then he will show himself what he is. 1. If a man be made, by the applause that is given him, proud, conceited, and scornful,—if he take the glory to himself which he should transmit to God, as Herod did,—if, the more he is praised, the more careless he is of what he says and does,—if he <hi type="italic">lie in bed till noon</hi> because <hi type="italic">his name is up,</hi> thereby it will appear that he is a vain foolish man, and a man who, though he be praised, has nothing in him truly praise-worthy. 2. If, on the contrary, a man is made by his praise more thankful to God, more respectful to his friends, more watchful against every thing that may blemish his reputation, more diligent to improve himself, and do good to others, that he may answer the expectations of his friends from him, by this it will appear that he is a wise and good man. He has a good temper of mind who knows how to pass by evil report and good report, and is still the same, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.8">2 Cor. vi. 8</reference>.

<div eID="gen14548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14549" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> will not his foolishness depart from him. <div eID="gen14549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14550" type="x-p"/> Solomon had said (<reference osisRef="Prov.22.15">ch. xxii. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">The foolishness</hi> which <hi type="italic">is bound in the heart of a child may be driven out by the rod of correction,</hi> for then the mind is to be moulded, the vicious habits not having taken root; but here he shows that, if it be not done then, it will be next to impossible to do it afterwards; if the disease be inveterate, there is a danger of its being incurable. <hi type="italic">Can the Ethiopian change his skin?</hi> Observe, 1. Some are so bad that rough and severe methods must be used with them, after gentle means have been tried in vain; they must be <hi type="italic">brayed in a mortar.</hi> God will take this way with them by his judgments; the magistrates must take this way with them by the rigour of the law. Force must be used with those that will not be ruled by reason, and love, and their own interest. 2. Some are so incorrigibly bad that even those rough and severe methods do not answer the end, their <hi type="italic">foolishness will not depart from them,</hi> so fully are their <hi type="italic">hearts set in them to do evil;</hi> they are often under the rod and yet not humbled, in the furnace and yet not refined, but, like Ahaz, trespass yet more (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.22">2 Chron. xxviii. 22</reference>); and what remains then but that they should be rejected as reprobate silver?  <div eID="gen14550" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv84"/><title type="x-s3">The Reward of Prudence.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv84"/> <div sID="gen14551" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, <hi type="italic">and</hi> look well to thy herds. <hi type="super">24</hi> For riches <hi type="italic">are</hi> not for ever: and doth the crown <hi type="italic">endure</hi> to every generation? <hi type="super">25</hi> The hay appeareth, and the tender grass sheweth itself, and herbs of the mountains are gathered. <hi type="super">26</hi> The lambs <hi type="italic">are</hi> for thy clothing, and the goats <hi type="italic">are</hi> the price of the field. <hi type="super">27</hi> And <hi type="italic">thou shalt have</hi> goats' milk enough for thy food, for the food of thy household, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> the maintenance for thy maidens. <div eID="gen14551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14552" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A command given us to be diligent in our callings. It is directed to husbandmen and shepherds, and those that deal in cattle, but it is to be extended to all other lawful callings; whatever our business is, within doors or without, we must apply our minds to it. This command intimates, 1. That we ought to have some business to do in this world and not to live in idleness. 2. We ought rightly and fully to understand our business, and know what we have to do, and not meddle with that which we do not understand. 3. We ought to have an eye to it ourselves, and not turn over all the care of it to others. We should, with our own eyes, inspect the <hi type="italic">state of our flocks,</hi> it is the master's eye that makes them fat. 4. We must be discreet and considerate in the management of our business, <hi type="italic">know the state</hi> of things, and <hi type="italic">look well</hi> to them, that nothing may be lost, no opportunity let slip, but every thing done in proper time and order, and so as to turn to the best advantage. 5. We must be <hi type="italic">diligent</hi> and take pains; not only sit down and contrive, but be up and doing: "Set thy heart to thy herds, as one in care; lay thy hands, lay thy bones, to thy business." <div eID="gen14552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14553" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons to enforce this command. Consider, <div eID="gen14553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14554" type="x-p"/> 1. The uncertainty of worldly wealth (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Riches are not for ever.</hi> (1.) Other riches are not so durable as these are: "<hi type="italic">Look well to thy flocks and herds,</hi> thy estate in the country and the stock upon that, for these are staple commodities, which, in a succession, will be for ever, whereas riches in trade and merchandise will not be so; the <hi type="italic">crown</hi> itself may perhaps not be so sure to thy family as thy flocks and herds." (2.) Even these riches will go to decay if they be not well looked after. If a man had <hi type="italic">an abbey</hi> (as we say), and were slothful and wasteful, he might make an end of it. Even the crown and the revenues of it, if care be not taken, will suffer damage, nor will it <hi type="italic">continue to every generation</hi> without very good management. Though David had the crown entailed on his family, yet he <hi type="italic">looked well to his flocks,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.29">1 Chron. xxvii. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.31">31</reference>. <div eID="gen14554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14555" type="x-p"/> 2. The bounty and liberality of nature, or rather of the God of nature, and his providence (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">The hay appears.</hi> In taking care of the <hi type="italic">flocks and herds,</hi> (1.) "There needs no great labour, no ploughing or sowing; the food for them is the spontaneous product of the ground; thou hast nothing to do but to turn them into it in the summer, <hi type="italic">when the grass shows itself,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">gather the herbs of the mountains</hi> for them against winter. God has done his part; thou art ungrateful to him, and unjustly refusest to serve his providence, if thou dost not do thine." (2.) "There is an opportunity to be observed and improved, a time when <hi type="italic">the hay appears;</hi> but, if thou let slip that time, thy flocks and herds will fare the worse for it. As for ourselves, so for our cattle, we ought, with the ant, to provide meat in summer." <div eID="gen14555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14556" type="x-p"/> 3. The profit of good husbandry in a family: "Keep thy sheep, and thy sheep will help to keep thee; thou shalt have food for thy children and servants, <hi type="italic">goats' milk enough</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.27">v. 27</reference>); and <hi type="italic">enough is as good as a feast.</hi> Thou shalt have raiment likewise: the <hi type="italic">lambs' wool shall be for thy clothing.</hi> Thou shalt have money to pay thy rent; the goats thou shalt have to sell shall be <hi type="italic">the price of thy field;</hi>" nay, as some understand it, "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt become a purchaser,</hi> and buy land to leave to thy children," (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.26">v. 26</reference>). Note, (1.) If we have food and raiment, and wherewithal to give every body his own, we have enough, and ought to be not only content, but thankful. (2.) Masters of families must provide not only for themselves, but for their families, and see that their servants have a fitting maintenance. (3.) Plain food and plain clothing, if they be but competent, are all we should aim at. "Reckon thyself well done to if thou be clothed with home-spun cloth with the fleece of thy own lambs, and fed with goats' milk; let that serve for thy food which serves for the <hi type="italic">food of thy household and the maintenance of thy maidens.</hi> Be not desirous of dainties, <hi type="italic">far-fetched and dear-bought.</hi>" (4.) This should encourage us to be careful and industrious about our business, that that will bring in a sufficient maintenance for our families; we shall <hi type="italic">eat the labour of our hands.</hi>  <chapter eID="Prov.27"/> <div eID="gen14556" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv85"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv85"/> <div sID="gen14558" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion. <div eID="gen14558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14559" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What continual frights those are subject to that go on in wicked ways. Guilt in the conscience makes men a terror to themselves, so that they are ready <hi type="italic">to flee when none pursues;</hi> like one that absconds for debt, who thinks every one he meets a bailiff. Though they pretend to be easy, there are secret fears which haunt them wherever they go, so that they fear where no present or imminent danger is, <reference osisRef="Ps.53.5">Ps. liii. 5</reference>. Those that have made God their enemy, and know it, cannot but see the whole creation at war with them, and therefore can have no true enjoyment of themselves, no confidence, no courage, but a <hi type="italic">fearful looking for of judgment.</hi> Sin makes men cowards. <div eID="gen14559" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen14560"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14561"/>Degeneres animos timor arguit—<l eID="gen14561" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14562"/>Fear argues a degenerate soul. Virgil.<l eID="gen14562" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14563"/>Quos diri conscia facti mens habet attonitos—<l eID="gen14563" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14564"/>The consciousness of atrocious crimes astonishes and confounds. <hi type="small-caps">Juvenal</hi> .<l eID="gen14564" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen14560"/> <div sID="gen14565" type="x-p"/> If they flee when none pursues, what will they do when they shall see God himself pursuing them with his armies? <reference osisRef="Job.20.24">Job xx. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.24">xv. 24</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Deut.28.25">Deut. xxviii. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.36">Lev. xxvi. 36</reference>. 2. What a holy security and serenity of mind those enjoy who <hi type="italic">keep conscience void of offence</hi> and so keep themselves in the love of God: <hi type="italic">The righteous are bold as a lion,</hi> as a young lion; in the greatest dangers they have a God of almighty power to trust to. <hi type="italic">Therefore will not we fear though the earth be removed.</hi> Whatever difficulties they meet with in the way of their duty, they are not daunted by them. <hi type="italic">None of those things move me.</hi> <div eID="gen14565" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen14566"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14567"/>Hic murus aheneus esto, nil conscire sibi—<l eID="gen14567" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14568"/>Be this thy brazen bulwark of defence,<l eID="gen14568" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14569"/>Still to preserve thy conscious innocence. Hor.

<l eID="gen14569" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen14566"/> <div sID="gen14570" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> For the transgression of a land many <hi type="italic">are</hi> the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding <hi type="italic">and</hi> knowledge the state <hi type="italic">thereof</hi> shall be prolonged. <div eID="gen14570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14571" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. National sins bring national disorders and the disturbance of the public repose: <hi type="italic">For the transgression of a land,</hi> and a general defection from God and religion to idolatry, profaneness, or immorality, <hi type="italic">many are the princes thereof,</hi> many at the same time pretending to the sovereignty and contending for it, by which the people are crumbled into parties and factions, biting and devouring one another, or many successively, in a little time, one cutting off another, as <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.8">1 Kings xvi. 8</reference>, &c., or soon cut off by the hand of God or of a foreign enemy, as <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.5">2 Kings xxiv. 5</reference>, &c. As the people suffer for the sins of the prince, <div eID="gen14571" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen14572"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14573"/>Delirant reges, plectuntur Achivi—<l eID="gen14573" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14574"/>Kings play the madmen, and their people suffer for it,

<l eID="gen14574" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen14572"/> <div sID="gen14575" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> A poor man that oppresseth the poor <hi type="italic">is like</hi> a sweeping rain which leaveth no food. <div eID="gen14575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14576" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How hard-hearted poor people frequently are to one another, not only not doing such good offices as they might do one to another, but imposing upon and over-reaching one another. Those who know by experience the miseries of poverty should be compassionate to those who suffer the like, but they are inexcusably barbarous if they be injurious to them. 2. How imperious and griping those commonly are who, being indigent and necessitous, get into power. If a prince prefer a poor man, he forgets that ever he was poor, and none shall be so oppressive to the poor as he, nor squeeze them so cruelly. The hungry leech and the dry sponge suck most. <hi type="italic">Set a beggar on horseback, and he will ride</hi> without mercy. He <hi type="italic">is like a sweeping rain,</hi> which washes away the corn in the ground, and lays and beats out that which has grown, so that it <hi type="italic">leaves no food.</hi> Princes therefore ought not to put those into places of trust who are poor, and in debt, and behind-hand in the world, nor any who make it their main business to enrich themselves.

<div eID="gen14576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14577" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> They that forsake the law praise the wicked: but such as keep the law contend with them. <div eID="gen14577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14578" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that <hi type="italic">praise the wicked</hi> make it to appear that they do themselves <hi type="italic">forsake the law,</hi> and go contrary to it, for that curses and condemns the wicked. Wicked people will speak well of one another, and so strengthen one another's hands in their wicked ways, hoping thereby to silence the clamours of their own consciences and to serve the interests of the devil's kingdom, which is not done by any thing so effectually as by keeping vice in reputation. 2. Those that do indeed make conscience of the law of God themselves will, in their places, vigorously oppose sin, and bear their testimony against it, and do what they can to shame and suppress it. They will reprove the works of darkness, and silence the excuses which are made for those works, and do what they can to bring gross offenders to punishment, that others may hear and fear.

<div eID="gen14578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14579" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Evil men understand not judgment: but they that seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> understand all <hi type="italic">things.</hi> <div eID="gen14579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14580" type="x-p"/> Note, I. As the prevalency of men's lusts is owing to the darkness of their understandings, so the darkness of their understandings is very much owing to the dominion of their lusts: <hi type="italic">Men understand not judgment,</hi> discern not between truth and falsehood, right and wrong; they understand not the law of God as the rule either of their duty or of their doom; and, 1. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> it is that they are <hi type="italic">evil men;</hi> their wickedness is the effect of their ignorance and error, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Eph. iv. 18</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> they <hi type="italic">understand not judgment,</hi> because they are <hi type="italic">evil men;</hi> their corruptions blind their eyes, and fill them with prejudices, and because they do evil they <hi type="italic">hate the light.</hi> It is just with God also to <hi type="italic">give them up to strong delusions.</hi> <div eID="gen14580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14581" type="x-p"/> II. As men's <hi type="italic">seeking the Lord</hi> is a good sign that they do understand much, so it is a good means of their understanding more, even of their understanding all things needful for them. Those that set God's glory before them as their end, his favour as their felicity, and his word as their rule, and apply to him upon all occasions by prayer, <hi type="italic">they seek the Lord,</hi> and he will give them the spirit of wisdom. If a man <hi type="italic">do his will,</hi> he shall <hi type="italic">know his doctrine,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">A good understanding those have,</hi> and a better they shall have, that <hi type="italic">do his commandments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.111.10 1Cor.2.12 1Cor.2.15">Ps. cxi. 10; 1 Cor. ii. 12, 15</reference>.

<div eID="gen14581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14582" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> perverse <hi type="italic">in his</hi> ways, though he <hi type="italic">be</hi> rich. <div eID="gen14582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14583" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. It is supposed that a man may <hi type="italic">walk in his uprightness</hi> and yet be poor in this world, which is a temptation to dishonesty, and yet may resist the temptation and continue to <hi type="italic">walk in his uprightness</hi>—also that a man may be <hi type="italic">perverse in his ways,</hi> injurious to God and man, and yet be rich, and prosper in the world, for a while, may be rich, and so lie under great obligations and have great opportunities to do good, and yet be <hi type="italic">perverse in his ways</hi> and do a great deal of hurt. 2. It is maintained as a paradox to a blind world that an honest, godly, poor man, is better than a wicked, ungodly, rich man, has a better character, is in a better condition, has more comfort in himself, is a greater blessing to the world, and is worthy of much more honour and respect. It is not only certain that his case will be better at death, but it is better in life. When Aristides was by a rich man upbraided with his poverty he answered, <hi type="italic">Thy riches do thee more hurt than my poverty does me.</hi>

<div eID="gen14583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14584" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Whoso keepeth the law <hi type="italic">is</hi> a wise son: but he that is a companion of riotous <hi type="italic">men</hi> shameth his father. <div eID="gen14584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14585" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Religion is true wisdom, and it makes men wise in every relation. He that conscientiously <hi type="italic">keeps the law</hi> is wise, and he will be particularly <hi type="italic">a wise son,</hi> that is, will act discreetly towards his parents, for the law of God teaches him to do so. 2. Bad company is a great hindrance to religion. Those that are <hi type="italic">companions of riotous men,</hi> that choose such for their companions and delight in their conversation, will certainly be drawn from <hi type="italic">keeping the law of God</hi> and drawn to transgress it, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.115">Ps. cxix. 115</reference>. 3. Wickedness is not only a reproach to the sinner himself, but to all that are akin to him. He that keeps rakish company, and spends his time and money with them, not only grieves his parents, but shames them; it turns to their disrepute, as if they had not done their duty to him. They are ashamed that a child of theirs should be scandalous and abusive to their neighbours.

<div eID="gen14585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14586" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> He that by usury and unjust gain increaseth his substance, he shall gather it for him that will pity the poor. <div eID="gen14586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14587" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. That which is ill-got, though it may increase much, will not last long. A man may perhaps raise a great estate, in a little time, by usury and extortion, fraud, and oppression of the poor, but it will not continue; he gathers it for himself, but it shall prove to have been gathered for somebody else that he has no kindness for. His estate shall go to decay, and another man's shall be raised out of the ruins of it. 2. Sometimes God in his providence so orders it that that which one got unjustly another uses charitably; it is strangely turned into the hands of one <hi type="italic">that will pity the poor</hi> and do good with it, and so cut off the entail of the curse which he brought upon it who got it by deceit and violence. Thus the same Providence that punishes the cruel, and disables them to do any more hurt, rewards the merciful, and enables them to do so much the more good. <hi type="italic">To him that has the ten pounds give the pound</hi> which the wicked servant <hi type="italic">hid in the napkin;</hi> for <hi type="italic">to him that has,</hi> and uses it well, more <hi type="italic">shall be given,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.24">Luke xix. 24</reference>. Thus the poor are repaid, the charitable are encouraged, and God is glorified.

<div eID="gen14587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14588" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> abomination. <div eID="gen14588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14589" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is by the word and prayer that our communion with God is kept up. God speaks to us by his law, and expects we should hear him and heed him; <hi type="italic">we</hi> speak to him by prayer, to which we wait for an answer of peace. How reverent and serious should we be, whenever we are hearing from and speaking to the Lord of glory! 2. If God's word be not regarded by us, our prayers shall not only not be accepted of God, but they shall be an abomination to him, not only our sacrifices, which were ceremonial appointments, but even our prayers, which are moral duties, and which, when they are put up by the upright, are so much his delight. See <reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa. i. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">15</reference>. The sinner whose prayers God is thus angry at is one who wilfully and obstinately refuses to obey God's commandments, who will not so much as give them the hearing, but causes his <hi type="italic">ear to decline the law,</hi> and refuses when God calls; God will therefore justly refuse him when he calls. See <reference osisRef="Prov.1.24">Prov. i. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.28">28</reference>.

<div eID="gen14589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14590" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Whoso causeth the righteous to go astray in an evil way, he shall fall himself into his own pit: but the upright shall have good <hi type="italic">things</hi> in possession. <div eID="gen14590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14591" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The doom of seducers, who attempt to draw good people, or those who profess to be such, into sin and mischief, who take pride in <hi type="italic">causing the righteous to go astray in an evil way,</hi> in drawing them into a snare, that they may insult over them. They shall not gain their point; it is impossible to deceive the elect. But they shall <hi type="italic">fall themselves into their own pit;</hi> and having been not only sinners, but tempters, not only unrighteous, but enemies to the righteous, their condemnation will be so much the greater, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.14-Matt.23.15">Matt. xxiii. 14, 15</reference>. 2. The happiness of the sincere. They shall not only be preserved from the evil way which the wicked would decoy them into, but they shall <hi type="italic">have good things,</hi> the best things, <hi type="italic">in possession,</hi> the graces and comforts of God's Spirit, besides what they have in reversion.

<div eID="gen14591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14592" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> The rich man <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise in his own conceit; but the poor that hath understanding searcheth him out. <div eID="gen14592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14593" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that are rich are apt to think themselves wise, because, whatever else they are ignorant of, they know how to get and save; and those that are purse-proud expect that all they say should be regarded as an oracle and a law, and that none should dare to contradict them, but every sheaf bow to theirs; this humour is fed by flatterers, who, because (like Jezebel's prophets) they are fed at their table, cry up their wisdom. 2. Those that are poor often prove themselves wiser than they: A <hi type="italic">poor man,</hi> who has taken pains to get wisdom, having no other way (as the rich man has) to get a reputation, <hi type="italic">searches him out,</hi> and makes it to appear that he is not such a scholar, nor such a politician, as he is taken to be. See how variously God dispenses his gifts; to some he gives wealth, to others wisdom, and it is easy to say which of these is the better gift, which we should <hi type="italic">covet more earnestly.</hi>

<div eID="gen14593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14594" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> When righteous <hi type="italic">men</hi> do rejoice, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> great glory: but when the wicked rise, a man is hidden. <div eID="gen14594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14595" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The comfort of the people of God is the honour of the nation in which they live. There is a <hi type="italic">great glory</hi> dwelling in the land when <hi type="italic">the righteous do rejoice,</hi> when they have their liberty, the free exercise of their religion, and are not persecuted, when the government countenances them and speaks comfortably to them, when they prosper and grow rich, and, much more, when they are preferred and employed and have power put into their hands. 2. The advancement of the wicked is the eclipsing of the beauty of a nation: <hi type="italic">When the wicked rise</hi> and get head they make head against all that is sacred, and then <hi type="italic">a man is hidden,</hi> a good man is thrust into obscurity, is necessitated to abscond for his own safety; corruptions prevail so generally that, as in Elijah's time, there seem to be no good men left, the <hi type="italic">wicked walk</hi> so thickly <hi type="italic">on every side.</hi>

<div eID="gen14595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14596" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh <hi type="italic">them</hi> shall have mercy. <div eID="gen14596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14597" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The folly of indulging sin, of palliating and excusing it, denying or extenuating it, diminishing it, dissembling it, or throwing the blame of it upon others: <hi type="italic">He that</hi> thus <hi type="italic">covers his sins shall not prosper,</hi> let him never expect it. He shall not succeed in his endeavour to cover his sin, for it will be discovered, sooner or later. <hi type="italic">There is nothing hid which shall not be revealed.</hi> A <hi type="italic">bird of the air shall carry the voice.</hi> Murder will out, and so will other sins. He <hi type="italic">shall not prosper,</hi> that is, he shall not obtain the pardon of his sin, nor can he have any true peace of conscience. David owns himself to have been in a constant agitation while he <hi type="italic">covered his sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.3-Ps.32.4">Ps. xxxii. 3, 4</reference>. While the patient conceals his distemper he cannot expect a cure. 2. The benefit of parting with it, both by a penitent confession and a universal reformation: <hi type="italic">He that confesses</hi> his guilt to God, and is careful not to return to sin again, shall <hi type="italic">find mercy</hi> with God, and shall have the comfort of it in his own bosom. His conscience shall be eased and his ruin prevented. See <reference osisRef="1John.1.9">1 John i. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.12-Jer.3.13">Jer. iii. 12, 13</reference>. When we set sin before our face (as David, <hi type="italic">My sin is ever before me</hi>) God casts it behind his back.

<div eID="gen14597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14598" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Happy <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man that feareth alway: but he that hardeneth his heart shall fall into mischief. <div eID="gen14598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14599" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The benefit of a holy caution. It sounds strangely, but it is very true: <hi type="italic">Happy is the man that feareth always.</hi> Most people think that those are happy who never fear; but there is a fear which is so far from having torment in it that it has in it the greatest satisfaction. Happy is the man who always keeps up in his mind a holy awe and reverence of God, his glory, goodness, and government, who is always afraid of offending God and incurring his displeasure, who keeps conscience tender and has a dread of the appearance of evil, who is always jealous of himself, distrustful of his own sufficiency, and lives in expectation of troubles and changes, so that, whenever they come, they are no surprise to him. He who keeps up such a fear as this will live a life of faith and watchfulness, and therefore happy is he, blessed and holy. 2. The danger of a sinful presumption: <hi type="italic">He that hardens his heart,</hi> that mocks at fear, and sets God and his judgments at defiance, and receives not the impressions of his word or rod, <hi type="italic">shall fall into mischief;</hi> his presumption will be his ruin, and whatever sin (which is the greatest mischief) he falls into it is owing to the hardness of his heart.

<div eID="gen14599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14600" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; <hi type="italic">so is</hi> a wicked ruler over the poor people. <div eID="gen14600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14601" type="x-p"/> It is written indeed, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people;</hi> but if he be a wicked ruler, that oppresses the people, especially the poor people, robbing them of the little they have and making a prey of them, whatever we may call him, this scripture calls him <hi type="italic">a roaring lion and a ranging bear.</hi> 1. In respect of his character. He is brutish, barbarous, and blood-thirsty; he is rather to be put among the beasts of prey, the wildest and most savage, than to be reckoned of that noble rank of beings whose glory is reason and humanity. 2. In respect of the mischief he does to his subjects. He is dreadful as the <hi type="italic">roaring lion,</hi> who makes the forest tremble; he is devouring as a hungry <hi type="italic">bear,</hi> and the more necessitous he is the more mischief he does and the more greedy of gain he is.

<div eID="gen14601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14602" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> The prince that wanteth understanding <hi type="italic">is</hi> also a great oppressor: <hi type="italic">but</hi> he that hateth covetousness shall prolong <hi type="italic">his</hi> days. <div eID="gen14602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14603" type="x-p"/> Two things are here intimated to be the causes of the mal-administration of princes:—1. The love of money, that <hi type="italic">root of all evil;</hi> for <hi type="italic">hating covetousness</hi> here stands opposed to <hi type="italic">oppression,</hi> according to Moses's character of good magistrates, <hi type="italic">men fearing God and hating covetousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.21">Exod. xviii. 21</reference>), not only not being covetous, but hating it, and shaking the hands from the holding of bribes. A ruler that is covetous will neither do justly nor love mercy, but the people under him shall be bought and sold. 2. Want of consideration: <hi type="italic">He that hates covetousness shall prolong</hi> his government and peace, shall be happy in the affections of his people and the blessing of his God. It is as much the interest as the duty of princes to reign in righteousness. Oppressors therefore and tyrants are the greatest fools in the world; they <hi type="italic">want understanding;</hi> they do not consult their own honour, ease, and safety, but sacrifice all to their ambition of an absolute and arbitrary power. They might be much happier in the hearts of their subjects than in their necks or estates.

<div eID="gen14603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14604" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> A man that doeth violence to the blood of <hi type="italic">any</hi> person shall flee to the pit; let no man stay him. <div eID="gen14604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14605" type="x-p"/> This agrees with that ancient law, <hi type="italic">Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen. ix. 6</reference>), and proclaims, 1. The doom of the shedder of blood. He that has committed murder, though he flees for his life, shall be continually haunted with terrors, shall himself <hi type="italic">flee to the pit,</hi> betray himself, and torment himself, like Cain, who, when he had killed his brother, became a fugitive and a vagabond, and trembled continually. 2. The duty of the avenger of blood, whether the magistrate or the next of kin, or whoever are concerned in making inquisition for blood, let them be close and vigorous in the prosecution, and let it not be bought off. Those that acquit the murderer, or do any thing to help him off, come in sharers in the guilt of blood; nor can the land be purged from blood but by the blood of him that shed it, <reference osisRef="Num.35.33">Num. xxxv. 33</reference>.

<div eID="gen14605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14606" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Whoso walketh uprightly shall be saved: but <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> perverse <hi type="italic">in his</hi> ways shall fall at once. <div eID="gen14606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14607" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that are honest are always safe. He that acts with sincerity, that speaks as he thinks, has a single eye, in every thing, to the glory of God and the good of his brethren, that would not, for a world, do an unjust thing if he knew it, that in all manner of conversation <hi type="italic">walks uprightly,</hi> he <hi type="italic">shall be saved</hi> hereafter. We find a glorious company of those <hi type="italic">in whose mouth was found no guile,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.5">Rev. xiv. 5</reference>. They shall be safe now. Integrity and uprightness will preserve men, will give them a holy security in the worst of times; for it will preserve their comfort, their reputation, and all their interests. They may be injured, but they cannot be hurt. 2. Those that are false and dishonest are never safe: <hi type="italic">He that is perverse in his ways,</hi> that thinks to secure himself by fraudulent practices, by dissimulation and treachery, or by an estate ill-got, he <hi type="italic">shall fall,</hi> nay, he <hi type="italic">shall fall at once,</hi> not gradually, and with warning given, but suddenly, without previous notice, for he is least safe when he is most secure. He <hi type="italic">falls at once,</hi> and so has neither time to guard against his ruin nor to provide for it; and, being a surprise upon him, it will be so much the greater terror to him.

<div eID="gen14607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14608" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> He that tilleth his land shall have plenty of bread: but he that followeth after vain <hi type="italic">persons</hi> shall have poverty enough. <div eID="gen14608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14609" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that are diligent in their callings take the way to live comfortably: He that <hi type="italic">tills his land,</hi> and tends his shop, and minds his business, whatever it is, he <hi type="italic">shall have plenty of bread,</hi> of that which is necessary for himself and his family and with which he may be charitable to the poor; he shall <hi type="italic">eat the labour of his hands.</hi> 2. Those that are idle, and careless, and company-keepers, though they indulge themselves in living (as they think) easily and pleasantly, they take the way to live miserably. He that has land and values himself upon that, but does not till it, but <hi type="italic">follows after vain persons,</hi> drinks with them, joins with them in their frolics and vain sports, and idles away his time with him, he shall have <hi type="italic">poverty enough,</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">satiated</hi> or <hi type="italic">replenished</hi> with poverty (so the word is); he takes those courses which lead so directly to it that he seems to court it, and he shall have his fill of it.

<div eID="gen14609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14610" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent. <div eID="gen14610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14611" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. We are directed in the true way to be happy, and that is to be holy and honest. He that is <hi type="italic">faithful</hi> to God and man shall be blessed of the Lord, and he <hi type="italic">shall abound with blessings</hi> of the upper and nether springs. Men shall praise him, and pray for him, and be ready to do him any kindness. He shall abound in doing good, and shall himself be a blessing to the place where he lives. Usefulness shall be the reward of faithfulness, and it is a good reward. 2. We are cautioned against a false and deceitful way to happiness, and that is, right or wrong, raising an estate suddenly. Say not, This is the way to <hi type="italic">abound with blessings,</hi> for <hi type="italic">he that makes haste to be rich,</hi> more haste than good speed, <hi type="italic">shall not be innocent;</hi> and, if he be not, he shall not be blessed of God, but rather bring a curse upon what he has; nor, if he be not innocent, can he long be easy to himself; he shall not be accounted innocent by his neighbours, but shall have their ill will and ill word. He does not say that he <hi type="italic">cannot be innocent,</hi> but there is all the probability in the world that he will not prove so: <hi type="italic">He that hasteth with his feet sinneth,</hi> stumbleth, falleth. <hi type="italic">Sed quæ reverentia legum, quis metus, aut pudor, est unquam properantis avari?</hi>—<hi type="italic">What reverence for law, what fear, what shame, was ever indicated by an avaricious man hasting to be rich?</hi>

<div eID="gen14611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14612" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> To have respect of persons <hi type="italic">is</hi> not good: for for a piece of bread <hi type="italic">that</hi> man will transgress. <div eID="gen14612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14613" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a fundamental error in the administration of justice, and that which cannot but lead men to abundance of transgression, to consider the parties concerned more than the merits of the cause, so as to favour one because he is a gentleman, a scholar, my countryman, my old acquaintance, has formerly done me a kindness, or may do me one, or is of my party and persuasion, and to bear hard on the other party because he is a stranger, a poor man, has done me an ill turn, is or has been my rival, or is not of my mind, or has voted against me. Judgment is perverted when any consideration of this kind is admitted into the scale, any thing but pure right. 2. Those that are partial will be paltry. Those that have once broken through the bonds of equity, though, at first, it must be some great bribe, some noble present, that would bias them, yet, when they have debauched their consciences, they will, at length, be so sordid that <hi type="italic">for a piece of bread</hi> they will give judgment against their consciences; they will rather play at small game than sit out.

<div eID="gen14613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14614" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> He that hasteth to be rich <hi type="italic">hath</hi> an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him. <div eID="gen14614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14615" type="x-p"/> Here again Solomon shows the sin and folly of those that will <hi type="italic">be rich;</hi> they are resolved that they will be so, <hi type="italic">per fas, per nefas</hi>—<hi type="italic">right or wrong;</hi> they will be so with all speed; they are getting hastily an estate. 1. They have no comfort in it: They <hi type="italic">have an evil eye,</hi> that is, they are always grieving at those that have more than they, and always grudging their necessary expenses, because they think the former keep them from seeming rich, the latter from being so, and between both they must needs be perpetually uneasy. 2. They have no assurance of the continuance of it, and yet take no thought to provide against the loss of it: <hi type="italic">Poverty shall come upon</hi> them, and the riches which they made wings for, that they might fly to them, will make themselves wings to fly from them; but they are secure and improvident, and do <hi type="italic">not consider</hi> this, that while they are making <hi type="italic">haste to be rich</hi> they are really making haste to be poor, else they would not <hi type="italic">trust to uncertain riches.</hi>

<div eID="gen14615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14616" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue. <div eID="gen14616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14617" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Flatterers may please those for a time who, upon second thoughts, will detest and despise them. If ever they come to be convinced of the evil of those sinful courses they were flattered in, and to be ashamed of the pride and vanity which were humoured and gratified by those flatteries, they will hate the fawning flatterers as having had an ill design upon them, and the fulsome flatteries as having had an ill effect upon them and become nauseous. 2. Reprovers may displease those at first who yet afterwards, when the passion is over and the bitter physic begins to work well, will love and respect them. He that deals faithfully with his friend, in telling him of his faults, though he may put him into some heat for the present, and perhaps have hard words, instead of thanks, for his pains, yet afterwards he will not only have the comfort in his own bosom of having done his duty, but he also whom he reproved will acknowledge that it was a kindness, will entertain a high opinion of his wisdom and faithfulness, and look upon him as fit to be a friend. He that cries out against his surgeon for hurting him when he is searching his wound will yet pay him well, and thank him too, when he has cured it.

<div eID="gen14617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14618" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> no transgression; the same <hi type="italic">is</hi> the companion of a destroyer. <div eID="gen14618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14619" type="x-p"/> As Christ shows the absurdity and wickedness of those children who think it is no duty, in some cases, to maintain their parents (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.5">Matt. xv. 5</reference>), so Solomon here shows the absurdity and wickedness of those who think it is no sin to rob their parents, either by force or secretly, by wheedling them or threatening them, or by wasting what they have, and (which is no better than robbing them) running into debt and leaving them to pay it. Now, 1. This is commonly made light of by untoward children; they say, "<hi type="italic">It is no transgression,</hi> for it will be our own shortly, our parents can well enough spare it, we have occasion for it, we cannot live as gentlemen upon the allowance our parents give us, it is too strait for us." With such excuses as these they endeavour to shift off the conviction. But, 2. How lightly soever an ungoverned youth makes of it, it is really a very great sin; he that does it <hi type="italic">is the companion of a destroyer,</hi> no better than a robber on the highway. What wickedness will he scruple to commit who will rob his own parents?

<div eID="gen14619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14620" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> He that is of a proud heart stirreth up strife: but he that putteth his trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be made fat. <div eID="gen14620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14621" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those make themselves lean, and continually unquiet, that are haughty and quarrelsome, for they are opposed to those that <hi type="italic">shall be made fat: He that is of a proud heart,</hi> that is conceited of himself and looks with a contempt upon all about him, that cannot bear either competition or contradiction, he <hi type="italic">stirs up strife,</hi> makes mischief, and creates disturbance to himself and every body else. 2. Those make themselves fat, and always easy, that live in a continual dependence upon God and his grace: <hi type="italic">He who puts his trust in the Lord,</hi> who, instead of struggling for himself, commits his cause to God, <hi type="italic">shall be made fat.</hi> He saves the money which others spend upon their pride and contentiousness; he enjoys himself, and has abundant satisfaction in his God; and thus his soul dwells at ease, and he is most likely to have plenty of outward good things. None live so easily, so pleasantly, as those who live by faith.

<div eID="gen14621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14622" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> He that trusteth in his own heart is a fool: but whoso walketh wisely, he shall be delivered. <div eID="gen14622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14623" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The character of a fool: <hi type="italic">He trusts to his own heart,</hi> to his own wisdom and counsels, his own strength and sufficiency, his own merit and righteousness, and the good opinion he has of himself; he that does so <hi type="italic">is a fool,</hi> for he trusts to that, not only which <hi type="italic">is deceitful above all things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.9">Jer. xvii. 9</reference>), but which has often deceived him. This implies that it is the character of a wise man (as before, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.25">v. 25</reference>) to <hi type="italic">put his trust in the Lord,</hi> and in his power and promise, and to follow his guidance, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.5-Prov.3.6">Prov. iii. 5, 6</reference>. 2. The comfort of a wise man: He that <hi type="italic">walks wisely,</hi> that trusts not to his own heart, but is humble and self-diffident, and goes on in the strength of the Lord God, <hi type="italic">he shall be delivered;</hi> when the fool, <hi type="italic">that trusts in his own heart,</hi> shall be destroyed.

<div eID="gen14623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14624" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> He that giveth unto the poor shall not lack: but he that hideth his eyes shall have many a curse. <div eID="gen14624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14625" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A promise to the charitable: <hi type="italic">He that gives to the poor</hi> shall himself be never the poorer for so doing; he <hi type="italic">shall not lack.</hi> If he have but little, and so be in danger of lacking, let him give out of his little, and that will prevent it from coming to nothing; as the bounty of the widow of Sarepta to Elijah (for whom she made a little cake first) saved what she had, when it was reduced to a handful of meal. If he have much, let him give much out of it, and that will prevent its growing less; he and his shall not want what is given in pious charity. What we gave we have. 2. A threatening to the uncharitable: <hi type="italic">He that hides his eyes,</hi> that he may not see the miseries of the poor nor read their petitions, lest his eye should affect his heart and extort some relief from him, he <hi type="italic">shall have many a curse,</hi> both from God and man, and neither causeless, and therefore they shall come. Woeful is the condition of that man who has the word of God and the prayers of the poor against him.

<div eID="gen14625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14626" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> When the wicked rise, men hide themselves: but when they perish, the righteous increase. <div eID="gen14626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14627" type="x-p"/> This is to the same purport with what we had, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.12">v. 12</reference>. 1. When bad men are preferred, that which is good is clouded and run down. When power is put into the hands of <hi type="italic">the wicked, men hide themselves;</hi> wise men retire into privacy, and decline public business, not caring to be employed under them; rich men get out of the way, for fear of being squeezed for what they have; and, which is worst of all, good men abscond, despairing to do good and fearing to be persecuted and ill-treated. 2. When bad men are disgraced, degraded, and their power taken from them, then that which is good revives again, then <hi type="italic">the righteous increase;</hi> for, <hi type="italic">when they perish,</hi> good men will be put in their room, who will, by their example and interest, countenance religion and righteousness. It is well with a land when the number of good people increases in it; and it is therefore the policy of all princes, states, and potentates, to encourage them and to take special care of the good education of youth.  <chapter eID="Prov.28"/> <div eID="gen14627" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv86"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv86"/> <div sID="gen14629" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> He, that being often reproved hardeneth <hi type="italic">his</hi> neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy. <div eID="gen14629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14630" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The obstinacy of many wicked people in a wicked way is to be greatly lamented. They are <hi type="italic">often reproved</hi> by parents and friends, by magistrates and ministers, by the providence of God and by their own consciences, have had their sins set in order before them and fair warning given them of the consequences of them, but all in vain; they <hi type="italic">harden their necks.</hi> Perhaps they fling away, and will not so much as give the reproof a patient hearing; or, if they do, yet they go on in the sins for which they are reproved; they will not bow their necks to the yoke, but are children of Belial; they refuse reproof (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.17">ch. x. 17</reference>), despise it (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.12">ch. v. 12</reference>), hate it, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.1">ch. xii. 1</reference>. 2. The issue of this obstinacy is to be greatly dreaded: Those that go on in sin, in spite of admonition, <hi type="italic">shall be destroyed;</hi> those that will not be reformed must expect to be ruined; if the rods answer not the end, expect the axes. They <hi type="italic">shall be suddenly destroyed,</hi> in the midst of their security, <hi type="italic">and without remedy;</hi> they have sinned against the preventing remedy, and therefore let them not expect any recovering remedy. Hell is remediless destruction. They <hi type="italic">shall be destroyed, and no healing,</hi> so the word is. If God wounds, who can heal?

<div eID="gen14630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14631" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn. <div eID="gen14631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14632" type="x-p"/> This is what was said before, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.12">ch. xxviii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.28">28</reference>. 1. <hi type="italic">The people</hi> will have cause to <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> or <hi type="italic">mourn</hi> according as their rulers are <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> or <hi type="italic">wicked;</hi> for, if <hi type="italic">the righteous</hi> be in <hi type="italic">authority,</hi> sin will be punished and restrained, religion and virtue will be supported and kept in reputation; <hi type="italic">but,</hi> if <hi type="italic">the wicked</hi> get power in their hands, wickedness will abound, religion and religious people will be persecuted, and so the ends of government will be perverted. 2. <hi type="italic">The people</hi> will actually <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> or <hi type="italic">mourn</hi> according as their rulers are <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> or <hi type="italic">wicked.</hi> Such a conviction are even the common people under of the excellency of virtue and religion that they will rejoice when they see them preferred and countenanced; and, on the contrary, let men have ever so much honour or power, if they be wicked and vicious, and use it ill, they <hi type="italic">make themselves contemptible and base before all the people</hi> (as those priests, <reference osisRef="Mal.2.9">Mal. ii. 9</reference>) and subjects will think themselves miserable under such a government.

<div eID="gen14632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14633" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Whoso loveth wisdom rejoiceth his father: but he that keepeth company with harlots spendeth <hi type="italic">his</hi> substance. <div eID="gen14633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14634" type="x-p"/> Both the parts of this verse repeat what has been often said, but, on comparing them together, the sense of them will be enlarged from each other. 1. Be it observed, to the honour of a virtuous young man, that he <hi type="italic">loves wisdom,</hi> he is <hi type="italic">a philosopher</hi> (for that signifies <hi type="italic">a lover of wisdom</hi>), for religion is the best philosophy; he avoids bad company, and especially the company of lewd women. Hereby he <hi type="italic">rejoices his</hi> parents, and has the satisfaction of being a comfort to them, and increases his estate, and is likely to live comfortably. 2. Be it observed, to the reproach of a vicious young man, that he hates <hi type="italic">wisdom; he keeps company with</hi> scandalous women, who will be his ruin, both in soul and body; he grieves his parents, and, like the prodigal son, devours their living <hi type="italic">with harlots.</hi> Nothing will beggar men sooner than the lusts of uncleanness; and the best preservative from those ruinous lusts is <hi type="italic">wisdom.</hi>

<div eID="gen14634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14635" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it. <div eID="gen14635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14636" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The happiness of a people under a good government. The care and business of a prince should be to <hi type="italic">establish the land,</hi> to maintain its fundamental laws, to settle the minds of his subjects and make them easy, to secure their liberties and properties from hostilities and for posterity, and to set in order the things that are wanting; this he must do <hi type="italic">by judgment,</hi> by wise counsels, and by the steady administration of justice, without respect of persons, which will have these good effects. 2. The misery of a people under a bad government: <hi type="italic">A man of oblations</hi> (so it is in the margin) <hi type="italic">overthrows the land;</hi> a man that is either sacrilegious or superstitious, or that invades the priest's office, as Saul and Uzziah—or a man that aims at nothing but getting money, and will, for a good bribe, connive at the most guilty, and, in hope of one, persecute the innocent—such governors as these will ruin a country.

<div eID="gen14636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14637" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet. <div eID="gen14637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14638" type="x-p"/> Those may be said to <hi type="italic">flatter their neighbours</hi> who commend and applaud that good in them (the good they do or the good they have) which really either is not or is not such as they represent it, and who profess that esteem and that affection for them which really they have not; these <hi type="italic">spread a net for their feet.</hi> 1. For their neighbours' feet, whom they <hi type="italic">flatter.</hi> They have an ill design in it; they would not praise them as they do but that they hope to make an advantage of them; and it is therefore wisdom to suspect those who flatter us, that they are secretly laying a snare for us, and to stand on our guard accordingly. Or it has an ill effect on those who are flattered; it puffs them up with pride, and makes them conceited and confident of themselves, and so proves a net that entangles them in sin. 2. For their own feet; so some understand it. He that flatters others, in expectation that they will return his compliments and flatter him, does but make himself ridiculous and odious even to those he flatters.

<div eID="gen14638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14639" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> In the transgression of an evil man <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a snare: but the righteous doth sing and rejoice. <div eID="gen14639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14640" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The peril of a sinful way. There is not only a punishment at the end of it, but <hi type="italic">a snare</hi> in it. One sin is a temptation to another, and there are troubles which, as <hi type="italic">a snare,</hi> come suddenly upon evil men in the midst of their transgressions; nay, their transgression itself often involves them in vexations; their sin is their punishment, and they are <hi type="italic">holden in the cords of their own iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.22">ch. v. 22</reference>. 2. The pleasantness of the way of holiness. The snare that is <hi type="italic">in the transgression of evil men</hi> spoils all their mirth, <hi type="italic">but righteous</hi> men are kept from those snares, or delivered out of them; they walk at liberty, walk in safety, and therefore they <hi type="italic">sing and rejoice.</hi> Those that make God their chief joy have him for their exceeding joy, and it is their own fault if they do not <hi type="italic">rejoice evermore.</hi> If there be any true joy on this side heaven, doubtless those have it whose conversation is in heaven.

<div eID="gen14640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14641" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The righteous considereth the cause of the poor: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the wicked regardeth not to know <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen14641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14642" type="x-p"/> It is a pity but that every one who sues <hi type="italic">sub form&#226; pauperis</hi>—<hi type="italic">as a pauper,</hi> should have an honest cause (they are of all others inexcusable if they have not), because the scripture has so well provided that it should have a fair hearing, and that the judge himself should be of counsel, as for the prisoner, so for the pauper. 1. It is here made the character of a <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> judge that he <hi type="italic">considers the cause of the poor.</hi> It is every man's duty to consider the poor (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.1">Ps. xli. 1</reference>), but the judgment of the poor is to be considered by those that sit in judgment; they must take as much pains to find out the right in a poor man's cause as in a rich man's. Sense of justice must make both judge and advocate as solicitous and industrious in the poor man's cause as if they hoped for the greatest advantage. 2. It is made the character of a <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> man that because it is a poor man's cause, which there is nothing to be got by, he <hi type="italic">regards not to know it,</hi> in the true state of it, for he cares not which way it goes, right or wrong. See <reference osisRef="Job.29.16">Job xxix. 16</reference>.

<div eID="gen14642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14643" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Scornful men bring a city into a snare: but wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> turn away wrath. <div eID="gen14643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14644" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. Who are the men that are dangerous to the public—<hi type="italic">scornful men.</hi> When such are employed in the business of the state they do things with precipitation, because they scorn to deliberate, and will not take time for consideration and consultation; they do things illegal and unjustifiable, because they scorn to be hampered by laws and constitutions; they break their faith, because they scorn to be bound by their word, and provoke the people, because they scorn to please them. Thus they <hi type="italic">bring a city into a snare</hi> by their ill conduct, or (as the margin reads it) they <hi type="italic">set a city on fire;</hi> they sow discord among the citizens and run them into confusion. Those are <hi type="italic">scornful men</hi> that mock at religion, the obligations of conscience, the fears of another world, and every thing that is sacred and serious. Such men are the plagues of their generation; they bring God's judgments upon a land, set men together by the ears, and so bring all to confusion. 2. Who are the men that are the blessings of a land—the <hi type="italic">wise men</hi> who by promoting religion, which is true wisdom, <hi type="italic">turn away the wrath</hi> of God, and who, by prudent counsels, reconcile contending parties and prevent the mischievous consequences of divisions. Proud and foolish men kindle the fires which wise and good men must extinguish.
