<div eID="gen14644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14645" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">If</hi> a wise man contendeth with a foolish man, whether he rage or laugh, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no rest. <div eID="gen14645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14646" type="x-p"/> A wise man is here advised not to set his wit to a fool's, not to dispute with him, or by contending with him to think either of fastening reason upon him or gaining right from him: <hi type="italic">If a wise man contend with a wise man,</hi> he may hope to be understood, and, as far as he has reason and equity on his side, to carry his point, at least to bring the controversy to a head and make it issue amicably; but, if he <hi type="italic">contend with a foolish man, there is no rest;</hi> he will see no end of it, nor will he have any satisfaction in it, but must expect to be always uneasy. 1. Whether the foolish man he contends with <hi type="italic">rage or laugh,</hi> whether he take angrily or scornfully what is said to him, whether he rail at it or mock at it, one of the two he will do, and so there will be <hi type="italic">no rest.</hi> However it is given, it will be ill-taken, and the wisest man must expect to be either scolded or ridiculed if he <hi type="italic">contend with a fool.</hi> He that fights with a dunghill, whether he be conqueror or conquered, is sure to be defiled. 2. Whether the wise man himself <hi type="italic">rage or laugh,</hi> whether he take the serious or the jocular way of dealing with the fool, whether he be severe or pleasant with him, whether he come with a rod or with <hi type="italic">the spirit of meekness</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.21">1 Cor. iv. 21</reference>), it is all alike, no good is done. <hi type="italic">We have piped unto you, and you have not danced, mourned unto you, and you have not lamented.</hi>

<div eID="gen14646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14647" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul. <div eID="gen14647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14648" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Bad men hate their best friends: <hi type="italic">The blood-thirsty,</hi> all the seed of the old serpent, who <hi type="italic">was a murderer from the beginning,</hi> all that inherit his enmity against the seed of the woman, <hi type="italic">hate the upright;</hi> they seek the ruin of good men because they condemn the wicked world and witness against it. Christ told his disciples that they should be <hi type="italic">hated of all men.</hi> Bloody men do especially <hi type="italic">hate upright</hi> magistrates, who would restrain and reform them, and put the laws in execution against them, and so really do them a kindness. 2. Good men love their worst enemies: <hi type="italic">The just,</hi> whom the bloody men hate, <hi type="italic">seek their soul,</hi> pray for their conversion, and would gladly do any thing for their salvation. This Christ taught us. <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them. The just seek his soul,</hi> that is, the soul of the upright, whom the bloody hate (so it is commonly understood), seek to protect it from violence, and save it from, or avenge it at, the hands of <hi type="italic">the blood-thirsty.</hi>

<div eID="gen14648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14649" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise <hi type="italic">man</hi> keepeth it in till afterwards. <div eID="gen14649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14650" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a piece of weakness to be very open: He is <hi type="italic">a fool</hi> who <hi type="italic">utters all his mind,</hi>—who tells every thing he knows, and has in his mouth instantly whatever he has in his thoughts, and can keep no counsel,—who, whatever is started in discourse, quickly shoots his bolt,—who, when he is provoked, will say any thing that comes uppermost, whoever is reflected upon by it,—who, when he is to speak of any business, will say all he thinks, and yet never thinks he says enough, whether choice or refuse, corn or chaff, pertinent or impertinent, you shall have it all. 2. It is a piece of wisdom to be upon the reserve: <hi type="italic">A wise man</hi> will not <hi type="italic">utter all his mind</hi> at once, but will take time for a second thought, or reserve the present thought for a fitter time, when it will be more pertinent and likely to answer his intention; he will not deliver himself in a continued speech, or starched discourse, but with pauses, that he may hear what is to be objected and answer it. <hi type="italic">Non minus interdum oratorium est tacere quam dicere</hi>—<hi type="italic">True oratory requires an occasional pause.</hi> Plin. <reference osisRef="Eph.7">Ep. 7</reference>.6.

<div eID="gen14650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14651" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants <hi type="italic">are</hi> wicked. <div eID="gen14651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14652" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a great sin in any, especially in rulers, to <hi type="italic">hearken to lies;</hi> for thereby they not only give a wrong judgment themselves of persons and things, according to the lies they give credit to, but they encourage others to give wrong informations. Lies will be told to those that will hearken to them; but the receiver, in this case, is as bad as the thief. 2. Those that do so will have <hi type="italic">all their servants wicked.</hi> All their servants will appear wicked, for they will have lies told of them; and they will be wicked, for they will tell lies to them. All that have their ear will fill their ear with slanders and false characters and representations; and so if princes, as well as people, will be deceived, they shall be deceived, and, instead of devolving the guilt of their own false judgments upon their servants that misinformed them, they must share in their servants' guilt, and on them will much of the blame lie for encouraging such misinformations and giving countenance and ear to them.

<div eID="gen14652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14653" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> The poor and the deceitful man meet together: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> lighteneth both their eyes. <div eID="gen14653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14654" type="x-p"/> This shows how wisely the great God serves the designs of his providence by persons of very different tempers, capacities, and conditions in the world, even, 1. By those that are contrary the one to the other. Some are <hi type="italic">poor</hi> and forced to borrow; others are rich, have a great deal of <hi type="italic">the mammon of unrighteousness (deceitful riches</hi> they are called), and they are creditors, or <hi type="italic">usurers,</hi> as it is in the margin. Some are <hi type="italic">poor,</hi> and honest, and laborious; others are rich, slothful, and <hi type="italic">deceitful.</hi> They <hi type="italic">meet together</hi> in the business of this world, and have dealings with one another, and <hi type="italic">the Lord enlightens both their eyes;</hi> he causes his sun to shine upon both and gives them both the comforts of this life. To some of both sorts he gives his grace. He enlightens the eyes of the poor by giving them patience, and of the deceitful by giving them repentance, as Zaccheus. 2. By those that we think could best be spared. <hi type="italic">The poor and the deceitful</hi> we are ready to look upon as blemishes of Providence, but God makes even them to display the beauty of Providence; he has wise ends not only in leaving the poor always with us, but in permitting <hi type="italic">the deceived and the deceiver,</hi> for both <hi type="italic">are his</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job xii. 16</reference>) and turn to his praise.

<div eID="gen14654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14655" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever. <div eID="gen14655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14656" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The duty of magistrates, and that is, to judge faithfully between man and man, and to determine all causes brought before them, according to truth and equity, particularly to take care of <hi type="italic">the poor,</hi> not to countenance them in an unjust cause for the sake of their poverty (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.3">Exod. xxiii. 3</reference>), but to see that their poverty do not turn to their prejudice if they have a just cause. The rich will look to themselves, but <hi type="italic">the poor</hi> and needy the prince must <hi type="italic">defend</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.3">Ps. lxxxii. 3</reference>) and plead for, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.9">Prov. xxxi. 9</reference>. 2. The happiness of those magistrates that do their duty. Their <hi type="italic">throne</hi> of honour, their tribunal of judgment, <hi type="italic">shall be established for ever.</hi> This will secure to them the favour of God and strengthen their interest in the affections of their people, both which will be the establishment of their power, and help to transmit it to posterity and perpetuate it in the family.  <div eID="gen14656" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv87"/><title type="x-s3">Parental Discipline.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv87"/> <div sID="gen14657" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left <hi type="italic">to himself</hi> bringeth his mother to shame. <div eID="gen14657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14658" type="x-p"/> Parents, in educating their children, must consider, 1. The benefit of due correction. They must not only tell their children what is good and evil, but they must chide them, and correct them too, if need be, when they either neglect that which is good or do that which is evil. If a <hi type="italic">reproof</hi> will serve without <hi type="italic">the rod,</hi> it is well, but <hi type="italic">the rod</hi> must never be used without a rational and grave <hi type="italic">reproof;</hi> and then, though it may be a present uneasiness both to the father and to the child, yet it will <hi type="italic">give wisdom. Vexatio dat intellectum—Vexation sharpens the intellect.</hi> The child will take warning, and so will get <hi type="italic">wisdom.</hi> 2. The mischief of undue indulgence: <hi type="italic">A child</hi> that is not restrained or reproved, but is <hi type="italic">left to himself,</hi> as Adonijah was, to follow his own inclinations, may do well if he will, but, if he take to ill courses, nobody will hinder him; it is a thousand to one but he proves a disgrace to his family, and <hi type="italic">brings his mother,</hi> who fondled him and humoured him in his licentiousness, <hi type="italic">to shame,</hi> to poverty, to reproach, and perhaps will himself be abusive to her and give her ill language.

<div eID="gen14658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14659" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> When the wicked are multiplied, transgression increaseth: but the righteous shall see their fall. <div eID="gen14659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14660" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The more sinners there are the more sin there is: <hi type="italic">When the wicked,</hi> being countenanced by authority, grow numerous, and walk on every side, no marvel if <hi type="italic">transgression increases,</hi> as a plague in the country is said to increase when still more and more are infected with it. <hi type="italic">Transgression</hi> grows more impudent and bold, more imperious and threatening, when there are many to keep it in countenance. In the old world, when <hi type="italic">men began to multiply,</hi> they began to degenerate and corrupt themselves and one another. 2. The more sin there is the nearer is the ruin threatened. Let not <hi type="italic">the righteous</hi> have their faith and hope shocked by the increase of sin and sinners. Let them not say that they have <hi type="italic">cleansed their hands in vain,</hi> or that <hi type="italic">God has forsaken the earth,</hi> but wait with patience; the transgressors shall fall, the measure of their iniquity will be full, and then they shall fall from their dignity and power, and fall into disgrace and destruction, and <hi type="italic">the righteous shall</hi> have the satisfaction of <hi type="italic">seeing their fall</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.34">Ps. xxxvii. 34</reference>), perhaps in this world, certainly in the judgment of the great day, when the fall of God's implacable enemies will be the joy and triumph of glorified saints. See <reference osisRef="Isa.66.24">Isa. lxvi. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.19.28">Gen. xix. 28</reference>.

<div eID="gen14660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14661" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul. <div eID="gen14661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14662" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a very happy thing when children prove the comfort of their parents. Good children are so; they <hi type="italic">give them rest,</hi> make them easy, and free from the many cares they have had concerning them; <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> they <hi type="italic">give delight unto their souls.</hi> It is a pleasure to parents, which none know but those that are blessed with it, to see the happy fruit of the good education they have given their children, and to have a prospect of their well-doing for both worlds; it <hi type="italic">gives delight</hi> proportionable to the many thoughts of heart that have been concerning them. 2. In order to this, children must be trained up under a strict discipline, and not suffered to do what they will and to go without rebuke when they do amiss. The foolishness bound up in their hearts must by correction be driven out when they are young, or it will break out, to their own and their parents' shame, when they are grown up.  <div eID="gen14662" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv88"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv88"/> <div sID="gen14663" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Where <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy <hi type="italic">is</hi> he. <div eID="gen14663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14664" type="x-p"/> See here, I. The misery of the people that want a settled ministry: <hi type="italic">Where there is no vision,</hi> no prophet to expound the law, no priest or Levite to teach the good knowledge of the Lord, no means of grace, the word of the Lord is scarce, there is <hi type="italic">no open vision</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.1">1 Sam. iii. 1</reference>), where it is so <hi type="italic">the people perish;</hi> the word has many significations, any of which will apply here. 1. <hi type="italic">The people are made naked,</hi> stripped of their ornaments and so exposed to shame, stripped of their armour and so exposed to danger. How bare does a place look without Bibles and ministers, and what an easy prey is it to the enemy of souls! 2. <hi type="italic">The people rebel,</hi> not only against God, but against their prince; good preaching would make people good subjects, but, for want of it, they are turbulent and factious, and <hi type="italic">despise dominions,</hi> because they know no better. 3. <hi type="italic">The people are idle,</hi> or <hi type="italic">they play,</hi> as the scholars are apt to do when the master is absent; they do nothing to any good purpose, but stand all the day idle, and sporting in the market-place, for want of instruction what to do and how to do it. 4. <hi type="italic">They are scattered as sheep having no shepherd,</hi> for want of the masters of assemblies to call them and keep them together, <reference osisRef="Mark.6.34">Mark vi. 34</reference>. They are scattered from God and their duty by apostasies, from one another by divisions; God is provoked to scatter them by his judgments, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">2 Chron. xv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">5</reference>. 5. <hi type="italic">They perish;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">destroyed for lack of knowledge,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.4.6">Hos. iv. 6</reference>. See what reason we have to be thankful to God for the plenty of <hi type="italic">open vision</hi> which we enjoy. <div eID="gen14664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14665" type="x-p"/> II. The felicity of a people that have not only a settled, but a successful ministry among them, the people that hear and <hi type="italic">keep the law,</hi> among whom religion is uppermost; <hi type="italic">happy</hi> are such a people and every particular person among them. It is not having the law, but obeying it, and living up to it, that will entitle us to blessedness.

<div eID="gen14665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14666" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> A servant will not be corrected by words: for though he understand he will not answer. <div eID="gen14666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14667" type="x-p"/> Here is the description of an unprofitable, slothful, wicked servant, a slave that serves not from conscience, or love, but purely from fear. Let those that have such servants put on patience to bear the vexation and not disturb themselves at it. See their character. 1. No rational words will work upon them; they <hi type="italic">will not be corrected</hi> and reformed, not brought to their business, nor cured of their idleness and laziness, by fair means, no, nor by foul <hi type="italic">words;</hi> even the most gentle master will be forced to use severity with them; no reason will serve their turn, for they are unreasonable. 2. No rational words will be got from them. They are dogged and sullen; and, <hi type="italic">though they understand</hi> the questions you ask them, they <hi type="italic">will not</hi> give you an <hi type="italic">answer;</hi> though you make it ever so plain to them what you expect from them, they will not promise you to mend what is amiss nor to mind their business. See the folly of those servants whose mouth by their silence calls for strokes; they might <hi type="italic">be corrected by words</hi> and save blows, but they <hi type="italic">will not.</hi>

<div eID="gen14667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14668" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Seest thou a man <hi type="italic">that is</hi> hasty in his words? <hi type="italic">there is</hi> more hope of a fool than of him. <div eID="gen14668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14669" type="x-p"/> Solomon here shows that there is little hope of bringing a man to wisdom that is hasty either, 1. Through rashness and inconsideration: <hi type="italic">Seest thou a man that is hasty in his matters,</hi> that is of a light desultory wit, that seems to take a thing quickly, but takes it by the halves, gallops over a book or science, but takes no time to digest it, no time to pause or muse upon a business? <hi type="italic">There is more hope of</hi> making a scholar and a wise man of one that is dull and heavy, and slow in his studies, than of one that has such a mercurial genius and cannot fix. 2. Through pride and conceitedness: <hi type="italic">Seest thou a man that is</hi> forward to speak to every matter that is started, and affects to speak first to it, to open it, and speak last to it, to give judgment upon it, as if he were an oracle? <hi type="italic">There is more hope of a</hi> modest <hi type="italic">fool,</hi> who is sensible of his folly, than of such a self-conceited one.

<div eID="gen14669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14670" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> He that delicately bringeth up his servant from a child shall have him become <hi type="italic">his</hi> son at the length. <div eID="gen14670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14671" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is an imprudent thing in a master to be too fond of a servant, to advance him too fast, and admit him to be too familiar with him, to suffer him to be over-nice and curious in his diet, and clothing, and lodging, and so to bring him up delicately, because he is a favourite, and an agreeable servant; it should be remembered that he is a servant, and, by being thus indulged, will be spoiled for any other place. Servants must endure hardness. 2. It is an ungrateful thing in a servant, but what is very common, to behave insolently because he has been used tenderly. The humble prodigal thinks himself unworthy <hi type="italic">to be called a son,</hi> and is content to be a servant; the pampered slave thinks himself too good to be called <hi type="italic">a servant,</hi> and will be <hi type="italic">a son at the length,</hi> will take his ease and liberty, will be on a par with his master, and perhaps pretend to the inheritance. Let masters <hi type="italic">give their servants that which is equal</hi> and fit for them, and neither more nor less. This is very applicable to the body, which is a servant to the soul; those that <hi type="italic">delicately bring up</hi> the body, that humour it, and are over-tender of it, will find that at length it will forget its place, and <hi type="italic">become a son,</hi> a master, a perfect tyrant.

<div eID="gen14671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14672" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression. <div eID="gen14672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14673" type="x-p"/> See here the mischief that flows from an angry, passionate, furious disposition. 1. It makes men provoking to one another: <hi type="italic">An angry man stirs up strife,</hi> is troublesome and quarrelsome in the family and in the neighbourhood, blows the coals, and even forces those to fall out with him that would live peaceable and quietly by him. 2. It makes men provoking to God: <hi type="italic">A furious man,</hi> who is wedded to his humours and passions, cannot but <hi type="italic">abound in transgressions.</hi> Undue anger is a sin which is the cause of many sins; it not only hinders men from calling upon God's name, but it occasions their swearing, and cursing, and profaning God's name.

<div eID="gen14673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14674" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit. <div eID="gen14674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14675" type="x-p"/> This agrees with what Christ said more than once, 1. That those who <hi type="italic">exalt themselves shall be abased.</hi> Those that think to gain respect by lifting up themselves above their rank, by looking high, talking big, appearing fine, and applauding themselves, will on the contrary expose themselves to contempt, lose their reputation, and provoke God by humbling providences to bring them down and lay them <hi type="italic">low.</hi> 2. That those who <hi type="italic">humble themselves shall be exalted,</hi> and shall be established in their dignity: <hi type="italic">Honour shall uphold the humble in spirit;</hi> their humility is their honour, and that shall make them truly and safely great, and recommend them to the esteem of all that are wise and good.

<div eID="gen14675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14676" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth <hi type="italic">it</hi> not. <div eID="gen14676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14677" type="x-p"/> See here what sin and ruin those involve themselves in who are drawn away by the enticement of sinners. 1. They incur a great deal of guilt: <hi type="italic">He</hi> does so that goes <hi type="italic">partner with</hi> such as rob and defraud, and <hi type="italic">casts in his lot among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.11">ch. i. 11</reference>, &c. The receiver is as bad as the thief; and, being drawn in to join with him in the commission of the sin, he cannot escape joining with him in the concealment of it, though it be with the most horrid perjuries and execrations. They <hi type="italic">hear cursing</hi> when they are sworn to tell the whole truth, but they will not confess. 2. They hasten to utter ruin: They even <hi type="italic">hate their own souls,</hi> for they wilfully do that which will be the inevitable destruction of them. See the absurdities sinners are guilty of; they love death, than which nothing is more dreadful, and <hi type="italic">hate their own souls,</hi> than which nothing is more dear.

<div eID="gen14677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14678" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be safe. <div eID="gen14678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14679" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. We are cautioned not to dread the power of man, neither the power of a prince nor the power of the multitude; both are formidable enough, but the slavish fear of either <hi type="italic">brings a snare,</hi> that is, exposes men to many insults (some take a pride in terrifying the timorous), or rather exposes men to many temptations. Abraham, for <hi type="italic">fear of man,</hi> denied his wife, and Peter his Master, and many a one his God and religion. We must not shrink from duty, nor commit sin, to avoid the wrath of man, nor, though we see it coming upon us, be disquieted with fear, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.16">Dan. iii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.6">Ps. cxviii. 6</reference>. He must himself die (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.12">Isa. li. 12</reference>) and can but kill our body, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.5">Luke xii. 5</reference>. 2. We are encouraged to depend upon the power of God, which would keep us from all that <hi type="italic">fear of man</hi> which has either torment or temptation in it. <hi type="italic">Whoso puts his trust in the Lord,</hi> for protection and supply in the way of duty, <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> set on high, above the power of man and above the fear of that power. A holy confidence in God makes a man both great and easy, and enables him to look with a gracious contempt upon the most formidable designs of hell and earth against him. If God be my salvation, <hi type="italic">I will trust and not be afraid.</hi>

<div eID="gen14679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14680" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Many seek the ruler's favour; but <hi type="italic">every</hi> man's judgment <hi type="italic">cometh</hi> from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14681" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What is the common course men take to advance and enrich themselves, and make themselves great: they <hi type="italic">seek the ruler's favour,</hi> and, as if all their judgment proceeded from him, to him they make all their court. Solomon was himself a <hi type="italic">ruler,</hi> and knew with what sedulity men made their application to him, some on one errand, others on another, but all for his <hi type="italic">favour.</hi> It is the way of the world to make interest with great men, and expect much from the smiles of second causes, which yet are uncertain, and frequently disappoint them. <hi type="italic">Many</hi> take a great deal of pains in seeking <hi type="italic">the ruler's favour</hi> and yet cannot have it; many have it for a little while, but they cannot keep themselves in it, by some little turn or other they are brought under his displeasure; many have it, and keep it, and yet it does not answer their expectation, they cannot make that hand of it that they promised themselves they should. Haman had <hi type="italic">the ruler's favour,</hi> and yet it availed him nothing. 2. What is the wisest course men can take to be happy. Let them look up to God, and seek the favour of the Ruler of rulers; for <hi type="italic">every man's judgment proceeds from the Lord.</hi> It is not with us as the ruler pleases; his favour cannot make us happy, his frowns cannot make us miserable. But it is as God pleases; every creature is that to us that God makes it to be, no more and no other. He is the first Cause, on which all second causes depend; if he help not, they cannot, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.27">2 Kings vi. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job xxxiv. 29</reference>.

<div eID="gen14681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14682" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> An unjust man <hi type="italic">is</hi> an abomination to the just: and <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> upright in the way <hi type="italic">is</hi> abomination to the wicked. <div eID="gen14682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14683" type="x-p"/> This expresses not only the innate contrariety that there is between virtue and vice, as between light and darkness, fire and water, but the old enmity that has always been between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>. 1. All that are sanctified have a rooted antipathy to wickedness and wicked people. They have a good will to the souls of all (God has, and would have none perish); but they hate the ways and practices of those that are impious towards God and injurious towards men; they cannot hear of them nor speak of them without a holy indignation; they loathe the society of the ungodly and unjust, and dread the thought of giving them any countenance, but do all they can to bring the wickedness of the wicked to an end. Thus <hi type="italic">an unjust</hi> man makes himself odious <hi type="italic">to the just,</hi> and it is one part of his present shame and punishment that good men cannot endure him. 2. All that are unsanctified have a like rooted antipathy to godliness and godly people: <hi type="italic">He that is upright in the way,</hi> that makes conscience of what he says and does, <hi type="italic">is an abomination to the wicked,</hi> whose wickedness is restrained perhaps and suppressed, or, at least, shamed and condemned, by the uprightness of the upright. Thus Cain did, who was <hi type="italic">of his father the devil.</hi> And this is not only the wickedness of the wicked, that they hate those whom God loves, but their misery too, that they hate those whom them shall shortly see in everlasting bliss and honour, and who shall have <hi type="italic">dominion over them in the morning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Ps. xlix. 14</reference>.  <chapter eID="Prov.29"/> <div eID="gen14683" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen14686" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14685" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Words of Agur.</title> <div sID="gen14687" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The words of Agur the son of Jakeh, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the prophecy: the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal, <hi type="super">2</hi> Surely I <hi type="italic">am</hi> more brutish than <hi type="italic">any</hi> man, and have not the understanding of a man. <hi type="super">3</hi> I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy. <hi type="super">4</hi> Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name, and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> his son's name, if thou canst tell? <hi type="super">5</hi> Every word of God <hi type="italic">is</hi> pure: he <hi type="italic">is</hi> a shield unto them that put their trust in him. <hi type="super">6</hi> Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar. <div eID="gen14687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14688" type="x-p"/> Some make <hi type="italic">Agur</hi> to be not the name of this author, but his character; he was a <hi type="italic">collector</hi> (so it signifies), a gatherer, one that did not compose things himself, but collected the wise sayings and observations of others, made abstracts of the writings of others, which some think is the reason why he says (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.3">v. 3</reference>), "<hi type="italic">I</hi> have not <hi type="italic">learned wisdom</hi> myself, but have been a scribe, or amanuensis, to other wise and learned men." Note, We must not bury our talent, though it be but one, but, as we have received the gift, so minister the same, if it be but to collect what others have written. But we rather suppose it to be his name, which, no doubt, was well known then, though not mentioned elsewhere in scripture. <hi type="italic">Ithiel and Ucal</hi> are mentioned, either, 1. As the names of his pupils, whom he instructed, or who consulted him as an oracle, having a great opinion of his wisdom and goodness. Probably they wrote from him what he dictated, as Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah, and by their means it was preserved, as they were ready to attest it to be his, for it was spoken to them; they were two witnesses of it. Or, 2. As the subject of his discourse. <hi type="italic">Ithiel</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">God with me,</hi> the application of <hi type="italic">Immanuel, God with us.</hi> The word calls him <hi type="italic">God with us;</hi> faith appropriates this, and calls him "<hi type="italic">God with me,</hi> who loved me, and gave himself for me, and into union and communion with whom I am admitted." <hi type="italic">Ucal</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">the Mighty One,</hi> for it is upon one that is mighty that help is laid for us. Many good interpreters therefore apply this to the Messiah, for to him all the prophecies bear witness, and why not this then? It is what Agur spoke concerning <hi type="italic">Ithiel, even</hi> concerning <hi type="italic">Ithiel</hi> (that is the name on which the stress is laid) <hi type="italic">with us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Isa. vii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen14688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14689" type="x-p"/> Three things the prophet here aims at:— <div eID="gen14689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14690" type="x-p"/> I. To abase himself. Before he makes confession of his faith he makes confession of his folly and the weakness and deficiency of reason, which make it so necessary that we be guided and governed by faith. Before he speaks concerning the Saviour he speaks of himself as needing a Saviour, and as nothing without him; we must go out of ourselves before we go into Jesus Christ. 1. He speaks of himself as wanting a righteousness, and having done foolishly, very foolishly. When he reflects upon himself he owns, <hi type="italic">Surely I am more brutish than any man. Every man has become brutish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.10.14">Jer. x. 14</reference>. But he that knows his own heart knows so much more evil of himself than he does of any other that he cries out, "<hi type="italic">Surely</hi> I cannot but think that <hi type="italic">I am more brutish than any man;</hi> surely no man has such a corrupt deceitful heart as I have. I have acted as one that has <hi type="italic">not the understanding</hi> of Adam, as one that is wretchedly degenerated from the knowledge and righteousness in which man was at first created; nay, I have not the common sense and reason of a man, else I should not have done as I have done." Agur, when he was applied to by others as wiser than most, acknowledged himself more foolish than any. Whatever high opinion others may have of us, it becomes us to have low thoughts of ourselves. 2. He speaks of himself as wanting a revelation to guide him in the ways of truth and wisdom. He owns (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.3">v. 3</reference>) "<hi type="italic">I neither learned wisdom</hi> by any power of my own (the depths of it cannot be fathomed by my line and plummet) <hi type="italic">nor know I the knowledge of the holy</hi> ones, the angels, our first parents in innocency, nor of the holy things of God; I can get no insight into them, nor make any judgment of them, further than God is pleased to make them known to me." The natural man, the natural powers, perceive not, nay, they <hi type="italic">receive not, the things of the Spirit of God.</hi> Some suppose Agur to be asked, as Apollo's oracle was of old, <hi type="italic">Who was the wisest man?</hi> The answer is, <hi type="italic">He that is sensible of his own ignorance,</hi> especially in divine things. <hi type="italic">Hoc tantum scio, me nihil scire</hi>—<hi type="italic">All that I know is that I know nothing.</hi> <div eID="gen14690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14691" type="x-p"/> II. To advance Jesus Christ, and the Father in him (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who ascended up into heaven,</hi> &c. 1. Some understand this of God and of his works, which are both incomparable and unsearchable. He challenges all mankind to give an account of the heavens above, of the winds, the waters, the earth: "Who can pretend to have <hi type="italic">ascended up to heaven,</hi> to take a view of the orbs above, and then to have descended, to give us a description of them? Who can pretend to have had the command of the winds, to have grasped them in his hand and managed them, as God does, or to have bound the waves of the sea with a swaddling band, as God has done? Who has <hi type="italic">established the ends of the earth,</hi> or can describe the strength of its foundations or the extent of its limits? Tell me what is <hi type="italic">the man's name</hi> who can undertake to vie with God or to be of his cabinet-council, or, if he be dead, what is his name to whom he has bequeathed this great secret." 2. Others refer it to Christ, to Ithiel and Ucal, the Son of God, for it is the Son's name, as well as the Father's, that is here enquired after, and a challenge given to any to vie with him. We must now exalt Christ as one revealed; they then magnified him as one concealed, as one they had heard something of but had very dark and defective ideas of. <hi type="italic">We have heard the fame of him with our ears,</hi> but cannot describe him (<reference osisRef="Job.28.22">Job xxviii. 22</reference>); certainly it is God that has <hi type="italic">gathered the wind in his fists</hi> and <hi type="italic">bound the waters as in a garment;</hi> but <hi type="italic">what is his name?</hi> It is, <hi type="italic">I am that I am</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.14">Exod. iii. 14</reference>), a name to be adored, not to be understood. What is <hi type="italic">his Son's name,</hi> by whom he does all these things? The Old-Testament saints expected the Messiah to be the <hi type="italic">Son of the Blessed,</hi> and he is here spoken of as a person distinct from the Father, but his name as yet secret. Note, The great Redeemer, in the glories of his providence and grace, can neither be paralleled nor found out to perfection. (1.) The glories of the kingdom of his grace are unsearchable and unparalleled; for who besides has <hi type="italic">ascended into heaven and descended?</hi> Who besides is perfectly acquainted with both worlds, and has himself a free correspondence with both, and is therefore fit to settle a correspondence between them, as Mediator, as Jacob's ladder? He was <hi type="italic">in heaven</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Father's bosom</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.1">John i. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.1.18">18</reference>); thence he descended to take our nature upon him; and never was there such condescension. In that nature he again ascended (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.9">Eph. iv. 9</reference>), to receive the promised glories of his exalted state; and who besides has done this? <reference osisRef="Rom.10.6">Rom. x. 6</reference>. (2.) The glories of the kingdom of his providence are likewise unsearchable and unparalleled. The same that reconciles heaven and earth was the Creator of both and governs and disposes of all. His government of the three lower elements of <hi type="italic">air, water,</hi> and <hi type="italic">earth,</hi> is here particularized. [1.] The motions of the air are of his directing. Satan pretends to be <hi type="italic">the prince of the power of the air,</hi> but even there Christ has <hi type="italic">all power;</hi> he <hi type="italic">rebuked the winds</hi> and they obeyed him. [2.] The bounds of the water are of his appointing: He <hi type="italic">binds the waters as in a garment; hitherto they shall come, and no further,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.9-Job.38.11">Job xxxviii. 9-11</reference>. [3.] The foundations of the earth are of his establishing. He founded it at first; he upholds it still. If Christ had not interposed, the foundations of the earth would have sunk under the load of the curse upon the ground, for man's sin. Who and what is the mighty He that does all this? We cannot <hi type="italic">find out God,</hi> nor the <hi type="italic">Son of God, unto perfection. Oh the depth of that knowledge!</hi> <div eID="gen14691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14692" type="x-p"/> III. To assure us of the truth of the word of God, and to recommend it to us, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.5-Prov.30.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Agur's pupils expect to be instructed by him in the things of God. "Alas!" says he, "I cannot undertake to instruct you; go to the word of God; see what he has there revealed of himself, and of his mind and will; you need know no more than what that will teach you, and that you may rely upon as sure and sufficient. <hi type="italic">Every word of God is pure;</hi> there is not the least mixture of falsehood and corruption in it." The words of men are to be heard and read with jealousy and with allowance, but there is not the least ground to suspect any deficiency in the word of God; it is <hi type="italic">as silver purified seven times</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Ps. xii. 6</reference>), without the least dross or alloy. <hi type="italic">Thy word is very pure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.140">Ps. cxix. 140</reference>. 1. It is sure, and therefore we must trust to it and venture our souls upon it. God in his word, God in his promise, is <hi type="italic">a shield,</hi> a sure protection, to all those that put themselves under his protection and <hi type="italic">put their trust in him.</hi> The word of God, applied by faith, will make us easy in the midst of the greatest dangers, <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.2">Ps. xlvi. 1, 2</reference>. 2. It is sufficient, and therefore we must not add to it (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Add thou not unto his words,</hi> because they are pure and perfect. This forbids the advancing of any thing, not only in contradiction to the word of God, but in competition with it; though it be under the plausible pretence of explaining it, yet, if it pretend to be of equal authority with it, it is <hi type="italic">adding to his words,</hi> which is not only a reproach to them as insufficient, but opens a door to all manner of errors and corruptions; for, that one absurdity being granted, that the word of any man, or company of men, is to be received with the same faith and veneration as the word of God, a thousand follow. We must be content with what God has thought fit to make known to us of his mind, and not covet to be <hi type="italic">wise above what is written;</hi> for, (1.) God will resent it as a heinous affront: "<hi type="italic">He</hi> will <hi type="italic">reprove thee,</hi> will reckon with thee as a traitor against his crown and dignity, and lay thee under the heavy doom of those that add to his words, or diminish from them," <reference osisRef="Deut.4.2">Deut. iv. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.32">xii. 32</reference>. (2.) We shall run ourselves into endless mistakes: "Thou wilt be found a liar, a corrupter of the word of truth, a broacher of heresies, and guilty of the worst of forgeries, counterfeiting the broad seal of heaven, and pretending a divine mission and inspiration, when it is all a cheat. Men may be thus deceived, but <hi type="italic">God is not mocked.</hi>"

<div eID="gen14692" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prayer of Agur.</title> <div sID="gen14693" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Two <hi type="italic">things</hi> have I required of thee; deny me <hi type="italic">them</hi> not before I die: <hi type="super">8</hi> Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: <hi type="super">9</hi> Lest I be full, and deny <hi type="italic">thee,</hi> and say, Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God <hi type="italic">in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen14693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14694" type="x-p"/> After Agur's confession and creed, here follows his litany, where we may observe, <div eID="gen14694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14695" type="x-p"/> I. The preface to his prayer: <hi type="italic">Two things have I required</hi> (that is, <hi type="italic">requested</hi>) of thee, O God! Before we go to pray it is good to consider what we need, and what the things are which we have to ask of God.—What does our case require? What do our hearts desire? What would we that God should do for us?—that we may not have to seek for our petition and request when we should be presenting it. He begs, <hi type="italic">Deny me not before I die.</hi> In praying, we should think of dying, and pray accordingly. "Lord, give me pardon, and peace, and grace, before I die, <hi type="italic">before I go hence and be no more;</hi> for, if I be not renewed and sanctified before I die, the work will not be done after; if I do not prevail in prayer before I die, prayers afterwards will not prevail, no, not <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord.</hi> There is none of this wisdom or working in the grave. <hi type="italic">Deny me not</hi> thy grace, for, if thou do, I die, I perish; if thou be silent to me, <hi type="italic">I am like those that go down to the pit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Ps. xxviii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Deny me not before I die;</hi> as long as I continue in the land of the living, let me continue under the conduct of thy grace and good providence." <div eID="gen14695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14696" type="x-p"/> II. The prayer itself. The <hi type="italic">two things</hi> he requires are grace sufficient and food convenient. 1. Grace sufficient for his soul: "<hi type="italic">Remove from me vanity and lies;</hi> deliver me from sin, from all corrupt principles, practices, and affections, from error and mistake, which are at the bottom of all sin, from the love of the world and the things of it, which are all <hi type="italic">vanity and a lie.</hi>" Some understand it as a prayer for the pardon of sin, for, when God forgives sin, he removes it, he takes it away. Or, rather, it is a prayer of the same import with that, <hi type="italic">Lead us not into temptation.</hi> Nothing is more mischievous to us than sin, and therefore there is nothing which we should more earnestly pray against than that we may <hi type="italic">do no evil.</hi> 2. Food convenient for his body. Having prayed for the operations of divine grace, he here begs the favours of the divine Providence, but such as may tend to the good and not to the prejudice of the soul. (1.) He prays that of God's free gift he might receive a competent portion of the good things of this life: "<hi type="italic">Feed me with the bread of my allowance,</hi> such bread as thou thinkest fit to allow me." As to all the gifts of the divine Providence, we must refer ourselves to the divine wisdom. Or, "<hi type="italic">the bread that is fit for me,</hi> as a man, a master of a family, that which is agreeable to my rank and condition in the world." For <hi type="italic">as is the man so is his competency.</hi> Our Saviour seems to refer to this when he teaches us to pray, <hi type="italic">Give us this day our daily bread,</hi> as this seems to refer to Jacob's vow, in which he wished for no more than <hi type="italic">bread to eat and raiment to put on.</hi> Food convenient for us is what we ought to be content with, though we have not dainties, varieties, and superfluities—what is for necessity, though we have not for delight and ornament; and it is what we may in faith pray for and depend upon God for. (2.) He prays that he may be kept from every condition of life that would be a temptation to him. [1.] He prays against the extremes of abundance and want: <hi type="italic">Give me neither poverty nor riches.</hi> He does not hereby prescribe to God, nor pretend to teach him what condition he shall allot to him, nor does he pray against poverty or riches absolutely, as in themselves evil, for either of them, by the grace of God, may be sanctified and be a means of good to us; but, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He hereby intends to express the value which wise and good men have for a middle state of life, and, with submission to the will of God, desires that that might be his state, neither great honour nor great contempt. We must learn how to manage both (as St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.12">Phil. iv. 12</reference>), but rather wish to be always between both. <hi type="italic">Optimus pecuniæ modus qui nec in paupertatem cedit nec procul &#224; paupertate discedit—The best condition is that which neither implies poverty nor yet recedes far from it.</hi> Seneca. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He hereby intimates a holy jealousy he had of himself, that he could not keep his ground against the temptations either of an afflicted or a prosperous condition. Others may preserve their integrity in either, but he is afraid of both, and therefore grace teaches him to pray against riches as much as nature against poverty; but <hi type="italic">the will of the Lord be done.</hi> [2.] He gives a pious reason for his prayer, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">v. 9</reference>. He does not say, "<hi type="italic">Lest I be rich,</hi> and cumbered with care, and envied by my neighbours, and eaten up with a multitude of servants, or, <hi type="italic">lest I be poor</hi> and trampled on, and forced to work hard and fare hard;" but, "<hi type="italic">Lest I be rich</hi> and sin, or <hi type="italic">poor</hi> and sin." Sin is that which a good man is afraid of in every condition and under every event; witness Nehemiah (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.13">ch. vi. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">that I should be afraid, and do so, and sin. First,</hi> He dreads the temptations of a prosperous condition, and therefore even deprecates that: <hi type="italic">Lest I be full and deny thee</hi> (as Jeshurun, who <hi type="italic">waxed fat and kicked,</hi> and <hi type="italic">forsook God who made him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">Deut. xxxii. 15</reference>), and say, as Pharaoh in his pride, <hi type="italic">Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice?</hi> Prosperity makes people proud and forgetful of God, as if they had no need of him and were therefore under no obligation to him. <hi type="italic">What can the Almighty do for them?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.22.17">Job xxii. 17</reference>. And therefore they will do nothing for him. Even good men are afraid of the worst sins, so deceitful do they think their own hearts to be; and they know that the greatest gains of the world will not balance the least guilt. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He dreads the temptations of a poor condition, and for that reason, and no other, deprecates that: <hi type="italic">Lest I be poor and steal.</hi> Poverty is a strong temptation to dishonesty, and such as many are overcome by, and they are ready to think it will be their excuse; but it will not bear them out at God's bar any more than at men's to say, "I stole because I was poor;" yet, if a man <hi type="italic">steal for the satisfying of his soul when he is hungry,</hi> it is a case of compassion (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.30">ch. vi. 30</reference>) and what even those that have some principles of honesty in them may be drawn to. But observe why Agur dreads this, not because he should endanger himself by it, "Lest I steal, and be hanged for it, whipped or put in the stocks, or sold for a bondman," as among the Jews poor thieves were, who had not wherewithal to make restitution; but lest he should dishonour God by it: "<hi type="italic">Lest I should steal, and take the name of my God in vain,</hi> that is, discredit my profession of religion by practices disagreeable to it." Or, "Lest I steal, and, when I am charged with it, forswear myself." He <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> dreads one sin, because it would draw on another, for the way of sin is downhill. Observe, He calls God <hi type="italic">his God,</hi> and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he is afraid of doing any thing to offend him because of the relation he stands in to him.

<div eID="gen14696" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Four Wicked Generations.</title> <div sID="gen14697" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty. <hi type="super">11</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a generation <hi type="italic">that</hi> curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother. <hi type="super">12</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a generation <hi type="italic">that are</hi> pure in their own eyes, and <hi type="italic">yet</hi> is not washed from their filthiness. <hi type="super">13</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a generation, O how lofty are their eyes! and their eyelids are lifted up. 14 <hi type="italic">There is</hi> a generation, whose teeth <hi type="italic">are as</hi> swords, and their jaw teeth <hi type="italic">as</hi> knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from <hi type="italic">among</hi> men. <div eID="gen14697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14698" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A caution not to abuse other people's servants any more than our own, nor to make mischief between them and their masters, for it is an ill office, invidious, and what will make a man odious, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.10">v. 10</reference>. Consider, 1. It is an injury to the servant, whose poor condition makes him an object of pity, and therefore it is barbarous to add affliction to him that is afflicted: <hi type="italic">Hurt not a servant with thy tongue</hi> (so the margin reads it); for it argues a sordid disposition to smite any body secretly with the scourge of the tongue, especially a servant, who is not a match for us, and whom we should rather protect, if his master be severe with him, than exasperate him more. 2. "It will perhaps be an injury to thyself. If a servant be thus provoked, perhaps he will curse thee, will accuse thee and bring thee into trouble, or give thee an ill word and blemish thy reputation, or appeal to God against thee, and imprecate <hi type="italic">his</hi> wrath upon thee, who is the patron and protector of oppressed innocency." <div eID="gen14698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14699" type="x-p"/> II. An account, upon occasion of this caution, of some wicked generations of men, that are justly abominable to all that are virtuous and good. 1. Such as are abusive to their parents, give them bad language and wish them ill, call them bad names and actually injure them. <hi type="italic">There is a generation</hi> of such; young men of that black character commonly herd together, and irritate one another against their parents. A <hi type="italic">generation of vipers</hi> those are who curse their natural parents, or their magistrates, or their ministers, because they cannot endure the yoke; and those are near of kin to them who, though they have not yet arrived at such a pitch of wickedness as to curse their parents, yet do not bless them, cannot give them a good word, and will not pray for them. 2. Such as are conceited of themselves, and, under a show and pretence of sanctity, hide from others, and perhaps from themselves too, abundance of reigning wickedness in secret (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.12">v. 12</reference>); they are <hi type="italic">pure in their own eyes,</hi> as if they were in all respects such as they should be. They have a very good opinion of themselves and their own character, that they are not only righteous, but <hi type="italic">rich and increased with goods</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.17">Rev. iii. 17</reference>), and yet <hi type="italic">are not cleansed from their filthiness,</hi> the filthiness of their hearts, which they pretend to be the best part of them. They are, it may be, swept and garnished, but they are not washed, nor sanctified; as the Pharisees that within were <hi type="italic">full of all uncleanness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.25-Matt.23.26">Matt. xxiii. 25, 26</reference>. 3. Such as are haughty and scornful to those about them, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.13">v. 13</reference>. He speaks of them with amazement at their intolerable pride and insolence: "<hi type="italic">Oh how lofty are their eyes!</hi> With what disdain do they look upon their neighbours, as not worthy to be set with the dogs of their flock! What a distance do they expect every body should keep; and, when they look upon themselves, how do they strut and vaunt like the peacock, thinking they make themselves illustrious when really they make themselves ridiculous!" There is a generation of such, on whom he that <hi type="italic">resists the proud</hi> will pour contempt. 4. Such as are cruel to the poor and barbarous to all that lie at their mercy (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.14">v. 14</reference>); their teeth are iron and steel, <hi type="italic">swords and knives,</hi> instruments of cruelty, with which they <hi type="italic">devour the poor</hi> with the greatest pleasure imaginable, and as greedily as hungry men cut their meat and eat it. God has so ordered it that the <hi type="italic">poor we shall always have with us,</hi> that they shall <hi type="italic">never cease out of the land;</hi> but there are those who, because they hate to relieve them, would, if they could, abolish them <hi type="italic">from the earth, from among men,</hi> especially God's poor. Some understand it of those who wound and ruin others by slanders and false accusations, and severe censures of their everlasting state; their tongues, and their teeth too (which are likewise organs of speech), are <hi type="italic">as swords and knives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Ps. lvii. 4</reference>.

<div eID="gen14699" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Four Things Unsearchable.</title> <div sID="gen14700" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The horseleach hath two daughters, <hi type="italic">crying,</hi> Give, give. There are three <hi type="italic">things that</hi> are never satisfied, <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> four <hi type="italic">things</hi> say not, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> enough: <hi type="super">16</hi> The grave; and the barren womb; the earth <hi type="italic">that</hi> is not filled with water; and the fire <hi type="italic">that</hi> saith not, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> enough. <hi type="super">17</hi> The eye <hi type="italic">that</hi> mocketh at <hi type="italic">his</hi> father, and despiseth to obey <hi type="italic">his</hi> mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it. <div eID="gen14700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14701" type="x-p"/> He had spoken before of those that devoured the poor (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.14">v. 14</reference>), and had spoken of them last, as the worst of all the four generations there mentioned; now here he speaks of their insatiableness in doing this. The temper that puts them upon it is made up of cruelty and covetousness. Now those are <hi type="italic">two daughters</hi> of the <hi type="italic">horse-leech,</hi> its genuine offspring, that still cry, "<hi type="italic">Give, give,</hi> give more blood, give more money;" for the bloody are still blood-thirsty; being drunk with blood, they add thirst to their drunkenness, and will seek it yet again. Those also that <hi type="italic">love silver</hi> shall never <hi type="italic">be satisfied with silver.</hi> Thus, while from these two principles they are devouring the poor, they are continually uneasy to themselves, as David's enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.14-Ps.59.15">Ps. lix. 14, 15</reference>. Now, for the further illustration of this, <div eID="gen14701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14702" type="x-p"/> I. He specifies four other things which are insatiable, to which those devourers are compared, which say not, <hi type="italic">It is enough,</hi> or <hi type="italic">It is wealth.</hi> Those are never rich that are always coveting. Now these four things that are always craving are, 1. The grave, into which multitudes fall, and yet still more will fall, and it swallows them all up, and returns none, <hi type="italic">Hell and destruction are never full,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.20">ch. xxvii. 20</reference>. When it comes to our turn we shall find the grave ready for us, <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job xvii. 1</reference>. 2. The <hi type="italic">barren womb,</hi> which is impatient of its affliction in being barren, and cries, as Rachel did, <hi type="italic">Give me children.</hi> 3. The <hi type="italic">parched ground</hi> in time of drought (especially in those hot countries), which still soaks in the rain that comes in abundance upon it and in a little time wants more. 4. The <hi type="italic">fire,</hi> which, when it has consumed abundance of fuel, yet still devours all the combustible matter that is thrown into it. So insatiable are the corrupt desires of sinners, and so little satisfaction have they even in the gratification of them. <div eID="gen14702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14703" type="x-p"/> II. He adds a terrible threatening to disobedient children (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.17">v. 17</reference>), for warning to the first of those four wicked generations, that curse their parents (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.11">v. 11</reference>), and shows here, <div eID="gen14703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14704" type="x-p"/> 1. Who they are that belong to that generation, not only those that curse their parents in heat and passion, but, (1.) Those that <hi type="italic">mock</hi> at them, though it be but with a scornful eye, looking with disdain upon them because of their bodily infirmities, or looking sour or dogged at them when they instruct or command, impatient at their checks and angry at them. God takes notice with what eye children look upon their parents, and will reckon for the leering look and the casts of the evil eye as well as for the bad language given them. (2.) Those that <hi type="italic">despise to obey</hi> them, that think it a thing below them to be dutiful to their parents, especially to the <hi type="italic">mother,</hi> they scorn to be controlled by her; and thus she that bore them in sorrow in greater sorrow bears their manners. <div eID="gen14704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14705" type="x-p"/> 2. What their doom will be. Those that dishonour their parents shall be set up as monuments of God's vengeance; they shall be hanged in chains, as it were, for the birds of prey to pick out their eyes, those eyes with which they looked so scornfully on their good parents. The dead bodies of malefactors were not to hang all night, but before night the ravens would have picked out their eyes. If men do not punish undutiful children, God will, and will load those with the greatest infamy that conduct themselves haughtily towards their parents. Many who have come to an ignominious end have owned that the wicked courses that brought them to it began in a contempt of their parents' authority.

<div eID="gen14705" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Four Things Little and Wise.</title> <div sID="gen14706" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> There be three <hi type="italic">things which</hi> are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not: <hi type="super">19</hi> The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid. 20 Such <hi type="italic">is</hi> the way of an adulterous woman; she eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have done no wickedness. 21 For three <hi type="italic">things</hi> the earth is disquieted, and for four <hi type="italic">which</hi> it cannot bear: <hi type="super">22</hi> For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with meat; <hi type="super">23</hi> For an odious <hi type="italic">woman</hi> when she is married; and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress. <div eID="gen14706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14707" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. An account of four things that are unsearchable, <hi type="italic">too wonderful</hi> to be fully known. And here, <div eID="gen14707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14708" type="x-p"/> 1. The first three are natural things, and are only designed as comparisons for the illustration of the last. We cannot trace, (1.) <hi type="italic">An eagle in the air.</hi> Which way she has flown cannot be discovered either by the footstep or by the scent, as the way of a beast may upon ground; nor can we account for the wonderful swiftness of her flight, how soon she has gone beyond our ken. (2.) <hi type="italic">A serpent upon a rock.</hi> The way of a serpent in the sand we may find by the track, but not of a serpent upon the hard rock; nor can we describe how a serpent will, without feet, in a little time creep to the top of a rock. (3.) <hi type="italic">A ship in the midst of the sea.</hi> The leviathan indeed <hi type="italic">makes a path to shine after him, one would think the deep to be hoary</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.41.32">Job xli. 32</reference>), but a ship leaves no mark behind it, and sometimes it is so tossed upon the waves that one would wonder how it lives at sea and gains its point. The kingdom of nature is full of wonders, marvellous things which the God of nature does, <hi type="italic">past finding out.</hi> <div eID="gen14708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14709" type="x-p"/> 2. The fourth is a mystery of iniquity, more unaccountable than any of these; it belongs to the depths of Satan, that deceitfulness and that desperate wickedness of the heart which none can know, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.9">Jer. xvii. 9</reference>. It is twofold:—(1.) The cursed arts which a vile adulterer has to debauch a maid, and to persuade her to yield to his wicked and abominable lust. This is what a wanton poet wrote a whole book of, long since, <hi type="italic">De arte amandi—On the art of love.</hi> By what pretensions and protestations of love, and all its powerful charms, promises of marriage, assurances of secresy and reward, is many an unwary virgin brought to sell her virtue, and honour, and peace, and soul, and all to a base traitor; for so all sinful lust is in the kingdom of love. The more artfully the temptation is managed the more watchful and resolute ought every pure heart to be against it. (2.) The cursed arts which a vile adulteress has to conceal her wickedness, especially from her husband, from whom she treacherously departs; so close are her intrigues with her lewd companions, and so craftily disguised, that it is as impossible to discover her as to track an <hi type="italic">eagle in the air.</hi> She eats the forbidden fruit, after the similitude of Adam's transgression, and then <hi type="italic">wipes her mouth,</hi> that it may not betray itself, and with a bold and impudent face says, <hi type="italic">I have done no wickedness.</hi> [1.] To the world she denies the fact, and is ready to swear it that she is as chaste and modest as any woman, and never did the wickedness she is suspected of. Those are the works of darkness which are industriously kept from coming to the light. [2.] To her own conscience (if she have any left) she denies the fault, and will not own that that <hi type="italic">great wickedness</hi> is any wickedness at all, but an innocent entertainment. See <reference osisRef="Hos.12.7-Hos.12.8">Hos. xii. 7, 8</reference>. Thus multitudes ruin their souls by calling evil good and out-facing their convictions with a self-justification. <div eID="gen14709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14710" type="x-p"/> II. An account of four things that are intolerable, that is, four sorts of persons that are very troublesome to the places where they live and the relations and companies they are in; the earth is <hi type="italic">disquieted for them,</hi> and groans under them as a burden it cannot bear, and they are all much alike:—1. <hi type="italic">A servant</hi> when he is advanced, and entrusted with power, who is, of all others, most insolent and imperious; witness Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.10">Neh. ii. 10</reference>. 2. <hi type="italic">A fool,</hi> a silly, rude, boisterous, vicious man, who when he has grown rich, and is partaking of the pleasures of the table, will disturb all the company with his extravagant talk and the affronts he will put upon those about him. 3. An ill-natured, cross-grained, <hi type="italic">woman,</hi> when she gets a husband, one who, having made herself odious by her pride and sourness, so that one would not have thought any body would ever love her, yet, if at last she be married, that honourable estate makes her more intolerably scornful and spiteful than ever. It is a pity that that which should sweeten the disposition should have a contrary effect. A gracious woman, when she is married, will be yet more obliging. 4. An old maid-servant that has prevailed with her mistress, by humouring her, and, as we say, getting the length of her foot, to leave her what she has, or is as dear to her as if she was to be her heir, such a one likewise will be intolerably proud and malicious, and think all too little that her mistress gives her, and herself wronged if any thing be left from her. Let those therefore whom Providence has advanced to honour from mean beginnings carefully watch against that sin which will most easily beset them, pride and haughtiness, which will in them, of all others, be most insufferable and inexcusable; and let them humble themselves with the remembrance of the rock out of which they were hewn.

<div eID="gen14710" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Four Things Little and Wise.</title> <div sID="gen14711" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> There be four <hi type="italic">things which are</hi> little upon the earth, but they <hi type="italic">are</hi> exceeding wise: <hi type="super">25</hi> The ants <hi type="italic">are</hi> a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer; <hi type="super">26</hi> The conies <hi type="italic">are but</hi> a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks; <hi type="super">27</hi> The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands; <hi type="super">28</hi> The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces. <div eID="gen14711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14712" type="x-p"/> I. Agur, having specified four things that seem great and yet are really contemptible, here specifies four things that are little and yet are very admirable, great in miniature, in which, as bishop Patrick observes, he teaches us several good lessons; as, 1. Not to admire bodily bulk, or beauty, or strength, nor to value persons or think the better of them for such advantages, but to judge of men by their wisdom and conduct, their industry and application to business, which are characters that deserve respect. 2. To admire the wisdom and power of the Creator in the smallest and most despicable animals, in an ant as much as in an elephant. 3. To blame ourselves who do not act so much for our own true interest as the meanest creatures do for theirs. 4. Not to despise the weak things of the world; there are those that are <hi type="italic">little upon the earth,</hi> poor in the world and of small account, and yet <hi type="italic">are exceedingly wise,</hi> wise for their souls and another world, and those <hi type="italic">are exceedingly wise, wiser than their neighbours.</hi> Margin, <hi type="italic">They are wise, made wise</hi> by the special instinct of nature. All that are wise to salvation are made wise by the grace of God. <div eID="gen14712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14713" type="x-p"/> II. Those he specifies are, 1. The <hi type="italic">ants,</hi> minute animals and very weak, and yet they are very industrious in gathering proper food, and have a strange sagacity to do it in the summer, the proper time. This is so great a piece of wisdom that we may learn of them to be wise for futurity, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.6">ch. vi. 6</reference>. When the ravening <hi type="italic">lions lack, and suffer hunger,</hi> the laborious ants have plenty, and know no want. 2. The <hi type="italic">conies,</hi> or, as some rather understand it, the Arabian mice, field mice, weak creatures, and very timorous, yet they have so much wisdom as to <hi type="italic">make their houses in the rocks,</hi> where they are well guarded, and their feebleness makes them take shelter in those natural fastnesses and fortifications. Sense of our own indigence and weakness should drive us to him that is a <hi type="italic">rock higher than we</hi> for shelter and support; there let us make our habitation. 3. The <hi type="italic">locusts;</hi> they are little also, and <hi type="italic">have no king,</hi> as the bees have, but <hi type="italic">they go forth all of them by bands,</hi> like an army in battle-array; and, observing such good order among themselves, it is not any inconvenience to them that they <hi type="italic">have no king.</hi> They are called God's <hi type="italic">great army</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.25">Joel ii. 25</reference>); for, when he pleases, he musters, he marshals them, and wages war by them, as he did upon Egypt. <hi type="italic">They go forth all of them gathered together</hi> (so the margin); sense of weakness should engage us to keep together, that we may strengthen the hands of one another. 4. The <hi type="italic">spider,</hi> an insect, but as great an instance of industry in our houses as the ants are in the field. Spiders are very ingenious in weaving their webs with a fineness and exactness such as no art can pretend to come near: They <hi type="italic">take hold with their hands,</hi> and spin a fine thread out of their own bowels, with a great deal of art; and they are not only in poor men's cottages, but in <hi type="italic">kings' palaces,</hi> notwithstanding all the care that is there taken to destroy them. Providence wonderfully keeps up those kinds of creatures, not only which men provide not for, but which every man's hand is against and seeks the destruction of. Those that will mind their business, and <hi type="italic">take hold</hi> of it <hi type="italic">with their hands,</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">in kings' palaces;</hi> sooner or later, they will get preferment, and may go on with it, notwithstanding the difficulties and discouragements they meet with. If one well-spun web be swept away, it is but making another.

<div eID="gen14713" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Four Things Majestic and Stately.</title> <div sID="gen14714" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> There be three <hi type="italic">things</hi> which go well, yea, four are comely in going: <hi type="super">30</hi> A lion <hi type="italic">which is</hi> strongest among beasts, and turneth not away for any; <hi type="super">31</hi> A greyhound; an he goat also; and a king, against whom <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no rising up. <hi type="super">32</hi> If thou hast done foolishly in lifting up thyself, or if thou hast thought evil, <hi type="italic">lay</hi> thine hand upon thy mouth. <hi type="super">33</hi> Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife. <div eID="gen14714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14715" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. An enumeration of four things which are majestic and stately in their going, which look great:— 1. <hi type="italic">A lion,</hi> the king of beasts, because <hi type="italic">strongest among beasts.</hi> Among beasts it is strength that gives the pre-eminence, but it is a pity that it should do so among men, whose <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> is their honour, not their <hi type="italic">strength</hi> and <hi type="italic">force.</hi> The lion <hi type="italic">turns not away,</hi> nor alters his pace, for fear of any pursuers, since he knows he is too hard for them. Herein <hi type="italic">the righteous are bold as a lion,</hi> that they <hi type="italic">turn not away</hi> from their duty for fear of any difficulty they meet with in it. 2. <hi type="italic">A greyhound</hi> that is girt in the loins and fit for running; or (as the margin reads it) <hi type="italic">a horse,</hi> which ought not to be omitted among the creatures that <hi type="italic">are comely in going,</hi> for so he is, especially when he is dressed up in his harness or trappings. 3. <hi type="italic">A he-goat,</hi> the comeliness of whose going is when he goes first and leads the flock. It is the comeliness of a Christian's going to go first in a good work and to lead others in the right way. 4. <hi type="italic">A king,</hi> who, when he appears in his majesty, is looked upon with reverence and awe, and all agree that <hi type="italic">there is no rising up against</hi> him; none can vie with him, none can contend with him, whoever does it, it is at his peril. And, if <hi type="italic">there is no rising up</hi> against an earthly prince, <hi type="italic">woe to him</hi> then <hi type="italic">that strives with his Maker.</hi> It is intended that we should learn courage and fortitude in all virtuous actions from the <hi type="italic">lion</hi> and <hi type="italic">not to turn away for any</hi> difficulty we meet with; from the <hi type="italic">greyhound</hi> we may learn quickness and despatch, from the <hi type="italic">he-goat</hi> the care of our family and those under our charge, and from <hi type="italic">a king</hi> to have our children in subjection with all gravity, and from them all to <hi type="italic">go well,</hi> and to order the steps of our conversation so as that we may not only be safe, but <hi type="italic">comely, in going.</hi> <div eID="gen14715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14716" type="x-p"/> II. A caution to us to keep our temper at all times and under all provocations, and to take heed of carrying our resentments too far upon any occasion, especially when there is <hi type="italic">a king</hi> in the case, <hi type="italic">against whom there is no rising up,</hi> when it is a ruler, or one much our superior, that is offended; nay, the rule is always the same. <div eID="gen14716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14717" type="x-p"/> 1. We must bridle and suppress our own passion, and take shame to ourselves, whenever we are justly charged with a fault, and not insist upon our own innocency: If we have <hi type="italic">lifted up ourselves,</hi> either in a proud conceit of ourselves or a peevish opposition to those that are over us, if we have transgressed the laws of our place and station, we have therein <hi type="italic">done foolishly.</hi> Those that magnify themselves over others or against others, that are haughty and insolent, do but shame themselves and betray their own weakness.
